As you can see by the number of hours displayed I haven't played "Tooth and Tail" very excessively. Hence - of course - my review might lack aspects other players have talked about in detail. However I felt like dropping a few words regarding a first impression.
As un-usual as it is - I rather read the negative than the positive reviews of a game, because usually people taking the time to express what they dislike is more reliable than a "Love, 10/10"-review. There is a lenghty post of somebody - shame on me, I forgot the user's name - who describes in detail what this game is lacking to be a really good RTS for him/her, and, if you buy Tooth and Tail expecting something like BroodWars or WC III you might feel disappointed. Most RTS are a lot about shortcuts and perfect micro-management, and while Tooth and Tail certainly touches these aspects - the gameplay feels very different. You cannot really divide your troops between bases and set them on "guard the area", while scouting and building (and protecting) a second base effectively. Personally - I don't mind much, but I can see why this is not appealing to other players.

For whatever reason the developers decided to "optimize" the game for using a controler. When I switched from keyboard to gamepad I got a differend feeling for the game, and it suddenly felt a lot easier (and also I stopped missing stuff that I got used to from SC/SC II; I think the "gamer's memory" always wants to extract data from previous "other games like this"-databank). Also one should always think of rallying the troops after a few steps - I forgot that every now and then, resulting in me standing there, facing the enemy alone, while my ferrets, squirrels and moles held a tea-party (but that is not the fault of the game; it's just a mechanic I need to get used to).
Also I don't really get why the in-game-models look like they were taken from an 90's game... but I got used to that quite quick. Still I think it's a bit of a shame, because, especially with Hopper, you easily miss out some interesting details. Hopper instantly became my favorite character when I saw her missing arm; people who know me will know why ^.^
However, if you are more a "casual" RTS-player and/or if you enjoy atmosphere and story over optimized gameplay and graphics I can truly recommend "Tooth and Tail". The amount of structures you can build is very manageable; you won't need to memorize a ton of units, buildings and upgrades (for more buildings and more different units). While a true RTS-lover will certainly miss this - I consider it as a good thing for casual (or even new) RTS-players. Also - a mission does not take 40+ minutes. An average mission takes between 10-15 minutes (if you are successful). Because I failed some missions several times - in the end some missions took me 30-40 minutes, but I don't mind. It never felt frustrating or unfair.
I would also recommend the game to people who like the "Redwall"-books, the movie "The Secret of NIMH", the "Packs!"-P&P RPG, and stuff like that. Because the world of "Tooth and Tail" feels like "Animal Farm" and the "Redwall"-series had a child. Talking to the Swine about "Harvest" and "being a breeder" is so evil... and yet so true at some point ... it made me chuckle on the one hand, and on the other hand I put the bacon back into the fridge and opted for some spinach for lunch. The soundtrack is neat, very catchy at times, and I like the replay-function and that the maps are randomly generated... however, the latter can bite you in the a** ; I already had a mission where it was too easy to defend my position, because the enemy could only attack from one side, while in another mission I was SO exposed (and I had to run around the map to find my ally) that my farms were blown up before my ally could be of any help.
I can't judge the multiplayer, and knowing me I "might" try it out - but it's not for sure. So far I am happy with my purchase, and I wouldn't mind at all if "Tooth and Tail" would become a solid franchise of its own.

What will you like about it:
+ A Sandbox Samurai game.
+ While the story is short (can be completed in 2 hours if you got passed the learning curve of the game) but the story can be branched in multiple different paths (almost similar to Zero Escape Series). It is also not possible to cover every mission in one playthrough because one story path will cancel the other alternative paths.
+ Awkwardly funny
+ It is fun to customize swords and fighting style
What you may dislike:
- Outdated graphics and animations
- Writing, voice acting and some characters are extremely awkward or bad. You could say it is "so bad, it's funny" as there weren't any annoying moments other than the guards shouting the same words over and over.
- Not much to explore. You could see every location in the game in around 30 min.
- Bad production value. Lots of missing sound effects in cutscenes and lots of quiet moments with no ambient sounds or soundtrack to support it. The developers were obviously on budget while developing this game.
PC Performance:
- This is a ported game from console by a Japanese developer. Therefor, you won't see much customization at all.
- It is better to play with an xbox controller (fully supported)
- Game does crash to desktop when you try to setup your resolution or other settings. However during Gameplay I did not get a crash to desktop.
Final word:
If you like Japanese culture and Samurais, you got to try this game especially when it goes on sale. It is not a masterpiece by far but you will definitly enjoy it.

this is one of those gems you find in the indie desert. from the rolling hills of bad games, the stifleing heat of the triple A game sun, the air so dry from early development hells.
comes this game. the jewel of the century, the last savior, the peanutbutter for your chocolate.
if you could not guess, i like this game, for numerous reasons too.
REASON 1
the artstyle is beutiful, i play on the worst settings (which honestly doesn't change much) and i love it. while some pixel art games are lack luster and unimaginitive. this game is not. the character designs are very well made, the animations are fluid, the designs are very easy to differentiate so you know what the enemy has. just very good graphics
REASON 2
the campain is fun. you might say "well i would think the campain would be fun!" most games that are simular to this one (there isn't many) don't have much of one if at all. the campain goes over the reason why the factions are at war and why each one fights. belefide fights for justice for his son, hopper fights for a democracy, quartermaster fights for order, and arcemides fights for power and food. i love the lore of the game and the characters, such as my favorite character is the skunk or "glorious AFB" as named in game, not because he is good/OP but because his lore states that he was an outcast to everybody untill war broke out and he became a public idol, but because of his entire life in recluse, he was akward and  did not know what to do with all the atention. i just thought that was funny. onto the next point!
REASON 3
the gameplay is phenominal. i love how this game plays out. you start (in multiplayer) with a few farms and much to do, you can build economy by placing more farms (max of 9) around your gristmill or place warrens which will spawn units. 3 per warren for teir 1 units, 2 for tier 2, and 1 for tier 3. once you have decided that one gristmill i not enough anymore, you can buy a new one with food that your farms produce. it costs 60 food to claim gristmills, place farms, place tier 1 warrens (20 food to spawn), spawn tier 2 units, and to place some defences. it costs 120 food for tier 2 warrens (60 to spawn) and 180 food for tier 3 warrens and spawns. there are many different units for each tier so all games are different, not just because of numerous units, but also because the maps are random, you can play against real people, and the timing you choose to strike. the units are
tier 1
squirels, they shoot pistoles
lizards, they throw spears
toads, they are suicide bombers
doves, they heal
and moles, they deal crits to structures and can be spawned directly, without a warren.
tier 2
skunks, they shoot gas (cause they're skunks) that lingers
ferrets, they are mobile mortar and are super effective against bullet hives
snakes, they do poisen shots
falcons, they are fighter jets, so flying glorified squirles that rapid fire, they are much slower than you would think
camelions, they are melee invisable guys
tier 3
owl, she is a mobile spawner capable (in this patch, might change) of spawning 6 mice that are not controled by you, they are melee so they run at the nearest enemy. (VERY EFFECTIVE AGAINST DEFENCES)
badger, the minigunner, she is slow to spin up but is super effective at destroying everything if kept alive
uncle butters, the boar. by far the best name, he sports a flamethower and is effective at lots of small guys, oh and he blows up into a huge fireball of pain and destruction, when he dies. but that might be tweaked
wolf, he is a unit buffer, makes farms produce faster, makes freindlies move faster, like sonic speed fast
the fox, the one unit in the game that is capable of sniping. she is very strong and can 1 shot most units.
sooooo, in a nutshell this is one of my favorite games, you should get it because the everyday playerbase is small and at most there is 6 people playing unranked at the same time. i highly recomend this game

Before I list the steps to "infinitely" enjoying this game, you will need a few things.
First, a small list of skills that you need to level up (preferably max out):
1- Victory Cry. This skill will cause more power-ups to drop. (most Important skill)
2- Mighty Roar. Increases damage against officers.
3- Attack Boost. Extra damage.
4- Rage Springs. Makes filling the Rage gauge much easier.
5- Quick Learner. Get more EXP. (Optional)
Note: You can change skills mid level/combat/stage.
Second, Ma Chao's ultimate six-star weapon (Radiant Flash Spear) as a secondary weapon.
Note: I find it much easier to cleave through infantry using this weapon while on horse back and easier to defeat enemy officers with a counter by using Rage Mode (while on horse back as well).
A mount of your choice (I prefer Red Hare).
Finally, to unlock the Yellow Turben Conflict in free mode (play it once in story mode under Other).
Note: For some reason, this stage infinitely spawns soldiers in the area between the ramp and the eastern garrison.
Now, steps to enjoy infinitely enjoy this game:
1- Choose the stage Yellow Turben Conflict.
2- Side with the Yellow Turbans
3- Equip an officer of your choice with the skills and weapon mentioned before along with a primary weapon of your choice.
4- Begin the stage, select a track of your choice.
5- Mount your horse and make your way through the stage and clear all the objectives as fast as you can.
6- After defeating Cao Cao's and Liu Bei's forces, rush and make your way to the "Eastern Garrison" and stay between the garrison and the ramp.
7- Fill up your Rage Gauge (either with a Musou Attack or EX Attacks) and start your
8- Keep an eye out for the Musou +1 power-ups as you defeat soldiers and keep picking them up as you go.
9- Make sure you dont run out of time. If the timer shows 5 minutes left, complete the stage.
Rinse and repeat.

I'm a newcomer to this series and  had never before played any Tex Murphy adventure. I got it in a bundle. At first, this appeared to be a rather cheap adventure-style game with some kind of retro charm. However, as I went along with playing it, I started to enjoy the story and the cheesy characters.
Gameplay-wise I found myself stuck several times with absolutely no clue how to progess. The searching and trying very quickly felt combersome and frustrating. While it *is* in the spirit of the adventure games of old, today I don't find the time anymore to come back and do the chores of what feels like hours of searching. Also, I had to use a walkthrough in a couple of places to proceed, only to find out that I either would never had realized the solution on my own (too confusing) or that I had all the right ideas but the game expected a very specific sequence of progression (which should be more open to similar solutions).
All in all, I recommend this game, although I happened upon it as a free extra in a bundle. I very much doubt that I would have bought it on Steam or elsewhere. Then again, this is a game with a main audience of longtime Text Murphy fans for whom this game is obviously created. Throughout the game, I always felt a bit excluded, like standing on the sidelines and not getting all the jokes. I then turned that into archaelogical curiosity, exploring the pieces of a culture remembering itself. That was kind of special.
Now that I know Tex Murphy exists, I would play a followup game. But then again, it felt lacking a little too much polish to be sold for 20 €.
Good ol' Tex. Just like UAKM or Pandora.

I guess there are a few things I'll say that could be considered spoilers, and spoilers are a nono for this game, so i'll be as vague as possible... I hope.
Dark Souls is a game that will change you as a player, and it might as well change you as a person too.
Impressive for a game of so much action and so little words.
My praises won't do the game justice, because all I can really convey in words is what most of the people already know.
But one thing I can say is: Forget about the "difficulty". People make it sound like everything this game is about is being excessively hard, It isn't true. The gameplay and mechanics aren't as hard to learn as actually understand what the game WANTS from you as a player.
It wants you to go forward, die a thousand times, and keep going forward and find your path, by yourself. You will get rekt, beaten up, destroyed, thrown off cliffs, burned, stabbed, crushed, get boulder'd indiana jones style, be flung, shot by arrows, magic arrows, exploded and many other violent deaths you can imagine. But that's the point after all, every single time you respawn at the bonfire, you'll have another piece of knowledge about your enemy, getting closer and closer to slaying them.
DO NOT BE DISCOURAGED!
Can you imagine? Could there be a more powerful and dreadful enemy than a warrior that would keep coming back with all his previous knowledge every single time you kill him... forever?
YOU ARE that guy, once you understand the real ♥♥♥♥ing monster is you, and that it's your destiny to put and end to the most vile creatures that have ever been, and to actually do it, it's a pretty fulfilling experience. I'd say Monster Hunter players would understand a lot of what i'm trying to say here.
Or you could die and give in to madness to turn hollow forever, which is really only a metaphor for rage quittng Dark Souls and never come back.
------
This game has so much more to offer than just raw combat... The story is truly amazing, and is told in such a way that only those who really want will get their answers. 'The world' will never tell you anything, you'll have to find the puzzle pieces by yourself, to uncover all sorts of stories, sad, frightening, desperate, of love, and even, rarely, a sliver of happiness.
A truly timeless - if flawed - experience. If someone blows off the original Dark Souls as unworthy on the premise that It's an older title and that there is Dark Souls 2 and 3, plainly ignore them, and go play Dark Souls, you will not regret it.

As an advant fan of Sonic the Hedgehog for about, all my life I can very well say that Sonic CD is a fantastic game.
However, it is very
from your typical Sonic game. In which, it's a very unique one.
This game (I find) is the
in the series. And I don't mean dark as in guns and devilish creatures (Shadow the Hedgehog) or a general dark story (Sonic Adventure 2, Sonic 360).
But it's the presentation that makes this game the darkest.
In this game, you have to find the Time Stones or venture back in time and destroy Eggmans (or Dr. Ivo Robotnik) generators in order to ensure a good future for Little Planet and it's unseen inhabitants.
However, if you fail to do either task, you will ensure a bad future.
A bad future is basically a bad ending. This means Eggman has won; he has ruined all the zones with mechanical machienery. This is evident with the pollution, the evil music (for the US OST anyways..), and overall disgusting look of seeing that nature has been corrupted.
That's why I find it the darkest game in the series (not to mention the creepy images in the sound test.)
Speaking of music, this soundtrack is AMAZING.
There is a common debate over which regional soundtrack is best, as the US s.t. differs from the JP/EU s.t.
I personally LOVE the JP/EU s.t. so much. In fact, I think it may be my favorite Sonic soundtrack ever.
The US one is great as well, it really fits the stages and the boss (threatning music).
While I love a lot of aspects in this game, I do have some problems as well.
One is the level design. I love the level themes, but the execution is..eh. I find that the levels in this game always have some sort of obstacle that stops all momentum. And while that's not bad once in a while, it gets ridicious as the game goes on. One minute you'll be zooming at the speed of sound then BAM! Either an enemy, item capsule, or something stops all that speed. Not to say the other classic sonic games did that, but I feel this one takes the cake in that department.
Another thing I don't care for...the special stages. I don't know if it's just me but I can never seem to get sonic in a good enough position to hit those damn moving ufo's! And not to mention, even when I jump RIGHT next to a blimp, it doesn't count.
I recommend traveling back in time using the posts to get the good ending like I did, because I honestly can't be bothered with those annoying special stages.
Finally, while I love that the bosses in this game are quite (might be some of the most unique bosses in Sonic history honestly), some of these too can get tedious (i'm looking at YOU pinball eggman)
Overall, with a great game, amazing soundtrack, interesting story, and cool levels, Sonic CD is definetly a great Sonic game. Some problems, but still an enjoyable title i'd say.
If I had to rate it, i'd give it a 8.5/10.

If you want my full thoughts on Sonic CD, you can listen to my review on
(Review itself starts at 18:12)
Sonic is a character that I grew up loving. I had a Sega Genesis as a child and played tons of Sonic 2 and Sonic 3 & Knuckles. At the time, I had no idea that the Sega CD existed, so I completely missed out on Sonic CD. Now, years later, I received Sonic CD in the Sonic Games Collection and excitedly sat down to play what I thought would be a nostalgia-filled romp in a franchise I once loved. Perhaps I've moved on from Sonic or maybe Sonic CD isn't the best example of a classic Sonic game, because I found the experience baffling at best and infuriating at worst.
Well, the game certainly moves fast, which no doubt was part of the marketing. Unfortunately, fast =/= fun. The game lacks a good sense of momentum. Sonic often goes from a complete stand still to flying across the screen, and vice versa, with no inbetween. This means that you feel very little control over the game at many parts and more often than not the game launches you into a death trap. Often these are unavoidable because the camera does not keep Sonic centered on the screen and you cannot see what is coming up and react to it. It's just poor design for a platformer and leads to a lot of frustration.
Also strange is the time travel aspect. I love time travel as a story conceit and as a gameplay mechanic but it's completely pointless here. The past and future versions of the level are nearly identical and destroying the robot machine in the past only effects the zone you are in. It's completely optional; you can literally beat the game without ever once time traveling. There are no puzzles based around the mechanic and you can get all the time stones without using it. It feels totally tacked on and without purpose.
The pacing of the game is problematic as well. Of the seven zones, only the final two offer any challenge. Most acts can be beated in under a minute, making the game incredibly short and unrewarding. The difficulty spike in the last two stages is simply unreasonable and is where you will spend the vast majority of your time. In particular, the race against Metal Sonic is one of the must unfair, rage-quit inducing sequences I have ever encountered in a game.
First off, I love the hand drawn cinematics. Gorgeous, fun, bright. They are what I wanted the game to be. Unfortunately, the game's actual graphics are much less interesting. Unlike other Sonic games where each level has a unique look and setting, all the zones here, including their past and future counterparts, look pretty much the same. Also troubling is that it is often unclear what is an object vs. something in the foreground or background. Something may look like a platform but you'll just fall through it when you try to land on it. Having graphics that clearly convey information to the player is essential for such a fast paced platformer and Sonic CD really let me down in that regard.
Sound design is pretty much what you'd expect, except that there are two different soundtracks. The North American one sounds just like previous Sonic titles but the Japanese one, which is turned on by default, is a bizarre sort of hip-hop fusion that isn't fitting to Sonic at all. Skip to
to hear what I mean.
I simple cannot understand the praise that this game receives. It is far from the strongest title in the Sonic franchise and has major flaws in nearly every part of its design. I can only recommend Sonic CD to those who loved it on the Genesis since it is a very good port. If you haven't played Sonic CD before, I do not recommend giving it a try now.

In this review, I will discuss THE GOOD (things I liked), THE BAD (things that were mechanically wrong or off with the game), and THE UGLY (more general stuff that really just shut me down about it.)
THE GOOD:
--Plays and feels like a CRPG! Mission accomplished!
--Party creation system is cool; you're able to travel around with companions from the story or custom mook-people who were designed in exactly the same fashion as you were. Your choice!
--Combat is a bit hard to learn at first, but fun and even a bit tactical when facing enemies on par with your level or higher.
--Pretty big game world, but not overly so.
--Health system is really good. It forces your party to take breaks from adventuring for fear of permadeath and gets rid of classic "we've been underground for a month!" phenomenon.
THE BAD:
--Healing is at a premium for all classes but one or maybe two. This basically forces you to have a priest on hand. Or a full party of Paladins. It detracts from any sort of party diversity and feels very min-maxy.
--As of recent patches, crowd control effects have been nerfed into oblivion. Maybe this is a "realistic" choice considering which monsters were buffed, but it makes some classes very uninteresting on some levels and complete garbage on others.
THE UGLY:
--This game has a lot more ugly for me than it will for others. I'm not trying to start a minor flame war when I say that I think Fallout 4 is a better roleplaying game than Pillars is. You may feel they aren't comprable, but I would disagree. It's a great CRPG, but I will explain later in this section why that isn't enough for me.
--Do not get Pillars if you want a coherent story. In the previous incarnation of this review, I stated that it suffers from Clockwork Orange Syndrome; the belief that making up your own language and implementing it willy-nilly is cool, but if you can't execute it properly, it's overwhelming and distracting. That's still true. It gets a little more cohesive later, but it stays pretty murky for quite a while, I felt; far too long for a game that's so hyped up.
--The crux of my Dislike: CRPGs often fail to be actual roleplaying games. The problem with MMORPGs, CRPGs, and even some ARPGs, is that they are all about a tidal wave of numbers crashing upon the rocky shore of the coastline of Other Numbers. Your characters will not feel special. Mine certainly never did. I knew nothing about the land I hailed from, I was given a great big bag full of cookie cutter dialogue options to flesh out my character, and nothing I could do made me truly care about him. Because of how foreign and unrelatable the game feels due to its original fantasy setting combined with the absurdly sheer density of lore, I just couldn't penetrate it. Min-maxing is practically a must on any difficulty above the easiest, for you must combat the numbers swarm! That's why they let you hire your own party, it's not to tell any kind of story. Your hirelings might as well be heavily armored, sometimes magically inclined sheep for all the characterization they're allowed.
Here's the deal. I'm an avid paper and pencil RPG player. While CRPGs are based off of PPRPGs, they have been corrupted. They are no longer roleplaying games, but rollplaying games. Do you see the difference? In a roleplaying game, character driven story is absolutely the most important aspect. In a rollplaying game, it's all just one big, impersonal clash of the dice titans as math jockeys swing their Holy Avenger +5s around.
Pillars of Eternity commits this crime. People complain on and on about Fallout because it doesn't hand them a story about their character; it doesn't force feed it to them. This is why people nowadays like the Witcher games; they have no concept of original, open characters. Not to say that the Witcher games are bad (the first two are), but the point is that I can't play Geralt the way I see him, only a handful of ways in which the developers see him.
Fallout 4, to me, is a better roleplaying game because I've played it through three times with characters that were WAY deeper than anything Pillars offered. They weren't deep in the game, but in the only place that mattered: my own head. FO4 exemplifies such an openness for imagination that you can be anything.
My first FO4 character started out optimistic and even excited about the chance for a new life and a chance to rebuild the shattered and insane wasteland, but eventually became jaded and nearly suicidally depressed after making some key story decisions later on. My second character was an older man who had married his secretary after knocking her up and didn't ever answer the hero's call, believing that the nightmare of the wasteland was just that: a cryogenically induced lucid dream that let him do almost anything in a playground of violence and nonsense. There were others, but I hope you get the idea. FO4 gives you a tiny bit of backstory, a voice, and that's it. Not that the game doesn't fall flat in a lot of areas, but the freedom to characterize is vastly superior.
A true RPG let's you do anything within the reasonable confines of the world. It's a practical sandbox. Pillars forces you into a corner with barely noticable character dialogue. There isn't even a bio screen to write. I'm the kind of player who LOVES Skyrim's journal mod because I would write my characters' thoughts in it.
If you skim over this review and decide you don't care about the aspects I've mentioned, I challenge you to tell any kind of significant story with your characters. I doubt it can be done. I don't hear water cooler stories about the imaginative bloom of characters coming to life in Pillars...just of jumbled numbers striking other numbers with their number swords. It's not a bad game mechanically speaking, I just really dislike that Pillars of Eternity doesn't nurture players' imaginations. It, like so many other games, simply placates our wonder while distracting us with admittedly good gameplay.

Pillars of Eternity is an uneven, yet excellent game.
Without spoiling anything, the story follows your made character as they get exposed to, basically, dark magic and is granted the ability to read souls. From here, you pursue your Nemesis across the realm in an attempt to find meaning and answer.
At times, Pillars is completely brilliant. The first 1 1/2 acts of the game is some of the best I've played. The story is riveting, the characters are interesting, the combat is complex and there's promise of some cool upcoming features that are hinted at in these early segments.
Unfortunately, the game mostly falls apart about halfway through Act II. The game loses any semblance of challenge it had, the story and characters and insane amount of side-quests all kinda boggle among themselves and the writing drops a few notches. You'll likely find yourself starting to get bored nearing the end of Act II (also right when I hit the level cap) and rush your way through Acts III and IV.
There are some cool features that I was excited about that don't seem to go anywhere. Building your own keep was a cool idea I haven't seen implemented anywhere in a game like this, but it actually does absolutely nothing in the game. Money is pretty infinite by the time you start building your keep. At that point, it's just time-gated. You can take prisoners.. but why? They just sit there doing nothing, occasionally offering bribes to be released. The crafting and enchanting systems are useless. Consumables are a joke (often taking longer to consume than they heal or buff). Some spells are ridiculously overpowered (Level 5 mage Charm is insanely powerful).
Even with all of this, I highly recommend this game. The visuals are fun, the characters and plot are largely interesting. The dialogue paths numerous and the endings multiple. The combat in the first half of the game is near perfect until you start getting overpowered.
Tl;dr: Pillars of Eternity has a slew of great ideas, some poorly or half implemented. But the core gameplay is amazing, the story is fantastic and the characters are interesting. The game is also 65+ hours long (supposedly 80-90 if you do all the content, but I rushed Act III and didn't do much in the way of side quests) and has a ton of content. B+

The most frustrating part about it all, is that the game has a lot of truly incredible things going for it. If it wasn't for the god awful combat system, this would be a masterpiece of a game. When your combat system relies solely on stats and not on clever enemy A.I and strategic planning, your game runs the risk of becoming incredibly shallow and grindy, which is exactly what happened to Pillars of Eternity. Don't bother.

A return to the golden age of isometric western RPG's with modern standards of visual presentation and gameplay.
Pros:
+ Excellent art direction and visual presentation.
+ Streamlined mechanics such as un-interrupted resting at the expense of supplies and frustration-less inventory management.
+ New races and new weapon proficiency system.
+ Retains the sense of adventure, progression, and wonder that previous games of the genre (Baldur's Gate, Icewind Dale, Planescape) had in spades.
Cons:
- Overzealous use of in-game text and dialogue to promote lore and story; this promotes skipping dialogue content and it becomes difficult to separate important story and quest elements from the trivial.
- Poor initial stat selection for non-player created party members; this encourages players to bypass otherwise interesting characters and side quests in favor of custom party members.
Overall, I hope to see a revival in this genre as I cannot stomach modern JRPG's and their cringe-worthy character design and adolescent aesthtetic.

It's easy to recommend for it's combat, it's voice overs and style, but at the same time this game has a pretty big flaw at it's core combat design and gameplay loop. As much as I like the whole nemesis system and taking revenge and what not, it is often a matter of time before you get swarmed with Orks and other captains making it often nigh impossible to really get the intended target. Now, I am sure people will say that is simply the grindy nature of the game, gaining strength and better abilities, playing it smart and getting better at dodging, but.... it kind of becomes a drag very VERY quickly (within 2 hours of gameplay) seeing yourself getting overrun with enemies and no reasonable chance of fighting the marked targets. Add to that the fact that 1. each time you die they come back stronger and 2. they already have plenty of resists and usually require a rather specific kill or execution because of it. As much as I like rogue-like games in other genres, buyers should kind of be aware this third person action brawler in vein of Batman Arkham series really feels a lot like a rogue-like. People who are in doubt but like the theme and what not probably should get it right now, it's definitely worth grabbing at only a $5'er. It will be extremely interesting to see whether or not the upcoming Shadow of War fixes all the flaws.

I recommend this game at full price. Upon writing this review, I have spent more than 49 hours in the game. This game is a classic, one that you'll enjoy for a long time. I can see myself spending 100+ hours exploring, fighting and trying to survive in the land of Gransys.
TL;DR: JUST DO IT!
PROS:
- Immersive: This isn't an easy game... but every fight is exciting. There is always a sense of accomplishment once you kill a boss. Leveling up and progressing in the game is also fun since you'll notice how easy it actually is to kill that one boss it once took you a WHILE to kill.
- Romance Everyone: Every human is romanceable, even some Pawns (i.e. Barnaby).
- Quests aren't boring: Usually, spamming quest after quest can be dreadful in some RPGs, but not here. The lore is also pretty easy to follow through the quests. You think it's just a simple escort mission? Well, think again!
- Dynamic: I love the game's animation, the skills, the environment, it's movement is so dynamic that it adds to the whole immersive experience. The voice acting is also superb, it brings life to the some otherwise dull-looking characters!
- Character customization: Play as M/F. Multiple body types are available, as well as color customization. Sufficient hair options (but i'ts just not enough for me, heh).
- You are not 'alone': (unless you choose to be). You can hire pawns in your party (up to four members) to help with your adventuring. You can hire pawns online and pawns which are greater than your level. These pawns 'import' experience they've had and give you tips during skirmishes (monster weakness, quest help, etc).
MEH:
- Generic design: the equipment and monster designs aren't really exceptional, they also lack variety, save for some. The majority of Gransy's environment is pretty boring (I guess I can say the monsters and their habitat complement each other :P). Haven't finished the game yet, but apparently, post-game monster designs add a bit of variety.
CONS:
- Lack of keybinding options: For PC players, this is a problem. You can't access the quests, maps and equipment directly. You have to go  through the main menu first before you are able to access them.

Well strike vector is none of the mentioned above! ^^
Controls are good, it is easy to make your vector do the things right, barrel rolls, flips, boost, switching between first and third person camera, aiming precisely, everything seems kinda very easily when you get used with it, also your vector immediately does takes the direction in which you want it to take, well playing with mouse is kinda hard till you get used to mouse sensitivity and adjust it fine. There is no lag in controls, no delay between actions, no slow response from the vector on key press which makes it even more fast placed shooter type.
And gameplay here!
You have several modes, deathmatch, team deathmath, capture the flag, bounty, which is incredibly fun with friends as vectors are quite fast, you fly thru any kind of stuff, surrounding pipes, moving platforms, chasing others, which requires form you to sharpen your skills, true and that makes it fun.
Every weapon is unique, from heat aiming missiles to plasma guns and machine guns etc, some weapons shoot slower or have lower range, others are fast and powerfull, but no worries you have settings even for that, you can choose to have more range on your weapon at the cost of damage or clip size or anything you prefer, you can try different combinations and strategies after every frag or fail too, if you can't score first time just change the strategy and try again, repeat in case of failure ;D, there is no locked items except customizations of your vector.
You have special weapons, EMP, mines which you can drop behind while being chased, additional boost with thruster and other perks beside those stuff which helps you in fights.
Monotone environment and bored flying around... nope. You have a space stations moving which floats around the spaces just as they should floating while you are trying to not crash into them, if you have enough skills you can attract your opponent and get him into the most difficult areas forcing him to smack himself into some object or wall while he chases you, it is very important to know the map well.

Grab emp and machine gun with long range and heat aiming missiles, just fly thru the combat area, hit the emp and then your opponents will not be able to escape from the missiles no matter what are they trying. Well it is a nice strategy but not always working as it should.
The only drawback is that strike vector has no bots or single player, it is only focused on multiplayer experience, for some luck you can host your own server with some commandline options mentioned in the forum and only people who got your ip address will play with you.
Good thing about it, dlcs are free any item will be unlocked except customization ones that you unlock with gaining experience, you just need to play it.

The objectives for each mission are varied and become progressively more difficult. You'll need to come up with some odd strategies to get all of the heroic objectives. The later missions will unfortunately feel highly based on RNG because the game procedurally generates every map, especially if you are going for heroic objectives. At the same time this makes the game feel less tedious because every map provides new challenges.
Multiplayer is available and is fun as well.  This is not a competitive game though.  The skill ceiling is fairly low and the community is very small.  You will run into the same players often.  Still it is enjoyable to play a few games, which are usually less than 15 minutes.  Queue times are usually less than a minute.
Overall, I thoroughly enjoyed it and if the setting or RTS genre interests you, you should pick it up.

Bought it on day  one of the Kickstarter, and I loved it. Absolutely loved it. Having played the early Tex Murphy games, I can honestly say that this is every bit as good as the previous games.  Goofy and cheesy, but in the best ways possible.

I first played many Tex Murphey games as a pre-teen back in the late 90s.  I never got to finish any of the games however, as CD-ROMs weren't very reliable back then and "compatability issues" entered common vernacular.  I looked up the series on steam in hopes that I could play some of the old games (I can!!) but when I saw there was a new game, I had to download it right away.  It was everything I hoped for.  I think I can appreciate it more now as an adult, since I'm sure most of the humor went over my head 15 years ago.  The game has complex puzzles but nothing that's going to stump you enough to give up.   Chandler looks exactly as I remembered it, and it was fun seeing old characters pop up (and some new ones!)  Old fans of the series should definitely buy this, and I think this is a good game for people who want to try something new.  Cute humor, interesting story, and hours of interesting game play.

This is a very weak recommendation.
It's great to see the entire cast of the old Text Murphy games back again.  The story is pretty good too, and the acting seems to have improved.  It's is based on an old Tex Murphy novel that begins right at the end of Overseer.  To explain the plot would be to give away the small twist thats right at the beginning of the story.  Suffice to say, the mythology is based on Tesla's work.
Unfortunately they also brought back the scavenger hunts from the old games that really make it not so fun to play.  When you finally give in the towel on a puzzle and look up the solution, only to find you missed something laying under a newspaper that was supposed to look like a wheel, behind a building with absolutely no hint that it was there, it makes the game not so much fun.  Now you realize you have to scan every single inch of every single location to make sure you haven't missed any inventory items.
Even with the magic flash light that makes things you can interact with sparkle, it's only slightly more bearable.  Primarily because the sparkles don't show up very well in the flashlights beam.
Also there are some puzzles in the form of simple brain teasers that seemed very out of place and lazily thrown in just to have a game with more puzzles.  Today's games have puzzles that are organic to the story.  Tex Murphy still lives in a world where people throw in Magic 15 puzzles to lock doors.
So if you liked the old Tex Murphy games, I would recommend this.  Just make sure you play on casual so you can use the hint system and even then, you might want to keep a walkthrough handy.

One of the best video game movies you will ever play / see. I've been a fan of Tex Murphy adventures since Mean Streets (coincidentally one of the first PC games I played). The narrative pathing (i.e., different endings based on decisions you make in the game) are great. The game play is fun, but if you hate puzzles, I recommend the Casual Gamer mode so you can skip the puzzles if you want. And there are quite a few brain-teasing puzzles. Thankfully, the only one I got stuck on (a sliding puzzle) was not mandatory to complete the game.
My only real complaint is that you can go entire hours without having a situation where you can die, so you're constantly moving around and clicking on stuff without fear. Then all of a sudden, there's something that can kill you and you walk right up to it without the game making you aware (you have to actually click on it for the game to tell you that it can kill you). This only matters if you care about reaching the highest award the game offers as a Detective. Other than that, you can die as many times without repercussion.
Pros:
-Great story line, must see/play!
-Puzzles can be fun
Cons:
-Can get frustrating trying to solve a puzzle (I recommend Googling a guide if you get stuck)
-Can get frustrating trying to find a missing object (again, Google a guide if you get stuck)
-Some of the puzzles are so complicated that you need to Google just how to complete them (Auxiliary Power reactor puzzle was one of them I did not understand how to work)

-Not much replay value. Once you complete it, you can check out the other endings on YouTube.

Does it have any problems?
========================
A big downside to the PC port is the unfriendliness of the control schemes. There are no button prompts for both keyboard and gamepad, and it makes the learning process a pain. Additionally, whilst playing co-op, two players have to share a keyboard. I don’t think I can remember the last game that delegated the arrow buttons and the number pad to player two.
Final Thoughts!
====================
Dynasty Warriors 8 feels like a fan service, almost to the point of frightening off new players. In my experiences with games that feature a huge character roster, you’re slowly introduced to the cast, allowing you to experiment and decide which character plays best for you. With 82 characters to select from, the inexperienced player will be overwhelmed by the choice. All said though, I was pleasantly surprised by how much fun I got from Dynasty Warriors 8: Xtreme Legends. There is so much content that you could spend hours just trying to skim the surface.
Not as good as DW4 but a hell of a lot better than 6. 1000/1000 Chinese peasants killed.

TL;DR Great game, worth picking up. However, no online co-op so don't buy for a friend with the intent to play online. Also use a controller.
If you're new to the whole hack-n-slash genre, then it's understandable how some people can see it as boring and repetitive because, let's be fair, it is the same stuff stage after stage. Fans of the series or the genre in general I think will indeed enjoy it. Compared to Dynasty Warriors 7 (please bring this to Steam), each character now has unique move sets and weapons. Animations are rather fluid, some choppiness here and there but can't win them all. Dynasty Warriors 5 fans would be pleased to know that the Rage attack has come back. Free mode has also returned, scrapping 7's Conquest mode, and Ambition Mode was implemented as a sort of town building side game where you can get more gold, weapons, levels for officers, etc.
Controller support is a thing, which is good because keyboard bindings are all over the place.
Sadly, there's no sort of matchmaking or online co-op that 7 had. Perhaps 9 (fingers crossed) will sort it out.
Much like 4 and 7, 8 has a kingdom based storyline that tries to follow the Rommance of the Three Kingdoms novel as best as it can (Note; I said novel, not History). A step up from 7 comes in two ways; first a small roster of 2 - 4 officers are selectable at the start opposed to just one, which leads to missions playing out differently, and there's a hypothetical route which explains the story should everything had gone right for the kingdom. Xtreme Legends adds Lu Bu's storyline and Jin returns.
My one criticism, however, is the lack of build up and drama. Particularly with characters dying, I feel that 8 just tried to hurry things along and play for next compared to 7. 8 loses a lot of emotion with most of its characters just vanishing off screen and, to be honest, unless you knew the story previously, you really wouldn't know what happened to them.
There have been criticisms regarding the voice acting in Dynasty Warriors game in general, and I honestly can agree to some extent. Some of the voice acting is a bit stiff (cough cough, Sun Quan) and seems poorly cut. Other characters make up for it, in my opinion. Sima Shi in particular gave a phenomenal performance.
However I do have to criticize the lack of voice acting in certain areas. While it would be a lot of content, and I can understand why to an extent, but storry narration and camps are dead quiet. I enjoyed listening to the narrative and chatting around the camp in 7, but sadly 8 did not follow up with that and left everything just text based. Once again, I'll hope 9 can fix this issue.
As for music, it's Dynasty Warrior greatness. Mixes of previous songs such as Welcome to China and Thousand Suns make their debut in addition to classics such as Men of Intelligence return.
Everything looks great. There are some clipping issues with clothing as noted previously and I've noticed in cutscenes certain cloth tends to jump up randomly or fall for no reason, but hey can't win them all.
Flat out avoid these. They're all cosmetic packs that have no impact on the game, which I can respect because I'm guilty of spending a lot on cosmetics in Dota 2, but they're too over priced. They all look stunning and I do enjoy that I could play as good old DW3 Xiahou Dun, but sadly it's not worth it in my opinion. However if you
want Officer Wang Yi or Fox Girl Xing Cai, then go for it; I'm a reviewer, not a cop.

The first few minutes when booting up the game, entering your name and playing the tutorial is a bit meh. But, boy, was that to change! The music and the way the game moves, really makes this game. It's a pity the rest of the graphics is a bit lacking: The enemies are a bit dull. Yes, they are huge, but very little details and variations. Did I mention the music? It's been a long while since I've heard this level of energic music, which actually fits the game. It's really the best you can get from a game music.
As for gameplay, it's pretty standard. Easy mode should be avoided, unless your try to play through the "campaign". The fun starts at Hard. You also have different modes. The campaign let's you modify your plane for each level, and level up perks, while the other modes is fairly standard: Choose a loadout and see how far you can go with what you've got.
So will this game be played more in the future? For sure! It's a game that I will pull out when I feel I just need to shoot something. Or perhaps challenge a friend. It hasn't got too much diversity in levels, so it isn't a game I will play for hours and hours.
Finally, is it worth my money and time? Fer sure! It could have been sold for even more than the current price, and still be worth a purchase. It's not the most unique shoot'em up, but it deserves to be in the collection of any fan of the genre.

Short story: It's a twin brother of Resident Evil 4 and Dark Souls console-PC ports. Outright bad, unoptimized and lackluster port of an extremely buggy game by itself that has interesting concept, nice gameplay and something people call 'charm'.
If you've spent hours and days modding Unreal, Quake, Far Cry, Dead Island or STALKER and are ready to spend 5-6 hours of your time to fix the most obvious bugs by yourself, then by all means buy the game and Breakdown DLC. If you are a "customer/consumer" type that wants to buy a product and enjoy it - STAY THE HELL AWAY FROM THIS GAME, it's ♥♥♥♥ed up and barely playable, dev team is small, bug fixing is slow, you'll only get frustrated by bying it.
Long story, pros and corresponding cons:
+ SImple and addictive hoarding gameplay
- Extremely poor coding: lots of ingame mechanics that should ADD things for you to use rewarding your efforts OVERWRITE your stocks instead and you end up losing tons of stuff you've spent hours to get. Includes ammo, meds, snacks, silencers etc.
+ Deep base and morale management systems
- Which are glitchy as ♥♥♥♥: your walls randomly require repairs regardless if any zombie hordes reach your base or not, Outposts (facility that you build in a building with some resource to get some of that resource daily) either don't give you anything at all (namely Medicine and Fuel outposts) or work regardless if you have resoureces to keep them running or not (Ammo ones). Skilled survivors that mow through zombie hordes like living tanks run away screaming if they encounter a single horde as a random event. And there still are more than a dozen of such bugs.
+ Gorjeous 'level up by use' leveling system: the more you run the more stamina you have, the more you slash, the better you slash, the more you shoot - the faster you reload etc.
- By now, you must've already guessed it. Yes, it's bugged, oh God it is. Damage source tracking is nonexistent, you get exp for killing zombies for your current weapon regardless of what killed them. Throw a Molotov at a horde and start slashing air in front of you - and you'll get a ton of exp for bladed weapons. Rinse and repeat.
- Hard-coded limit on the amount of things you can have (due to xbox memory limitations). After 15 or so hours of gameplay you'll start spending more time juggling stuff around deciding what to keep than actually looting new stuff. All items and guns are repaired daily for free and you'll end up destroying 70% of things that you've spent hours to get because there is physically no way to use up that much and no way to store that much either.
- Game was patched and overhauled so many times that many changes aren't logged anywhere, there is also no manual. For example, the game says that levelling up Cardio skill (run a lot) increases your available stamina. In fact, it also increases stamina regeneration rate and decreases rate of stamina consumption when you sprint. And there is a ton of things like this, go figure stuff out.
- No multiplayer
- Very poor PC optimization (controls are mostly fine though)
- Poor physics
- Zero modding support, loads of bugged hard-coded stuff that is unfixable via CryEngine's configs and xml sheets.
- Very few features and game mechanics half of which are bugged
- Eventually zombies become so numerous (mostly at night) that game engine is unable to handle that much and zombies become immune to any form of harm, but they still can harm you! Ensures loads of fun.
- Inconsistent realism: for example you need a special tier 3 facility to repair vehicles, that takes a ton of time and resources to build, yet melee weapons and guns are repaired daily for free with tier 1 facility and neither of two requires a mechanic nor some kind of resource. People that are sleep deprived treat it by consuming FOOD and so on. Eventually it gets mind-blowing.

I can go on like this for hours. I've actually fixed some of this stuff, some was fixed by guys at forums and Nexus, devs themselves rolled out 5 patches already but still it feels like an alpha or a tech demo of some sort.

One of very few games that capture "survival" within its gameplay, State of Decay is an ambitious take on building and maintaining a community in a world with danger around every corner. Starvation, sickness, and death due to failure to recover from injuries are all present. Additionally, among the survivors, they may run away from home, or go missing (sometimes permanently), all while the resource pool you have is drained every (real world) day. There are a lot of scary moments in the game that come about in a completely organic fashion. Stealth works as intended, and the enemy AI acts as it should when you're sneaking around. Action in the game is very competent and exciting. It seems like the ideal survival game.
Of course, there is a "but" that follows. The game is buggy. Not just a little buggy, either - the game is very buggy. You can't go five whole minutes without seeing a zombie clip through a fence or get stuck on a piece of the landscape. However, most of the bugs have little effect on gameplay, and thankfully, stealth is in no way negatively effected by said bugs, and combat rarely is either. However, if you do come across a bug that nips you in the butt, there is no way to undo it, which leads me to my next point, which is saving. Saving your progress in this game sucks. It just does. There's four files you can use, but you can only save one playthrough to each, and the game autosaves, with no hard saving at all. As a result, you can be screwed over for the entire playthrough if you make a simple mistake, such as falling from a height, which leads me to my next point - controls. Controls aren't necessarily bad, but they're definitely in need of improvement, especially for when you're in melee combat. The controls do a servicable job otherwise though. Another problem is the quest system. You receive quests through somebody at home communicating with you over a radio. Its a good system, or at least, it would be if she wasn't contacting you every single minute about one quest or another. Its so bad that there are mods that do away with it that are actually called "Nag be gone!" and "The 'Stop Harassing Me Lily!' Mod", both of which work by the way. The game lacks any multiplayer, which is both a good thing (nobody destroying your community overnight) and a bad thing (game experience feels very lonely, and most players would benefit from cooperating), and there is not going to be any multiplayer added to the game. The game also persists while you're not playing, which can severely damage the experience of some people. There are mods that address this too, and even allow you to shut it off, so those with little time to play the game on a regular basis can still play (although the game requires such a large time investment that I would honestly recommend another type of game instead). There's no conflict against humans in the games - its entirely cooperation with fellow survivors, which will probably be disappointing for some, but I feel that the game is better for such an exclusion. State of Decay can also get quite dull and repetitive over time, which, again, can be solved, if only temporarily, with mods, which I suppose should bring me to my next point.
For many of the faults of the game, there's mod support out there that addresses a lot of it, and some mods overhaul the game with drastic changes that alter the dynamic. Mod support won't keep the game alive forever, but the current ones out there can definitely extend the life of the game and rectify many major problems with the game.
All in all, State of Decay is one of three survival games I've played that seem to actually capture the essence of what "survival" really means, and doesn't simply slap on "survival" because there are zombies in the game like some people actually do with games like Dead Rising and Left 4 Dead. If you have a survival itch that won't go away, or have any interest in the genre, I highly recommend getting State of Decay, and its DLC "Breakdown", on a Steam sale. Otherwise, honestly, you might be better off playing something else.
tl;dr 6/10, buy this game if you're interested in or enjoy the survival genre, and check out mod support for the game as well.

Well, as it's already been stated by many, this is a revisit to Baldur's Gate (1 & 2). It doesn't have the story depth of the characters of those classics, and it doesn't quite match up to the immersion of Planescape: Torment, but when it comes to isometric cRPGs this is one that stands out. You won't have the, "Squeak SQUEAK" of the "Boo" that is Minsc's hamster or the haughty judgementalism that is Jaheira in the character interactions, and you certainly won't get the gender-changing possibilities of your companions, but . . . it's not bad for a crowd-funded game.
If you're expecting that level of depth and that's what you're looking for, you're not going to find it with this game. There is, however, interaction and some degree of character growth of the NPCs that can join your party. All NPCs have personal quests - not as rewarding as BG2, for instance - but it's there.
Having said that, this is an isometric cRPG that allows you to create a character of your choice and choose, at your leisure, a party of either pre-built NPCs you meet in-game or recruit and define for youself. Your party grows in strength and experience, you stylistically decide how to develop yourself and your NPCs to suit your expectations, and you go through the game playing these decisions against the battle encounters you face.
And that's kind of where it breaks down. The story - the plot - is interesting, but what you will find is that you approach all conflicts and battle in pretty much the same way. "I put my 'tanks' or 'warriors' here, and everyone else destroys the enemies from afar." is not an unfair description of how most fights go. If you're in it for the story, then great - it's like playing any RPG, such a Dragon Age: Inquisition, on casual mode. If you're in it for hardcore combat challenge, then you're just going to end up with larger groups of enemies against whom you already have effective strategies and tactics to defeat.
Point is, the battles get repetitive. The story is there between the battles, but the story doesn't progress without the battles. Looking back, all those years ago at Baldur's Gate and Planescape: Torment, it probably wasn't much different. But at least at that time it was novel ideas and made me a captive audience. In this re-incarnation, it's the same thing except I know what to expect, and that diminishes the overall experience.
I recommend the game, however, because of the story. That is, ultimately, why we play RPGs. I want to know what happens next; I am the protagonist and get to make choices that may affect future consequences, and I have a BIG♥♥♥♥♥DAMN SWORD that can cut you in two. As a revisitation on older cRPG games, it's nothing less than awesome. Graphics are decent, soundtrack is great, voice-acting is okay - there's just enough to bring those memories back from the 90's. And since I'm sentimental, I'll run with that.

I dont know how to do reviews so here a good recipe for banana bread
2-3 very ripe bananas, peeled
1/3 cup melted butter
1 cup of sugar (can easily use 3/4 cup, or drop it down to 1/2 cup if you want it less sweet)
1 egg, beaten
1 teaspoon vanilla extract
1 teaspoon baking soda
Pinch of salt
1 1/2 cups of all-purpose flour
METHOD
Preheat the oven to 350°F (175°C), and butter a 4x8-inch loaf pan.
In a mixing bowl, mash the ripe bananas with a fork until smooth. Stir the melted butter into the mashed bananas.
Mix in the baking soda and salt. Stir in the sugar, beaten egg, and vanilla extract. Mix in the flour.
Pour the batter into your prepared loaf pan. Bake for 1 hour to 1 hour 10 minutes (check at 50 minutes) at 350°F (175°C), or until a tester inserted into the center comes out clean.
Remove from oven and cool completely on a rack. Remove the banana bread from the pan. Slice and serve. (A bread knife helps to make slices that aren't crumbly.)

As a Tex Murphy fan, I was stoked after hearing about the newest installment, and boy was I eager to play!  But after playing half-way through, I found myself questioning whether I should even bother finishing the game.  It was only through sheer force of will and a weird, nostalgic obligation, that I managed to see it through to the end.  *sigh* So where to begin?
Let's first talk about the things it did well:
Revisiting Chandler Avenue and reuniting with the old cast was a treat for old Tex Murphy fans like myself.  And honestly, I didn't mind the mediocre graphics, as it felt reminiscent of the old Tex Murphy games.  The FMV sequences were well-done for the most part, and I enjoyed exploring areas without running into loading screens or having to change discs. (I know I'm throwing a bone here, but it's the little things that count, right?)  Unfortunately, that's where the good ends.  Now on to my personal gripes:
What's with the talking, Tom Servo gadget?  In the beginning and throughout the game, I was questioning the purpose of this supposed "character".  Other than the tutorial, and occasional out of place quips, it didn't really add to the story - or much of anything else for that matter.  Tex's  inner monologues could have easily replaced this character - so why even bother with this?
When initially exploring your apartment and Chandler Avenue, you come across seemingly random objects which upon closer inspection, will play back clips from the old Tex Murphy games.  While it's a nice trip down memory lane for fans like me, the references seemed out of place for the game's story.  I understand the intent, but the clips felt rather shoe-horned in, and were unnecessary to the story's progression - not to mention confusing for those who are new to the franchise.
In terms of game-play, the pixel hunting wasn't a big deal for me.  What was a big deal was having to cope with:
1.	Awkward and unpredictable stealth mechanics (which will kill you)
2.	Navigating security systems via clunky controls (which will kill you)
3.	Dealing with random enemy patrols with questionable aggro radius (which will kill you)
All the while looking for obscure objects hidden in the environment to progress further in the story.  It was an immense frustration, and made me want to quit several times--it was just, not, fun.  Now if the stealth mechanics were actually fleshed out and developed, I don't think it would have been a problem.  As it was however, the deaths felt cheap, and you can't help but feel as if the game is working against you.
The story...oh man, the story.  For the record, this contains *SPOILERS* - so don't say I didn't warn you.
The story picks up where the last game left off, with Tex suffering from amnesia from the past seven years.  Now it's up to you to figure out what happened.  Pretty straightforward, right?  As you progress, you're introduced to more characters from your 'previous' life that you have no recollection of.
However, one of the major flaws of this game is that you never fully interact with ANY of these new characters...at all!  I found myself scratching my head, trying to put names to faces and their overall place in the timeline of events.  When I asked questions to folks around town, I had to remind myself who the heck "so-and-so" was and why did I care?  Overall, the story telling suffers from a severe case of exposition.  You are TOLD who these characters are, and what your prior relationship with them was, but in terms of experiencing these relationships first-hand throughout the game and having meaningful interaction with any of them?  Pfft! Forget about it.  This is because the characters are either:
A.)  Dead
B.)  Soon to be Dead
C.) Meet in 2-3 FMV scenes only to be never seen or heard from again
The game lacks context in so many areas, that as a player I was left struggling to put the pieces together.   On top of that, the game adds soap opera-esque plot twists, as if the story wasn't convoluted enough! (Chelsee was actually the daughter of Margaret Leonard but was given up for adoption because of....reasons.  And J.T Donnelly was actually the past incarnation of Tex Murphy... WTF? Seriously?!  What does ANY of this have to do with ANYTHING!  *slaps forehead*)  Jesus, in terms of trying to make sense of the story - don't even bother.  The way the game plays out, it's like getting handed pieces of a jigsaw puzzle, and asking you to piece it together - in the dark, while riding on a roller coaster.
TLDR:
I really wanted to like this game, but even as an avid Tex Murphy fan - I felt this was a bit of a disappointment.  It had potential, but with frustrating stealth mechanics, convoluted story-telling, and dangling plotlines with no resolution or relevance to the story - I cannot in good conscience recommend this game.
I hope that if future installments are made, they get rid of stealth/patrol sequences, tighten the story (less plot holes please!), emphasize more character building and interaction, get rid of 'transition' characters (i.e. Tom Servo, Ariel, St. Germaine) and rely less on references from the older games -- it will make it infinitely more enjoyable.
If you're a Tex Murphy fan, pick it up when it's under $5.  I can't see spending more than that.  If you're not a Tex Murphy fan - skip this one, and instead pick up "Under a Killing Moon" - it's dated, but it's definitely a solid and entertaining game.

The Binding of Isaac: Rebirth will always be one of my favorite games. I have over 100 hours into the PS4 version (came with PlayStation Plus) and purchased it on PC for modding and a fresh start. It has been a thrill to play this game and I'm even more excited to try Afterbirth once I feel I am done with Antibirth (a free mod expansion which adds a ton to the game). The Binding of Isaac is a top-down, rogue-like game that I have heard resembles the original Zelda games in many ways. It revolves around beating the game several times and unlocking new items, bosses, and increases in difficulty as the game progresses. Overall, the design was meant to take hours and hours to unlock everything while still providing a fresh experience each run, which this game does very well. The flow of the game, the controls, the items, the synergies, all of these things make the game enjoyable for long periods of time so be wary of the fact that this game is a time drainer. One real run may last about an hour usually. There isn't a lot I can say bad about this game other than it can be extremely difficult at times once you get further in the game, probably to keep you playing longer. Other than that, it's a well thought out game with a pretty great developer who really wants to please the community. I would encourage purchasing Afterbirth as well from all the great things I've heard about it and it is often bundled with the base game. I have no comment on Afterbirth+ though. Overall, The Binding of Isaac is the definition of a game that gives you a huge "bang for your buck" by providing hours and hours of entertainment. It really is a must have for any new PC gamers.

For the longest time Sonic CD was my #1 favourite video game; a title possessed of a rare quality for the time it was released.
Developed as a showpiece for CD-ROM technology, it was hoped that Sonic CD would pave the way for a new generation of quality disc-based games and whilst it is a fine title in its own right, ultimately the grand vision never materialized like Sega once hoped.
Sonic CD appealed to me as a youngster for its sharp 2D graphics and flourishes of 3D, for its excellent soundtrack (in the European/Japanese version at least) and its robust palette of different levels.
Sharing much in common with the first game in the series, this lesser-known title in Sonic's library consists of 7 different stages interwoven with the theme of time travel. When Sonic passes certain posts in the game world he gains the ability to transport himself through time by gaining enough speed for several seconds (an obvious inspiration from Back to the Future).
Each stage features a design for the current time period (whether it's a good/bad future, present or the past) complete with new colours, different enemy patterns and an alternate arrangement of both the level layout and music. Such variety for a game released in 1993 is stunning (as each level essentially comes in four flavours) and it helps set Sonic CD apart from the generally lacklustre titles that call the Sega Mega CD console home.
Although the method of time travel is clunky, it remains an interesting mechanic and part of the game's advanced challenge as the only way to secure a truly good ending is to visit levels in the past and destroy a robot-producing factory present in each one.
When you add in an impressive 3D bonus stage, a time attack mode and other unlockables that save to your console's internal memory; you've got a truly great Mega CD title that keeps very small company.
This HD remaster on Steam was helmed by wizard programmer Christian Whitehead and is the best way to experience Sonic CD today, and after many years the game is finally reaching the larger audience it deserved on current generation consoles and mobile devices.
The time this game spent as my #1 video game was time admittedly obstructed by nostalgia, as very few people I spoke to then had any knowledge of this special game at all; making the whole thing feel like a more personal experience than usual.
The gameplay isn't as fast or exciting as Sonic the Hedgehog 2, the challenge is a bit lax and the overall level design does leave a lot to be desired.
But Sonic CD is still a good game and it's one that has aged remarkbly well thanks to this gorgeous HD remaster.

State of Decay, an arcade-ish zombie "sandbox" game by Undead Labs. "Sandbox" because you have the possibility to do what you want (in game limitations of course), without any time limits.
There is a story, but it's not what you should buy this game for. It's the fun from killing zombies, and building a community to survive.
"Building a community"? Yes. You have it in here. You start out small, with some people barely tying up an end with the other end, and you are supposed to help them survive. Or you can just ignore them completely and go kill some zombies. Up to you.
The combat is pretty enjoyable. The game doesn't have any tutorials on to how to kill that walking corpse, but you will figure it out fairly quickly. Or just check the wiki. There are few types of zombies, from the normal shambling ones, through sprinting ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s and ending with a juggernaut that requires some effort to take out.
Gameplay itself is also done well. You can get into nearly every building you see, you can look around for supplies to help your group survive, you can swap between characters. And there's character progression.
Many people recommend playing on a pad, but I actually have no difficulties to play on a keyboard & mouse.
Graphics are nice, even for a X360 game, made on CryEngine 3. AI is good enough (as for a zombie).
If you are looking for a game where you kill zombies, run around and do stuff, and where it "tries" to simulate an apocalypse, then this is it.
I got this for full price, and I am not disappointed. There's a living modding community going, so the game has at least some years of life more. Although, if you do not care about a story mode, and you prefer just a survival sandbox, you should also get Breakdown DLC.

I'll start off by saying this game definitely has clunky moments. Inventory management is annoying, moving and shooting during combat can become frustrating, and the character animation during conversation can be a little stale at times.
However, the story and world building are absolutely fantastic, and it's made the
series one of my favourite science fiction IPs. The codex is very rich and well written, the environments speak volumes on their fictional history and the exploration feels grand and important. The Mako (the vehicle which you control to explore worlds) can for sure be annoying to handle at times, due to the poor terrain design, but it still feels so cool to go down to planets, look around, and go back up. I really feel like some intergalactic space pioneer!
The companion characters are all dynamic and interesting, and the villains are intimidating. I rarely skipped conversations in the game because it feels like every person, whether it's a main character or some random NPC, has something interesting to say about this massive universe beyond the stars. I also love the designs of the aliens, spaceships and architecture; each part makes the world feel so real. Paired with the amazing soundtrack, it makes me want to join a space program and get the hell off Earth.
I'd give this game a 9.0/10.0. I know that seems a little high considering the negatives I've mentioned but everything this game does right outweighs everything it does wrong. It's such an impressive debut to an intellectual property, and is an instant classic.
Honestly an experience I cannot forget, and one that I have chased ever since.

This game tries to take the twitch shooting of quake and the ship fighting of Freelancer and combines them into an ugly hybrid monster that you don't like but at the same time has a super adorable face and you're all excited for it's potential when it grows up.  The ability to stop flying instantly and change direction instantly kills any aspect of chasing someone through a cool map, if that's what you're here for, and the ability to start flying instantly and with an amazing turn rate kills any close combat twitch shooting.
Not to mention, the gamemodes are DM, TDM, CTF...it's hardly new and interesting.  It's the same old boring modes except with ships.  Where's the cool assault type maps?  UT04 had this down with the one assault map where teams pilot ships in space and attack a base.  Where's that in this game?
Then again, even if it was in, if you came for awesome flying ship fights you'll be disappointed and if you came for quake style fights in the air you'll also be disappointed.  Game has amazing potential but doesn't capitalize.  If you like flying fights play Freelancer and if you like twitch shooters play Quake, because this game unfortunately isn't as good as either and the inclusion of both modes in a mediocre way doesn't make up for the way in which they, individually, are mediocre in this game.
This ignores the whole "grind for guns" part of the game, which is total crap.
I'd recommend if:
Remove ability to instantly switch from close range hover to long range flying mode (this kills quake style fights).
Remove ability to instantly accelerate/deccelerate (this kills flying fights).
Add an interesting game mode.

All in all, it's a really enjoyable RPG experience that every fan of the genre should give it a try. More specifically, I felt like the combat of the game is one of its strong points since it runs smoothly and offers great variety in its playstyles. The player is not limited to a specific "vocation" (class) as it can be easily changed and unlock access to a whole new array of skills and different weapon types. The skills are quite varied and make for interesting combinations, though you have to choose only three at a time. You can dodge with the daggers, block with a shield and all in all the mecchanics work really well. Your pawns (companions) can make the difference in the battlefield since they provide assistance and actively engage enemies or at least draw them away from you.
When it comes to customization I was exceptionally pleased as the player is offered with many options in character creation and you can even change the voice, skin color, makeup and hairstyle (plethora of choices) at a barber shop as many times as you like during the game. The armor sets were plenty and diverse. You get your standard protective armor, some special items with peculiar shapes and forms and even the less protective, though definitely aesthetically pleasing pieces like lingerie and revealing robes.
As far as the story goes, it's not anything impressive and at times can be perplexing with the whole pawn-arisen concept. You get the big bad dragon who threatens to destroy everything and you need to stop him (or not). The setting is, as expected, medieval and everyone calls you "ser" even if you play as female. They tend to speak in a more refined and unnatural way like they're constantly trying to find exquisite synonyms for words (maybe a "side effect" from the japanese translation).
My biggest flaw of this game is definitely the save system. It's plain frustrating that an rpg game doesn't let you keep multiple saves so that you can try different outcomes or simply to return to an earlier stage. Not only that but it doesn't even have a proper "load" function since if you wish to load your saved game you need to exit to the main menu! Others rightfully complain about the travel system as well, since there is no fast-travel like Skyrim but that can be dealt with an "eternal ferrystone". Another slightly bothersome point is your "beloved", who basically serves the role of your love partner. Thing is that the system determing him/her functions in a weird way and you can easily end up with the wrong person (happenned to me), who, unfortunately, plays a pivotal role in the story.
So, apart from the "save" issue, I thoroughly enjoyed the game and I'll definitely give it another go (New Game+), since you can basically keep going till you drop :)
