Well, as it's already been stated by many, this is a revisit to Baldur's Gate (1 & 2). It doesn't have the story depth of the characters of those classics, and it doesn't quite match up to the immersion of Planescape: Torment, but when it comes to isometric cRPGs this is one that stands out. You won't have the, "Squeak SQUEAK" of the "Boo" that is Minsc's hamster or the haughty judgementalism that is Jaheira in the character interactions, and you certainly won't get the gender-changing possibilities of your companions, but . . . it's not bad for a crowd-funded game.
If you're expecting that level of depth and that's what you're looking for, you're not going to find it with this game. There is, however, interaction and some degree of character growth of the NPCs that can join your party. All NPCs have personal quests - not as rewarding as BG2, for instance - but it's there.
Having said that, this is an isometric cRPG that allows you to create a character of your choice and choose, at your leisure, a party of either pre-built NPCs you meet in-game or recruit and define for youself. Your party grows in strength and experience, you stylistically decide how to develop yourself and your NPCs to suit your expectations, and you go through the game playing these decisions against the battle encounters you face.
And that's kind of where it breaks down. The story - the plot - is interesting, but what you will find is that you approach all conflicts and battle in pretty much the same way. "I put my 'tanks' or 'warriors' here, and everyone else destroys the enemies from afar." is not an unfair description of how most fights go. If you're in it for the story, then great - it's like playing any RPG, such a Dragon Age: Inquisition, on casual mode. If you're in it for hardcore combat challenge, then you're just going to end up with larger groups of enemies against whom you already have effective strategies and tactics to defeat.
Point is, the battles get repetitive. The story is there between the battles, but the story doesn't progress without the battles. Looking back, all those years ago at Baldur's Gate and Planescape: Torment, it probably wasn't much different. But at least at that time it was novel ideas and made me a captive audience. In this re-incarnation, it's the same thing except I know what to expect, and that diminishes the overall experience.
I recommend the game, however, because of the story. That is, ultimately, why we play RPGs. I want to know what happens next; I am the protagonist and get to make choices that may affect future consequences, and I have a BIG♥♥♥♥♥DAMN SWORD that can cut you in two. As a revisitation on older cRPG games, it's nothing less than awesome. Graphics are decent, soundtrack is great, voice-acting is okay - there's just enough to bring those memories back from the 90's. And since I'm sentimental, I'll run with that.

Tooth and Tail is a simplified RTS with a delightful soundtrack and beautiful art style. The game functions on a very basic rally system. Your hero rallies your troops and you can either choose to attack move, fall back, or hold position with your units. The maps and spawns points are randomly generated, which adds to the chaos of the game, but it makes the game feel less competitive. There is an option to use premade maps in ranked play, but, here's the thing, the player base is so small right now, it's hard to find a match.
Even though I enjoyed this game immensely, I find it very hard to recommend the game  because it's really hard to find matches. The game has been out about 2 months and the player base is very small. Don't get me wrong, there is a campaign mode, and I'm sure it's great, but personally, I prefer to play my RTS games in multiplayer, against real people, and if there isn't anyone to play against, I just don't play the game.
Tooth and Tail has a lot to offer if you're new to the RTS genre, but if you're a seasoned RTS player whose looking for a competitive game, you'll probably want to look elsewhere. Seasoned players will feel like they slightly oversimplified the genre. You cannot effectively micro and macro at the same time in this game. You either choose between building structures that automatically spawn troops or attack moving on the enemy. The way the rally system works doesn't allow you to do both at the same time.
That being said, I'm going to still review this game positively, it's a great game, and I enjoy that they managed to make an RTS game that doesn't take 45 minutes to play unless you cheese. They've actually made some improvements on the genre. Personally, I think the system that allows you to draft your troops is amazing and I hope to see it in future games.
I'd still be playing Tooth & Tail, but it doesn't have the player base to keep me engaged. I can only hope that there is a surge in players, because it would be unfortunate if the multiplayer scene for the game just fades away. Tooth & Tail is a genuinely great game, I just feel like a lot of people missed it.

I am a huge fan of Tooth and Tail. The controls are simple and intuitive, which I believe is important for an RTS aimed at newcomers to the genre. Also, the gameplay is intense and fast-paced while still emphasizing strategic play (as this is the appeal of RTS games), which I enjoy. The singleplayer campaign is difficult, which may be a good or bad thing depending on your tastes. I personally enjoy a good challenge, but sometimes, certain missions can be quite frustrating. The dark premise of animals fighting a war to eat each other is one that definitely piques my interest. Overall, I would recommend Tooth and Tail.

I enjoy various video games genre and I have more than 500 games in my steam library. And out of all of them, this small yet very catchy rts ranks 1st in number of hours played. It feels a lot like a lighter, shorter, version of SC2, with the main difference being your unit control is being framed by your commander (which acts as a living cursor), rather than your sheer ability to multitask everything at once. Some might find that feature strategically restrictive, but I think it actually makes for an interesting and original take on the rts genre. It also makes this game learning curve much smoother.
The units are well designed, in their function and in their appearance (graphic style and voice), the musics are excellent for all 4 commanders... I don't have anything really negative to say about this game to balance my review. Except maybe, the solo campaign alone barely makes the game worth its normal price. While it does have 25 missions, with various objectives, intersting dialogues, and an elusive lore about civil war and cannibalism, the real catchiness of the games lies in its multiplayer mode. The games are short, fun and rarely feel the same as the previous ones (partly thanks to the randomly generated map, which are great for diversity, for the modest cost of adding a little bit of luck, as some maps may turn to be unfair). The matchmaking is very efficient, though it tends to prioritize quickness above similarity of skills as waiting time goes on. The community is very active and sympathetic and the game gets balance updates almost every week, which adds even more variety to the strategies. Did I mention you get to pick 6 units types among 20 before every game? I think variety is the word that describes best my opinion of the game. And quickness.
Much good. Worth the 20 bucks.

Controls are simple and easy to learn. In spite of this, this game manages to largely maintain what makes a good RTS.
The game has a reasonably long single player mode with various missions with unique rule sets that tells the tale of animal civil war. Many of the missions can be quite difficult, particularly due to the random nature of the maps. Fortunately, the main component of this game is the online multiplayer.
If you enjoy RTS games, this one is hard to skip.

While on the topic of Town of Salem, I'm gonna bring up the game Throne of Lies. At first glance it just looks like a copy of Town of Salem but it is so so so much better in my opinion. And I say that as someone with probably 30+ hours in ToS. First off, there's so many more roles in the game, but not enough so that it gets exhausting. It's like the perfect amount so that it keeps the game very fresh without being a slog to learn everything. Additionally, the game has a very streamlined built in class list that tells you every single thing about the class, so you don't need to worry about not knowing what class do.
So the way the game plays is as follows: The "Good" faction is the Blue Dragon, and they're in every game. Then it randomly chooses a "Bad" faction, either the Unseen or the Cult. The Unseen is like the traditional mafia, The Cult is a bit weirder. Every game has a Prince, a King, , 2 of either The Cult or The Unseen, 2-4 Neutral classes and 8-10 random Blue Dragon classes. The king can be Good, Evil, or Neutral which makes for very interesting games.
The game plays pretty much the exact same as ToS. A 90 second day for discussion and voting for treason followed by a 30-45 second night (can't remember which). However, this gameplay is where ToL is ahead of ToS by leagues. First off, there is not a single dull class in ToL. For example, in ToS, if you get Survivor or Retributionist, it's pretty boring because you can't really help your team win directly through what you do. Obviously with the survivor all you have to do is live, which is really boring. Nobody wants to do nothing except for survive. It's fun to learn secrets about people and be involved in the game, and the survivor actively stops you from that. Additionally, the Retributionist can be extremely valuable to the town, but the only thing they can do is revive someone. It can be one of the most valuable skills in the game, but the player doesn't feel like they did much. ToL gets rid of those issues entirely.
First off, every single class has at least 2 abilities, some have up to 4. The abilities are split into Day and Night abilities. Day abilities can obviously be used during the day and they have an immediate impact. For example, look at Political Pressure on The Aristocrat. It forces a player to vote another player up for treason and remove their ability to vote again. You can use this to completely screw over another player by making them look super suspicious. It's a very fun and unique ability. On the other hand, Night abilities are used during the night and almost always have their effects done at the end of the night. For example, look at the Psychic's Link Minds. At night she has the ability to link her mind with 2 other players, allowing the to talk privately during the night. This is an example of an ability that doesn't occur at the end of the night. This is another very cool and useful ability.
Every class is able to directly influence other players in the game and learn about them or kill them, which makes for much more fun games. Many of the abilities are so unique and cool that it adds much more flavor to the game than ToS. For example, look at the Illusionist, the Unseen version of the Psychic. She has an ability where she can delete the chat history of a player. That is such a fantastic idea for an ability like holy♥♥♥♥♥♥ It has the potential to completely ruin a player's day it such a cool way. The game is sprinkled with awesome abilities like this.
The Unseen and the Cult are able to stay relevant throughout the entire game. Both of them have leaders which are able to convert Blue Dragon people to their faction, with each BD class having its own unique Unseen class. You could play the game for so long and still never experience all the classes because of how the conversions work. It takes such a specific set of circumstances to get any given Unseen class.
All in all the game is just a much better version of ToS, especially because the playerbase isn't divide between DLC and Non-DLC. If you love ToS, this game is definitely worth picking up.

I rate the game Saviors (also known as Star Saviors) 4/5. Good.
Perhaps the best thing about this game is that it is only 2 dollars and it gives you an amazing amount of gameplay for the price of just 2 candybars. In many ways Saviors is very, very similar to Revolution Ace or Raptor: Call of the Shadows. This is a "schmup" (Whatever that stands for) game which features multiple play modes but particularly focuses on a main campaign wherein you choose a ship and progress through a series of areas upgrading your ship as you go. The campaign is done fairly well as are the various other modes of play (survival, arcade etc.). This game really shines in terms of how many options it gives you, particularly the fact that this game can either be really easy or really hard depending on which difficulty you choose (and a moderate difficulty really is moderately difficult). On the downside, like in Revolution Ace and Raptor: Call of the Shadows, the environments you fly over just creep along in an incredibly lethargic manner. There really isn't very much of a thrilling sense of speed and to make matters worse, the environments you fly over tend to be fairly boring. Despite this downfall though, Saviors is still fairly fun and it's main campaign has a nice, though predictable, little story told using between-mission dialogue scenes (and bizarre, creepy, computer-generated misshapen character faces. I try to pretend that's just how humans ended up looking on that planet in the distant future).
+Many different game modes to choose from and many, many different ship types to play, all unlocked from the start.
+The main campaign is long and challenging and fun with a wonderfully done difficulty curve from easy up to extremely difficult. The main campaign gives you lots of upgrade and ship customization options as you progress and lets you reconfigure your ship if you need to redo an area.
+Several difficulty levels. Easy really is easy. Hard really is hard.
+Pretty good music though perhaps a bit too much of it is in a sort of odd happy-go-lucky style which dramatically decreases the game's sense of tension. But hey, at least it isn't frenetic Japanese techno music yet again.
+The main campaign actually has a story (which it explains, in fairly shallow interpersonal terms using text only). Some of the dialogue can be funny. One character does nothing but mouth off at the guy giving you objectives and another character is completely fixated on making big explosions.
+Nifty and important and well implemented control scheme which lets you fire certain weapons out the sides of your craft if you need to. Good, responsive controls in general.
+Good screen and menu layout.
+This game seems to be completely devoid of bugginess.
+Seriously, you can get this game for 2.00 and it lasts almost as long as Raptor: Call of the Shadows.
+/-Adequate graphics but the environments, particularly as drab and boring as they are (and overly clean looking) should have whizzed by at a great speed to add interest to the game's graphics but instead merely creepy along at a snail's pace making the game graphically boring.
+/-Large variety of enemies but despite their variety the enemies and their projectiles are not very creative looking. In terms of gameplay the enemies tend to fight in a fairly bland and offer fairly conventional challenges to gamers familiar with this type of game.
-Bizarrely animated and rendered character faces. Really, I'm not sure the developers of this game could have made a more creepy looking set of characters if they'd tried,
-Mediocre and repetitive sound effects.
-Fairly boring boss fights.
-Despite the many different game modes, the bland enemies and boring boss fights and boring visuals make this game seem, well, boring after a while. Probably a good game to play just once in a while along with other, similar games. But hey, what can you expect for 2 dollars?

A fantastic social deduction game similair to Werewolf or Mafia games only with a conversion mechanic. This increases the skill-ceiling immensely and ensures every game is unique: in other words, it is like ToS for clever people ;)
The design and graphics of the game is honestly beautiful, it is all set in a Medieval castle called Castle Adiart, and each class has their own unique bedroom which you see every night. In the morning all the dead bodies are found in a random location of the castle, giving it a real murder-mystery vibe. On top of that there are tons of cosmetic items which you can buy with money EARNED THROUGH THE GAME to increase your immersion at no real expense.
For me the best thing about ToL is the community. As it is a social deduction game by far the most important enjoyment factor is the players around you - how your team mates act, how toxic they are. The Mods and Devs work tirelessly to get rid of any trolls or toxic players (which are normally few and far between) which can be evidenced by the vast amount of salty reviews from trolls who have been banned :D. The Discord server is a great friendly place, and the Imperium42 forum is so friendly to the point that I am suspecting everyone else may be NPC's.
All in all 100% worth the 10 quid and will guarantee hours of gameplay.

The binding of Issac is a mixture of Legend of Zelda type game play, permenent death, and dark themes. Thats the best way to describe this game. You play as a boy named Issac, who escaped his mother trying to kill him by jumping into a basement full of horrors. You collect items and trinkets along the way to further Issacs gross apearance. There is SO MUCH♥♥♥♥♥♥IN THIS GAME IT IS INSANE. The game revolves around your tears (Creative attack syestem) which you controll with your arrow keys. You can get items (as already said) and upgrade your tear attacks. You can also get passive upgrades which can control the enviroment around you. You go floor by floor, going to bosses and then going down the trap door to get to a new floor. On these diffrent floors you can find shops, devil deals which require heart containers to get items, angel deals and much more. As you progress in this game you get new bosses, new items to find with each run, and even new final bosses and endings. If I remember correctly this game has about 16 endings. "Woah, thats alot of endings!" I hear you say like a surprised otter. And yes, you are correct because this game is PACKED with content. You can also unlock new characters to try the depths with who each start with their own damage/health/speed and items spawned with. If you want a really interesting character, try azzazel. A black demon with wings thats tear attack is to fire a mini lazer. Cool right? In conclusion the Binding of Issac is worth every cent. I have spend 180+ hours into this game and I have not even unlocked all of the achivements. If you are to buy this game I would reccomend buying the 2 expansion packs, Afterbirth (ew) and Afterbirth +. Both of them are amazing (to be fair the new final boss for Afterbirth + is a little BS) and add tons of new content. 10/10. This is in my top 3 favorite games of all time. ♥♥♥♥ing amazing.

So while Sonic 2 was being developed in america the poeple that still remained in Japan decided that they would make a Sonic game anyway. What came out of this was Sonic CD released in 1993 for the Mega-CD addon for the Mega Drive/Genesis if you live in America. The one im reviewing is the 2011 re-release by yours Christian Whitehead so there will be notable differences from the origional but the core of the game is exactly the same.
Lets cover the story first. Eggman has chained up a planet that visits sonics world every year or so called Little Planet. Eggman chained the planet to a mountain to stop it from leaving and gradually starts to covert it into a base of operations. Sonic just wont have that and heads up there to stop Eggman. But along the way he has to collect the Times stones (or rather NOT-Choas Emeralds) to stop eggman just reversing what he just did. If you collect all the stones little planet leaves and all vegertation is restored. If you don't then Sonic will let the planet free but because eggman has the stones he just warps little planet back to the way it was, chained to the mountain and you effectively just do the same stages over and over agin until you get the good ending. Along the way he encounters Amy Rose who almost immediently get capture by yours Metal Sonic and robot built by Eggman to match Sonics everything but mostly speed. He defets metal sonic and rescues amy. Huzzar???
Well now gameplay. Sonic feels and controlls almost identical to sonic 1,2 and 3+K and he can still jump on enemies, run through loop-de-loops, and do the spin dash but less enfasis is put on the spin dash in this game and more is put on  this new (and one off) move called the super peel out. To charge it you simply look up and press the action button, sonic will go to a figure of 8 and when you let go you blast off so fast the camera sometimes cant keep up. But dont get too used to it as it only appears in this game and 2 game gear titles.... The ♥♥♥♥ Sonic Team? The main focus of t5his game is time travel. Scattered around each stage are posts that say past or future. If you go past them and build up enough speed you'll travel in time to whenever. once you get there you need to find the robot generator destroy it and in tern make a good future. You need to do this for every stage or you get the bad ending. The stages themselfs are a mixed bag. They are Palmtree Panic, Collision Chaos, Tidal Tempest, Quartz Quadrent, Whacky Workbench, Stardust Speedway and Metalic Maddness. Palmtree Panic is a pretty decent, Collision Chaos well chaos is correect theres stuff that will send you all over the place. Tidal Tempest is Labyrinith Zone on steroids. Quartz quadrent is good and you can breeze through it pretty qiuckly. Whacky Workbench: I hate this level there are springs EVERYWHERE and navigation is a pain in the♥♥♥♥♥♥ and by the way does anyone agree that the colour palet for this game is a bit OTT? Stardust Speedway, oh by they really over did it here. Its like starlight zone but with springs everywere and trust me you will get dizzy. You think after taking doen metal sonic the game would end but no theres one more stage. Metalic Maddness: Eggmans personal base and its not all that hard just long. Well if you dont like time traverling you can try andother method. By getting 50 rings and jumping into the goal ring like sonic 1 your transported to the special stage where you control sonic is sorta-full 3d and destroy some UFO's. Destroy them all and you get a time stone. collect them all you are garrentied the good ending so no need for timetraverling. Thr bosses are a lot more gimiky now like you have to destroy bubbles to get to eggman and you have to race metal sonic to the end with eggman on your tail with a instent kill lazer. I like the boss concepts.
In terms of looks it shows off what the Mega CD was capable of with vibrate colours and textures but as i mentioned before they overdid it on the colour palet which makes the stages look a bit too OTT. The soundtrack acctally differs wether u live in the US or JP/EU but thanks to christian whitehead you can now choose which soundtrack you want to play. each version is awesome and id say they are about equal in terms of greattness. You can also unlok tails in this version with the ability to fly and all.
So overall Sonic CD (well the rerelase) is a pretty awesome game but it does have its share of problems. For one the stages can be quite short and most should only take u about a minuite or so to complete and the game is full to the brim with springs. The amout of springs in theis game is jsut as worseas the amout of speed boosters in sonic 4! But dispite these if you havcent tried out Sonic CD I recomend triing it out, its a solid game from a solid developer.
SCORE: 8/10
PROS:
Super Peel Out
Boss Concepts
Fantastic Music
CONS:
Too Many Springs
OTT Colour Pallette

Pros:
- Looks pretty bearing in mind how old it is.
- Great OST, choice of US and JP version with some nightmare inducing songs in the US version.
- Good variety of levels.
- Level design is sometimes good.
- New super peel out mechanic means you can go faster than just spindashing which is pretty useful.
- Special stages in 3D which actually handle pretty well.
Cons:
- Some of the levels are terribly designed e.g. wacky workbench, where it is near impossible to build up speed and you feel like the entire level is actively trying to stop you from getting anywhere.
- Pointless time travel mechanic where you have to find a sign to go to the past, pass through it, and gain a good speed for about 10 seconds which is VERY hard in some levels unless they have areas designed for you to do this. You travel to the past and have to explore the entire level (bearing in the 10 minute time limit) to find some objects to blow up so you can get a good ending. Hard when past signs are rarer than future signs and half the time you end up accidentally going to the future because you can't slow down, which has no real benefit other than a lack of enemies when you clear out the objects in the past. You have to do all this crap to get a good ending for each level, although I heard you can just do it the old fashioned way, getting enough rings and doing the special stage at the end of each level.
- Some bosses are pretty badly designed or a massive pain to beat, like the pinball boss.

This is a very thoughtful, fully-realized game world where I want to spend time. The main reason is Chris Jones' stellar sense of humor, and his interactions with other cast members.
The game play is point-and-click, and there are puzzles with various levels of difficulty. I was pretty pleased with myself for figuring out the one where you have to activate the six power points. Nice little thrill there, after experiencing a a few minutes of despair looking at a seemingly-unsolvable puzzle. The only puzzle I skipped was the slidey puzzle over the fireplace. I guess it was late and I didn't feel like exerting my brain much. The hint system here is simplified. I kind of liked the old hints/points system better, but that's a fairly minor nit to pick.
There is a good deal of exploring to do as well. I had more than a little bit of trepidation willfully walking into a big maze, following some kind of giant spider. But I was rewarded for my bravery (after dying a few times).
It was a treat to see Todd Bridges from Diff'rent Strokes in here (and now I'm showing my age). Also, June freaking Lockhart. There are a bunch of great character actors that will have you thinking, there's a familiar face. It was fun to look at the cast on IMDB. My favorite character beside Tex would have to be the mutant Louie Lamintz, who in real life is a lawyer practicing in Utah! Brilliant, just brilliant. Really enjoyed the acting bits. The only one that somehow seemed a bit wooden was Holly, but hey, she's a hologram, what do you expect? And I don't want to hear from you hologram activists!
The "paths" hinge on your romantic interests. I haven't seen all the endings. I elected to stay true to Chelsee the first time through. Anyway, some of those scenes are a touch cheesy, not necessarily in a bad way, but I always kind of got a kick out of Tex getting rebuffed at every turn in the previous games. He seems to have somewhat better luck here, although it's sort of important to the story. And there is a double-slap moment that's pretty good. So I'm more than satisfied with this aspect.

The game description invokes some big names, but let's establish one thing right away: This is not a game that follows in the footsteps of games like Ikaruga or Radiant Silvergun; the production values on display and certain design decisions keep Star Saviors from that epic tier level of shmups. Fortunately, Star Saviors has a lot of things going for it that make it absolutely worth playing, particularly if you're new or not so skilled at shmup/bullet hell games.
A major talking point is the price. It's very low for a game with as much content and competence on display here, and in a way I almost feel like the price sends a message that the game is crappier than it is. However, there's a very noticable low-poly almost amateur level to the character models and story presentation, but in a shmup game this isn't of importance and it's bizarre how much the story is pushed by the developers considering their study of the "shmup greats".
But enough of all that, you say, how does it play? For a one dollar game, pretty damn well. I jacked it up to 1440p and blazed ahead at 120 fps, with smooth movement and easy dodging using a Dualshock 4. Games like Ikaruga have a certain elegance to the way the enemies approach and attack you, and in many ways a perfect run of a shmup like that is a beautifully coreographed dance between the player and the AI. In Star Saviors' case many enemies just come at you without an identifiable pattern, but it's clear a lot of throught and time was put into making sure that it felt good to shoot the enemies and to have bullet patterns that are always dodgable.
As a veteran of this genre, I thought the game was quite easy at first. The ships have a shield that can take a hit before you start losing "hull damage", meaning that you can fail to dodge quite a bit before losing a life. If you are a veteran, however, Star Saviors has multiple difficulty modes and customizations to tailor the experience to you. To be clear: You can approach this game at any skill level with the genre and have a good time, with veterans missing some more advanced systems and newbies able to ease themselves into the genre using this game without being overwhelmed at the start.
Ikaruga has a brilliant chaining system with the color changing, Radiant Silvergun had a massive variety of attacks on one ship as well as chaining based on the colors of the enemies. Sine Mora has a beautiful presentation of it's story and art design. Star Saviors does not meet any of the lofty levels of these greats, but the price is an unaviodable factor that makes it much easier to accept the things it does do right. If you love this genre and play it to death, a buck towards these devs might help to allow them to continue refining their craft and maybe realize their dream of releasing an epic-tier shmup. You'll have a good time regardless on the higher levels, and the RPG-like ship customizations after each story level offers a nice change of pace. If anyone has made it this far and has an interest in the genre, but might feel intimidated by the often high level of difficulty and skill required - this is absolutely your excellent starting point and the price couldn't be easier to swallow to see if these kind of games can be for you. If it turns out that they are, do realize that there's a next level and proceed to move on to more pricey but higher quality titles like Astebreed, Ikaruga, Radiant Silvergun, and any game made by Cave.
Star Saviors may not reach the high goals set by the titles it aspires to, but it's amazing that a $1 title can even make an honest attempt at that level. I recommend it to anyone who's curious or even anyone who enjoys arcade space shooters. I'd say the amount of words and time I've spent even talking about a game at this price level should say a lot.

On top of that there are tons of cosmetic items which you can buy with money EARNED THROUGH THE GAME to increase your immersion at no real expense.
For me the best thing about ToL is the community. As it is a social deduction game by far the most important enjoyment factor is the players around you - how your team mates act, how toxic they are. The Mods and Devs work tirelessly to get rid of any trolls or toxic players (which are normally few and far between) which can be evidenced by the vast amount of salty reviews from trolls who have been banned :D. The Discord server is a great friendly place, and the Imperium42 forum is so friendly to the point that I am suspecting everyone else may be NPC's.
All in all 100% worth the 10 quid and will guarantee hours of gameplay.

It's hard for me to review this game because I don't really know what to compare it to.
My best attempt to categorize it is to call it a PVP version of Papers, Please, but with a fantasy setting. I don't think it's a very good description, but it's the best I've got.
The game is very fun, especially for the low price, and it has (at time of writing) quick queues for matches and a good community. Each match is pretty much always fun, and it only gets better once you get familiar with the rules and mechanics. Graphics are unimportant for this type of game, and I appreciate being able to run it on pretty much any computer that isn't more than a decade old.
Only issue that I can think of is that every patch so far has changed the rules a bit. Always read the patch notes. Developers are clearly trying to find the right balance for a few mechanics, and that's a good thing, but in a game with such emphasis on knowing the mechanics, a sudden change in mechanics can be very disorienting.
The only suggestions I have are that I would like to see enduring statistics for individuals. I don't want anything public, necessarily, but I'd like to know how many times I've won while playing the Prince, etc.
And maybe consider putting the King in slot 1 on roster by default. Sometimes feels like whoever's #1 in a game is thrown under the bus by their prominent placement. Since there's always a King, I'd think the King would go in that most prominent position by default. Of course, #16 is also marked out, but not as much as #1 is, I think.
Also, the Physician having to choose between healing and exhuming puts him at a great disadvantage, so much so that it's rare to see anyone use Exhume to great effect. I think if Exhume were a daytime ability (I know graverobbing is not a broad-daylight activity, but bear with me) it would make Physician preferable to the Alchemist for some people, and would also keep the Physicians from being too bored in the daytime (where they presently have no abilities and generally no reason to engage the other players).
Other than that, I have no suggestions. One of the best I've played in a long time.

All obvious, though Wits is to speed up your search time and find more items.
You get to set up a new location for home base, set up outposts to help survivors that wonder get back home and there are many different resources. The main resources being Food, Ammo and Medicine whilst the two others are Petrol and Building supplies which can be used to help improve your homebase. Building watch towers, libraries, bunkers, storage areas, medical centre and so on. All these give different boons and improvements to your stats.
You also get many new missions to help improve the survivor's Moral. Not only yours, but of others that appear around the area with many chocies slightly altering the game world. The ending is a little flat, but I'm more than interested in buying a DLC for this game and see where it leads from there. A must sell for anyone who loves the zombie apocolypse genre and wants to play one with not only decent combat, but also survival mechanic that's not too detailed either.
However there are glaring issues. When you find supplies and leave them for later you can't remotly get other survivors to get them later. You can only do that whilst in the house. You are unable to dump the supplies you find in the boot or back of a car, which would make long-distance scavenging easier and not a endles chore. The ending is rarther bland as it could've been far more interesting taking this game on the road and developing a better plot, like finding what caused the zombies.
Survivors do not accompany you unless part of a mission or you invite them along which costs 100 influence. When they do accompany you, you can't ask them to pick up supplies to carry for you or any other items. There is also no "luxery Item" thing either which could've been used, like in Dead State, to help raise moral and keep people in a positive mindset, despite this being a end of the world kind of deal.
All in all, not the best game in the world, but it's worth a look if you're into the whole zombie apocolypse thing and you'd like to see it done with some time and resource management in it.

Among the original Sonic games this is the one I find myself returning to the most. The art and music of this game is, in my view, the pinnacle of the original Sonic series. Not only does each stage have three iterations of its music - there are two different soundtracks to choose from (JP is best). Each level presents a good balance between brevity and intricacy, and are a pleasure to go through on subsequent playthroughs.
The time travel mechanic is somewhat awkward to execute, but allows for a multitude of interesting level designs and overall replayability. This aspect of the game is also completely optional. Sonic CD also features one of the more interesting special stage modes, although the faux 3D style is a small step down in terms of visual presentation.
This game does have the usual minor shortcomings found in the series. The bosses are creative, but generally too easy to beat. Most zones present little challenge to get through, although wacky workbench is perhaps the most irritating stage in history. I would say it is a shame this game doesn't seem to have the recognition the mainline sonic games have enjoyed. Updated features and achievements definitely make this one of the best Sonic games to get on Steam. I recommend this game.

Sonic CD is one of my less favourite classic Sonic games - the level design is the main problem as the game encourages you to go fast (especially with the time travel element), yet punishes you for going fast by having a spike wall right in front of you or something similar. There is often no clear path forward as springs just send you back and the stage having multiple floors just confuse matters. At times the screen is too hard to discern objects from the backgrounds simply because the artists went a bit overboard. Powerup placement is a bit questionable - for example near the first boss is an invincibility box which means there's zero risk of dying.
And yet it's really hard to hate this game. It is ultimately a game that was designed with a lot of love and feels more like a sequel to the first game than Sonic 2 did. For all its faults, it still has a great aesthetic and feels more like a Sonic game than anything in the last 10 years does. The graphics were great at the time and still look good today and the soundtrack holds up just as well.
This version has a nice selection of options including various screen resolutions (including a windowed mode), a few extras, four save slots and achievements. It's pretty good value for money and if you can get it on sale, you're more than likely to get your money's worth out of it. If you played the original Sega CD/Mega CD version it's much the same and you're mostly buying it for the convenience of having it in your Steam library (which is why I've only got about 20 minutes of game time as I write this review), but these other features add to it, too.

THIS GAME IS SO MUCH FUN. Entertaining, irreverent, hilarious -- a total joy to play. I haven't had this much fun with a game since I was a kid. I love it.

All in all, it's a really enjoyable RPG experience that every fan of the genre should give it a try. More specifically, I felt like the combat of the game is one of its strong points since it runs smoothly and offers great variety in its playstyles. The player is not limited to a specific "vocation" (class) as it can be easily changed and unlock access to a whole new array of skills and different weapon types. The skills are quite varied and make for interesting combinations, though you have to choose only three at a time. You can dodge with the daggers, block with a shield and all in all the mecchanics work really well. Your pawns (companions) can make the difference in the battlefield since they provide assistance and actively engage enemies or at least draw them away from you.
When it comes to customization I was exceptionally pleased as the player is offered with many options in character creation and you can even change the voice, skin color, makeup and hairstyle (plethora of choices) at a barber shop as many times as you like during the game. The armor sets were plenty and diverse. You get your standard protective armor, some special items with peculiar shapes and forms and even the less protective, though definitely aesthetically pleasing pieces like lingerie and revealing robes.
As far as the story goes, it's not anything impressive and at times can be perplexing with the whole pawn-arisen concept. You get the big bad dragon who threatens to destroy everything and you need to stop him (or not). The setting is, as expected, medieval and everyone calls you "ser" even if you play as female. They tend to speak in a more refined and unnatural way like they're constantly trying to find exquisite synonyms for words (maybe a "side effect" from the japanese translation).
My biggest flaw of this game is definitely the save system. It's plain frustrating that an rpg game doesn't let you keep multiple saves so that you can try different outcomes or simply to return to an earlier stage. Not only that but it doesn't even have a proper "load" function since if you wish to load your saved game you need to exit to the main menu! Others rightfully complain about the travel system as well, since there is no fast-travel like Skyrim but that can be dealt with an "eternal ferrystone". Another slightly bothersome point is your "beloved", who basically serves the role of your love partner. Thing is that the system determing him/her functions in a weird way and you can easily end up with the wrong person (happenned to me), who, unfortunately, plays a pivotal role in the story.
So, apart from the "save" issue, I thoroughly enjoyed the game and I'll definitely give it another go (New Game+), since you can basically keep going till you drop :)

I bought this game on sale and played it purely because of Mass Effect 2's Metacritic score. 100 hours later, I'm onto my fourth playthrough of the trilogy. Though the combat can feel clunky and outdated at times, the story progression more than makes up for mechanical flaws.
My two main criticisms of this game:
1. Traveling takes an eternity. Vehicle portions are supposed to give you a sense of the size and scope of the world, but end up wasting your time as you drive past stretches of empty land. The fetch quests on uncharted worlds are also fairly annoying, and don't give much of a reward.
2. Inventory management is a real pain. If you've played other RPGs before you'll know what I mean. You pick up all the stuff you come across out of habit, only to realize that 90% of it is worse than your current best weapon or otherwise unusable. When you have to juggle the inventories of six squadmates as well, it can become a chore rather than the usual joy of customization.
Other than that, if you pick up this game during a sale, you won't regret your experience. Mass Effect 2 eliminates my two previous criticisms as well, making it another worthwhile purchase if you have the time and funds.

Mass Effect can be surprising. You start the game, expecting just another RPG in space. You're quickly pulled in by the story and the characters. You then start to have stakes into how your character (your own Shepard, with her/his own choices) models the universe around.
Mass Effect is now a game with dated graphics, with at times dubious game design choices. But this game is able to strike such an emotional cord within yourself that you can excuse it for almost anything it pulls you through (except these times exploring with the Mako over high terrain... You'll want to have a one-on-one with the designer of this part before long.) But the whole trilogy is so great, you should really take the time to make it through the first game.
Then you start playing the rest of the trilogy. Maybe even several times.
The relationships are great, and taken over the whole franchise, they will make you find the same sweet spots for these characters as Firefly was able to do in TV series.

Strike Vector is a fast paced, balanced shooter that is non-forgiving and goes beyond the limits of what is humanly possible. Strap on a tank of NOS to a Formula One car and tell it to fly. Now set that beast loose in a china shop. That is Strike Vector.
Thankfully you have the ability to slow down the pace by transforming into harrier mode which allows you to maneuver on a dime or act as a mobile turret platform with the ability to take precision shots at your enemy.
First impressions: you will absolutely hate this game. You will be beaten to a pulp championing the bottom of the brackets yelling bloody murder at the screen as your eyes are unable to process the visuals. The trick is to think of the harrier mode as an extension of your body and to incorporate it into every aspect of your gameplay. Next, find a weapon system that complements your play style. Going to camp? Use the plasma rail. Looking to chase non-stop? Use the gatling cannons. Looking for a happy medium? Use the rocket pods.
The celling of the game is set stupid high by the ridiculous use of speed. You NEED to bring the game down to reality by playing at a level that is comfortable for you. Until you find your niche you will be disappointed in yourself and put blame on the game as an excuse for your incompetence.
CTF is awesome; TDM is an absolute adrenalin rush.
Everyone stands on the same footing. There is no auto-aim, auto health regen or unlockable weapons. The game is pure skill and very reminiscent of gameplay mechanics found in old school shooters such as those found in the Quake generation.
Give this game the time that is deserves and you will find it extremely entertaining and rewarding.

I came into this game, not knowing what to expect at all. I had bought just another Humble Bundle, and this game happened to be in there. I selected one of the titles which had a pretty interesting name. Tesla Effect: A Tex Murphy Adventure.

When examaning a wall in this game, at one point Tex says "Is this the fourth wall? Because I don't want to break it." It's just plain hilarious, and yet interesting. I love point-and-click adventures, and this takes it a step further.
At first however, I was not at all impressed with the quality of the game. I loved the dialogue, but the acting and whatnot from pretty much any actor other than Tex, felt out of place. However, the story was intruiging enough to keep me playing, and I gotta say, it was worth it. After a while I got accustomed and didn't even mind the acting; here and there it's bad, sure, but it's got it's own vibe.
This game is so refreshing from any other game I've played. I would absolutely recommend you checking this game out. You won't regret it.

Of note : I only recommend this game for the people who loved the old point&click adventures of the 1990s.
This game has a lot to love for the old farts of us who played the old P&Cs.  The same branching dialogues, the same silly puzzles that usually aren't difficult, and the same questionable logic which determines which random objects go together to make functional objects to solve problems.
Pros:
~ The 4K camera work looks great.  The quality of the FMV portions look fantastic.
~ Cheezy dialogue and acting.  It's a YMMV thing, but I love it.
~ For those who have followed Tex through his recent adventures in the Pandora Directive and the Tex Murphy Radio Saga, it attempts to tie up all the loose ends and explain what has all happened.  It's a pretty well written story.
~ Multiple endings based on dialogue decisions, and while some are better than others, Sapphyre's is great.
~ The game is legitimately funny.
~ All digital, so NO DISC SWAPPING HALLELUJAH!
~ Tons of references to the earlier games, especially Under a Killing Moon.
Cons:
~ The puzzles aren't really as difficult as you would think.  And the game follows a fairly predictable thread of 1.) Talk to people on the street 2.) Find items needed to get into a place  3.) Find items in place, and solve puzzles, 4.) Rinse, Lather, Repeat.
~ The camera work is great, but the in game 3D world looks like it came right out of 2003, in a not good way.  The world is much more open than previous games, and there aren't the frequent, epic length loading screens, or disc swapping THANK GOD.
~ If you didn't play the earlier Tex Murphy games, especially Overseer and Pandora Directive, it may be difficult to grasp the story.  Under A Killing Moon is suggested, because it's the best, but doesn't contribute as much to the story.
Ultimately, if you're an oldschool Tex Murphy player, a fan of Point & Click games, interactive movies, or like comedies with a film noir setting, you may love this game.  If you're not into those, you could probably pass on it.

Pillars of Eternity is a good CRPG that feels held back by a bland story and combat that gets easier and tactically simplier as the game progresses. There is plenty of content to explore (including a personal castle to upgrade and a deep dungeon to explore for fancy loot, room for actual roleplaying with extensive dialogue options, and unique classes that alone are enough to make me want to replay the game) but the majority of it is too similar to previous games in the genre to really stand out on its own. While I love Obsidian, this repurposing of old ideas and design choices just doesn't feel like the dream project it was supposed to be.
PoE gives you plenty of important decisions to make and lets you know every chance it can that these decisions matter. However, one very important sequence of events near the halfway point in the game in particular stood out in breaking that illusion. At one point you reach a crossroads between two factions, one of which you previously sided with. Various speech options let you continue to side with them or roleplay other options. However, the Big Bad shows his face and spits on your decisions, making your previous questing and choices moot. It is very frustrating to play through because you're just stuck there watching it play out with no input on what is happening, only to suffer the consequences later. Something more cryptic happening off-screen during these events would've been better writing and would've had the same effect without being so frustrating to play through.
The end boss also feels very contrived and added for the sake of having a last boss for a video game. Most of the game you're chasing him and always 2 steps behind him and yet in this last bastion he decides to face you face-to-face. I feel like he was supposed to be an Irenecus clone but he comes off feeling whiny and shoehorned. I would've really preferred pushing him and the "twist" leading up to the final area into a sequel or expansion because it really detracts from the rest of the game.
While I enjoyed my time with PoE, I find it hard to recommend. Overall, it felt quite bland and dry compared to CRPGs of old with only the few unique classes and the deep character interactions really standing out to me. If you've played CRPGs before and are on the fence about this, try a pillar of the genre such as Baldur's Gate 2 or Icewind Dale before dropping cash on this.

The single player isn't bad and I've played a few missions of it to learn about the game's different unit types. However the game really shines in multiplayer. Tooth and Tail's random map generation actually works nicely, allowing players to get an advantage by scouting the map and adapting to whatever terrain is available. The strategy and tactics used in multiplayer are similar to those used in something like Starcraft, but you don't have to mash the keyboard at 400 actions per minute just in order to be competitive. There's still plenty of nuance about how the different units interact and you can still micro-manage your army in a meaningful way. The game is awesome and if you like 1v1 RTS it's easy to recommend.

There's a lot to love about this game. It has a fantastic score, great art, and some really cool lore and atmosphere. The final mission design is really neat and innovative in a way I've rarely seen in strategy games. It tries to bring the RTS genre, one of my personal favourites, to a wider audience.
But it just wasn't fun or rewarding to play, at all. It's distressingly far from being fun.
Now I knew that this wasn't going to be a typical RTS, so I tried to temper my expectations. And for the first hour or so, I thought it was kinda neat. But very quickly, playing each new level became an exercise in grinding frustration. I think a lot of it comes down to this: Tooth and Tail tries so, so hard to "distill" the real-time strategy game experience that it ends up making compromises that just don't work.
The key conceit of the game is that this is an RTS where your character does everything your mouse cursor would in another RTS - command units, plant buildings, claim resources, etc. This makes the game playable on a gamepad. It also means that you can't divide your attention across the map, even for scouting purposes. You can scout, or command attacks, or build, or claim resources, but you can never multitask. And unless you're returning to your existing base, you can never switch your visual focus instantly to another part of the map.
Imagine playing an RTS game where you need to use the WASD keys to slowly pan your camera around the map instead of clicking on a minimap, and you can only interact with things in the exact centre of the screen. And you can't pan the camera over forests or cliffs. Oh, and also, weather and terrain effects slow your camera down too. Fun, right?
This might not be such an issue if the fundamental scenarios you're playing through weren't designed in the spirit of the RTS genre. You're still getting attacked on multiple fronts often by multiple enemies. You still need to juggle production in your home base with commanding troops on the front. But shifting your attention between different points of focus is glacially slow, you effectively can't divide your forces to engage on multiple fronts (you can issue orders to specific classes of units, but even then all units of that type are affected), and the gameplay is paced so frenetically that tiny errors or miscalculation spell doom.
That's not to mention the fact that your production buildings eat resources automatically to produce units on a timer, so you can't prioritize production orders once you've got your facilities up and running, meaning the more you build the less control you have over what actually gets made.
I'm sure this game will be fun for some people, and clearly a lot of hard work went into making it. But as an avid fan of most RTS games, I went from being kind of interested to hating the gameplay within the span of a few hours, and I'm not entirely sure forcing myself through the whole campaign was worth it.
Damn good music, though. Go check out the soundtrack if nothing else - Austin Wintory is a master in the space.

Tooth and Tail is a fine example of how to produce a game loaded with atmosphere, which is truly rare nowadays. There are little details thrown in that really add to the setting, such as the voice acting, ruined buildings, bits of chitchat between characters, and unit descriptions. Tooth and Tail is essentially An American Tail meets Russian Revolution meets Hannibal Lector. None of the animals want to eat plants, as that's deemed "uncivilized" - except for the pigs, who farm grain and end up on the dinner plate as a result. "Civilized" animals - according to the Civilized faith themselves - eat meat and only meat, treating fruit and such as less than famine food. In the end, it's all about who gets to eat the meat and who gets to be the meat.
As of writing this, I still can't get past the seventh (or eighth?) storyline mission but that doesn't matter to me. You can play against the AI in one-off battles and other players, if you wish. The focus on units is natural, given that your only resource in the game is meat and that inevitably runs out in good time. The only limit to what kind of units and structures you can have is the amount of meat you have. There are three tiers of five units each and the simplicity of their design belies an insane degree of complexity in how they can be utilized. I can't recommend this game enough... unless you lop off an unwante dlimb and/or organ and let me eat it.

The best way to describe Way of the Samurai 4 is to call a choose-your-own-adventure game. Your character is a voiceless blank slate whose personality never changes but the choices you make in the game effect other characters and the state of the world. Certain locations will change, characters will become enemies or allies and your end-goal will change. Within the game is an Event Tracker in which you can see that various story paths and branches you can take.
There are also a vast amount of customization options for your samurai. Gender, clothing, accessories, swords, styles, you can customize every bit of it. Accessories can be manipulated in any way and can appears/disappear when your sword is sheathed or you are wielding it. Likewise, you can collect sword parts and design one according to your tastes and as you master different moves, you can create your own style using your favorite movesets you've mastered over the course of your playthroughs.
The graphics are servicable. The character models and world are good enough to get you immersed but not enough to WOW you. The combat animations, however, are well-animated and are fun to execute. The combat, likewise, is servicable. It has enough depth to keep things interesting but not so much that it overwhelms novices and not enough to satisfy hardcore fighting fans.
Overall, it's a game that can be easily picked up and played. The writing is light-hearted and quirky so it's very easy to get invested in the characters and world and most play-throughs last a couple of hours. You can skip all the storylines entirely and just focus on doing side missions to earn money to buy new clothes and upgrade your swords, or you can focus entirely on the plot. It's a gem of a title that'll entertain if you looking for a different kind of "open world" where your decisions change the flow of the story.

Way of the Samurai 4 may just be amongst the weirdest games I've played. While at first it looks serious, soon it becomes clear that the game is a huge joke, and is so in a positive way. That's not to say it's not fun, or not serious at times.
The gameplay itself can best be summed up as grindy. Combat relies on you beating up people to learn their moves, then beat up other people with those moves to get better at them. It takes a fair amount of time, and for the most part is pretty simple, with combat becoming difficult later on due to high health bars and instant kill moves. The swordplay itself is actually fun, with most of it making sense, even if the most efficient strategy I've found was to simply kick everyone.
There are a variety of side-quests and activities, ranging from forging your own swords out of the scraps of your enemies' to  seducing every major NPC in the game, and a few side-quests which further improve replayablility.
Replayability is a core aspect of this game, as it relies on a sort of New Game+, where you finish the story in only a few hours, then go back and play again, keeping all your items and most progress. This continues on and on, until at some point you can tackle the actual main storyline of the game.
The story is nothing too special, but it makes up for it with silly stereotypes and stupid gimmicks, as well as an interesting twist or two. There's 3 big storylines, as well as the actual "main" one which is unlocked further, and a variety of different events happening depending on your progress and choices in previous palythroughs, all neatly shown in a menu. It's definitely worth to paly through the game multiple times as you are expected, because that's when the game begins to get more interesting.
There also are a large variety of unlocks, from the ability to play a female character, to clothes, to the styles and outfits of major NPCs and the ability to play Hardmode. These can be purchased with currency gained upon completing a single playthrough.

The first 5 minutes of Hektor really draws you in. Straight away from the title screen to the excellent intro sequence and the very first dead end you realise things in this world are not always what they seem.
The game’s story is told through audio logs and much like the rest of the sound in the game these are excellent. While I am not usually a fan of this type of storytelling they are brilliantly voice acted and really make you care about the story and feel for the characters behind these notes. I would even go so far as to say these are the best audio logs I have come across.
The sound design is also wonderful and creepy and the mutterings and noises that accompany the main score are a key element of the games atmospheric success.
I finished the game in about 4 hours and while I enjoyed it I felt it could have been longer. The predator could have arrived earlier and been fleshed out a little more and I equally had a few unanswered questions related to the story.
While not perfect for a debut indie title Hektor is a fantastic horror game that I would easily recommend. At £14.99 the game is a little on the expensive side and I could imagine a slight price drop helping to persuade fence sitters. A unique experience that’s worth checking out and fun for all the family… well maybe not.

A meager 10 hours is not sufficient for me to claim to be a capable player in this game, but enough hours to ensure that Throne of Lies really is a fine game for fans of Hidden Role and Social Games. Tabletop games like Avalon and Battlestar Galactica are what introduced me to this genre and Throne of Lies really takes what they have to offer and ups the ante with various roles and ways to interact.
While the idea of the game is not anything new, its execution is delightful. The various roles take time to thoroughly learn and the social aspect of the game ensures that gameplay doesn't get dull quickly. The game is constantly updated (at least now, few weeks from the launch) and balance changes seem a delightfully important duty for the developers.
I have to give negative comments on the technical functionality. The UI is ugly, sometimes the game hangs when connecting to a game and joining the game as a group of friends is wonky at times. Especially for roles that have things to do on the first day and night the wonky connection can prove very annoying.
This aside, Throne of Lies has quite unique attraction to it. The simple presentation is immediately forgotten after the game starts and all player focus is aimed at the action itself. The technical problems will hopefully the ironed out and balance perfected. I wasn't sure if I should get this game at first, but I'm glad my friends decided for me.

I've been warned several times, but this one in particular irks me:
I'm priest, which is a very important class for the blue dragon. During the update I was playing priest it was particularly important not to put a mark on your back. Then, a psychic links me with the king. The king has a tendency to die d4 in about half of the games, so I didn't want myself on his logs. So I didn't claim. My argument ingame at the time was "king can be evil too.. lol" or something along those lines.
The next day the psychic puts me on the stand for this, rather then waiting for any of the ACTUAL investigative classes to check me. Furthermore, they don't wait for the prince to jail me (so I could have a chance to talk to him without the others knowing). They execute me for treason on the spot. I only had 30 seconds to sum up this argument, so I said something along the lines of "One of these days you'll learn king can be not bd". Not the greatest way to put my argument, but I was under time pressure you know?
All in all, not too upset about that much. It's a social game, and I really didn't think they were going to execute me D2. But low and behold the moderators issue me a warning for throwing the game. Firstly, we WON that game. Secondly, overbearing much?

Depending on who you ask, Sonic CD was the best Sonic game ever made. For me, it's difficult to pick the best between this, Sonic 2, or S3&K. They are all excellent and have their own strengths. Sonic CDs strengths are the audio quality thanks to being a Mega CD title, the level design, and the core mechanic of travelling through time, along with the Time Stones instead of the usual Chaos Emeralds.
On a technical level, the sound quality is superior to the Mega Drive Sonic games, however I feel that the tunes are just not as catchy or memorable as the BGM found on the cartridge games. Both the Japanese and Western soundtracks are included with this release on Steam, and while the consensus is that the Japanese soundtrack is great and the Western soundtrack not-so-great, I personally find them both to be rather hit and miss. Both soundtracks definitely have their 'This is a sweet track' and 'lolwtf' moments.
The controls are your standard classic Sonic, movement left, right, up and down, and a jump button. One improvement in this release is you can set the spin dash and peel out moves to work like Sonic 2, 3 and S&K. In those games the instant you let the direction go (down for spin dash, up for peel out) the move was executed. In the original Sonic CD game, there was a warm up period you had to go through before the move actually came out, which made them a bit clunky to use. The game works fine on keyboard, I have not tried with a controller but I'd assume it's fine with that too.
Graphics wise the display has been modified to fit either 16:9 or 16:10 aspect ratio correctly. There are also filters that can be turned on to soften and smooth out the image.
The level (or zone) design is the most colourful and chaotic of the classic Sonic games, with lots of pastel colours in the palette, and a level layout that utilises a lot of vertical space and many different routes to take to get to the end of a zone, making them both pleasing to the eye and lots of fun to play. Both the colour and layout of each zone change when Sonic travels through time, which brings us to the time travel mechanic that's unique to Sonic CD.
Sonic starts each zone in the present time. Scattered around each zone are sign posts that say either 'Past' or 'Future'. After touching one of these sign posts and running at full speed for a few seconds, Sonic will travel to either the past or future, depending on what was written on the last sign post he touched. Both past and future versions of a zone use a unique colour palette, as well as having different layouts. The past is more forgiving in that there are less badniks and obstacles like spikes about, however there are two different possible futures that Sonic can visit.
Initially travelling to a zones future will take Sonic to the zones 'bad future'. There are a lot of badniks roaming about, a lot of traps like spikes and crush traps, the colours are dark and drab, it's generally a very unwelcoming place to be. However, it doesn't have to be this way as Sonic is able to prevent these 'bad futures' by travelling to a zones past and destroying a badnik making machine. Each zone has one of these machines, they can also be found in the present and bad future time periods, but can only be destroyed in the past.
When one of these machines is destroyed, that zones future will become a 'good future'. It also kills all badnik robots in that zone. There are three zones that make up a 'Round'. The third zone of each round is always set in one of the two possible futures, and is where boss battles take place. When both zones one and two have good futures, the third zone is automatically a good future too. However if Sonic fails to make both zones one and two have good futures, the third zone will be set in a bad future.
Reaching the goal post at the end of a zone with 50 or more rings with allow you to access the special stage. It is in these special stages that Sonic can get the Time Stones. The special stages in Sonic CD play similar to Mario Kart on the SNES but in full screen. They are quite tricky to play, as it is difficult to judge distance due to the lack of depth perception of 2D sprite graphics. I can offer some advice with these special stages, you need to jump earlier that you think you do.
Part of the replay value of Sonic CD is trying to make every zone in the game have a good future. Another part is collecting all seven time stones. Like all classic Sonic games, you can beat the game without collecting any of these time stones or making any good futures, but you will not get the 'real ending'.
This is a great game for people who loved the old classic Sonic games and maybe missed out on this one back in the day, due to it being released on the ill fated Mega CD. It plays and looks great, features some of the most creative level design seen in the classic Sonic games, and features the debut of both Amy Rose and Metal Sonic. Tails is also available as a playable character (needs to be unlocked). I recommend this game.

This game comes so close to being one of my favorite games of all time but trips on it's shoe laces as it gets within 10 feet of the line.
In Dragon's Dogma you assume an unassuming individual of your creation who is left heartless by a dragon and you have to get your chest engine back. And ... save a Kingdom or something in the process?
The game is handled in a very interesting way, it combines a handful of genres/influences in a way that I throughly enjoyed... but kept throwing it's weaker bits in my face so much that it was hard to understand why none of the playtesters of the PC port/remaster... whatever this is didn't notice the flaws.
Combat... Combat... Combat.
The fighting in this game is great, it feels hack and slash but mixes in subtle strategy. The class system opens up to give you some nice customization in terms of gear and abilities as the game goes along. Being able to give your companions some semblance of personality through 'teaching' them behaviors was a system that should've been explored more. The most intersting part of combat is the Shadow of the Colossus style grapple you can do with larger monsters, even hang on when some of them take off. It gives a real sense of scale as well as despiration as you find yourself clinging to a monster to get that last bit of damage in before it takes off, or hanging on for dear life as you are swung around wildly and using the monster's weaknesses to set up power plays to stack on damage.
Nearly everything else
I say that both as an overexaggerative joke... but like... 40% serious.
The travel between places is a bit tedious, the fast travel system isn't exactly functional for a good portion of the game, and then when you get it, it's so disjointed from the paths you need to go back to you probably will roll your eyes and then run to said spots anyway.
Your comrade/pawns... *sigh* Is obnoxious to say the least. You can make an attempt to fix this by 'teaching' them to not talk as much, but you have little to no control over the pawns created by other characters. And often will find that you'll engage in combat only to have the same 3 lines shouted 3 times over and over again until the fight ends.
The story? ... If you can call it that. You show up, heart is stolen, you kill somethings, nonessential dialogue drowns a good portion of the actual story so i doubt you'll pay attention to what happens. You'll unknowingly push forward and find yourself at the climax of the story wondering what actually even happened.
All in all : 7.2/10
It sounds like this game is a mess but it's a surprisingly lovable mess. The annoyances are something you seem to grow numb to and it just becomes a case of: When is my next big monster fight? Obviously if the narrative was tighter and better written, characters and story more memorable, and the overworld quirks (faster travel and companion customization) were dusted off a bit better it'd be an AMAZING game but what it lacks there it makes up for in core quality. The cycle of fighting, exploring, fighting, getting gear, leveling your character and doing it all again is so fun that you forget about the other parts until you have to go back to town and run a few fetch quests that make you groan a bit.
Get it. It's well worth it, just be ready to sigh a few times through the game.

This game is one of my favorite games of all time and there is so much good to this game. The plot in the main story line is pretty good but still could be improved, but that is one of my only complaints about the actual game. The combat feels tense when you first go against something like a Cyclops or Chimera, but as you play and get stronger the fights become easier and easier as you learn what they do and how they react which is something that other games lack. Certain games will just improve old monsters for a new challenge making it dull and uninteresting, while this game will add entirely new creatures for that challenge. I will say that played ~1000 hours of this game on console, and there are still things I find that I haven't seen, but that probably is because I constantly made new characters. Speaking of characters, the character creation in this game is one of the best I have ever used with how detailed you can make a character. You can edit your characters to precisely what you want them to be, whether it is a silly looking one, a badass looking one, or one that you think fits your playstyle. And what I love about this character creation is how some of your stats are dictated by your physical looks, so a large muscular one can carry more than a tiny weak one. The class system is also one of the best because it allows you to experiment with what you like and what is best fitting for your character without having to create a new one each time. The only game that does this better is Skyrim, which has in my opinion the best way of ranking abilities up. Many would call this a Skyrim and Shadow of Collosus rip off, but it is neither of those, It in itself is an amazing game and is polished to an edge, and while there are similar mechanics to both of those games it is not copy paste at all. I love the pawn system in this game because of how it allows you to see what other people have done that make their characters who they are and can help new players with what to do. My only complaint/peeve is how lazy people will just use a pawn and rate it without actually saying how they did, or just keeping their pawns in an outfit from the storage and never changing it (WHY CAN"T YOU SPEND SOME TIME TO MAKE A CHARACTER AND NOT JUST A USLELESS TOOL!?). But this is just lazy people's way of doing things and has nothing to do with the game itself. If I had to rate this game I would give it a 99/100 as it is almost the perfect game in my opinion.

- General knowledge: there is a tremendous amount of hidden and not obvious stuff that influences your gameplay e.g. at character creation your weight and height influence how easily knocked down you can be and how your stamina is drained, how cool is that? A ton of other stuff in terms of gearing and character progression  -- get ready to read the Wiki a lot if you want to get good, but not required for a casual playthrough.
- Combat is a combination of Monster Hunter Tri,  Dark Souls (fun and kid version of Dark Soulds I'd say) and Shadow of the Colossus. Having played The Witcher, Dragon Age and other RPG series I can confidently say Dragon's Dogma leaves all these games in the dust, and it came out in 2012! Just superb.
- World is immersive and I felt sucked in by it. It felt so polished and what stood out for me is the lantern and day/night cycle. Bring a lantern if you go outside when it's dark!
Is it worth the 30 EUR price? YES! For me this is almost a must have if you're an RPG fan. But, it's often on sale, so I'd wait till then.

Graphics:  Colorful, enjoyable, not top of the line, but to be honest, that isn't the appeal of the game regardless.
Gameplay: Utterly Horrific.  Even with a Controller, it's the weakest part of the entire game.  Combat is boring, grindy, and for a game which you face multiple enemies they do not even offer a proper way to switch between targets.   It's pretty much a Fighting Game with solo fights among groups of many with a Dynasty Warrior style power attack that allows you to wreck an entire group when needed.  Gets boring quick.
Story: Not to bad, the concept is sound, presentation isn't exactly that impressive though.  You have around ten different possible endings with different branches that can take you two those endings.  So definitely has variety in story going for it.  Counting on your choices you can literally play the game a few dozen times and still get something originality out of it.    Best part of the game really.  If you like Tell Tale games, I can promise you would likely at least enjoy this game for that.
Characters:  Definition of Stereotypes across the board, and some of the worst character design I can imagine at times.   They feel like a poorly conceived anime.  Presentation of characters is so bad that it is almost embarrassing, the villains are pure cartoon villains with no illusion that they're villains for example.
Playability:   It isn't the most stable game.  I've encountered a few Crashes, but nothing to really complain about.  Playing the game itself it's a nightmare at times.  Mountains of Menus for literally everything you do often.  Combine that with the boring combat in the game, it can get quite tedious.    Over all the entire game itself is tedious.  If you want to make a good sword you have to grind tediously, if you want to max your combat skills in a specific martial art, you have to grind tediously, if you want to make enough points to unlock everything you have to grind tediously.  Grind, Grind, Grind and more Grind.  For a game with so many different endings/possibility in the story they though it was necessary to throw tedious grind into a game that really didn't even need it to begin with to boost what might be 20-30 hours of content into 50-100 hours of all grind.   Something that did nothing but hurt the game honestly.
In conclusion.  I like the game about as much as I hate it.  I had some enjoyable moments, even some laughs at some of the story and cutscenes.  Other times I wanted to literally bite one of my fingers off to keep myself from screaming at utterly horrible experiences I encountered.   Being I do not to give this game a "Negative" score, as that would emply it is a bad game, which to be honest, I think it is not a bad game, just not a good game either, it's kind of in between.  I really do not want to recommend it to anyone.  I think I will continue playing it just to say I've unlocked everything, but the grindy aspect of the game means I can only do that in short burst.
