Splinter Cell Blacklist is the best Splinter Cell effort since Chaos Theory, and one of the best pure stealth games I've played in years.
Traversal is a dream. Sam moves fluidly and intuitively. You feel like a cat prowling around these levels, stalking enemies, and darting quickly to and fro outside their paths of patrol. Sam Fisher's hand to hand takedowns are superbly satisfying, particularly the deadly variants with his karambit knife. The choreography there is spectacular, and unlike some stealth games such as Human Revolution, the takedowns never get old. The game is also designed in a way that rewards you for your playstyle, no matter how decide to play. Want to play ghostly, never touching enemies, and never leaving a trace? Me, too! You get a lot points for that, which you can use to unlock better gear and weapons. Want to take down every single enemy you come across, alternating between fighting, popping off a couple of shots, then throwing down a smoke grenade and disappearing into the shadows? They give you quite a few points for that, too. Want to just go balls out and play the game like you're John Rambo, throwing incendiary grenades and fire an unsilenced heavy gun? Totally viable way to play the game, and, yup: They give you a boatload of points for that, too. This game has succeeded in allowing the player to drift between full stealth and action shooting in a way that many stealth games have tried over the past couple of decades, but few have succeeded in doing. It does exceptionally well at allowing you to play the game the way you want, and seamlessly transitioning between different styles. I's an amazing accomplishment, and it's the biggest reason why this is such a good game.
The replayability I touched on is another asset of the game. Sam Fisher is so customizable that this game could also be described as having RPG features. You can customize all of his gear and weapons to help him better perform either at stealth or combat. You receive money for accomplishing things like takedowns or disappearing after alerting enemies, and then use the money to purchase pants, better goggles, better guns, and more. It does more to allow you to play the game the way you like, and that's something I can always get behind, especially from a company as typically reprehensible to consumers as Ubisoft generally is. It also creates a ton of replayability and does a lot to keep you coming around. Just look at my stats: I've put 60+ hours into this game and have replayed it several times. That's more than I've put into any Splinter Cell game since Chaos Theory.
A big part of the success here is how bad♥♥♥♥♥you feel while playing the game. I mentioned how strong the hand-to-hand takedowns are, which is a big part of it. Another is the mark and execute feature that's been carried over from Conviction, which I absolutely adore. It functions in this game as an excellent "Oh,♥♥♥♥♥♥quot; tool to use if you're about to be spotted by an enemy. Check out the surroundings, mark the enemies, and commence sneaking. Take a wrong turn and get spotted? Hit the button and Sam instantly takes out anybody within range that you've marked, bailing your dumb♥♥♥♥♥out and giving you another shot to keep sneaking. It's a great way to incorporate a kind of undo button into a genre as unforgiving as stealth. I'm not sure whether the developers purposely intended for the feature to be used in this fashion, but it works great, especially considering that you can now use mark and execute at extremely long range when equipped with sniper rifles, which is a neat feature.
I've played several Ubisoft games the past few years, and none have run very well aside from the Far Cry series. This game, happily, runs like a dream. It looks great, too. Textures are excellent, and motion capture for the actors is terrific. I do think the game loses quite a bit without Michael Ironside, though, and I question why Ubi even deigned to put Sam Fisher in the game to begin with. The justification was that they needed a younger actor to do the motion capture, which is understandable. But Sam has to be in his late 50s by this point. Why not just reboot with another character altogether, and relegate Sam to the Lambert role of the older games? Ironside is an excellent voice actor, and the series is worse off without him.
Anybody who has read my reviews in the past knows that I have a big problem with checkpointing in stealth games. There's nothing more frustrating than sneaking through nine tenths of an area, getting caught at the very end, and dying, only to be put right back where you started and having to follow everything you just accomplished again. It's unbelievably frustrating, and it has no place in modern video games that could easily provide a free save feature. If you don't like save scumming, then don't do it. I don't. But not having free saves is a terrible design choice and it harms people who play the game on the hardest difficulty, which I frequently choose when playing stealth games. This game, sadly, does feature checkpointing, which is one of my few complaints about the game. However, the checkpoints are frequently very manageable, which does some mitigating to the repetitiveness caused by their presence. They are still annoying, though, and I have no idea why game designers continue to use them.
The story is another weak point with this game. It's your typical Call of Duty-esque American military story, with the gruff hero saving the world from the sneering villain. I thought Conviction actually had a really great story, but unfortunately this game doesn't continue what they shot for with that one. Gone is pretty much all of the Tom Clancy flavor out of the series that was present in the first three games. This is all Hollywood action movie, which is disappointing, but doesn't matter much in the long run since the game plays so fantastically.
I also found the music wanting. Chaos Theory had what I consider to be the best soundtrack in any video game, ever, and this game lacks Amon Tobin's stunningly beautiful score that that game featured. Tobin did such a great job with Conviction, despite having only two songs present in the game, that I would linger on that game's menu just to listen to the excellent menu track that he composed. The fabulous sound design in Conviction does not return, either, but it's manageable here. Seriously, Ubisoft, Amon Tobin is a god. Bring him back, please. We miss him.
Another complaint I've got are the stupid first person shooting segments of the game. I can see the value of using them to break up the pacing and add something different, but come on, people who buy Splinter Cell games buy them for stealth gameplay. If I wanted a shooter, I'd play Battlefield. I'd rather Splinter Cell sticks with its strengths.
The multiplayer and co-op features in this game are some of the strongest since Chaos Theory as well, and I'd be doing a disservice to the game if I didn't mention them. I don't play much competitively, but I had a blast with the co-operative segment of the game. I only wish it were a bit more meaty -- It's easy to blow through all of the co-operative levels in just a few hours.
Overall, you could do way worse than Splinter Cell Blacklist. If you're looking for a pure stealth experience, this is your game. It looks great, it runs great, and it plays great. It's got great replayability. The minor nitpicks I have with it do nothing to really damage the experience. This is a great game, and it's a promising return to form for the Splinter Cell franchise. If you're a fan of the stealth genre, you'll adore it. If you're not, it's still worth playing, as it's a solid game even when played just as a third person shooter with some stealth features.

Dispite this being the weakest game in the franchise, and a god awful boss fight, this game is still a great one.
Many people who played the other installments in the series would most likely not be happy with it, as it seems to get away from the pure stealth aspect and instead offers players a wide variety of ways to get past certain situations, appealing to more people depending on how they chose to play, and based off of the situation.
Running and gunning is possible, but is very difficult as even on normal difficulty you die in just a few hits, so stealth is highly encouraged, but not mandatory, a feature in games that I greatly appreciate.
Overall, Splinter Cell Blacklist is a fun game, it may not stick true to it's roots, and has occasional bugs (lighting, enemy AI occasionally being pants on head ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥,) and the absolutly terrible boss fight, but it's still a great game, and worth a play.
TLDNR: 7/10 Would recommend.

Even in the very first missions, this game proves that procedural generation and RNG have to be actually well thought out in order to be good.
Every mission in this game is randomly generated, including the story missions - only the mission goals (and conditions) are predetermined.
It is entirely possible that a mission simply cannot be fulfilled (especially with the bonus goals) if the level was generated in a way that gives you only one path through enemies defenses, places you miles apart from you ally, etc.
If you're lucky, a mission will be doable, if you are not, you will restart until you get lucky.
In most cases, the main mission goal is doable even in sub-par generated levels, but being able to fulfill secondary goals will require many attempts.
And not because of lacking skill, but entirely because of the random level generation.
I'm certainly the last person not to like random generation, but here, it was clearly done in order to avoid thinking much about mission design and that is just lazy development, not to be rewarded.
It is a shame that such laziness destroys the otherwise great ideas in this game.

Miscreated is a multiplayer open world survival game similar to games like DAYZ and H1Z1.
After picking this game up on sale for $10.99, I was not expecting much as this genre is hard to get right, but I was pleasantly surprised. I have also played a lot of DAYZ and ARMA 3 Breaking Point, and this game definitely has those two beat.
Firstly, the game runs very optimized. Framerates are good, and the lag is nonexistent. Solid net code here. The Cryengine looks great and provides some nice effects (dynamic weather, footprints in sand, water and grass effects).
The gameplay is what you should expect from this type of game, very tense. If you die, you will lose all of your looted gear. This game is best played in a group so you can scavenge together for vehicle parts to more easily move around the map.
The map is currently unfinished, but proves a large area to play in which is more than enough for the current 32 player max servers (this may go up in the future).
The DEVS are very active and the game is being updated constantly.
I highly recommend trying this out, especially if you find it on sale!
CONS:
- No auto run button :(
- No prone (not so bad, helps to stop campers)
- Currently you can't tell friend from foe very easily in a group (hopefully they will add some sort of marker in the future) so watch your friendly fire!

State of Decay is an XBLA port for the PC. I'm not saying that as something negative, but just shedding some light on where the game originated. Overall, the game is fun, but it does have it's issues. The most noticeable issue for this game is it's lack of proper Mouse support. The game DOES support Mouse and Keyboard, along with Controllers, but mouse settings have a built in Mouse Acceleration setting that CANNOT be disabled. Undead Labs have mentioned "working on the mouse" but have yet to correct this issue.
The problem with this is that I prefer to play my PC games with mouse and keyboard. "Use a controller" should not be a fix for this issue. Besides the mouse being handled terribly, the game is actually very fun. It isn't a hardcore survival game by any means, but there's nothing wrong with that. The only reason I would not recommend this game is because of how the mouse has been ignored, when realistically the mouse and keyboard are the two most important things that should have been a priority over everything else.

With so many Zombie Apocalypse Titles out there, the whole scene is getting boring rather fast, but I must honestly say that State of Decay is a great game.
It's the same as most other zombie apocalypse game do everything you can to survive scavenge, fortify your base and so on and so forth but they did it a bit different.
You start off with 2 friends Marcus and Ed at a campsite in the mountains where you meet up with a couple of other survivors who ask you to look around a bit to see if you can find any other survivors, the first person you meet is Maya, a soldier who was out by the lake with two of her friend, sadly her friends were overrun and killed by the zombies. Your little group of 3 then make your way back to the ranger station only to find everyone there has also been killed. You get hold of a two way radio and from there the actual fun begins when you head toward your first home base.
Once at your new home base you need to make friends, you only have access to certain gear if you do your part and put in the leg work. Now you are going to do a lot of running in this game, a lot of button mashing fighting and you are going to get very upset at yourself for making stupid mistakes that get you killed, because if you die then you’re dead. That’s it that character that dies is gone forever, never to be seen again. SO DON'T DIE... Remember you are not super human.
The game is not very hard but at the same time it's not very easy either at first you run up to every zombie you can find to beat up to see all the different cool moves your character has to take down zombies but as you progress you learn one very important thing, being overrun is dangerous, too many zombies in a small space could be fatal and so you find yourself avoiding contact later in the game.
So what makes the game great? Well here's a list of why I think it's a great game.
1. The story progresses if and when you want it to, though there are plenty missions available you don't have to do them all.
2. If you scavenge supplies and you find more than you can carry you can call in for help. Leave the premises and a friend or two will go get the remainder of the supplies.
3. Relocating your home base, as your circle grows you need more space, and different home bases give different "Rewards"
4. The Zombies are balanced out, it’s not like most other games where there are little or no zombies, or they are massively over populated and you have almost no chance of survival.
5. The vehicle damage is very realistic, you hit a fence or a couple of zombies a few times and you are going to start getting radiator problems.
But there are also a few bad things in the game.
1. You find yourself doing the same thing over and over again a lot in the game.
2. The game has no manual save option, which makes it more realistic ( I actually like this ) but it's bad for when you make a stupid mistake and end up dead then you sit there afterwards and think why the hell did I do that.
3. This is probably what bugs me the most, the whole time you are playing the game it feels like you are sitting behind a console, and I am a very big console Hater and I am not afraid to say it. For over a year now, I've been desperately searching for a good game that could make me like video games again. I liked the old Mass Effect, I liked Fable, I loved the fantasy genre in general, but I'm super picky with the vibes and combat, as I hated every minute of playing Dragon Age. I kept hating games more and more recently, and lately, playing games feels like a chore. Then I bought this game, and I found everything I could have asked for from a videogame. It has action, it has story, it has character interaction and relationships between you and the NPCs, it even has extensive character customization instead of forcing you to play the character they made themselves. It felt like they just took all the good things out of all of my favorite games and mashed into to one perfect mass of fun. When I first started it, I expected it to be ok at best, but after just a little bit of gameplay, I couldn't stop grinning. Graphics are by no means superb - but still good, the storyline and lore are meh and very forgettable, the voice acting is sub-par at best... so why then is this one of my favorite games of all time? Simple. Every flaw in this game is completeley overshadowed by the things it does right.
From a gameplay standpoint the game does an excelent job of immersing you into the world of Dragons Dogma by the design choices in how the game is played and character progression is handled. First off, the character customization in this game is phenomenal and you can easily spend over an hour getting your character (him/her) to look exactly as you want down to the color of each individual eye. Furthermore the cutscenes in-game present your character exactly as they look at that point in time, which is really cool. This character customization carries over to the in-game class and vocation system, which you can select or change at will via discipline points earned by completeing story quests, side quests and slaying monsters. The vocation system includes your standard mage (magic), strider (bow & daggers), fighter (sword & sheild), and many other interesting ones.
The game's combat is arguablely definitive of the rpg genre and fights are handled in real-time, allowing you to move freely, unleashing skills and performing stunts as long as your stamina bar doesn't deplete.  Great character animations and fluidity of movement  only enhance this experience. I would like to add that the boss battles and battles against larger foes are handled very well in this game, allowing you to latch on to them and climb their bodies while you hack away at them in epic fashion. And some enemies are truly impressive at that ( large cyclopes, dragons, griffins, ogres, human bandits, and zombies are only SOME of the foes you will encounter, and they are animated INCREDIBLY!).
The game further immerses you into its world by how traveling in the world is handled. Fast-travel is limited, and can only be performed by acquiring or purchasing port crystals and ferrystones - and then placing them at points on the map you travel to and using them accordingly. This makes traveling truly feel like a journey in an epic fantasy world, as you need to prepare and stock up on tools and curatives to combat the monsters and bandits lurking about in the world as you journey to your destination. NIGHTTIME travel is a highlight, as visibility is VERY poor and enemies are stronger. You will need a lantern and flasks of oil for sure.
Now, to get to one of the games most significant features: the pawn system. With it, you can select one 'main pawn' (a travel companion with the same level of customization as your main character to include comabt) and two other pawns that have been created by other players. Pawns can be found through a rift stone or by wandering about in the world via an online functionality. Your main pawn levels with you, but the other two will need to be eventually switched out if they are too weak or die. Pawns do well enough to make you feel not alone on your dangerous journey, with their significant help during combat, and their rambling about the world of Gransys and information about enemy weak points. But they often say the same things over and over which is annoying.............
There is very much more i can say about the game, but you should pick it up for yourself and learn as you play. It is flawed, but still a very awesome game, and once you get hooked on it, it can easily become an over 100 hour game. The included bitter black isle expansion, is very difficult, and equally rewarding if you can overcome its challenges.

For starters, if you play this before Mass Effect 2, you will thank yourself. This game includes squad mates that are in just about everyone's favorite ME character list, and the choices you make here will affect relationships in each of the sequels.
My favorite thing about the Mass Effect series is the freedom to choose squad mates among your team that suit your playstyle and form your own unique story. Since my own character was tech-focused, my team members could make up for my shortcomings with tankiness and raw power. Others may enjoy using squaddies that supplement you with crowd control or hacking abilities.
It's no secret that Mass Effect 2 had polished away game lengtheners and the micro-managing aspect of RPGs, but this will be the only time in the series you can gear up characters beyond the guns they use. The most interesting or strategic type of loot is the type of bullets your gun uses, so you may switch types to take advantage of enemy weaknesses.
Mass Effect is a lovely series, and I hope you make the time to enjoy it as much as I did.

I have to be honest, I am glad that I went into this game pretty much blind to the reviews here....
I got this game as a gift since I have recently been trekking through games like this (see: Outlast) and a friend said the game looked pretty cool.
To be fair, the concept and story are solid. I think that in terms of a framework for the game, there is something to be said about the way it is structured. Yes, the environments are repetitive, but it actually makes sense as the plot unveils itself. Where this game goes wrong is in execution, lack of interaction and just plain laughable aping of the genre.
PROS:
+ Good enough story to keep you entertained
+ Interesting twist to the effects on your vision as you move through the game, makes it very difficult to concentrate if left unchecked
+ Plenty of opportunities for good old jump scares!
CONS:
- Terrible enemy design... I stood behind a box and watched the 'predator' run straight at me with no regard for the obstacle for about a minute straight. Basically, he couldn't make a decision to go around the box. Also, the sound effects for when he gets close are really bad
- M. Night Shamalamadingdong twist that kind of smothers the build up
- Feels way too much like a bad Outlast
- Achievements are glitched, how do I get all the ones for dying AND not dying or taking damage in one run?
Overall, you can spend $10 in many ways that would leave you worse off. However, this game is not as polished or fleshed out as its peers, leaving you disappointed at what could have been. Maybe worth a sale purchase if you are burning money in your wallet, but otherwise, I'd steer clear unless the game sees some major upgrades.

The binding of Issac is a mixture of Legend of Zelda type game play, permenent death, and dark themes. Thats the best way to describe this game. You play as a boy named Issac, who escaped his mother trying to kill him by jumping into a basement full of horrors. You collect items and trinkets along the way to further Issacs gross apearance. There is SO MUCH♥♥♥♥♥♥IN THIS GAME IT IS INSANE. The game revolves around your tears (Creative attack syestem) which you controll with your arrow keys. You can get items (as already said) and upgrade your tear attacks. You can also get passive upgrades which can control the enviroment around you. You go floor by floor, going to bosses and then going down the trap door to get to a new floor. On these diffrent floors you can find shops, devil deals which require heart containers to get items, angel deals and much more. As you progress in this game you get new bosses, new items to find with each run, and even new final bosses and endings. If I remember correctly this game has about 16 endings. "Woah, thats alot of endings!" I hear you say like a surprised otter. And yes, you are correct because this game is PACKED with content. You can also unlock new characters to try the depths with who each start with their own damage/health/speed and items spawned with. If you want a really interesting character, try azzazel. A black demon with wings thats tear attack is to fire a mini lazer. Cool right? In conclusion the Binding of Issac is worth every cent. I have spend 180+ hours into this game and I have not even unlocked all of the achivements. If you are to buy this game I would reccomend buying the 2 expansion packs, Afterbirth (ew) and Afterbirth +. Both of them are amazing (to be fair the new final boss for Afterbirth + is a little BS) and add tons of new content. 10/10. This is in my top 3 favorite games of all time. ♥♥♥♥ing amazing.

Pros:
- Good atmosphere
- Good sound effects
- Multiple zombie types
- Sustainance isn't redicilously hard to find like it is in DayZ
- Base Building
- Blueprints provide progression
- Plenty of cars to use
Cons:
- Base building is so limited, that the question of why it even exists in the game comes to mind
- Despite having open inventory slots, carry weight makes survivability extremely difficult
- Only one storage container allowed per base. Starting off, each storage container has less than 14 slots
- Blueprints are too rare to justify their purpose, even non-end game ones
- Even though food and drinks are slightly more abundant than in DayZ, it's still a "Tapeworm Simulator"
- Cars usually require a lot of resources in order to maintain/restore
The amount of Survival-Based games are not in short supply. DayZ, 7 days to die, Rust, Hurt World, Reign of Kings, etc. With each one released, we get closer to making that ideal survival game. Is this the ideal survival game that is foretold in the Bible, Quran, and the Torah? ♥♥♥♥ no.
I got banned from the DayZ forums permanently for explaining how DayZ was a Tapeworm Simulator. This game is another tapeworm simulator, having to eat food every 5 minutes or suffer starvation. Here's the best part though -- you are limited by how much you can carry... not by how many spaces are open.
Accuracy in survival games is indeed a good thing. It's neat to learn about herbs, medicinal treatments, how to address injuries, etc, but if things are too realistic as far as player limitations, it becomes tedious.
Yes, there is a base building feature... Go ahead, have at it. With the weight limitation, one-box-per-base, and plot mechanics, this is more of an in-game joke than an actual feature.

Preface: If you're looking to get this because you enjoyed Terraria's challenges and expect something similar from Starbound, you're going to be very sorely disappointed.
After years of painstakingly-slow development Starbound ended up being a lot of nothing. There aren't any triggerable challenges I know of, there aren't any 'events' so to speak, the overall gameplay variety is comparatively sorely lacking and once you find your niche weapon(s) –which for me was explosive assault rifles and high ROF daggers for dealing with melee enemies– you'll quickly find you don't need/want to use anything else.
I pity my friend who spent more to get the 4-pack from which he gave me a copy, because unlike Terraria there seems to be no motivation to continue playing this once you've finished the storyline.
As such I would sooner suggest you get Terraria over this game if you're looking to get either of these as a newcomer and want more engaging gameplay. If you don't care so much about the gameplay and simply want to 'build stuff' then Starbound might be more to your liking.

It hurts me to write this negative review, because I love the studio and it looks and feels really nice. The atmosphere is great, and the art and music compliment if perfectly. But it just feels so... off. As an rts, it's so strange not being able to really control your units. Mostly they follow their own AI, attacking enemy units whether you want them to or not. There's no way to direct units to an area without going there yourself, and you need to select either your entire army, or one small group of units to move. It's just not what I'd expect, and despite my efforts to force myself to like it I just can't.

Tex Murphy was a FMV (full-motion video with real actors) point-and-click adventure series back in 1990. I did not play previous games back then, so this is a newcomer review.
The idea of playing the role of a private detective in a cyberpunk world with a bit of humor is interesting, but the game has its flaws.
- First of all, there are many reminiscences to previous games. They are supposed to touch the hearts of the series veterans, but looked out of place for me. The same can be said about most of the game - many things feel out of place (for example you are in a cyberpunk city, ok, and then you're solving ancient Egyptian puzzles all of a sudden) but I heard it has this cheesy feeling on purpose since all the games were designed like this. Not a design I like, but whatever.
- The story was also a bit hard to follow for me, a couple of times I struggled to understand what I just uncovered while Tex acted like it is clear as day for him. I don't think I could tell you the uncovered story from start to finish even if I wanted to. Perhaps it makes more sense to those who played previous games.
- Graphics outside video sequences are so-so (Unity engine), but they are light years ahead of previous games of course. I don't think I have the strength of will to play the previous ones if navigation there is represented via static images like in old Myst.
In spite of these cons, I'd recommend this game if you like detective stories and adventures.
+ FMV with real actors looks good in Full HD.
+ Gameplay with finding clues and combining things is good if you like adventure games. Puzzles are manageable (I resorted to walkthrough just a couple of times, there is also a casual playing mode where you can skip puzzles if you don't like them).
+ There are multiple endings, too bad I didn't get the things as I wanted In the end (so-so ending without love and such). Choices that lead you to one or another are rather obscure (this is not so good).
Overall, I recommend playing it if you like point-and-click adventures and don't mind the cheesy setting. For veterans of the series it is a must buy I presume.

Tooth and Tail is an RTS about four different factions of animals fighting it out to see who gets to eat who.  Before you click out of this review because you aren’t an RTS fan, it should be noted that this RTS is for people that both hate and love the genre.
The usual resource management that is required of most RTS games has been distilled down to one resource, meat.  Other micromanagement elements that are not a factor in this game are worker management, upgrades, or even creating soldiers.  When you create a farm or burrow (the building that creates soldiers), they automatically produce the soldiers and workers you need.  There is a larger focus on combat and strategy which makes matches faster, more frantic, and fun.  I do miss base building, but it is refreshing to play an RTS with a different twist to it.
The campaign starts you out as the leader of the Longcoats, a father who starts a rebellion after having just watched his only son get chosen as a dinner course and eaten right before his eyes by the faction called the “Civilized”.  The voice acting and cinematic set up the Longcoats as the protagonist, but once you complete all of the missions during their section of the campaign, there is no satisfying conclusion or continuation of their story.  Each faction has their own ideologies and methods of keeping everyone fed and throughout the campaign you get to see each side’s point of view.  This constant switching of ideologies completely throws out the notion of a story that the game started with.  You see the Longcoats in future missions, but the emotional development that that introductory cinematic seemed to be setting up never pays off.  That being said, the ending is definitely an interesting one that I don’t want to spoil, and the story is worth seeing through to the end.
Also, the campaigns difficulty is all over the place.  Some missions are extremely easy while others had me consistently restarting hoping to figure out what I’m doing wrong.  This inconsistent difficulty is exacerbated by the fact that every single map in the game is randomly generated.  This means that spawn points and the layout is completely random even during the campaign.  I think this was a bad decision for the story mode and should have had set maps to keep the gameplay more consistent.
I normally don’t even play the campaign to RTS games and instead spend most of my time in the offline skirmish and online modes.  These are where the game truly shines.  Matchmaking for ranked matches was quick, and I never experienced any lag spikes while playing.  Something that I didn’t expect would be included in the game is local split screen to both PC and console.  This adds so much replay value especially during this generation of consoles consistently doing away with the mode all together.
Something that is missing from offline and online modes are the rule sets that are present in the campaign.  There are so many unique variables added to each mission throughout the story such as freezing effects, damage outside of your base, and much more.  Adding these rules outside of the story would allow for players to be creative with scenarios and add even more replay value.
With all of that being said, I really enjoy Tooth and Tail.  The campaign may be extremely frustrating and patches are even coming out to fix the difficulty of some of the missions, but overall, I had a great time while playing the game and plan to continue to play it online or with friends.  I give Tooth and Tail a solid 7.5 out of 10.
This is a really good game and I highly recommend it if you love or hate RTS games. I really look forward to seeing how these developers continue to grow and improve the game in the coming months.

"Real Time Strategy Distilled" is the perfect slogan for this game. - Very well balanced, addictive RTS that is accessible for everyone.

CONS

The best new RPG I've played in a few years, one of the amazing things about Pillars of Eternity is the depth of the world created for the game right from the get-go. To talk about Pillars without mentioning Baldur's Gate and other infinity engine games to those who've played them would be an oversight, and part of what made these games so enjoyable was the rich complexity of the setting, specifically D&D's Forgotten Realms for Black Isle's fantasy games, they were placed in. One might also notice the infinity engine's sci-fi branch, the Fallout games, are also somewhat of a hit these days with the amount of anticipation for the upcoming Fallout 4. For these predecessors, creating an enitrely new world for which Pillars to take place in would be daunting at the very least. Yet a comparably deep world is exactly what Obsidian has accomplished, with the nations, factions, and cultures they've created for the world of Eora.
The story is also stellar, as is Obsidian's trademark, with choices in game mattering so much because of the branching consequences that follow them in game. The plot of Pillars is nothing short of novel-worthy, as the conflict and mystery are both relatable and allegorical.
PoE's class system, while elegant and based on a wonderfully created new RPG-system, may be one of the areas in which the game isn't perfect. Though most classes are fun to play and plan out, some, such as the Chanter, simply don't have as much to do as others. This is not necessarily a bad thing, as fighting classes in modern video game RPGs are given an absurd amount of fighting moves and abilities simply to keep up with their caster kin, but then perhaps make up for this by having more environment/setting related abilities, such as better stealing for the rogue or more social abilities for the chanter, multi-classing and multi-player, while definitely an afterthought, could be included as well as they were in other games.
Despite this the characters are certainly fun to create and role-play, weather finding spells for your wizard's spellbook (something that is appallingly absent from RPGs these days) to creating new followers from scratch at taverns (!), to adding bonuses to crafted items, Pillars is highly enjoyableas a game with near endless variety and a future world to build on.

I've been seeing Pillars of Eternity appearing on my recommended queue for a while but put off purchasing it. I finally bought it on discount and have to say it has been thoroughly enjoyable to play.
The plus:
- Engaging, challenging, and deep combat with an assortment of skills, abilities, and spells. You can have a party of up to six which I really like. You can choose to micro-manage or let the AI take its course.
- Pre-made characters are interesting, each one with its own story and side quest. I especially like the dialogue that happens between characters at random as you travel, almost like Dragon Age: Inquisition.
- Expansive dungeons and maps that are open for exploration. Od Nua, or the 15 level dungeon is especially enjoyable. I had to come back to it every now and then as it grew harder every level.
- Satisfying customization when it comes to your character and party-mates. I re-trained my characters many times just to try new things. You can do that at any inn, for a fee of course.
- The availability of choices. Technically speaking, you can end a quest whatever way you like. You can be the good guy, the bad guy, or the-in-between guy. You can even kill the quest giver if you feel like it and loot all his goodies.
- The writing is exceptionally good, almost like reading a fantasy novel. But beware, you will be bombarded by endless walls of text. More on that below.
The not-so-plus:
- I found the art style to be very dated, almost unappealing. A far-cry from Divinity: Original Sin which looks absolutely gorgeous.
- Difficulty spikes. I had to push down the difficulty to Normal at one point. There were fights which were a breeze only to find the next one impossible. This game is downright hard and frustrating at times.
- The writing is good, but the sheer amount of it has prompted to me to skip the dialogue on some occasions. Oh, and the voice acting is for a very small potion of what you will be reading.
- The story and plot aren't very interesting.
The Verdict:
Overall, this game is fun and I recommend it. I have already bought the DLC.

Fantastic game that possesses what many modern games lack: a soul driven by an engaging narrative. The world and the violence contained in it feel purposeful, and that you are been driven toward a worthy goal, which you discover what exactly it is along the way. It is entertaining and contain masterfully written narratives.
Pros:
Great Gameplay
Entertaining combat
Well crafted side quests
Companions with personalities
Engaging Narrative that breathe life into the world
I love the endurance system, which for the most part negates the need for post-combat healing
Con:
Item progression does not feel unique or rewarding. In term of appearance and stats, higher leveled and unique items are not distinct from their lower level counterparts.
Despite the rough start and challenging tactical combat that is apparent at the beginning, the game steadily becomes too easy, even on hard mode. A full party of 6 will right click through almost everything. I restricted myself to play on hard with a party of 4. Even then, combat feels very trivial at mid to late game, esp if you are a min-maximizer.
Lackluster lore. The world PoE set in is enormous in scope. Yet there are few information available about the kingdoms and territories outside of Dyrwood, the country that the game contains itself in. There is no Middle-Earth type of feeling as you dive into its world.
That's all I can think of for now. Nonetheless, the game is well worth the purchase and is a true Baldur's Gate II successor.

DYNASTY WARRIORS 8. Based on the historical story of the Three Kingdoms, this franchise concentrates massively on destroying literally everything in sight that has a sword, spear, bombs, even someone with a wheeled halberd and quite honestly, really strange hair. More than ever, this modern adaptation of Dynasty Warriors focuses more than ever on strategy and thinking ahead, giving it more of a well rounded feel instead of absolutely destroying everything in sight (which you can still do).
Before I go any further, this is a port of the PS3 version of the game, not the PS4. You can see the comparison here, although the PC version looks better than what's shown ton the PS3 version in the video.
English voices:
Japanese voices:
Gameplay wise, if you've played 3, 4 or 5, there's a world of difference here. Everything is much more massive - 1000 kills per battleground is no longer a gigantic struggle to do as there are more than plenty of troops to slaughter. Strategy is more of a thing now and it is pretty fun. Going around completing missions for the leading commander, such as taking a base, or defending a wind shrine to generate wind makes the game feel as if you're really advancing the story. If you're wondering about the godlike music in this game, no need to worry. The DW8 (shortened title for the game) official soundtrack is amazing if you give it a chance. On the plus side as well, if you didn't enjoy music, you can play a select amount of songs from DW3 all the way to DW7 for the nostalgic purposes.
For example;

This track is played during the Battle of Chibi, really amazing stuff. The Free Mode in this game is the best one they've put out yet, giving the player the freedom of any officer, with any bodyguard and with any side for any battle. It'd take you a long time to explore each and every difference each officer makes. Finally, a fatal flaw with any beat 'em up game, this game is EXTREMELY repetitive so unless you can really enjoy the playstle, the repeitiveness may kill your experience.
Story is extremely improved on, so much so that the game plays stuff out to almost chronological order and to historical fashion. You may find that a few things aren't as accurate as you might have thought so, but most are covered. On top of this, they've introduced a new mechanic into the game called Hypotheicals, which are basically "What if?" routes that leads to a dramatically new ending for each of the factions - Wei, Wu, Shu, Jin and Lu Bu's story, Lots of content here to be explored and mess around with.
Graphically, the game falls short here. DW8 is not the prettiest game, but it gets detail where it's needed. The battleground for Fan Castle is extremely low detailed, even on maxed settings. My graphics card, R9 380 struggles to get a perfect 60FPS on max settings but I have never seen the game dip below 30FPS. CGIs in game are not exactly great, but like before, they get the detail in and thus the job done, if not to a unsatisfactory standard. The weapons are also detailed but to an extreme detail. In other words, nothing in this game is meant for super close examination because you will almost always find a flaw or an issue with whatever it is. Another issue that people may or may care about is that there is no physics engine in this game. Capes, drapes and even hair (pony tails, or any form of long hair) will flap around like crazy if you even take a step. While funny looking, it may ruin a serious moment.
Overall, Dynasty Warriors 8 is a great game that has been improved on greatly versus the console versions. While it doesn't look the best, the music, the characters and most of all, the story of the Three Kingdoms is one hell of a time waster. 100 hours in and I'm just starting to get to the real end game. You may find me often in game because of nostalgia purposes but I really do mean this - if you're looking for a fantastic beat em up game with plenty of story and content to go around for more than 130 hours and if you don't mind some repetition, this game is a fantastic purchase.
Very fun, relaxing, and simple game. If you've ever played the flash game "Tanks" and liked it, this is the game for you.

First, a little ethos-building: I'm a horror game fanatic. Any title boasting even a whiff of creepy atmosphere, sign me up. Cardboard-creaky monsters, cliched storylines, monumentally dumb protagonists? I don't care, sign me up. I also regularly champion indie games. I've played my fair share and count several of them among my absolute favorites. I've played, and loved, so many "bad" games, I even write a blog as testament:
Now that's done, you can probably see what I'm about to say from a mile away: I'm going to have to give Hektor an enthusiastic thumbs down. Ouch! It's hurts me more than it hurts you.
The main problem here is the translation from idea to actual gameplay, in my opinion. Hektor is (or was, at launch) much touted as "that game where the environment keeps changing all around you like a big head trip." Well, this is true; hallways twist and turn, sometimes evaporating into thin air behind you when you're not looking. Familiar doors appear in front of you, and suddenly you find yourself walking through a deja-vu loop of hallway-room-hallway-room, straight out of some Twilight Zone episode. I'm trapped inside a room, that's inside a room, that's inside a room! AHH!! Or do a 180 to reveal that the path you just traversed has turned into a dead end brick wall.
OK, cool. But when the environments are all incredibly samey (I mean, you pretty much have identical sets of dirty white concrete hallways, closets, wooden desks and doors ad nauseum here--you will NOT find any smidge of variety in this game whatsoever), the long-term effect of this constantly shifting environment...lands with a thud. Who cares? It all looks the same anyway--what does it matter if it's shifting about willy nilly? It ends up not being interesting nor creating any real sense of confusion, tension, mystery, or horror. Darn it.
In fact, it engenders the opposite...a nagging feeling of ennui. I literally found myself saying out loud:
"Clearly, it doesn't matter which hallway or door I choose, which direction I turn, or what I do. The game ends up sending me where it needs to in order for me to progress. I don't need to memorize locations or anything. All I really need to do is just push the thumbstick forward and the game will build itself around me until I get to the end." Yup, pretty much sums it up.
I'm surprised the developers didn't consider this possible effect before committing to this questionable design decision. Talk about alienating your player.
Next, if you take that effect and add to it the fact that the "predator" stalking you throughout the game can kill you upon sight (you have no way to defend yourself; nor can you outrun it; nor can you even effectively hide from it--seriously, there's nothing you can do but stand there and wait for the game to kill you and restart)...well, you end up having absolutely no connection to what is happening, no sense of agency, no sense that any of your actions matter at all. And the puppet-like predator loses all sense of horror the second time you see it--and you will see it repeatedly as it hacks away at you robotically before the screen goes dark. I try not to play the "comparison game" too often honestly, but in this case for some reason, I couldn't help but think how far, far, far away Hektor is in quality from anything Frictional has ever created (for instance). These developers don't have "it," and I don't see them finding "it" any time soon.
As a note-picking-up simulator that attempts to tell a shadowy covert-government-sponsored-brainwashing story (I guess?), it has some pretty well done voice acting. And the music is so suitably depressing (and professionally recorded), I assumed it was simply canned music from some licensed collection. But it appears the sounds were recorded specifically for the game. Kudos on that.
But it's not compelling enough (or properly fleshed out enough) as a narrative to make you care about it or the poor souls inhabiting this world. Hektor tries to do some interesting things, but it's a weak, weak indie. And what the heck does Hektor mean, anyway? That's the flavor which was left in my mouth after the final cutscene played followed by the credits. A weak, meandering fog of...nothing, really.

Graphics are by no means superb - but still good, the storyline and lore are meh and very forgettable, the voice acting is sub-par at best... so why then is this one of my favorite games of all time? Simple. Every flaw in this game is completeley overshadowed by the things it does right.
From a gameplay standpoint the game does an excelent job of immersing you into the world of Dragons Dogma by the design choices in how the game is played and character progression is handled. First off, the character customization in this game is phenomenal and you can easily spend over an hour getting your character (him/her) to look exactly as you want down to the color of each individual eye. Furthermore the cutscenes in-game present your character exactly as they look at that point in time, which is really cool. This character customization carries over to the in-game class and vocation system, which you can select or change at will via discipline points earned by completeing story quests, side quests and slaying monsters. The vocation system includes your standard mage (magic), strider (bow & daggers), fighter (sword & sheild), and many other interesting ones.
The game's combat is arguablely definitive of the rpg genre and fights are handled in real-time, allowing you to move freely, unleashing skills and performing stunts as long as your stamina bar doesn't deplete.  Great character animations and fluidity of movement  only enhance this experience. I would like to add that the boss battles and battles against larger foes are handled very well in this game, allowing you to latch on to them and climb their bodies while you hack away at them in epic fashion. And some enemies are truly impressive at that ( large cyclopes, dragons, griffins, ogres, human bandits, and zombies are only SOME of the foes you will encounter, and they are animated INCREDIBLY!).
The game further immerses you into its world by how traveling in the world is handled. Fast-travel is limited, and can only be performed by acquiring or purchasing port crystals and ferrystones - and then placing them at points on the map you travel to and using them accordingly. This makes traveling truly feel like a journey in an epic fantasy world, as you need to prepare and stock up on tools and curatives to combat the monsters and bandits lurking about in the world as you journey to your destination. NIGHTTIME travel is a highlight, as visibility is VERY poor and enemies are stronger. You will need a lantern and flasks of oil for sure.
Now, to get to one of the games most significant features: the pawn system. With it, you can select one 'main pawn' (a travel companion with the same level of customization as your main character to include comabt) and two other pawns that have been created by other players. Pawns can be found through a rift stone or by wandering about in the world via an online functionality. Your main pawn levels with you, but the other two will need to be eventually switched out if they are too weak or die. Pawns do well enough to make you feel not alone on your dangerous journey, with their significant help during combat, and their rambling about the world of Gransys and information about enemy weak points. But they often say the same things over and over which is annoying.............
There is very much more i can say about the game, but you should pick it up for yourself and learn as you play. It is flawed, but still a very awesome game, and once you get hooked on it, it can easily become an over 100 hour game. The included bitter black isle expansion, is very difficult, and equally rewarding if you can overcome its challenges.

Surely the combat is better than Skyrim? Nope, it's class based, you can only play 8 classes and only start off with 3, Skyrim has way better combat because you can dual wield, bash with weapons, use any weapon or spell you want without restrictions because there is no class system, class systems are generally cancer unless theres plenty of classes to make up for the lack of depth, this game does not have that. The only thing this games combat has going for it is that you can climb on enemies, that's it, otherwise it's just a wannabe Dark Souls. Atleast in dark souls there was no restriction to what weapons and armor you could use, all classes did was change your starting gear and stats. Mount and blade has much better combat aswell as in that game there is also no class system, you just pick up a weapon and use it, and there are multiple directions you can block and attack from without having to turn, and there are also throwing weapons and longarms. Also, very important, THIS IS NOT AN RPG, role playing games do NOT have a preditermined backstory, you are the "arisen" no matter what just like how in skyrim you are the "dragonborn" no matter what. Did i mention Skyrim is not an RPG either? Mount and blade is an example of a real RPG, you make your own backstory in that game and start out as a new entity. If theres one good thing i can say about this game is that it has a large variety of enemies compared to Skyrim. The UI is clunky and terrible in this game, going into inventory to use potions is a chore, you cant bind switching weapons to scrolling, walking inside of inclosed spaces gets wonky sometimes, and picking up items is hard due to thirdperson. Game starts you off with a companion whether you want him or not, very immersion breaking. Very few ways to grind in the beginning without doing quests because enemies are too powerful. You can't swim in this game, and if you try to, you will black out and be teleported outside of shore, making the game very linear. Some bosses have way too much health for their size, or just enemies in general, in the beginning, goblins and wolves tank hits from bow and arrow fire, without fire enchantment, they're unbeatable, unless you're high level and have much better equipment, atleast in skyrim your level 1 character could actually stand a chance and having a companion wasn't mandatory. No reason to pick up this game for 30 dollars when you can get Skyrim and Dark Souls and Warband for 20.

Pick it up on sale, boys!
Adrenaline fueled rushes through the woods and through the night are sure to follow a purchase of this game. Spawn in with a flashlight, collect your buddies, and pray to God that the next person you run across is bluffing when he holds that shotgun up and there aren't really bullets in there. Miscreated is a VERY hardcore PvP game, with your entire inventory getting wiped upon death. The looting system is so brutal and unforgiving that the easiest way to (and I'm guilty of this a few times) collect supplies is to stalk someone for 30-40 minutes, wait for them to get really well geared, and then just pounce on them and take ♥♥♥♥ing everything. This feels EXCELLENT to be on the giving end of, and is one of the worst feelings of the world on the recieving end.
Finding a car feels great, fixing it up feels great, killing people in it feels great, losing it feels TERRIBLE. This is the cycle of Miscreated; Good to Great! to Awesome! to YES! to ♥♥♥♥ MY LIFE!!!!!!!!!!, and then back in a circle. It is so glorious I can't even really give it justice.
Miscreated focuses on PvP, with very little PvE. There are a few towns to search through, ALL hotzones for people to be waiting to ambush you. The big city (Hayward Valley) is visually impressive and shows the developers have some REAL talent for capturing atmosphere and putting in excellent mechanics into their world (the hotel with the elevator was a real hoot the first time around).
Very clear problems: Inventory space is far too limited. Weight system is so restrictive, it makes me want to cry. Also building system could use some work as my buds and I have died several times from clipping issues into walls when getting out of cars in our bases.
Like I said, buy it on sale.

It seems the 5 years between Chaos Theory and Conviction had everyone forget what made the series so different than everything else.
"Stealth Action Redefined" was the original subtitle of Splinter Cell. I always thought that the point of a secret agent was that his existence remained as much a secret as possible. In SC:B, it's quite the contrary.
The SC fans will likely opt for the Ghost approach. In SC:B, being a Ghost means you can be seen by the enemy as long as you knock him out within a second. You can knock out as many people as you want, shoot out light bulbs, destroy cameras, you name it. The next morning, nobody will remember a thing and will probably blame the destroyed light bulbs and cameras on a power surge or something.
You'll go on this mission where you must hack some computers, and where, if you're "detected", the enemy will wipe out the data and the mission will be a failure. But apparently, if you knock out the entire base before hacking the servers, it's not suspicious at all and they won't wipe out the data, because, bleh.
And if you remain completely invisible without leaving as much as a drop of sweat, the game rewards you with a lame 11000 points and a few thousand dollars. If you opt for wiping out the whole base, you'll get 20000+ points and even more money. Even shooting light bulbs rewards you with money.
Everything that was challenging in the previous games is now gone.
It's a somewhat fun game, but it's pretty far from what made Splinter Cell "redefine the stealth action" genre. Sadly, I don't think it's ever coming back

QUICK REVIEW:
Runs great, plays great. Do miss chaos theory style play where it was slow but methodical. Faster paced works fairly well though.
Single player was fun. Various customization options and playstyles provide a different experience for people, adding loads of replayability. Story was a run of the mill Tom clancy plot - SCARY GROUP ATTACKS 'MERICA STAHP THEM BAD GUISE. Was very entertaining to play though and you feel like a badass no matter what playstyle you use.
Side missions are hard and most have an optional Co-op feature. Co-op feels neutered compared to chaos theory's: it had a well planned unique experience unique only to co-op. Outside of one or two Co-op only missions, an extra person doesn't add much to the experience other than maybe a different path to take and it's possible to execute fully armored hostiles.
Spies VS Mercs returns and is still pretty "Mehh". Core gameplay of this is the same as ever - spies sneak to objectvies while mercs control FPS style and try to stop them. Spies control much better than they used to back in the day BUT mercs are still awkwardly wonky. The subpar FPS controls feel super out of place from a company that delivers rainbow six, ghost recon and Far Cry titles.
Overall it's a fun package if you enjoy single player stealth titles like old splinter cell games or metal gear solid. If you're expecting a great multiplayer experience you will be underwhelmed. Worth the time and money especially if you wait for a discount on the price.

The thing I enjoy the most about this game is how strong its building and customization aspects are. The exploring aspect of the game will get stale once you reach the final stages, but you can milk A LOT of fun out of building houses, bases and villages and populating them with NPCs. You can hire a crew with different little perks and choose their uniform, you can set up a little museum planet where you store all the rare artifacts you collect in your journeys, you can use the wiring mode to make lots of different contraptions a la Minecraft, etc. Even though I found the main quest to be fun enough, the game shines the most when you try to make your own fun. Also, even though the setting is pretty silly/comedic, the game has surprisingly well-crafted lore.
If you compare it to Terraria, you'll probably find the boss fights / combat aspects lacking, but on all other aspects I'd say Starbound does quite a bit better.

You can scare off or kill your save points. Need I say more?
But really, it's a very Japanese game in just how absurd it is and how it both takes itself very seriously and not seriously at all. The story progresses in a really unusual (and sometimes irritating) way. Basically, time moves each time you enter a new zone and events happen at certain times in certain areas. You can technically ignore all the story and just do your own thing or you can follow one route by helping one group. It really requires a lot of trial and error and your first playthrough might just be learning the path that the overarching story takes so you can better plan your second one.
Really interesting concept, although it's really only fun if you're patient. If you don't like the idea of missing huge pieces of the story just because you took a wrong turn, this game isn't for you. Otherwise, it's an absolute blast.

Samurai Simulator sounds like it should be a slam dunk idea. However, the slodgy combat and dopey game world really brought this down for me.
Swordfights feel like two men hitting each other with pool noodles. There is little strategy to the combat -- your best bet is generally to whale on your best move or two until the match is over. Parries don't seem to work well, so it's anybody's guess as to whether you or your opponent will have the upper hand after a block. Meanwhile your swords are rapidly turning to dust with each strike and parry.
The game contains three major factions. One is a set of rabid nationalists, another are the local government / wacky BDSM connoiseurs, and the last are the British (a 12-year-old girl named "Laura Rita [get it?]", a gay man from a 2005 anime, and an Amazoness named "Melinda Megamelons." They're all tremendously stupid, and I couldn't bring myself to give a rip what happens to any of them. Why play this again and again to see how the story changes when everybody is lame?
There's also a glut of dopey minigames: fishing, bdsm tortures, "night crawling". None of it really says "samurai" to me.
The budget combat makes choosing a storyline a chore, and the crummy world makes choosing a storyline pointless.

Let me just say I hate adventure/point and click games because they have the most annoying and obtrusive gameplay. This game is no different. You hunt around locations in first person picking up random items that you are supposed to somehow know that you can make random nonsensical combinations and then think to use them 30 min later on a part of the background that doesn't let you know you can use items on it. When you aren't doing that, which is 75% of the gameplay, you are solving sometimes annoyingly frustrating, random, and lacking direction puzzles, and sometimes fun puzzles. The place where this game shines is the story. I have never played a game with FMV's before, and this game does a great job with it. I have not played a Tex Murphy game before this one, and while you may miss some connections and characters, the story does a good job of staying grounded in the present. The cutscenes with real actors make the story feel more real and thus more interesting, than pixels. I found myself invested in the story and wanting to know what happened. I dreaded actually playing the game, but I loved watching it. I also loved all of the optional dialogue and many branching paths. I loved how I got to do an extra part because I chose to bang this one chick. The dialogue options could have been better in the sense each one is basically one word, and you have no idea what that word leads into. I would pick a word and then I would see the option was sarcasm and not sincerely saying the word, but the game didn't let me know that. Other ones just gave no real description what you said and it was open-ended. For that reason I had to replay some dialogue options with reloading, which they could have minimized by giving a better understanding of what you are going to say. Hey if Bioware can, so can they. The game graphics are actually terrible, like from a game in 2008, but I didn't play this for the boring annoying gameplay. You will need a walkthrough for a lot of solutions. It is super annoying how games like this, because you need to use EVERY single thing you find, that if you missed 1 little thing in 1 little drawer in one of the 10 rooms you had to look through, you'll be stuck, but you won't know why, because the game expects you to somehow never miss anything. And other parts in facilities, where you are supposed to know you need to go up to this 1 room and then back down 2 flights and go to this specific room to use it, are the definition of stupid. Still, because of the branching paths and FMV and interesting story dealing with Tesla, some grounded in truth and superstition, I give the game an up-vote. But it would be higher if it were actually "fun" to play. 6.5/10.

A great pulpy detective story, marred by plodding hidden object searches, and generic adventure game puzzles. The characters and cutscenes are superbly written and a joy to behold, and the game really hits its peak when it gives you a mystery to unravel and an open space for you to find clues within.
However, half the game's puzzles seem to exist just to exist. Too often I was left in an interesting location, with uninteresting objectives. At one point, I found a sliding block puzzle in an old woman's mansion and simply quit because it completely broke immersion for me.
Still, an enjoyable experience, and a tentative recommendation. However, if you're looking for gameplay that actually makes you feel like a detective, I'd recommend the Sherlock Holmes' or Blackwell series' instead.

I've played through all but Overseer of the previous Tex Murphey adventures when they first came out and had varying amounts of nostalgia for them, but I much prefered the later fully FMV entries in the series and Tesla Effect is a really fun conclusion.  Now I have to actually go back and finish my playthrough of Overseer, which I have kicking around somewhere.  But back to Tesla Effect.
The best parts of the whole thing are the cast.  A few are soooo bad it's hilarious, most are decent, and a few, especially Tex himself and Rook, are really great.  Lots of laughs.  The humor from the previous games has survived.
The story is interesting at first, but about 2/3 of the way in, things start getting weirdly complicated, like four or five people were writing while off on their own and then feeding their plotlines into the final product with only occasional collaboration.  I mean, you could follow what was happening, but it got pretty dumb by the end.  Also, while I very much appreciated the handful of branching choices, I would have liked more contextual clues when they popped up.  On my first playthrough I got one of the odd endings that didn't feel like it really fit the overall story up until that point, because of a single choice I took to be a joke at first.
Gameplay is all about picking up everything that is pick-up-able, examining and trying different combinations of items, as well as asking every single person you encounter about every single topic available.  Death traps are situational and sometimes annoyingly cheap (I'm looking at you stealth section and lab exploration).  There is no combat.  It is a point-and-click adventure, afterall.
The puzzles range from simple speed bumps a small child could solve, to the occasional head-scratcher needing a bit of trial and error, to the classic adventure game standby of "now what were the devs thinking when they came up with this one", where you have to imagine what would make sense in the immediate context rather than what would work in real life.
The FMVs were all very clear and polished, while the rendered art style was classic Tex, and barely updated.  The devs were clearly writing a love letter to the series, the characters and the old school fans.  I had a great few nights running through this with nostalgia goggles on, and will probably do so again after I finish Overseer.  I would highly reccomend this to any fans of the early 90s FMV adventure genre, and it's a must have for anyone wanting to see one last Tex Murphy case.  If you're neither, however, odds are you'd be better off just watching a Let's Play, if only for the cutscenes, because the older style and sensibilities will probably be lost on you.

Warning: I have no nostalgia for older titles in this genre. I did not complete the game for reasons which are clarified below.
What the game got right:
This game is very cheesy. The cutscenes and character interactions, the one-liners from the PI you play as -- those are the strong points of this game. The FMV parts of the game are really well done: the resolution doesn't make you feel sick, the green screen is just viewable around the edges of the characters but not too distracting. The 2k resolution for the FMV sequences is probably nice for people who have the hardware to display that kind of thing.
What it got wrong:
However, I would not recommend this game. It just doesn't feel like a game. On top of that, the graphics of the main street you first walk around it sicken me. It feels like Deus Ex. Both games were set in the future, and both games look like they were made in 2000. Deus Ex WAS released in 2000, but Tesla Effect was released in 2014. There's a car I saw on Main street that looked almost
like a flattened blackened, car from DE. I know this is a game which is trying to appeal to older folks and older gamers by mimicking older games, but
. It's hard to go from 1080p FMV sequences to crappy everything else. It's immersion breaking.
So, as a game, I would not recommend this. It's like you're swimming in an ocean of outdated graphics and mediocre gameplay, and every FMV sequence is a breath of fresh air before you have to plunge your head back into the ocean to get to the next part so you can breath in the FMV again. Some people say, once you get immersed in the story, the graphics will become insignificant. Maybe. I did not get immersed in the story, and after quitting the game once, had little inclination to go back.

You basically need to plan ahead, position your party so that they don't get flanked (There's backstab mechanics in this game.), and not to get clustered, incase an AOE comes your way. I found out later that Carrie Patel was narrative lead - which explains a lot, I actually bought one of her books (I was really hyped for this game) and couldn't get past first 100 pages which is a rare thing for me.
There's a ton of useless NPCs with some stories provided by backers (usually bad ones) - and although you can avoid them, they clutter cities and pubs and the whole idea of having them is completely silly. Other characters talk a lot but have nothing to say. I am a guy who enjoys "games you can read through", but I expect some decent level of writing, not just an outlet for some untalented nerd's graphomania.
And don't make me start on game mechanics. All stats are dump stats, only your level matters.
Crafting and enchanting feels like... crafted... 2 hours before release.
Main antagoinst has charisma of shredded carrot. I actually couldn't even care about the story or what was going on, it was so boring. First off fan boi’s please down vote and move on as negative fan boi explosion comments will immediately be deleted with… pleasure….
Let’s start with the pro’s of game since there are only a couple.

Never could. PoE has whole new classes and “mathy” stuff built from the ground up. What do you have when it is done? A total chaotic mess. Character creation and stats make absolutely no sense whatsoever, leveling up is a bore because they have fleshed the entire process out, and to top it off they have extremely low level caps because (I suppose) the numbers were just getting too big (didn’t have enough hands?).
3.	A game that focuses on “reading a book” while everything else gets the shaft. If you don’t LOVE reading your story, RUN THE OTHER DIRECTION. If you try to just skip all of the hundreds of pages of painful reading in hopes that you will just be able to figure things out on the fly you will quickly find that you are wandering around aimlessly with no clue what to do with a journal that is about as useful as most of the reviews for this game.  “Find the cliff from the vision”… 11/10
4.	Bugs, glitches, and failures. Items will disappear from your inventory, save menus will all of the sudden not show dialogue (you just have to guess where the “yes please save” is SUPPOSED to be on the screen because it just isn’t there) saves corrupts, and loading screens, OMFG the loading screens by the end of the game are seriously minutes long and you have a half dozen of them to even get back to your “keep”. The rest of the time you are left wondering if what they did was better at all, just “different”. Loot is terrible, there is a total lack of ANY memorable boss fights or unique monsters, classes mean absolutely nothing (there is a “rouge” class that literally has no benefit to “lock picking” or any other “thief like skills”) and can be summed up basically as either “damage takers” or “damage dealers”, (There is no “thief” in the party or “ranger that will help you navigate magical woods” you just have people who take damage and those that deal it) crafting is a joke (anyone can just throw some dirt and money at an object and make it better) and item management/economy has been thrown out the window (you have a “unlimited bag of holding” from the very start of the game so you just pick up EVERYTHING and sell it, money becomes worthless… oh, but you can only hold 2 rations of supplies to heal yourself with… lmfao) and the list could go on but you get the point.

I had played through both Baldur's Gate games extensively back in the day and I have played this game a lot before making an opinion.
It began as a kick starter and stays true to the gameplay of the Baldur's Gate and Icewind Dale games. You have an isometric view and guide your hero through story driven quests whilst recruiting up to 5 NPCs with their own dialogue options and personalitys. The story is interesting and manages to be fairly original, immersing you in a new universe to explore. You have a world map to navigate and the White March expansion adds an increased level cap, weapons that level up and a new area with quests.
I haven't completed the game yet as I have hit my level cap near the end of White March 1 (14), and suspect that White March 2 will increase it further (16?) so don't want to lose out on exp. Some of the fights are still difficult on normal and I have found myself going back to them once I powered up a bit more. The weapons/spells are varied enough for a fantasy universe and the side quests interesting.
You also get to look after a stronghold near the start of the game. This to me was more of a minor distraction and something that could be built on in the sequel, although it still performs many useful functions and the basis for the endless paths quests.
As a fan of Baldur's Gate I think the developers have done a great job, and I hope they continue to build on this franchise. I am now looking forward to White March 2 so I can beat the end boss or rage quit trying...

Given that I am a long time role-playing gamer and an admirer of Bioware's works since Baldur's Gate and Neverwinter Nights, I decided to give Mass Effect a go.
I heard quite a lot about the game before playing it, and I've finished Dragon Age: Origins not long ago, so I knew a little bit what to expect. Even though I never was a big sci-fi fan, and I've always preferred a fantasy setting, I tried to be objective in my assessment nevertheless.
The visuals are pretty impressive for 2007 and help to create the perfect atmosphere for a space adventure.
The music is also fitting and of high quality, as well as the sound effects.
My first complaint is related to the voice acting. It's probably because I played Mass Effect after playing Dragon Age: Origins, which, in my opinion, is a game that has one of the best voice acting in the history of computer games. Still I could not help but notice that many characters lacked distinctive personalities. I would say that the only exceptions are Wrex and Tali (well, and maybe Liara).
The battle system is a bit similiar to a shooter, due to the setting. Still the engineering and biotic abilities provide for a nice variety of options to choose from.
The character development system is neither too complicated nor too simple. As you level up, you gain the points that you can spend on some abilities determined by your character class. Nothing revolutionary, but it works well.
The story is pretty good. It will not blow your mind, but it provides for an entertaining gaming experience. Some of your choices affect other characters, and you may use your save file in Mass Effect 2 (I still haven't played it myself). But it seems that there is only a couple of choices that have really important consequences and that are inevitable.
The optional quests are not a strong point of the game. Surely, there are many side missions with different pretexts, but, in the end, almost all of them consist in terminating the enemies. And the usage of the same buildings in various missions only serves to make the experience even more boring.
My verdict:
Mass Effect is a really good sci-fi RPG. It cannot be compared to the genre classics, but may help to introduce the casual players to the genre. If you like space operas and games that can offer more than just shooting everything that moves, you will likely enjoy playing Mass Effect.
