Tooth and Tail does two things that make it worth your time to venture into the terrifying world or multiplayer RTS:
1) Having your commander act as a mouse imposes a real cost on microing and caps everyone at the same movement speed for issuing commands. Your opponent won't be able to perfectly micro their units AND macro at their base.
2) The short match times allow you to lose, learn and repeat blindingly fast. Get crushed, watch a replay, see what you did wrong, or what creative build the opponent used and apply it to the next game.
With these two points you don't have to commit giant swathes of times to learning the game and seeing real improvement. They allow you to focus more on bigger picture stuff such as your builds and tempo. Simply excellent!

I've been playing RTS games for a pretty long time. And Tooth and Tail is probably one of the best entry level RTS games I can think of, right next to Army Men RTS, particularly for players who might have a background in MOBA style games. It plays well, the art designed killed it, sound design is stellar, and gameplay is simple to grasp.
Don't take that to mean this game is easy. I'm an RTS Veteran, and this game threw quite a few curve balls at me due to the randomized maps. Yes, randomized. Every map - campaign AND multiplayer - is generated when you play it. This means that instead of memorizing maps you actually have to go scout yourself with your commander (your physical presence on the battlefield). The downside is that this means any potential competitive scene is going to be hamstrung unless more symmetrical maps can be generated.
But for $20 dollars this is a stellar game for someone looking to get into RTS, and a veteran looking for something new.

This game breaks all the oldschool RTS rules- there are no extensive menus, tech trees, or huge unit rosters to tangle with... and somehow it's one of the most enjoyable RTS games to come along in a very long time! A brilliant introductory RTS game for any newcomer to the genre, it's contorller compatible and forgiving on the easier modes. If you're an RTS veteran (like me) and you want to match wits against one of the best enemy AI out there today, then turn up the mode and it'll give you a run for your money. Better still, as of this writing Tooth and Tail has a vibrant multiplayer scene, so you can take on real people too.
At it's heart though, the game is pure fun. The story mode adds a ton of charm, while the brilliant AI and map generator menas you'll never have two matches alike. It's incredibly easy to get into, yet impossible to truly master; I haven't gotten bored of it yet, and the way the updates and ballance tweaks have been going, I doubt I ever will.
Whether you're looking to match wits against friends, human enemies, an utterly ruthless computer AI, or just have fun commanding an army of drunken squirrels and a flamethrower wielding boar, this game will give you hours of enjoyment.

Tooth and Tail turned out to be a great game that lowers the barrier of entrace into RTS genre without sacrificing strategical depth.
To get your attention right away: Tooth and Tail is a competitive indie RTS. The backstory of the game is revolution in an animal world: animals revolt against other animals.
The game essentially addresses the issue with most rts games, where high skill level is necessary to even start thinking about competitive play. The most radical change is that you can’t scroll the map freely. You control a commander unit that you can move directly (keyboard/mouse or gamepad), this unit scouts the map, orders the other units and places buildings. Here’s how it is handled: your initial building, gristmill, has spot for 8 farms. You have 3 farms in the beginning of the game. Each farm costs 60 food to build and produces 1 food per second. As game progresses, new gristmills on the map can be captured.
You can build defensive buildings, new farms or “lairs” for the animals. The lairs automatically produce soldiers (while your supplies last), and you can then order those units around either by commanding them all or by selecting a specific unit type. The unit commands are pretty much straightforward: button click can mean attack, holding the mouse button while highlighting the enemy makes everyone focus it, or running away and keeping the mouse button pressed means your army retreats with you.
In total, there are 15 unit types and 5 defensive buildings. You pick 6 of these in any variation before the multiplayer battle, thus adjusting your strategy for every battle separately.
At the state of the previous patch (1.0.3) – on my ranks it felt that the game has the “rush meta” - I could win most games by building small units, but I’ve checked out the tournament videos and they showed much more elaborate plays.
Overall, the game matches are extremely short and intense. I personally never had a game longer than 8 minutes.
The aesthetics are the strong point of the game. The pixel art is cartoonish, but once you think about this, it gets pretty brutal. It is implied that the animals eat meat of others, which adds a cannibalistic feel to the game. Some might tell you: wait a second, in the animal world it’s called “carnivorous”. To that, I can answer: “The animals in the game have anthropomorphic features, so you can’t distance yourself from looking at them from the human angle.” So in the end, the game that is light on the art implies heavier subjects, making a unique dark atmosphere.
The drawback to this is that it’s sometimes hard to distinguish between walkable and unwalkable tiles. You’ll be getting stuck with your hero, simply because some places that seem to be passable turn out not (mostly in bushy tilesets, gets quite extreme in singleplayer, especially the mission where you have to free multiple squads of your soldiers).
All maps (even in single-player campaign) are generated randomly. That means that a lot of matches in single-player will be made easier if you get lucky. In competitive you can get screwed because of that, but it surprisingly does not bother you much: first, it teaches you how to adapt better. Second, if you are placed at a worse position than your opponent and lose: no big deal, it only took 5 minutes.
The strongest point of the game is the entry threshold: if you enjoy watching RTS games, but can’t get into competitive scene because those games require lots of concentration / time to get good, Tooth And Tail might be a good alternative. Since you control one commander, it takes the pressure off micromanaging tons of units / controlling the minimap / bases like crazy. You can start the games quickly, quickly win or quickly lose. The amount of strategies and possible plays still big due to unit variety and strategical decisionmaking (expansion vs offense). Overall, I can safely recommend Tooth and Tail to both RTS fans and people who are willing to get into the genre.

I loved the music, art-style and pseudo-Russian language, but the biggest problem for me was the maps. Random generation is a good way to shake up the gameplay and avoid patterns for the player to get stuck in, but at times it seemed that the AI received an unfair advantage or I would get stuck in the terrain. This revolved between annoying to downright frustrating, and some missions/matches felt like I won or lost based on the map, not through any skill of mine. In addition, the centralized method of controlling your troops, though simple and effective, made more complicated strategies difficult to carry out.  The game was charming and unique, but not without its flaws.

PROS:
-As an alpha i was not expecting this game to look as good as it does when i first bouhgt it, the graphics are incredible and its going to be prime time when it fully comes out.

Pros:
Epic mini-boss battles, especially for its time.
Character appearance customization is good with many options.
Good amount of classes add replay value.
Fairly large open-world.
Cons:
Game-breaking  save system. You can only have ONE SAVE. Want to  role play as a different character? You have to erase your old game and start a brand new one. The game tries to offset this by allowing you to switch your character class fairly easily, but if you like to role play as a different person for each class you're going to have to delete your previous character.
Any body of water deeper than your waist kills you. Yes, you heard me right. A fog monster that you can't see or fight just kills you, and the game reverts to your last save point.
Game-breaking quest bugs. In this game you have three NPC allies known as 'pawns', one permanent that levels up with you, and two that you will periodically switch in order to get higher level pawns. If they die, you can recover them at a 'rift stone' which are easily found throughout the map, but any items you gave them will have vanished. This includes quest items. I made the mistake of giving some very heavy quest items to a pawn that then got knocked off a bridge and into water, and that was that. I could get the pawn back, but the items I needed to complete the quest were gone forever.
The same monsters spawn in the exact same places on the map.
Graphics are hit or miss for 2012, but some of the npc character models and animations are truly horrible. Voice acting does not match npc movements half the time.
Crafting system is overwhelmed with useless items.
Overall, I'd recommend skipping this game unless you're okay with the single-save function. It had a lot of promise, but except for the boss battles Skyrim is a far, far, far better game in every way. If you have to get this, wait for a good sale.

Picked up the game on a whim. I'll try to be polite when reviewing this, but I don't think that will hold.
Graphics: 1/5. There are absolutely no graphics settings other than resolution, and it seems like the developers changed the textures from PS3-level graphics to something that belongs more on a PS2. For a game on PC, port or otherwise, this is...atrocious.
Sound: 2/5. The voice acting is wooden, and the sound effects are somewhat...underwhelming. I literally cringed at the hit sounds when fighting; the sounds seem more appropriate in a low-budget anime.
Gameplay: -5/5. So you've got lacklustre combo-based fighting, coupled with some of the least well-explained combat mechanics in any game. Sure, they explain heavy and light attacks, and directional combination attacks; and then you realise halfway down that there are grab attacks, that are never explained. Picking up items and equipping them requires a strange combination of keystrokes on both hands which does not pause the game while you switch to a weapon that isn't broken; enjoy eating a knuckle sandwich from your opponents in that time and get floored.
Update: There are yet more frustrations with the game's method of implementation. Being framerate locked to 30/60 fps for processing causes odd behaviour during button mash sequences. Combat is normally locked on a linear course between two combatants, ala Street Fighter; but because the camera does not rotate to show the two fighters side-on to the screen, this causes directional commands on a mouse-keyboard system to become awkward. When an enemy is to the bottom right of the screen, and your character is top left, what does sidestepping become? It's never clear in this case. If you have a PS4 controller or a X360 controller, this may be corrected - but why are you playing a port instead of the original?
Add to the fact that combat breaks whenever the two combatants aren't on the same floor level, and you've got even more problems. If there's so much as a narrow pillar in between you and your opponent, congratulations, someone else gets a cheap shot in your back because you aren't duelling them any more. Fighting next to stairs is next to impossible for this reason, as you are very likely to either knock them off the stairs or you get knocked onto the stairs, breaking combat.
Overall verdict: 0/5.
Easily the worst $20 I've ever spent on a game. Controls? Makes Fallout 4's menu system look like a godsend. Default key mappings are truly, utterly bizarre; in-game manual does not explain majority of basic combat maneuvers.

State of decay is an amazing zombie survival game. It doesn't rely heavily on the "jumpscare" which I love. The game isn't soley built on fighting zombies. It's about surviving the long game. In order to succeed you need to scavange, set up outposts, upgrade your home base. You need to look for weapons for yourself, but also buidling, medical, food, and ammo supplies for your group to survive.
You need to manage relationships with other groups of survivors by rescuing them, or ignoring the pleas for help so you can run another mission that you need for supplies.
You need to manage your folks as well, playing as one character can hurt you in the long run, you need to play multiple folks and level them up as well. If your singlely played character dies you're in for a long tough road ahead.  The game does a great job reminding you of this as each player will fatigue when they've been outside the safe zone for too long, so you are reminded that you need to swap characters.
The best part is for a zombie survival game you dont' need to kill zombies. There are no drops, no added bonus to offing them, other than keeping you and your home safe, so hiding in bushes, or staying quiet to save ammo and mele weapons isn't peanized one bit.

The autoaiming in melee is very frustrating, if there are more then two zombies ... you get it, it happens a lot.
And never ever think that you are save because you cleared the surroundings of a house and then enter it to clear the house itself. There will be hordes of zombies spawning right in those surroundings, if you use a single bullet ... your survivor is dead meat if that happens.
Caring for your homebase feels like SIMS on Crack. Once you get home from a mission someone feels scared. Once you are back from helping the scared guy (you go on a zombie hunt near your base) someone is ill and another one caught in some house so you need to pick him up. Before you even get to anyone of the new missions you learn that there is a new infestation in a house right next to your base. And all the time missed opportunities to help or rescue other survivors. And this happens with only a dozen survivors. I am really scared of ever getting more then this.
And the most annoying feature ... if you leave the game and get back to it after a week (because maybe you work, go to school or whatever real life you got) your base is almost empty of ressources, at least mine was.
After a patch my very skilled sniper character (took a lot of work and bullets to get her to it) lost all her levels in ranged combat but one. WHY?
All in all I have to say that the game is good and has got a lot of potential. Maybe if you love SIMS and DAY Z this game is the right for you. Otherwise you can get very frustrated ... A LOT.

"Blacklist" is the Best Splinter Cell game so far...
+ Visually and aurally spectacular. From a luxury yacht with a disco lounge to a petroleum plant on the Louisina coast, everything just looks right in Blacklist. It's so easy to get realism wrong (and everyone to trot out their favorite barely-understood phrase "uncanny valley"), but this game just looks and sounds excellent
+ More diverse gameplay. By explicitly embracing 3 different game modes, each level has been designed to support different play styles. It's great fun to go back to levels you now know and try them in different ways.
+ Strong story and performances. The story is the expected "a madman wants to plunge us into World War 3!", but it's really the relationship among Sam and his team that is so well done. Don't skip the dialog scenes!
+ Meta game works. Excellent progression and unlock system allows you to buy what you want mostly when you want it. The challenge system is also a powerful incentive to try different play styles
+ Lots of content. I'm probably 30+ hours in and have barely scratched multiplayer. I could easily spend 70 - 80 hours mastering the levels in the different styles. And multiplayer is, quite literally, endless.
What I didn't care for...
- Co-Op. Too much emphasis on Co-Op outside of MP. There are entire levels of the game (Briggs levels) that require co-op. But honestly, I don't really like to Co-Op with internet randoms, so I missed those levels.
- The AI is sometimes oscillates between truly unaware and hyper aware. Particularly on some of the later Embassy waves the enemies on the other side of the map instantly know when you've silently thrown a grenade
- DLC was weak. But I'm just trying to think of things to say here. Seriously, it is a fantastic game and I'm sorry I was so late to the party.

Tesla Effect is a love letter to the old FMV genre that stands on its own merits as a modern title. You play as a bumbling cybernoir detective named Tex Murphy in this reboot of a series that had its last installment in 1998. This game was crowdfunded by fans so newcomers (like myself) can feel a little lost but the story opens with Tex losing his memory of the last seven years which can help ease you in to the universe.
The gameplay is fairly simple. Full motion video cutscenes are separated by 3D envrionments that you must explore to find clues and solve puzzles in order to progress. The puzzles are not very difficult and you'll find most of the challenge comes from finding small items hidden in obscure locations. These scenes are made more lively with Tex's commentary as you observe different items in the games world. Depending on how observant and you are and your profficency for puzzle-sloving this game will vary from around 8 to 16 hours. I took just shy of 14 hours to complete my first playthrough and the only other FMV title I have played is the old X-Files game.
The real charm from this game comes from its characters and acting. It feels like watching a cheesy B-Movie in the best way possible. There are some real gems of good delivery to be found complemented by awkward lines that will make you grin. Tex himself is absolutely lovable and you will meet several genuinely interesting people along the way. The game doesn't take itself too seriously and focuses on being as enjoyable as possible.
Overall it's a well-executed modern interpretation of the old FMV adventure games and I am so glad I picked it up. If you are on the fence watch the "OMG FMV GOTY" trailer (it should be the first video on the store page). It sold me on buying this in under four minutes and I haven't looked back since.

PROS:
+ Fantastic gameplay that feels like a real RTS
+ Challenging campaign with good difficulty curve
+ Engrossing story and memorable characters
+ Incredible OST
+ Fast, fun multiplayer
+ Steady updates from the developers
CONS:
- RNG maps can make some campaign missions nigh impossible
- Some Heroic objectives are almost entirely luck
- Lack of control over micro can be frustrating
Generally, when a game's premise is that it's a simplified, streamlined version of a genre I love, the end result is something that feels like it's been watered down, like there was a good game and things got taken away from it.
Tooth and Tail turns that expectation around.  It feels like it was built from the ground up to be a solid RTS, rather than from the top down to be "an RTS with less things".  The gameplay is smooth, intuitive, and most importantly it hits a lot of the small elements of what makes playing an RTS game fun.
Beyond just gameplay, Tooth and Tail has an incredible setting.  From the first words in the cinematic opening to the last note in the end credits music, you'll feel pulled in to the grimdark humour of an extremely twisted version of Redwall.  The story has enough little twists and turns to keep you interested, and plenty of big moments, without suffering from the convoluted plots and often plodding pace RTS stories tend to suffer from.  As your armies starve and loyalties constantly shift and falter, every mission has a clear purpose to drive you to complete it.  The cipher-language Vyehsal and leitmotif heavy soundtrack help to tie everything together to create an immersive world that's easy to get invested in.
That said, the game is not without faults.  The biggest problem by far is the randomly-seeded maps.  While the maps are a main feature of the game, and the seeding generally keeps them to a fixed theme, there are some campaign missions that are completely reliant on whether you're unlucky enough for your first mill to be right next an enemy base, or which unit campfires spawn near you, or where the meat pickups are.  Especially with how challenging later levels can be, it gets frustrating when your biggest challenge is getting a reasonable map to play on.
Micro also feels frustrating at times.  While the streamlined controls are generally easy to work with, there are few things more irritating than positioning your army exactly how you want it, only for it to be destroyed by one accidental tap of "rally all".  Not being able to cancel orders or group unit types feels like a missing feature.
All in all, whether you've sunk countless weeks of gameplay into Brood War or your only interacting with the genre was an accidental purchase of Brutal Legend, Tooth and Tail is a fantastic RTS game you owe it to yourself to play.

Let me say this up front: I probably should not be trusted with first-person horror games. I'm a very jumpy person and tend to get very immersed in games, so first-person horror is like a waking nightmare for me no matter the quality. Keep that in mind when I say that Hektor creates a palpable sense of isolation and dread, and despite that I still hated it.
Honestly I was all set to review Hektor after about 20 minutes. In that time I never saw a monster or moved the plot forward in any way. Instead, I encountered three things that made me never want to play it ever again. The first was the intense, unshakable nausea that the game's sanity effects inflicted on me. Your character has some sort of dementia that causes their vision to constantly swirl and lose focus, and only a few minutes of fighting that in cramped, darkened hallways was enough to make me want to hurl. There are pills you're supposed to take regularly, ostensibly for your sanity, but they have no effect on the visual agony you are constantly exposed to.
The second was the layout of the game. Which is to say, there isn't any. Hektor's big gimmick is that the levels are procedurally generated on the fly, changing the places you just came from. This means you can walk down a hallway, poke your head in an office, go back down the hallway, and end up in a completely new place. This might sound cool to fans of House of Leaves or Grave Encounters, but think about what that means in terms of game flow. There is no way for you to get to a specific place in a level. Every time you round a corner, there's no way to know where you're going to end up. And this is bad because you need to reach certain rooms in a certain order to progress. So that means a lot of running down the same halls over and over until the game decides to cycle you into the area you need to be. I won't deny that it's an unsettling effect at first, and there's more than one good setpiece using it, but it really saps the appeal of exploration and makes progressing needlessly bloated.
The third was the♥♥♥♥♥♥hallway. There are fully voice-acted notes to be found from the different inhabitants of the Hektor complex. Some of these are pretty banal, like a guy wondering where his buddy is or a secretary commenting on the guy that always stares at her in the office. Then you end up in the dormitory wing, and find a note from the secretary about being♥♥♥♥♥♥♥every night. So you're listening to this girl describe her fear and discomfort whilst being♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ and then you realize that YOU CAN HEAR HER BEING♥♥♥♥♥♥♥in that very hallway at that very moment. Hektor, being a spooky game, has spooky voices that say things like "Run" or "I'll find you", but in this case it's a lot of "No please stop" and "Why are you doing this" between choked sobbing. There's even a cherry on this♥♥♥♥♥♥sundae, which is that the procedural level generation might make you run through the dorm wing multiple times. And yes, every time you pass through, she's being♥♥♥♥♥♥♥
I don't know what the point of Hektor is, and after all the physical and mental discomfort, I don't really care to know. There are plenty of first-person horror games that don't make me want to throw up or force me to listen to endless♥♥♥♥♥♥being acted out. They might not be as graphically impressive or well voice-acted, but at least they won't make me sick in nearly every sense of the word.

Dying to an orc isn't the same as dying to a hollow in Dark Souls, where your mistake is obvious and you only have yourself to blame. The quicktime events are dumb and add nothing to the gameplay, nor does the absence of a lock-on system, even a soft one. Countless times I died because I flipped over, or jumped onto the wrong enemy. And when there are literally 50 brutes wailing on you, it's almost impossible to fight back.
The controls are clunky (mounted combat is horrible in particular), and the combat is difficult for all the wrong reasons, so why did I keep playing? Not the story (forgettable), not the setting (not a huge LotR fan). I didn't even find the nemesis system all that interesting when most of the captains remained dead throughout my playthrough, and only became a threat if I purposefully hunted them. I... I just don't know, but I really liked climbing around and exploring the setting, and especially the stealth and archery missions. And at a certain point, right around when you enter the second area, you are strong/skilled enough to make combat inessential. You can roam, sneak past mobs, kill only what you need to, and run away. No lingering consequences.
So, play the campaign, do some side-quests, and ignore the DLC (more of the same, padded heavily with collectathon nonsense). And don't feel too disappointed with the ending. You play hide and seek with a BBEG who I guess was introduced in the opening cutscenes, but he is absent between the prologue and final mission.
9/10, Better Assassin's creed then Assassin's creed

But, that is also the charm of a deduction game, to try and find your allies.
Unfortunately, a majority of the players that I have played with do not try to actively win, but rather passively stay alive.
I would recommend the game to people, who enjoy deduction games, and encourage you to keep trying to use the chat even if you get no to little response from your fellow players. Although, as of this moment of writing the review, I cannot say if it is because of the servers or players, but there have been many leavers/dc in recent games that I have played. This of course negatively impacts the game, and it is understandable since the game is currently trending and the development team is understaffed as of my knowledge.
I would say the game is a plus in terms of its genre, but the high amount of leavers/dcs and players not actively trying to win makes the game less appealing. Steam not does have a "neutral-button" so I will have to give it a thumps down, due to the massive amount of leavers/dc and passivity from the players, that I have encountered.
My review is only based on my opinions and my own circumstances, which I have encountered. I would recommend giving the game a try, since the issues I have listed can be fixed with the help of the devs and community. You may also be lucky and not encounter the same problems that I have when you decide to try the game.
P.S I would like to believe that I have a 50% winrate or slightly higher due to actively participating in chat and trials, but I have not tracked winrate, so I cannot really say.

Wow. I'm ashamed I waited so long to buy this game. I've kept a close eye on Miscreated for about a year now and never made the purchase until a week ago. Major reason being: DAYZ. Dayz killed it for me. I dropped 35 dollars on dayz in 12/2012 and have logged over 700 hours of gameplay into that game so my review and comparison of these two games should hold some weight on anyone who's on the fence about buying miscreated.
First off: I would give this game about 8/10 where I would give dayz a 5/10.
Miscreated is everything the dayz devs wanted dayz to be.
Let me just get the cons of miscreated out of the way.
1 - The map is a little small. They are increasing the size though
2 - the graphics are cleaner but they lack the realism dayz had. Especially in terms of vegetation
3 - the firefights don't seem or feel as real as dayz's did. IDK if it's because the way the guns shoot or the amount of damage it takes to bring down a player.
That's honestly my only problems with this game thus far.  Of course it's in alpha so there are some bugs to work out but that's to be expected and it's nothing even close to the problems with DAYZ.
Basically, I've played dayz for almost 4 years and the only changes to the game I've noticed is I don't break my legs when walking on a pair of shoes, there are now barely functioning vehicles, and a little bit more guns.
Miscreated is actually fun when looting. The items just aren't on the floor in the middle of a living room. They spawn behind TV's, on top of wardrobe's etc..
Character interaction is massively superior to dayz. It's not just the community that's better, but I have noticed people don't just kill the♥♥♥♥♥♥out of you for no reason in miscreated. I've been killed of course, but I understood why I was killed. I'll be honest, in DAYZ, I was a bandit all the time. I wouldn't even consider talking to other players after about 6 months of playing because everyone was so damn back-stabby that you couldn't trust anyone.
Another pro of miscreated is the optimization. I don't get very many frame drops or rubber banding or anything of that sort. Even in the biggest cities.
I don't remember the name of the biggest city in the game because I have only been once but I was so impressed. The detail they added to buildings blows dayz out of the water. After playing for about an hour I logged off and found myself wanting to call in sick to work the next day to keep playing haha. I still haven't done that yet but It's definitely on my mind.
Another perk is VEHICLES. THEY WORK. You won't get your truck stuck on a fence post or any nonsense like that.
Also, LOOT RESPAWNS. You don't have to pray for a server restart to refill the loot. It just happens. I don't know when or how but it does.
So basically, if you're a dayz guy/gal and tired or bored of the same bs then check out miscreated. You won't be sorry. Plus, from what I hear, the dev's actually care about their customers so hop on the miscreated train and leave those ♥♥♥♥♥♥ careless dayz dev's in the past.

Got this game at a giveaway, so I had no "strings" attached to it, but man I love this game (Despite the fact that I've never heard of it before).
Pretty cool high-octane dogfighting action with a unique "vectoring" system where you can switch your fighter from Vector Mode to Harrier Mode. Switching quickly between the two modes will enable you to change direction very quickly; enabling you to pull off many tricks that would seem impossible in conventional dogfighting games like Ace Combat. Along with that comes the detailed and immersive world (not only graphical fidelity, but also really interesting aethestics) along with well thought out map designs. Kudos to the devs for this too. The amount of customization makes me feel at home and there's quite some freedom in it (though not unlimited).
But of course, not all games are perfect. Even the ones we love. From the reviews I read, Strike Vector (at its release) was very lacking in presentation, but the devs quickly fixed that, so it's okay now. Another point to work on is the fact that the game doesn't have a very big player base; despite the game being constantly updated. I played this game for a few hours, and I keep seeing the same names. Doesn't happen much in other online games that I play. I find it really hard to improve myselfif I keep playing with the same people over and over again, not mentioning that it becomes especially boring if they do not improve as well. And perhaps, a matchmaking system would be able to fix this along with the unbalances when more experienced players are stacked in one team.
Do I recommend it? Depends.
If you have $6 to spend on a random game; then yes.
If you don't have $6 to spend or would rather buy something else with that $6 dollars; then no.
But if you're just looking for a unique and exciting dogfighting experience, you've come to the right place.

"State of Decay" is quite simply a REALLY good game. I love to become thoroughly immersed in the environment of whatever game I'm playing and when "State of Decay" gave me a little scare (admittedly the only one) I knew this was happening! I happened to be concentrating so hard on my nighttime supply searches that a zombie crashing through the window over my shoulder made me jump in my chair! Now that's a good time!
The game includes several nice RPG elements like being able to select special abilities for each character you control (reached 12 characters in my full playthrough, which means it was a little like playing an RPG with a party of 12!) but this is limited by their pregenerated list of stats. The basic 4 are Cardio, Fighting, Shooting, and Wits, with some characters bringing in largely useless additional stats like being good at sports trivia (???). It is here that the game's regrettable lack of voice talent becomes plainly obvious as several characters seem to be voiced by the same people, somewhat detracting from the overall experience, especially when your chosen NPC backup sounds exactly like you!
You also have control over what buildings to construct for your base, which is also governed by the size of the structure you inhabit and pre-existing buildings. These can have fairly basic functions like a store room, or play a role in increasing one of your stats more rapidly (a library speeds up "Wits" improvement which in turn lessens the time it takes you to search for supplies). Vehicles are a useful part of the game (unless you want to run EVERYWHERE), although the selection is unfortunately very limited. Why no abandoned harvester in a field with which one could mince zombies into fertilizer?! It is important to note here that the game seems to take place in more or less real time - if it says it's going to take about half an hour for people in your store room to have a go at preserving some food then it's actually going to take half an hour. The game does also seem to take the time that the player spends away from it into consideration as well, advancing day to night if you've been away for a sufficiently long while and adjusting your supplies accordingly. I found that I quite liked this feature in general, as whenever I came back to the game I had left the previous day I was always met with a report of the previous game day's activities (characters who returned from missions, supplies utilised, random events, etc.)
The game's graphics are generally of a very high standard, but the individual characters can occasionally appear "cartooonish", even at the highest settings, somewhat detracting from what is otherwise a thoroughly immersive experience of survival in the zombie apocalypse. "State of Decay" is straightforward in terms of format - gather supplies while completing smaller side missions as the main plotline contines - and it can even become quite tough on the odd occasion when you've become a little over-confident in a character's fighting skill and try to take on the world all by yourself! This is when the "Perma-death" feature of the game hits home hardest, as the long hours that you've devoted to exploring with a particular character, constantly honing their combat skills, suddenly come up against the brick wall of a zombie horde and no more painkillers!
Admittedly, "State of Decay" is still a little buggy: zombies regularly get stuck in walls and can't be hit or shot until you decide to leave them alone. Then they jump out and chew into your neck?!  I must however say that no bug was ever able to sour my experience of what is a great representation of the zombie apocalypse genre and a solid purchase for anyone looking for a diverting and enjoyable action-RPG.

Oh where do I begin?  WofS4 is an amazing game full of freedom, bloody combat, sword collecting, martial arts mastering, midnight love making sessions, and best of all you decide your path.
You start as a simple samurai entering a town on the brink of war between the police, forigners, old guard, and the government.  Through your actions, you will decide the fate of each one... or you can just get drunk, sleep at the inn, and take the next boat out of here.  This game revolves around new game plus in that way.  You can start fresh any time, keeping what weapons and moves you earned, and later money and items.
Previous enemies will become allies, previous allies that were plot central will become unimportant.. it all matters what street you walk down, and what fight you wish to pick.  The game has a very helpful time scroll to help you keep track of events.  Though as I said, you can easily just mess around and accomplish nothing.  Take up some fishing, do some gambling, find random women to sleep with in the most Japanese of ways possible...
There are A LOT of weapons you can collect, and even more since you can take apart and put back together new combinations.  Not only that but there are hundred or so fighting styles, with hundreds of moves that you can master.  Most of them are even useful.  The character customization is rather deep as well, allowing you to trick out your character with masks and accesseries that you can not only place, but move them XYZ anywhere on your body.  This game is great for completionists as well as people who just want a good story, and feel like a samurai.
Worth every penny, but I do have one gripe that I want to get off my chest.
Weapons have a charm system, like a tic-tac-toe kind of thing when making a weapon.  To get something really good takes a LOT of grinding.  I mean it is worth it, but it can take awhile.
Besides that...  seriously, get this game.  Give it some time, and you will learn to enjoy it.

Splinter Cell: Blacklist is the game the series has always wanted to be.
It acts as a culmination of every cool idea the series has ever had, finally finding that middle ground between the hardcore stealth that used to define the series, and the faster, more approachable and dynamic gameplay introduced in Conviction. It still isn’t perfect, as Ubisoft has stubbornly held onto a few of the less severe problems of the franchise, but for all intents and purposes Blacklist is far and away the best entry the series has ever had, which coming from someone who has enjoyed every Splinter Cell game ought to mean something.
The biggest problem of past Splinter Cell games up to Conviction was their strict adherence to set paths through levels, which were often difficult to discern and as a result required trial and error to get through. They presented you with a huge assortment of gadgets and tactical moves but rarely allowed you to use them unless they explicitly planned for you to, essentially removing any player choice with how you tackle a mission.
Conviction in contrary was the series rebirth, removing many of the extraneous stealth options but introducing levels that were far more open, and allowed a greater amount of freeform play. It transformed the series from one in which you were constantly vulnerable to having you be that danger, hunting down enemies and making your way through areas like a hi-tech ninja.
Blacklist as I said before takes the best aspects of both these fairly different experiences and rolls them into a gloriously dynamic bundle of options and an endless supply of ways to make use of them. For once you are no longer punished for playing however you want to play, be it sneaking through levels leaving no trace you were ever there or rolling in guns blazing and allowing no witnesses, and paths and opportunities for every playstyle have been designed into each level, never locking you into one particular way of playing but giving you the choice the take on encounters any way you see fit.
Expanded climbing options offer a level of verticality to levels that further extends your tactical abilities, often allowing access to secret paths or surprise takedowns. It made me conscious of the environment and how I could best make use of it, and nearly without fail anytime I looked for a solution it was there waiting for me.
I always felt in control playing Blacklist, whether I was hiding from hostiles or taking shots at them, and this freedom makes for an experience that’s extremely empowering and encourages you to try out different approaches. I’ve never replayed a Splinter Cell game, but Blacklist gave me reason to revisit levels and see what I might have missed the first time around and a scoring system that rewarded exploiting every tool in my arsenal. Being able to customize said arsenal further allowed me to tailor my playstyle how I wanted, ranging from which guns and gadgets I used straight down to the color of the LEDs in my goggles. These choices all mattered and I was able to see my abilities increase as I progressed and gained better gear, giving me yet another reason to go back to older missions and see how much I had improved.
Unfortunately, much of this doesn’t factor into the 4th Echalon side missions (which also act as the coop mode, though most can be played solo if you want). These smaller supplementary missions tended to lock me into a particular playstyle and in many cases harshly punished me if I attempted to deviate from it as I had been able to the entire campaign. It’s not that these missions aren’t still enjoyable or are particularly poorly designed, but they represent a step back to some of Splinter Cell’s most archaic design principles in a game that takes so many strides to finally distance itself from them. There are a few moments in the campaign when this happens as well,, but thankfully they are generally brief and at least contextually make sense.
Context is more important this time around, as Blacklist continues Conviction’s trend of finally giving me a story that I could be bothered to follow. The plot is a fairly standard Clancy terror conspiracy with an outcome of World War 3 proportions, but it’s told in a way that removes the dry, technobabel of past narratives with one that’s far easier to follow and allows for substantially more characterization. Your team at 4th Echalon is comprised of characters with actual personality, with little exchanges you can take part in between missions adding to the subplot of the personal dynamics between such a small, tightly knit team. It has a lot of ground to make up still, but the fact that I wasn’t skipping cutscenes because I actually cared and was interested in what happened is a marked improvement and hopefully will continual to improve as the series goes on.
There are still a handful of stubborn rough edges clinging to Blacklist from Splinter Cell’s past, but the overwhelming improvements and intelligent design present kept them from ever being more than a minor nuisance. I’ve loved Splinter Cell since its exception, but this is the first time that I feel almost everything has come together as planned, with smarter level designs, an excellent sense of progression, and the allowance for so many different playstyles that could likely all make up their own games. It’s everything I’ve wanted the series to be and then some, and I'm almost giggy thinking about where it could go now it's gotten to this point.

My opinion is kinda split on this one. the one hand the writing is compelling, the character and party options are staggering, the art is pretty, the quest solution options are plentiful, and the dungeons have a decent variety of traps and secrets.
However, there are some issues that dragged down my enjoyment of the game.  Melee is based around "engagements" where a melee unit gets a free attack if an enemy tries to retreat from it. However, this also applies if the enemy tries to shift at all.  This is... problematic in the narrow corridors and dungeons that make up half of the combat arenas, with maybe one or two of your units clogging a doorway that could fit four if engagment allowed shifting of positions.  I now loathe this mechanic, which could be fixed by simply allowing units to slide around each other without breaking engagement.
The interface is muddy at best.  Battles are obscured behind a cloud of muddy particle effects that don't settle until one or the other side is dead, leaving you looking at a cluster of indistinguishable green and red circles and imagining the epic battle that must be going on under the looney-tunes cloud of dust.
I'm a fan of taking tactical advantage of terrain in a fight, and this game did nothing to scratch that itch.  Different dungeons are tactically interchangable.  I was particularly disappointed by several abilites with strong pushback being thwarted by the fact that every deadly cliff and pit of acid is guarded by an invisible wall.  After a while I found myself using the exact same opening combo of brute-force abilties to defeat mooks and bosses alike, leaving the majority of my characters' talents unused.
I wish I could recommend it wholeheartedly.  But I'm not sure slogging through another dozen fights to catch the story are worth it.`

A New School Game for Old School Gamers!
Pillars of Eternity brings back the Infinity Engine style RPG that many of us played and loved. Taking inspiration from Baldur's Gate. Icewind Dale, and Planescape: Torment, Pillars of Eternity offers up a great experience for anyone who was a fan of those old games and are looking for a new game to play in a similar vain. It definitely lives up to its status as a "spiritual successor." While playing, it has the depth and story of Baldur's Gate, a soundtrack and tactical combat of Icewind Dale, and the walls of text and fluff that Torment had.
Even if you have not played those styles of games, Pillars is a great game to play still.
The positives of Pillars of Eternity include:
1.An in depth character creation system including many different races and unique classes (and backgrounds!) that only fuel the RPG experience
2. A unique system that still has a pen and paper feel to it
3. A game that facilitates role playing a character and developing them.
4. Both recruitable NPCs and the ability to make your own recruitable party members.
5. An engaging story set in a unique and interesting world
One of Pillars downsides is it lacks the multiplayer mode that Baldur's Gate and Icewind Dale had, but hopefully an update or DLC will add it. If not, I sure hope a sequel does. Now you may not view this as a downside, so that may not be a concern to you. Also wish the Stronghold function had a little more depth to it.
All in all, Pillars of Eternity is a great game that harkons back to the old days of some of the best RPGs and can now consider itself amongst their ranks. Get it. Play it. Enjoy it.

This game really scratched the itch for me--I love adventure games, especially ones with full motion video, though I somehow missed out on the Tex Murphy series back in the day. Playing Tesla Effect, I kept thinking--man, we are REALLY missing out by not having more FMV in modern games. Live actors, especially likable ones with a good script to work with, add so much emotional depth to a game that just can't be delivered via 3D models. Furthermore, the FMV is integrated here very smoothly into the gameplay, and even when the segments run long, you're so invested in the story that you don't feel the game is playing itself.
I guess the game won't appeal to everyone, but I am very happy to have found it. I played it through to the end without ever feeling bored or frustrated. Furthermore, all of the nods to the older Tex Murphy games (they include a lot of the footage from those games in the forms of flashbacks) have whetted my appetite to try them out, too.
This game is more focused on story and characters than Myst or Riven and the like. It's also helpfully broken into "days," which you can get through in an hour or less if you don't have all day to play. The dseigners also did a good job providing you with just enough areas to explore and options to try that you don't get overwhelmed, yet still feel that you're the one solving the case.
In short, I really enjoyed this game and highly recommend it to anyone who likes adventures. One thing's for sure--if I ever see a new Tex Murphy game on Steam, I'm buying or pre-ordering that baby. This game would've been well worth paying full price and then some.

I bought this game solely for MP and haven't been disappointed.
70 hours out of a game at this price point? Hell yeah! And I'm still enjoying it.
(I've barely scratched SP, played one or two missions before diving straight into MP - read other people's reviews for that - SP just isn't my thing)
In North America at least it isn't hard to find a game. Sometimes it takes a few minutes to get into one but honestly that's not long. But man, the MP is fun. Games are dynamic, varied. I'd say the balance is pretty good - it encourages variety and experimentation. Obviously there is a "meta" but it hasn't stopped evolving - which is a good sign.
ALSO: Another reason why Tooth and Tail is great is because of the design of the game, you can’t be outclassed by someone with crazy APM. This makes macro strategy way more important. I usually prefer turn based games so this is appealing to me, and why I prefer Tooth and Tail to other RTS.

Having played this game all the way through (on my brother's account) and in the middle of a new playthrough, I can definitely say that Dark Souls is one of my favorite games of all time. It's certainly not flawless (*cough cough Demon Ruins and Lost Izalith COUGH*), but all of the good things about it overshadow the bad things almost entirely.
You are the Chosen Undead in a decaying world, near the end of the Age of Fire and the start of the Age of Dark. All of the heroes and gods have either died or gone completely insane, and it's your task is to usurp the Great Lord Gwyn to either get a Dark Age going, or make everyone's crappy lives last a little bit longer. The story is kind of like Half-Life where you can be as involved in the story as you want to. You can ask, "why does this huge blob of fire with a face and giant tentacles get miffed when I looted that corpse," and dig a little bit deeper in to the story, or you can say, "GIANT DEMON'S ANGRY? YEEEEAH LET'S DRENCH THE WALLS WITH HIS BLOOD AND♥♥♥♥♥♥ON HIS FAT DEAD BODY!"
The world of Dark Souls drips with atmosphere in a way which no other game I've played has captured. The whole kingdom of Lordran and the environments related to it are so detailed and well thought-out, and the amount of ways that most areas are connected makes the game feel so much more than just loading screens stapling levels together. Although, it feels like the way you get around some of the areas was designed after making the area itself. For instance, a portion in the city of Anor Londo requires you to traverse up a random buttress that gives you no clear visual indication of being able to climb up it. Another thing I love about the world in Dark Souls is the fact that, if you can see a huge tower or monument or whatever in the distance, chances are you'll go there some point in the game and that there's something in there that wants your head on a silver platter.
The gameplay of Dark Souls is challenging, but fair (except Demon Ruins and Lost Izalith COUGH). Many of the weakest enemies can still pose a threat later on in the game if you let your guard down, but it rarely feels like your death was the game's fault. Taking down the baddies, big or small, requires skill, timing, and memorization of their attack patterns. You could get squashed flat in to a pancake several times in a row by a giant knight, but once you know all of his attacks you can kill him in no time flat like the medieval Neo made out of beef jerky that you are.
Overall, Dark Souls is a must-play for anyone looking for a significantly challenging game, deep story, and plenty of fun.

I have played shellshock live 2 on the browser for quite a while before I played the steam version. One thing I did not like in the browser version is in game purchases which they took out in the steam version. So I am really happy about that. It gives everyone an even ground and provides fair combat.
I love the steam version and would recommend it to anyone having an interest in artillery games.
Here is the pros and cons for shellshock live.
PROS:
1. Simple yet elegant graphics design. One does not get bored looking at it.
2. The massive amounts of weapons to obtain and upgrade. At the time I wrote this review, there are 367 weapons including the upgrades.
3. Active developer and community. The developer works with the player community to constantly improve the game with new content, new features or bug fixes.
4. Many game modes to choose from ( 8 I believe). With countless customization options that will satisfy every need. For example, you want to play with players your level, you can do that, you want a more fun and challenging game play, you can set mods to one weapons and wind to high etc.
5. 4 sections of tank upgrades to master!
5. And many more!
CONS?
1. Time consuming. Is it? I have played for 60 hours and I am already level 83. I know the game is a grind, but isn't every multiplayer game? For example, I played warframe for 360 hours, or grinded for 360 hours. Shellshock live in my opinion is a grind, yes, but compared to some other "popular" games out there, it is not a grind at all. I know low level is frustrating and everyone wants to level up, everyone wants to win. But be patient and you will eventually reach level 80 in 100 hours. Besides, the real grind starts at level 90. Unless you're hardcore and want to get every single achievement. Which I advise to not to do if you want a social life... Don't make such a big deal out of it!
2. The music gets repetitive after a while and sounds boring, but that's not a big deal. Just run some music in the background or something.
3. Hackers? This is also a big deal according to a lot of people. IT IS NOT! I have yet to see a hacker in the 60 hours i played. And besides, the latest updates reinforced security to eliminate the piratically non-existent hackers. And also, people complain about rulers......... yes, there are people who use rulers, but there are multiple ways you can take care of this. First, play a game with them, and lose, then set atmospheric nudge to ON, or set high wind, and then play the next game, and then accuse them of using a ruler, and they will be too ashamed to admit it and leave...  and yeah.
Overall, shellshock live is a really fun and addictive game to pass the extra times you have. There is so much to do, so much to learn and so much rage when you miss a shot.... ayyyy.

I love this game but its has a lot of flaws, if you dont mind those you will have a REAL fun time.

Is one of the best RPG's I've played. While the story might be a little weak at times, its overall premise is interesting and the lore added by the Dark Arisen DLC is compelling.
Magic in this game actually feels powerful. You can summon giant maelstroms in the middle of a fight and watch it suck and vault enemies up into the air before hearing their bones break as they land. You can summon meteors from the sky to kill giant enemies like ogres and cyclopes, gryphons and cockatrices. If you're not into magic, you can go the strider route and climb onto enemies Shadow of the Colossus style and slice them up. Warriors and fighter abilities don't feel weak, they actually put weight into their attacks.
You have followers in this game that are called Pawns. You make your main pawn (where you can customise their entire appearance, from their height to their weight -- both of which have gameplay effects. Larger and heavier pawns can carry more items and can also weigh down enemies like dragons to stop them from being able to fly. Smaller pawns are more nimble and are better at dodging attacks) and can hire the pawns of other players. Pawn AI improves the more you play with them, they will learn enemy weaknesses and abilities, can assist you with quests and will become knowledgeable about areas you visit.
Pawn behaviour changes depending on their inclination and how knowledgeable they are. Utilitarian pawns will try and take advantage of enemy weaknesses better and more often than non-utilitarian ones. Your mage/sorcerer pawn saw an undead warrior? It'll bless your weapons with fire/holy magic to help take them down better. I've had non-mage/sorcerer pawns pick up things like exploding barrels to use as weapons, too.
Fights against dragons, wyms and drakes are fun. Listening to them taunt you in Wyrmspeak during battle makes the fights feel more personal and intense. Watching them swipe a pawn (that you might be very fond of, lmao) into their grasp  before trying to possess them so that they'll turn against you makes you feel even more invested in taking them down.
I just love this game because so much thought was put into it gameplay-wise. Wandering around at night is dangerous, but you have a lantern (that needs to be refilled with oil occasionally) that'll light your path.  So imagine how spooky♥♥♥♥♥♥becomes when a harpy grabs you out of nowhere and drops you into a river or some other body of water, which then puts out your lantern. No oil flasks? Better hope your pawns picked some up, then. Harpies like to grab, a lot. If your pawn/arisen is small, they'll have less trouble snatching you to try and kill you by dropping you from a height. If you're heavier, they might not be able to lift you off the ground. If you're with a well-trained pawn, they can catch you to save you from the drop or might be savvy enough to attack/kill the harpy so that she releases her grip ASAP.
This game has a lot to it, and I hope Capcom will make a sequel in the future.

I first played this on my PS3, then picked up the PC port of the game when it was on sale.  As you can see from my play hours, I've completed the game and I can honestly say (having played the whole thing all the way through on two seperate systems) that it is one of my favorites.  Is it perfect?  Oh, no.  Definitely not.  Most of the complaints you see here are valid ones:  Occaisionally laughable voice acting, goofy and sometimes extremely awkward dialogue, tendency towards jogging sim, etc...
Having said all of that, I can also say that it has a huge beautiful world that is filled with visually interesting things to explore, find, and kill.  The combat system is fantastic, esspecially when fighting big monsters.  Magic is suitablely epic and fun (though I'm partial to the slightly less epic Arcane Archer and his game-breaking ricochet shot). The in-game soundtrack is excellent and, in some places, downright pretty.  Despite its flaws this is a genuinely fun and interesting open world game.  One downside:  The original game had a super-fun rock-n-roll theme that they ditched for what sounds like someone's significant other's opportunity to make it big.  It's downright awful.  Bummer because I actually bought and still listen to the original song.  What can I say?  I'm an anime pop junkie.

This is an excellent game.  It has got a lot going for it, and it also has some oddities that you may like, or you may find flawed.
What I liked: It has an excellent fighting system.   Fighting groups of enemies can feel very satisfying once you figure out what moves you like, how well they chain together, and how often they stun or knock down enemies.  It can feel very artful, which drives you to want to progress more, gaining more moves or trying different professions.  Scaling the large enemies is always very fun as well.
The character customization is neat, as you can be huge, small, etc.  The outfits can be mixed and matched to make very unique styles, and almost all of them are excellent.
The Pawn system is super enjoyable.  You get to make your own, building them, dressing them, affecting their personality, and then you get to hire two more from other players, should you wish.  Anyone in turn can hire your pawn.  This creates an exciting dynamic, where you want your pawn to be cool enough to be picked, and you develop wordless partnerships with other gamers through their pawns, rehiring them as you both level up.
What I didn't like: The story has a weird focus and a weird pace, and in many ways doesn't care what you want.  At more than one occasion my character made out with people I did not intend, either because simply doing a certain sidequest requires it, or due to a romance system that requires effort to keep it from going wrong.
Sometimes the dialogue is klunky.  Everyone says "aught" entirely too much, but it's not the worst.
Pawns have a tendancy to babble on annoyingly.  You can affect their personality to keep it down, but still.  The problem here, is that it is never small talk, never friendly jibbing, no human talk.  It's always them offering a tip, which is a problem when you've heard it a million times, and makes their personality suck.  It's all quite tolerable though.
Thing's I didn't like but I know others did:  The story is super nontraditional.  I'll call it interesting, but I felt no pleasure about it.  Other's I know loved it.
There is an enormous focus on end game dungeoneering.  I'm the type of gamer that doesn't see the point of fizzling on after the grand finale, so I like to do everything before the last boss and be done.  This game expects you to do end game dungeons, has a more difficult post game word, and finally a new game plus that gets you ready for the Dark Arisen content which is too difficult to attempt after only one playthrough.  Excellent news for some, not quite what I'm here for.  This content has it's own narrative though, so it's not just a bonus dungeon, it's another chapter.
All in all I really enjoyed it, and I would love to see a sequel where they improve upon this already excellent game.

From a game developer's point of view, Way of the Samurai 4's concept is pure genius: create as few assets as possible and combine them to get as much variety as possible. And in practice, unlike many other such attempts, it works out surprisingly good!
From a player's perspective, there are a few things to consider before you dive in though. If you only want to go through the story, then you will probably get the worst ending in 2-3 hours of gametime and will feel let down, not having seen the vast majority of what the game has to offer. If you don't like the goofy humor of the game (you can check the screenshots to get a very good idea), you're gonna have a bad time. If you expect a AAA PC title with next gen graphics and full customizability, you are going to be disappointed since this is the port of a 5 years old console game with only very basic PC options, most of which are in the form of configuration files. (There's nothing inherently wrong with the port though, or at least it worked just fine for me and my XBox 360 controller but your milage may vary.) If you want to play every game on the hardest difficulty, you are probably also going to have a bad time. Although the only two options for a new character are Easy and Normal, these are more like Diablo's difficulty settings. You are not expected to play the higher difficulties with a new character.
With all that in mind, there's plenty of ways (of the samurai, wink-wink) to have fun in this game! First of all, you there's the main story with a bad ending, 7 easy to get endings plus 2 hidden endings you can get through manipulating events in previous playthroughs. That's right! The when you get to an ending, you will recieve a score based on how you performed and get Samurai points you can spend on unlocking new features like the Hard and Harikiri difficulty level, special customization options for your character or even new weapon style categories like Dual Wielding and Guns. Then you can start a new platyhrough with the same character, keeping your weapons, styles and also some of the major changes in the village will carry over and those changes will affect your new plathrough!
Then there's also the Dojo where you can train pupils and fight challengers who can drop special styles, there's nightcrawling which is a pretty stupid but fun "dating" minigame, you can fish, you can do random missions for random NPCs for a little money, you can do questlines for a few named NPCs for lots of money, you can do some epic side quests if you do all questlines and get unique styles and weapons, you can forge your own weapons from parts, you can upgrade your weapons, you can get unlockable enchants on your weapons, you can fight with a fish as a weapon... The list goes on and on.
So yeah, I would recommend, if you don't expect it to be too serious and are willing to spend the time to explore the game in multiple playthroughs!

As I'm sure most know at this point, Middle-earth: Shadow of Mordor is a 3rd-person, open world game, in the same vein as an Assassin's Creed title. Your character, Talion, has been "denied death," and is now linked to the "soul" (?) of an Elf. You are cursed, and must break this curse if you are to join your slain family in the afterlife.
This is a nice touch, as it makes every death "canon." You become known as a ranger who can't die, with Orcs referring to you as the "gravewalker."
However, I found that a lot of the game didn't resonate with me, someone unfamiliar with the world and lore of Tolkien. The inclusion of Gollum was a nice touch though - he mirrors the movement and speech that you witnessed in the films. For those in my situation, I wouldn't recommend spending time gathering collectibles. This did not enhance my experience - the amount of upgrade currency given by each collectible is really quite inconsequential, and you are given no reward for "catchin' 'em all." The collectibles seem to be "winks" to people familiar with the lore.
The most fun parts of the game, in my opinion, are:
* Some of the sword and bow legends, where you must kill an insane amount of Orcs in one battle.
* The Ratbag story arc, where you aid an underwhelming Orc in being a warchief.
* Systematically taking down the warchiefs, especially once the brand ability is unlocked.
* Some of the final main story quests in each section, "The Black Captain" and "Lord of Mordor" quests.
So many of the abilities that Talion learns are fun to use, from stuns to beast riding to branding enemies that can later fight for you. The rune system is also interesting, and I found myself switching runes in and out depending on the situation I found myself in. All of the upgrades are worthwhile, and completing the weapon legends seems to be the best way to earn upgrade currency.
The game can be quite difficult if you attempt to go after Orc captains immediately. Often, the orcs will be immune to whatever approach you're taking, and they quickly call their friends into the fray. You'll think you have a captain isolated, only to find yourself quickly surrounded by 30 orcs. Sometimes more captains run into the battle, each with their own abilities and specific ways they must be defeated. Don't be afraid to run away and heal with one of the many healing plants in the vicinity! I'd recommend starting with a few things other than dealing with Orc captains (like main quests), and feel like it's a good idea to always have intel on one before making a play.
Torvin's quest line was probably my least favorite - a jolly little dwarf. He's just very similar to jolly little dwarves that exist in every game where there are dwarves. I also found the outcast rescue missions, survival challenges, and hunting challenges to be not worthwhile. Additionally, the finale of the game is a bit underwhelming.
Overall, the game is a good time. Movement and combat feel good, and toying with the nemesis system is a lot of fun. I'm looking forward to the sequel later this year.

My opinion is kinda split on this one. the one hand the writing is compelling, the character and party options are staggering, the art is pretty, the quest solution options are plentiful, and the dungeons have a decent variety of traps and secrets.
However, there are some issues that dragged down my enjoyment of the game.  Melee is based around "engagements" where a melee unit gets a free attack if an enemy tries to retreat from it. However, this also applies if the enemy tries to shift at all.  This is... problematic in the narrow corridors and dungeons that make up half of the combat arenas, with maybe one or two of your units clogging a doorway that could fit four if engagment allowed shifting of positions.  I now loathe this mechanic, which could be fixed by simply allowing units to slide around each other without breaking engagement.
The interface is muddy at best.  Battles are obscured behind a cloud of muddy particle effects that don't settle until one or the other side is dead, leaving you looking at a cluster of indistinguishable green and red circles and imagining the epic battle that must be going on under the looney-tunes cloud of dust.
I'm a fan of taking tactical advantage of terrain in a fight, and this game did nothing to scratch that itch.  Different dungeons are tactically interchangable.  I was particularly disappointed by several abilites with strong pushback being thwarted by the fact that every deadly cliff and pit of acid is guarded by an invisible wall.  After a while I found myself using the exact same opening combo of brute-force abilties to defeat mooks and bosses alike, leaving the majority of my characters' talents unused.
I wish I could recommend it wholeheartedly.  But I'm not sure slogging through another dozen fights to catch the story are worth it.`

A New School Game for Old School Gamers!
Pillars of Eternity brings back the Infinity Engine style RPG that many of us played and loved. Taking inspiration from Baldur's Gate. Icewind Dale, and Planescape: Torment, Pillars of Eternity offers up a great experience for anyone who was a fan of those old games and are looking for a new game to play in a similar vain. It definitely lives up to its status as a "spiritual successor." While playing, it has the depth and story of Baldur's Gate, a soundtrack and tactical combat of Icewind Dale, and the walls of text and fluff that Torment had.
Even if you have not played those styles of games, Pillars is a great game to play still.
The positives of Pillars of Eternity include:
1.An in depth character creation system including many different races and unique classes (and backgrounds!) that only fuel the RPG experience
2. A unique system that still has a pen and paper feel to it
3. A game that facilitates role playing a character and developing them.
4. Both recruitable NPCs and the ability to make your own recruitable party members.
5. An engaging story set in a unique and interesting world
One of Pillars downsides is it lacks the multiplayer mode that Baldur's Gate and Icewind Dale had, but hopefully an update or DLC will add it. If not, I sure hope a sequel does. Now you may not view this as a downside, so that may not be a concern to you. Also wish the Stronghold function had a little more depth to it.
All in all, Pillars of Eternity is a great game that harkons back to the old days of some of the best RPGs and can now consider itself amongst their ranks. Get it. Play it. Enjoy it.

This may be my 1st review for an RPG-based game. Normally, I find myself getting bored in RPG's, especially since starting over the game means going through the exact same steps as before. In fact, of the many types of games I enjoy to play, I'm not sure RPG's are even in my top-5. Then, comes Pillars of Eternity:
For a game essentially "built from the ground up", it far exceeded my expectations. The story is very unique and keeps your attention. The way you interact with others means endless replayability (be evil in 1 game, and noble in the next). The combat was fairly new to me. Took some time getting used to pause mid-fight to tell my companions what spell to cast or enemy to attack. Once you are used to it, you can quickly learn how to take on very dangerous enemies. And the graphics are excellent. Everyone says with a game like this "every class has its plus and minus, but this one is better". While true, that is a huge understatement. Each class works completely different, and although there have been plenty of arguments as to who the best "class" is, they are all powerful in their own way. My main experience is with a Druid, Wizard and Fighter (Fighter being my favorite so far because, well, it's fun).
Overall, this is a game almost anyone could enjoy. Unique, lots of fun, very in-depth, great gameplay and graphics. 9/10

I'll preface this by saying that I've never played a Tex Murphy Adventure before Tesla Effect.  They were very much on my radar and I remember quite well wanting to play Under a Kiling Moon when I was young.  FMV games for the most part were a flash in the pan fad that really overstayed their welcome in the early/mid 90's.  Some did it very well and are among my favorite adventures (Gabriel Knight 2: The Beast Within,) some were flawed but still highly enjoyable (Phantasmagoria) and some were pretty abysmal (anything released on Sega CD.)  Tesla Effect falls promptly into the middle catagory.
The story, characters, presentation and FMV are pretty fantastic.  The acting is terrible but in the best possible way.  Any positive things I have to say about this game all center around those aspects.  The game environment and gameplay on the other hand did leave quite a bit to be desired.
The world itself is pretty ugly by todays standards.  It was like navigating a 1999 poly environment.  I guess you could argue that works for the game since it's a return to a medium long dead since the 90's. The gameplay relies HEAVILY on finding items as every adventure games should.  The real trouble here is that the items and world are so murky and blocky that they blend together.  I highly recommend playing on "casual" settting because your flashlight will call sparkly attention to these things.  Even then it was still difficult finding them.
I feel bad for complaining about this game because it has so much character.  I just wish more time and effort were put into the gameplay.   Also I hugely enjoyed the easter eggs that pulled video from the original Tex adventures.  They really made me want to go back and see what I was missing.  Sadly they were missing from the final half of the game or I was just missing them.
Still a recommended play for anyone looking for a nostalgic trip back to 90's FMV

I have a lot of problems with Tesla Effect: A Tex Murphy Adventure, and I really really wish I didn’t. I want to make sure before I spill out all my complaints I make this very clear: games like this need support, dev teams who are willing to take the risk faithfully resurrecting the genres and characters many of us cherish from our childhood should be applauded. No matter how much I dislike this game I think that it was a competent remake of a classic game that has a strong cult following and a lot of loving support. I would be a hypocrite if I condemned this game for being itself simply because I’m not into the content while at the same time begging for developers to bring back Banjo Kazooie.
With all my respect for the resurrection of the Full Motion Video (FMV) crime adventure on the table, I thought The Tesla Effect was not very good. Right from the beginning, inspecting objects around the opening area leads to a multitude of (what I presume to be) clips from the original Tex Murphy games. They are abysmally cheesy and for someone who never experience the franchise in the past, they feel like inside jokes that I’m completely left out of. The cheese I can absolutely forgive because the original games were from a very different time culturally and technologically, however the feeling of being left out as a new player is really disheartening. Next up is a very personal and subjective complaint with very little merit in a review of a game like this, but I find FMV cutscenes to be disturbingly unnerving. Every time a cutscene would trigger I was so uncomfortable. I’m not sure if it’s the clash of real people against digital backdrops or if it’s just that principal of the uncanny valley, either way I just could not stomach that art style. On to a very different issue; I’m not sure how the original game played, but not being able to walk while moving the mouse is absolutely ridiculous. I don’t care if that was part of the “charm” of the original game or not, having to walk forward, stop, look left with the mouse, and then be able to walk forward again is just inexcusable. Finally, I have never had a game run my rigs so hot before. On my brand new laptop (which I frequently use to play games like Space Engineers Civilization BE and Bioshock Infinite) after only 15 minutes of play I was unable to use the keyboard. I typically hit around 40-45C near the GPU but running Tesla Effect caused the majority of my keyboard to hit 50 degrees!
I support the developers with all my heart and I think more risks like this need to be taken, but Tesla Effect was just not right. Between personal and mechanical issues, I would not recommend this game to anyone.

The thing I enjoy the most about this game is how strong its building and customization aspects are. The exploring aspect of the game will get stale once you reach the final stages, but you can milk A LOT of fun out of building houses, bases and villages and populating them with NPCs. You can hire a crew with different little perks and choose their uniform, you can set up a little museum planet where you store all the rare artifacts you collect in your journeys, you can use the wiring mode to make lots of different contraptions a la Minecraft, etc. Even though I found the main quest to be fun enough, the game shines the most when you try to make your own fun. Also, even though the setting is pretty silly/comedic, the game has surprisingly well-crafted lore.
If you compare it to Terraria, you'll probably find the boss fights / combat aspects lacking, but on all other aspects I'd say Starbound does quite a bit better.
