My expectations were met. The game is a fun ride through and through; but it has has some questionable design choices that I feel drag it down.
The gameplay is exactly what you'd expect from a classic sonic game. And to it's benefit, Sonic CD is more inspired than most of the other sonic games. When you step into a level,  you quickly come to understand the depth on display here. There are essentially three different phases for every one stage; meaning you can flip through different pallets and scenery by hitting a post and going fast. While this does wonders to help keep the game interesting, the real opportunities to flip the phase are limited unless you are clairvoyant or unreasonably reckless. In a game about going fast, Sonic CD seems to want to slow you down quite often, which is an issue.
What's also an issue is some downright bizzare boss and game over music. A slowed down, pitch shifted version of a laugh accompanies a creepy tone. It's abundantly clear that this is supposed to be Dr. Robotnik laughing at us. The game plays this theme every time you see him. And I get that the point of the game is to stop him, but really? You couldnt've picked a less jarring theme for boss fights? This, compounded with the fact that Dr. Robotnik is seriously out of good ideas, as most bosses can be beaten by slapfighting them, turns bossfights into a chore.
It's good, but just barely so.

I never got to play this when it first came out on the Mega CD (there weren't many around), but I'd always wanted to give Sonic CD a go and am glad I did. It has great gameplay, interesting bosses, lovely graphics, and one of the best soundtracks around, all topped off with fantastic intro and ending videos. The game isn't too hard, but a couple of the later levels are challenging (like the race against Metal Sonic). The only bad thing is that the bonus stage is a bit dull. Sonic 2 on the Megadrive is often said to be the best Sonic game, but if you don't know Sonic and can only get one, then I urge you to get Sonic CD instead. 9/10

Bought this game because I need to blow off some steam after studying for a major examination.
Basic premise: there are 20-30ish classes that you can be assigned to. There's the Blue Dragon faction (the ""good guys"") who don't know the alignment of anyone else, the Unseen and Occult (the ""bad guys"") who know who's on their side, and the neutral people who are out for themselves. It becomes a game of trust building and deceit. Do you have what it takes to make people trust you? even if you're a repear waiting to stick your sickle into their back?
In my favorite recent game, I ended up as the reaper; a stand alone class who reaps people's souls. You're all alone in this role and if the court votes to throw you out, there's little you can do about it. So what does one do? Deflect, decept, and deny. Build up relationships and then toss em away when they are no longer useful. That's the mind of a reaper.
But the game is incredibly, incredibly complex. The dead can and do talk with the priest class meaning anyone you backstab can come back to haunt you. Observers can spy on your every move while nobles send maids to spy on your secret converstations. The prince can jail anyone but the king and demand they account for their actions all while not knowing if the king they serve under is good, evil, or neutral. In total, there are kings, nobles, dutcheses, aristocrats, priests, seers, psychic's, prince's, seers, drunks, alcoholics, reapers, cult leaders, masterminds, assassins, hunters, alchemists, fools, and many more.
Who will lie their way to the throne? Only time will tell.
10/10 would lie my way to the throne again.

I've played plenty of FPS games where your character is a bipedal humanoid, firmly bound by gravity. Seeing that Strike Vector gives players a "hover" mode made the game seem like a good choice to transition from the traditional FPS to the flight shooter.
However, Strike Vector is plagued by the same combat formula other flight shooters have: find enemies, chase each other in a circle, break out of circle to get a shot, and end up being destroyed because if you're not flying in a circle, you are inevitably an easy target for some other player.
If you're familiar with flight shooters, you might still like this game, and you might emphatically disagree with my analysis of the combat. However, if most of your games are from other genres, Strike Vector is not a good introduction to flight shooters. It has a very steep learning curve, has not advanced significantly beyond others of its type, and does little to appeal to anyone who isn't a hardcore flight shooter player.

Pros:
-Flying feels awesome. Controls are reactive and well designed.
-All but cosmetics are available from the start. No grinding to unlock better weapons.
Cons:
-Not many people are ever online. It's rare to find more than 2-3 games which have more than 3-4 people.
Overall this has the potential to be a really awesome competitive aerial FPS. It's tons of fun, looks good and is very cheap. It just needs more people playing it.
Hopefully it being on sale will help with that.

If you're looking for a fun, aerial shooter you may want to pick up this game. Every weapon option is available from the beginning, so older players have no advantage over the newer ones, save for experience. The maps have a dirty, industrial aesthetic theme, and flying through them in first-person is a refreshing change of pace from the usual terrestrial shooter. Players can unlock custom spaceship parts and wing art to personalize their crafts, but these rewards do not grant any additional abilities or buffs.
If you want to fly around in a spaceship, blast away foes, or just want to play something different Strike Vector is for you.

The game play is just as advertised, fast and loose, a bit rough and unpolished feeling. The aesthetic and theme are great and seem pretty damn inspired, this game just oozes "cool". There’s a fair amount of customization by way of multiple weapon combinations and augments, which is nice, it’s not too deep, but nice. Even though the controls feel a bit unpolished navigating through tight corridors and speeding through an insane amount of obstacles whilst gunning down an opponent is beyond satisfying.
In my limited playtime I’ve encountered a few glitches, mostly terrain clipping. It’s pretty difficulty to distinguish what can stop you dead in your tracks and what is just window dressing.
The game has its moments, and they are fantastic. But it feels lacking, not in one particular area, but overall, everything seems to need some sort of fine tuning to be “just right”. Strike Vector is a mixed bag.
It’s seemingly full of promise, however …

I have played many zombies games including Left4Dead, DayZ mod and its current alpha and grown a little tired of the genre. Thankfully State of Decay invigorates my interest zombies games again. The game is a mix of role playing, action and base building and it balance those elements very well. Once you get into the game you will be hooked for hours even days. It has a number of bugs and quite rough around the edges but nothing game breaking. On the negative side, the main story ends abruptly and there are several graphical glitches from time to time.
Each heroes/survivors has her/his unique trait and abilities so you will be having fun playing as every one of them( characters in the game can get tired and sick) It is also one of the better open world games in recent years. The landscape is pretty varied from small and big towns to fields and jungles. Scavenging alone is pretty tense especially if you have a horde or ferals nearby.
If you ever intend to get the game, don't forget to purchase the awesome Breakdown DLC. Best described as a survival mode where they drop you in a random location on the map and you have to build your base from scratch, recruit survivors, find and fix an rv to escape to the next level. Each level gets harder and harder until it becomes nearly impossible. There are also new heroes to recruit in each level requiring special conditions to unlock them. Breakdown is the real meat of the game.
I rate this game 9 zombie headshots out of 10.

Star Saviors another one of the bullet hell genre of games, does it do anything more than what others have done ? no. But it is fun like others ? like hell it is (no pun intended).
Graphics - Buller hell games really don't need that much graphic power, with using simple meshes (like this game does) it works perfectly. But this just can't be overlooked, the character models are taken out of a nightmare, and just put in there to haunt you for the rest of your life. If you can just pass this simple detail, everything else is fine. 6/10
Music - Empowering, just the music it needs for the type of game it is. Mostly heard is metal, with a few dubstep sounds mixed within. If you love that kind of music, you are going to love this game. 7/10
Cinematics - None
Story - You as the reader, have probably heard this story over and over again, the story where you are the chosen one and you have to save the world. Now this may come as a suprise, but this game actually changes it (no it doesn't). You follow a relatively average campaign through the galaxy to prevent a war that is going to unfold at any moment. Also the game tells you multiple times that you are the chosen one, and that you are the only one who can do what you are doing. Although at the start of the campaing, you are given the choice between 3 characters, and while you are doing what you are doing, the other 2 characters are doing the same, but remember how you are the only one capable of doing this ? Well you are not. 5/10
Content - For a game this cheap, it does have quite a bit of stuff hidden within it. A story campaign, which is roughly 18 missions, 3 character choices at the start, which have quite a bit of background story to them. Futhermore, the more you advance through the story, the more weapons and perks you unlock for your skills. Oh forgot to mention that each of the playable characters have a different playstyle. The first one is slow but with hard hiting weapons, the other one is fast with low to average damage, and the last one is average speed with average damage. Also it does other modes, separate from the campaign one. 8/10
Controls - Responds perfectly to any command that you give, which is a must have for these type of games. 8/10
Gameplay - Really fast paced, you don't have time to think about what you are going to do, as you are bombarded all the time. It does get progressively harder with every level, as it is expected. The bosses man were they hard, mostly that one at the 13'th level, but nothing a second (if only it were 2 tries) attempt couldn't fix. 7/10
In spite of that, Star Saviors is a pretty solid entry for a game this cheap. It does have its flaws as does every game, but it does way too many things really well, that you can just look past the flaws. If you like these type of games, you won't regret buying this one.
Final Score: 6.8/10

Fantastic social/deduction game based on concepts used by Town of Salem. Every player is assigned a random role at the beginning of the game and every role has a unique job to fulfill in the game. None of the players know anything about eachother including things like role or faction. So the person next to you might be an ally, an enemy or a neutral role who can either help you or kill you. Or he might be a dumbass, who knows?
The game is a struggle of gathering information and figuring out who is who in order for you to reach your win condition.
It does have flaws though. There's tons of "quality of life" features that are not present in the game but could be easily implemented with a few patches. For example, clicking your Journal icon while having the Journal already opened closes and opens the Journal again instead of just closing it. Sometimes the interaction between abilities are confusing or not explained well enough but it's not bad enough to impact your enjoyment of the game.
Closing thoughts: I love this game and I recommend it to anyone who liked Town of Salem or tabletop games in general.

A very unique experience with tight, refined gameplay that, while theoretically simple to execute, has an intense layer of depth in strategy and movement, leading to a very difficult but very rewarding real time strategy game. The control scheme, while simple, provides exactly as much control as you need to execute whatever strategies you might need. The music is dark, but rowdy and playful, the writing is brimming with character, and the art style is clean enough that you can tell exactly what's happening on the battlefield at any given moment.
The dev team is clearly passionate, and very transparent. They have a public Trello where you can see the intended progress of the game, with features they're working on, and they even stream parts of the games' development, showing how they fix bugs, and discussing their logic behind the changes they make, while being open to feedback.
The campaign has a couple of difficulty spikes, and the multiplayer population is a little bit low right now (though plenty enough for you to find matches whenever you want), but other than that I have no major problems with the game, and hope to see it continue to develop and grow. It's very difficult at first, and you might find yourself losing a lot of early multiplayer matches, but it's very rewarding to learn and get better at, with a strong replay system with real time graphs helping you figure out what went wrong.
Worth your time and £15, for sure.

One of the best examples of level design, 2D or 3D, that I can think of.  Way ahead of its time, when I think about it.  Looking at any point of any level, there are usually at least 3 routes running parallel that you could be taking.  Perfect balance, in my opinion, of speed and precision platforming; the game lets you run as fast as you like through certain sections, while others require reactions, timing and control.  While the latter sections may be somewhat challenging, none of them are infuriatingly difficult and you're unlikely to find yourself stuck at one section for any length of time.  The Past/Future mechanic is brilliant; switching between times changes the level around a bit to make it harder or easier in certain places, and this can be used to your advantage but only if you are able to build up enough speed to travel in time.  It adds an extra dimension to speedruns, and multiplies the already huge amount of ways to beat a level.  Boss fights are short, sweet and creative, varying hugely each time.  As for the port itself, it's a great port; about the best I could hope for.  There's a main menu and a save system that has up to 4 save slots.  There's proper audio options, you can use the old spin dash animation if you like, and you can apply a Sharp, Smooth or Nostalgic (i.e. classic) video filter.  It appears to be pretty happy running in Windows, no bugs that I've found and alt-tabbing brings up no issues.
Overall, no real gripes besides the lack of story.

Shadow of Mordor offers a fairly interesting story set in the LOTR universe.  This originally put me off on the idea of playing, but I'm truly glad I put those "movies turned into games" notions behind me.  While it takes place in the LOTR universe, the characters, plots, and idea is unique (you won't see Frodo, and I've only heard one mention of Gandalf).
The plot is fairly simple: revenge, but the main character is stuck in between the Wraith world and the world of the living, giving him special abilities and weapons.  You're left to uncover the reason you've been cursed to roam this border world, unveil the past of the Elven Master bound to your own soul, all the while trying to eliminate the Uruk threat to the land.
Missions:  they serve as a good push for the story as well as offering new unlocked abilities and fun stories.
Side missions:  overall my favorite part of the game.  Each one is unique, challenging, and best of all: fun.  Really good ways to utilize the abilities you've unlocked as well as earn more dosh to unlock some more!  I've read other reviews that complain about repetitive side missions.  The OUTCAST side missions are a bit of a grind as they are all "Save #5 slaves, don't be detected, yada yada" and these missions FAR exceed the number of other side missions. They are still fun if you choose to do each one differently from the last.
Gameplay:  if you're a fan of Assassin's Creed (I sure am - that's what led me to this game...) then you'll enjoy this, as it's structured nearly identical.  This is a positive thing - trust me.  That being said I found the KB/M controls wonky, weird, and un-enjoyable.  Highly recommend a gamepad (I hooked up my PS4 controller to the PC) to get the best experience.
Graphics/Audio:  Pretty standard for the games of today.  I had no issue running this on ULTRA settings with high framerate.  The game looks very nice and runs great, but it's not the best thing that's happened to computer graphics in the past few years.
Final impressions:  Overall the game seemed very easy.  The orcs have very limited sight (unless you're on one of those damn cloak&dagger missions...), but this is 'countered' by the fact that they completely swarm you once you're spotted and they don't go down in melee battle very easily.  All of the 'optional objectives' were easily obtained (getting your more money) and the missions can easily be completed on 1-2 attempts (except, again, those dagger side quests, which took more than 10 attempts for some of them...)   Completionists (like me) can excpect 30-40 hours of gameplay, so for a game of this structure, it's pretty short.  The two maps you get to raise hell on are also fairly small - you can run from one side to the other in a matter of minutes.
This game is WORTH at least one playthrough if you're into Assassin's Creed / FarCry type games.  Again, don't bother using KB/M, hook up a controller.

I've always wanted a relalistic survival game with some focus on exploration and hunting for resources. Don't starve was at the top of my list for it and now this game can join the ranks. There's already a lot in the game and the devs have kept hard at work by releasing massive amounts of new content every month or two (A nice treat to get me to get back into it for another long session). There's plenty to talk about so its time to take a trip to steam reviews favourite pro's and con's:
Pros:
This game is perfect for some adrenaline pumping exploration in the form of finding loot at the bottom of the sea whilst being chased by sharks.
The AI is spot on in my opinion, not every animal has an immediate intention of killing you. Sharks mainly show this by first being curious by swimming up and nudging on your boat. If you react they become aggresive and will only when you're not focusing on them. Very Realistic and adds a touch of diffuculy when fighting them.
Lots of items and crafting with an ever expanding list. The game makes it pretty tedious when collecting resources if you want a good setup. This isn't a bad thing because its very realistic (again something I want) as well as it promotes you to not only find items through sunken boats and planes so you dont need to craft them but also make resource collection more effective.
There are a lot of aspects of survival such as; hunger, health, temp./ Weather, sickness and injury. Their currently in the process of being implemented fully but a solid start.
There is a lot of uniqueness for ships and the ocean floor as well as sea life (with more on the way).
Cons:
Friggin rendering distances, each island has its own biome and once you leave any island not rendered gets the same stock image. Its impossible to tell which island you left all your stuff on.
The island design is repetitive and some uniqueness such as a volcanic island or islands with mountains, lakes, forests. A range of different islands with different things will be a great addition to the game.
More diffuculty in travel. I would like to prepare for long distance journeys, pack my boat with walls full and stack everything I need without it gltiching out of the boat and set of for adventure. Make people want to be mobile with more options boat-wise and variety in islands will be great.
The game needs to be tougher. I've stated many aspects for realism are being added but I can survive with a rock indefinetly and some potato plants with a 2 minute grow time, a few crabs and a bucket of water over a fire spit.
Overall I still heavily recomend the game and believe I will be clocking in some heavy hours and I hope you get it too.

If you like horror games this game is a must!  Hektor is like a mix of Amnesia and The Stanley Parable.  Amnesia because no weapons and you find items and it's like The Stanley Parable because you'll walk down a corridor to a dead end then turn around and find your path completely changed.  One time I kept walking through a looping sequence and didn't know where to go so I decided to turn around and walk the other direction...only to find the path changed and was able to go to a new area!  Another interesting fear factor to this game is that unlike most horror games that drive the fear and jump scares right from the beginning, Hektor sort of toys with you for a while.  It leaves you wondering when it's going to do it.  Dark corridors, lights blowing out, whispers in the dark...at one point I was nearly begging for the game to just come get me so I'd have some form of closure, LOL!  Play this game at night with headphones on,
Very creepy!
Irregular paths, changing environment.
Unpredictable scare moments.
Find items to proceed - sense of quest.
Things will come get you...but when?
No real storyline.

Pills - you take them to keep your sanity but they don't seem to do very much.

Rare glitch - toward the end of the game I encountered a glitch where the area kept looping.  Normally this can happen if you require an item but not in my case.  There was no way out of this loop.  If this occurs just restart the game and it should get back on track.

Serious Review:
Probably ( in my opinion ) the best splinter cell since Chaos Theory, if not one of the best stealth games. The stealth is challenging, rewarding and so so so satisfying. I can't count the amount of times I have slinked across a pipe, crossed an entire building complex or sneak across an entire ventilation system without disturbing a soul and just sit there for 5 minutes, drowning in my own happiness.
Unlike the last couple of Splinter Cells, this game encourages stealth so very much. In fact, it seems to punish going loud much more than other games would. It takes about 3 shots from an assault rifle going at full auto to bring you down. It is, however, still the easiest way to get through a level. That is why it is the worst, you get little to no rewards and you feel nowhere near as good. That, and going assault is just plain boring.
But when you start to utilise your gadgets, surrounding, and enemies themselves? You have a vast amount of ways to complete a level and half of them don't even involve disturbing people. One of my favourite moments was using my drone to scout out an area, and find key points to lure targets. Once inside the area myself, I would place sticky cameras in the aforementioned key points. I moved each guard with lures and the like to these areas, and in quick succession, released sleeping gas from the cameras and sprinted for the door. One survived and attempted to attack me. Lucky he was next to the door, and before he could fire a shot, I had him as a human shield. As previous intel suggested the next room would be impossible to sneak through. I use sonar vision to detect my enemies and equip a crossbow with  sleeping gas bolts in it. Perfect, the enemies up ahead are tightly packed. I mark them out and crash through the door with my hostage, using the execute function to fire 3 bolts at my marked enemies. The following cloud of green gas is enough to knock out all 6 enemies in the group. I grab the intel I needed to acquire. Mission accomplished.
And that was just a side mission.

is a Point & Click detective film noir FMV adventure game. Waking up with the past 7 years as a gap in your memory, you set out to put the pieces together of who you became during those years, and find out why you lost your memory.
: This is a new sequel to well beloved FMV franchise of the 90s. All recurring characters, 8 of which I can think of, are played by the same actors as those who left us off in
,
and
, which is quite an accomplishment 16 years later, although only 7 years have passed in-game. The memory blank allows players of the previous games to jump right in where they remember the story, which is where Tex remembers it. Jokes are corny but Tex's smirk remarks are always worth a smile, giggle, or even laugh. The game has 4 different endings, and even branching path as entire levels could only be played with certain paths, like the Sewers, the Blue Dragon, and many flashbacks. There are many Easter eggs of clips from past games of the franchise, as well as many locations where points can be gathered by looking at the many portraits of Kickstarter backers on the walls (every single one of them with a personal one-liner from Tex!).
: In the first person perspective, the textures are awful, and I mean it. Any FPS players will be turned off by the game's graphics, and is obviously not where the attention was put. The game is somewhat short for an adventure game, and you don't feel as much as a P.I. as you did in previous games and barely spend any time in your office, or getting "cases" from clients. Money and shopping were completely removed from the game. The puzzles were for the most part easy, while the conversation options that define how your story will unfold are utterly vague, often misleading.
: ★★★☆☆ - It's up to you
Heck, I had fun playing this game! There is no doubt everything that did carry over from the franchise was an improvement over previous games. Shadow of Mordor offers a fairly interesting story set in the LOTR universe.  This originally put me off on the idea of playing, but I'm truly glad I put those "movies turned into games" notions behind me.  While it takes place in the LOTR universe, the characters, plots, and idea is unique (you won't see Frodo, and I've only heard one mention of Gandalf).
The plot is fairly simple: revenge, but the main character is stuck in between the Wraith world and the world of the living, giving him special abilities and weapons.  You're left to uncover the reason you've been cursed to roam this border world, unveil the past of the Elven Master bound to your own soul, all the while trying to eliminate the Uruk threat to the land.
Missions:  they serve as a good push for the story as well as offering new unlocked abilities and fun stories.
Side missions:  overall my favorite part of the game.  Each one is unique, challenging, and best of all: fun.  Really good ways to utilize the abilities you've unlocked as well as earn more dosh to unlock some more!  I've read other reviews that complain about repetitive side missions.  The OUTCAST side missions are a bit of a grind as they are all "Save #5 slaves, don't be detected, yada yada" and these missions FAR exceed the number of other side missions. They are still fun if you choose to do each one differently from the last.
Gameplay:  if you're a fan of Assassin's Creed (I sure am - that's what led me to this game...) then you'll enjoy this, as it's structured nearly identical.  This is a positive thing - trust me.  That being said I found the KB/M controls wonky, weird, and un-enjoyable.  Highly recommend a gamepad (I hooked up my PS4 controller to the PC) to get the best experience.
Graphics/Audio:  Pretty standard for the games of today.  I had no issue running this on ULTRA settings with high framerate.  The game looks very nice and runs great, but it's not the best thing that's happened to computer graphics in the past few years.
Final impressions:  Overall the game seemed very easy.  The orcs have very limited sight (unless you're on one of those damn cloak&dagger missions...), but this is 'countered' by the fact that they completely swarm you once you're spotted and they don't go down in melee battle very easily.  All of the 'optional objectives' were easily obtained (getting your more money) and the missions can easily be completed on 1-2 attempts (except, again, those dagger side quests, which took more than 10 attempts for some of them...)   Completionists (like me) can excpect 30-40 hours of gameplay, so for a game of this structure, it's pretty short.  The two maps you get to raise hell on are also fairly small - you can run from one side to the other in a matter of minutes.
This game is WORTH at least one playthrough if you're into Assassin's Creed / FarCry type games.  Again, don't bother using KB/M, hook up a controller.

Some brief background to put my recommendation in context:
I missed the original isometric RPG era by a few years. By the time I discovered them, I'd been through a series of games with more modern design that made it tedious to play older games that lacked the conveniences to which I was accustomed. I loved the character building aspect in theory and tried to get into them multiple times, particularly with Beamdog's "enhanced editions", but still found the experience to be frustrating and unsatisfying. I felt like I spent more time alt-tabbed trying to understand what every ability score meant than I did actually playing the games.
This last point is where POE separates itself: transparency. Nearly every statistic, ability, spell, etc. can be easily understood in-game by simply mouse hovering over the text. Statistics are streamlined: there's no worrying about which attribute will increase melee damage versus ranged or spell; one statistic affects all damage dealt. Another statistic affects your chance to hit with weapons and spells. There's also transparency during the combat phase. When you hover over enemy creatures, you'll be able to see their damage reduction to each particular weapon or element.
Another difference comes through how you equip your party. There are no weapon or armor restrictions; if you want to put the heaviest armor you can find on a mage, you have that option (though action speed will be affected). Weapon selection is interesting as well with each type having a different perk: some weapons deal two different damage types depending on which is more effective against the target. Others bypass damage reduction. Some add to your defensive ability, while others improve your accuracy.
Perhaps one of the biggest differences between the old isometric games is the introduction of "per encounter" abilities. These are abilities that can be used a certain number of times each battle and then return after the party finishes combat. It adds an active aspect to combat that didn't previously exist for non-spell casters (and even with spell casters for those of us who were overly conservative).
The story, dialogue, and lore aren't overly compelling, but the world and general atmosphere are interesting enough to draw you in a bit.

This is effectively the successor we've been waiting for BG2. Does it hit as hard as BG2? No, it's hard to do that. BG2 existed in a kind of beloved universe by nerds, cultivated with a rich goofy history from Dungeons and Dragons.
This attempts to do it's own thing, though common fantasy tropes are brought in. None the less it's interesting and takes a strong themeatic focus upon the concept of the soul, which here is a particular thing with particular qualities, capable of being approached in an almost scientific manner.
The gameplay is essentially turn based though real time, you will pause often. AI can be preset for companions to make it flow easier and I've found it to work fine. The classes are many and interesting while the stat system is a little more forgiving, as usefulness is spread out wide amid the stats. It's hard to build yourself into a character hole.
The dialogue and reading is plenty. Play this game ever night, a little bit, before you go to bed. It's like cozying up with a book. It isn't supposed to give you an adrenal rush, but be an enjoyable journey.

BiteSize Review - Middle-earth: Shadow of Mordor
The Good:
- Game is very well optimized, will run on older and new systems
- Game looks great in spots
- Combat is really satisfying
- Can play either play loud swinging your sword or be stealthy with your bow and dagger
- Nemesis System means randomized orcs, so each one has his own personality and perks to fight against
- Deathcams make each kill really satisfying and has impact
The Bad:
- Story is pretty much forgettable (you good, they bad, kill bad guys)
- There are really only two levels to explore and both are essentially the same large open areas with ruins scattered around
- Even though each orc is unique, after awhile of killing them very few will stand out as you plow through their ranks
- You use the same weapons throughout the entire game (though their runes can be changed at anytime)
- Timed/Protect Missions gave me cancer
- Large install size (just under 60GB)
The Verdict:
This game came out of left field for a lot of people when it was released. It was not advertised very much and the game play was fun and it was really well made. The setting was unique and never seen in the movies, and the nemesis system made each encounter somewhat special with each stinking orc. The best part of this game was that you could back stab orcs, combat them with your sword and then take out a few with your bow and all of this combat flowed and worked really well together.
The combat is what kept me playing this game for more than 20 hours. There were a few issues with game though, the story was forgettable and the levels had a few interesting spots but were mostly large open areas with ruins scattered around etc. The DLC added a bit more replay-ability but once you got through the story missions there is really not much else to do. You could keep playing and killing orcs but after 20 hours or so it does get kind of old.
Overall I would highly recommend this game to people who love action games and LotR fans. It's very well made and if bought on sale you can definitely get your money's worth.

What's there to say about Hektor?
For starters, it's actually a well done horror title. While not entirely unique, it does enough right, and does it differently, to stand out from what is an overcrowded genre.
Hektor casts you as a patient of some sort, exploring and trying to figure out just what is going on. As you visit different rooms, the game literally does change the environment around you. Running around a corner only to hit a dead end, you'll see a room has appeared where you just came from, or a hallway leading to various other rooms. It's quite jarring, and works well to keep you guessing.
Because it is a horror game, there are a few jump scares. Nothing too crazy, and most you won't expect, but they're not overdone. Where Hektor shines is its tension, or rather, the tension it puts on you. There may not be a jump scare around every corner, but you will wonder what's going on for the entire game, especially when you hit the dream sequences. There's quite a lot of 'wtf' moments, for sure.
Graphically, Hektor looks nice. There aren't a lot of effects (smoke, particles, etc.), but the environments are nicely done. The acting is also good, whether it's the voices you hear throughout the game, or the notes you find scattered about.
On the flipside, Hektor is relatively short. You can finish it in about two hours, give or take a few minutes (or underwear changing breaks). There is no replay value to the game, as once you've beaten it and figured out what's going on (as best you can), there's no incentive to play through again. Perhaps to clean up the achivements you may have missed, if you care about those, but otherwise, no.
A worthy purchase, when it's on sale. For the normal retail price ($21.99 CDN), it's a little pricy for the length of the game. Jump scares are good, but not overdone, and the overall being on the edge of your seat makes it a good experience.

10/10, and here's the story of why:
Dark Souls and I have an odd relationship. I purchased it 4-5 years ago on my Xbox 360 after reading of how it was "The Hard Mode" version of Skyrim... It was.
After the tutorial (If you want to call it that), it throws you in the middle of nowhere with really no direction on where to go unless you're an elitest. I died countless times, was invaded, stabbed, and probably cursed more times than I ever did at a game. I never beat it; I just gave up.
2 years later, I picked it up again, since my boyfriend at the time suggested we should play it together. It was okay, but still didn't beat it. Didn't care for it at all.
Fast Forward to February 2016:
I decided to finish the game at all cost after watching two friends of mine post "Let's Play" videos of it. One was playing a first run blind playthrough; the other was slightly in my shoes, but he knew more.
I finally beat it, noticed my time (180 hours) and said the gawd awful words that sucked me in," I think I could do better..."
<< Present Day>>
Now I speedrun Dark Souls for fun(1hr 38min. It's not fast, but it's definitely better than my very first run), and each run just seems to make the game's charm grow on to me.
I highly recommend it to anyone that hasn't experienced the double-edge sword/love-hate relationship of Dark Souls yet. And even if you're like me and die countless times, I encourage you to continue going. There's nothing more satisfying than beating Ornstein & Smough for the first time on your own.

It took long enough for someone to create a spiritual successor to Tank Wars and Scorched Earth, but there's something truly wrong when even the lowest-hanging fruit on the developer tree can churn out something as average as Shellshock Live and still be successful.
The entire game is about grinding. First you have to grind your tank up levels to get new and better weapons, and then you have to grind the weapons to get upgraded versions of them. As with all grinding, this quickly gets tedious and really kills the enjoyment of the game, and is REQUIRED to get on a level playing field with most of the playerbase.
Then we have the weapons. In-game stats for them are not available, and they're horribly unbalanced...yet the game the dev thinks it's perfectly fine to randomize what weapons every player gets. An option to allow players to pick their weapons before a battle would be a nice choice to have.
The UI is beginner-quality bad. Oversized buttons, useful in-game information only appearing for a handful of moments and a complete lack of server options once the game has started besides quitting the game. Is it so hard to code in a votekick option? And then there's the bizarre concept of having a large targeting circle surround the tank. It took 10 seconds for players to realize the 100/86 rule and make it more of a crutch than a useful UI asset.
There are plenty of game modes to pick from, but some of them are outright ruined by basic game elements. Assassin involves targeting another specific player exclusively. There's nothing to stop the other player from just constantly running away from you to deny you victory, and doubly so if the "Move First -> Shoot First" mechanic is enabled.
The mere fact that this game can still be a blast to play in multiplayer shows how entertaining a Tank Wars clone game really is, but this is the worst such clone I've played in 25 years.
Not recommended until the developer overhauls the entire game from scratch - but considering the game is close to leaving Early Access, I highly doubt he's even gonna bother with that. Spend your money elsewhere.

I had no idea what FMV games are previously to playing Tesla Effect. I also had no idea who Tex Murphy is. Anyway, I really enjoyed it and can hardly wait to get my hands onto other similar games.
This game just left me thinking why on Earth it isn't more popular. It's got all the right ingredients: lots of jokes and humorous lines (puns and "dad jokes" all over, enjoyable even when cheesy or goofy), a quite interesting storyline (a bit childish at points but still decent), intricate puzzles for those looking for a challenge that can be quickly turned into reasonable puzzles for those that prefer a more relaxed approach, and best of all, the FMV part!... Nowadays there's no way a CGI-designed character (NPC or whatever) could look anywhere close to real humans played by actors. And this makes the game so immersive and captivating. Yeah, the acting is a bit awkward here and there, but I wasn't expecting Oscar performances anyway. And some characters are actually well-played (and I loved Jodi Russell's smile - the actress playing Taylor Lamintz). The overall graphic quality was pretty good as well. The hint (Smart Alex) system is well-done too. There are even multiple endings based on the choices you made throughout the game.
I guess the only left to blame is the lack of attention and care from the publisher. State of Decay is a polished single-player open world zombie survival game. It requires you to take on the mindset of a survivor than just another player. After slowly taking my time and beating the single player campaign in about 25 hours (100%), here are some highlights from the game..
Pros:
- The game is not actually hard BUT the consequences are tremendous if you do ♥♥♥♥ up (you'll be instilled with a feeling of loss)
- Resources are finite. It can be counterbalanced with resource investment into sustainability (for survival).
- You don't just play one character. You raise up a community. The more time to take into building up the group as a whole, the greater your chances of survival.
- Vehicles are considered a resource. If you take better care of them, you'll find that they can do more than just get you from point A to B.
- 25 hours worth of content (main story and side quest included).
- For a single player game, the NPC companions are quite capable. They don't take the lead but they don't fall behind either.
Cons:
- The story is quite average.
- Vehicles are overpowered. They can kill everything except for one special infected.

Sonic CD is a 32-bit platformer that is strangely about exploration rather than speed. It's still more momentum-based than your average Platformer games, but the game itself centers around "going fast" only so far as travelling through time.
There are 4 versions of each stage. If you complete a Stage with 50 or more rings, you get to play the Bonus Stage. The Sonic CD (PC) lets you choose between the JP and US music for the whole game. Each stage has a Present, Past, Good Future and Bad Future. By default, the "Future" is the Bad Future and you have to go into the past & explore the level to find & destroy a robot teleporter thingy. After you destroy the teleporter, all enemies (but not obstacles) in the level are destroyed in the Past, Present & now Good Future.
As I said before, there's a different piece of music for each stage. The Present & Future feature .mp3 audio tracks, while the past features PCM (PC-Music) audio music that's programmed in a manner similiar to classic PC game music such as Warcraft II, Diablo, or Command & Conquer, so it sounds more unique. What might throw you off when you first play the game is that the MP3 music tracks have people singing sometimes; what I had to remember was that this is a 32-bit PC game, not a 16-bit console game!
There are a few gameplay/level features that differ from the original Sonic CD, the most major being after you have played through each stage as Sonic you can then play through the game again as Tails, with an appropriate (and adorable) updated sprite for Sonic CD. Playing again as "Tails" is basically easy-mode. Completing the game as Sonic gets you the credits-roll of the original Sonic CD staff & credits music, whereas playing as Tails through the game gets you the credits roll of the 2012 PC remake (of the 1996 PC port...).
What is important to note for a diehard Sonic fan, is that this is a remake of the 1996 PC version of Sonic CD. It has nothing to do with a ROM hack nor does it have anything to do with DOSBox.

Tooth & Tail is fast-food RTS (pun intended). But it's not like McDonalds. It is more like Chick-Fil-A or Chipotle -- something comparable to a true restaurant meal but cheaper and more convenient.
T&T is one of the most approachable RTS games on the market.
- Your cursor is a unit that you move around, so you don't have to be a fast person to be good at T&T.
- The game is easy to learn, so you don't have to study unit and tech trees to be an adequate player.
- The matches are about 12-15 minutes long MAXIMUM, so you don't have to worry about being stuck for 2 hours in a long match.
- Maps are random, so you don't have to memorize maps to win games.
- Controller support for console peasants <3
Yet all of these features come with no loss of depth or crunch. The simple but merciless economic system will absolutely separate winners from losers. Micro can still win battles without rapid clicks. T&T managed to keep the exciting and challenging components of the RTS genre while removing its deepest approachability flaws. What you have here is a charming, quick, welcoming game with crunchy RTS strategy sufficient to satisfy a hardcore RTS gamer and a casual LAN party gamer.

I am leaving this negative review here just to address my issues with this game. NOTE THAT IF YOU WANT TO JUST READ A SUMMARY OF THE REVIEW, SKIP TO THE LAST PARAGRAPH.
So let me describe a typical session of playing this game with a freind or two. So we start by selecting a server. Most of the servers seem similar so we usually just go by whichever one has the best ping/ or amount of players, not knowing if the server will be there again tomorrow if we wanted to continue our progress. So we all load in, and have to find each other. We will loot nearby buildings for loot and look for a road that can lead us to a town so that we can all meet up there. eventually we end up meeting in a town. From here we either get killed from behind, starting over again looking for each other, or we are actually able to loot the town. Usually upon looting a town we find lots of food, drinks, clothes. We will also find on a more uncommon occasion; a backpack/bag, melee weapon, guns and ammo that almost never go with one another. So now that we got a melee weapon each that we can fend outselves off from zombies with at the least, that is unless we get killed by a player with a gun after we have looted.
So from here we will just move onto the next town and loot to hopefully find a gun to use so we can try to defend ourselves, or we will base build provided we found an axe. Now i always thought we would be able to spawn at our base when we die. I recently found out however, that this isnt true. So what is the point of a base then? I mean zombies are only near towns and parks it seems, so there is no need to defend yourself from zombies if you arent even near those places, and also players can just destroy your base and steal whatever you had stashed inside it anyway. So why even bother with building one?
The point is my friends and I really dont have much to look forward to when playing this game because even after hours of playing we cant even come across a gun to defend ourselves. We know we can just loot the military base airfield, but palyers are either camping there, it has already been looted, or we do end up getting lucky and finding a gun or two. And if we do find a gun or two, then what? Lets say we kill a player and get more guns and ammo. Okay, now what? we are eventually just going to die and lose our stuff to another player and have to start over from scrach. And if we ended up going to our base to stash our stuff, then we have to worry about a player raiding it and taking it from us. Now we are getting into the realm of grinding the game out to be successful. A couple of hours a day just wont cut it. You will die a lot, lose the stuff you spent hours looting, having to start over, and having to repair your base and re obtaining everything you once had, after a raid. Too many hours would have to be put into the game in order to stay on top of all of this. Unless of course you get lucky finding a gun from the start, lucky to kill a player, lucky to find that that player had a stash of guns, and lucky enough to repeat this over and over again. I wish this game well. I want to see it succeed and become more as i can see myself falling in love with it. It just needs these issues to be fixed.

Hektor is an interesting game with a very well put together atmosphere, and concept; however, what it makes up for in looks, it completely lacks in playability.
***NOTE: AS PER MY EXPERIENCE, THE CHARACTER FEELS LIKE HE IS DRUNK OUT OF HIS WITS AT ALL TIMES; THERE IS NO RELIEF FROM THE NAUSEA INDUCING SWOOPING AND SWAYING OF THE CAMERA. DO NOT PLAY THIS GAME IF YOU SUFFER FROM MOTION SICKNESS. YOU MORE THAN LIKELY WILL VOMIT***
=======
CONS:
- Movement/Game Machanics/Headache in a box: The motion sickness + headache inducing combo of the visual aspects (a la "psychosis") are terrible. Trying to navigate my way through the game, I found myself more aggravated at the fact that I couldn't see anything well enough to properly grasp the scope of the game than being scared, frightened, or slightly immersed. I was just frustrated, dizzy, slightly nauseous, and disappointed.
- Scares: I really didn't find this game scary in any aspect. Why? See above.
- Puzzle-solving: It's a drunken scavenger hunt with a shifting hedge-maze thrown into the mix.
PROS:
+ Good atmosphere: ...when you actually notice the atmosphere. (Hard to understand? You haven't played Hektor..)
+ Audio/visual: For what is present in the game, it's not bad. I get an "Amnesia" or "Penumbra" vibe from it big-time, and it does it well enough that it could be a good game, overall. It COULD be. It just needs to lose the "psychosis"/"pill-popping" mechanic. It's terrible.
+ Shifting Areas: I really enjoy the feeling of having the world shift around me as I move through it. It's really unique, in a sense, as most games don't do this sort of thing, and it impressed me for a moment when I was playing. However, that feeling quickly fell to frustration as I desperately tried to cling to my senses of perception as I played, and not feel the need to avert my eyes. Again, the swooping mechanic draws my attention away from the positive, and all I could focus on was my frustration at having to fight to get anything done :/

Time for an update on my review.  I know what the hours say on my profile, but the Steam system is very inaccurate I'm afraid.  It does not count offline hours, while it does count online hours where the client is open and not being played at all.  So far I am running a little over 200 hours split between two laptops.  My initial review was short due to my short exposure to the game.  As that exposure increases I will keep this review up to date.
Currently I still give the game a thumbs up.
Pros:
Active development and regular progress.  Most of what I have seen being worked on lately has been very labor and time intensive.  They are very active in bug fixing and are visibly working with testers from the player community to correct these bugs.
Developers release client updates fairly often,  I can think of at least 4 client updates in the past 2 months, and I think there was actually 5 but that last one was pretty much just bug fixes only.
Communication between the developers and the community seems to be pretty good and frequent these past few months since my initial review.  They are using a company website, two Trello sites, facebook, twitter, and Steam for communication so it is spread out a bit, but the moderators and some of the community seem to be working together to consolidate these onto Steam.
They have been using suggestions from the community in the game development, which is a very nice thing to see, and it also shows that the developers do in fact listen to the community.  Something I like to see, even though it can be distracting at times for developers.
While visible content has been thin the feature systems seem to be evolving and progressing, and more visible content is starting to be released.  The depth of the immersion is starting to intensify with upgraded weather and ocean systems.  I cannot state that the next update will in fact produce the increased content and features as stated, but so far the developers have kept to their word as much as humanly possible and as such I tend to trust that this next update will be everything that they have claimed.
The developers have expanded their dev team and the increase in output has been very obvious since they hired a new dev.  Another strong indicator that the game is not only active in development but that the developers are in fact motivated to produce this game.
The game has some strong community support with a number of key individuals who help provide more formal testing and assist other players with questions and solving issues.  One of the more reliable signs of a good game design, btw.
Cross platform support.  Currently the game supports both Windows and Mac OS, and they have stated an intent to support Linux in the future.  Most games are developed for a single platform initially and additional platforms are supported after release of the game, in order to allow the development team to focus on game completion first.
Cons:
Low visible content at the moment leads some players to become bored after a short period of play, say several days to a few weeks worth.  However this does seem to be changing with the new updates and the game is still in early alpha.  So this is a limited negative and I believe based upon historical evidence that it will be rectified shortly.  I could guess by the end of this month, but that would be just a guess, not fact.
Cross platform development.  I feel that with such a small development team this MAY have been a bad choice, to develop for multiple platforms at the same time rather than wait until the game has been released for the first platform.  There are pros and cons to this, and I listed it as both for that reason.
Other Observations:
One of the things that I have found refreshing with Stranded Deep is that by design the game allows for a wide range of play styles.  The developers have been building Stranded Deep as a survival game, and yet they have ensured that players have enough features and lattitude to survive their own way or style.  Most survival games either require you to survive by their "rules" or at the least they mark off some form of point system for not surviving by their design goal or method.  Stranded Deep seems more about the immersion into that world and it's environment and leaves you to figure out how you will survive on your own.  The path you take is up to you and the game supports it.  A unique approach yet far more realistic than others in the survival genre.
The game is great with first impressions, but lacks multiplayer.

Stranded Deep is a very good game considering it's early access state. Overall I would recommend this game for patient gamers. If you prefer action and are not very patient than this game will be very boring for you, if not than you'll love it.

90% of combat is keeping the party in formation, so the enemies don't run past the tanks, and no one gets gibbed. That's it. Your "choices" are to initiate combat perfectly to get a good formation, and then pause constantly to keep it together. That's

a popular style and stick to it? Perhaps games have publishers for a reason.

Pillars of Eternity is a classic fantasy roleplaying game in the likes of Baldur's Gate. You can play solo or in a party made from characters met along the way or custom made ones. If you like RPGs you have to play this. Period.
There is a lot of everything, reading, talking, fights, quests, items. It is just a great game. But to elaborate a bit. I loved Baldur's Gate 2, it was freaking amazing. I might be biased towards every game that looks and feels similar. And PoE is like BG2, just better. Did I mention there is a lot of everything here? You create your main character and can even create your whole party if you so desire, but the NPCs that can join you along the way are some great personalities and it's a pleasure to travel with most of them. The main story, as the mini stories of each npc, is well written and quite interesting to unravel.
VISUALS
The game is pretty. You travel through, forests, cities, countryside, dungeons and various other environments, and all of them look amazing. Fighting in the rain, in tall grass, with magical lightnings strucking here and there looks as cool as it sounds. Characters look very nice and with all the various clothing options it's fun to play dress up. All the spells look flashy enough, but not to the point that you cannot see through the fireworks. Just look at the screenshots, aren't they pretty?
AUDIO
Very fitting medieval tunes most of the time with Globus-like majestic battle tunes. I found myself actively listening to the background music more than once. Voice acting is very good, it helps that the character's lines are well written. No Minsc here, but I was very fond of Eder and Aloth. Other than that lightnings kaboom, fireballs whoosh, magic missiles whizz. All is well on the audio front.
GAMEPLAY
Have you played Baldur's Gate? Or any BG inspired RPG? Lots of classes, and interesting too. Active pause or real time fights. Party management. Very good new concept or endurance vs health. During fights you use endurance to make an action and enemies deal dammage to your endurance and health. Endurance regenerates automatically if you win a fight and you can use spells or potions to regenerate t during a fight. Health is regenerated on rest only. Very interesting concept and it works really well. Other than that it's all your standard RPG fare. Done right. Quests, bounties, killing stuff, upgrading your stronghold, everything is here. Also enough of difficulty settings and acheievements for all you masochists out there.
Basically if you like RPGs you own it to yourself to play this one. It's that good. Main story with all the side quests and full stronghold upgrade took me ca. 60hrs on normal difficulty with expert enabled (no hints). I had two extremely difficult fights, one being one of the first bounties - ogres - and the second the Adra dragon. Other than that the difficulty was... normal. Excellent game.

Pleasantly surprised by this game. I am one of those people who thought Chaos Theory was the best thing to happen to the Spilntercell series. I still think it's the best, but Blacklist was really, really good. Like it's just under Chaos Theory in my Splintercell ranking. The story is predictable, but well acted, and well done. Lots of gadgets for you to play with, lots of side mission stuff. I did NOT like the upgrade system. Unlike Chaos Theory you need to earn 'cash' and upgrade your gear. Honestly I used a trainer and bought everything after the first mission. You're part of a government agency that is so far off the books the Hubble telescope couldn't see it, and yet you have to 'earn' all of these items that basically 'free' in all of the other Splintercell games.
The change in controls coming from Chaos Theory is quite jarring. The first thing you'll notice is how 'macro' your movements are compared to Chas Theory. No more half steps here, or moving inch by inch. It's foot by foot now. If you a Chaos Theory fan play on perfectionist. It's the hardest, but the most rewarding when you get it right, and the most fun. Night vision is not quite as good as past games. It starts out super grainy, and get's clear after a few seconds. A few precious seconds. I love/hate the gaurd modes now. Once they're suspicious their movements are randomized, and they search the ENTIRE area upping the challenge. They'll even go back to back searching to guard themselves from attack better. Sitcky cameras are NOT recovereable anymore however. So use them sparingly. I found myself using mostly just my hands and bit of crossbow through the levels. As you may have heard in other reviews, the light and sound meters are gone. When in full shadow your gear lights will flare, and sam will go gray. Sound is more of a "was a really being that loud?", and the game responding "I don't know, WERE you really being that loud?" kind of thing. It will tell you through ambient response, which I kind of liked. It makes the world feel a bit more immersive, as you're focused on the game, and not a meter.
At times (not many) the game will force you into 'combat' situations. They are well done, and force you to think on your feet if you don't plan contengencies or explore before accomplishing objectives. You may find that taking chances is can be rewarding. The loss of the meters seems to have translated into guards being more forgiving if you move quickly through the line-of sight.
The only side missions I did were the ones for Grim. They were very fun, and done very well. Like actual mini-missions pulled from the main story. I tried the missions for Charlie, but just couldn't stay motivated enough. You have to complete a lot of waves of enemies in a GOW Horde style to get a mission complete, and it makes if very, very, very hard to do this stealth style. Run-and-gun and mixed style fans will probably like it. I also didn't do the missions for Briggs, as my play style is very slow, and conservative, and I didn't want people messing up my grand plans for how to complete a level. I may try it in the future though. Speaking of Briggs, there is some FPS style action in the later stages of the game with him. I did use some deadly force in these, but they can be done with minimal levels of this.
All in all I LOVED this game, and highly recommend it. It doesn't punish you for any play style except sloppy play (letting hostages die, going super mega slow, leaving bodies in exposed places). The gameplay is tight, and consistent. Just about everything in the game is very well polished and shows a loving attention to detail. That wonderful feeling of accomplishment you get from sneaking past a whole level of guards like a ghost is here, and if you get caught you don't feel cheated, just maybe a bit disappointed that your plan didn't work out. I got this game for free with my AMD card, but I would have absolutely paid full price for it if not for my fear of a departure from what made Chaos Theory so great. Make no mistake this game full of action, but it's so well placed, paced, and put together that it never feels wrong. There's always a good reason for it. They learned their lessons from Double agent, and Conviction, took the best bits of all the Splintercell games, added a few shiny new pieces, and came out with a near masterpiece in the end.

As someone who grew up playing computer games in the 90s, Tesla Effect offers a fantastic return to an era when the capabilities of the computers of the day were pushed beyond their boundaries with spectacular results. While Tesla Effect won't tax any modern computer, it still offers a compelling game with good graphics, which will hopefully stand the test of time.
I'm a diehard Tex Murphy Fan. When I first started the series with Under a Killing Moon and its four CDs under DOS, I was instantly hooked. Having played the games that followed, I was always keen for more, so when Microsoft bought Access and effectively killed Tex Murphy, especially after the cliff-hanger that ended Overseer, I was devastated. Thankfully, due to a successful Kickstarter campaign, we now have a conclusion to that story, with spectacular results.
Tesla Effect continues the same formula as its preceding games, which is actually not a bad thing. If you've ever played Under a Killing Moon, Pandora Directive or Overseer, then you know what you're getting into. In terms of gameplay mechanics, Tesla Effect benefits greatly from being produced in the modern era, with fantastic graphics and a solid control system in place that's a massive improvement from the clunky controls (relatively speaking) of the prior games.
Tesla Effect continues the trend of Full Motion Video (FMV) embedded within a digital game world the franchise was famous for, which offers a great experience. While most games these days tend to use digital models for people, Tesla Effect, and its preceding games, capture real actors and place them within their digital environments. This provides for (IMO) a much better story delivery method, which has always been used to great effect in the Tex franchise.
While the game can be played stand-alone, it's probably better if you jump back to Overseer as its story bleeds into Tesla Effect's to a degree. There's plenty of homage to the franchise, which should bring great excitement to fans (Which I certainly loved!), but it may not have the same effect on those who've never played the series before.
Tesla Effect essentially boils down to a detective adventure game within a 3D world you can explore. It is loaded with lots of puzzles for you to sink your teeth into, as well as a witty story rife with choice. You will be expected to look closely at the environment to find elements to assist you on your quest, which at times can be a little irritating as the items are either obscure, or blend into their environments a little too well, but the reward for correctly identifying, combining and utilising the items is satisfying.
All interactions with characters are provided through simple but vague options which you can choose. Importantly, the game is designed such that the choices you make as you interact with the characters have the ability to shape the game's ending, which is nice. Each of the options provides an interesting and often humorous reply from Tex, sometimes leading to your downfall if approached poorly.
For fans of the series, all of the key actors are back and this is absolutely fantastic. It's great to see so many actors from the franchise put their hands up to recast their roles after such a long time, which provides great continuation for the series and continues to anchor the game in the franchise's world. The new cast members for this game, such as "The Soup Nazi", also work well, but there are also a few other well known celebrity actors included in the game too, much like in the earlier games.
Overall, if you're a Tex Murphy fan, most definitely pick this up. If you've never played Tex Murphy games before, you owe it to yourself to try out what was, in my opinion, one of the greatest gaming franchises of the 90s. If you’ve never played Tex games before, pick up the preceding three games and give these a go too. While their graphics become increasingly dated and ordinary with age, their stories and detective mechanics are what really make them shine, and therefore, still worth pursuing.
Tesla Effect: A Tex Murphy Adventure, is a game I most highly recommend!

It’s like going back in time. To 1994, to be exact, when Tex Murphy: Under a Killing Moon came out. It was a live-action, point-and-click adventure game, with bad acting, cheesy special effects, but a story that was pretty interesting and gameplay that backed it up nicely.
A great throwback to two decades ago, with an interesting story, and the same cheesy special effects and acting. It’s brought down by blurry graphics and a multitude of clipping issues, and is overly short. Play it in Gamer mode, not Casual, for the best experience.
+ Story. Like the previous games, the story is what makes this game. It’s humorous, serious, and at times, weird and offputting. But that’s the draw. There is lots to take in, from the required story portions to the optional questions you can ask pretty much anybody, all in typically cheese FMV.
+ Acting. The acting is cheesy, and not the greatest, but it beats the previous games. Tex really is a character you’ll want to hate.
+ Puzzles. Some of the puzzles are odd, but most wind up fitting nicely into the theme of the game. However, they’re all pretty easy, and you shouldn’t have any issues whatsoever with any of them.
- Clipping. My word, the clipping is atrocious. You’ll clearly clip through windows, doors, gates and holes. It’s as if the dev’s didn’t even try to add collision detection. The worst is when you clip through a wall you clearly should be ducking under, but can’t because there’s no duck option, yet when you watch the subsequent cutscene, the people duck under through. It’s odd.
- Poor graphics. Very poor graphics. Walls and backgrounds are blurry, the flashlight looks weird. A non-static point-and-click game doesn’t need to have the fanciest of graphics, but these are just bad.
- Very short. The game can be completed in a couple of hours, and if you play on Casual mode, every object that is of importance sparkles for you when you shine the flashlight over it. Playing in Gamer mode removes the sparkle, as well as stops you from asking for hints, but it’s still over very quick.

Snappy one-liners, great voicework, good level design, and lots of FMV goodness.  Tesla Effect really hits home with a newschool take on an oldschool FPS adventure formula.  Highly recommended if you liked other Tex Murphy games or if you ever played games like Return to Zork growing up as a kid.

Fast paced, unforgiving, yet fun. Strike Vector is an entertaining arena-shooter hailing back to the days of Quake 3 or Unreal Tournement where you duke it out in fully customisable variable geometry fighters through grimey industrial vertically stacked arenas at many fasts per second. Gameplay combines elements of Unreal Tournement arenas, Hawken-esque vehicle combat and a subtle hint of Starfox.
You'll die at first, a lot, but you'll have a smile doing it, and before long you'll be ploughing other peoples grinning faces into walls instead of being on the recieving end so try not to be put off by the cliff-like learning curve (If you won't jump off a cliff, you are going to get vertigo when you see the arenas)
Like most arena shooters the game is perfect for being able to step in or out and have 10 or 20 minutes of fast-paced action with no commitments (A lost art in today's gaming with dailies and grind that punishes players for not religiously playing their one game), though persistance rewards new skins and customisation options for your ship.
Sadly, the community right now seems to be lacking numbers, but perhaps word of mouth might help that.
It's worth remembering how that this is a PvP arena game, if you have a PvP allergy, or just dislike the genre, then it's unlikely this game will do anything for you. But if you miss the "good old days" then this is a blast from the past

This game takes a little work to get good at, but when it finally clicks, it is VERY satisfying to play. But you're going to have to take your lumps on the way.
It's very unforgiving to start with, but it has a very high skill ceiling.  On the upside, that means you will always be able to improve your skills to get that much closer to mastery, which is very satisfying -- but on the downside, it means that you will get slaughtered at the beginning by seemingly superhuman players, and you kind of have to shrug that off if you want to improve.
Another thing I recommend is that you put on some ACDC while you play - it enhances the experience considerably.  Also, increase your mouse sensitivity to at least 50% in the in-game options.  It makes a world of difference!
The community, from what I've seen, is very small, friendly, and dedicated.  If you're new and having trouble, definitely let people know, and they'll probably go easy on you and show you the ropes.

Way of the Samurai 4 is a game where a visual novel meets an action-packed samurai flick. It's really hard to categorize. You have an extensively branching plot and non-linear events from a visual novel on one hand, and elaborate combat, upgrading, crafting systems along with an open game world on the other. It's a rare and unique experience one should try themselves.
Way of the Samurai 4 is set in a post-isolationist Japan, with the country being more and more influenced by the foreigners, with some of the natives being ok with it and some of them - not so much. The stage is set in Amihama city, and you have 5 days to become part of the events and resolve the struggle in one way or the other. So how do you change the fate of Japan in just 5 days? By taking part in story-based and side-missions of course! The game has huge replay value, as almost every mission has different endings, and completing them will unlock something new in the game world or the story. Your event progress and opportunities are conveniently illustrated by a built-in flowchart, so you'll never miss anything.
So, how extensive is the story branching? You have three main routes with ending variations and an independent samurai route, which makes for 10 different endings combined. Like in a good movie, every branch and ending gives you a piece of a bigger picture of the events in Amihama. So it's not like a regular game which you beat once and put on the shelf — it's meant to be cleared multiple times in different ways. This is where having a story span of only five days comes in handy.
To make things more interesting, the results of your actions are transferred between playthroughs, as are your belongings, skills and the in-game flowchart. You've managed to convince the smithy's apprentice to return to his trade and succeed as the town's blacksmith? He'll be there working as a blacksmith in your next playthrough. You've been too aggressive in the town, acting as a bandit? Don't be surprised to find more patrols, as a response to the increased crime-rate. There are also other, more subtle changes.
With all the dialogues and decisions, this is still an action, combat-centered game. The combat system features multiple weapons, skills, stances and styles, but there's more to it: you have the ability to craft new weapons and improve existing ones, you can also fight melee or even switch to non-lethal moves (Kojima's Seal of Approval), you can even create your own unique fighting styles! So it's easy for those who just picked the game up, and sophisticated enough to give something fresh to seasoned players.
Now, technical side of the things. Way of the Samurai 4 is a port of a niche PS3 game back from 2012, which wasn't AAA even back then. Some things were ported as is and were not improved from PS3:
- 30 FPS lock;
- Game world is divided in lots of rather small locations;
- Texture resolution left as is. Game has nice visual style, though;
- Save system still has limited amount of slots;
The default keyboard controls were made by scattering actions all over the keyboard. The problem shows itself when it occurs to you that you either need to move your hand from WASD / the mouse to do something, or grow a spare hand. The mouse support is ok, but still, using a gamepad is highly recommended.
Despite every port-related problem and keyboard controls, this is a fun game to play and a unique experience that you probably won't find anywhere else. Most people have missed this gem, both upon its original PS3 release and this PC port, with SteamSpy estimating sales at less than 50K copies. Don't be like them! Amihama city awaits you for a samurai showdown.

I would like to go ahead and say that, while my PC version only has about thirty minutes on it, I have more than fifty hours in the console baby version of this game.
Way of the Samurai is a series that just kind of stuck with me every since I played the first one back in my younger days at the tender age of 53. I feel like I have a lot of common with the Ronin of old on account that we're both homeless and fight people for swords.
You play as a wandering Samurai, one that you customize with name, face, and clothing before sending him out into the world. After taking a boat ride to the port town of Amihama seven years after the foreign black ships showed up, demanding that the Japanese inhabitants buy their hats.
Once you get off the boat, your master-less Samurai is swept into conflict between the Pro-Shogunate government an the nationalist isolationists. It's up to you to decide whether you also want a funny hat or putting up “Keep out” signs wherever you go.
The game itself is a third person action game with a few RPG elements. You're free to go around town and find your own things to do like find side quests, fight random encounters, or scrounge for rice balls to eat like the miserable sack of crap you are. You can collect and take apart swords from fallen enemies, and even have a smith build your very own sword with the parts you collected from the dead, increasing it's stats over the course of your play through.
When in battle, you have a few moves at your disposal to make sure you don't end up like a background character from an old Akira Kurosawa movie. You have your standard attack, dodge, block, and parry. But what sets WOTS apart from other sword fighting games is the fact that you can change your fighting style with the use of books that enemies sometimes drop. These new martial arts, unless they're for spear or fist fighting, are usable with any sword and changes both your Samurai's stance and attack patterns completely. It's a neat thing that keeps combat interesting, finding a art that suits you instead of sticking to the default stance and attacks.
The story is...Strange, and that's coming from a garbage eater like me. The story revolves around a conflict between the pro-government forces and the anti-foreigner movement: The Prajna. The background itself wouldn't be all that strange if it wasn't for all of the strange characters. I don't know if it was the localization team or the director of the game itself, but WOTS4 is fairly sillier compared to the other games in the series. And that includes the one with the cowboy samurai.
The game is short, but that's kind of the point. It takes place over the course of four days with a different ending depending on your actions. I think there was 14 or 20 or so endings all together. So there's fun in finding all the ends. Or just saying “Screw it” and leaving the island via boat all together.

In the PS3 version of this game, there was a feature called Tsujigiri, or Cross-roads killing in English. What this feature was was a Dark Souls like element where other player's characters to show up in your game. They could be super powerful or weaker than you, and if you managed to kill them you would be able to take their sword as a prize, sometimes ending up with a sword much more powerful than the one you had with you.
