What Can I say about State of Decay? Playing this game feels a lot like how walking dead would've been if it wasn't in an interactive story format.  The gist of this game is to scout around for supplies in order to survive.  You can be as sneaky as you want to be, or go guns a blazing if you want the challenge of alerting hordes.
The graphics aren't too bad for a cheaper microsoft studios game and the gameplay does change with each play through.  There's some glitches here and there, mostly animation clipping or disappearing zombies but nothing game breaking.  Voice acting is acceptable.
My one HUGE complaint about this game is how it progresses even when you're not playing.  Your supplies decay at a rate per day that persists offline. Shadow of Mordor is an open world third person action game based on the Lord of the Rings franchise, following the story of Talion who seeks revenge on Mordor.
The story in Shadow of Mordor takes a while before it gets interesting, but the further you come, the better the story gets. This together with the fantastic cinematic and voice acting, can make the game really immersive. You are free to choose how you approach missions, whether it's going all-in, playing it stealthy or using enemies against each other. While playing through the game, you'll notice the scenery in this game is gorgeous, there's 2 different worlds for you to explore and they look amazing. Thanks to Photo-Mode it's really easy to make great screenshots as well, this is an editor that pauses the game and enables you to apply filters, move the camera, change fov etc.
Shadow of Mordor introduces the Nemesis system. The Nemeses also known as Sauron's Army, are the Uruk and Olog leaders that are generated uniquely with each playthrough of the game. Each nemesis has their own personality and will rise or fall within their social structure as the game progresses. They are affected by Talion's actions, and each will react differently to Talion's actions in Mordor, be it fight, flight, or some other reaction. Resulting in enemies reacting differently when you meet them after they've already killed or almost killed you. Enemies also have unique fears/strengths to discover which will be important in battles.
Combat is really well done and comparable to the Batman series, it looks amazing and plays great. The combat in general is quite easy (making the game easier as well) but is just really satisfying. You will have 3 options for combat, either go in with your sword and slice through orcs and finish them with some brute finishing moves, stealth kill them through sneaking or keep your distance and snipe them with your bow. Next to combat, movement is really well done. Sneaking over buildings, climbing and hanging on the side of walls Assasins Creed style, everything feels great, smooth and just works. However controls can feel a bit wonky at times.
Throughout the game you'll earn points to upgrade your weapons and skills. From movement to combat abilities. Everything can be upgraded and it's really fun to discover all the new upgrades. This gives motivation to keep on playing even after the Story mode(Which has a decent length of 10-15 hours). Cause there will be enough to do in the world of Mordor. Even after finishing the main missions, there's tons of things to do like: Taking down warchiefs/captains, rescuing people, Doing challenges, finding collectables and more! After you're done with everything, there's DLC that adds more missions/outfits.
Some downsides of the game however, are for example: some missions can feel a bit unnecessary because of repetitivity, some battles are really anticlimactic and the game can be quite easy due to its easy combat at times. Side characters could've been used better as well, some of them are easy to forget.
Overall, i would highly recommend Shadow of Mordor. It's a great game with lots of content, a decent story, satisfying combat and great scenery! However, the game is more oriented towards stealth gameplay, so make sure you like that.

This is the first game in the Mass Effect series.
And like many other first games, this one has a lot of flaws.
But the positive up front:
The game opens up a unique and interesting new universe to explore and expand. Really, the most interesting thing about this game is the world. Even though it may not have aged well in terms of graphics, there is still a lot of stuff to look around for.
This game also introduces the dialogue system, for which the Mass Effect series is famous for. That includes that your character can go down different paths and has to make hard decisions from time to time. But this game only scratches the surface of that and many other things that get explored much deeper in the following games.
All in All:
Pros:
+ good story (nothing major, but with a few very cool twists and ideas)
+ new and unique universe
+ introduces certain very interesting gameplay mechanics - Combos in combat, dialogue and decision system
Cons:
- graphics haven't aged well
- gameplay is very clumsy
- at times a bit repetetive
Still, I think this is a game you would not regret playing.

To Deaf & Hard of Hearing gamers out there:
Do not buy the game. It is far from deaf-friendly! When the game was first released, it was shown on the store page that the game had English subtitles available. Sure enough, there was an option to turn on subtitles within the game. The problem? It didn't work at all, the settings would reset themselves once you actually started playing the game. Even after trying several proposed fixes, it did not come anywhere close to working.
Then I found out that despite the option being there, the subtitles were actually not implemented yet. Emphasis on the word "yet." I asked for an ETA on the subtitles, never got a response.
A few weeks later, I decide to give the game another shot, see if it had actually been completed as per the game's store page. I checked the game's options and was confused to find that the subtitles option had vanished. There was an announcement stating they had updated the options to properly work but no mention of the subtitles. Checking the store page revealed to me that the developers had quietly removed the check under "Subtitles" section under the "Languages" header.
Do not buy the game unless you want to go into the game without subtitles and not knowing what the hell to do besides wander around like an idiot suffering from constant vertigo.
Shame on the developers for not sticking to their word.

I have just finished my first playthrough of Mass Effect. Until recently, I had given it a wide berth, beacuse I don't really like shooter-games (the first Max Paine and Ratchett & Clank being exceptions). A friend convinced me that ME is not so much a shooter but an RPG. Considering the amount of praise the game has received I finally wanted to give it a try, and now, after seeing the end credits roll, I have two words to describe Mass Effect: Overrated shooter.
I don't want to go into rant-mode, so I'll just try to sum up what bugs me most:
- Story: Many people say how great a sci-fi story ME is. I say: no. Neither is it very original, nor well told: endless info-dumps, barely connected chapters (i.e. main worlds), utter predictability...
- Characters: On first glance, most characters seem interesting, but soon you realise that they do not influence anything and are not influenced by anything. The few dialogues uncover the backgrounds, which is interesting, but has no effect whatsoever. Wasted potential.
- Dialogues: Way too patriotically American, excuse me, Alliancian for comfort. Much gung-ho militarism, covert and open racism. The rest... well, I get the impression that Shepard can't be all that bright, so his dialogue options have to reflect that.
- Explorations: Copy-paste worlds, copy-paste side-quests. Not even interesting enough to say more.
Actually, ME is not a bad game, but unable to live up to its' fame. Do I regret playing? No, I had enough fun and the game is dumb enough to play after a tiring workday. Can I recommend ME? Depends. If you're looking for a sci-fi story, a role-playing game, or both, better look elsewhere. If you like a shooter with the playing time blown up by dishing out more and more of the same, mostly easy battles- go ahead.
My thumb down has the following reasons: I can't give a weighted rating, which would be 5/10, negative reviews often get more attention and, most important: I was promised something that ME simply is not.

Pillars of Eternity is a classic fantasy roleplaying game in the likes of Baldur's Gate. You can play solo or in a party made from characters met along the way or custom made ones. If you like RPGs you have to play this. Period.
There is a lot of everything, reading, talking, fights, quests, items. It is just a great game. But to elaborate a bit. I loved Baldur's Gate 2, it was freaking amazing. I might be biased towards every game that looks and feels similar. And PoE is like BG2, just better. Did I mention there is a lot of everything here? You create your main character and can even create your whole party if you so desire, but the NPCs that can join you along the way are some great personalities and it's a pleasure to travel with most of them. The main story, as the mini stories of each npc, is well written and quite interesting to unravel.
VISUALS
The game is pretty. You travel through, forests, cities, countryside, dungeons and various other environments, and all of them look amazing. Fighting in the rain, in tall grass, with magical lightnings strucking here and there looks as cool as it sounds. Characters look very nice and with all the various clothing options it's fun to play dress up. All the spells look flashy enough, but not to the point that you cannot see through the fireworks. Just look at the screenshots, aren't they pretty?
AUDIO
Very fitting medieval tunes most of the time with Globus-like majestic battle tunes. I found myself actively listening to the background music more than once. Voice acting is very good, it helps that the character's lines are well written. No Minsc here, but I was very fond of Eder and Aloth. Other than that lightnings kaboom, fireballs whoosh, magic missiles whizz. All is well on the audio front.
GAMEPLAY
Have you played Baldur's Gate? Or any BG inspired RPG? Lots of classes, and interesting too. Active pause or real time fights. Party management. Very good new concept or endurance vs health. During fights you use endurance to make an action and enemies deal dammage to your endurance and health. Endurance regenerates automatically if you win a fight and you can use spells or potions to regenerate t during a fight. Health is regenerated on rest only. Very interesting concept and it works really well. Other than that it's all your standard RPG fare. Done right. Quests, bounties, killing stuff, upgrading your stronghold, everything is here. Also enough of difficulty settings and acheievements for all you masochists out there.
Basically if you like RPGs you own it to yourself to play this one. It's that good. Main story with all the side quests and full stronghold upgrade took me ca. 60hrs on normal difficulty with expert enabled (no hints). I had two extremely difficult fights, one being one of the first bounties - ogres - and the second the Adra dragon. Other than that the difficulty was... normal. Excellent game.

Best Euroshmup I've ever played.
This is the euro STG style done RIGHT! Specifically the european PC breed of shooters with RPG elements. Fair bullet patterns, lots of upgrade fun, a full arcade mode and plenty of challenge. Music is awesome if not a bit repetitive. Backgrounds can leave a bit to be desired, but the graphics are mainly in the bullets, which look spectacular, with plenty of colour and variety. Story mode is long, I'm not sure how long, I'm 18 levels in. They're mostly all really well-designed levels, albeit a bit easy on Normal mode. It won't you go back to earlier levels and annihilate♥♥♥♥♥♥with your upgraded weapons, and you only earn upgrades if you survive the level you're playing. This means there's no grinding to be done, which is a plus, and you'll simply have to retry the levels until you can beat them. A level select at some point would be helpful to practice stages without going through the entire story mode. Getting stuck on a hard level can be frustrating since you can't go back to an earlier level to cool off, and you can't have multiple saved games, so you're stuck there unless you wanna start over from the beginning, but at least then you can use a different perks upgrade strategy if your previous one wasn't working. Earned weapons you can switch between anytime, and only the perks are permanent. But you can undo your *most recent* perks upgrade and pick a different one at (I believe) any point.
More to be written once I have some more time with the game.
If you're on the fence about this game, you've probly played a few lackluster euro-type shooters or you've noticed the slew of mediocre $2.00 shooters on Steam and other platforms. Well this is nothing like that, this is a super fun game that that uses many elements of the euro style without being weakened by sloppy design or cheap deaths. If you're not into the story mode and messing with weapon sets and perks, the arcade mode is perfect, you just pick a preset weapon configuration and that's what you have for the whole game. There's also a Survival Score Attack mode.
Don't pay attention to any of the game's descriptions on Steam. This game has little to do with Raiden or Radiant Silvergun andf almost nothing to do with Ikaruga. It's also more about being a UK PC RPG STG than it is about being a bullet hell. There are fast bullets like Raiden and Various weapons, vaguely similar I guess, the RSG, but that's quite a stretch. I really feel the ad copy for this game gives the wrong impression. Think Tyrian 2000. This game is like Tyrian 2014, and all for the better.

My review for this latest installment in the Splinter Cell franchise is well overdue! To cut it short: It's an excellent game. It was the first game I played (upon release) that had the enter/exit cover option, and in the beginning I wasn't sure if I liked it, but it definitely grew on me. It allows for superior tactical planning.
You definitely have a choice here how you want to handle a mission, and you can tailor your load-out to match. I find that I usually prefer a good medium between stealth (ghost) and silent takedowns (panther). The third option, assault, ultimately turns into chaos and that is not really how a Splinter Cell (by definition an operative who is a silent infiltrator that has the freedom to choose on how to proceed) works. I find that a non-lethal takedown usually works quite well, but there are situations in which pacifying a room permanently, is definitely a good plan (e.g. hostage situations) if safe to do so and if the mission parameters allow for it. There are definitely some targets tht need to be captured alive!
During the game you will have the option to upgrade your gear which will also provide you with much better intel while you're deployed, and will give you better abilities to protect yourself. Spending available Uplay points on available suit options is also definitely helpful, if you're pondering that. They're both worth it.
Some have complained that the "execution" system (you gain up to three points for silent takedowns which you can then use to automatically execute marked targets with a headshot) is making things too easy, but ultimately the truth is that you have to work for that option to become available and it is not an automatic "recharge". You will, however, find several weapons crates during a mission that will allow you to restock on ammo and gadgets.
If you liked any of the previous Splinter Cell games (and if you like tactical/stealth/military games I can't see why you wouldn't), then this is definitely a recommendation. Get to your next best (online) store and exfil with this game. Mission accomplished.

A great reboot of a long lost genre of games. Adventure FMV games were at their height in the mi-90’s as CD-ROM’s were becoming a popular option in desktop PC’s. While a great deal of these games contributed greatly to killing the genre, it had its merits and gems, with the Tex Murphy series being a clear stand-out. However, did the series deserve a second life?
Upon it's 2014 release, and 20 years later, Tex Murphy's back and it’s rather refreshing to encounter in a sea of modern military shooters, generic game mechanics and poor story telling. While the graphics are slightly below modern standard, the actors have aged (some better than most) and the medium dead, it is a thrilling ride with great narrative, funny dialogue and challenging quests and puzzles, it is proof that games can still be creative, entertaining and intelligent.
In an era were games are judges by sales figures, it is a great relief to see a game that journeys back to when they were made for gamers and not for profit. A lesson to where the industry should have been headed instead of what we have now.

With only a few hours on my belt I'm not sure if I should be reviewing this already, but oh lordy do I love this game. It's really hard to get into, but after an hour of straight practice I finally got my first kill, and both me and the game got better and better since.
Short version:
++ Graphics
++ Concept
+   Gameplay
+   Variation
+/-   Hard to learn, fun to 'master'.
-  No Team balancing
-  Could use more players
-- Balancing issues with some loadouts
Long version:
High-speed dogfighting in the most maneuverable fighters you've ever flown give you such an adrenaline rush that you get the feeling you need to stop playing after a while, but you never will. The fast respawns and instant-changes you can make to your fighter make it addicting and very action-packed. The minor customisation is fun but doesn't seem to give anyone an advantage which is great, it makes you try out everything the game has to offer.
Some loadouts seem to be used more then others though. Like the dual Plasma-canon 'Sniper' set-up, which is just guys floating around on their own trying to shoot people from the very edge of a map and running away to the other edge with bonus-boosters the moment danger gets near. This seems rather weird for a game that is about out-manouvering your opponent rather then out-shooting them. I'd rather not see this weapon in the game as it seems cheap and forces other players to use the same tactic, turning the server in an all-around sniping-jiggle match. Which is, quite frankly, really really boring for such an exciting game.
So I guess there are some balancing issues that need to be fixed, including how one team can consist out of just lvl 50 veterans while the other team is nothing but newcomers. The game should be able to balance teams properly like any other online shooter, so that's a weird oversight imo.
Oh but did I mention that the graphics are gorgeous, but still keeps playing at 60fps even on old computers like mine? Beautiful! Lag might sometimes be an issue though depending on the server that you're on. The maps are beautifully crafted and they're all unique with their own style, hazards and way of traversing it. Some are very open with lots of debris flying around while others have narrow corridors and require precise control of your craft. They all bring their own challenge and variation and they have kept me perfectly curious and entertained so far.
Never a dull moment! Hop into your Vector and join the high-speed, high-stakes battlefield in the sky!

This is one of the best games I have ever played.
Purchased <2 weeks ago, have already played for 66 hours. Some of the roles I like less than others, but overall the replayability is insane... the game as a whole never gets old. Buy it.
It is chiefly a social intuition/communication game mixed with strategy/puzzle/logic. It pits two factions aginst one another with a host of "neutral" classes that make things even more messy. The variety of roles is impressive, and 16-person games are amazingly fun.
I have learned more about human nature in this game than any other game, and it is very VERY fun to take advantage once this knowledge is gained.
For example, playing as an Evil King, my goal is to destroy the team I supposedly lead without making my evil allies suspicious enough of me to kill me off. This challenge requires creativity, sublety, and constant tactical revision.
Playing as an investigative role on the good team, your job is to sniff out the bad guys. Just don't communicate too frequently or too openly with the other good guys (who you can't be totally sure of anyways and need to individually vet) otherwise you will become a target.
You get the idea. I could go on but I won't. Buy it, well worth the $10. Get a few friends interested as well and it will become even more entertaining.

Flawed? Eh... if I sit down long enough I'll find a flaw anywhere. My internet is bad (and so am I) so take this review from one filthy casual who plays story mode and bots.
Story: In short, I like it. Dark, certainly. But full of character. Every interactable thing with in the hubs gives you a little slice of story. Without devulgeing any story up front, I'll just go ahead and say the KSR is my favorite faction, if a smidge misguided... but who isnt?
The end made me think for a bit. Funnily enough, minimal amounts of writeing in the from of dialouge were used to set up a big finale, and in the end, the big reveal was done relitivly quietly save for the shooting and explosions in game. No exposistion, they got that over with before the mission... the entire game is dotted with it in fact.
It leaves the fate of all beasts heavily alluded to, but very vauge at the same time. Comendable work if I say so. It left just enough room for doubt and head cannon to run rampant.
Multiplayer: Well now I can only speak as a comp-stoming casual, but I will say that the computer is not entirely brain dead. If your looking for practice runs to test army builds and the like, I sugest starting at Easy and working your way up. From what I can see, random maps are a mixed blessed curse all in one. You can have your game extrodinarily trashed at the start from where your mill is. Do note, its not impossible to recover from. I think if I were to say, sugest this for tournament play on a more advanced level, some sort of tweaking, or full on unchangeing maps, would be nessisary.
I did mention it was a 'blessed' curse. Take an RTS, say 'Wargame', or 'StarCraft'. There is a map on that game you like. You know it very well. You know its exploits. Because your playing on that map, you have some odd form of 'home field advantage'. The other experianced players will probably put up a goof fight, but anytime the matchmaker gives you a fresh, green newbie, you break them before the game is started, or toy with them while you build to your supply cap. Then steam roll them.
Cant do that in this game. I mean... you CAN, but you got to work for it.
So all in all I say good game. Matches last 5 to 15 minutes. to be fair, if you break 15, something went wrong. Your forced to think on your feet, and find new ways to micro in a game where most people just grab a blob of units and throw them at enemy mills. I hope the developers keep working hard on this game, I'd love to see more from it in the form of units, story, or mechanics (like the map thing I mentioned earlier). Glory to the KSR, send them all to the Kitchens, and have fun.

The first installment of the Mass Effect trilogy proved to be a solid start in Bioware's space opera. While the best is yet to come, the game was meant to be the building blocks of an entire universe, which is Mass Effect's strong point.
Bioware is (or was) widely known for good writing and better characters. Mass Effect follows the story of Commander Shepard, the somewhat generic military-type protagonist that can be seen in a multitude of games. The plot is simple (save the galaxy from impending doom) but fitting for an epic journey. Keep in mind that the game was designed as a trilogy, so Mass Effect is just laying out the carpet towards "saving the galaxy". While the main story is captivating enough, with a few twists that change the stakes you're fighting for, it's the characters that shine.
During the opening hours of the game, you suurround yourself with various crew members and companions that are unique individuals. As any respectable RPG would do, dialogue is a massive part of the game, and conversing with the crew members is probably the highlight of the "writing" part. Each have their own stories, some more interesting than the others, and while the game does not offer very much character development, the excellent character writing is one of the main pillars of Mass Effect.
When embarking on this voyage, Bioware had to create the entire universe from scratch. This is where the creative team shined. Comparing to other space games, the world was created to be very relatable. Everything was made to be believable, like interplanetary travel, weapons that are more like railguns rather than lasers, and so on. It was specifically designed for the player to accept it and understand it without the need of a dictionary.
It's a world filled with interesting things that encourages exploration. The world wants you to learn about it, making you walk around and just checking out the area. The scenery is great in the "handcrafted" areas of the game, like the Citadel or various main-mission planets, but falls flat when entering the side-quest zone, which is repetitive "almost same planet but with different climate", "same base with same assets, just different enemies" and "same damn enemies I fought with 10 minutes ago".
From a level-design point of view, the game walks a line between railway and open field. More areas are quite linear, with you just following the trail of enemies to the objective, while other areas offer a more vast playing field that are 1 kilometer wide and 1 meter deep: mostly nothing to do but drive to the next point of interest.

Mass Effect is basically a cover-based action game. If you're not talking to somebody or enjoying the sights, you're fighting enemies in an area littered with cover. The gameplay, while not very engaging, is decent enough to get you through the game. Most abilities are not impressive so you'll likely find yourself just pumping rounds into an enemy until it dies. While it does add a "magic" element with Biotics (the Mass Effect equivalent of Force powers), the style is even more boring and unrewarding than going full Rambo.
The game suffers a lot from lack of quality of life features. Lack of a fleshed-out journal and quest tracking, horrible inventory management and so on. As an example, you will likely have an inventory full with the tons of weapons that you pick up from enemies or loot containers. First, you'll start going through your squad members, checking each weapon (one by one) if it has stats that are better than the currently equipped. Then you'll either want to sell the remaining loot or turn it into omni-gel, a sort of currency that lets you bypass the god-awful "unlock chest/door/etc" minigame. You will have to sell each weapon (one by one) to the vendor or turn them (one by one) into gel. I'm not kidding when I say it will take up several hours of your total game time.
Physics are ... I'm not even sure how to call them. Wonky? I think "wonky" is a good word. The first ride in the player's only vehicle, a futuristic armored personnel carrier, will be either hilarious or nausea inducing due to the wonky stuff.
AI is very basic, with most of them just charging your location while using cover from time to time. No tactics, even on harder levels. Companion AI is either frustrating or hilarious (depending on your point of view) and you will oftenly see them shooting a wall or just shooting you in the back. They spare no effort to shoot through whatever (or whoever) is between them and the enemy NPCs.
While not the greatest (even for its era), the graphics still hold out and are good enough to be easy on the eye. As dialogue is probably the biggest part of the game, character design was clearly favored, with the player character and NPCs that are were clearly given more attention than some of the environments. The basic lip-sync works remarkably well and gives life to the scenes. While some environments are gorgeous (the Citadel, Ilos, etc), side areas feel rushed and unfinished. Planets feel like one plot of land with varying topography: no trees, reused assets for points of interest, basically a barren zone that requires you to imagine what that alien planet might look like given enough time.
On a side note, the modding community created a HD texture pack for the game that breathes new life into it. It does not match current graphical fidelity but makes the experience far more enjoyable.
Now let's talk audio. As before, a huge amount of time was used for dialogue. Being fully voiced, it was a big step up from previous titles. The great cast brought to life all the loveable characters that the player suurrounds himself with.
While most of the voice acting is top notch, the overall sound quality is dragging the game downwards. Due to technical limitations, most areas have you listening to two sounds: background music and footsteps. Out in vaccum, it's understandable but in other areas it's immersion breaking to a degree.
Despite all the minor flaws, I loved Mass Effect. I loved the characters, I loved the world, I loved the design. It became a classic despite the shortcomings and paved the way for the even greater Mass Effect 2. I totally recommend the game, especially when it's on sale.

First, let me clear up a few things right off the bat:
With those out of the way, here's my honest experience with the 1st game in the franchise.
I came into this game with almost no knowledge of mass effect, save for the memes, the hatred of vehicle segments, and the odd,"Tali is best waifu," comment I'd see out on the internet. What I expected was a mediocre space tale paired with a discount Captain Kirk simulator.
I was kinda wrong.
Mass effect took my expectations and atomized them, and I can confidently say that this game easily rivals modern titles. The story was actually enjoyable here, and transcended beyond the typical "Aliens kill puny humans" tale that permeates many a space game. Instead, it takes unique characters, an abnormal premise, a (usually) pertinent choice system, and combines them to make a unique set of events that the player can feel responsible for.
Speaking of which, the choice system is easily the best part of the game, something that anyone who's even heard of mass effect probably understands. Sometimes, the simplest of decisions can lead to an unfortunate incident, or it can drive the odds of a situation in your favour. For the most part, big decisions can be seen from a mile away, so they usually have consequences the player can already foresee. However, the little choices that massively change your experience are the absolute best to discover.
(Don't ask why I'm not spoiling a decade-old game).
'Course, the game's not perfect, and a lot of it's age shows through a few key things.
Outside of those few gripes though, the game is pretty well-done from a 2017 POV. The combat is great, the gunplay is decent, you'll get invested in the characters as you learn their stories, the cutscenes are still great by modern standards, and the story is expertly-crafted. This is probably the first game where I went out of my way to read/find all of the lore, as every piece of it made the world feel more and more plausible in the future. If you're a fan of games with solid stories and well done characters, pick this one up. Same if you like seeing your choices actually mean something. It's got some flaws, but they're easy to look past when the world immerses you this much.

Pros :

- Very interesting storyline
- Good third-person shooter gameplay - and it's saying much since I am not a fan of shooters
- Characters are good : full customisation of the main character and interesting social interactions (including romance, which is great!)
Cons :
- The buildings/environments are all the same in secondary missions, so it gets a little bit repetitive if you want to do everything. I ended up skipping the secondary missions.
- No possibility of continuing the game with the secondary missions when you end the final mission (so everything you have not done until there will remain undone)
- Not enough romance choices imo :p
Globally I enjoyed this game very much, and went on with the full trilogy. I absolutely recommend it for anyone who likes RPGs and/or Sci-Fi.

I got this game on a whim because I once played this series like... a decade ago. DW3/4 to be specific. And even though I know full well that this sort of game is basically meant for consoles, I managed to play it just fine once I adjusted the key bindings to stuff that worked well for me. Anyway... game.
If, like me, you have played these games before, you pretty much know what you are in for. If you have never played any of these games, I'm not quite sure what else is quite like it. Basically it's a fighting game, except it is on large battlefield maps where you murder thousands of random and a handful of named NPC's while following objectives in order to complete each level. If that sounds repetitive... well it can certainly be that. It's the ultimate hack and slash-fest game, and if you get bored with murdering insane numbers of enemies, then chances are this game is not for you.
The game is based upon the Three Kingdoms era of Ancient China (184-280, roughly), and, despite the absurd outfits and personalities of many of the characters in the game, it is actually fairly consistent with what is known about the period. Or rather, it is consistent with the famous novel 'Romance of the Three Kingdoms' by Luo Guanzhong, which is basically a work of historical fiction that takes real events and bends them a bit according to the whims and views of the author. Which, of course, means that certain characters (particularly Shu-Han characters like Xuande/Liu Bei) are depicted as noble honorable sorts fighting for justice while others (like Mengde/Cao Cao) are depicted as villanous and driven by ambition. I don't want to dig too deep into this because there most likely are entire books written about how Luo Guanzhong messed around with the characters, but the depictions he made are pretty much what are found in this and all previous DW games. The nice thing though is that if you read between the lines (or maybe it's just because I am very familiar with the source material this game is based off of), you can see the flaws in the author's bias in the game as well. Namely that Liu Bei was a massive hypocrite every bit as ambitious as his rivals, and that Cao Cao, while not exactly the nicest guy around, wasn't the hellspawn other characters (like Liu Bei) called him.
Anyway, the game follows the story decently well, though some creative license and trimming down obviously has happened. I still liked how the game depicted things most of the time. Perhaps my favorite was Lu Bu's campaign which, while maintaining the massive "OMG ITS LU BU" hype that all DW games have had, reveals exactly why the real Lu Bu got himself executed in chapter 19 of a 120 chapter book: that he was dumb as a brick, betrayed people constantly, and never listened to anyone's advice. While the old DW games I played did have storylines for him, they didn't take the historical route that this game's (default) story path takes. The same goes for the numerous character deaths shown, though many of these are made more dramatic than they actually were.
Also, while the playable character cast has increased to the point of total insanity (including some that may not have even existed or actually fought on battlefields), I did like that, in the time between DW4 and this, they added a number of characters that rounded out the cast further by including some of the other lesser-known strategists (Chen Gong, Lu Su) and characters who rose to prominence in the later parts of the story (Deng Ai, the sons of Guan Yu/Zhang Fei, as well as the entire Jin faction who were the ultimate winners of this whole mess). I thought that was a nice treat since these sorts had been badly neglected in past games, where everything seemed to stop at the year 234 (when Kongming/Zhuge Liang died), which was roughly the chronological halfway point of the entire story.
Ok, I better stop and just finish this up.
In short, It's a DW game. That means that on the one hand, the combat gets repetitive, many of the characters are very hard to take seriously, and many of the story events are overdramatized to the point of being kind of ridiculous. On the other hand, there is a MASSIVE amount of content (and all those DLC's for this "Complete Edition" are purely cosmetic), big battles are kind of fun, and one can even argue that the storyline's inherent cheesiness may actually be more a positive than a negative.
If you have never played one of these games before, this is the one i'd look at because (to my knowledge) it's the newest one and has an insane amount of content even compared to its predecessors. If you have played these and liked them before... why not? If you didn't like these games however, then most likely this will do nothing to change your opinion.
For all it's goofiness and repetition, DW is still entertaining enough for me to waste sizeable amounts of time with it. Hooray and stuff.

This game is for anyone who is a fan of the genre, and also for anyone who doesn't know what FMV is. I personally never played Tex Murphy games before, so I can't say if it's a good sequel or not. It has a detective mystery, jokes and some (mostly unoriginal) puzzles. What does feel both very familiar and, at the same time, very new, is the live actors and filmed cutscenes. You know, the games and movie makers strive for decades to make computer generated faces look realistic, and yet you can always learn to tell it's a fake. It's surprisingly refreshing to see actual live real human people talking to you from the screen. Even if their acting skills are not Oscar-winning :) And it's cool to watch pre-rendered cutscenes with flying cars and special effects. The clever way developers combine 3D world where you can walk around like in any FPS game, with full motion video dialogs and cutscenes, was also a pleasant surprise for me. The gameplay is mostly about dicovering pieces of the mystery through dialogs with real actors in full motion video, and walking around and finding hidden objects in full 3D. It's a good solid game, relaxing mostly, I'm enjoying it. And it makes me want to see the FMV genre developed further, with more games and more creative ideas on using real actors in a gaming environment.
So, my personal opinion is that Tesla Effect is a nice game, but not a blockbuster; what it really deserves a big praise for, is showing that FMV gaming still has a potential. If you're a fan of adventure titles, you're most likely to enjoy it, but if you're just curious to know what FMV is like in 2014, I'd recommend waiting for a sale.

I've been on Steam for a long time but this game is the first one to motivate me to write a review - it was that good :) As a hardcore point-and-click games fan, I somehow missed the hype around Tex Murphy series when previous installments were released. This is the first FMV game I've ever played and this is what I liked about it:
- Quality of graphics and FMV scenes exceeded my expectations. Transitions between cutscenes and in-game content is smooth and 3D environments in general are a real eye candy (for a game this type)
- Story is interesting, full of some (sometimes) cheesy humour but overall very engaging - the cheesy parts are actually funny and enjoyable rather than annoying. Acting is great but then again, you won't see much of acting from the secondary characters in the game (mostly short dialogues)
- Puzzles are logical for an adventure game and mostly enjoyable rather than frustrating. The game auto-saves a lot, so even if you happen to die (which in some parts of the game may happen a bit more often), you won't have to replay anything
- There is a decent hint system (pretty much an in-game walkthrough), so if you get stuck, you can always review the solution of this particular puzzle/episode of the game. I used the hint system a few times in the beginning of the game until I got used to the mechanics of character control and interaction and almost haven't used it since
- Hunting for items/interactable objects can sometimes be a pain in the butt, since it's much harder to do pixel hunting in 3D environments as opposed to 2D environments used by most point and clicks/adventure games. I am playing the easy mode which makes an item "sparkle" when you use the flashlight but I still had some difficulties noticing several items in the game (they were only noticeable when Tex approaches them closely). I think that this happened 2-3 times so far, so definitely not a frustrating experience (if you play it on the hard mode, some items may be very challenging to find :))
Playing the game felt a bit like L.A. Noire (due to its unique Film Noir like setting), a bit like Fallout 3 (in terms of exploring relatively spacy areas and buildings) and a lot like a very good adventure/point and click game. I even went ahead and bought all other Tex Murphy adventures even though I probably won't be able to stand the old graphics for too long but as all point-and-click games fans know, these games are not about the graphics (e.g. Wadget eye games) :)
I sincerely hope they will make another one or remake one of the older ones - I will buy it instantly.

If you've never played a WotS game, it has some of the most realistic sword combat this side of Bushido Blade.  Instead of the typical sword-fighting game where you simply mash one button continuously to do ridiculous combos, you actually need to use a bit of thought and quite of a bit of timing to be successful here. When I'm not playing State of Decay, I wonder why I can't stop playing it. I should find the combat repetitive - it's simplistic, and doesn't reward you for doing anything but overpowered trip attacks to incapacitate zombies. I should find the fetch quests annoying - if it's not some moron wandering into a zombie party, it's a moron who wants to go kill the 'freak' zombies. I should find the glitches and bugs a deal breaker, but I still boot the damn game up, over and over again.
I know I shouldn't, but I find that I really like this game and can't stop playing it. It's got that 'one more mission' addictiveness that draws you in, and it doesn't complicate gameplay with too many moving parts. Kill zombies, find materials, don't die. It is repetitive, but in the same way that Mount and Blade was repetetitive. It's the same map, the same people, the same combat, over and over again, but it's still fun. It's fun burning mobs with molotovs, it's fun finding those much needed supplies, it's fun splattering zombie heads all over the grass.
That said, the story game isn't worth more than a playthrough, and even then, honestly? It's really only valuable for introducing you to the geography. Breakdown is where the real fun is, and though it is a bit of a scumbag move to make you pay for a feature that really should have been in the game, put together the game is still less than thirty bucks. For the number of hours you'll get out of it, it's a pretty good deal. If you do get the game, grab the mod that lets you put bags in the back of trucks. Trust me, huge improvement.
Buy this game if you enjoy searching for stuff, don't get bored bashing in zombie heads, and appreciate the survival side of the zombocalypse.

The hallways of a mysteriously decrepit and deranged research facility beckon your escape, but the weakening of your mental state refuses to make navigating your way to freedom an easy task. The voice of a mysterious girl describes to the player acts of unspeakable injustices from within the confines, and your descent into the sanity depleting design of this strange complex leads you on the hunt for more information. Why are you here, what is the purpose of this wretched place, and who is this girl leaving you notes telling of a sketchy employment situation gone horribly afoul?
is a rare breed of psychological horror gaming, one with impeccable pacing and constant flow. Never feeling slow, never sluggish, tedious or breaking the pace, it keeps you one-hundred-percent on your toes and pressing ahead without the will to ever look back.
The story and the mystery surrounding the fates of the facilities inhabitants is told through the discovery of notes left behind by past workers, and cryptic visions from elements of this bleak environment. The voice acting is fantastically done and part of what keeps the player so immersed in the harrowing events unfolding through the snippets of writings uncovered and a real sense of urgency, confusion and terror can be heard with each increasingly dire development of the story.
Moving through the story of
takes you through a range of odd environments and surreal imagery. Starting with the harsh reality of the trashed and abandoned research complex and slowly evolving into more vibrantly obscured visions of lush red curtains and fancy tiled floors as if you've stepped right into an episode of
, but which of these surroundings are merely a figment of your imagination?
The beautifully orchestrated soundtrack is instantly chilling and ominous, worming its way through your ears and into your mind where you can feel every sharp note of the violin effecting your psyche. The echoing of unnerving metal scrapes in the distance, the buzz and crackle of old and failing light fixtures all work together to create a heavy atmosphere that constantly builds tension only to all explode in your face with every twist of the plot and your pysche.
Hallucinatory visual effects that plague our character creates a chaotic and fittingly confusing effect, and your only solace is the scarce Benzodiazepine pills scattered throughout the facility. This in part is what gives
such a uniquely bizarre and frantic situation for a horror game, and a unique concept not seen since the likes of the legendary
in terms of how much your mind is being screwed with. The wavy and twisting effect of your ravaged mental state making you feel as though you are losing your vision, causing you to squint and focus your attention on the distortion of the screen even harder until that one disturbing/shocking moment takes you off guard.
Not only does neglecting to take your pills bring about the mind altering hallucinatory effects, but stirs the vengeful and twisted souls of past test subjects of this cruel place. Always ahead of you if you rush and forget to scavenge for pills but never too far behind if you lose your way and slow down, the threat of seeing one of these sanity depleting and terrifying creatures is what drives your carefully paced search for escape and answers.
The random and deliberately confusing nature of the ever-changing hallways around you and the constant transformation of the mysterious facility is an incredibly innovative mechanic for the genre. The straight-forward and almost repetitive nature that plagues most modern horror games gets a much needed spicing up and the cold, gray, lifeless hallways we're so used to from the genre now feel much more alive, more
and
.
is one of those elusive and unforgettable horror titles that manages to keep me consistently glued to the screen, only to severely regret my undying attention at the harrowing realization that I'm not alone in these dark and desolate hallways. The creepiness is in full force thanks to a genuinely mind-bending atmosphere, nothing ever feels forced and the scares are all derived from the mysterious unknown factors and macabre questions swimming around your mind. Even more impressive is that this elegant and disturbing journey into a twisted facility was hand crafted and coordinated by a team of five very dedicated people working from various locations across the globe.
Amongst the droves of same-y horror titles and their cheap thrills,
stands out as one of the few sublimely twisted experiences with a hallucinatory touch and just the right amount of mind♥♥♥♥ery causing you to question the reality of every last step you took. Where have you really been and what really happened, where are you going and will you ever get there?

"You must gather your party before venturing forth"
PoE harkens back to the cult classic of 1998; Baldur's Gate. However it does not follow any DnD ruleset at all. Instead it invents the wheel with its own set of rules that may be confusing for a good handful of hours at first - to say the least.
While traditional DnD states that health is the primary attribute for how healthy a character is, PoE mixes in endurance that factors in on every encounter. You will regain endurance (up to a certain point) after each fight, but health is not. Think of it as fatigue and hp. Long battles will drain your endurance, while the number of encounters you take before camping will drain your hp. Unless there are permanent effects in play, you will regain full hp and endurance after camping - for which you'll need supplies to do so.
It's certainly an alternate take on RPG and while the game offers plenty of atmosphere, a solid soundtrack and voice work, the aspects of how the game calculates damage, modifiers and character "wellness" takes time to get into. I wish they just stuck with regular tropes here as after over 10hrs in I still have troubles figuring out how all of this ties together.
However, once you get the ropes of how Obsidian has rethought the DnD-ish battle system, which may take you some time, it makes sense. It is unorthodox and off the beaten path, but works within the universe they're trying to paint - and it's a mindbafflingly beautiful one.
The world of PoE, Eora, is so full of life, little details, npcs, side-quests and things to explore you'll never run out of things to do, see or aim towards. The expansions provide even more content, leaving you busy for weeks on end.
The more I've played of PoE the more I'm sucked into its welcoming arms as a gaming experience like no other. Not since Baldur's Gate and American McGee's Alice have I been so immersed in a digital world like this, and that's quite a feat. Obsidian has treated its roots and legacy with great care and it shows. It's a masterful reinvention of the wheel once you carve past what may look like arbitrary and awkward combat mechanics at first. They certainly takes some getting used, especially the mechanics of suppressed stats (modal or active), meaning items with the same bonus don't stack. Have two items that yield +1 intelligence? Well, you're only getting one of them, the other gets suppressed.
Pillars of Eternity provides a very similar experience to praised cult classics like Baldur's Gate, but with its own twist and uniqueness to combat. For hardcore savants of Baldur and Icewind lore it may be a bit offputting at first, but for everyone else it's a masterpiece to behold. Even the savants may appreciate it over time, like I myself did.
Do yourself a favor and lose yourself in a world that harkens back to a time RPGs were isometric, dangerous and required you to gather your party before venturing forth.

Of all the most venerated modern game sci-fi series, Mass Effect is BioWare’s signature conglomeration of modern RPG designs focused around cinematic storytelling as well as improving game design over role-playing mechanics. This change is nothing new as BioWare has cared little about role-playing; instead, they focus on an established character for the player with a moniker (ex. the Bhallspawn, the Warden, the Champion, etc.). What makes Shepard more personal than previous attempts is that the player has more time to shape their Shepard into a person. The direct continuity makes the ninety-hour journey to save the Galaxy truly an epic that has yet to be matched by BioWare, even with the likes of Inquistion.
Through the series, there is an obvious, yet unseen, difference between each game that players have noticed, and the main change is how BioWare has cultivated each RPG with a new framework for decisions that works in tandem with its narrative. If BioWare’s games were a garden, then Mass Effect would be best described as a hedge, Mass Effect 2 a pine tree, and Mass Effect 3 as a Red Oak.
The original ME is often touted as the most “choice” based of the three as you can select planets in whatever order that you wish. Side-quests also have branching paths that can be done in any order that give the illusion of a player-created experience when in reality the story is made of linear threads interwoven in masse. Players can choose to snip off side quests that snag the experience, trim plotlines now or later, and they can proceed however they choose after the initial beginning (root) is set. The most damnable thing about the choices in ME1 is how disjointed it is from one-another, and the result is often immediate, not in the future.
ME2, however, approached the non-linear design with more gates; instead of sending the player off in any direction, the player is gated behind the branches that must be done before he or she can proceed higher on the trunk. The player will need to complete three side-objectives before they can proceed with the main one. What was lost in the illusion of non-linearity is made-up by the game improving the decisions players make. Side-objectives, as a result, are engaging, choice-based stories that have more lasting consequences not only when the game came back to focus but also in its final act. This leads into the notorious “Suicide Mission” where companions, if they or the ship are not prepared, will result in permanent deaths for ME2 and 3. (The only downside is these consequences are predictable and you would have to go out of your way to screw it up.)
This final mission is the hacked-away stump where ME3 begins as not only is the storyline connected but the leveling system begins where the player stopped. Unlike the previous game that brought Shepard back to Level 1, ME3 chooses to make its first act a long, semi climatic climb up before it begins to branch out. While the ending has its sore spots, the ultimate result of reaching the top is to marvel at the journey not only this game took you through but the previous journeys that led you to the finale. It’s only when you factor in the added branches from the expansions does ME3 truly surpasses ME2 in terms of its storytelling and choices, especially with the Leviathan DLC that clears up the reworked ending as well as the Citadel DLC that adds nearly eight hours of dialogue-focused choices to bond with companions.
Long lasting bonds, for better or for worse, are not only ME3’s saving grace as it’s the dominant traits carried through each game. The amount of alterations between three games’ choices truly does color each player’s experience even if the ending itself may not possess the full spectrum of its shades.
In terms of side-casts, ME is perhaps one of the greater showcases of how to handle side-characters compared to other RPGs including BioWare’s past titles. BioWare’s past games relied mainly on filler companions with quirks with Baldur’s Gate and Neverwinter Nights and DA suffered from having characters too closely tied to special roles. Alister and Morigan come to mind whereas the Dwarf is unremarkable because he is unimportant. There is no happy division of these two types of characters.
Most characters in ME, like Shepard, are not destined for a predetermined role or are many venerated by their races with the exception of Tali who comes off as an ambassador of all Quarians in the first game. Garrus, Wrex, Liara, Ashley, Kaiden, James, Miranda, Jacob, Jack, EVI, Samara, Morinth, Javik—almost all these characters, even bland ones, showcase some unique personality that becomes better with each game such as Ashley and Garrus, and most are simply individuals separated by race and/or factions. Even the main antagonists, Saren, the Illusive Man, and Reapers, all have a sense of personality and relation with the player. This sense of camaraderie as well as tension, which is the key factor that makes it better than DA, can sometimes manifest itself as permanent decisions that will kill of a character in the first or second game, or even the third if you made decisions in the past.
One gradual change that I find stranger to role with is the heavy-handed focus of romance. Now I should preface that I am not against these inclusions, but I have to wonder if the time put into a selective group of bone-able people really adds to the experience. This became apparent when my third run began and I romanced with a squadmate before sending him to his death, only to get Liara coming into my chambers even though I acted disinterested with her. The game basically structures itself to show off some softcore T&A no matter who you choose. ME1 is perhaps the most egregious example as ME2 and ME3 doesn’t have these forced moments, and, to be fair, the alien/human romances are often more tastefully handled with actual romance put into them. (Garrus is simply a Casanova to enjoy.) However, as each game adds more crewmates outside of the squad to the bang-achievement list and as people demand for same-sex options because they cannot simply roleplay as someone else, the inclusion only becomes more questionable if it’s necessary for an RPG.
As my Dragon Age series overview lamented, the lack of a “Buy Everything Together!” edition really hampers the experience of Mass Effect, perhaps even more than the DA games. Whereas each DA game is indirectly related to one-another, every story is directly felt and referenced in following games, which boggles the mind why the “Trilogy” version would need another $90 of story-related DLC to get the full experience. It might be a sign of malice but it’s more likely that EA forgot about the BioWare points’ system as you have to go out of your way to purchase these downloads, so it’s more about incompetence.
This statement about DLC cannot be expressed enough; the difference between base-game ME3 and the complete version with branching storylines of the mystery of Leviathan, the Omega “renegade” retreat, and the personal touches of Citadel make ME3 the real ending of the game. It’s somewhat ironic that when I completed ME3 I forgot to include the Extended Cut, and the ending, as a result, was more coherent—aside from the Normandy and squadmates—that it felt like it was there all along. While not everything is closed in the Milky Way Galaxy, the sense of finale reaches the penultimate goal of the ME to create a universe centered around the player with enough memories of a Galaxy, good times and bad, that is worth revisiting to save it once again.

The introduction to a series hailed as one of the best interactive space operas of all time (surpassed only by its sequel, I believe). Easily worth every ounce of praise. Every minute spent in play is a minute well spent, whether on the first time through or the fifth.  Interesting encounters, fascinating world, great voice acting, gripping story, decisions that matter (and have lasting consequences). Incredible.
Only real gripes: the interface and inventory management. Interface: It takes a while to get used to the HUD closing in during combat, targetting for the abilities of your squadmates and the fact that not every ability can be configured as a hotkey. Inventory: not enough notice on when you're about to run out of space. 150 items sounds like a lot... until you get the 'almost too full' notification at 135 and you're in a place where you can't offload existing items ('cause sometimes, you'd want to keep what you just found rather than reduce it to omni-gel). Small complaints given the sheer magnitude of awesome this game will throw at you.
9/10, two thumbs up. Would let the Council die again. ;-)

The reviews for this game were pretty mixed, but I decided to pick it up anyway. I'm completely new to the Tex Murphy games and FMV games a whole. The only others I'd really seen were the phantasmagoria games and the handful of Wing-commander games in the same format, which were kinda like interactive movies.
This game is no different, but it was cool to see a dead genre reborn. The game was definately one for the fans, and you can tell a lot more work went into the FMV sequences rather than the game-play itself. The acting is very cheesy a lot of the time, just like most FMV games. For example, in at least two scenes, actors were supposed to be dead, but you could see them still breathing.
The puzzles in the game were pretty basic and the puzzle difficulty ranged tremendously throughout the game. Sometimes I had to use brute force to pass a puzzle, other times I managed to solve them very quickly.
With all this said, I still really liked the game and would happily buy and play a sequel. Hopefully we may also see other FMV games return in the future.

This games too cheesey to recogmend. If you are afan of the old games you may get a certain feeling of nastalgia from playing it. Having not played any of them beyond a demo for under a killing moon i cant comment to the accuracy to the old style.  Regardless, the world which you walk around in is graphicly below par for a game made this side of 2000. I realise this game was funded through crowd funding, but this doesn't excuse the old textures and graphic models used, not a slap dash approach to CGI rendered animations. Accepting that a substantial amount of the budget did go into making the cinematic cut scenes doesn't excuse them from being lazy elsewhere.
The story though did have a certain amount of charm, even if it lacked in the complexity i normally enjoy. The puzzles for the most part were easy to solve and weren't really much of a challenge. The only exception being one which required you to have looked at something a lot more carefully then i did. Several were confusing only in the lack of instructions. Show me what appeared to be a drafts bored and then i find its actually a puzzle where i cant have more then 1 of each tile on each row. Solution was easy once i realised my goal. In some ways this is a hall mark of the style and not really something you can hold against the game, though it is nice when the items aren't limited to only one use.
The cheeseyness of the acting though either makes or breaks this game...you will either love it for it, or you will find it distracting from the story telling. For me it was somewhat distracting, i could see what they were trying to do, but the actors just didn't feel up to it. To me it felt like they were overacting.
The world felt empty, apart from a few roaming insta killers, there was no real interaction with anyone outside of their preset boxes.
When it came up i had considered supporting the kickstarter. Having now played the game, i'm really glad i didn't.

Honestly, I haven't played an RPG with as much depth, story, and awesome universe in such a long time. The last time I got this absorbed in an RPG was the Witcher 3...and this game is almost 4 years old now.
Don't let the graphics dissuade you. Yes they are a bit aged, but it's still a beautiful looking game. The animations, spell effects, particles, lighting, everything is just masterfully done. The day/night cycle adds a whole new depth to the gameplay that I haven't seen. Small details in the gameplay like grabbing onto monsters and attacking them on their backs, or watching your pawn pick up a wounded ally and drag them to safety just add more to the immersion. The AI for your pawns isn't perfect, but being able to customize your pawn as deeply as you can your main character really adds to the experience. It creates a sense of control over your party and being able to hire other player's unique pawns is just such a cool bonus.
I've only scratched the surface of this game, but I'm deeply looking forward to delving deeper into the story and universe.
Combat, is perfectly done by the way. The game does a fantastic job at making you feel like a bad♥♥♥♥♥whether your a warrior, archer, or mage, but it never feels easy. If you make one wrong move you can die just as quickly as you would in a game like dark souls. It's not as difficult as dark souls, but you definitely need to use your tactical advantages whenever possible. The combat shines so bright in this game and I've never seen spellcraft and archery done this well. This game puts a game like skyrim to shame in terms of combat mechanics in my eyes.
The only downside I have for it, is that you don't get a mount until far later into the game. This means you have to sprint everywhere which feels some what tedious, but forces you to explore. I just wish that the stamina bar wouldn't drain while your out of combat and running around. In cities and towns you can sprint to your hearts content, but when your out in the wilderness it drains pretty quickly from running. I can't really imagine having to play this game as a mage who has very low stamina. I've never been one for fast traveling, always felt like it ruined part of the experience of a game for me. I wish they had a mechanic like witcher 3 had where each city had signs that let you fast travel or that gave you a horse or something. I've never been a fan of the skyrim-esque fast traveling.
Overall I give this game a 9/10

I like the game, but my big complaint is that the rewards structure is kind of ♥♥♥♥ed up. Why does the game only reward you for sticking to one of the three pure styles? The game is tedious to play 100% ghost, but playing 100% panther makes it really difficult to immerse yourself as a covert military operative. I tried to do a combination of both styles (trying to stay hidden but using weapons when necessary), but the game seemed to punish me for my decision when scores were tallied at the end of each level. I guess you can ignore the scores and the game telling you that you failed to reach the designated goals as a ghost or as a panther, but for me it felt unfair to be punished for trying to play pragmatically in synch with the story.

This iteration of the Splinter Cell series really puts my feelings for Ubisoft to the test. As far as single-player goes this is by far the best stealth-game I've played. Multiplayer (especially co-op missions) has the potential to make it one of the all-time greats, but that's where Ubisoft just didn't pull through for whatever reason. It's full of bugs that make prolonged game-sessions prone to all kinds of glitches that rarely turn out in your favor, mostly they screw you and potential hour-long efforts over for good.
Of course as it is with most Ubisoft games it is pretty much abandoned now update-wise so as much as I hate Ubisoft for their ways of doing business I have to admit that the game and its mechanics are pretty much as good as it gets as long as the god of multiplayer-bugs has mercy on you.
Bottom line: This game is too much fun for me not to play it but I would prefer it if Ubisoft at least delivered a finished product, be it on launch-day or through updates at a later time.

It may not have the say amazing stealth gameplay that Chaos Theory had, but at least it does not over the top action like Conviction.

tldr:
too long part:
As a SC veteran, I gotta say things changed a huge deal since Chaos Theory but I really enjoyed basically everything this title has to offer gameplay-wise. Controls feel pretty smooth and natural after a short while and the infamous Assassins Creeds "press this button to either live or jump off a cliff" syndrome is not showing its presence as much.
AI difficulty settings offer an adequate challenge for everyone, while the games arcade side keeps you fairly rewarded for everything you're trying to achieve. No matter which mode you are playing, every little step forward feels good.
Some people find the economy of unlocking stuff rather questionable but it's definitely not a reason to make you stop playing the game.
If you've never played a Splinter Cell game before, it's not a problem - there are no essential references to earlier games which allows anyone to embark on this Jack Bauer's "24-style" storyline with decent actors and moderately catchy story (pro-american as hell but you can't avoid that these days it seems). The game attempts to go rather back to its roots while still trying to maintain the action-hungry audience and does a very decent job at that. You can play the game the way you want and that is awesome.
As far as the coop campaign goes, unless you have a friend to play with, the odds of matchmaing giving you a guy on the same note as you are pretty slim. There is also a nice horde mode which is good for farming money and practicing your abilities. Both modes are a lot of fun and youll most likely play each map and mission more than once. Important note is that your cash is shared in both COOP and MULTIPLAYER which is awesome and it lets new players get into the game more easily.
Basic matchup is 1st person heavy armed mercs VS 3rd person agile spies. Modes with mixed teams and lot of variation are available. Some maps seem imba one way or another but since its not competitive, nobody really cares.

Judging by the media and art regarding the release of SC: Blacklist, I was convinced that the series had taken a relatively bad turn for the worst as in transforming the setalth game into a military third person shooter. Albeit the initial doubts and suscpicion I harbored for the title, I purchased it shortly after release and was pleased to be welcomed with the same generally solid SC: Conviction framework, in addition to sporting missions and levels more akin to the well received SC: Chaos Theory, which focused more on conventional stealth and leaving enemies unharmed rather than hunting enemies from the shadows. Aside from one or two missions which are story oriented ( such as the introduction mission which can be skipped) the levels can be completed entirely on ones own terms. Due to the nature of Splinter cell being a stealth game, the favored approach of most players would be to kill as few enemies as possible without alerting others or raising suspicion from cameras, but akin to others in the series, Blacklist allows for no-kill completion by using the tazer and non lethal hand to hand combat, which offers a generally more intense challenge due to the range limitation and need of disposing unconcious enemies. In terms of story, the game does not offer anything particularly interesting which is slightly disappointing, but the game does feature some great locales and mission sandboxes, so that's a plus. All of the aforementioned details pretty much sum up the gameplay experience in my own words, although in terms of visual aesthetics; the game performs exceptionally well for a Ubisoft PC port, and the level design and texturing is quality work, even for being an Unreal engine game, it manages some remarkable ligh and shadow work in addition to convincing animations.
Ultimately, the game suceeds in most aspecrts regarding what formulates into a enjoyable and elaborate stealth game, although it stumbles in the story department, Splinter Cell: Blacklist is a worthy entry to the series and a must have for those who were  slightly off-put by the fast paced nature of Conviction, as it approaches mission design with a more open, sandbox framework.

The way of the samurai series has always been a uniqe mix of Role playing/fighting, and both aspects of the game are masterfully done in the fourth entry.
- Fighting mechanics -
The game offers 82 uniqe fighting styles and a ton of different weapons. You can also create your own fighting style or weapon to suit your personal taste. Styles include dual wielding, spear wielding, ninja styles, and duel ninja styles. You can even use a pistol or rifle.
The combat itself is easy to jump into and difficult to master. The learning curve isnt very steep compared to most fighting games, so if you (like me) arn't usually a fighting game player, then you can still hop in and have a good time.
- Role Playing -
Few games make me feel like my actions are directly influencing the outcome of the story like sam4. The game is meant to be played multiple times and offers 10 different endings. There are even some hidden events and missions that are well worth finding.
Although the game itself can be overwhelming early on, if you like fighting games, role playing, or are intrested in feudal japan, then there's no game i can recommend more. It'll be well woth the price tag.

Way of the Samurai 4 takes place in the humble port town of Amihama during the mid 19th Century, several years after the arrival of the “black ships” from the West ended Japan’s long history of cultural isolation. It's a third person action adventure with nice graphics, great music, horrible kb/m controls (you can get used to it or you can use a controller) and some really weird characters.
It's Ryu ga Gotoku Ishin/Kenzan meeting a Telltale adventure. On a smaller scale. You side with one of the factions and go through several days of key events up to resolution on the last day, which might be as soon as 4th or as late as 7th. The time moves forward whenever you do a main story mission and you can do whatever you want in-between. You can own a dojo, master a huge amount of sword styles, gamble, have fun with the ladies, do some side missions, go fishing or play dress up.
The main story line, whichever of the 10 endings you go towards, should take around 3 hours. Probably faster on your subsequent playthroughs. And there should be subsequent playthroughs as 10 endings mean you have to complete the game at least 10 times to see them all. As the true ending requires you to complete some very hard boss fights, you might need to complete the game way more times to buff your character (it carries over to the new game). And if you want to 100% this game you're looking at 120-140hrs of grinding. I've completed this more or less five times now, with some grinding done here and there, and after 20+ hours it's still fun. But I like Japan...
I liked:

* graphics (despite clipping everywhere)
* the Japanese weirdness
* huge amount of things to unlock
* it's a samurai game in Japan!
I disliked:
* some evil stuff that you do on the evil path was... evil
Get this:
* if you like Japanese weirdness
* if you like medieval Japan
* if you like grind
Don't get this:
* if you're easily offended
* if you don't like grind

Okay, most reviewers got most of the bases covered. Yes, it's actually an RTS with all the micro and macro and metagames involved, yes, it's great with a controller, yes, the devs are active, yes, Quartermaster is a waifu (one that's inferior to Hopper). And yeah, there's local splitscreen multiplayer, holy crap. And a spectator mode, and replays, and all the good stuff you want out of an RTS. Really can't think of anything it's missing. Okay? Okay.
Here's one thing other reviewers tend to whine about instead of being helpful - the campaign and its perceived difficulty. Not gonna say some missions aren't annoying, not gonna say the game's not hard. Just one thing - and I'm gonna take a page out of the modern games journalist's book here so bear with me - this is Dark Souls of RTS. It's not unfair, it just makes you work for your victories. You are expected to attempt each mission multiple times, fail over and over, develop a strategy, then win. Matches are short, you'll fail in 2 minutes, try again, no problem. Each mission has a hint, use that. Check the rules, scout the map, check your composition, know your units, formulate a strategy, win. Don't brute force missions, that won't work. It's a strategy game. You are meant to make meaningful decisions, not spam and pray. It's not the most APM-intensive game under the sun, you only ever have a few units to work with, so it's all about that execution. If you can't deal with your lack of progress, take a break, think about your strategy, your life, your emotional debts, and try again.
With that out of the way, on to the actual review:

The controls for this game are straightforward and easy to learn. You move your tank left and right and then you move your turret left and right and increase how much power to put into your attack before you fire your weapon. However, a lot of the weapons are weak in power and you have a leveling system not only for your tank, but also for the weapons that will change what the weapon does and more power to the weapon.
The multiplayer aspect of the game comes built in with a server browser, private lobby creator and gamemode modifiers fir for creating the perfect kind of carnage for you. Fancy a gametype with extreme wind? Do it. Fancy a gamemode where damage only counts by a rebound? Do it. Fancy a gametype where you can only use one weapon? Do it.
ShellShock Live is not simply a multiplayer game. You can skirmish against bots to test new weapons (although this won’t earn you any experience). There are also single player missions that force you into specific scenarios and challenge you to fight your way out. There are over seventy of these single player scenarios, and reaching certain milestones unlocks even more weapons, levels, and upgrades. This huge amount of upgrading, customization, and unlocking means that after just a short amount of progression, you will see a huge variety of builds among different tanks. Some people may focus on just one weapon, trying to upgrade an already powerful shot to an even more ridiculous one. Some people may spread their weapon progression out so that several different options have slightly more powerful versions. Some people may focus on mobility, some on armor, and some on powerful critical hits. There is no wrong way to play the game. And if you dive in with a group of friends (as anyone who has played a game of Worms: Armageddon can attest to), the trash talk and the salt are both very real. Overall, the community seems pretty welcoming. Even if you do not know anyone who plays, jumping into a multiplayer game is not terribly intimidating. I would recommend running through a bit of the campaign first to get a few levels and upgrades under your belt before diving right in, lest you be overwhelmed by the superior firepower of your opponents.
