In this review, I don't want to focus on the gameplay, the graphics or the technical aspects of the game (which you find in many other reviews), but on a specific issue I'd like to explain to you. This is, of course, very subjective and based on my personal experience, but if you're interested in my view, keep reading.
Anyway, one of the things I like most about this game is the message behind it (or rather, how I interpret it). Back in the day, I played all classic Sonic games on the Genesis. In these games, technology has always been evil and formed the counterpart to nature, which was depicted as inherently good. This conflict was black and white, and only one could prevail. And because almost every machine you encounter serves Dr. Robotnik, you always fought against them. This bugged me a lot as a kid, because I was (and still am) a fan of all kinds of technology and machines. My favorite stages were usually the completely artificial, factory-type stages like Chemical Plant Zone, Metropolis Zone and Flying Battery Zone (I liked their music, too!).
But Sonic CD is very different in this aspect. You still fight against Robotnik and his machines, but there is another representation of technology, shown by the good future of many stages. Once you liberated the past zones of Palmtree Panic from Robotnik's machines, you expect the same happy, perfect, Green-Hill-esque Zone you saw in the present, but it is very different. Suddenly, the palm trees are replaced by mechanical versions (and it's still as happy as expected). The whole stage is now outfitted with an artificial irrigation system. The same thing can be observed in Tidal Tempest, which starts out as a relatively technology-free zone and turns into a high-tech greenhouse. Technology and nature coexist in harmony and technical progress is shown in a positive light. It improves nature instead of destroying it.
But that's not all. The bad future in Sonic CD does not just show a “perfect” mechanized world, but rather a broken down, decayed wasteland. This underlines the fact that Robotnik is not an ambassador of technology, but an egoistic megalomaniac who simply uses technology as a tool for his plans. The player can see that once Robotnik succeeds, he ruins the place no matter if it started out as a natural or high-tech zone. It is also quite apparent that the mechanization of the stages in the future is not the work of Robotnik. It will happen either way, driven by unknown forces. Robotnik is just the one negatively influencing the development (or not, depending on how you play).
At the same time, nature itself is presented different as well. The only natural area you see in the game which closely resembles the “standard” natural stages in the other Sonic games is the present of Palmtree Panic. The present of Tidal Tempest already looks suspiciously evil despite being mostly natural. But what's really interesting is the past. Here you can see a different face of nature, which is often ignored. The past zones show a primitive, uncivilized world which is often as dangerous for the player as any other zone. This contradicts the usual “pure” view of nature which is often shown in games and other media.
The bottom line is that while technology can very well be used to serve humanity and improve life, it can also cause a lot of harm if it's not handled correctly or misused for personal gain. This mirrors my own interpretation of technology and appears to me as a much better message compared to a simplistic conflict between the idealized, inherently good nature and the demonized, artificial technology in the other games. Maybe I'm reading too much into the game, but that's how I interpret it. And for this reason, I like Sonic CD very much.
Thank you for reading.

I was excited to play Sonic CD, to say the least. It seemed to be just the right blend of speed and exploration, and up until about Tidal Tempest, the third zone, it seemed to be so. But more on that in a moment.
Now, there are many great things about this game. The story is fresh without being overcomplicated. The time travel mechanic was a nice idea, and works very well in theory. The art direction is pretty sweet, too; everything looks great, except maybe there are too many overly bright colours, and maybe the sprite art is occasionally ever-so-slightly wonky, but the graphics are still very good, especially for their time. And the soundtrack (the Japanese one, at any rate) is absolutely fantastic.
In fact, I think everything about this game is great, except for one vital component.
The level design is absolutely abysmal. The levels are confusing to navigate; there are far too many things which you don't have time to react to before you take damage from them; there are far too many springs, including ones which launch you directly into enemies which you couldn't have possibly known were there... it doesn't feel like a Sonic game. When I play a Sonic game, I expect exhilarating speed, along with some straightforward platforming to break up the pace occasionally. What I do not expect is to be tossed around the stage like a blue spiky ragdoll into enemies, hazards, etc, that not only did I not have time to react to, but oftentimes I didn't even
, even as I was sent flying into the next deathtrap. It felt like the game was working against me.
Palmtree Panic was enjoyable, if a little confusing at times. Collision Chaos, while perhaps aptly named, was pretty much the same. However, the moment I dove into Tidal Tempest, I thought "Hmm. How am I meant to travel to the past if there is water everywhere, slowing me down and preventing me from reaching 88 miles per hour, so to speak?" After failing to make a good future in Act 1, the answer was clear: I couldn't. And as the game went on, things just went downhill.
Quartz Quadrant was the worst. In that particular zone, there are hidden springs EVERYWHERE, so good luck just running in a straight line. Wacky Workbench wasn't that bad, but I really couldn't hope to achieve anything between being bounced everywhere and electrocuted. And as for Stardust Speedway, when I entered, I thought "Great! Finally, a level actually fitting for Sonic, the character whose 'thing' is that he goes fast!" And while this zone did feel much more fitting for a Sonic game, the whole place being built up of the eponymous speedways with no set pieces to distinguish one from the other made it more confusing than ever!
All in all, I did not have a good time with this game. A lot of the time, it not only feels frustrating and bewildering, but unnecessarily so. At the end of an Act in Quartz Quadrant, I saw the signpost pointing to the end and thought "YES! FINALLY! I CAN GET OUT OF THIS DREADFUL PLACE!"... only to run into one last spring pointed backwards. The placement of that spring was what made me really start to hate the level design. It seemed more than anything to have been put there to annoy the player; I mean, what other purpose could it have served?! It was right at the end of the level, so it was obviously out of reach of everything. Why was it there??
But I digress. The level design seemed bizarrely bad compared to all the other elements of the game. Even the 3D special stages weren't that bad, but the in-game levels? Absolutely atrocious. And yet, I seem to be in the strange position of recommending this game. Why? Because pretty much everything apart from the levels themselves is fantastic.
It's certainly not my cup of tea. But rather, it's more like a cup of coffee. It looks great, and smells great - and I don't mind having a taste. But I couldn't stand to drink the whole thing.
So in conclusion: don't buy this game if you're easily frustrated. Just watch a Let's Play and/or search for the soundtrack on YouTube. However, if you like being challenged relentlessly, go right ahead. And if you just want to experience the lush visuals and snazzy music and don't mind the level design, go right ahead. And if you're just a masochist, go right ahead.
Final scores:
Story/Ideas 8/10
Graphics/Art direction 9/10
Music 10/10 (6/10 for the comparatively "meh" US version)
Level design 3/10

Shadow of Mordor is made by WB Games, and is very similar to Mad Max in the general gameplay and engine.
Initially the game has a lot of issues, no FOV slider, poor camera, limited GFX options, and 100fps lock, but by messing around with settings files and 3rd party programs I was able to get the game in a much better state.
The game is story driven, however I found the story to be very mediocre, this game really shines when it comes to the gameplay, which it has ample amounts of. The game revolves around fighting Uruk, killing chiefs, getting revenge, and later creating your own army, the system for these mechanics is innovative and very fun!
The graphics are very good, although optimization is about average.
The soundscape is excellent, and the game has a good atmosphere.
The DLC for the game adds a reasonable amount of extra content which will provide another 10 hours or so of gameplay.
The game does suffer some flaws, with minor bugs, animation locking, and a very poor story, but it is such a fun game to hack and slash through that I can only recommend it. If you liked Mad Max then this is definitely worth checking out and can be bought at bargain prices online.

After over 100 hours I finally finished Pillars of Eternity and I think I'm ready to write this review.
Is this game good? It's more than good, it's great. It's not only one of the best RPGs of all times, it's also one of the best games I've ever played. It has great story, beautiful graphics, sound and music, deep mechanics and everything what good RPG game needs. But don't expect revolution, this is just step ahead in comparison to best classics like Baldur's Gate.
So what you may expect? Pillars of Eternity is pure old-school RPG in modern times. Engine is very classic, but modern in the same time. So you have 2D view, but with zoom. Combat is in real time with active pause. There is a lot of reading and dialogues. You will spend a lot of time to manage your party stats, skills and inventory. I played in hard difficulty and it was necessary to survive.
What about world and mechanics? There is new world and RPG mechanics made by Obsidian, but it has a lot in common with Dungeons and Dragons. It's heroic fantasy with many races (there are elves and dwarves too) and classes (like paladins, warriors and clerics), which combines elements we all know and love, with some new ideas, which is great. One word about spellcasters. I love the way how each magic class is different to each other, they use totally different spells and strategy, there are many fresh ideas here.
Also other thing is great. Best dialog system I've ever seen. Here you may feel your how your reputation and stats affects your dialog options.
But not everything is perfect. There are some things in that game, that would be improved, like your castle for example. This is clear that potential of this idea isn't fully exploited. Sometimes I felt like this part of the game was done in a rush.
VERDICT:
If you're an old-school RPG fan, this is must have for you. With this game you will feel the same magic as you felt playing Baldur's Gate.
If you're younger player, I'm not sure you will be so delighted as I am. I can recommend this game to everybody but I know there are many people which expect more intense RPGs in modern style. So if you like to read a lot and think what to do, try this game and find the ancient magic.

This is the first review I'm ever writing, but I'm doing it because I think Pillars of Eternity deserves it so so much.
The game has an amazing story line, great dialogue and high quality writing. I'm a great fan of fantasy novels, and I felt like reading a book while actively engaging in it.
There are so many NPC characters, and you have the option to learn about their history and their motivations. It really helps to flesh out the whole game world and make it more immersive.
The gameplay itself is also a lot of fun. I love micromanaging my team of 6 characters, and this game satisfied all my needs. There are just so many possibilities to customize a character and put together a functioning team. When faced with unforeseen challanges, it is fun to be concerned with both positioning of characters and activation of their miriad of skills.
I also need to commend the art. There is so much detail in each map, and it looks wonderful. And the background music complements it beautifully.
There is really only one single criticizm I have. I didn't like the character models much. But it didn't in any way retract from my gaming experience. Maybe a little bit... I can't say for sure.
I recommend this game to EVERYONE. Great game, indeed!

I wanted to like POE and I played it through to the end but there are just too many issues. First of all there is WAY too much dialogue and lore to sift through. Instead of adding to the immersion it really becomes a chore. I can't imagine doing another play through primarily for this reason.
With the exception of the Roderic's Hold quest the game is relatively linear and there are few choices you can make that materially effect the world. The castle upgrades seem tacked on and pointless. The skill system is very basic and doesn't allow for much specialization. Characters will often end up with similar stats and the only ones that seem to really matter are lore, lockpick and traps.
They've updated some basic party AI for this game but it is woefully insufficient. Programmable AI was a feature in IE games 15 years ago. So there really is no excuse for the lack of its inclusion originally.
As it is the system they have doesn't work effectively on the higher dificulty levels. Be prepared to click hundreds of times in a tough battle rather than have your party follow a simple script. There is SO much combat in this game it really does become a grind and I don't understand why people defend the massive amount of micromangement it requires.
The load times in POE simply take way too long. I have an average system but I've heard that even players with good rigs still suffer from bad load times. This shouldn't be an issue for a 2D game running an old engine.
The plot is meh and the characters aren't particularly memorable. This game is a dungeon crawler first and foremost and more like Icewind Dale than BG1 or 2.
The party AI and dialogue just kill it for me but if you're a fan of this genre it might be worth a play through if it's on sale.

This game nearly flew under my radar, but it's great. Choose your own samurai adventure in a bustling port full of nutty Englishmen, sadistic princesses, sinister ministers, xenophobic rebels, and all kinds of oddballs. Clothing options are plentiful, and as silly or serious as you want them to be. Be that jerk who interrupts people all the time with inane banter! Start a dojo and drag any warm bodies off the street to be your pupils! Help out those in distress by saving their marriage, or murdering witnesses! Find or forge all sorts of weapons, learn dozens of fighting styles and even invent your own!
It's not perfect, though. Combat can be uneven, as there's no telling how strong your opponent will be until you start trading blows, but beyond that it's on you to pay attention to an enemy's movements and respond accordingly. Fighting styles take work to unlock their full potential, and with so many to learn, it's hard to give them all a fair shake. Speaking of which, you need a well-staffed dojo with a good rep to really get into the unique fighting styles, but it can and WILL get attacked regularly by challengers, who will likely kill your students and ruin your rep if you don't drop everything and rush over to beat them.
All in all, though, it's a fun experience and well worth getting into.

An enjoyable, crowd-funded detective game that's really half-game, half-movie (it's a 16GB download!).  Good acting and interesting storyline that can branch into 5 different endings.   Except for some annoying 'jumping-through-the-hoops' at times (some puzzles and items quests were a bit 'unintuitive'...), it was, overall, an entertaining ride. Good writing and appropriate music, too.
On the downside, there are some graphic scenes of violence (Tex getting beaten unconscious with an iron rod, which I did NOT find funny...), depictions of decapitation, and certain 'adult' themes, all of which make this game inappropriate for pre-17s.
What I also liked about it was that it appears to be designed to help raise awareness about the life of Nikola Tesla and his work.  If you get a chance, read up on some of Tesla's monumental discoveries and their importance in not just our daily lives (e.g. AC power, brushless motors, etc.) but also in the implementation of certain advanced technologies (e.g. wireless transmission of power, resonant systems, scalar electromagnetics, etc).  Helps fill in the missing 'forbidden' knowledge purposely omitted from most college-level Physics courses these days...
Check it out.
(Note: Acquired via a bundle)

This is an excellent entry-point for anyone who has been interested in the RTS genre, but been dissuaded from dipping into it due to them often being time-consuming and unmanagable. It is also a great game for any RTS veteran like me as it takes what I love about RTS and handily removes the fluff and gives you the very essentials of what makes a good real-time strategy game.
But that does not mean the game is easy or lacking depth. Make no mistake, Tooth and Tail makes great use of a couple key mechanics that ensure quick games, punish turtling and the small unit roster has ended up not feeling small at all. Every unit is interesting and capable, with clear strengths and weaknesses, which allows for deep strategies and counter-plays.
The game comes with a good and varied single-player campaign which has an interesting story arc. There are oth online and offline multiplayer options, and local as well where two players can split-screen which I haven't seen in a game in ages. For offline play the bots put up a decent fight and are good target practice before stepping onto the online ladder.
A couple things I liked:
1. Random maps mean that no game feels exactly the same. You don't run across Summoner's Rift or whatever a hundred times.
2. The unit roster seems small but each has an important role and defined function, meaning that no matter how you set up your army you will have strengths and weaknesses. This leaves a lot of room for experimenting with strategies which is great.
3. The theme is unique and great, the art is very nice to look at and the pixel-art gets the job done and then some.
4. The mini-gun toting badger is mega-fun.

tldr; I uninstalled this game because I got lost in it for 8 hours at a time. It affected my work. That never happens.
I'd never really played Mafia or Werewolf much before, but a friend gifted me a copy of the game, so I decided to try it. It took 3-4 games before I understood how it worked, but even that learning period was
engaging. A game lasts around half an hour, and during that time you're constantly writing things down, trying to figure out who is what role, who is a threat to you, who your allies are, and how you can navigate the situation. If you're evil, you're furiously establishing your cover story while also trying to kill off the good guys. Every word you say is a ploy to advance your position, every letter scrawled in your journal (which is visible on your death) is calculated.
And when the court puts you up for treason, but you've covered your tracks so perfectly that they pardon you? That's
. When you take a gamble and kill someone who's story doesn't check out - and you were right? That's
. It's a kind of thrill I haven't ever gotten from a game before, and man was I addicted. It's not the kind of game that you expect to lose a whole evening+night to - but that won't stop you from being surprised when you look up and it's 4am on a work night.
It's well worth your money.

An extremely expansive universe to explore, unique weapons and abilities, and randomly generated mobs and terrain around every corner? What's not to love about Starbound?
I preordered this wonderful game for $40 (thats more than double the standard price) and I do not regret a single moment of it. I've logged over 100 hours in this game and I have loved seeing it grow and expand as the developers put in new mechanics and storyline features as the community suggests them. Chucklefish Games is an amazing studio that reads all of the posts on their forums and add new wonderful features from them.
If you haven't played Starbound it's an amazing sidescrolling open world game (such as Terraria) with randomized elements from games such as No Man's Sky (this is better, of course.) The game is really easy to run only requiring an i3 processor and pretty much any video card. The graphics are unique and creative in the restrictive pixel style. Chucklefish Games is always adding new features and little storyline elements for players to explore. If you feel like developmentis ever slow, you can browse the never-ending list of mods on the steam workshop. I've mentioned the storyline a lot and that is because Starbound has a truly well thought out story. There are several playable races each with their own storyline and origin. You can find many books in-game describing past events and how the universe came to be. There are also clues within many of the game's dungeons that hint at later plot events that are extremely fun to decipher.
I'm going to end off this review with a comment on Starbound's soundtrack. It is absolutely beautiful. Even if you aren't going to buy the game, I would reccomend spending the five or so dollars on the soundtrack to listen to anywhere. I listen to it 24/7 in the car or on walks because of how relaxing and beautiful it is.
Keep up the good work Chuclklefish Games.

I always played this game via Sonic Gems Collection on GameCube, but when they released Sonic CD onto Steam, I picked it up. If you don't know, Sonic CD was released in 1993 for the Mega CD (Sega CD in the USA) a quite obscure Mega Drive/Genesis addon, and it introduced characters like Amy Rose, Metal Sonic and it was also the first Sonic game to feature a save feature! And the FMVs were really well animated. If you're a true Sonic fan, this game is absolutely perfect for you! Especially the Steam version which allowed you to play as Tails (as an unlockable character), and at a cheap price, it's absolutely a Sonic Magnum Opus. Pick it up now!

I don't quite know what to make of Mass Effect 1.
On the one hand, it's the kind of game I would like- an RPG-esque space opera with spaceships, alien races and end-of-the-universe stakes. In spite of the mouse being very laggy in the Wine wrapper I created for this, I did reach the end of the game and ended up with the satisfied warm and fuzzies that saving a virtual universe as a messianic, unifying, misunderstood saviour figure gives you. I finally got to fly the Normandy and have a chat with Chakwas- to me, two of the most memorable characters in this game. That was good.
But. I don't know but what, but. Maybe I don't identify with Shepard. Maybe the graphics and cinematic approach were just a tad too dated for me to enjoy. Maybe I don't like games that feel like a relatively straightforward path to a predetermined end with small variations. Maybe- though this would be to the game's advantage- I had already watched a couple of let's plays and thus missed out on the surprises. Maybe I had just finished Dragon Age Origins and had my appetite for a great game sated by that. The voice levels were occasionally off. Maybe a combination of the above.
This game is neither fish nor fowl. Is it a cinematic adventure of epic scope? Check? Is it an RPG? Check? Is it a third-person shooter? Check? Puzzles? Check? Relationship Simulator? Check? Ultimate Shepard Simulator (MKI)? Check? Sometimes the parts come together to become a greater sum than they are individually. Currently playing ME2, there is a part of me that wishes that the design team had committed to one style of gameplay, rather than try to mix many prominent flavours into something that is pretty to look at- occasionally, but never came together as a nuanced challenge to reflex and intellect for me, while sending me strong signals that it should be.
This Mass Effect is, to me, above all an experiment in the genre of interactive film, in that it tells a relatively linear story that does not give the player much choice in affecting how they will be involved in its unfolding. Success is rewarded by cutscenes and additions to a cluttered inventory. In some ways, it does make use of subjective narratives (as in player-generated narrative) through leveling, the exact path the player chooses to get to the ending and a few choices which make the story feel personal. But every playthrough is going to be a variation on a relatively rigid theme, with little choice but to tread the known paths in hopes of discovering those that are unknown, or hope of approaching situations in entirely new ways. Therefore, while it succeeds in telling its story, it never felt like a story I was really in- for the most part, I felt like I was watching Shepard do these things without ever really seeing through her eyes.
I finished the game with the feeling that this had been much easier than expected, and less fun, in spite of the very good storytelling and ambitious scope and many good things I had heard (and seen) beforehand. It never really tugged at my heartstrings, or made me ponder why I was  choosing this path of action and not another. At the end, I felt like I had spent most of my time running around, shooting whatever popped up in my crosshairs and had occasionally heard some words in between- most of which I had forgotten by the time the credits rolled. And the companions, though well-written, felt too archetypal to be truly memorable. I did not emerge with a sense of individual journey, or virtual growth- it was always clear that Shep would save the universe. I was just riding along on her back.
The closest approximation I have for this game is a trashy novel you read on the beach. It grips you while you're in it, occasionally throws you with something stylistically inappropriate, gives you the occasional chuckle, rare insight and some soft-core porn. For science.
And yet, you would recommend this novel to your friends, remembering that it was a good read for the holidays and that you enjoyed it more that you disliked it. And then you discover the sequels…
If you want to learn the story of mass effect but dont mind the gaming and graphics you should play it.

Shadow of Mordor is made by WB Games, and is very similar to Mad Max in the general gameplay and engine.
Initially the game has a lot of issues, no FOV slider, poor camera, limited GFX options, and 100fps lock, but by messing around with settings files and 3rd party programs I was able to get the game in a much better state.
The game is story driven, however I found the story to be very mediocre, this game really shines when it comes to the gameplay, which it has ample amounts of. The game revolves around fighting Uruk, killing chiefs, getting revenge, and later creating your own army, the system for these mechanics is innovative and very fun!
The graphics are very good, although optimization is about average.
The soundscape is excellent, and the game has a good atmosphere.
The DLC for the game adds a reasonable amount of extra content which will provide another 10 hours or so of gameplay.
The game does suffer some flaws, with minor bugs, animation locking, and a very poor story, but it is such a fun game to hack and slash through that I can only recommend it. If you liked Mad Max then this is definitely worth checking out and can be bought at bargain prices online.

Dynasty Warriors is a very fun series but it's not for everybody. It is essentially the epitome of a hack n' slash game as you are dropped onto a battlefield immensely strong and are given thousands of mooks to have your way with. There are enemy officers that provide a bit of a challenge every now and then but once you've mastered the relatively simple combat system there is not much that can stand to you. I heavily enjoy the gameplay however the common criticism that it is very repetitive is entirely valid as there is not much variety in the combat. The story mode is pretty compelling if you're into wuxia stories but if you're not into the gameplay then you are going to have a pretty rough time having fun with this game.
I very much enjoy the series but my recommendation to newcomers to the series is to play a friend's copy before buying for yourself. Since the entire story is included with every game you don't need to worry about being unfamiliar with what's happening and that helps make it accessible. Definitely worth buying for fans of the series but avoid the DLC. There's not much going on there.

> i make my way to an airfield to find some loot. needed a gun and a backpack mostly.
> found a colt .45 and a backpack, along with food, bandages, etc.
> i'm set. i start my journey towards the cities.

> he sees a bright light coming from a tower, so we decide to go there check it out.
> on route, we see a lot of light coming from the trees across the river, we get curious, so we make our way there.

This is not a souls like game. It is very very different. It is not a bad thing, I still really enjoy the game, but do not buy it solely based on the notion that it is souls like. It isn't.
In Dark Souls you are a nameless adventurer who has to face overwhelming odds in beautifully designed set piece areas where the challenge is how you approach things and your skill to defeat overwhelming odds. Epic bosses require you to study their attack patterns and weaknesses (usually by dying to them) until you can finally apply what you know to achieveing your victory. Everything and just about everyone are against you and it's all up to you.
In Dragon's Dogma you are an Arisen, a hero who had his heart eaten by a dragon or something, who is what most heroes are in rpg games- the one true savior type deal and all that. Bosses feel less epic, you usually just climb on the damn thing while your 3 npc followers are all constantly yell directions at you. Congrats you did it on your first try, it only had to be 4v1. Hope they dont annoy you, because they are ALWAYS talking. It's just a typical action rpg, with strong story elements and a LOT of dialogue. You run around an open world and complete quests while everyone praises your majesty as the hero. Dying in this game is less skill and more from an enemy bursting you down from full health to nothing in a hit or 2 because you tried to do a sidequest. (I mean really, why are the bandits dual wielding knives repeatedly slashing me for like 30 a hit but the dudes with a sword and shield do 200-300 a hit) Better save often though, your near instant death means you may have to traverse all the way down the entire road all over again for a solid 20 minutes just because the game went from small packs of wolves and goblins to 20 camoflaged lizard people. Do I sound salty? A bit yeah. If it was Dark Souls Id hit and run and dodge and win gradually but all you can do in this game is spam attacks and hope the enemies dont figure out that killing you is instant victory. Your skill only matters up to a certain point, but really you may as well start running the moment your 2 handed sword's fully charged up special move does only 4% of a mob's hp because your level isnt high enough.
Despite the differences and my complaints, it's still a good game. Just dont think you were going to play a game even remotely similar to a souls game. If the npc pawns had any personality (aside from how you tell your main pawn to act in certain situations) and werent being replaced constantly it'd be closer to Dragon Age. Probably the best comparison really, just without the heavy moral choices and awkward sex scenes at camp.

To start with, this is a very very good RPG, definitely worth the $10-20 you can find it frequently on sale at. I personally paid $11, and have received 37 joyous hours of gameplay (as of writing this). I have not done everything there is to do in the game, but am well aware of what I didn't do.
The main story takes a bit to do, it starts off great, though it can leave you wondering what in the hell you're supposed to do next (usually wandering around for a few minutes or doing a quick google search resolves that, it's annoying but far from a deal breaker).
The combat system is reasonably well-developed, with a wide variety of options and tactics available to you. The bosses are all moderately difficult to dangerous, mainly dependent on your gear level. There is *major spoiler* a giant Dragon, and unlike Skyrim where you can literally oneshot him on legendary difficulty (I've done it using daggers + x30 sneak damage), this game has a great, cinematic, and rather protracted fight against the dragon. It's definitely an epic encounter, if nothing else the game would be worth buying just for the dragon fight alone.
There are 9 classes, each class has a different playstyle, and you can swap to any class upon reaching the Capital (done relatively early in the game). There are the 'radiant' style quests that you get from noticeboards, 'go kill goblins, go kill this hydra, kill 10 chimeras, kill 60 bunnies', they are there to be taken, and supplement your XP and gold incomes (sometimes they award items too), taking all but the escort quests will usually be the best option, you can finish most of them by just doing the regular stuff you'd be doing otherwise.
Graphics wise, I'll be honest, it's textures are ancient. It's level designs are ♥♥♥♥ing amazing, and it's color choice, set design, and just overall look and feel of the game are spot on. Except in cutscenes where it was painfully obvious (zoomed in, you can see the character animations + textures more than usual)  you won't even notice that the graphics are ancient.
Bosses can be really really dangerous dependent on how undergeared you are, and fighting some enemies while unprepared will spell certain doom. I thought I 'overprepared' for the fight with the main baddie, I barely lived, best bet is to always overprepare what you thought was already overpreparing.
The game works on a weight system, with weight you have available based on a combination of your height, dimensions (leg length, arm length, etc.), weight thresholds determine how fast you can regenerate your stamina, run faster, etc. Being taller makes you heavier (good or bad; being smaller makes you regenerate faster as a byproduct of weighing less, but can also carry less), adn increases your reach (weapon attacks). Being smaller gives you options in a place I won't spoil, but just think like a mole and it'll come to you. Being slowed means at times you won't be able to dodge out of an important attack, or have enough stamina generation, though that may be offset by having more and important curatives available, heavier armor, or better reach.
Combat can be quite tactical, and might at first seem pretty basic (the game does a decent job at not overwhelming you early on). If something seems too difficult to fight head-on, consider running away, or fighting smarter. A raging Ogre can be tricked into running off a cliff or ledge to his death, just be careful that you aren't accompanying him.
*IMPORTANT if you do pick up the game, upon arriving in the Capital, grab that Unlimited/Eternal Ferrystone so that you can use fast travel to and fro freely (otherwise it's extremely limited to single-use Ferrystones), Fast Travel is limited to the capital Gran Soren, your starting village, Cassardis, and anywhere you place a Port-Crystal. They are big glowing purple stones, you will find one at the bottom of a certain place you explore relatively early in the game, and more later on. They can be picked back up after use, they cannot be placed in 'dungeons', only the open world.
Overall, the game is definitely worth checking into. The story is great, there is a lot of underlying meaning that might be casually overlooked, and the story does NOT end with killing the Dragon, to give you a heads up, don't quit after killing the big bad, b/c there's more.
I'd give it a solid score of a 10/10, for the price, there is no reason not to purchase this. It offers a lot of what I wish other and traditionally 'better' RPGs have, it has plenty of flaws that earn it well-deserved flak, but it makes for a great experience none-the-less. The boss-fights are great, and the true bosses of the game, namely the Dragons, are pretty interesting design wise. The story is innovative and different, and the whole story serves up a greater point, the entire story is in fact an allegory, which is not something you find in a Bethesda game.
It WILL be rough at times, don't get me wrong, that's usually when you're trying to rush through the content. The enemies don't scale with level, so they'll be freakishly powerful early, and laughably weak later on (though at some points they can or are replaced with empowered variants). If your pawns get annoying, you can always turn their sound off in the options menu, or sit them down and tell them to shut the ♥♥♥♥ up.
To leave you with a quote from Mr. Scaly himself, "This is not fate, nor duty's call. This battle is your own, waged of your own free will."

Stranded Deep is, in my opinion, the best survival game available. It takes place on an archipelago in the deep ocean, surrounded by water and hungry sharks. It is a very realistic game, having many aspects of real survival. It is a very enjoyable game to play and is a great game for survivalists looking for something a little different.
PROS:
-No external threats like zombies or monsters like most other survival games. Just Mother Nature and her wrath
-Other than a few small details, it is a very realistic game
-Unique environment. Very few survival games I've seen focus on the ocean
-Makes it necessary to adventure, as the island you live on will run out of material eventually
-Health, hunger, and other stats do not take up screen space...you hold a button to view them
CONS:
-It is too easy to reach the point of "set for life." If you have enough crabs and sticks, you're pretty much covered.
-Breaking limbs will kill you eventually and, from my own experience, is rather easy to do
-The crafting and building systems are a bit strange
All in all, the pros outweigh the cons, making this game well worth the money.
Props to steam for letting me return this game twice.

In terms of raw player driven fun, this RPG is in another league entirely from its contemperaries. The sheer amount of TECHNOLOGY in this game has never been topped, in my opinion.
There is a quest, where you must find a ring to open an ancient treasure chest, you can take the ring to a counterfeiter, get an exact duplicate, and when it comes time for the NPCs to use the ring to open the chest, it fails(Because it's a counterfeit.) I really like Tooth and Tail, and it is definitely a good game to me, however I do have a few grievances that I think need to be addressed. In order to address everything I will be going into story spoilers so if you want to experience the story for yourself without knowing then just skip over the story section of this review.
Gameplay: Solid, simplified, easy to learn RTS. I completely think that the developers nailed it with what they were aiming to create, which was an RTS simplified. Some argue that the game is too easy, or that it relies too heavily on RNG due to the random map generation for every game. I counter that by arguing that this is isn't like the huge, in depth RTS's out there where your games last 30min-1hr in length, where you can go in with a grand strategy and outplan your enemy. In this game you need to go in to matches with an open mind, you need to see what you have to work with, learn what your enemy is working with, and plan around it, and plan around the plan of your enemy, Games last about no longer than 10min, so every decision you make from grabbing an early expansion to investing straight into units, it all matters, especially if you are reacting to a move from your opponant. In the end, I think that there is a wealth of strategy to be had having the game this way, especially without knowing what units your enemy will bring or what the map will have to offer.
Design: The world of T&T has a beautiful pixel style art design that is fairly simple and it fits the simplicity they were going for in developing the gameplay. The artwork for the actual unit portraits, and the leader portraits is all very well made as well, allowing you to get a really detailed look as to what your units actually look like. The music is also very nice, each faction getting a few different themed tunes that suit their theme, such as the KSR getting a brass orchestra and the Civilized having curch organ in the instruments.
Multiplayer: Some people have reported issues with multiplayer, having no one in their region to play with, but here in America that is not an issue so if you are in the US and Europe then I assume you wont have trouble. Anyway, the multiplayer functions just like the campaign, but with no special map conditions and you are up against a real person. There is even a competitive mode where you can climb the ranks and be featured on the leaderboard. I have not had any issues with connection, or finding matches, so I am going to say that, for my experience, it has been good.
Story: This is where I have to give and take points away, and where you should stop reading if you dont want spoilers. So, Tooth and Tail sets up this amazing parody world akin to the Russian Revolution, with its story being told through interactable people and environment objects in the four bases. It sets up this tragic tale of the murdered Tsarina, the only one able to hold society together, and then the four factions began to tear eachother apart when times got rough. You learn about Bellafide, leader of the Longcoats out for vengence for his son, having been murdered in the harvest. Hopper, the one armed revolutionary out to rally the poor and neglected members of society to create a democracy for better rights, and an election for the harvest. The Quartermaster of the KSR whom is lost after the death of the Tsarina, no longer having the head of state to give direction to the organization, trying her best to do as she believes the Tsarina would think was best. And finally Archemedes, the high priest of the Civilized trying to do the will of his order while also dealing with his own morals on right and wrong. Unfortunately, the game gives only 5-6 missions per faction story line, giving you hardly any time to really explore society or the main characters, and to top it off you are limited to only exploring the tiny faction bases rather than more open areas to really get a look at what the world looks like. To top it off, the ending is absolutely horrible. Your final mission is to end the war, and so one would assume that we would see some sort of resolution to all of our main characters stories, right? No! Instead, the game ends with the pigs rising up and killing everyone, presumably ending the war for their own order to rise up. So, do you like the four protagonists? Too bad their dead! Do you like exploring their story archs? Too bad their dead! This is where the simplicity of the game is painfully crippling, because it leaves you wanting more, and not in a good way! It feels incomplete, rushed, with an unsatisfying ending. This could be remedied by giving every faction its own in depth storyline with at least fifteen missions, letting you also explore outside of the main faction HQ to see more of this world and what it is like. The story spans over a year, at least, so there is so much time to work with! And if they toss out the stupid pig ending then they have even more time to work with post "the end". So many people I talk to are wishing for more, for an open world exploration of this T&T landscape, for better story campaigns, and for a better ending.
I really hope this helps people make their decision to get T&T, and if a dev possibly sees this then my final words of advice to you are these: DO MORE! You have a rich setting in the palm of your hand with a fanbase that wants more, use it! Fix your campaigns, add more locations to explore, hell add some sort of world map to explore or something, but just add more! As it sits you are currently crippling yourselves with what you have available.

Tooth and tail is a stripped back pixel art RTS.

Map generation is an issue because sometimes you can get screwed over when you do not have enough farms near you or your base is surrounded by high ground. A improvement to competitive would be to have a competive playlist where the maps are random and another playlist where they are not. This would cater to everybodys desires.
For the future i would like to see more units introduced into the game as well as regular balence updates to create metas. This would give the game a League of legends feel where the game is always fresh with new units and balence changes. Overall i would reccomend Tooth and tail to anyone and at a $23 price point this game is definately worth your time.

Really fun game. Combat is kind of Arkham/Assassin's Creed style, and though it can get a little repetitive, the animations are awesome and varied, so killing hordes of orcs doesn't get boring. Though those parts of the game are good, the really great part of this game is the nemesis system. Orc captains and warlords all have unique strengths, weaknesses, personalities and appearances. When you kill or help them, you affect the power hierarchy of the orcs. This makes the world really feel responsive, and every makes every death feel meaningful. Its a really cool system that they're hopefully going to expand on a lot in the sequel.
The only real downside of this game is how easy it is. It's pretty easy to escape any difficult situations, so, unless you really overcommit to a kill, it's hard to die. But that's pretty minor, and the rest of the game is extremely good.

Second try of writing a review as my first one was rather unforgiving...
TLDR:
Not wholy oldschool but pretty good. As a fan of the old infinity engine games you should really try it. Younger RPG lovers should also get it.
Now I'm a seasoned Planescape and Baldur's Gate (also NWN) expert so I'll use those classics as reference in mind.
Graphics are nice but old style, Divinity looked more modern but still every equipped armor shines neatly.
Music is Conan style, no surprises but good and fits. Sounds like Baldur's Gate.
Voice acting - good but we expected this.
World and lore is a copy of forgotten realms essentially. Standard fantasy you'll feel right at home.
Rule system is somewhat on par with D&D2 and slightly inferior to D&D3, no multi-classing either.
Party, choice of the assorted fleshed out companions, those have a lot of personality, bicker as always and come with a quest. You can also create more adventurers for small coins if you rather want custom characters. Companions are on par with the averagely made Baldur's Gate companions say Corgan, Keldorn or Mazzy and better in cases. No Minsk, Imoen, Morte or Annah though.
Quests - those are very good.
The main story is high above average game standards. Souls, reincarnation, unearthing the past, all of that. After reaching act 2 the plot gains some depth.

Being a veteran of the first three "Way of the Samurai" titles, and the teams original "Way of the Ninja", I had pretty high expectations going into the game. And, while they weren't all met, for every expectation not met they had a new aspect added in to make up for it.
Now, for a brief "in-a-nutshell" rundown of what the seires has always been to start us off:
Play as a Samurai; Wander about a town/providence that's dealing with an internal conflict; Get one of multiple endings based on your choices.
Now that you're caught up on the basics let me tell you some of that info about this entry to the series.
When playing "Way of the Samurai 4" one of the first things you'll notice is that the game is HEAVILY story-based, as you watch a multi-part cut-scene that will take around 10 to 15 minutes (though, this is broken up by a tutorial on how to fight, which does keep you in the action). However, this introductory story segment does extremely well at introducing all of the main characters to the player. Allowing us to decide which groups we like, and which ones we don't, right off the bat (though, your perception of the groups will change over time). This, in turn will help you determine whom you wish to assist throughout the game, if any of them.
That's right, this story-based game allows you to completely bypass the story, and just do whatever you want to do. So, you can be a noble Samurai warrior, a renegade, a dojo master, or just a person who likes to fish (Though, let's face it, if you're playing a Samurai game, you're in it to kick some♥♥♥♥♥.
Now, a big difference in the story aspect of this entry to the series, is that the game provides you hints as to where you can go to progress the story, through the use of an "events" option in the pause menu. Whereas the older entries determined what happened to you, based off of where you were at different times of the day, which changed as you moved from area to area in the old games (though, in this entry, time is only passed by either witnessing a story event, or having your character sleep).
Personally, I think this change was for the better, as it allows the player to do a lot more, without the risk of missing an event they wanted to interact with.
Now, onto the other main aspect of the game: "The Combat".
Combat, in this game, is not as you would expect it to be (if you're starting the series from here). While a glance would make it look like it's a simple hack-n-slash action game, there's a fair amount of tactical thought that put into each strike (on any difficulty above easy). There are your standard quick and heavy strikes, as well as blocking and dodging, yes. But, there's also different aspects to each move, such as being a guard breaking strike, a push to knock your opponent off their guard, grabs, parrys that counteract pushing strikes (and much, much more!). When fighting in this game, messing up once against an opponent has the chance to mean instant death. So, you need to plan out what your going to do in real time, as you watch your opponent's movements carefully.
This kind of combat is much more engaging to the player, and makes every victory feel satisfying.
Now...The controls do take a little bit to get used to, and are god aweful if you're playing on keybord (Due to this game being a port of a console game to PC). So, it's highly recommended that you play with an Xbox controller, if possible. I can't say much more about the controls, other than: "Pay attention to the tutorial".
This game is, in fact, a 30fps game. And, if you're a fps snob, then you're not going to like it. However, the game looks good, and isn't hindered by being at 30fps at all. So, if you're playing to enjoy games rather than frames, you're gonna like what you see.
In the end, this game isn't perfect, but it is a lot of fun. And I highly recommend it.
Final Score: 8/10

This is a hard game to review, and a harder game to give a score or rating to.
The combat is somewhere between Dark Souls and Dyansty Warriors, with grand flashy combos and special moves, but a delicate 1v1 life-or-death flavour.
The crafting and skill trees are beyond deep, with nearly a hundred different martial arts styles to choose from, and five different weapon types (Katana, Spear, Dual Katanas, Guns [Muskets and Pistols] and unarmed kung-fu style fighting).
The story is branching, fairly deep, and at times highly engaging, with clever plot twists, likeable and complex characters to get you invested, and a lot of replayability as you wind your way through the story tree in new ways to see every mission and eventually get the true ending.
I think a lot of the sound design is good, with solid sound effects and a pretty excellent Spaghetti Western/Samurai soundtrack that would make Morricone proud.
Very deep character customization system.
The humour is clumsy at best, as the localisation team tried to keep all of the quirky humour from the Japanese release in the game. Unfortunately, at least in my opinion, most of the humour falls very flat, and the game would have been a lot more fun for me if it had been played off as a serious game. Some moments are entertaining for the sheer insanity factor, but the novelty quickly wears off.
Nightcrawling is just a ridiculous mechanic, which in my opinion damages the tone of the game greatly while offering little in the way of reward.
Very little in the way of graphics settings, which is a shame because, running at the default settings from the PS3 release of this game, it's pretty average looking. Sometimes the graphics shine, other times they're downright ugly. It's a mixed bag.
No English voice-over! This would have made the experience a lot more enjoyable for me, personally, although some may prefer the authenticity of the voices here.
Barely any tutorial or documentation makes learning the mechanics of the game difficult at best, downright cryptic at worst.
You MUST have a controller to play this game, in my opinion. Mouse support has recently been added (which beats the old keyboard layout) but is still inferior to an XBOX 360 controller. Luckily, the controller support is superb; plug it in and away you go, no fuss or settings to tweak, all button presses on-screen represented with the correct icons.
The issue here is, a lot of these cons and pros are highly subjective; some people may enjoy the quirky humour, and although I express I personally dislike it, I also think it wouldn't be the same game without it, and I might even enjoy it less if it were absent simply because it adds a certain light-hearted character to the game, as if the game doesn't care what you think, it's going to be batshit insane anyway.
All in all, WotS4 offers a great deal of gameplay, an exciting experience and a deep story for a fairly low price, and even lower on sale (£9.99 at the time of writing).
I personally think it's worth every penny, but some may hate it. My advice is to buy it, try it, and get a refund if you don't like it; you'll know soon enough as this game is certainly love-or-hate.
I'd also like to mention that the developers for this game are superb. This game has only been released on Steam in the last few months, but the developers have been incredibly active in updating and improving it, adding highly requested features and plenty of bug fixes with each patch.

Okay, is this game Saviors or Star Saviors? It's called Star Saviors on the main page, but the actual picture's title and the title on my download list says "Saviors". Well, which is it, Steam?
Before I go completely off track, I was mildly surprised by Star Saviors. I know the Bullet Hell audience (a couple of my friends are part of that niche), and let me just say that they can be about as damned annoying as anime/manga fans.  Especially when a new Bullet Hell game comes out! Well, I decided to try this one out just for craps and giggles, and was a little more surprised with what I got than what I was expecting. This game isn't a masterpiece, but I had a lot of fun- while I was expecting a more dull game.
Star Saviors functions like the classic "your ship moving constantly forward, with all the other ships trying to blow you up", fashion. You fly, and you shoot. But what Saviors has that made me love it a lot more than the old 1940's plane games I used to tear up back in the day, is that those amazing weapon upgrades that'd normally disappear in one hit in those arcade games are full-on upgrades you can unlock and combine with your weapons in whatever style you want, to maximize damage. No specific pattern of bullets is better than the other, since they all upgrade in damage at the same time, and that I really, really liked. Even the upgradeable perks system was a nice touch.
Now, there IS a huge difficulty curve in this game you have to get over, and it can be a bit annoying at times, when you've got a sliver of health left on a boss and you die and have to start all the way back at the beginning, but it still manages to be fun with all the adversity I faced- and I even found it addicting.
The story's short (as the main game's campaign is roughly 2 hours), but it's a little bit better than other indie arcade-reminiscent games I've played in a while. Mind you, I'm not saying this is Oscar-material. The enemies have no personality, and the guy and girl that follow you do no service to the plot (and honestly, no one on your Saviors team actually helps you shoot down enemies, which is weird at the end on one of your teammates says, "I shot the most of them!"... BS! I shot ALL of them!"). And the character's faces look like a clay face forced back into an uncomfortable stare that are being telepathically controlled through their lips... It's honestly creepy to look at. But as far as characterization goes with the father and son, gave a small but nice touch. The other plot points were nonsensical and did nothing at all for me, but the moments when your dad encourages you and wants to make sure you stay safe were a slight touch of "something more" that this game has.
Again, it's not perfect. The plot is really pointless, as you aimlessly fly from zone A to be, gunning down enemies, finishing a boss fight, and doing... something to forward your progress on saving your home planet. But it's still a fun game to throw 20 cents on. It's certainly worth that.

This is a very solid shooter experience, and it was made by just three people.  This is exactly the sort of gem you hope to find from small indie teams.
The graphics and music are above average, the control is tight, there are a lot of options to customize your experience, and several different game modes to keep you going.
There are 18 levels to complete to make it through the story.  After each mission you are allowed to pick perks, as well as customize your main, secondary and special weapon.  As you get deeper in the game more options unlock.  You can also choose one of three pilots, and each ship has its own unique flavor.  Missions are a mix of standard enemies and bosses.  Most moves are telegraphed ahead of time, giving you a split second to plan your next move.  You can also alternate your fire between going all guns forward for full damage, or split your damage three ways and shoot ahead of you and to each side.
The story sections are the weakest portion of the game.  There is nothing unique, the writing is not very natural, and the pilots don't look great in the speaking sections.  There is an alien invasion, and only your commander saw it coming, now go blow everything up.  The end.  Fortunately, all story sections can be skipped.
Very worthwhile game if you enjoy this type of shooter.  A solid entry, give it a try.

Cons:

in a longer version, this translates that the game looked promising, with its large world, cool combat mechanics, adn pretty decent ai. it kinda gets dumped on by the way the npc's are presented. some are just superbland shells that say two lines and then they are gone, some talk to you like you should know them or like you would know who they want you to target, but the reality is, you only just arived at the place after a pretty crazy series of events which dont really seem that logical to begin with. now, if it would atleast give me things to find that would describe this place i am in (even tho i should have been told allready as an intro, after all, our character lived in this world allready) i would be able to forgive that weird order in which things happen, but it just doesnt offer anything. you learn about the followers, but everything else is just nothing.
now i wont lie: i likes the large enemies that i fought. i dont really think it made as much sense that they where there, but i liked the way there where many ways to pitch in on such large fights (i found it very satisfying to learn that arrows actually stagger cyclopses for a good while). besides the big targets, i really didnt find too much variety or interresting enemies. just piles and piles of goblins and wolves, with some zombies at night.
one more thing which made me ask for a refund in the end, was the fact that, after two hours of free exploration, killing some tough cyclopses etc, i saved my game before trying a jump, and guess what, i couldnt load that save. from the deathscreen to alt-f4ing and using main menu's way to load the game, it just didnt do a thing. did i just fumble with that save? no. i made 5 saves before that point, and it gave me a "saving game, blablabla" message. kinda defeats the purpose of doing anything at all, if its not going to be recorded/saved unless i reach some checkpoint of the main storyline, which wasnt really anything to begin with>.<'
so no, i cant say this game deserves any real attention. i would like for the combat mechanics to be implemented in a new game with a vastly better storyline, and even the ai system deserves to be re-used, but the main game itself is just a pile of garbage.

Shellshock Live is a very relaxing game with a frantic assortment of crazy weapons to throw at your opponents. Your mission: shoot stuff at tanks to destroy them. It's literally that - no more, no less. You can shoot with everything - grenades, frogs, fish, sillyballs, MOONS, pooping birds etc.
Gameplay is simple:
At the start of the game you spawn with the set amount of health on a (randomly) chosen map, which can be in different team compositions, 1v1 through 4v4, or 1v7, or a free for all-murder-everyone mode. You get equipped with a set of weapons randomly selected from the ones you have unlocked so far. During your turn, you can select a weapon and a trajectory to damage your opponents. ez life.
It has a level-based system in two separate segments: you can level up to unluck new weapons and perks, and you can level up your weapons by dealing damage with them. You can level up by playing missions, or playing multiplayer games. Your progress depends on your participation (kills/dmg etc, with a bonus for being MVP), the amount of trickshots you hit, and - additionally - you level up for unlocking achievements. With each new level you unlock a new weapon and an "upgrade gear" with which you can increase one of your perks (damage boosts, shield boost, mobility boost and.. luck boost).
Leveling up weapons will result in having the possibility to get an upgraded version of the original weapon, which can increase damage, range, area of attack, number of projectiles, or simply the ease to use.
It comes with a bunch of different playmodes and settings to finetune the game to your preference for you and your friends
As an easy to play, laid back multiplayer game it's very suitable to pass time or to hang around with friends (definitely recommended to play with friends; which greatly enhances the joy you can get out of the game). It has a slightly nice balance between luck, skill and silliness, although on higher levels, the weapons you get can often already decide the game.
Pros:
- Entertaining gameplay
- "Simple yet effective" graphics
- Nice music and sound effects
- ideal to play with friends
- also suitable for grinding levels/achievements for those that need that to keep them playing
- Your tank can be a beachball. (not really, but it can be round and beachballs are round)
- MOONS
- GUPPIES
- BOUNSPLODE
- Piñata music
Cons:
Only one I can really think of, which can provide quite a drawback: At later levels, the game is frequently already decided by the weapons you get equipped with. There are a few weapons that are vastly more powerful than others, and the higher you get, the more this applies. This effect stacks with your positioning (which you can alter to an extent though, if you upgrade mobility); some weapons only work in close proximity or in certain areas. This goes up to a point where getting poor weapons, or only close-range weapons when in a longrange position, can result in rendering you unable to be efficient at all. While I would not consider winning the main point of the game, it can make quite a dent in your playing experience.
All in all this game is definitely worth it. I've received it as a gift, and have fond memories of playing it. Havent played in a while, both due to lack of time, and because the friends I used to play with rarely play it nowadays (the latter definitely influences me as its much more fun to play with friends). All in all I would definitely recommend!

Game is much more stable and the main menus deal with adjusting the resolution nicely.  So developers are obviously working on defects.

Here is how those few hours went.
Spend the first hour looking around, finding food, collecting cool stuff. Hammers, hatchette, cloths, back packs.
After a while you decide you have too much stuff and need somethere to put it, You spend the next hour finding a nice secluded spot and start building.  After that hour you find that you can't place any items down until you have a sign post, which requires a nail.
You take a very long walk to try and find a nail to make your sign post.  After you search many stores and gas stations you come up empty.  You follow the road for another hour to make it to the next town.
BAM! Someone blows your head off with rifle from 300 meters away without so much as a "HELLO".
"Respawn" you are asked, I don't think so.
Oddly, I found myself recommending the game, just don't get attached to anything you find.  Someone WILL take it from you.

I've had Mass Effect in my list for a long while and now I'm kicking myself for not playing it earlier. Mass Effect is now officially one of my all-time favorite games.
The writing and characterization in the game is superb. If you are an action junkie, this might not be the game for you because, while there is a lot of action, it is interrupted by a deep storyline with lots of cut scenes. While I loved the complex characters and breadth of story, you may not.
The scope of the game is amazing. There is one main plot, a few major plots, and a bunch of side missions. You can really spend a lot of time exploring and completing the side missions.
As you proceed through missions, you acquire equipment upgrades and new team members. While you eventually have quite a few team members, you can only select two to accompany you on missions. Each member has specialized skills and you have to use strategy when assembling your away team.
The combat is one of the weaker aspects of the game. It's just not that challenging. But that was a minor annoyance because the story, characters, and side missions were so good.
I'm looking forward to playing 2 and 3 now!! What a superb game.

A cool concept for a very fun, micro-heavy strategy game. It could be incredible entertaining in multiplayer, but its single-player campaign is completely marred by horrid combination of random map design and static resource collection/survival missions. The result is that it often places you in highly indefensible positions where you are completely dependent on the map positioning for resource collection rather than using farms. To add insult to injury, the enemies in these missions can often build anywhere and come from anywhere. The mechanics do not support the kind of strategy game they have created and often results in missions feeling completely unfair until you suddenly win because it gave you a kind map layout. Sonic CD is a platformer game starring famous hedgehog from Sega and was originally released for Sega CD in 1993, making use of CD technology. And having two different soundtracks for JP or US region. It was later released for PC, having improved intro and ending movies, without limits of Sega CD. And now it was rereleased and improved for smartphones, PS3, Xbox360 and Steam.
What's new in remastered version? It was ported onto new engine, allowing new menues, small stuff and even support of widescreen. It kept full movies from PC version. It even used rotation and scaling where it made sense, where Sega CD used choppy animation. And it even added new content, with ability to choose preference of Spin Dash from Sonic 2, ability to choose US or JP soundtrack, leaderboards (for your time attack fun too), achievements and even ability to select the ever cute Tails the Fox, that wasn't originally in Sonic CD. You have to beat game once to unlock him and even has ability to fly from Sonic 3 too. Lacks intro and ending movies though. Yes, he got new animation frames.
The only bad thing I can think of is that Japanese soundtack main songs lack lyrics, instead replaced with custom-made instrumentals. They lack some of charm.
Now, if you have to descripe Sonic CD in one line: it's Sonic 1, but more gimmicky and easier.
And it's not a bad thing, since Sonic 1, like most classic Sonic games, was one of the better pure-platformers out there (I mean, no attack button or such). With more movement-based awesome physics, both while running or rolling, simple control, nice pacing and multiple branches, it was great. It also had unique rings-health system, where you would survive a hit as long as you had at least one ring, while scattering them all around.
Sonic CD retains most of the greatness, and despite being released after Sonic 2, got the looks and control feels of the first part. Background look much more complex and game uses CD audio, which may not sound chiptune-like, but still has great tune to it. Japan version at least. US soundtrack is more of generic thing, with some dark tones here and there.
Sonic have to travel onto the flying little planet, which has time-teleport troubles and is controlled by Eggman, just to kick his egg butt once again. Oh, and to save planet. And Amy. And battle with Metal Sonic. Your mission is still same, to get to the end of the level, each of 7 levels having 3 acts, the third one being a boss act.
Bosses are one-trick ponies. They are easy, but have some gimmick going on for them. While other Sonic games have more of classic challenging bosses, each taking 8 hits, Sonic CD ones use various trickish mechanics, giving them a wackier cartoonish feel. For example, one of the bosses requires Sonic to keep running over conveyer belt of sorts, speeding it up and making friction melt the bottom part of Eggman's machine.
And bad sides, once again, bosses are too easy once you know what to do. Or even if you don't. Final boss isn't that much of problem either, as you can just rush him down with the forgiving ring-health system of Sonic games.
You will also notice that level design is all over the place. It doesn't feel tight or much of challenge, instead being more of easy maze, having unneded branches and areas. And for sure you will notice Past and Future signs. Well, why, it's yet another gimmicky approach to game design, the Time Travel!
Once you pass over time travel sign, you will get ability to teleport either into Past or Future if you will be able to keep maximum speed for more than few seconds. This will make you learn the level layout, either to find the best cleanest path or to just abuse some springs that will send you into loop. The main difference between Past or Future is level layout and visual theme being slightly altered. It's not really a big deal.
But in the Past is where you can find two important objects: Flying engine destroying which will kill all the enemies in the act and will turn Bad Future into Good Future, while destroying Metal Sonic hologram will make animals appear in the level again. If you destroy all engines in all levels, you will get good ending. Hard work!
There is little reason to visit Future though.
But bad thing is, such exploration for Past and engine still negatively affects level design when player just wants to beat them in traditional way. Time Travel barely adds anything to the gameplay, because by time you would go to Past to destroy all enemies, you could easily beat the level. And if you are aiming for good ending, then there is actually even easier way to get it: Collect all Time Stones from Special Stages! Once you collect all time stones, you will get Good Future in all levels from that point and you will always have good ending, making time travel obsolote.
Thankfully, modern version gives you a special achievement for doing all hard Time Travel work, giving at least some reason to do it at least once.
Oh. And Special Stages, that you get by having 50 rings by the end of stage, are awesome in this one. Using a trick similiar to Mode-7 kart games on SNES, you control Sonic on 3D flat track, who has to jump and crush down every UFO that patrol around, under time limit. Running over water will deplete timer quickly and a special UFO will appear that gives time bonus once you have only 20 seconds left. This is my favourite Special/Bonus Stage of all Sonic games, it really is fun to control.
And yes, this remaster upgraded special stages visuals greatly. Instead of having choppy pre-made animations frames for UFO enlarging as you come closer to them game now uses real smooth scaling for them. It allows you to measure just how close you are to them so much better.
Sonic CD is still fun platformer. But it's too easy to feel much of accomplishment and gimmicks are distractive game design. Time Travel feels unneeded and tackled on, but there are people who actually like this Past-searching quest. Some people dislike this game, others call it the best. I say, go for it, try it, you may love it.
It got old Sonic charm at least.

The worst part, and perhaps the most insulting thing about Hektor, is that it isn't scary at all. Outlast was scary, Alien Isolation was a stressful and harrowing experience. Hektor? Hektor is a complete disgrace to the horror genre of games. Watch any of the lets-plays that are currently on Youtube. Not a single one of them is enthralling, immersive, or in the least bit frightening. Many claim that the game's atmosphere is intensely creepy, and that they would prefer a game like Hektor to one filled with jump scares. Sure, jump scares alone do not make a horror game. Neither do games that are all about the long drawn out creepy atmospheres that eventually amount to nothing.
You can only play so much of Hektor before you feel cheated and violated, like the boy who is strung along by a candy man with all the promises of a sweet future, only to end up in the back of a windowless van. No, there is nothing causing that sound that appears to be made by the wheels of hospital beds rolling across the corridor. Its just one of the many sound assets that the game randomly plays every now and then to build up 'atmosphere'. In fact, I haven't seen a single hospital bed move in this game. How about those creaks and groans and that squeaky violin sound you hear as the background music reaches its crescendo? Yup, just more of the same. Sounds with no force of a credible threat behind them. And do you know why there is no hiding in this game? Because there is no need to - the game is a bloody walking simulator. The only threats in Hektor reside in the creatures that you will encounter in this game, and what a disappointment they are.
The developers advertise this game as having a horrific monster that tirelessly pursues you. Yes there is only one monster in the game capable of killing you. But the only times you experience being chased by this presence is halfway through the game when you first come across it, and towards the end when the game artificially ramps up its difficulty level by putting the creature in your path. Beyond those two occasions, you almost never encounter the creature, much less get 'pursued' by it. Additionally, it is difficult to be afraid of a monster that has pathing issues. There was one occasion when the monster ran continuously into a box that was in front of me as it tried to get at me.
Besides this monster, the game scatters, with no logical rhyme or reason, half naked deathly pale people around the map. These death-camp prisoner of war lookalikes cannot hurt you physically, but are capable of reducing your character's sanity level if you are near them when they scream. The first time you encounter one of these people is a decently shocking experience, but towards the later part of the game, their presence is at best an irritating encounter as the game uses the same audio asset for their screams, and at worst you might end up laughing in their face, especially when you see their ridiculous transition from person into a reddish spectre.
Who are these people-like things? What is that monster that chases you? What is the Hektor program? Who are you? Why are you at the facility? How did you come to develop your psychosis? Why do you guzzle antipsychotic medications like M&Ms? You'd probably have a better chance of getting that information from God than this game. In fact, Hektor hardly explains anything properly. The game conveys its tale singularly through badly written journal or diary entries that are randomly distributed throughout the entire level in a humdrum and erratic manner.  Walk into the intelligence room for the first time, pick up a journal entry. Walk into the intelligence room again at a later time, great there are 2 more journal entries to pick up. What the ♥♥♥♥ is this? Shouldn't the intelligence room be empty now given that I have just explored it earlier? The entire attempt feels so lazy, so half-hearted. It destroys any remaining immersion that one might have in the game up to this point.
The main story is simplistic. It is also full of boring cliches. How many times can we pretend to be interested in the stories told by the people who eventually develop the 'crazies', or some aggravated form of 'stockholm' syndrome? Leave that for the bad movies, it is their rightful domain. You are supposed to be making a horror game that scares us, unnerves us, that makes the hairs on our skin stand as we uncover the story bit by bit. And this is the best you can come up with?
$14.99 is too much money to spend on this utter filth and garbage. $14.99 is too much money to spend to be insulted by the developers, who think they can masquerade this bad cashgrab as a 'psychological horror game'. The only thing that is horrifying about this game is our ridiculously low expectations when it comes to paying for and hyping garbage like this on Steam.
If you enjoyed 'Daylight', which is another horror game with procedurally generated levels, you might enjoy Hektor. They are both equally bad. Another option is to skip both games, and simply watch a let's play from one of the better youtubers out there. It will require a considerable amount of good acting skills on the part of the youtuber to beat some life into this dead dog's body.
Otherwise, FASTER FASTER... avoid Hektor. You have been warned.
