Dynasty Warriors 8: Xtreme Legends Complete Edition
You might wonder why a complete edition game has a separate available dlcs and are sold at crazy price. Long story short, it is a single product of normal DW8 + DW8XL, which in ps3 are 2 different products with different story combined into one. It's a good thing if you ask me since—you don't have to buy both of them like the previous dynasty warrior games normally do—to fully enjoy the experience of slaughtering thousand of peons in the name of benevolence while following romance of the three kingdoms story.
"Ok I get it. So what's so good about the game itself?"
Tl;dr?
A fun game to learn history, based on a famous chinese historical novel "Romance of The Three Kingdoms" and at the same time a good stress reliever while you're mashing and alternating between normal attack and charged attack to try different combos with over 80 characters to try, each with different weapons, movesets, traits. Most of them, if not all, were real figures from the three kingdoms history.
"More details. I need to know what I'm getting myself into."
Rather than explaining the game, I would like to compare the game to the previous dynasty warrior series since explaining about the dynasty warrior itself will take forever. Don't worry, you'll get it even if you haven't played the previous games.
Like I said before, this is the combination of DW8 (base) + DW8XL (expansion), hence complete edition. It is the first in the franchise to combine both since in the previous games, the base game only has a historical story mode while xtreme legend expansion adds an alternate story mode but still playable without base, and you have to buy both to get the full experience between history and hypothetical story. Well you get the point.
Like the previous games, DW4 and DW7. Rather than every characters, DW8XLCE focussing the story on each kingdom. This is probably a major change since DW6 and could be proven to be efficient, at least for me, as you don't have to play every characters in the game with most of them having a same battle (ex : both Gan Ning and Ling Tong have Battle of He Fei in their storyline). And if you really insist to play every possible characters in the same battle, you can do it in free mode. Each battle in each kingdom story has a notable characters in that battlefield which you must pick, each have different and important role/objective. Furthermore, all of playable officers in that battlefield still get experience and level up. This is great and saves a lot of time if you want to try or level up every characters because you don't have to start as weak as level 1 and can take on a higher difficulty.
Thanks to xtreme legend expansion, each kingdom's storyline has a historical route and additional hypotethical route. A historical route is, pretty much self-explanatory, a route where you follow the story based on a real historical event of three kingdoms. There's not much you can do in here. Even when you're able to beat or already defeated every dudes in the map, if the victory condition tells you to surrender/retreat, so be it.
Whereas the hypotethical route is basically what-if scenario. What if x didn't die on y battlefield? What if x didn't get injured? What if they win at z battlefield thanks to x plan? You have a certain conditions in certain battlefields to fulfill in order make those what-ifs come true, hence opening up a hypotethical route. And I tell you all of them are epic.
Next is weapon system. Okay so other characters level should be decent thanks to auto-leveling at story mode, so what about their weapons? It would be sucks to play on hard with sufficient level but still using a starting weapon, right? Well don't worry, because every non-playable officers you have killed in the battle will drop a random weapon. And since it's random, if you have played enough you will obtain new additional weapons for every characters. The higher the difficulty or the later the stage, the better the weapon of course.
Aditionally, every characters can use every weapons (or rather, movesets) in the game regardless of fighting style. In extreme case, a mighty Lu Bu can use Xiao Qiao's fan and becomes very feminine as carried like a princess. Vice versa. Well puting that aside, it makes your life easier if you don't have a decent weapon for a character and too poor to make/buy one so instead you decided to use a stronger weapon of other's character, though you can't use their ex attacks.
There are a lot of things too which I failed to include in this review like ambition mode, bodyguard and their skills, ex attacks, weapon affinity and storm rush. Well just play and experience it yourself.

I've been a die hard fan of Dynasty warriors since I was 4 years old (lol), that's when I played the first hack and slash dynasty warriors game. Despite that I'll still give a subjective review of the game.
I loved it because you could just be a soldier in a battlefield, something I always wanted. The games have changed a "little" since then. Some for better some for the worse.
Anyway lets start




The game is based on the novel the romance of the three kingdoms, which is based on the historical time period of china that the three kingdoms occured with a bit more fiction involved and a few characters that didn't exist but it includes all the major fights and events.
You are just a badass soldier in a battlefield, with godlike powers that can kick everyones♥♥♥♥♥ Until Lu Bu comes along and kicks your♥♥♥♥♥. Over
if I recall correctly and each has their own unique weapon and moveset. There is simply no way you won't find someone you like.
There are campaigns for every one of the three kingdoms. + The jin kingdom and a Lu Bu campaign. If you don't know who Lu Bu is shame on you.
Each campaign has the "true" path and what would have happened if (insert kingdom) had won (insert battle) plus a few extra stages that cover some other battles.
It also includes a free mode in which you can select whichever character you like, play whatever battle you desire siding with whatever army you feel like.
Also a challenge mode with a few other "mini games" per say which challenge you to beat a highscore and then there's the ambition mode. Which is a much more grindy empires version of the game. You select your character, build your own empire, fight and recruit officers etc.

Long, long, long time Tex Murphy fan here, one of the ones that was actively pining away for a new Tex after Overseer abruptly ended.  I have to sadly say, that at this time, I am not impressed.  I'll keep it simple...
-The first person camera is poorly done, and leaves me with severe sea sickness like queezy feeling, even for hours after I save and close down the game session. (fiddling with the field of view in options helps but doesn't completely fix this problem)  I've played First person shooters for years, and I don't have this problem with AAA designed FPS titles that perfect the veiwing angle, which eliminates motion sickness for me
-Opening game story/writing is very bad
-dialog writing and acting delivery is extremely bad and lacking the charm of the old Tex games.  Tex was never known for great acting, but he was known to pull off bad acting and all sorts of hokiness with a fantastic endearing quality and I'm just not agreeing with it in this new release.
-the early game puzzles are really lame (Spoiler' ' an overly complicated and obnoxious game of simon and running all over town without much aim or directive just to find a ladder and have some forced introductions with currently useless new characters who aren't very interesting ' ')
-I cannot stand the Mystery Science Theatre sounding PDA voice that is constantly a part of the game, it's the voice of the personal electronic organizer.  I'd rather be alone with Tex's internal monologue and not annoying interuptions of MST voices popping in with awful one liners and insults.
I only played through the first hour or so of the game + I finished the entire demo before the final game was released.  I found the demo to be a tad bit better than the intro of the new Tex game, so perhaps the game gets better as it goes on, but with nothing so far that I find endearing or appealing combined with the naseau inducing first person camera implementation, and I don't think I'll be back to find out if I'm missing out or not.
Personally I'd rather replay UAKM or Pandora Directive or go replay Myst III, IV and V than try this again anytime soon.
Sorry Tex, I still love ya, but please, try again.

There's nothing quite like a Cosmo D game, but that's a good thing. An adventure game in the style of Gone Home or Myst but with a healthy dose of surrealism and a killer soundtrack, The Norwood Suite is Cosmo D's most polished and intriguing game yet.

Just finished TE and found it to be one of the most enjoyable games I have played. Now, fair warning, this is a point-and-click adventure game, so if you do not like that type of game, then you probably won't love it the way I do. However, if you do like that genre, this is a wonderful game for you. If you played any or all of the Tex Murphy games from about ten years ago--Under a Killing Moon, The Pandora Directive--then you are in for a double treat. Many of your favorite characters are back, and Tex is played by the same actor with all the wisecracking and corny P.I. jokes (of course). One of the things I got the biggest kick from is the flashback sequences drawn from the old games triggered by objects in the environment (remembering how Tex got a hole in the brim of one of his fedoras was one of my favorites). The flashbacks appear to be the FMV from the old games displayed in a little letterbox in the center of the screen. The new FMV shot for this game is high-def and full screen and looks and plays beautifully. There is a casual mode for beginners with hints as to what to do next and objects that are needed for the story highlighted by Tex's trusty flashlight. More experienced adventure gamers are going to want to play without the hints or the object-highlighting, but either way this is a great ride--especially if you played any of the earlier games. I played without the help, and while there are a few items that took a bit of work to find and a challenging timed puzzle at the end of the game, I only had to rely on the Universal Hint System two or three times.
So a great point-and-click adventure for anyone, and a special treat for Tex Murphy fans from earlier games, Tesla Effect is not to be missed.

I have been playing Pillars of Eternity for a while now and this has to be one of my favorite games in the past couple of years. Obsidian has managed to make an incredible game that is steep in lore and exploration that made this Dungeon and Dragons nerd pack up his dice. Now I have never played Baldur’s Gate or any tactical RPG. The combat system is more fun than what I was expecting, however, I must advise watch where you put or team members for I have blocked my barbarian and fighter in a corner many times by not paying attention. This game does involve READING and lots of it, for it replaces what might be a cinematic event in another game with a “choose your own adventure” event that you have to read and make your choice. During these parts it really makes the D&D aspect shine, for I can imagine a Dungeon Master explaining this to me and the other players gathered at the table.
Exploring the world can take a while to do especially when you come across an NPC or cave that you might want to explore which will lead into a side quest. As I was going through the different areas in the world you will come across some NPCs that if you help will open up different dialogue or events later on. I helped a man early in the game which led to me getting a free pie at the inn in town.
The side quests come as an easy distraction as they did in Dragon Age: Inquisition. Going and trying to get to the main quest (which by the way I am still on the third quest) I come across a new companion or one of my other companions say why they are traveling with me and ask for help which unlocks a side quest and I say “let’s go!” completely ignoring and forgetting what I was doing. After I die a few times I realize I have gotten off track and try and finish the main story, yet another NPC talks to me and offers gold or to hunt an Ogre and I am right back to where I was. Having these amazing side quests make the game feel long which makes you feel you’re getting your money’s worth.
Overall the game is amazing for fans of Dungeons and Dragons along with RPG enthusiasts. So if you’re looking for a great game or looking for one that will hold you over until another game comes out pick up Pillars of Eternity.

The Intro:
Stop. Don't let the big red square in the top left of this review fool you into being defensive. I LOVE this game, probably more than any of you reading this review. That being said let's talk about the one, ONE problem with this perfect game.
The Problem:
It's dead, man.
The Good:
For all of you who don't know, Strike Vector is a dogfighting game as fast paced as you see in the trailers. Speaking of which, the trailers do a good job describing the game: The graphics are pretty, the action is tense, there is aesthetical customization. On combat, there are varied weapons,  passive abilites and "use once every so often" abilities like cloaking and a huge speed boost. (8 of each) The other positive reviews explain that in more detail, so I won't waste your time and regurgitate said information.
That being said, the game is HARD to learn. Basically you have to get used to the controls, master switching harrier and jet forms, get used to flying in tight corridors, and ONLY then can you hope to face others in pvp. You'll still get creamed a few times, but if you need advice, just type something in chat and they would tell you.
Sure it was frustrating back then when everybody was better than you, but they would be nice and try to be helpful. THE COMMUNITY WAS HELPFUL, MAN. A PvP (As in dead flipping serious, "you are not rewarded for messing around") game where the fighting is intense had a helpful community. That to me, is amazing.
The Bad:
But nowadays, there isn't a community. I, (and you included) could open up the game, click on the servers tab, and find for the amount of players on each server, ZERO across the board. Sure, some people will comment, "That is rediculous, just the other day I was playing and there were five servers with a moderate amount of people." I have NEVER seen that many people other than when i first got the game: 2 months ago, specifically April 12. (As you may tell, the other review are way before or around this time, so at most the main problems were bugs and there is no mention of a dead playerbase.) Even then the playerbase was shrinking and nowadays its maybe one person on a server for an hour. Just to humour those people, however, lets do the math; A server usually has 16 players max, but "a moderate amount of people" suggests it would be roughly half or 3/4 full. So lets say per server there is an average of 10 people. Times that by 5 and what do you get? A playerbase of 50 people. Ladies and gentlemen, that's not much, at all. It's certainly not fitting for a AAA game that this is. Morrowind has a bigger playerbase, Duke Nukem has a bigger playerbase, even MOTHER FLIPPING Ace of Spades has a bigger playerbase. Also please take into account that the figure is outdated by two months and nowadays its one guy on one server flying around for an hour and leaving.
The Fix:
So this is surprising; Usually you have a crummy, unoriginal, game that doesn't have a player base no matter HOW much advertising they do, but in this case it's the opposite. You have an awesome game that hasn't done much advertising. The only way I found out about this game was because my friend had it, and because it went on sale for like two days. Ideally, they do more advertising, people realize how cool and original this game is, the devs have a large playerbase and víola! You have a successful game.
I'm no expert, but as a person who buys games, (you are one of these too), I really like Steam sales, also anything on the "Featured" page on the store catches my eye. Sure, advertising costs money, but if they do both of these things, they will have an actual playerbase, become deservingly popular, and attract more people. Haven't you ever seen the, "put a dollar in the jar and people will come trick?"People like popular things.
The Tl;Dr:
It's dead right now, so don't pay 12 dollars for a AAA multiplayer game with no other players.
Update:
So I've done some dedicated server checking and the figures are still low. Sometimes they're in the tens, twenties, even fifties of players but this is usually right after a sale and the number drops off quite quickly. The average of the entire server population is still below ten if not absolute zero which it usually is, so I still can't delete this review.
2) Contrary to popular belief, tricking people into buying a game is not the right way to increase server population. People are throwing around really cool ideas in the forums like singleplayer, better customization, co-op challenges and other neat stuff that would not only make this a fuller game but also keep people playing. The devs also make a few comments here and there. You should check it out and give the game and the forums some love.
Also, my review just happens to have magically disapeared from the store page, so I figured it was as good of a time as it could be to update the review.

I'll be deinstalling the game to free up HD space again, but I feel sorry that I'm missing out on what appears to be a great game for others. But it's just too complicated for me. And I *did* finish Planescape. Thrice.

Tl;Dr: This game is very good, its unique take to the RPG genre is very well done, and bold enough to take many innovate changes to the formula whereas by comparison other games have very simple takes and are too afraid to be more than just average and boring. This game is a step in the right direction for open-world RPGs.
----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
The game does suffer from some flaws as do all games, but ultimately the game rises above it's flaws fantastically.
The combat in this game can be approached by using different classes or "vocations" and the use of NPC allies that you can recruit from other players and make yourself known as "pawns". Additionally, the game makes use of a myriad of objects to use in mid combat, from dousing the enemy in oil to light them on fire using arrows, or literally throwing poison jugs at an enemy's face, or my personal favorite, using magic gems.
But to the point of the enemies, this game as a nice variety of what you can fight: goblin variants, human bandits, trolls, chiemeras, spoopy skeletons and ghosts, tentacles, giant floating eyeballs, dragons, hydras, lizardmen, and more. A lot of these enemies have a specific way of dealing with them that can make the fight a lot easier if you do things right, other fights will punish you for being dumb and ignoring a fight's mechanics. In this regard, combat often takes interesting turns in some cases, especially late in the game.
The game's combat also makes use of a sort of fatigue system, w/ damage taken gradually being able to be healed by magic less and less, making you use healing items to restore health that has been fatigued. The game also lets you grapple your enemy and quite literally climb them in any way you choose if they're large enough. Otherwise, the game lets you outright pick them up and throw them wherever you want, the same with items in the area, like throwing cinder blocks or jugs at them. Finally on this point, stocking up on items is absolutely essential midway to late game, as refusing to take a moment to stock up can make things much, much harder than they need to be if not outright resulting in dying due to your negligence. In this regard, the game adds a sort of item management to the game that actually does matter, whereas more notable games like Skyrim forces you to just carry mana/health potions without need for anything else. In this game you can carry a myriad of items with equally as varied uses.
The only downsides to this game are the lack of life from the NPCs in the game, any sandboxing of AI is restricted to the main hub in Gransys, mostly, and they are just there for decorative purposes, they themselves cannot be interacted with whatsoever. Likewise, the NPCs who do offer services are literally in the same place 24/7. All of this basically creates a feeling where your character is one of the only few people who are actually in the game, with mannequins filling the gaps in the world.
Interestingly enough, as a final note, this game's travel system is almost non existent, forcing you to mostly run to where you need to go until you reach a certain point in game until you get Ferrystones (teleports tied to certain locations already in game or that you can place down yourself). HOWEVER, the game was designed w/ this in mind, and as such, the land is traversed without too much difficulty, but the teleporting useing Ferrystones shaves off a lot of time when you get them, since late-game results in running around a lot.

Building your character is very freeform, with your starting class not limiting you to any specific role, so that you can adapt your playstyle as you progress.
All in all, Dark Souls is a masterpiece, and I would urge anyone to at least give it a shot.

This is the game that kicked off the trilogy, and it's definitely got some good stuff in it. It's like someone curated parts of various works of science fiction, such as the crews and space politics, and the action-y elements of Star Wars (including pseudo-science-y powers called biotics allowing for gravity manipulation, etc., and mixed them all up in one video game.
The gameplay itself is a little lacking and hasn't aged well. You drive around on planets that are largely empty of anything to do, and there are a very small number of planets and a space station with a decent amount of tasks to keep you busy. Some of it comes off as pure busy work, while other parts are actually decisions and activities you made and completed, which transfer over to the sequel and you will get e-mails from characters you helped, or even see follow-up stuff in the sequel in response to what you did in the first game. That said, the third game is very divisive and your choices are pretty meaningless in the ending to the trilogy.
The best part about the original Mass Effect, in my opinion, is the establishment of the setting and the lore. It does a great job of introducing these new races and giving you a feeling of he galaxies the game is set in. Truth be told, a person could probably skip this game entirely in terms of getting the best gameplay the trilogy has to offer, because it's the first game's biggest weakness, but if plot and transitioning decisions are important to you, then you definitely want to start here.

I have to say that Tesla Effect turned out to be a lot better than I had imagined. The good things that made the old 90's games so enjoyable were still there: the gloomy, post-apocalyptic sci-fi setting, the tounge-in-cheek-film noir/detective investigative style, the wonderfully sleazy jazz soundtrack, and the cheesy, daytime soap-/b-level class acting. I was even pleasantly surprised that the graphics were as good as they were, with overall really nicely rendered 3D, even if worked a lot better with the environments/bakgrounds than anything that was supposed to resemble people.
Still, Tesla Effect is by no means any masterpiece - for a game that took a lot of the great things from the original franchise and tweaked, improved and polished it, there was a surprising amount of things left in that you figured would have been removed. Just like previous games, there are a lot of rather frustrating and tedious logic puzzles that break the mood of the story by not really feeling like they are connected to anything in the games story, apart from being an excuse to throw in slider puzzles to lengthen the gameplay. But then again, those have always has been present in the Tex Murphy games, so I suppose it's not too surprising, but Tesla Effect definately seems to have A LOT more of them than previous games. (And yes, there even is a kind of a short maze puzzle. Not an old-school-bad maze, but still.) I would definately have liked more of the inventory- and investigative puzzles.
However, the absolute worst thing is probably the extremely annoying bug that seems to be a common problem for a lot of people, where the audio/graphics of the game stutter and lag to point of almost making the game unplayable at times. That did remove quite a lot of the enjoyment from the game, and hopefully it's something that will be patched/fixed in the future.
So, in the end, would I recommend Tesla Effect? Well, yes. If you played any of the earlier games and liked them: absolutely.  Tesla Effect captures the exact same feeling and mood that made both Under a Killing Moon and The Pandora Directive thourougly enjoyable. Story-wise, it's a nice and interesting plot that tries to tie together a lot of loose threads, and partly succeeds, even though it doesn't carry quite the same weight of conspiracy and thrill of it's predecessors. You might enjoy it even if you haven't played the previous ones and just like post-apocalyptic sci-fi/film noir, but I think a lot of the charm does come from its association with the previous games. An enjoyable, if not perfect return from San Francisco's most bumbling gum-shoe.

Ah damn, this is a hard review to do...
Well, I love the serie, you know? I was so pleased to see a new episode coming out. FMV is all my youth after all. I rushed on Harvester when it was re-released, own both the 7th Guest and the 11th Hour and enjoy them almost as much as first time.
And if I must be honnest I would go down on my knees for some Phantasmagoria or Gabriel knight but this is a totally different story.
Ok, so this new Tex.
Those new gen FMV's are gorgeous, I connected my notebook to my 55" TV and were all "WOW" like when I saw Tex HD. The intro is great, sweating Blade runner from all its pixels.
The first minutes were plain joy, a nicely done optional tutorial and then, here I went on my own ready to investigate this new open world. Then...
Well, yeah, then...
THEN, I realized that the game is just no more than FMV's and a nice scenario continuing the main serie story.
Let me explain myself, the game got a single and only bad point: it's realisation is rubbish. It seems like the team spent all the budget on the movie part and the rest of the game, the interractive "real" playable part, was build using HL 1 engine. It's cheap, cubic, empty for the most part with plenty of 3D models repetitions trying to furnish the maps but failed.
The level design, if I can call it that way, is madly wrong and screams: "So boring to do those additional buildings, anyway you would have no interraction on them except maybe an optional object to find so why try harder".
No joke, I saw some better textures on Minecraft...
Click on one of those "useless buildings" and enjoy Tex repeating again and again the same comment.
Countless amounts of objects here and there triggering some "flashback" style videos getting the player back to the old episodes of the serie but with no links with the actual story would then finish the work and make you understand that the Dev's are just imploring you hands joined to buy the older episodes.
Another epic fail was the translation. For those who master english, no problem at all. Characters are all on ol'time noir movies slang and they sounds great.
Heh, me bad. english isn't my mother's tongue so I turned on the subtitles.
I'm not stupid. I pretty well know that slang or expressions are sometimes really hard to translate as they sometimes got no compare on another language but dude!
Who the hell did you guys picked to do the job? We have litteral translation here, word for word. Not any comprehension of the original meaning and worst, on some dialogues with multi answers choice it becomes plain luck to choose witch one you must or want choose from...
So after all that was said, you would certainly ask yourself: "So, good or not?"
For myself, as a real lover of Tex' debuts, it will definitly be a YES. I played some serious ♥♥♥♥♥ way more awfull than that and enjoyed them.
For new incomers, those who never played Under a Killing Moon and even don't know what is it, don't loose your time here.
If you're just curious about the franchise, get yourself one of the firsts.

A fantastic hybrid of Assasins Creed's traversal and The Batman Arkham series combat set in the lore rich world of LOTR. This game really impresses. While not perfect, much of the action is fluid and interesting.
The story feels very much in line with the novels and films, and could be a hidden missing chapter, though perhaps focused more on a tropey heroic arch as opposed to Tolkiens more 'humble overcomes power' narrative. But it works really well for the game.
The nemesis system is brilliant pitting you against Uruks who have grown stronger by defeating you in battle. Hunting them down and trying to break the  their power structure of the Uruk army is a fun enough system you could just focus on that and be entertained for many hours.
The only major concern I have with the game as a whole is a slightly disjoined feel to the pacing of the story and other elements. Though lore filled, many of the mission structure elements feel sort of bolted on. it doesnt feel like it builds so much as things happen randomly. Sometimes its a quicktime event or a following mission or a big battle with many enemies, but it isnt structured like it had a purpose, and there isnt any tension or sense of you getting closer to an end or climax it just sort of comes to a close.
All in all it is a very solid game and very much enjoyable. If only it had felt more epic overall as all of its parts are perfect to make this happen.

I so badly want to give this a 👍 but I just can't.
Did it keep me playing all the way through? Yes.... Was I having fun the whole time? Hmmm... no.
So much of it is surrealism for the sake of surrealism and I spent the whole game waiting for a pivotal revelation that just never came. It's a couple of hours of glimmering fetch quests strung up on a faux Tree of Life.
I had a brief glimmer of hope when I faced the Goonies piano puzzle, but then that was it.. everything else was errand boy  blasé.
I respect what the developer is trying to do here, I truly do, but he is on his way to composing his opus and rather than wait until it is perfectly constructed, he has unleashed it in a formative state that leaves the listener disappointed.
♩ Interesting Music
♩ Cool Premise
♩ Intriguing Character Developement
♭ Poorly Constructed Narrative
♭ Sloppy Surrealism Instead Of A Meaningful Story Arc
♭ Almost All Fetch Quests
♭ Wastes An Opportunity To Help The Player Grow Their Musical Vocabulary
All of that said, I WILL be looking forward to the developers NEXT game because I think I can see where he is trying to go and I'd love to be there when he masters the execution.

I bought Miscreated from -50% sale, thought to myself
I wasn't expecting much since I've been crawling through all sorts of survival games in the past and they all seem to revolve around the same idea:
- Major catastrophic scenario / Post Apocalypse
- Hunger, thirst, weapons
- More PvP than PvE
- Zombies / Mutants
And Miscreated fits right in there. You are a survivor, scavenging for gear, food and crafting materials - trying to make the best out of a bad situation. You're surrounded by mutants and other players, also known as "the bandits". I know, I know. There are good guys there too. (until you give them a weapon and accidentally turn your back on them)

Hells, we've all seen this scenario by now. What makes this game different from that one certain zombie mod over a war simulation game or it's standalone offspring, is that Miscreated is actually built just for this. It's not a "somewhat working" adaptation of some other game and it feels damn good to play a zombie survival game that actually has a fluent inventory system, very nice graphics and great performance all around.
The world seems detailed, the ambient sounds, light and shadow effects etc. but as I'm writing this (December 2016) it's still missing the wildlife, weather system and the "feel of danger". The world feels huge and the current player cap of 36 players feels very low on such a big place. It almost feels like you need a drop of luck to even see another player, though I guess that makes to post apoc feel more like, well post apoc.
Your only actual threat at the moment are the other players - there's only a few squishy mutants walking around and you see them quite rarely. I did see some bigger tankish variations too but only once. I'm optimistic these things will get more attention in later development.
There's enough of different types of gear, clothing, vehicles and gunporn in game already which makes Miscreated in it's current state very much playable and enjoyable. Oh, and from what I've gathered you make a character into a server and it stays on
server.
There is no server hopping, moving into a good position, then switching on to another server to grind the same loot over and over again.
--
Of course the game is nowhere near complete being in early access, but I do see a lot of potential in it already. From what I've seen and tested, many of the mechanics in game at the moment do work nicely and the vehicles & base building is a nice addition too. I'm eagerly waiting for more content to the game.
If you're a survival game fanatic like me and like to see the sights before the riffraff settles in, I think now is the perfect opportunity to give this game a spin - and for a wallet friendly -50% price!

Let's talk about these in more detail.
So you never played a shoot 'em up before, or you are not good at all in those games, but there's something fun about dodging bullets and firing away your laser spreads at hundreds of incoming enemies. Well, here's your game. Two game aspects will make the ride nice for the casual shooters or players that hate ultra high difficulty. The first one is the shield system. In Saviors, you effectively have two health bars: your shield and your ship's armor. You don't immediately die after being hit once, instead, your shield takes the damage, and different enemy bullets do different damage. Once your shield is depleted entirely, any damage goes directly to your ship. But, unlike your ship's armor, if you can stay out of harm's way for long enough, your shield will recover. It can even fully recover. This means one bullet doesn't mean the end and it can actually ease the new players into the bullet hell basics of dodging, making them better at the genre. The second aspect of the game that welcomes the new players is, of course, the many different difficulties.
On the topic of offense, Saviors has it's own merits as well. Your ship will use three weapons at once at all times: main weapon, secondary weapon and missiles. Your shooting button will fire two weapons at the same time: the main shot and the secondary shot. Another button is assigned for missile launch. You can also choose between two attack modes at any time. The standard attack mode will fire both main and secondary weapons forward. The alternative mode enables your ship to fire the secondary weapon sideways while still firing the main gun forward. There's a vast number of weapons you can choose from in the game. In story mode, you unlock new weapons as you progress. There's an arcade mode where you can choose among many different preset types. Each different weapon will have it's own strengths and weaknesses. Some weapons will cover a lot of space with a large spread. Others will have narrow spread but high damage. Others will fire in bursts of high damage. Others will have weaker, continuous fire that deals better damage over time. Others yet work like shotguns.
The story mode is unusually lengthy. The shoot 'em up genre will generally offer you about 5 stages and that's it. Saviors offers 18 stages. Slightly smaller stages combine with the death system to make progression smooth. Every time you die you have to start the stage over, but since they are not immense stages, it will give you better sense of progression and success than infinite continues.
The music has a rather strange choice of synths mixed with rocking guitar on fast electronic beats. It feels weird at times and exciting at others. And there are other times too when it's weird and exciting at the same time when the strange synths work at some great tunes. Exciting blood pumping OST is what every shooter should have and Saviors delivers in a unique way that will have you consider buying the OST.
The poor aspects of the game are outweighed by the good ones by a far margin. Nevertheless Poor character designs, personalities and dialogs will make you skip the story every time. The art is kinda ugly all around as well (menus, backgrounds, "hud" etc). It doesn't wreak the fun, but it certainly doesn't help.
Finally, the price is perfectly fair even at full. The game could actually be more expensive.
Highly recommended.

This game is like a budget version of Yakuza with a choose-your-own-adventure style twist.
For the first time in a long while, I actually got really immersed in a steam game *and* enjoyed it. Maybe because this was originally a console game, but I digress.
A couple gripes to get out of the way beforehand: The camera sucks, and sometimes the game will crash on startup or talking to the clothing store owner.
Way of the Samurai 4 is fantastic. Combat isn't too special, but offers enough variety to float the rest of the game along, which is where this WotS4 really shines. The character customization in this game opens up a ton of hilarious possibilities, and having your goofy idiot character show up in cutscenes acting serious is part of what I genuinely enjoyed. I went through the true ending as a cowboy resembling Woody from Toy Story, and it was a great time.
There are 10 different endings, the 8 that have you align with a certain faction are rather flat, for lack of a better word, but attune you to the fact that things could be much better, this kind of grooms you to obtain the true ending. Additionally, going through each path reveals different plot points that occur while you're doing other things in subsequent playthroughs.

I have been a big fan of WOTS since it came out on playstation2.   for this review i am not critiqueing the concept as a whole but rather the changes between the previoius titles, and WOTS4.
i do not recommend this game for the following reasons:
- the camera is still terrible.  in this day of great video games, we expect that the camera can detect when we are completely unable to see what is happening in the game.  this game fails in that respect and you will often find yourself unable to see anything other than a wall, and have to stop moving and fighting to rotate your camera to a new angle.  unacceptable.  This mechanic has been broken since inception and should not take up to WOTS5 to be fixed.
-moveset saved to character.   Your moveset is no longer tied to which weapon you use in any way.  This has to be the big one for me.  why i gave it a negative review.  In the past, WOTS was a sword collecting game for me.   I would play the game through every possible ending in order to obtain every sword.   Now that movesets tied to your character via skill books, and are obtainable from any random drop, this best feature is removed.  You no longer need to find the ending in which you can kill that elusive gang leader in order to get his awesome sword so that you can finally bust out that jumping spin, because all you gain is......   a fancy hilt for a possibly below average crafted weapon?  booooooo.  terrible change.
-crafting system.  Again, this crafting system furthers the removal of sword collecting.   You obtain moves via skill books dropped by random enemies.  You now disassemble different weapons and then reassemble their mixed parts to make your swords.   These homemade swords are able to have great bonuses if you simply enter and exit the shop menu.  Go ahead and fight almost nobody, and craft yourself an OP weapon.   Difficult to obtain boss weapons not only dont grant you new moves, but the chances that they will hold any useful bonuses is minimal to zero.   broken system.
Until the game becomes better patched, I will not have anything to say about it, which is sad considering it's a major favorite title of mine, and a reason I purchased a PS3.

Alongside Sonic 3, this would be the go-to example of what makes a Sonic game- Sonic CD, for a game made roughly 20 years ago, feels like it was made yesterday, with it's beautiful visuals, amazing sountracks, and smooth gameplay, any platformer fan would be insane to ever skip this one over.If there ever were a truer example of why Sonic isn't all about speed, I can't find one. Sonic CD gives you speed as a tool to meet your ends, but it heavily discourages it in favour of precision, thought, and exploration, while it still feels faster than your average platformer.
One of the most fun elements of Sonic CD is it's integration of time travel into the core gameplay, whether it's simply seeing what each beautifully designed level looks like in each of the four different timelines, or to find all the different objectives this non-standard Sonic platformer has to offer.
If you want to get the most enjoyment out of this game, take some time to explore each timeline in each area. Take a look at the bleak, dark bad futures, then go back into the past and destroy Eggman's machines so that you can create a good future, all while admiring the thematic changes in music and art that come with each timeline.
Sure, the game's design can be headache-inducing at times, but it's a short adventure that will leave you with some fond memories, and it'll certainly make you want to listen to those soundtracks over and over again. Plus, the animated cutscenes and multiple endings are a nice bonus.
Honestly, if any Sonic game needs a spiritual sequel, it's this one! Time travel is a simple yet very interesting and game-changing concept. And unlike the recent Sonic Boom titles, exploration and nonlinearity in this game feels RIGHT. it's a damn shame this game was on a system that was all but a failure, but thanks to the power of remastering, we are here able to play it in glorious HD. Do yourself a favour and pick this game up, I have a feeling you'll like it.

Plus, since players can be converted to another faction mid-game, sometimes your strategy will completely pivot (and sometimes you can be pulled off the losing side on to the winning one.)
The game does have a few bugs to be worked out, and my game does crash from time to time, but for a $10 game still in beta it's worth every penny.

I wrote an extended letter to the devs, I highly reccommend reading it if you're at all interested in this kind of game.
Letter to the Devs -

Mafia is fun because there is no opportunity to metagame. You have to read reactions, faces, body language, and speach in addition to actions. All of these subtleties are lost on a digital version. Town of Salem falls to the same problems that Throne of Lies has.
Games like Trouble in Terrorist town (Garrys Mod), while flawed are superior to Throne of Lies because it changes the fundemental way the game is played.
In Mafia, all the players sit in a room and play according to the honor rule of not reading your card aloud.
In Town of Salem and Throne of Lies, players sit in different rooms, and play by the same rules, with the honor rule unenforced.
With TTT, players are not trying to emulate the same game. You're forced to play differently, even if the goal and idea is the same. It's not just MAFIA BUT ONLINE, it's "Like mafia, but with shooting and crime solving"
It's not good and I don't reccommend it to anybody, even if it has good ideas.

Nowhere near as fun as others make it sound like. Let's start with the movement, it's bad. It's hard to describe, but it feels like you're getting tossed around instead of running or walking.
The game itself isn't so bad, but it's pretty much nothing like the description. You don't get to make Your own base in a way you'd expect, you have around 5 or something options of already set locations to create bases, you can create outposts, sure, but they're really glitchy and won't even get created most of, if not all the time. I've tried creating 3, lost a ♥♥♥♥ton of materials but nothing happened. Though, base customization sucks. You just sellect what you'd like to have in already decided spots around the base (You can have beds in the kitchen. No I won't make a sexist joke here), and upgrade them by pressing "Upgrade" then having to wait ♥♥♥♥ing 10 - 30 minutes for it to become upgraded.
The way you discover other people is also stupid. Basicly what you do is, you find others that have set up their own base somewhere, and say "Oh hey would you rather our base instead? It's way cooler." and hope they join. There are no survivors out there that really feels like they NEED help at all, which honestly ruins a lot of the point for me.
The zombie spawns are way to much. Zombies are fun to kill, deffinetly, but it's just too much considering the game takes Place in small villages. It feels like I've already killed 10 times the actual population to this city, and if you're gonna claim that the zombies "wandered into the town", then why did they do that? What the ♥♥♥♥ is so special about these mostly isolated towns that made so many zombies want to go there? If there actually IS a reason for that, the game doesn't explain it at all.
Oh and another thing is the way the special zombies appear into the game. The game is based around missions, (the developers can deny that all they want), and the special zombies just appear in ONE missions because it just so happens to fit in, and then suddenly they're a normal sight everywhere. That just doesn't make sense, at least provide some kind of explanation to why.
Though the worst of all is the "Nothing respawn" feature. What they mean with "nothing", is ABSOLUTELY nothing. This may sound like a good idea, but considering this is supposed to be a survival game, it means you'll run out of food, weapons and medicine, so you can't actually survive. This is gamebreaking for me, all the other things I could deal with, this I can't.
The game isn't really worth replaying, because you know you won't be able to ACTUALLY survive and will have to restart AGAIN, and besides, there's nothing more annoying than having to start all the way from the bottom when you had already made a decent base and had some nice equipment.
The game does have a lot of cool features though, I love how when you're talking to someone over the phone and enter combat, your character will say "Hang on a second" and then say "Ok continue" once you get out of it instead of just talking while fighting. And of course there's the "Your character is tired/beat up, choose another one and let this one rest" function. That's really cool. It does mean you won't really get attatched to anyone at all, but it's a lot better than "Eat Food to restore health, stop bleedings, remove pains and cure broken limbs" function most games have.
Though despite that, I wouldn't recomend the game at all, at least not for the price it's asking, but seeing the effort that was clearly put into the game I can't really say that it should cost less.
Tl;dr? BAD GAME. NO BUY. BAD.

Several hours into this game and Tex has infiltrated a creepy cult, and been told of an invention that would remove the veil between the living and the dead.  Also, a guy jumped to his death in front of Tex's eyes, right before Tex was propositioned by two entirely separate ladies.
In other words, this game put a smile on my face.  If you love stories and characters at all--and don't mind a presentation that at times can feel a little "stripped down" (but charmingly so)--then I can guarantee you'll enjoy this game.  The light humor and noir atmosphere certainly don't hurt either.
If you're wondering if you have to already be familiar with the Tex Murphy games to enjoy this, the answer is no.  Take it from me, as I've never played any of them before this one.  In fact, I only have a vague knowledge of what they even were based on hearing them being mentioned so many times on adventure game forums.  (I also once downloaded and listened to the humorous "Tex Murphy Radio theater" based on these characters.)
I was aware of the Kickstarter campaign that got this game made, however.  And I find it miraculous that for such a low budget, they were able to produce this polished an experience.  (The team must be friends with a lot of people in the industry.)  No, it does not look like a "real" movie.  It's not quite that cinematic.  But coming from someone whose previous experiences with FMV (Full Motion Video) games included Gabriel Knight 2 and Phantasmagoria, this has to be just about the most polished FMV game ever made.  This may be damning with faint praise, but you can easily find clips and stills of the game in action on the net and decide for yourself if the "FMV" look is something you can enjoy.
Special mention has to be made about the music though.  I said before that the look of the game wasn't quite on par with a "real" movie.  Well, the same can't be said for the music.  It's fantastic, and would easily fit in with any high-budget mainstream film.
I do also want to make special note of the acting.  I see some people have called it "cheesy" or bad.  I could not disagree more.  Most everyone in the cast is very good, and any "cheesiness" seems to be ithrough intentional over the top hamming it up--all in good fun.  I think if at times it comes off as a bit amateur it is through no fault of the actors themselves.  Basically, this was shot in a very "matter of fact" way with HD cameras that don't entirely convey a purely cinematic look.  Add to that, for the "interrogation scenes" the actors have been instructed to stand dead center in front of the camera and looking directly into the lens the entire time.  It's really hard to come across as natural under such circumstances.  The fact that they largely manage to do so is a credit to them.
Anyway, if you're a fan of the adventure genre--specifically because you're a fan of story and character--then you should give this a whirl.
***
I do have a few criticisms, though.  In no way do they make the game unworthy of purchase, but just know that they're there:  I wish that the streets you navigate through had been populated by some NPCs so as to create a more alive feel to the world.
It should also be noted that the latter stages of the game are not as much fun as the first half.  Other reviews have mentioned the unfortunate presence of "pixel hunting" in this game.  While that's true, let me just clarify what that term means in Tesla Effect.  In the old days of adventure gaming, pixel hunting meant that one had to move their mouse all over the screen and click on just the right spot for the game to recognize they'd clicked on the correct object.  That's not quite what it means in the case of Tesla.
There aren't truly any areas of the screen to confuse the player as to its "clickability."  Nor are there any objects so small that one can't precisely place their mouse over it.  (After all, when Tex turns his flashlight on, any such objects that tex needs to interact with immediately sparkle.)  What IS an issue however is that the latter half of the game is largely taken up with First-Person Doom like navigating around some real-time environments while Tex/you must find different objects, push buttons, etc.  I know most people wouldn't find such gameplay an issue.  In fact, first person, Blair Witch-like experiences are (unfortuantely) what most gamers have come to think of when you say "video game" to them.  For a lot of people, videogames are nothing BUT that.
However, that's not the kind of experience I treasure in a game.  I enjoy games (particularly Adventure games) for the characters and story--elements that Tesla Effect has in spades at the beginning, but which gradually dissipate as the game goes on.  Unfortunately, as the player wanders around these vast, sterile 3D environments (the multi-floored "Tesla Society" building being the worst, in that it never ends), much of that sense of character and story is lost.  Yes, sometimes you'll hear Tex's voiceover comment on something when you encounter a locked door or whatever, but it's not enough to remove the sense that, yup, you're currently playing a game similar to 99% of games that people play these days.
The cut-scenes and sense of story do return at the end, thankfully.  However, it's not until after the player has slogged their way through a lot of tedium.

I have been a fan of Tex Murphy since Under a Killing Moon – nearly twenty years! That said, I will not do this game or the community a disservice by writing anything less than a fully honest review. The game succeeds far more often than it fails, but is far from perfect, so I will not score it 10 out of nostalgia, or 0 out of disappointment.
First, let me give this game a score out of ten. In my opinion, it falls somewhere around 7.5. I think this game will please Tex fans and newcomers alike, even if it isn't perfect. If you like a good story or adventure games, then check this one out. If you like it, I highly recommend trying out Tex's past adventures.
Let me start by talking about what the game gets right. First and foremost is the story/cutscenes. Tex Murphy is definitely back and they hit the nail on the head, bringing the right balance of humour and drama to the story and protagonist. The story is a satisfying conclusion to the cliffhanger of Overseer and with multiple story paths and endings provides some good replayability. I have completed the game  twice and got two endings. One was near perfect, the other was mediocre, but easily avoided in the future. The characters in the game are mostly quite good, with some familiar faces returning to Chandler Ave, and a few new ones. I particularly like Mojo, the owner of one of the new establishments on the street.
The multiple paths and endings brings with it something new to Tex Murphy. Unlike The Pandora Directive, the path you choose will affect your ability to access several locations and will uncover different story elements. While these are all relatively small, most come with puzzles you won't get playing the game along another path. My only wish is that this was more pronounced than it was. The  gameplay is about 90% the same regardless of the path you're on.
The gameplay is what you'd expect from an adventure game: inventory and “logic” puzzles. While easier on this front than it's predecessors (more on this later), it was still fun. The atmosphere in several of the locations is excellent, particularly the last big location in the game, which manages to capture some of the atmospheric elements that made The Pandora Directive so good. The main musical theme of the game is also excellent.
While all of these elements are good, they all fall a bit short of what they could have been, and keeps Tesla Effect from beating out Pandora or UAKM for best Tex Murphy game.
While the story is quite good, it can feel a bit rushed or disjointed at times, like just a bit too much wound up on the cutting room floor. Sometimes you're thrown from one scene to the next with a bit of exposition in between – rather than returning control to you. You also can't visit locations whenever you want, even when there's no reason to disallow it – e.g. Why can't you return to the resort whenever you want, even if there is nothing to do there? This all gives the game a very linear feeling.
While I noted that characters are mostly good, one in particular stands out as not: Smart Alex. Your new PDA sidekick (voiced by Kevin Murphy) feels out of place in a Tex adventure and is rarely very funny. Instead of hearing Tex's inner monologue, we're too frequently left hearing Smart Alex – this is of particular note during the death sequences. I miss Tex lambasting himself for violating PI rules, or calmly explaining that he was mauled to death by a pack of hungry coyotes (try breaking the alien abductor in Pandora for that one). All in all, I don't think this hurts the game too much, but it is part of what holds it back from being the Tex masterpiece I had been hoping for.
While multiple paths are interesting, they seem to revolve exclusively around which woman Tex would like to romance, which is unfortunate. During the Kickstarter, it was promised that the three paths would be to find out what happened to Chelsee, uncover the truth about yourself, or find the people who were responsible for shooting you at the end of Overseer. I don't feel this was really delivered on. While the Chelsee path is there, the other two don't seem to be. It would have been more satisfying if the woman Tex ended up with was caused by which path you're on, not the other way around. Though Pandora's pathing was a bit too rigid (try getting the good or bad endings without a walkthrough – few people can), it was stronger as it relied on your actions as a whole (are you good to everyone, bad to everyone, etc.).
As I said earlier, the gameplay is a bit too easy. There are fewer logic puzzles in the game than in the past and not enough head-scratchers. Only for one or two puzzles did I feel the need to take out a pen and paper. Objects are also frequently too close to where they will be used. I assume this was to save players from wandering around, but to me that was part of what makes an adventure game an adventure game. I want to feel stumped, if even for a just a few minutes. With the full walkthrough system right in the game, this would have been possible without frustrating players who just want to move on. It would have also been nice if the “Gamer” difficulty (which doesn't let you access hints or bypass puzzles) had some differences that made it more challenging than the Casual difficulty setting.
The graphics are good, but certainly nothing to write home about. I don't really care, either. To me, graphics always take a back seat to everything else (unless they impact the gameplay somehow). That said, a few environments are a bit too empty, giving them an incomplete feel. The sewers are particularly uninteresting and made moreso by the fact that they are just a maze. Even in the more complete feeling areas (which is the majority, don't get me wrong), there are so few things for Tex to look at. One of the greatest things about the previous games were Tex's humourous comments about mundane things, but almost every location has too many things that can't be interacted with – things ranging from vending machines to hot tubs to miscellaneous stuff on a shelf can't be looked at, but all of these things would have been in any of Tex's previous adventures.
In summary – 7.5/10 :
Pros:
Good story, with plenty of Tex humour
Good cast of characters (mostly) with some excellent newcomers
Multiple story paths and endings provide replayability
Some good adventuring gameplay
Atmospheric locations come close to matching Pandora's and UAKM's
Cons:
Some story feels rushed or incomplete in a few places (not enough to seriously affect enjoyment, though)
Story pathing relies too much on which woman Tex wants to be with
Gameplay is a bit too easy at times given that stumped players would have a hint system at their disposal
Some sparse environments
Too few items can be commented on by Tex
Smart Alex

*Tom Clancy's Splinter Cell Blacklist - 6/10*
Dissapointing and average singleplayer, but a solid co-op and a very well made multiplayer.
Singleplayer - 5/10
The singleplayer falls flat. What is suppose to be the best part about Splinter Cell is the worst. This game feels more like an action movie than an actual tension filled stealth game. There's even obvious moments in the campaign where they are forcing the action onto you. You feel like a one man army with all your mines and grenades. And with all the enemies, tight spaces, and bad level design, it feels like the game wants you to go all out rambo. These are the problems that make the game a straight forward action shooter. That's the complete opposite of what Splinter Cell is suppose to be. Where's the REAL tension that the older Tom Clancy games provided?
And the plot, oh god, It's terrible... Cliched, unoriginal and generic. "Oh my god! Terrorists are attacking USA, WE MUST STOP THEM!!!" Simple and stupid. The characters all feel dull and generic, even Sam Fisher himself. Also, where's the dark humor that the other Splinter Cell games had?
Co-op - 6/10
Now this would be a wonderful co-op if it weren't for the several bugs it has. It's still very fun. There is a decent variety of missions and all of them are exciting and fun to play with a friend. Unfortunately, everytime I play the co-op I encounter several bugs. I always encounter another new bug sooner or later. Other than the annoying bugs, the co-op is solid.
Multiplayer - 7/10
The best part of the whole game. Spies vs. Mercs is extremely fun, unique and surprisingly deep. I love it. You play as either the spies who have to hack 3 locations or mercs who are heavy gunners that have to stop the spies from doing so. Both teams have different abilities and gadgets. Whenever a spy activates the hack, the match fills with tension. The spy that activated the hack has to hide from the mercs. If the spy dies, the hack turns off. It's awesome when you see a merc go right by you unaware where you are. As a merc, you have to find this spy before the hack reaches 100%. You also have to watch your back as a spy can sneak up behind you and kill you. There's also a good amount of strategy involved and it makes for a very fun competitive game.
There are only 5 gamemodes, but SvM Blacklist is really the best one. The others are okay, but nobody really plays them unfortunately. Sometimes, the game doesn't balance out the teams very well. I've experienced matches with high levels vs very low levels. The turning radius in this game is also pretty wide for some reason. Other than those problems, the multiplayer is great.

Cool gameplay. Cool music. Cool skin-tight latex body suits that demonstrate the effectiveness of P90X.  However, the lack of Michael Ironside's voice and performance prevents Blacklist from reaching maxmium coolness. A weathered man, a father, a war vet, I imagine Sam Fisher is pushing 55, yet in this rendtion of the Splinter Cell series, he is voiced by a pubescent child who is prone to lashing out at his inner party. It's as if they're making some lackadaisical attempt to turn Sam Fisher into a young and hip action icon that is possessed by teen angst, opposed to the sardonically dark humour that we've grown accustomed to over the years. I don't mind if they're trying to reinvent the protagonist of Splinter Cell in order to appeal to a younger generation, but if that's the case, put Sam Fisher to rest and don't sully his image more than you already have. Introduce a new Splinter Cell--this reverse aging thing is just too weird for me.
Also, Fisher, arguably one of the most skillful agents of espionage of all time, lacks the ability to take cover in a standing position, which I found odd.

Perhaps the most underrated entry of all the 16-bit era Sonic games, this 90s Acid masterpiece should be in every platforming aficionado's Steam library. Time travel, challenging mode-7 like bonus stages and branching mazelike levels that are altered by where in time you are serve as a testament on how well Sega used the CD medium to maximize the formula's potential, making sure to punish those that think Sonic is only about going from left to right fast. Far from being just a rushed port, the Steam release upscales the game with widescreens in mind, features both the Japanese/European and the US version of the two excellent soundtracks and tops things off with bonus modes and achievements.

*Sonic CD.
A game that in my opinion is one of the best Sonic games ever. In CD time travel is incorporated to add to the replayability. Now I have bought this game for my console, phone, tablet and now pc. The pc version is, in my opinion the best. It's a great, solid game that has a suprising amount of depth packed into it.
Also worth mentioning was some additions to the cast including Metal sonic and Amy. I found the game to be both challenging and fast (pun intended), but it also didn't lose any luster along the way. In the end though it's good to just sit down and play a classic Sega game that reminds you of Sonic's better days.
-Good story
-Classic gameplay
-Gives a nostalgic feel
-Sonic doesn't have a bandana
*7.8/10

This is the game that kicked off the trilogy, and it's definitely got some good stuff in it. It's like someone curated parts of various works of science fiction, such as the crews and space politics, and the action-y elements of Star Wars (including pseudo-science-y powers called biotics allowing for gravity manipulation, etc., and mixed them all up in one video game.
The gameplay itself is a little lacking and hasn't aged well. You drive around on planets that are largely empty of anything to do, and there are a very small number of planets and a space station with a decent amount of tasks to keep you busy. Some of it comes off as pure busy work, while other parts are actually decisions and activities you made and completed, which transfer over to the sequel and you will get e-mails from characters you helped, or even see follow-up stuff in the sequel in response to what you did in the first game. That said, the third game is very divisive and your choices are pretty meaningless in the ending to the trilogy.
The best part about the original Mass Effect, in my opinion, is the establishment of the setting and the lore. It does a great job of introducing these new races and giving you a feeling of he galaxies the game is set in. Truth be told, a person could probably skip this game entirely in terms of getting the best gameplay the trilogy has to offer, because it's the first game's biggest weakness, but if plot and transitioning decisions are important to you, then you definitely want to start here.

The sequel to a free game called Off-Peak, The Norwood Suite improves the formula in almost everyway in a much longer addition to this story.
The Norwood Suite's lush microcosm of an eccentric music scene had me completely entranced, loved it / played through twice.

Cosmo D's style is something to experience. The Norwood Suite is the most "game" of the three games that have been released but the main focus here is really the feeling and atmosphere. If you haven't already, check out Saturn V and Off-Peak, they're both great introductions to what to expect and offer similarly immersive audio-visual goodness.
Basically, this game is all about headspaces, if you had to distill it to mechanics it's a short adventure game story where you assist the hotel guests and staff by finding various items scattered about, gaining access to rooms, learning more about the Modulo company, hotel staff and the quirky residents hanging out around the place as you listen in on their conversations. More importantly, The Norwood Suite, and all of Cosmo D's games offer some fantastic, top notch music. Instrumentals fade in and out dynamically as you make your way through the hotel, setting background ambiance for certain characters or locations, every section of the estate is a new piece of the soundtrack, so as you access more places and grab items to complete fetch quests and puzzles, you're being treated both through your eyes and ears.
The visuals obviously are a little wonky, character models look borderline silly, sometimes almost distorted or warped with how their arms or legs bend in some poses, but they're visually diverse and satisfyingly weird; business people with green lipstick and bright dyed hair, a musician with a neon pink eyepatch and an eyeball necklace, and the various portraits of Norwood himself whose outfit is so outrageous that part of your main objective to progress in the game is to recreate an 8-piece costume as a disguise. Some models are noticeably shoved through each other and have collision issues and I did have some brief bouts of framerate dips as I played, but the game succeeds for me because the way everything is put together really is captivating to explore. Sifting through any screenshots of the game you can see it's visually striking and that's one of its biggest strengths alongside the music.
It's not going to blow away anyone on merit of gripping gameplay, and I'd even say you move a little on the slow side navigating the hotel, but for the price and given the last two games Cosmo D has graced us with free of charge, I had no problem at all dropping full price for the game and soundtrack. If you're on the fence, I would download Saturn V and Off-Peak from Cosmo D's website, see if you like them, and if you do I definitely recommend picking up The Norwood Suite. I've got a little ways further to go on my playthrough but I needed to take a short break and give this one a big thumbs up! Keep it up, Cosmo D!

My favorite part of Twin Peaks wasn't the quirky dialogue, the disorienting mix of humor and horror, or the random animals (although the random animals were awesome). It was the places. The hidden places, the secret places, the places you could only get to in dreams, or through magic.
The Norwood Suite is one of those places. It's actually a LOT of those places.
It's like Gone Home and Amnesia: TDD and The Beginner's Guide in that you're in a strange place, you have to investigate it, you have a role that isn't immediately clear, and the focus is on storytelling over violence/destruction/construction. It's open-ended, but not in a way that feels loose or arbitrary -- there is a story, and there are many parts of that story to be discovered.
Every review talks about the music, and, yes, the music is amazing (and important to the game play), but the atmospherics of the game -- the backgrounds, the hotel rooms, the cliffs and outside areas, and (yes) the secret passages -- are what make me keep digging deeper. It's a beautiful, lush game, but the beauty is always one step away from you, hidden in some corridor you just haven't touched yet, and you keep looking for ways to find it, to get there. Maybe it's that masquerade party at the end that they won't let you into without a costume. Maybe it's one of those things you need to find, like the missing keys to the grand piano or a way of talking to characters (they all speak in musical notes, and it sounds like individual pieces of a bigger song that we can't hear all at once...unless, maybe, there's so me way to?).
Anyway. It's a weird, deep, beautiful game, and I love playing it. I hope you do, too.

Terraria in space? No.
Terraria is a great game, but it is extremely linear. You beat it once, and there's not much reason to play it again. Starbound on the otherhand has a vast, nearly infinite world for you to explore, mine, farm and frolick. Procedurally generated quests, craftable items, armors and weapons will keep you busy as your rifle through countless biomes on an array of different planets orbiting all sorts of stars.
I started playing this game back when it was new to Steam, and everyone was afraid it was going the way of the early access cash grab games; there weren't many features, but lots of promises and poor communication. Luckily the developers turned that around to become super and create a fantastic game. I've created and played through to the final tier of equipment over a dozen times, with and without mods.
Oh yeah. Mods. Holy crap Chucklefish set up something fantastic for modders. The modding community is helpful and active, constantly updating their mods the most recent stable version, and there are TONS of really neat mods. Frackin' Universe is one of my personal favorites, as it nearly(or at least) doubles the amount of stuff you can do, mine, find and forge.

The concept of this game is spectacular; A giant open state infested with zombies, and building to scavenge, all while maintaining the safety and wellbeing of your group of survivors. It really sounds like a seaso of the Walking Dead. But I did have to constantly remind myself "it's just a game from the Xbox LIVE Arcade".
While the game did have a lot of diversity in its characters (not just in appearance, but how they perform due to their background) It still hasn't really roped me in to actually caring about them. By the end of the standard game (before Breakdown) each and every survivor was "expendable" to me to the point where I'd sacrifice them in situation that may only cost a little bit of food. Maybe it is due to the sudden wave of survival games that have deep narratives and player choices, like the Last of Us or the season of the Walking Dead, but this game didn't hit any major marks in character development. So that combined with a bit of a choppy engine, and monotone gameplay would bump this to about a flat C if you want a rating.
But if you just want to waste zeds and splatter them with dozens of Honda Civics, then I can definitely get behind this game.

doesn't mince words or waste time. It throws you right into the heart of a laser-heavy space battle and lets somebody else do the explaining. In honor of that, I will try to be brief.
is a "gamer's game." It is fully aware that it is a game, and seems to be fine if you are, too. Immersion is only one path to greatness as a video game product, and this game shows that you don't need to re-invent the wheel if you've got a really good wheel.
The gameplay is incredibly smooth. Three buttons and arrows, and go get 'em, tiger. I had never heard the slang term "bullet hell" for the scrolling shooter genre, but it took about twenty-five seconds to make perfect sense.
nails a very difficult design concept: the controls should fit like a glove, but that doesn't mean that every task should be intuitive. A few formations will make you think twice or leave you guessing, but unlike so many games that use unpredictability and no-win situations to cheaply raise difficulty, you can always hunker down in
and juice a little more playtime out of sheer instinct.
My big complaint - and the reason that I don't recommend it for everybody, everywhere, is that its presentation is that of several very good parts that don't make a cohesive whole. I have to admit that I do favor the ability to immerse myself in a game world, and each of the elements here don't quite go together. The sprites and particles have different reflective properties, and neither quite look like they are a part of the world painted by the backgrounds. The soundtrack is vivid and pulse-pounding, but it sounds like it was for a completely different game and overpowers the sound effects by default. For this style of game, I get that many gamers mute the game audio and throw on their own esoteric techno or speed-metal soundtracks, but as a casual gamer, I like to see the little touches that give me more than a series of well-designed levels: they give me a world to play through.
gets truly difficult, but it definitely starts off at an inviting level, so people new to the genre (like me) can work their way in. At all levels, though, it gets perhaps the most important part of this genre right: you will have one or two moments per level where you ask yourself, "How on earth did I get myself out of that one?" It's intense and addictive. This is a superbly-designed game at a very attractive price. If you like space shooters at all, or want to find out if you do, buy right away.

I played two previous Tex Murphy adventures when I was younger: Killing Moon and Pandora Directive.  This new game is better than both of them.  It still features most of the original cast that you know and love but vastly improves on the control interface.  Gone is that clunky old "push the mouse button to move, use the arrow keys to look up and down" interface.  It's now a streamlined WASD movement configuration that everyone is used to by now.  It still has the great puzzles and sense of humor.  I highly recommend it.

Tex is back and that's a darn good thing!  Everything I enjoyed about the Tex Murphy adventures, the silly and witty puns, the surprisingly deep storylines, the crazy cast of characters and engaging puzzles are all here in the Tesla Effect.  This time, they're wrapped in shiny Ultra HD and the video is SHARP!  There's definitely a tongue-firmly-in-cheek, silly Mystery Science Theater 3000 flair to the sets, costumes and makeup for the filmed scenes - but that's a REALLY good thing!  It feels like you're playing a B movie which is exactly what the Tex Murphy adventures have always been.  To lose that kitchy appeal would completely ruin the experience.
Tesla Effect is kind of a love letter to the fans, bringing back a large number of the cast from previous games.  There are a few jokes that won't quite zing if you haven't played the game before, but do not be discouraged if this is your intro to the Tex Murphy canon.  Thanks to some lovely flashbacks, new players can familiarize themselves with the past games' plots and characters.  NOTE: I still encourage anyone to play the previous games because they are wonderful - I actually replayed Under A Killing Moon, Pandora Directive, and Overseer before playing Tesla Effect.  These games have stood the test of time.  Sure, the graphics are dated, but the story, characters, gameplay and puzzles are just as much fun as they were when I first played them years ago.
Chris Jones still has me cracking up as the titular character, Tex Murphy, and the rest of the cast is obviously having a ball as well.  The puzzles are overall very good - similar in difficulty and creativity to those from the past games.  There are multiple endings (of which I have only found 2 thus far, but I hear there are at least 4) which are unique and worth replaying the game for.
My only minor gripe is that the in-game graphics were only ok.  And that's mainly because so many of the textures were low resolution and some were sloppily applied to the models.  While this didn't detract or deter my enjoyment of the game, I would have liked to have seen a little more care put into the in-game graphics - the same kind of care that was put into the film sequences.
Overall, I thoroughly enjoyed playing Tesla Effect and I hope that Tex Murphy will be back again soon to again save the world from annihilation.
