Cool gameplay. Cool music. Cool skin-tight latex body suits that demonstrate the effectiveness of P90X.  However, the lack of Michael Ironside's voice and performance prevents Blacklist from reaching maxmium coolness. A weathered man, a father, a war vet, I imagine Sam Fisher is pushing 55, yet in this rendtion of the Splinter Cell series, he is voiced by a pubescent child who is prone to lashing out at his inner party. It's as if they're making some lackadaisical attempt to turn Sam Fisher into a young and hip action icon that is possessed by teen angst, opposed to the sardonically dark humour that we've grown accustomed to over the years. I don't mind if they're trying to reinvent the protagonist of Splinter Cell in order to appeal to a younger generation, but if that's the case, put Sam Fisher to rest and don't sully his image more than you already have. Introduce a new Splinter Cell--this reverse aging thing is just too weird for me.
Also, Fisher, arguably one of the most skillful agents of espionage of all time, lacks the ability to take cover in a standing position, which I found odd.

It is a sad and sorry state that Splinter Cell is now in.  This will be my last and it will also be the first that I haven't beaten.  I can't even be bothered to play more than a couple of levels in.  Splinter Cell, as it was intended, is simply dead.  Even the controversial Splinter Cell: Conviction was at least an elegant change of pace with a very simplifed and fast paced gameplay to fit with the narrowed vision of Sam's character.  And still, at least Conviction cared about stealth still.  And the game definitely had a strong sense of style.
But Blacklist?  It's a clunky attempt to serve two very different masters.  For all the "AAA" bells and whistles, I find that it an insult to anyone who has played the old games - even Conviction.  The stealth is just downright awful.  I'm usually a big fan of minimalistic HUDs, but there's a reason why Splinter Cell games generally used them sans Conviction.  It was always complex.  It tracked your noise.  It tracked your concealment.  The inventory system was intricate and tracked every little gadget.  It knew that players needed this information.  Blacklist?  It can't be bothered.  It's too busy being pretty to care about half of it's gameplay.  It's too busy being an action flick to care about shadows and noise and concealment.
And to top it all off, Ubisoft is too cheap to even bring back Michael Ironsides.  Or perhaps Mr. Ironsides saw exactly what I'm seeing here.  Splinter Cell and Sam Fisher are dead.  And now I have to watch this farce run around in their skin.  It's quite revolting.  It's a good thing Tom Clancy isn't around to see this.

When I first heard of Strike Vector, I had to check it out on Steam. I watched the trailer and I was sold. I had to get it. And I was not disappointed, quite the contrary: it was one of the most fun games I've played for a long time.
It's a chaotic, fast-paced 360-degree multiplayer shooter that plays -absolutely beautiful-. It has diversified weapon/perk combinations, the sense of classic online shooters, great visuals, maps that actually differ from each other, multiple game modes and so on. It's got a tight learning curve, so the first few days will be bumpy rides (quite literally), but that won't be a problem if you got the stones to handle it.
The two flight modes work beautifully in unison. Switching between modes happens fast and fluently and is essential to master. Jet mode is for fast travel and dog-fighting, hover/harrier mode for aiming, fighting at close quarters, fast turns, braking and so on.
I heavily recommend to anyone who's up for a good flight and a good fight.

Pillars of Eternity. Widely acclaimed as a spiritual successor to Baldur's Gate and Icewind Dale. While I do not doubt the truth of such claims, I would like to offer my perspective as someone who's never played Baldur's Gate or Icewind Dale, and thus approach PoE with fresh eyes.
For a start games in the fantasy genre which PoE sits in are plenty on Steam. Indeed I have an earlier review of Spellforce, a game which was somewhat forgettable for me despite brave attempts to capture the spirit of fantasy RPG. As I hadn't played Baldur's Gate nor Icewind Dale, PoE's first job as to sell itself to me on the steam store page. I approached it with some skepticism initially and wasn't entirely sold on the top down isometric view. The game's content, gameplay, mechanics, lore etc however, reminded me of my evenings of pen and paper RPG games I've had with friends, and that convinced me to give it a try.
It was a decision I would not regret. Character creation is one of the biggest parts of any good P&P fantasy RPG game, be it Dungeons and Dragons or Warhammer. The character creation of PoE made me feel exactly like I was starting a P&P RPG game. It wasn't so much as customising my character's look as it was fleshing out my backstory, allocating stats etc. I spent almost 3 hours alone in character creation.
The story is well written, well paced. The lore is rich, you feel like you are in a wonderful fantasy world to be explored. While having individual maps instead of a massive world like any of the Elder Scrolls games makes exploration less of a focus, nonetheless it's still good fun discovering new places. The combat system takes a while to learn and master, and having a game manual would really help, but by and large the mechanics of the game aren't too difficult to pick up. When playing it I had a sense I was playing a game with Elder Scroll's rich lore and setting with Diablo's graphics and interface, both franchises I absolutely adore. As a setting for individual role playing in, it's right up there with Elder Scroll games.
There aren't many games which have made me think "I really love the fantasy genre". Fable was the first that got me started. Warcraft, especially WoW, got me deep into it. Elder Scrolls cemented my love for the genre, and I didn't think it was possible to take my love for fantasy to a new level, but Pillars of Eternity has somehow managed to do that. Playing it brings back the sort of emotions I experienced the first time I played Fable, WoW, Elder Scrolls. All the more amazing given the isometric top down projection and fixed maps PoE utilises instead of first person or over the shoulder views in an open world those other games share.
With the rich amazing lore as its foundations, I can see PoE being the beginning of something great. A grand new fantasy franchise to go alongside giants such as Warcraft, Elder Scrolls, Warhammer etc. PoE has recently released its first DLC, I am sure the first of many. This is a game franchise with a great future to come, and I am not only glad I am a part of it from the first game, I hope to bring along as many of you on this adventure as I can.
Edit: already PoE is being held up as the new benchmark. Issue 283 of PC Gamer has a review for a similiar isometric view RPG game called Kyn with this exact phrase: "The more I played, the less it reminded me of Pillars of Eternity..."
Also I wrote this review before I read the PC Gamer's review of PoE. Here's part of the opening paragraph: "Almost an hour had passed, and I was still on the character creation screen. That’s how I knew, before I’d even started, that this homage to classic computer role-playing games like Baldur’s Gate, Icewind Dale, and Planescape: Torment was authentic...."
And here's another part of the next: "It’s the most captivating, rewarding RPG I’ve played on a PC in years, and I’ve fallen in love with the intricate, richly painted world they’ve crafted."
Seems familiar? Those were exactly the same things I've said about PoE that's made me fall in love with. This game is a must try for RPG fans. Get it, you won't regret it!

Pillars was pitched as the next generation neverwinter, the next baldurs gate, the next single player DnD replicating simulation and in this it is a perfect game. There is no black or white in Eora. You'll often ask yourself whether or not you did the right thing. Doubt creeps in and you justify your decision because it was what made most sense at the time.
It's no longer just the endless whispers of lives past that keep you awake. Blessed sleep plagued with visions of people and places you know and don't know. Cries of mercy, faces of foes you struck down, looks of betrayal, of gratitude...Hours would pass, the camp awakens and you make ready for the day. As you walk to the next town, you hope that they don't need help with anything.

Pillars of Eternity set about to be the spiritual successor to Baldur's Gate, Icewind Dale, and Planescape: Torment.
Nailed it.
Offering a wide variety of difficulty options and many ways to play, this game is both a reminder of our past for those of us who enjoyed the afforementioned games as youngsters, and a great primer for the genre (and, dare I say, a possible fresh start for the genre?) for neophytes to it.
If you enjoyed the old D&D games (or similar ones, such as Arcanum) you'll want to experience this fantastic journey.
If you haven't played any of this genre before, but like epic story telling, challenging tactical combat, some of the best voice acting *ever* in a video game, and gorgeous immersive worlds, give PoE a try. It will test your tactics and your morals in the best possible way. Expect some small stumbling blocks if you've never played a game like this before, so if you're not comfortable getting used to a new style of game you may not want to pick this up before watching some let's plays of it. By an hour or two in you'll be as comfortable with PoE mechanics as you've been with any others.

First: this is one of my all time favorite games of all time; it is a very good game... That being said, let me break something down:
- If you want a full, unique, and overall well-rounded story experience, do not buy this game. Being a story and lore junkie will only make you want your money back.
- If you want exciting boss fights, balanced character progression, a deep class/skill system, and challenging gameplay, this game WILL pull you in.
Starting off with the story, it is dull and you WILL forget things and become lost... Well, you can only forget things if there are things to forget so maybe not that... Deep down, yes, the story is kinda interesting and sometimes does allow for good atmosphere*; however, this only happens after completing the mian quest. So, agian, skip this game if story is something you like... That isn't what this game is about. Think of it like this: the start of the story and generic fantacy with a bit of sparkle, the entire middle of the game is a massive blob of random filler, and the end is weird and interesting but still leaves you satisfied.
REMEMBER, gameplay is the gem! It is the only reason it is good! Keep that in mind at all times, thank you.
The filler that I mentioned is not just story filler, the great majority of it is fun, introducing different monsters and quests for you to do, giving you some really great fights. On the surface, the class system seems simple... But once you break off the first layer and look into it, the combinations and skills and augments allow for some really great build; through stat progression and building, weapon finding and upgrading, for both you and your companion, you will feel extremely satisfied with how bad*** your character becomes. Many reviewers of this game call it a hack and slash but it is much more than than.
Think of game in which Dark Souls, Shadow of the Colossus, Monster Hunter, and a hand full of good MMO mechanics all had a fancy love child but it's story was writen by the Two Worlds devs, trying to make the most basic of fantacy plots, then once you finish the main plot, the dev team didn't know what to do and they knew they had to do something so they rolled with the most random final ever, completely telling you to forget about the main plot line and told you to FOCUS ON THE WEIRD *** HOLE IN THE GROUND.....

I admit that when I first picked up Dark Souls back in 2011, I thought the challenge and community hype around it sounded amazing, and wanted to give it a go myself, I managed to scrape past the Asylum Demon, but immediately hit a wall with the Taurus Demon, thought that the game was too challenging and unfair, I didn't pick it up again for 5 years. However the videos of people playing and discussing lore, really dragged me back into Souls games. I picked up Bloodborne, which I thoroughly love, this got me playing in a new way, and really let me understand how these games work, what their essence is. I went back to play Dark Souls, and so far, I am loving it even more than Bloodborne, and it has quickly become one of my most favourite games of all time.
This game is a masterpiece (with quirks), it is punishing, it is frustrating, but you will never enjoy a game more than this one - once you have acquired the taste. This is the thing with Souls games, they have to be acquired, they are complex, rewarding and genuinely engaging, but you have to learn to enjoy the sensation, you have to let it click in your mind that you have to think in a certain way, but once mastered, the feeling from throwing yourself at boss after boss, to getting to the top of the fortress, or breaking through the darkest depths to face that boss, to be kicked out on your rear again and again but gathering up and charging again, when that boss falls, there is no game I have ever played that makes you feel so good about what you've achieved. You can love this game, you will love this game.
TL;DR Game is hard, but once hat will stay in your heart forever.

This review is relating is a comparison of Terraria to Starbound. It assumes that you have played Terraria and enjoyed it.
Pros:
- Adds additional Biomes and planets within the same saved game. This is achieved by having different planets with multiple biomes. This allows for more diversity when exploring above ground.
- The difficulty of surviving on a planet changes from planet to planet. This allows you choose how difficult you want to make the game for yourself. You can go to a harder planet with less gear or an easier planet with more gear.
- Story line and quests which add encourages you to progress rather than having to drive your own progression
Cons:
- While there are some interesting things to find underground (ex hidden villages and bonus dimensions) there isn't much to encourage you to continue exploring the underground of a planet. Eventually once you've upgraded your ship and mined enough raw resources, there is no insentive to keep digging. Adding more interesting things to find on planets, like rare items or rare events, might encourage more planet exploration rather than hoping from planet to planet.

Tesla Effect is one massive love letter to 90s FMV adventure gaming, and a *very* faithful follow-up to a long-gone series (for better and for worse).
Working with their lite Kickstarter budget, Big Finish Games delivered a full-length adventure game loaded with (generally) well-acted cutscenes, great music, devious puzzles and alternate endings. They had a lot of ambition going into this project, and they somehow managed to pull it together into a solidly engaging 10+ hours of detective-ing.
Sure, the game's central plot - in which our hapless hero attempts to piece together the last seven years of his life, whilst on the trail of Tesla's lost inventions - is convoluted and sometimes poorly explained...and the humour frequently dives into dated dad joke territory...but if you're at all interested in this series or 90s adventure gaming in general, this is a solid addition to your library.
Be warned though: the game also revives some of the major faults of 90s adventure gaming. Several sections of this game suffer from severe pixel-hunting-itis (less of a problem in Casual Mode, but potentially rage-inducing on the standard difficulty setting), there are some minor awful stealth segments, there's an extremely lazy bit where you have to solve a "the chicken and the fox can't be on the same boat" puzzle...and yes, there's even a maze full of spiders.
Still, it's nothing worse than what the 90s threw at us. It's worth bearing through it for the overwhelmingly fun, nostalgic, and authentic Tex Murphy experience that this game has on offer. Thumbs up from me!

State of Decay is an easy game to recommend, provided you have a tolerance for the occasional bug and jankiness.
It starts out on a bit of a low point, throwing you and buddy-character into a zombie apocalypse with absolutely no explanation; it gives you the impression you accidentally skipped some important cutscene. From there, the entire first area is, predictably, a tutorial, but it informs you of game systems that are disabled until later. It's all very confusing at first.
But once you get out of the tutorial and into the game world, it really shines. This is a zombie survival game where survival comes first. You need to scavenge supplies and food every day for your group of variable survivors to stay safe, and you need to deal with group conflicts and sudden bad circumstances. For the most part, the seams seperating dynamic content from the scripted are very well hidden - in truth, there are scripted characters and plotlines to follow, but the bulk of the cast is generated as you play, as are world factors and interpersonal conflicts. What you solve and what you leave to the AI to deal with makes a big difference as the dynamic side of the game adjusts to your influence or absence. Even when you're not playing.
Also, this game is punishing of mistakes. You can swap through whatever characters you have influence over, and they all excell in different areas through character-specific blends of skill trees. As long as you play to your strengths and keep an eye out, you'll be fine, but if you get reckless it only takes a few good hits from a horde to take a character down. Once a character is down, they're dead. This game features harsh perma-death. But that's part of the thrill; never have I been so desperate to escape a bad situation as when my favourite character was a stumble away from death. By the way, if you take the easy way and just order another character to do the job for you, they carry all the same risks.
The game is not without its faults though. The combat is a bit clunky, and there are plenty of bugs around (although you learn to notice what they are and how to compensate). Given the massive cast size and permadeath for every fallen character, it's remarkable that every character is voiced, but you quickly figure out how this works and it loses its magic shortly thereafter. Still, the effort is admirable.
If you want a zombie-survival game that's more about the group management and day-to-day survival aspect of the setting, it's hard to do any better than State of Decay. It's clunky, but it's way more in-depth than it should be.
(As an additional suggestion: The game generates conflicts and relationships between characters on it's own, but playing into it yourself is a great boost to the drama value.)

State of Decay, is a zombie game that focuses on survival. Population size is dwindling along with the resources you can find throughout the city you explore. Time is not on your side, the world will persist even when you are not playing. Finding a fortifiable location to barricade from zombie hordes is critical to winning the game.
As you progress through the story you are given certain facilities to use as your headquarters, once you hit a certain point of the game you are allowed to re-allocate your base.
The main game focuses on a balance between survival, difficulty and story. Any character you play can be killed off by zombies and stay dead. There is no way to bring them back other than starting over again or attempting to exit the game before it auto-saves. Some characters clearly have better traits than others especially the first guy you play as. If you let them die, you will be disadvantaged. Training multiple characters to be strong and capable of survival is critical.
The DLC is survival oriented with the story stripped out, which results in a good experience, not interrupted by constantly redoing cinematics or certain missions over and over. Instead, it allows you to play at your own pace and repair the van to proceed to the next difficulty. Every trip reduces the total amount of resources within the city, scales the damage of the enemies up, and reduces the amount of cars available.
A major con to some people but also appealing to others is the persistent world. Alot of people dislike the fact that while you're away from the game the resources are depleting every day. The people who play more hours a day have a much greater benefit than those who play few hours or attempt to play it casually.

I've really enjoyed the first few hours of playing State of Decay, although I feel like the game won't last for very long. It feels like the game is half over already. Maybe that's because I've been doing the same things over and over.
State of Decay creates a wonderful atmosphere for you to experience zombie survival in. The setting is a group of small towns in America and you have to set up and manage a small community of survivors whilst scavenging in the abandoned houses for supplies. There is a real feeling of development as you level up your characters skills as well as developing your home base to become more sustainable and efficient.
Melee is fun. Plain and simple. Great finishing moves that, despite being very repetitive, really drive home the zombie apocalypse feel with lots of blood and braaaiaiiins.
The character you start with can die. This may take a while to happen to you, or it may never happen because you are smart and conservative. Just don't stay out all night doing missions and gathering supplies, because they WILL get you eventually!
There are many hours of enjoyment to be had in this game, hopefully I haven't gone through most of them already.

Splinter Cell Blacklist takes you back to the roots in terms of gameplay (well, kinda). In most missions you are given the choice of how to deal with your enemies. You can certainly use the direct approach that was prevalent in previous Splinter Cell games but most of the time you won't get very far if you run in guns blazing. Usually it's easier to pick enemies off one by one without alarming other guards. There you have another choice, being lethal or not. For those who seek a real challenge there is the so called "Ghost" approach which requires you to skip enemies entirely and try to find ways around them whitout getting caught. This requires a lot (and I really mean a lot) of patience because the AI is one of the best I've seen in recent games.
You can upgrade your base of operations to provide bonuses on your missions and buy and upgrade all your equipment to suit your playstyle. Before each mission you choose which guns and gadgets to bring and with the right upgrade you can even change them mid-mission whenever you find a weapons cache.
The story isn't up to e.g. Bioshock standards but its decently interesting and has some twists, enough to keep you interested until the end. Admittedly, the story is a little short but there's still the multiplayer mode.
The scenery and graphics are amazing and the missions take you all around the world with very different environments. The voice acting in this game is superb... and I don't mean the main characters only. Depending on the location of the mission guards usually talk in their native language like russian or spanish.
Tldr: A worthy successor to the Splinter Cell franchise and a really fun game.

The Short:
This game has a tonne of potential and it looks pretty good while not requiring a space computer to run smoothly. And that's it's issue: tonnes of potential that's unrealized with paltry playmodes, lack of tunables for flight characteristics, no real game to speak of besides basic arena play, a flight system that's got an identity crisis. With all these problems, it's hard to invest into a game that feels more like a tech demo than a game. Get it if you want to try 6 axis arena shooter because there aren't many out there. Honestly, this game needs more development time! I like this game, but I want to ENJOY this game, and the problems listed above and below are preventing that.
The Long:
Fix the flight controls. This is a game with a flight identity crisis. If you want to do newtonian flight, do newtonian flight. Don't add by default things like drag, bank and roll characteristics of airplanes and then yaw is missing. If it's a spaceship with awesome rocket boosters, FLY IT LIKE A SPACESHIP!
I wanted a Macross/Robotech game, but what I got was a half finished game with a learning curve that's more vertigo inducing than rage quit inducing (yes I turned off the auto roll, but still feel like i'm in a clothes dryer everytime I turn). If you want to have fun with a learning curve, I'd wait until they have more refined controls. The network lag between when you press thrust and when it actually happens is mostly suicidal unless your in a wide open pocket. The radar...eesh it's just too primitive to provide enough information for snap quick decisions, so it's a learning curve in itself for tactical. Targeting is playing wack-a-mole while getting vertigo. This game needs a lot more tunables for in flight sensitivies (turn rate, pitch rate, roll rate, and again there's no yaw in flight mode...ugh...). Just too many issues with the flight to be enjoyable.
Now lets get to the game: There is none to really care about.
This is as tech demo as you can get. Yes, it's a tech demo. By this day and age, pure arena battles are really just tech demo's.  I give you gun, a flight kit and some symetrically laid out floating boxes with a score counter.  Game balance does not exist when you make all the weapons available but employ no economy, graduation system or classes. There's nothing for us to invest ourselves into: No Story, No Character/Class Development, No Economy!!! No game to invest upon!
Is there skill involved: yes to the extreme. This takes the lessons from the old school shooter in learning curve, but in this day and age that being the sole premise is not enough for many to invest their time in.
Do I want my money back? No, since I bought it half price and the developer is still adding content.
I recognize the hard work this team has done to get this far.
Is it worth the full price it's asking? That's up to you. If you are a diehard fan of this type of flight sim and an arena junkie, it's passable given the unique 6 axis play. There are better develop shooters out there, but none with the level of freedom available. Accessibility to these freedoms is a real problem with this game though.

Pillars was pitched as the next generation neverwinter, the next baldurs gate, the next single player DnD replicating simulation and in this it is a perfect game. Pillars of Eternity meets all its objectives, fulfills all its promises and offers up an engrossing story along with a refreshing new fantasy world. If you've ever liked tactics, parties and dungeon delving this game is a single player gem.

There is no black or white in Eora. You'll often ask yourself whether or not you did the right thing. Doubt creeps in and you justify your decision because it was what made most sense at the time.
It's no longer just the endless whispers of lives past that keep you awake. Blessed sleep plagued with visions of people and places you know and don't know. Cries of mercy, faces of foes you struck down, looks of betrayal, of gratitude...Hours would pass, the camp awakens and you make ready for the day. As you walk to the next town, you hope that they don't need help with anything.

Pillars of Eternity set about to be the spiritual successor to Baldur's Gate, Icewind Dale, and Planescape: Torment.
Nailed it.
Offering a wide variety of difficulty options and many ways to play, this game is both a reminder of our past for those of us who enjoyed the afforementioned games as youngsters, and a great primer for the genre (and, dare I say, a possible fresh start for the genre?) for neophytes to it.
If you enjoyed the old D&D games (or similar ones, such as Arcanum) you'll want to experience this fantastic journey.
If you haven't played any of this genre before, but like epic story telling, challenging tactical combat, some of the best voice acting *ever* in a video game, and gorgeous immersive worlds, give PoE a try. It will test your tactics and your morals in the best possible way. Expect some small stumbling blocks if you've never played a game like this before, so if you're not comfortable getting used to a new style of game you may not want to pick this up before watching some let's plays of it. By an hour or two in you'll be as comfortable with PoE mechanics as you've been with any others.

Are you a min/maxing, character optimization obsessed freako'saur? Prepare to lose your sanity.
You will literally become a beast steak farming, goblin murderer for the 1st 20 hours of the game, while playing every class except possibly the one you are building for. This is thanks to how the vocation system's discipline points are awarded as well as a desire to build (read: multi-class 200 levels) towards the coveted stats of 500 attack rating or 600 magic attack rating with as many stamina points as possible. Also don't forget to multi-class for augmentation perks without actually leveling your character. You'll definetly want to learn how to speed run a Ring of Preserverance at level 5 before going any further into the main quest. You'll also want to learn some basic marketing skills to encourage others to rent your pawn companion for early rift crystals which are used to "identify" random gear drops. This means making an interesting looking companion with a catchy name. (yes, the easy route is to put some time into making a scantily armored floozy).
Ready to play?

I hope you like managing conditions. There are dozens of conditions AND curatives in this game. From various Hardspud sauces (is this vodka?) and herbs for healing Health and Stamina, to Secret Softener (giggle) for when you need to be umm...more regular.
Ultimately, did you play Skyrim and Dark Souls yet? I guess you could give this a go if you need to kill more time rather than do something productive.

It's told direclty, unlikely Dark Souls, but primarily has one, overarching plot that you find out in the end encompasses everything you've done. By the end, you are left with a sense of closure that everything you've done has led up to this, whether you knew it or not. Even NG+ has a
explaination, unlike most games that introduce this mechanic.
The encounters are more akin to Dark Souls, with mini-bosses scattered throughout the map that require strategy including mechanics such as climbing on larger enemies, which is very entertaining if a bit unwieldy. It's an open-world however, so you can explore 95% of the map from the beginning of the game, although that doesn't mean you should!
The game reaches a critical point approximately 1/3rd of the way through, after a major battle. At this point the world around you changes, and the entire map changes, giving reason to explore areas you've already been. It's an interesting mechanic I wish would have been explored in games like Skyrim, where I see the story could have used that "End of the World" drama this game presents so well, pushing you forward in the story.
Couldn't recommend this game enough in the drought that is good Fantasy RPGs of the last 1-2 years, with no signs of that changing anytime soon.

Or would you rather manipulate politics to your will? JUST DO IT. Or, if you're like me, you'll have a hand in everything. They allow you a lot of freedom in the fights, and scaling them to work on their weak points was definitely the part that has stayed with me.  Overall, definitely worth a playthrough.

This game is a work of love. From the same developers that created Monaco, Tooth and Tail is a simplified take on the Real Time Strategy genre.
I will not comment on the story mode, as you will have to find out for yourself if it's to your taste (I loved it), so I will just speak for the multiplayer aspect and general gameplay.
Instead of complete per-unit micromanagement, you control groups of units that encompasses all troops of the same type. Instead of giving orders to these units directly, you control a Commander that moves around the battlefield. The controls are simple and only uses two buttons. With these two buttons you control either your whole army, or a specific group of troops with three basic commands, which also share the same buttons: Rally, Retreat and Focus.
To create troops, you must first generate resources. You start with a Gristmill and a bunch of farms (Think of the mill and farms in Age of Empires) that serve as your base. The farms generate Food, which is the only resource in the game. You spend food to create Warrens, defenses, build more Farms, or capture more Gristmills. The Warrens are your essential unit-production buildings, each of them pumping out troops one at a time.
To win the game, you must either destroy all of your enemy's Gristmills or force them to starve. The first is pretty self-explanatory, but the second occurs because there's a limited amount of resources on the map. After five minutes, your farms will become fallow, and cannot be replanted. Should you find yourself with no active farms, you have 60 seconds to capture a Gristmill and build a farm (The timer isn't reset when capturing a Gristmill, so think fast.) or eliminate your enemy's remaining Gristmills. The matches, due to the constant pressure on maintaining a line of resources are surprisingly short, so if you couldn't get into the RTS genre due to the time factor, this might be to your liking.
This game is so far one of the most enjoyable RTS experiences I've played, and I keep coming back for more. If you're interested in this kind of genre, give Tooth and Tail a try. I can assure you that you won't be disappointed.

And there is only one save file. I generally save frequently on video games. And I make sure to save BEFORE I go into a dangerous situation. That way, I can reload and try again if I fail. 5 out of 10. Add 3 points if you are a fan of Tex Murphy, you like FMVs or you plan to play this on casual mode otherwise steer clear.
There are two difficulties in the game, Casual and Gamer, my impressions are from playing the game in Gamer, in my opinion this game was made with Casual in mind.
This is a "point and click" adventure game that sadly is full to the brim with two particular adventure game tropes; item & pixel hunting.
Almost EVERY puzzle of this game is about finding out of place items, particularly small ones.
It gets very frustrating, specially when a particular section requires you to literally hunt tiny broken pieces to assemble a symbol and STILL every other puzzle afterwards is the same "find hidden items in the environment" until the end.
Unlike other adventure games before it, puzzles don't have two or more ways to solve and they don't particularly require much deduction to figure them out, either you have that screwdriver or you haven't found it.
The game becomes more of a visual novel if you play it in casual mode, since your flashlight will highlight items in the environment and you can skip puzzles. There are choices to be made that will change your story and Tex's relationships, other choices won't change the story but it is fun to go back to them and see the reactions to the different decisions in glorious High Resolution FMV.

Tex Murphy: Tesla Effect is a very good adventure game with a plot worthy of the series. Being an FMV game might turn some people off, but it’s worth checking out if you’re a fan of noir or apocalyptic stories. More casual players might shy away from it, particularly those who aren’t big fans of tough puzzles, but over 7,000 people had faith in the concept to make the game a reality. It’s not without its flaws, but thanks to two different difficulty settings most of these can be overlooked or worked around. While it’s not classic point-and-click, the first person exploration might bring over shooter fans who want a more relaxed exploration-based title that uses controls very similar to today’s FPS games.

Tesla Effect takes me down nostalgia lane harder than any Mario game ever could. It's probably mostly a game for people who played the older Tex Murphy games ~20 years ago, but if you're into noir and don't mind some not-quite-modern 3D graphics, then you're absolutely in for a treat even if the basketball behind Rook's Pawn Shop doesn't immediately bring a smile to your face.
Having recently played through Under a Killing Moon in anticipation of Tesla Effect getting released I must say that it's incredibly true to the old games. Whenever the term "space opera" is mentioned, one imagines space battles sprawling across millions of stars, armadas clogging up space and heroic characters ready and willing to uphold justice and peace in the galaxy - tropes undoubtedly inspired by series like
and
. In fact, these and other series have for a long time remained the main contenders for the title of the most influential piece of the genre, with entries in movies and games amassing thousands of dollars of income and generating wider fan bases. It was not until the year of 2007 when a Canadian game studio
, with years of experience and a 2003's
behind their backs, would release a revolutionary RPG of unmatched scale -
.
The game is set in the 22nd century, where rapid advancements in technology thanks to the discovery of Element Zero allowed humans to progress as a species and enter the Galactic Council, granting them galaxy-wide recognition. As time passed, humanity became more involved in the interstellar affairs, including war conflicts, ultimately leading to a covert operation on a human colony Eden Prime - the starting point of the game.
Playing as commander Shepard, customized to your liking, you take on a thrilling chase after a renegade high-class agent Saren - a Spectre, one who can use any means necessary to uphold law. He, however, abuses his powers and goes rogue, and it is Shepard's mission to bring the traitor down. Little does he or the Council know in the haste, however, that a much larger threat is looming over the Milky Way...
The plot, written dy Drew Karpyshyn, aims to challenge the likes of
in its scale: from the lush sceneries of Eden Prime to the gritty and unforgiving magma-filled world of Palaven, the journey takes Shepard and his team of loyal soldiers across the galaxy to strengthen their numbers and unveil Saren's intentions. The story catches your breath since the very first moments and makes you sit on the edge of your seat up until the grand culmination, and plot twists are not a rare sight: what initially comes off as something blatant and easy to grasp the concept of reveals to be much more complex later.
Beautifully written and designed, each with their own backgrounds and motives, the characters in this game are some of the most memorable in the video game industry. Every member of Shepard's crew feels unique, and if all the right conditions are met, can even become a love interest, even though that's completely optional and influences the plot lightly.
Being a game from 2007,
shows its age in the way it looks: the animations are on the stiff side by today's standards and graphics are nothing to write home. That being said, the aforementioned aspects are but minor inconveniences for those who truly care about these aspects of a game and in no way hamper the experience one can receive.
The way the player handles Shepard and their crew is mostly similar to other third-person RPGs: there are weapons to shoot at anyone who gets in the way, skills to utilise and choices to make. A defining feature of the series is the "tactical pause": binded to spacebar by default, any time the key is held down, the time freezes, allowing for a more tactical approach to the situation the crew find themselves in. Skills can be selected to be used simultaneously on the adversaries, weapons can be switched and markers can be set for your crewmates to either take point, assault someone or hold back - all in a matter of seconds, leaving enemies clueless as they are tossed around the battlefield. The introduction of this "pause" allows for easier crew management and more control over the party in the middle of a battle and is overall a welcome addition.
features one of the most compelling dialogue writings in role-playing games: words alone define characters and turn tides of wars raging across Milky Way, and the protagonist can often influence how an encounter turns out merely by saying the right phrases with enough "Hero/Renegade" points, which are accumulated as you manage to persuade people either by being compassionate or ruthless with them.
to this day remains an influential entry in the space opera genre of videogames, serving both as a solid beginning of one of the most renowned game series and as a fantastic standalone role-playing game. With excellent writing and thrilling gameplay, the game still holds up despite the age, owing all to the fact that the effect it produced on the gaming community was truly massive.

It really feels like Bioware weren't quite sure what their vision was for this game. It is a typical Bioware RPG in the sense that it follows a very compelling story in which you are at least given the illusion that your choices matter. But it is delivered to the player through such clumsy means it's almost as if everything else was an afterthought.
I'm sure the combat system means well - but it's a real bad hombre. Due to the truly awful AI (both friendly and hostile), half-baked cover system and lack of truly interesting enemies, every fight feels the same. It's all just dudes with or without guns and sometimes dudes with guns that make you fall over. To clarify, there are actually quite a lot of different enemies to face throughout the game; but they all act and feel the same. Your party members don't follow orders so well and that tends to get them killed, especially early on, when they aren't so tough. I just gave up on giving them orders entirely. Sometimes you are thrown into a combat environment where the odds are stacked so heavily against you, the only way to survive is to abuse the horrible AI while taking things extremely slowly. Once you are familiar with how to consistently deal with the combat it's very unlikely that you will ever die - that is, unless you get insta-killed by a burrowing thresher (not a fun way to lose). But even they are predictable.
In completing every side mission I could find I probably close to doubled my play time in this game. Unfortunately, doing so was ultimately pointless and mostly unrewarding. They are, for the most part, composed of copy-pasted locations and enemies with little variation. I spent a long time wrestling with the Mako to explore the surfaces of many dull, empty planets. I remember the data for one planet in particular mentioning the atmosphere being completely inhospitable for any life forms larger than microoganisms. But in searching the planet I came across multiple colonies of weird space monkeys. It may be an expansive galaxy full of exotic aliens and wondrous technology, but it sure isn't consistent. Another planet was home to ancient Prothean ruins that housed a mysterious floating metallic sphere. Upon inspection, Shepard fell unconscious and witnessed the life of a primitive humanoid through his eyes while his species was studied by Protheans. It sounds like a cool story, and it would be if it had actually happened. What I actually got was a few paragraphs of text describing the event. I'd expect this from Bioware... nearly two decades ago in a game like Baldur's Gate - in that game everything was text so it didn't feel out of place. It was quite jarring and left me with a bad taste. Some of the side missions touch on very relatable, very human stories - but they're over so fast, with so little time to become invested in them. They are missed opportunities.
The characters of Mass Effect individually get enough screen time to exhibit a reasonable amount of development. They are all believable and play their parts well - wearing their personalities openly. Conversation is the primary method for the game to deliver lore; this is something it does very well. I didn't read a single journal entry outside of the mission log and I still feel that I learned more than enough about the galaxy, it's races and their history just through conversation with a whole host of different characters. It was absolutely an enjoyable way to be exposed to the fascinating and intriguing Mass Effect universe. I would say this is where the game shines brightest - it's story, characters and lore. Despite most of the mechanics being a mess, this is what carried me through the experience and this is why I thoroughly enjoyed it.

tl;dr: This is easily the worst Splinter Cell game I have ever played.  Do not buy it.
And the long version:
The writing is absolutely awful: the plot is stupid, boring, and nonsensical; the dialog is cliched and hackneyed (with the amusing exception of Kobin, who is supposed to be an unlikable scumbag, but is easily the most endearing character); the characters are completely forgettable (again, with the exception of Kobin); the action falls into the very worst traps of "action tv" with 'splosions and technobabble going off all over the place; and nearly all of the technical discussions are wrong (now, I may be crazy, but I've always found it odd that video games, which, you know, run on computers and were created by people who understand computers, don't have a very good track-record with using the things in-universe; the answer is probably that writers remain as uninformed and ignorant as always).
Sound design is fine, but nothing special.  Voice work varies from character to character: Kobin is great, Charlie and Briggs (two more supporting characters) are OK, Grim is Canadian now (seriously, listen for her "out"s and "about"s—it's subtle, but it's there—but do it on YouTube because you should not buy this game), and Sam is no longer voiced by Micheal Ironside, which is actually a huge problem: the new guy, however good an actor he may be, simply cannot deliver the same gravitas and sincerity that Ironside could.  Also he doesn't sound quite like Ironside, which is suprisingly distracting.
Map design is bi-polar, veering widely from abject linearity to twisted mazes filled with instant-game-over lasers.  Every once in a while, though, it manages to come together and be good—the Chicago water-treatment plant, for example, but such cases are rarities.
We'll get to gameplay in a sec, but first let's talk about the Paladin.  My thoughts are "why do we need a Mass Effect/StarCraft II-style 'interactive' hubworld? why? why do we need that? is it because we're following the leader and those other games did well, so our game must do well, too, if it has these elements?"  If so, Ubisoft not only failed to understand why those games did well but also failed to rip-off properly the gimmicks they thought were the selling points.  The Paladin does not need to be interactive.  The player does not need to talk to the characters, especially when they have nothing to say (except for Kobin).  It's a huge waste of resources and time for the designers, devs, and players alike.
And now for the game mechanics: they are servicable, usually causing only slightly more problems than they allow the player to solve.  And that's where the game shoots itself in the head.  "*Usually* causing only slight more problems than they allow the player to solve"—"usually".  Every once in a while, for reasons known only to the good folks at Ubisoft, who should all be berated for not fighting against this harder (or at all or even proposing it), the game mechanics will be altered, sometimes in little ways, sometimes in big ways.  There's a bit where the player loses control of Sam and takes control of Briggs.  For reasons which completely escape me, these sections are played, with no warning, in first-person perspective (and with equipment that the player cannot choose, to salt the wound).  In all coop missions featuring Briggs as a playable character, he handles exactly the same as Sam, as one would expect, so why the sudden shift in handling?  No idea, other than the preposterous "this is too easy, let's shake things up a bit".  No, thank you, Ubi.  I don't like things being shaken up.  And, futhermore, if I wanted to play a CoD-style forced-stealth mission, I would be playing the Chernobyl mission in Modern Warfare.  No, I'm actually here to play Splinter Cell.  I would really like to play Splinter Cell all the way through this Splinter Cell game.  Shocking, isn't it?
Continuing that line, we have the final boss fight.  The team (and the player) have spent the entire game chasing down this poorly-written (but actually quite well-performed) villain, Sadiq, and Sam finally has him cornered... but Sam isn't wearing his suit, and he doesn't have his gadgets or spare mags for his pistol, and he just gave his rifle to Briggs, who isn't actually in this fight—he's on the sidelines, injured and unable to help in any way.  So this stealth game, which has relied on Sam's supersuit, gadgets, guns, and ability to fight only the dumbest enemies who easily lose track of intruders, becomes a game of "Redlight, Greenlight" as the player tried to work his way, unarmed and unarmored, toward the boss, who is standing conveniently in one place until he decides that the player is taking too long, at which point he will retreat to a spot even farther away from the player, and the process repeats.  If the player should manage to sneak up on Sadiq and try a take-down, Sam and the boss will engage in fisticuffs, and the player will be asked with no warning to try to use the mouse to aim the boss' gun at him while the boss resists.  If the player fails, he has to start over again from the beginning (no mid-boss-fight checkpoints for us!).  If he succeeds, the boss will beat the tar out of Sam and then vanish, dropping his gun in the process.  The player is not allowed to pick up the gun.  The player then has no choice but to try to walk Sam, who is quite injured at this point, slowly toward the next objective.  After just enough time to be obnoxious, the boss will tackle Sam from behind, at which point, the player is presented with a quick-time event to grab the boss' knife.  If the player fails, the game resets to the start of the boss fight.  Again.  If the player succeeds... well, I don't know what happens then.  I only managed it the once, but the boss had tackled Sam into a crate, which obscured the action, so I couldn't see what was happening.  I think I managed to pass the first QTE only to die to the second.  After trying the fight several dozen times, I gave up in frustration.  I may try again in a while, but I'll certainly never try to play the game a second time, and I'll recommend to anyone who asks that they not try to play the game the first time.
To reiterate: This is a bad game.  Do not buy it, and do not play it.  Find something better to do with your time.  Have you read "The Killing Star" by Charles R. Pellegrino and George Zebrowski?  It's really good.  Your local lending library probably has a copy or could get one for you through the inter-library loan system.  And, who knows, you might make a new friend while you're at the library.  That'd be cool and worth your time, unlike this game.

Sonic CD is a 2D platformer that has you as a hedgehog finding your way through labyrinth like levels. Between getting from the start to the finish of the level, Sonic can collect rings. These rings are insurance. If you get hit with rings, they all spray out of the hedgehog. If you get hit without any rings, Sonic dies and its back to the last checkpoint. If you have 50 rings at the end of the level, you can jump up into a giant ring that lets you do a bonus stage for a chance to get a chaos emerald. The bonus stage feels like Sega's version of Sonic running around a Mario Kart track. After every 2 levels comes a boss level that has you stock up on rings or lives before you face the boss Robotnik. The game breezed by in a few hours without me noticing.
For those that haven't played any Sonic games from the 90s, the controls are simple enough to use one button. That one button is jump if you're standing or running. If you're ducking and push the button it charges up a spinball. When you release the down direction, Sonic will fire off with a super boost of speed. If you press down while running, Sonic tucks into a ball that will damage enemies.
The real gimmick of Sonic CD is the ability to go into the past or future. You do this by first hitting a sign and then going so fast that you will either go to the era. It feels like nothing more than a pallet swap. There are changes here and there, but you won't need to visit one era or another to progress. Plus there is a screen that takes Sonic to the era and it stops the gameplay. There's not that much variety in gameplay. Even the brief water levels only slow down Sonic, forcing you to find air bubbles to breathe. He can't swim or anything.
For the explorers out there, jumping between past, present and future will reveal secrets. Visit the past to improve the future. When you make two levels have good futures, the third level will take place in the good future. Without the exploration, every level goes by after a few minutes.
New to the series is a Metal Sonic who kidnaps Amy shortly into the game. At some point you will need to race Metal Sonic to get her back. It adds to the unique boss fights. The boss battles are what make the game stand out from other old school Sonic games. You need to defeat each Robotnik boss in different ways other than the traditional 'hit him.' Some you'll need to run fast while dodging objects. Others you'll need to go up on hovering rocks and still others involve chasing him.
Since the game came out between Sonic 2 and 3 there are only a few items to find in boxes. Items like extra lives, 10 extra rings, super fast shoes, temporary invincibility and a shield barrier that lets Sonic take an extra hit. There is nothing new that you won't find in the first two Sonic games.
Unique to the Sonic CD is an animated cartoon introduction and then another when you beat the game, before and as credits roll. Both are nice to look at and pretty brief. They add some much needed flair outside the game to make it feel different from the other old school Sonic games. Sonic CD shouldn't take more than 3 hours to complete. Once you complete the game, it unlocks Tails as a playable character. Tails is a fox that plays the same as Sonic, but if you tap the jump button in mid air, Tails can helicopter around for a while. I can understand why he is an unlockable character, because with him it becomes far too easy to just hover over entire levels.
The game feels easy up until a point, which lets new players get far into the game before it gets challenging.  To add to how easy the game is, if you use all your lives, you start at the same level you were at, instead of restarting the zone. The backgrounds are beautiful and have a lot going on. The levels feel large enough to get lost in. The real challenge is traversal, because the enemies are quite forgettable. Sonic will be bouncing off of springs, doing loops, running up ramps, zooming through tubes, running against treadmills, avoiding crushing blocks, hopping on enemies, running around what I can only call gears, but they're not and much more. It didn't feel to me like there were many moments for Sonic to get up to top speed.
Even with the future and past dynamic, the game feels like a big sidestep from Sonic 2. There is nothing new here, but is that a bad thing?

To tell you the truth, I never played Sonic CD before, but this was my first time playing, and it was a pretty good start!

The visuals in this game, while not particularly impressive, are still quite beautiful. Everything looks peaceful and pretty like a tropical island should. However, there are some graphical glitches, particularly with the lighting. Weird waves of shadows pass over the island every morning which is really annoying. If you look at the sun through the heat waves coming from a campfire it gets this blinking black swirl in it. And at night, you can cause a lunar eclipse by holding a coconut in front of the moon. I kind of like that one, though. It makes me feel like a god. My biggest issue with the visuals, though, is that from a distance, every island is represented by the same generic "icon" on the horizon, so they all look the same. Also, you don't cast a shadow or have a body when you look down, so there's that. Maybe you actually died in the plane crash at the beginning and you're really just a ghost who thinks he's still alive?
I realize that the developers probably decided to go with a minimalist UI to increase immersion, but there's something they seem to have overlooked. The player can't feel what the in-game avatar is feeling. Therefore, without a visual indicator there is no way to know when you are hungry, tired, etc. A message will pop up when you are about to die of hunger, but by that time it's almost too late to do anything about it. (EDIT: Okay, I found the hunger/thirst/health indicators. You have to hold up your watch with "F" and left click and it changes the display. So the UI is there, you just have to search for it. Would have been nice if that had been mentioned in the tutorial.) Also, the inventory doesn't make any sense. Four big sticks, four heavy rocks, and four tiny sardines all take up the same amount of space.
Which leads me to another issue. Half of the design elements of this game seem to have been chosen for gameplay reasons and the other half for the sake of realism. For instance, yucca and potato plants regrow after a day or two once you harvest them. On the other hand, palm trees never grow and never grow back after you cut them down. If you get sick or poisoned you will NEVER get better until you use an item to cure yourself. My sea urchin poison lasted about a month and a half before I found antibiotics. Also, a campfire will burn perfectly fine in the rain. Either this was a decision made to make the gameplay slightly less tedious, or it's just a result of the game being incomplete.
The biggest issue plaguing this game, however, is the lack of content, though I do realize that this is an early access game and therefore not complete. Still, there are very few resources and foods that you can find on the islands (which all pretty much look the same, btw). The foods are coconuts, fish, crabs, and potatoes (hello scurvy) and the building/crafting resources are sticks, rocks, lashings, and palm fronds. There are other items you can find and use, but as far as I can tell you can only find them on shipwrecks and they're only used to craft two things: the boat motor and bandages. Most islands only have 1-2 shipwrecks (3-4 if you're really lucky), most shipwrecks have only one container (although bigger ships have more), and one item per container, except lockers. Some containers have nothing in them and if you're lucky like me a container will spawn inside a tree so you can't retrieve the item. It took me 54 days in game to find a compass and 55 days to find the last piece I needed for the boat motor and antibiotics to cure the sea urchin poison I got around day 10.
So here is what needs to be done to make this game as awesome as it can be (and it has the potential to be really frickin' awesome):
-Drastically increase the variety of:
+naturally occurring foods and crafting materials
+interactive AND non-interactive flora and fauna (why are there no birds or flowers?)
+size and distance between islands (for instance a large island or a group of smaller islands within swimming distance of each other should be possible)
+the placement and number items in containers (more than one item per container, more than one container per shipwreck, containers found in other places than shipwrecks, such as washed ashore on the beach).
-Fix the lighting issues I mentioned above (except the moon one, and maybe the player shadow if I'm right about the ghost thing).
-Add dynamic events. Here are some ideas:
+Dolphins jumping and playing near your island or raft.

I bought Dragon's Dogma during Summer sale for 12$, I heard it was good game but didn't really expect much, thought it was just "another RPG" but it turned out to be one of the best RPGs I've ever played.
It's hard to compare DD:DA with other RPGs, I'd say it's Japanese Skyrim but Skyrim gameplay is nowhere as deep. DD:DA is a mixture of all the good things you've played from other video games: the non-linear sandbox structure from TES games, the giant boss grabbing mechanic from Shadow of The Colossus, the badass combat mechanic from Devil May Cry, the challenges that require survival and management skill from Dark Souls and classic RPGs. Because of this, DD:DA is one of the most underrated, fun and well-designed RPG ever made.
Pros:
- Perfect combat system (if not almost). As mentioned, the combat has elements from action games such as Devil May Cry, Dark Souls,... every monsters have weak spots that you must learn while fighting them, and there are some epic giant boss fight slightly similar to fighting a colossus in SoTC. What makes combat so satisfying are the badass animations and badass skills, combine with the sounds and gore effects, you can feel every strikes you inflict on the enemy. You can also change class easily and enjoy your own playstyle without having to worry about "optimal build" and what not.
- Pawn system: you must create a custom companion for yourself, its appearance, personality, class will be your invention. As you progress, this pawn will learn from you and become more aware with the world such as how to find a weak spot on monster, how to do a certain quest easier,... The online feature of this game is that you can let people hire this pawn of you to help them as you can hire people's pawns to help you. It's a complex system but it's very rewarding and gives meaning to your progress. To keep it short: you are giving life to an AI.
- Rich character customization system: you can pretty much create anyone, just Google "Dragon Dogma Character Creation" and you will see what I'm talking about. Also, armors and clothings are excellent designed and varied to serve your fashion obsession, there are also well animated cloaks to increase your character's badass-ness.
- Great music.
- The big bad dragon is twice the size and twice the challenge of Alduin, he also says things that will leave you pondering, I kid you not.
Neutral:
- Lot of people say this game has no story at all, I disagree. Story in this game is minimal and somewhat predictable, but it's there and it has some interesting lore that you must figure out by yourself. And if it helps, I'm the kind who prefer story over gameplay and I think this game does great enough for its minimal storytelling.
Cons:
- Notice board quests aka MMO fetch quest: while they can be fun to do in early game and makes the game feel alive, there are just too many of them and most of it are more trouble than it's worth (e.g: take this guy to that place that's at the end of your unexplored map, kill 50 of this thing that you just killed a bunch of them an hour ago,...). So It's only recommended to do these quests if you are interest in the reward or looking to farm exp.
- Due to the vague, non-linear structure of the game, the chance for you to miss something is high and the consequence can be severe. So it's recommended to check out the missable quests guide if you don't want to missing out.
- Some voice actors can be laughable bad.
- The above are just minor things, however, there is one thing I really dislike about this game: the terrible late game grinding, especially Dark Arisen's content. If you want those fancy late game loot, you must either spend another 20 hours to grind for it or using trick to still grind for it but in an hour or two, because these rare loot have a dropping chance of 2%, seriously. It gets worse with the DLC where the game will prevent you from using the farming method from base game, and while the loot have better chances to drop in DLC, you will most likely get the same loot 3-4 times while wasting a bunch of currency that's mostly coming from people who hired your pawn, so you will definitely be screwed if no one hires your pawn.
In the end, over 100 hours of fun for a 12$ game is more than I could have asked for. I can say that I've never been addicted to a non-linear open world RPG like this since Skyrim, and it means this is the kind of game that will stuck in my hard drive for a very long time.

The most fun aspect of Dragon's Dogma was the combat system. It features a grappling system unlike i've seen in any other game, And that together with a wide variety of special abilities that are unlocked and can be switched in and out via certain innkeepers, it made fighting a very dynamic and interesting situation.
As an RPG it's very limited, The only real roleplaying i found was to choose who will be your "beloved" But what kept me immersed in the situation, more often than not were the very talkative and helpful pawns.
Pawns are beings in dragon's dogma that look like humans, except they want for nothing, never age or die and live only to serve (how convenient) Your own custom pawn presents a very interesting dynamic in which you can make up for your character's weaknesses by having a constant companion who levels up along with you, although their AI is limited and some vocations are less ideal for them.
Vocations are the way you can decide what your characters job is. They determine which weapons and skills are available to you as well as what stats you will gain on a level up. There are basic, advanced and hybrid vocations:
First you will get Fighter, Strider (A rogue) and Mage.
Their advanced forms are Warrior, Ranger and Sorcerer,
The hybrid vocations are not available for pawns, they are:
Mystic Knight, (mage/fighter) Magic Archer (mage/strider) and Assassin (fighter/strider)
I personally found a lot of joy just running around the territory, which is not only beautiful, but it’s also filled with encounters all over that will keep you interested to find more. I personally found that the sheer number of herbs and spices you could combine was overwhelming, but in reality you only need to remember like 5 combinations of things to make healing and stamina items for your long adventures.
Bitterblack Island is an interesting beast, in that you could just run through it and get pretty high tier loot. But you’re not gonna be able to use it unless you collect a lot of Rift Crystals. But that’s completely up to you if you want to grind the place which is like, level 30-40 at the barest minimum. and that level increases as you progress through.
With all this said i heartily recommend this game if you enjoy a good adventure in a fantastic action/RPG made by capcom.

Dragons Dogma is a very solid action RPG with great combat, a simple but effective and fun class system, and a beautiful open world. I played Dragons Dogma: Dark Arisen on PS3, and must say that the PC version fixed some key issues. One key issue really. The PC version lets you turn pawn chatter off. I would highly reccomend this game to anyone who is a fan of The Elder Scrolls, Demons/Dark souls, or any other open world or action oriented RPGs.
------
Pros
>Fluid fun combat
Simple combat combined with fluid class ablities integrated, imagine combat similar to souls games except ditch the clunky targeting mechanic.
>Extensive character creator
This is one of the best character creators out there, you can really make pretty much whatever you want. It might be the best character creator Ive seen outside of an MMO, it has a body customization thats unmatched allowing you completely change the height and build of characters, on top of this, your weight and height effect you in game!
>Beautiful design
I love the washed out color palette Dragons Dogma uses, it reminds me of Resident Evil 4 or the first Dark Souls. On top of that, Dragons Dogma has beautiful enviroments ranging from cliffside beaches, caves, forests, to one of the best designed medieval cities in a video game. Theres something artistic about the game design that other games, even ones with highly superior graphics, tend to lack.
>AI
Dragons Dogma has a pretty good AI, I dont think Ive ever had a moment where I thought the AI did something that was outright stupid.
>Open world
Beautiful Open world, slightly more restricted than Bethesda games with available paths and areas but still an entirely open world game.
>Boss fights and grabbing
Shadow the Collossus boss fight mechanics, allowing players to climb on large enemy monsters to attack vunerable areas such as eyes or necks.
>Music
Dragons dogma has fantastic music, absolutely beautiful, Id reccomend the soundtrack in addition to the game,
Cons
>Only one save file at a time
I dont know what the designers were thinking when they decided to only allow one save file on the game, there are ways to work around this but they require playing with game files which is a hassle and always has the risk of accidentally goofing up and losing a character.
>Game length
I am very slow with my RPGs and completed most quests before finishing the game, still, Id estimate it only took me around fourty five hours. Thats fine for the length of a main storyline but I know there are people out there who didnt do every side quest like I did who beat the game in half the time.
>Story
If you like cryptic up to interpretation stories that go totally over your head akin to Dark Souls, youll love the story of Dragons Dogma. Everyone else will be left going, "Huh?" and "Wait, what?" at the end of the game, like I was.
>Travel
There are affordable fast travel stones you can purchase now in the game but with only two destinations to travel to and having to unlock and set other fast travel points, getting around Dragons Dogma can be a chore.

I got this game because I needed to quench my thirst for a new and innovative flight combat game, and also is was on sale.
I'll start with the good things, the game looks great, I don't have much to complain about it.  Nothing special, but they do the job.  The game is fairly easy to jump into, creating your own personal vector is quick and easy.  The controlls for this game are great!  No joystick required, I actually think it would make the game worse!  I've encountered no controll problems within the game.  Gameplay is very innovative and fast paced, you can either hover, or whiz around the map.  There are plenty of weapons to choose from, but the game lacks balance in terms of weapons.  The maps are all very different from one another, we just need more of them.
Now with the bad things, let's start with the UI.  Yeah sure you open up the menu and it looks fine, but when you get into the games is when you encounter problems.  All of the text is in lower case, and in arial font.  It's like they forgot about the whole in game UI and just put in a rough draft.  The "killcam" or whatever's text is the worst, the "emblems" for the players look dreadful, and the names of the guns are different from their original title.  For example if I get killed by and "LMG", it won't say "LMG", it will say "lmg1".  It's very annoying.  My next complaint is with the "booster" pads.  Their placement is just awful, I'm not even sure if their supposed to be a bonus or a trap.  When you go into a booster, you have absoluetly no control of your Vector for about 3 seconds.  Plus everyone will see you because the boosters are loud as hell, so you're going to get shot.  Sometimes their placed right at spawn, killing at least half of your team at times.  You have to go in right in the center of the booster if you don't want to hit something.  If you touch an edge, you're dead.
If you like flight games, wait for this one to go on sale, it's not worth $25.

Tooth and Tail is definetely a charming RTS game with a unique art-direction and gameplay mechanics, beautiful soundtrack, pleasing graphics (even though pixelated ones) though is seriously underdeveloped and sketchy. In this game, the general of your army acts as a cursor, which handles the deployment affairs, while units attack enemies on-sight and do the basic jobs on their own. Maps are procedurally generated, which is good and bad at the same time for the obvious reasons. But the main subject here is the core gameplay, which feels kind of smartphone-y, like it belongs more to the phonegame market rather than the PC market. Unit variety is small, mechanics are scanty and the matches don't go on for too long, rarely ending in more than 20 minutes. It has a pace of a game you play in a vehicle or while traveling to kill time with big emphasis on zergrushing and blitzkrieg tactics.
Nonetheless, I'll give it 6.5 / 10, because it can still deliver a good dose of fun for a casual player, a really casual one.

Say what you will of the graphics, love them or hate them this game is RTS to its core. I have to admit I wasn't a fan of the pixelated direction they took, but when I got my hands on it I found myself incapable of putting it down. The game is easy to learn but challenging to master; mainly due to the fast pace of the games. The theme of the game is also fantastic. I was a fan of the Redwall books and even if you aren't or don't know what those books are there is something extremely satisfying about a vickers machine gun toting badger laying waste to your enemies while being healed by volunteer medic pidgeons!
The campgaing is enjoyable and surpisingly grim, but where the game truly shines is in the multiplayer. Yes, the maps are procedurally generated which can mean an inherant advantage/disadvantage at times. But, that is where I found myself really being hooked. Yes there was some disadvantage to a particular map, but I was able to find some aspect of the map that I could use against my opponent. At times you are gonna get wrecked because the map was just not in your favor, but given the fact that the matches are short (10min or less) and the fact that that very same disadvantage could mean your advantage in the next game means it really isn't a problem.
First and foremost, this is an RTS game for RTS lovers. HOWEVER, for those new to the genre who may have never thought of playing one this is an oustanding game to discover RTS games. That being said, for $20 this game is a steal! The devs are committed to their product and have been doing a fantastic job of keeping the community up to date on where they are and where they plan to go. Considering the enjoyment I have had with it I cannot help but reccomend this game as a solid buy that is worth every penny.

I highly recommend this game to anyone on the fence about it. $20 is easily a fair price for a gem of a strategy game that seems to have come out of nowhere.

Ever wanted to be a samurai?
To throw caution to the wind and run around town in a loincloth, brandishing a sword?
To beat people senseless, then force them to join your dojo?
Or how about sneaking into someone's house at night to wisk little old ladies away to the inn for a frolic?
If you said yes, to any of these things, this could be the game for you!
WOTS4 isn't a game for everyone. I've heard a lot of people say something to the extent of "It's like GTA in fuedal Japan!"...which isn't quite accurate.
The game IS open world, and it does have quite a few things you can do in it, but about the only real similarity here is the open world part.
The story isn't anything amazing, and the game is pretty short, but the fact that your decisions and actions (or even inactions) will have a big impact on the story is a big plus. This also affects the ending you will get, as there are several different ones.
Fail to protect someone during a fight? No, the game's not over, but that character is now dead. You will go on.
It also has a pretty quirky (and at times perverse) sense of humor that reminds me of some of the old Japanese samurai drama/comedy shows. It doesn't take itself too seriously, and clearly doesn't expect you to either.
The game isn't without it's faults though, and many of them are pretty easy to see. The AI isn't the most brilliant. People in town will walk around, bump into each other frequently, and either apologize or end up picking a fight.
The scripted scenes at times look like everyone's waiting for the "slower" character to realize he's supposed to say something. Animations aren't always the best, and the graphics, while they do the job, aren't exactly stunning. There's also the shortness. It took me just over 2 hours to beat the game on my first play-through. (Though I focused pretty heavily on the main story, and didn't do many sidequests.)
There's a lot of good though, that really overpowers the faults. The game is actually fun. The corny humor is refreshing, and there's plenty of things to do in the game.
The sword fighting system is quite nice, and responsive. On easy mode button mashing might get you through most things, but on higher difficulties you'll need to be more careful. I also love the variety of skills, weapon upgrades/mods, fighting stances, and so on that you can use.
The number of endings and different ways of playing mean that even though the game is short, it has a pretty good amount of replay value.
Overall:
Pros:
-Fun Gameplay
-Quirky humor
-You can be a naked samurai with an afro, and mustache, and nobody cares.
-Replay Value
-Your choices direct the story
-Lots of character, weapon, and fighting style customization options.
-You can try to pick up women and get rejected, just like in real life!
-The old blacksmith looks like an asian Duke Nukem.
-At $25, it's pretty inexpensive.
Cons:
-Rather Short
-Graphics reveal it's a PS3 port.
-Oddball glitches here and there (though they're more funny than harmful.)
-Cut scenes are pretty robotic, though entertaining.
-Kinda stupid AI.
Overall I'd give it a 7.5/10, mostly from sheer fun value.
