Good old Chinese Genocide simulator.
Dynasty Warriors (DW) has been around for a while now, and I'm sure most of us have played it at least once, giggling like a maniac at the sheer level of destruction we wrought on these poor, unarmoured peasants.
It's not uncommon to get over 1000 kills in a single level - and there are a lot of levels.
DW is based of the Romance of the Three Kingdoms, a semi-historical narrative based on the period of the Three Kingdoms in ancient China. There are 4 main campaigns available - Wu, Shu, Wei, and Jin - with a fifth campaign based on the exploits of the infamous Lu Bu. Each of these campaigns has a split that occurs the second time you play them (assuming you hit all the requirements), allowing you to complete either the historical end, or an alternative end (which generally isn't as bleak as the history can be. What? You thought ancient Chinese warfare has happy end?).
The gameplay itself is the best I've seen from the series, and it allows you to take two different weapons (which was new to me). In a way, it's kind of like a fighting game between two officers, it's just that hundreds of mobs get in the way.
The character roster is also insane, with dozens of playable characters, each with their own unique attacks.
In terms of optimisation, it runs really well for me - I get a near constant 60fps, only dropping when there are a LOT of men and particle effects on the screen.
In short, DW8 is easily the best DW game I've ever played, and you should really give it a shot.

Tex Murphy was a staple of my growth into manhood and I have an incredible amount of nostalgia for the old series. When Tesla Effect hit Steam, I purchased immediately, because I had a feeling they were going to deliver and make a decent adventure game.
Man, was I way off-mark.
They made an INCREDIBLE adventure game. Like, really friggin' nailed it. Most adventure games nowadays suffer from uninventive puzzles (use a broom to sweep, use gun to shoot), but Tex Murphy is the first game in the last decade that has made me feel like I was enjoying the adventure games of my youth, exploring and inspecting everything, fitting together random, disparate items in hopes of gaining some positive outcome. And, more often than not, the game can be brain-bendingly difficult, which means that finally discovering the answer is so incredibly satisfying.
Big Finish Games really struck the anvil while the fire was hot with this game. The music is amazing. The cutscenes and atmosphere are dead-on some of the best cyberpunk/noirpunk I've seen, and the FMV in this game is far and above the best I've seen across any medium. Even the actors are quite good at keeping you immersed in the game.
There are only a few problems. The textures are fairly low-resolution in the game, but considering the amount of FMV and the fact that the game is a love-letter to late 80s-early 90s adventure games and isn't over 30gigs, I'm completely okay with it. The game is of a really decent length, but a lot of that may have been because I spent so much time exploring every possible nook and cranny, so you could feasibly finish this game in a few short hours by powering through. Additionally, there were some areas where I found a few holes in the world that I couldn't get through, but could still see through the map, which is a bit of a problem.
Otherwise, though, this game is a solid 9 out of 10 for me. If you aren't a fan of the originals, this might be a pass for you, but I highly recommend at least giving the demo a shot and deciding for yourself if you want to purchase it, because I guarantee it is at least worth some of your time. This is the first time I have ever seen a franchise resurrect itself in another era of electronic media and not only pay PERFECT homage to it's predecessors, but grown and delivered a compelling experience of it's own. It's also the only adventure game I've played that understands it's audience's sense of humor and level of maturity.
Please please please give this game a chance, for your own sake, and support a great developer, so they continue delivering amazing gaming experiences.
-Palin

20 years ago FMV was a very new and cool concept in PC gaming.  It promised to bring ultra realism and a whole new level of immeration in gaming.  Unfortunately the games that came out with FMV were less than steller.   One game series that went all in on FMV was the Tex Murphy series of adventure games.  Tex 3, 4, and 5 (Under a killing moon, Pandora, Overseer) all featured this new technology.  The Tex series was an enjoyable if cheezy adventure game series that focused on an out of luck PI who was 2 parts buffon and 1 part saint.  The draw initially was the FMV but the series milked successfuly the humor and puzzle elements for all they were worth.  For the most part the Tex series enjoyed moderate success with gamers but not at the same level of a Monkey Island or a Sierra title.
Now we have yet another Kickstarter romp though an old game series that is long since dead.  Very dead in fact....   Its been 16 years since Overseer left Tex fans on a clifhanger.  As one of those fans I have to admit I was excited at the prospect of seeing the old Tex in action again and finally geting a proper send off for a beloved series.  Its painful for me to admit but I REALLY wanted to see another game in this series.  Enough for me to fork over 100 bucks 2 years before it was released. In this case I think it might have been better to have Tex stay dead.
While the game industry has moved on its clear the designers either havent or thought they had to stick to the old forumla because TeslaEffect is basicly a slight upgrade from their last outing.  The backgrounds are so pixulated that I think I am back playing in 1997.   Some of the actors are either not professionals or just mailing in their performances (similar to what we saw in UAKM).   The puzzles seem random and dont tie into the world and its story.  When playing as tex and choosing from a text bubble the options are so random it really doesnt matter what option you choose or to even bother to read them.  Clearly the skills of the storytelling and game design for these folks havent advanced a day from the late 90's
The story itself is corny (what you would expect from the series) and at times hard to follow.  There are many many gems hidden for Tex fans to reminace about the past.   Its mostly overdone and in poor quality, which leaves this Tex fan disapointed.  As of this date (May 2014) there are many bugs still in the game, most are of the audio nature.  The game can get offsync with the audio and at times the audio will cut completely out for a few seconds.
Bottom line is that if you really really really must see a new tex game its probably worth it to you to spend the 15-20 bucks for the cost.  The other 99.999999% of the population however should stay away.   Literally this game is made for about 20-30 indiviudals who stayed true and talked tex in message boards (Unoffical Tex Murphy) all these years.
Me I thank Tex for the fun we had in the 90's but to me he died in that speeder in Overseer.
Happy trails Tex

While I enjoyed the early portions of the game the overall sameness of it beats you to the ground, sadly. There is a crafting system implemented like most games that fall into the "Survival" category but, it is just far too limited to be worthwhile. Head over to the Wiki for a better idea of what I mean. You'll find it to be adorably finite and while were on the subject would it be so horrible to have one of these type of games come with a complete crafting list in-game? You shouldn't need to be go to a search engine, smart phone, or tablet to find out how to accomplish a basic task. Not talking about a secret or some special feat here.
Next up the sharks. I happen to love sharks always have since I was a child and I love the fact that games are staring to make a point to have them where they fit in. However, every time I witness one of these astounding marine creatures it's always met with a sigh. Their always this blood thirsty enemy and are way too damn plentiful. Sharks are predators no one with a pair of brain cells to rub together will argue that however they are animals first and foremost. There are times when they hunt and other times when they're surprisingly docile. I remember seeing a Go Pro video on YouTube of a Hawaiian model diving down and swimming with Great Whites. She would get up close to them, touch them, and even grab onto their dorsal fin to get pulled. Most incredible thing, they didn't even so much as nibble on her! As long as she didn't hurt or threaten them they couldn't cared less if she was there. No developer seems to fully grasp this.
When you're in the water and the Tiger Shark makes an appearance it should be terrifying, especially if it's a Sand Tiger. Nope, swim up to it start hitting it and it'll just swim away and by swim I mean it simply moves slightly faster than regular. It seems more annoyed than angry or fearful that your trying to kill it. Not once did one of these Tigers make any concerted effort to so much as injure me if I was striking it. Recently they gained the super power to teleport but, that's another issues entirely. When I came across a Black Tip Reef Shark I was surprised by it's nature. That being that it was the correct one for this animal as both species (White and Black) Reef Sharks are passive towards humans in real life, once again, as long as their not threatened. I can say I was impressed. One last incident before I move on and a joy for you it involves that much feared predator the Great White.
I'll set the scene for you, I'm in the middle of the midday Pacific paddling to a nearby island. Halfway there a bump shifts me on the raft. I look around quickly, peering into the ocean in search of what might have caused it only to have my heart leap into my throat. A Great White Shark was circling my insignificant raft attempting to put me into the water! I kept paddling as there was little I could do to repel the beast. I crossed my fingers and prayed for success in my journey to the neighboring spit of land. Another bump vibrated through my raft, I look once more only to see another Great White circling! I persist yet again with my situation growing all the more dire as I proceed. Then again a bump. Though I dread, I look once more to see that the two had become five! And then my immersion was broken. Really? Not only do I have the reverse fortune to be harassed by one Great White but, five of them!? Since when have these creatures become the "Wolves of the Sea"? When did these typically solitary hunters come together to get a acquire a measly morsel like myself that couldn't so much as sate the appetite of one of them let alone five? Point being fix the animal nature and appearance rate fellas.
I brought such mention to the sharks as they're a big part of the experience with each encounter being memorable so point to Beam Team Games on this one. However, after the rudimentary survival, traveling, wreck diving, crafting, and shark fighting you'll find there is very little else to do. There are no objectives or goals to aspire to complete and after a short while your left bored. There is a severe lack of motivation in these style of games to continue playing after an hour or two and that needs to be addressed. I read that such things will be implemented into the game at a later date as well as controller support and co-op which I look forward to but, at the moment it's a bit bare. I get how the developers have organized how they intend to update this game. First the world with it's animals and weather effects then making sure the performance is rock solid. It's just that I wish they did all that before Early Access as I feel would have yielded a better overall experience instead of this rather basic one. Could we also get some ambient music like in the trailer, dependent on where we are and what's taking place. Just to liven up the experience, you know what I mean?
I sincerely hope that Beam Team Games put more and more effort into "Stranded Deep" as this, with what little it has, does manage to standout from the pack. Even though that may be based more on it's local then anything else. I however cannot in good faith recommend this to anyone outside of the most avid of players of this genre. What it is at the moment is a glorified demo and showcase of what's to come more so than what's already on offer. If your wondering why I glanced over the gameplay is because it's sadly unexceptional, very by the numbers minus the wreck diving that just blurs into it's self given the time. I don't hate this nor do I berate the team behind it. Honestly I wish them the best of luck and hope this game becomes everything they wanted it to be.

Wait, have I not reviewed this game? It's pretty much the best. If you like twin stick shooters, dark humor, and more or less infinite replay value with runs that surprise me to this day despite having 300+ hours clocked on it at the time I write this, you're probably already playing it, but if not, you should be.

If you liked the original Legend of Zelda for the NES then this is a must-play. It also has a rather interesting backstory to uncover through somewhat cryptic hints. You also may like it if you liked Super Meat Boy, as it has quite a few references to that game.
Honestly, I've never had a single issue with this game. I don't know why anyone would EVER give this game a bad review other than them just not liking it in general, and that's just personal preference. No, this game isn't for everyone, but it is what it advertises to be, and more.
Here's a checklist. If you enjoy these, then you'll probably love this game like I do.
-Nearly infinite replay-ability
-Difficulty that progresses as time goes on
-Very hard to 100% complete, leaving you occupied for a VERY long time (I have 100 hours as of this being posted and I'm not even halfway done with fully completing the game)
-Interesting item combos that will surprise many
-Very similar to the original TLoZ for NES as mentioned above
-Backstory that's entertaining to explore/look into
I could go on, but it'd be ridiculous to list the hundreds of positive things this game has for people to look forward to.
Anyways, with all of that being said, there are only THREE main things that may ward people off. Those things are:
1. Difficulty. While the game may start off easy (depending on how lucky you are sometimes), it DEFINITELY gets bone-crushingly hard after a while.
2. Gore/Grotesque. While I highly doubt anyone would deny a game for gore (especially because this game has pixel graphics), this game certainly does have blood and just straight up nasty stuff in it. No, not the 18+ kind of nasty, but the disgusting kind of nasty. This never really bothered me because of the cartoon + pixel-style graphics, but I could kinda see how someone would be bothered by it.
3. Religion. If you are a very religious Christian, you would probably hate this game's backstory as it has to do with Christianity and can be perceived negatively. Without spoiling much, the most I'll say is yes, you can make deals with the devil, but that option is entirely up to you. In fact, not choosing to do so makes it more likely for angels to grant you rewards. However, if you're really serious when it comes to Christianity and take religious elements in games very seriously, you may not want to play this. It's really hard to explain this without spoiling much, but if you don't mind it being spoiled, I recommend you watch the 'Game Theory' video on this game. It goes in depth about this topic and explains a lot of things.
With all of that being said, I see why people would dislike the game, but I, for one, certainly don't, and there certainly isn't any reason to not recommend it. 10/10 all the way.

5/10  - That's being generous.
Baldur's Gate this certainly isn't
Pros -
1 - Graphically it's adequate. A step up from the games it claims to be emulating but certainly nothing to get all hot and bothered about. After 15 years, this type of game should look better than BG and BG2. Why people are going mad about this is as if its a new innovation, is beyond me.
2 - I'm struggling to think of a 2.
Cons -
1 - Character generation. Too many crap classes so that you either go for the old faithful fighter (dull, very dull) or a cipher (gets dull real quick). It all comes down to random dice rolls anyway, so it doesn't really matter what points you put where.
2 - As a game, either you're going to be new or old. If you're going to have new races, don't have elves or dwarves. Either forge your own identity, or don't. This just feels like a lazy attempt to pretend POE is somehow a new experience wrapped in a nostalgic bubble. By either description, it falls way short.
3 - Wow the items are dull. Looting your local grocery store would result in more interesting items than you'll generally find at the end of a dungeon in this game. You'll grind your way through generic mob after generic mob, just to find a chest full of crap. So then, you're left with crafting, which while available, feels half hearted and ill thought out. They added crafting as a tick box exercise, rather than make the effort to make it rewarding.
4 - Combat. Okay.....open You Tube and find the Benny Hill theme. Then start a combat. Play the theme as your enemies target your spell caster. Watch the spell caster flee around the screen, followed by the enemy, followed by your tank hopelessly trying to reacquire the enemy.
5- Combat. It's so bad it deserves more mentions. Combat will go like this. Fire off the spell you always fire off. Switch to your standard attack. Go downstairs. Make some dinner. Ring a friend. Come back to find the party still trading boring blows with boring enemies. This is if you're lucky.
6 - Combat - If you're unlucky, you'll fire off a spell and set your tank(s) fighting, only to find that your ranged attackers have bizarrely ceased to attack and are now stood around doing nothing. That or they've been killed by the super teleporting shadow monsters that appear on top of them. In this case, you have the choice to either try and run, dying immediately due to the absurd game mechanics, or stand and die anyway. Your spells are mostly useless, so you'll be presented with a big list of crap to choose from each time you level, rather than spells that feel useful. In 30 hours, I have never found an item with any kind of wow factor. Nothing that I equipped gave me any sense that the effort of slogging my way through the generic, uninspiring dungeon was actually worth it.
7 - The NPCs. Talking to strangers at the bus stop is more rewarding than engaging these generic, dull characters in conversation. They have as much life when they've been killed as they do alive. They have no reason to follow you and nothing much to say when they do. Baldur's Gate etc are old games now, but they managed to produce real characters. Fifteen years later and POE has undone this. I didn't care if they lived. I didn't care if they died. In an RPG of this price in 2015, that's just not good enough. I didn't expect Mass Effect character development, but I certainly hoped for more than walking cliches, that largely dissolved into taciturn automatons after their initial, uninvolving dialogue.
8 - The Lore/World - Lots of lore can be a good thing. It's been done well in other games. It's not done well here. It's like a commitee pulled together a load of standard fantasy fiction and slung it together to create a world notable only by it's staggering blandness. Blah, blah, elves, dwarves, blah, blah, ancient ruins, blah, blah dungeons. It's all so lazy and predictable.
9 - Having to rest to somehow regain your ability to use magic is a mechanic that was crap fifteen years ago. It belongs in table top roleplaying gaming, and that is the type of player attracted to POE. They want to play D&D again, but no one does anymore, so they wax lyrical about POE instead. That kind of limiting, tedious mechanic doesn't appear in computer RPGs anymore for a reason. Unless you're an old school roleplaying gamer, with the accompanying problems with OCD, this kind of mechanic has no place in computer RPGs.
10 - Price - If you loved BG and BG2, then maybe you'll like this. I didn't, but you might. Wait for a sale though. To price this in a similar band to Witcher 3 or DAI is ridiculous. What you're getting is a  facsimile of games that are 15 years old. There's nothing new here and certainly not one iota of innovation. I would argue that POE is in fact a huge step back from the old games it seeks to emulate. Don't pay full price for this. It's not worth it when you can pay a fraction of the price and pick up the original and vastly superior genre games from the early 2000s, like Baldur's Gate or Neverwinter Nights.
Conclusion- For the price, this just isn't good enough. POE is bogged down by a bland world, uninvolving characters and a dull, bugged combat system. I spent hour after hour hoping it would get better. That somehow the world would come to life. It never did. For 5.99 this game would be okay. For 34.99, it's a been one huge and, frankly unacceptable disappointment. It piggy backs on the reputation of much older and far superior games, without ever matching their achievements. Baldur's Gate will be remembered in another fifteen years. Barring bargain basement sales, POE will have been forgotten in fifteen months.

: Obsidian Entertainment
: Paradox Interactive
Note: I will try to be as spoiler-free as possible.
Note #2: I don't think I can do this game justice, but I'll try anyway.
==========
Quite possibly the best isometric CRPG to be released in recent years, Pillars of Eternity is an entirely new world expertly crafted and filled with lore created in the style of the classic Baldur's Gate and Icewind Dale games. Any fan of these games will instantly fall in love with Pillars of Eternity and it's similar design.
==========
Played from an isometric top-down view, Pillars is packed with things to do. You play the game entirely by mouse, pointing and clicking to navigate each area, converse with NPCs, battle enemies, and more. One of the best things about this game is that it is extremely detailed and immersive with it's superb storytelling. Pretty much exactly like the titles mentioned above. There is a literal TON of reading, as everything is presented to you in much the same way a dungeonmaster or storyteller in a tabletop game would. Every detail is spelled out for you, and you get to make you own choices in each dialogue. Most of these choices have a profound impact on the outcome of whatever quest you are on (people
and
die!), and even the main storyline.
You start out by creating a character from a huge list of options. There are a small handful of races, several classes, and you can even choose some regional differences for each race. You could easily spend and hour or more creating your first character. Along with your "main" character, there are 8 (10 with The White March Part I add-on) unique companions you can recruit. You can also create more characters to join your party after a certain point. Each character can be customized the way you see fit from an extensive list of spells, abilities, auras, talents, and equipment.
One of the big features of Pillars is the Stronghold. Shortly into the game you come into ownership of a stronghold called Caed Nua. Caed Nua, once owned, can be upgraded and repaired to offer you a variety of new features, goods, and services. For example, you can build an Inn that will allow you to rest. Another example is you can construct a barracks which unlocks the character creator. Also found underneath Caed Nua is an extensive maze-like dungeon, which can be explored throughout the game, with each floor getting more difficult.
There are many options in battle, and probably the most helpful (but sometimes annoying) of which is the Auto-Pause feature. This can be set to activate when any number of events occur, such as a character's Endurance dropping too low. Pausing allows you to survey the battlefield and make the best decision possible to turn the tide back into your favor.
An important part of any RPG is inventory management. With a game of this scope, there are naturally a ton of different items: weapons, armor, accessories, food, potions, scrolls, crafting ingredients, and more. With all of these items, you need a way to store and manage everything. Thankfully, each character has their own inventory, and you can freely move items between them at anytime. But the biggest boon to item management is the Stash. On your inventory screen, you will see a large button with a Treasure Chest on it. This is your Stash, which can be accessed from nearly anywhere, at anytime, and is seemingly infinite in capacity. If it has a limit, I never found it!
Most RPGs are packed full of quests and tasks, and with this comes th eneed to manage them. The quest log in Pillars is pretty detailed, giving a sort of summary of any actions taken during a quest. This is extremely helpful, in that if you take a break from the game you can easily come back and jump right back to what you left off on. This is a common complaint of some of the larger RPGs, that when picking the game back up after awhile players have no idea what they were last doing, so they start over. Pillars eliminates that problem entirely.
When you reach the edge of a map, you are able to leave the area and return to the World Map. From here, you can travel to any previously visited location no matter how far across the map it is. This fast travel is extremely helpful in navigating the world and completing objectives.
==========
If you liked the graphics of Baldur's Gate, then you'll love the updated style Pillars of Eternity offers. You can zoom in and out at anytime, and the closer you zoom in, the more detail you will see on nearly everything. The characters in particular are very well done, as are the environments and maps of each area. They all look superb.
I simply cannot say enough about how good this game looks. All of it is very well-made and designed, and really draws your eye to the details. It's just so detailed and beautiful as a result. The only downside is that there isn't too much variety. The entire base game map is mostly woodlands and forests, and all of the dungeons look really similar...stone and darkness. It isn't until you get the White March Part 1 add-on that you start to see more varied environments (SNOW!).
==========
Absolutely amazing. The soundtrack is wonderfully immersive, and extremely well-done. Making the soundtrack available in the store was a great move. Once I'm able to afford the Champion Edition upgrade, I'll definitely get it JUST for the soundtrack alone. I'm a huge fan of video game music anyway. I found no problems with any of it. Every track was expertly paired with the right situations in-game for full immersion.
The sound effects are extremely well done too, even footsteps. This is a game I play with my sound up full blast, there's a lot of details in each area that's conveyed via the sound. Each area has a lot of ambient effects, like crickets in a woodland setting or stones shifting as you traverse a dungeon.
==========
This game ran flawlessly on my low mid-tier rig. No hiccups whatsosver. No framerate drops, lag, stuttering, or random crashes. The framerate did appear to be capped at 30 though, as I never saw it go over that. I'll need to pay attention next time I play and make a note about it.
One of the main complaints (well, only complaint) I have with this game is that inbetween every single area you will run into a loading screen that takes anywhere from 5-15 seconds to clear off. Thankfully, these screens feature some beautiful artwork and often helpful tips about the game, so it's not too big of an issue.
==========
Pillars of Eternity is a MUST PLAY for fans of the CRPG genre. A truly immersive and expansive adventure that you can play your way. If you enjoyed any of the games mentioned at the top of this review, you *need* to have this game in your library. And with the recently released White March Part 1 add-on and accompanying patch that added some much needed features to the game (Party AI), it's gotten even better! Don't pass this up, it's well worth the price of admission.

Where to Begin....
First the things I like.....
Gameplay isn't bad for me. I like the graphics and the world that is created. Also the interesting characters that the world has in it and the way you form your group to explore and quest that world.  Some of the monsters are really interesting too. You can build an interesting character and then upgrade him or her and even change him or her if you want along with you main pawn too. You also get to travel with a group of helpers that provide interesting infor and comments as you go. You even get to swap out your helpers as conditions change. All this is great and fun to play with.
Now for one thing that drives me crazy. A role playing game is about following a course and a path to an end. This can be a long around path or a short one. It can be thru any number of mazes, trials, tricks, or other distractions and you still are givening the feeling you are "getting there" even if you don't know how. Along with these twists and turns, the player needs to feel that he is making progress toward a goal. (Completing a quest, working toward the end of the game, etc.) This game presented me with the one problem I have run into over and over again in certain role playing games.  That is finding yourself lost when trying to complete a quest by not being able to find out where to go due to  not having enough hints or pointers showing you the way. I've run into this a lot in this game. For example, "Find an item" and the NPC tells you to ask a certain person, but the map gives no clues where to look or points to an area that seems totally disconnected from what you're looking for.  Also, the game makes an assumption that the player "will know" what to do in certain situations when, in fact, the player may not have a clue. I've noted a number of times the game popped up a message and before you could read it it's gone and when you check the quest information, you can't find the infor you need. I've spend a great deal of time wandering around trying to find information to complete a quest and having a lot of trouble doing so. This gets very frustrating at times and sort of spoils the game play for me. To me, if a game points you toward a area, place, or person, and then, even if you take a round about route, you should be able to find that area, place, or person by being given hints, markers, and pointers as to where to go. I found this confusing in this game.
OK, all that said, I have enjoyed playing this game so far. I like this game, or I wouldn't be playing it anymore. I really suggest anyone considering this game get it and spend some time in a very interesting world it creates.

) is a light RTS featuring 8 bit graphics, a refreshing
-inspired setting, and an enjoyable but dark-in-tone campaign with a twist. The game's atmosphere and characters ooze charme and the blend of 8 bit gameplay assets and high-definition UI elements is executed very well. Mechanically,
confines both player control and field-of-view to a singular commander unit which serves as a glorified mouse cursor for base builiding and army movement orders. This significantly reduces the mechanical skills demanded from players and makes the game playable via controller, which is rare for an RTS. However,
mistake this game as easy.
The singleplayer (SP) campaign, which lasted ca. 9 h for me, serves mainly as an introduction to the 20 unit types. I enjoyed it despite some missions suffering from very uneven difficulty and pacing issues as a result of the randomly generated nature of the levels playing havoc with the predefined objectives. After finishing the campaign, Skirmishes against bots are your only further SP option. Unfortunately, bots up until Hard difficulty pose basically no challenge but harder bots will cheat, rendering them ineffective as a learning tool to prepare you for multiplayer (MP) matches.
Speaking of which, Unranked MP in my personal experience proved disappointing as there are few open lobbies at a time and many host seem to be afk. Luckily, Ranked MP - the main
of
- is well populated. Matches are shorter compared to other games in the genre, with rounds usually lasting 5-15 min. Despite
's deceivingly simplified gameplay mechanics, Ranked MP is punishing, revealing a surprising depth to the gameplay that casual RTS fans will struggle to live up to. This competetive streak clashes with the game's layed-back attitude concerning the control scheme and the aspect of random map generation, the latter of which can lead to very interesting but occasionally one-sided MP map configurations.
Casual RTS fans like myself will struggle to keep up in Ranked mode after finishing the medium-length campaign, which is enjoyable but by all means one big tutorial for MP. Bot matches get stale quickly. On the other hand, seasoned RTS veterans might long for more unit variety and more involved micro- and macro-management options, as well as oppose the random nature of the MP map "pool". In the end I'm left wondering who the audience for this game actually is.

Seemingly light on the surface, this 5-10 minute RTS feels action packed and beautifully made. Enviroments, Sound design, and gameplay are all crisp and satisfying. Usually i am one to criticize a game based on it's resource collection/management, but in Tooth and Tail it feels very fitting to the atmosphere and mechanics of the game. Wonderful introduction to the genre for someone who doesn't like the micro and laundry list of duties in a traditional RTS.

Innovation in a genre that hasn't seen much lately.
Tooth and Tail reminds me of Hearthstone or Heroes of the Storm in that it's a game that takes an existing genre and then works out how much complexity can be removed while still preserving the feel of gameplay.  Missions take 15 minutes or less, yet *feel* like the 30-45 minute battles of Dawn of War or Starcraft 2.  It's a brilliant distillation of all the genre's most thrilling aspects, but skipping 90% of the buildup.
I will note that economy optimization is minimal.  If you're looking for an Age of Empires style RTS where economic micro plays a prominent role, Tooth and Tail isn't that.  The economy in Tooth and Tail reminds me of The Battle for Middle-Earth or Dawn of War 1 (with Overwatch commands always on), where it's mostly about territory control.
Beyond gameplay, the game has a rather charming aesthetic that I've described as "the country Fievel's family was fleeing from in An American Tail."  It's a Russian revolution era world filled with talking animals who are fighting each other specifically to eat one another after multiple failed harvests.  The decision to use Russian-sounding Gibberish instead of voice acting is a little odd, but I assume it was to streamline the voice acting process (so you don't constantly hear your commander say the same 3-4 lines over and over).  The setting is equal parts warm and dark, reminding me, again, of Don Bluth's late-'80s, early 90's films.

A fast-paced RTS that keeps you on your toes. Humorous tone, great soundtrack, challenging but helpful campaign and over-all great gameplay. I may be biased because I love RTS games, but this is probably one of my favorite games now.
There are a few things that could use a little polishing, but overall I'd say it's a very good game and is enjoyable if you don't let a couple of losses get to you.
The maps are randomly generated, which provide good replayability to campaign, multiplayer and make the game unique each time, but does have the problem of occasionally screwing you up, but they have been making good efforts to try and keep it fair. No two situations are ever the same due to this map generation though, which is good!
The controls are so simple I don't think it'd take more than like 15 or less seconds to go over them. Gamepad support is also very good I hear, especially since it's an RTS, which typically would be impossible to make for gamepad.
The units are (debatably) pretty balanced as well. If you know what you're doing, you can at least last a while if you balance out food and unit production, regardless of what units you pick, and (once again debatably) every unit has a good counter.
It supports up to 4 players of both online and local (I think) multiplayer. Matches can range from FFA, 1v1s, 1v3s, 2v2s, etc. There is both ranked and unranked. Leaderboards exist too for the more competitive people.
It's quick and easy to get into online matches, but if they have a slow internet, it can be a pain to deal with the periodic freezes. Not much can really be done about that though. :/
Battles are fun and intense. There's been a few times where I was sure I was going to lose and then end up somehow wiping out their entire army with freshly-spawned units, or them losing due to starvation despite having them blowing up my last gristmill. The fact that you have to physically throw your commander into the fray and risk getting killed on-the-spot is one of the more intresting points that also helps kind of make you feel involved.
But either way, the sound of gunfire filling the air and the light of exploding artillery while the map goes up in flames is truly beautiful--chaos at its finest.
If you've ever heard of Redwall, the theme is pretty much that + World War I. Pretty interesting and fun. The story isn't exactly much but it does at least line up with the missions well! I haven't beaten it yet though.
Anyways, I definetly reccomend this game. If you like war-themes, RTS games, or animals, this is a great game for you.

This game is AWESOME.
It tends to be based around what so many new mainstream shooter games are based, but with a cool twist - a very spy-like game play.
Instead of running in guns-a-blazing, you can choose (and in some cases you have no choice) to do the mission the quiet, non-detectable way. The tools provided for you to work out your strategy are really fun to use. Makes you feel like a very gadgety spy.
That is also the other thing cool about this game... there's no A to B way of doing a mission. You are given the freedom to choose how you approach a mission. You can go in from the side, from top to bottom, or from the main entrance. It doesn't matter. It's about what works for you.
Even more, the co-op is great! Figuring out how to work together in order to get through a mission undetected is some of the most fun I've had with gameplay.
I definitely recommend this game. It rates well in all fields!

So, this game is great. You play a Samurai, arriving in a town with strife happening. Normally, one would not make any kind of difference... but because you play a Samurai, you can make a difference, with your legendary skills. Or die in day one to a nameless thug and be forgotten.
The combat is fun. It is easy to learn and hard to master. The true strength of all of the way of samurai games, is the replay ability. The story is generally short, but packed full of so many options and multiple endings that you can spend a very long time of samurai slaying hours to complete it all.
Many different swords you can collect and many styles to fight with. And, if you are truly a master, you can make your own style. "Haven’t messed with this yet."
If you are a fan of the previous Way of the Samurai games, you will like this one. I personally disliked 2 and 3, but this one feels right.
The main fault I feel this game has is the... really bad dialogue. The first of the series came out on the play station 1. Seeing is how this one is many years later, I don't think they really improved the quality of the dialogue very much. So few choices, but they make up for it because so many choices can lead to so many different things. However, far as I can tell, it also seems to be Japanese only with English subtitles. I feel this was to try and hide the fact that the voice acting is so terrible.
I also would have liked a bigger map, more places to go, more people to fight! I remember the... second? At Night the entire map turned into a warzone with everyone trying to kill everyone. Last thing is weapon durability. In the first one you could keep the same weapon and, with fighting correctly, could never break your sword.
In this one, no matter what you do, your sword loses durability points as you fight with it. Imo, this is kind of a negative. It almost feels like I have to use a secondary sword, and get kills on that one and save the good sword, with hardly any kills on it for the tough guys. Max durability is also imo kind of low.
Beyond that, I love this game a lot. I see myself playing it a lot. I hope to see some real DLC that adds maybe more to the dojo, another few areas even? Just.... More! What is here is solid and I want to play it through multiple times... but as always, if there was more to play through, it would be, well, more fun. :p
If you like sword fighting games, I would definitely pick this up for the low price tag it is.

I wasn't born in the nineties, but man, is this game good. The game was released for the ill-fated Sega CD, which had games that were badly made, mostly due to the fact that they relied on FMV too much, and the technology just wasnt there yet. Sonic CD was arguably the only good game for the Sega CD, and arguably the best Sonic game ever made. Sonic 2 was the first game I ever played, and this one just blows it out of the water. The Sega CD had some good features besides FMV, it allowed higher quality music, which even though the 16-bit music of the other sonic games were catchier, it still allowed great songs to be put into the game. The first issue i found, which worried me at first, was that i did not recognise the music in the intro. The intro music is just epic, but it appeared to have been replaced by a new song. Luckily, i found out that in the menu screen, if you go into the soundtrack option, you can switch it from the japan version to the american version. Another issue, was that the game appeared to be blurry, but once again, after digging into the options menu, i found an option to change the graphics to the original graphics. Another thing that Sega CD offered was larger games, and slightly improved graphics. Since this game came out before Sonic 2, it made sonic 2 look bland. It had some 3D moments, which were a bit too much in my opinion. The game has an awesome function where if you run past a sign that reads "future" or "past" fast enough, you can go into the future or past of a level, where its either ruined by robotnik or still in it's natural state. Another thing that Sonic CD had which Sonic 1, 2 and even 3 didnt have was the ability to save your game. People always left their consoles on so that they could finish Sonic 1 and 2, which was a problem. I personally think that if the Sega CD didnt have so many FMV based games, it could have been saved and even have had a better version of Sonic 2, which was actually going to be Sonic CD, before being redone. The Sega 32X was beyond saving, though. It should have been a separate console, which was pretty much what it was replaced by. The game remains pretty much untouched, which is a great thing. the only thing is that there are options to change the game, but you can turn them off.

Let's be serious.  This whole game is about one battle with metal sonic in a bad future, and it'll make you wish the entire game was about that alone between the actual fight and the music that accompanies it.
And you'll get this game (probably on sale) just because of that, and like it.

“Great sword-swinging fun!  A good game that has suffered (then mostly recovered) from console import issues.” (8/10)
Pros:
- Fun and challenging combat – easy to learn the basics, difficult to master, not a button masher for the most part
- Short but well written, branching storylines
- Player actions/choices matter
- Plot twists!!! (Again, player choices actually matter.)
- Massive replay value
Cons:
- Issues as an console import – includes occasional audio and graphics bugs, random game freezes/crashes, keyboard controls are cumbersome at best (glitches have improved drasticly after patches)
- Bootstrap method (money --> upgrade weapons --> harder quests --> more money --> repeat) character progression required during early hours of gameplay
- “Choices Matter” mechanic can be unforgiving at times, requires a “save early, save often, and in different slots” approach.
- Later fights may be a bit too difficult/hardcore for casual players (player vs. 25 mobs just as strong as them), even when playing on “Easy” mode.
Overall, Way of the Samurai 4 has been a terrific game for me.  Fun but challenging gameplay has been paired with great characterization and fantastic storytelling, to present a game that virtually has it all.  The branching plot lines are easy to follow thanks to the Event calendar, but pack surprise twists as your every action can affect the plot…  This game certainly deserves the “Choices Matter” tag.  In my case, I accidently killed the pharmacist NPC during a street brawl, only to find out he was needed for a later story event (and a scene reminding you he had been killed was included as part of the quest!).  There is so much to do that it is quite impossible to accomplish everything in a single play-through, and the game has been designed as such, having the bulk of your inventory and consequences for some of your actions carry over to the next save.  As a result, WotS4 also benefits from immense replay value.

Sonic CD is a pretty good game that took advantage of some great ideas, but after multiple playthroughs, I felt that it was marred by noticeable flaws which dragged down what would otherwise have been a solid game.
Time travel enhances the exploration factor to Sonic's already multi-tiered level design by creating secondary objectives that require seeking out specific objects, in addition to changing the terrain for each time zone. This gameplay element is reinforced thematically; if you don't find the badnik spawners, the zone enters a Bad Future where Eggman has soiled the landscape... but if you do destroy them, things look even better than in the Present, and as a bonus all of the enemies are destroyed. I always feel a certain sense of satisfaction from going to the Past, destroying the spawner, and then going into the Future of that same level to enjoy the scenery and rack up rings and 1ups ("I did this, and now I'm reaping the rewards"). You can also create a good future by collecting all of the time stones (which also gives you the "good" ending, as miniscule a difference as it is).
There are two main problems with this factor of the game: the sole method of travelling through time is obnoxious, and the secondary objective is ultimately not well incentivized.
Time posts allow you to try to build up speed; once this hedgehog reaches 88 mph, a cutscene will play and Sonic will then find himself in the same spot forward or backward in time. Well... it's inaccurate to say you go through time by "building up speed", it's more that you go at "run speed" for a certain amount of time, then the HUD indicator starts blinking, and if you're still at running speed for a certain amount of time, you complete the time travel sequence... otherwise you lose the ability.
This system is stiff and unforgiving. Sonic's camera doesn't give you enough room to plan ahead for certain terrain when going fast, which makes it very easy to lose momentum just after you reach the "blink" mode. Unless you stop, walk around the act, and strategize a track that you can sprint through, it's usually more favorable to find two springs close to each other so you can bounce around and circumvent the challenge in a stupidly easy fashion. It all feels very clunky and not exceptionally well skill indexed.
It would have been more favorable if Sonic could go through time by finding giant rings or something similar, like at the end of the levels or in Sonic 3's hidden rooms. Actually, why not make it so that Sonic's peel-out mode instantly transports Sonic to the next time zone so you don't even have to create this ugly speed system for it? The peel-out isn't even that great of an addition to begin with; the spindash lets you do pretty much the same thing but in roll mode.
The other thing is that it's honestly a lot easier to create good futures by just beating the special stages. You don't have to go through the time post ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t or hunt for the spawners, and plus you only have to do it seven times if you're good enough (there are twice as many spawners in comparison, not counting the Metal Sonic holograms), and so if you just want to beat the game optimally and quickly, you really just have to ignore the Past for the most part, which devalues a good chunk of the gameplay. And hell, even if the game allowed you to start every level in the Past, you'd still have to figure out where the spawner actually is, which sometimes feels like finding a needle in a haystack. And once you find it, there's usually very little opposition keeping you from actually destroying it, which makes it a bit underwhelming.
I love the idea behind the time travel gimmick, and it's a great fit for Sonic's levels because of how diverse and multilinear they are to begin with. However, I also believe it's not as good of a fit for Sonic's _mechanics_ as it would have been for other platformers, like Metroid or Castlevania, or even something fairly simple like Mario. Levels with time travel dynamics work best when it creates design space for puzzles, exploration, and combat. While Sonic does inherently have a good deal of exploration, it's far more focused on the momentum-based physics than it is on gimmick puzzles or even badniks, and so it's difficult to really expand on this through the game's gimmick.
Speaking of badniks, this game is hands-down the easiest of the classics. Sonic Team had some of the best ideas for bosses in this game, but they're squandered due to positioning/blink time exploits on the player's part as well as overall just being too forgiving. There are very few death pits in this game in general, the only one even coming to mind being on the last level, and the final boss itself is a joke. It's still possible to game over if you're new at the game, but otherwise the difficulty curve is very shallow.
The environments are really gorgeous and diverse, probably some of my favorite from the 16-bit era. IMO this is what actually makes the game memorable. I will say that the backgrounds are a bit too "busy" in terms of contrast, which sometimes makes it a little difficult to follow the action.
This port allows you to choose between the American and Japanese soundtrack, and both are nice in their own ways. The Japanese version has the kind of "bounce" and focus on melodic motifs that you would expect from the Sonic franchise, but Spencer Nelson centralizes more around rock and ambience, which is a great fit for the Future levels. This port in particular creates looppoints to all of the original tunes, and some of the American tunes even take advantage of extended arrangements previously only featured in the album "Sonic the Hedgehog BOOM". Overall a very nice sound package. (Now if only we had American "Past" variants... )
If you already knew about this game and are wondering which version is the best, it's definitely Steam's. If you're wondering if this is the go-to Sonic game... some diehards will tell you otherwise, but I would say Sonic 2 and Sonic 3 & Knuckles are preferable in terms of gameplay. The boons of the time travel gimmick aren't present in these games, but both games offer a more satistfying challenge and are quite a bit longer than Sonic CD. If you just want a decent platformer on Steam, then I would recommend this.

Setting aside the fact that this was the only Sonic the Hedgehog title released for PC back in the '90s, what really sets this game aside from other Sonic titles is the Past/Present/Future phasing.  Every stage is effectively 4 maps (Past, Present, Bad Future, and Good Future).  That was a big f**in' deal for its time because this is one of the earliest games EVER to have a Good Ending/Bad Ending.  Even today, that's especially rare in the platformer/sidescroller genres.
Complete with fully animated cutscenes and the option of US/JAP soundtracks (both compliment the game very well) Sonic CD was truly ahead of its time and set the stage for a "Good Future".  10/10.
Note: This game is the same level complexity as the original Sonic the Hedgehog and Sonic the Hedgehog 2.  No special bubbles or aerial combat abilities and unfortunately no Knuckles.  This title introduced the Amy and Metal.

(Contains slight gameplay spoilers) TLDR; Great game! 10/10 for me, personally, based on enjoyment. Becoming one of my favorite games. Period. New or old fan, great game! It's definitely worth the money. Also, the DLC means nothing, it's basically purely cosmetic. Weapons and stages being arguable for this, but still... The game is complete. I wanted a few hours on this game visable before I made a review (as I've had a lot of offline hours which I don't believe is counted), and now that I have that, I've played subbed and dubbed for a bit (subbed more), have completed Ambition Mode (half way through my second run), have completed some of the Amibition challenges such as 100 win streak, beaten a few storylines, few max chars, etc. I think I've played enough to justify a reasonable review. I should also mention that I skipped DW8 and went straight to DW8 XLCE, so I know nothing about DW8.
Okay, so this game is quickly becoming one of my favorite games ever... Honestly. I absolutely love the added difficulties. For one that finds Chaos a bit too demanding in previous games (such as DW5), but wasn't fully content w/ Hard, I feel like Chaos was toned down a lot in this game, and I very much so appreciate it. Now they also have Ultimate, which is basically the old Chaos.
I'll move into the characters here. Oh, this is my favorite part... Every character is viable now. They made every character viable somehow. You still have officers that are clearly better than others, and some characters lack a lot, but they're still viable and they don't feel like a chore to play as anymore. The stats in this game are more like Samurai Warriors 4, where every level you gain you get added hp / attk / def, and different moves unlocked, to be expected imo. There's a Scholar in Amibtion mode that you can pay gold to increase your stats (useful once you've reached max level [150 in this game] which your attk caps about 900-1.1k, same w/ def. but I believe you can have around 1.5k? I have gotten to 1.4k so far).
I guess I'll start w/ the game modes here...
Amibtion mode is extremely fun for me. It's sorta like Conquest where there's a lot of character interaction, but it's handled differently, and now it doesn't feel as grueling as Conquest felt at times. Basically, Ambition Mode in a nutshell is "Make a new home for the Emperor! Make it grand, make it amazing!" And when you defeat an officer they join you. You need officers and material to improve your infrastructure (such as your blacksmith, etc.). Sadly, if you don't play Ambition Mode you basically miss out on 3/4th of the game. I'm sure if you hate Ambition mode, it'll be a chore, but trust me, you want to at least level up your blacksmith, which is stupidly important (note: you can use your blacksmith options in Free Mode, but to have your blacksmith options unlocked in free mode, they must be unlocked in Ambition mode, that's why I say this. After you're done w/ the blacksmith you can just as easily never go back to Ambition again, and you don't miss much in Free Mode or Story Mode anymore). There are 5 types of Ambition Mode stages. There are Great Battles (battles w/ quite a few officers to help build up your officer list, etc.), Skirmishes (to gain supplies, Fame battles that have you basically escort your main officer to an exit point for fame, Duels which focus on getting all the famous officers to join you, and the post-game Amibtion mode which is my personal favorite, which focuses on trying to defeat a false emperor, and to get to this point you must convince the other officers to (re)join you and battle your way to the final stage. I think it's the most fun I've had in a Koei Warriors game in a while. It can become repetitive, but it doesn't always drain away the fun. You play small stages like conquest mode in DW7 where things are a bit small but there are plenty of troops in the great battles, duels, and post-game Ambition stages.
The Story mode is excellent. I was really let down by the DW7 story mode (as I skipped 6, so I'm not sure if it'd apply for that game as well), and I disliked how DW7 did story mode, felt like a huge hassle and I never fully finished it, I personally liked the character focused story modes of the earlier games... But this game... I think they nailed exactly what I loved about the previous games where it's still character based to an extent, as it feels as if they touch w/ every character, especially the ones you choose to play as, but they also keep it faction based. I say faction due to the Kingdoms you can choose from being Wei, Wu, Shu, Jin, Other, and Lubu. Every faction has an off-branch around mid-story that something else can happen once you complete challenges to change the outcome of a battle, which I genuinely enjoy greatly. I'm more than happy to re-do story mode stages to complete these challenges to see where it'll take me.
There is also a hypothetical route for Wei, Wu, Shu, and Jin. I have not been in the Other story mode yet to check it out, and sadly, Lubu doesn't have a hypothetical route. These focus more on the "What ifs?" as I believe Koei explained at some point, and I love these routes, they're super fun for me...!
Now, Free mode... I'm very happy they have a free mode in this game title now. I see nothing really wrong w/ it, but I think it falls off for me due to my love of Ambition Mode, and how much I enjoyed the Story Mode in this title, but I have played several (not many) free modes. Seems fairly good though and every Free Mode stage has different challenges to complete if you'd like (I believe if you complete all of these challenges you unlock a trophy / achievement).
I'm regretfully running out of room, and I don't believe I'll delete anything above, so I'll try to wrap this up quickly. Challenge mode is decent. I'm glad they included it though. Modes include Rampage, Bridge Melee, Speed Run, Arena, and Inferno. Sub is great, Dub is slightly sub-par due to the generic officers DRIVING ME UP A WALL INSANE. But the dubbed famous officers are just like the previous games. Take what you will from that. They did a good job imo w/ weapon attributes and character skills. Leveling is great and welcomed (max level being 150). 19 "new characters" when compared to DW7. If you drop who have been in previous titles (including 7E) you reach 14. Excluding ones from DW8 you have 5. Anyway, I'll digress here shortly w/ one last thing to say... Is it worth $50? Yes. I bought this during a sale, but I've definitely already gotten $50 worth of enjoyment from it already. Should you wait for DW8XLCE to go on sale? Maybe. It's definitely something that you *should* pick up if it's on sale and you have more than enough money. Those are my final thoughts on the game, I do believe. I hope you found this review helpful enough to make a good judgment on the game.

It's been a long, long time since I picked this game up. I remember watching my friend play in total awe as he flew through the atmosphere and mined out little rocky satellites in orbit.
Well, the game did lose some of what made it as purely unique and awe-inspiring as it was before 1.0. However, it is still an enjoyable game for its incredibly diverse open universe and its sensible progression system. There were some things that didn't translate well into a story-based game, such as the more shoehorned bosses like the mech and dreadwing, but the story did add numerous things which I feel helped it in so many ways. A collection of likable characters, if minimally involved, still seem to be relatable in some ways.
Aside from the numerous bugs and gltiches upon the full release, many of which remain a problem, Starbound will be a game I will fondly remember decades down the line. I hope Chucklefish continues to nourish this game for a long time, and eventually I hope it remains an Indie classic among the likes of Minecraft and Terraria.
Also, it did No Man's Sky better than No Man's Sky, so there's that.
1 Year Edit: It's been a long time, and while the game has continued to develop in its 'stuff to do' aspect, many fo the issues I pointed out still remain. It's a painful experience speaking to Esther on a world you have completed the game in, and several of the major glitches in planet generation are still present. That said, the mechs and space statons were a breath of fresh air in a game that had threatened to forget its roots. I haven't played in a while, but what has been added of late ahs been a blast.

I recommend this game, although I must include some reservations.  I'll start with the negative and then work my way up to the positive.
Casual gamers should probably avoid Pillars of Eternity.  Although it is a well-crafted, enjoyable challenge, the story is not quite compelling enough to justify the investment of time and practice.  Admittedly, you can certainly make it through the game without a deep understanding of its mechanics, but most of the fun of this genre revolves around careful tactical planning and well-planned character design.  This is exacerbated by the abilities of the game's core NPCs.  Many of them are set up in ways that do not not take advantage of their character class and you will need to spend some time optimizing their abilities so that they work together cohesively.  Without offering any spoilers, I'll simply warn that the finale of the game can be surprisingly difficult and a casual player who is not using a walkthrough will probably find it immensely frustrating.
Having made this disclaimer, I should now clarify that I think Pillars of Eternity is fantastic.  I still think that Baldur's Gate II and Planescape:  Torment are two of the best games ever made, and Pillars of Eternity is a worthy successor to the genre.  In fact, if you've played Baldur's Gate or Icewind Dale in the past and found it even remotely entertaining, then you absolutely must play Pillars of Eternity.  You should have no trouble learning the ropes of this new game.  People who have experience with tabletop RPGs will likewise have an easy time grasping the mechanics and underlying strategy.
Comparing it to other games within the same genre, I think that Pillars has unique strengths.  Including firearms in the game was a great choice; it is incredibly satisfying to mow down enemies with a blast of your blunderbuss.  This is a definite improvement over games such as Baldur's Gate and Icewind Dale.
Pillars also has a few weaknesses, which I hope will be addressed in future installments.  The most significant drawback is the use of backstory/lore.  The game has a habit of dumping lore over you like a bucket of water.  There are numerous "wall of text" moments where you feel like you should be taking notes to keep track of all of the names.  This is a mistake, I think; I would encourage the designers to use lore as a spice instead of a main dish.  Lore should peek out from the corners of the story and the environment.  It should invite you to explore further on your own, rather than pulling you along by the hand.  Make the lore seep subtly through the music, the setting, and the storyline, and then sit back and invite the player to learn more on his own initiative.  Perhaps this will become easier with future games because the world will be semi-established.
Regardless of these drawbacks, I still recommend the game for people with an interest in the genre.  Casual gamers will likely find the learning curve too steep to be interesting, but then again, I doubt that a lot of casual gamers will stumble across this review anyway.  If you have an interest in this RPG genre, you absolutely need to buy Pillars of Eternity and support the company who brought this back to life.  I am so glad that Obsidian has taken steps to revive the genre and I will certainly be purchasing future installments and expansions.

In a time where good RTS (Real-time-strategie) games are becoming rarer and rarer, i, as a huge RTS-Fan, am very happy to see, that new developer try themself on this "dieing genre" and try to create something new.  And after i played the game very intensive in the last days, i think i have now seen enough of the game to make a final statement.
The controls of the game are very cool and very unique and i havent seen anything simular in any RTS game so far: While in all other RTS games, you scroll with the mouse over the map, to send your troops or to build your buildings, here you take direct control of a commander, who functions as a mouse cursor in other rts games. This leads to the situation, that your view is fixt and you cant just go from on side to the map to the other with one click to see whats going on their. And with the left and right mouseklick you are sending troops to your current location of your commander to attack enemies. This results in a very basic and simple control of the game: While in the usual RTS-Games like Star Craft 2, a good player has to develop a very high APM (Actions per minute) to compete against others, since the faster you are, the more things you can do, which resulted in the situation, that if you want to become good, you have to learn to move your fingers around your keyboard as fast as a professional pianists, and also older people could never compete with younger people, since they cant reach such high APM`s anymore. In Tooth and Tails, the basic control (you can even play it with a controller without having any penalities) take much of the huge hurdle away that you have to overcome, and the difference of a good player and a bad player is now only the logic, like which units to buy and when to attack where, rather then the micromanagement like it is in the other RTS-Games.
The Plot of the game is very unique. In the animal world, food sources are getting lower and lower, and so, the animals did develop an interesting solution to overcome this problem. They become full carnivores, and while they theoreticly could eat vegetables, most of them prefer to starve to death before they would do something so "uncivilised" like eating the foog of beats (everything that is not meat) But with this new food-culture, their comes a nother problem. Their are disagreements who should get food...and who should be food. So 4 factions did develop, loosly based on the russian revolution and everyone tries to be the last side alife to feast on the corpses of the fallen enemys.
This is the mainplot in the Campain in which you play as every of the 4 faction in their deserate fight to decide the war for them. Each faction has a very interesting lore behind them, (the blue longcoats for example are capitalistic revolutionarys who produce illegaly alcohol to finance their revolution, the red commonfolk are the communists of the animalkingdom, poor, but many animals, that dont want to bear the oppression from the upper class and the Civilised, are the old religios leaders of the land who think that only their religion should decide who should life and who should become food.
The missions of the campain are well done, while they begin very easy they become very hard later on and you really have to develop a specific tactic for each mission. Also very well done is the design of the mission. While their are also some "build your base and destroy every enemy" missions, their are also many missions where you really have to think from zero, missions in which you have to survive a certain amount of time, or to rescue allys from prisons as quickly as you can. Also their are "Heroic quests" that are optimal quest that you can fullfil to get achievements. And while the missions will get very difficult at the end, i have to admit that the heroic quests are some of the hardest challenges i have ever overcome in any videogame, expecially some of the last heroic quests are almost impossible to fullfil if you are not lucky with your map.
And here we come to a VERY big negative point of the game (in general, but especially in the campain) Because every map in the game is made by a map generator, it will generate the map on some fixt points (like the enemy will always start with three bases, of their are 5 possible mills that you can conquer in the map etc. but the layout of the map is randomly made. And this leads to the situation, that when you are lucky with the map, and you start at a location that is easy to defend while the enemys location is very open, you will win even the hardest levels with ease, while when the situation is the opposite, then the heroic quest, if not even the mission itself is impossible to win. Because of this the later (harder) missions become very very RNG based, you can have a perfect idea about how to win the map, but if you are not lucky you can play as good as you want, you will not get it. So especially if you want to finish all the heroic quests you need a huge frust toleration and you have to restart the map over and over again, until you finally will get a good map.
I understand that creating such an map generator is a very complex and difficult thing to do, but honestly i wish they would just have made balanced hand-made maps in the campain, because their was non RTS game, that i have every played that had sometimes so ridiculous bs maps like Tooth and Tails. But thankfully the developer are aware of the problems and try to fix the issues with the maps in the campain so i think the chances are very good, that in the future the campain will be a more enjoyable experience.
With the easy control i was sceptical that the Multiplayer will be to casual, that you didnt improve yourself and it will be more a luck than a skill game. But after i have played the Multiplayer for some time now, i can see that my concerns where unfoundet. You have to improve to get better rankings, their is a huge difference between a beginnger and a good player, and while the skill-gap is of course not as high as in "real competitve" games like Star Craft 2 or AoE, it still takes time and practise to become a good player. The matches are all short (between 5-10 minute) that makes them very action intensive but also not to stressfull since you can just join a new game in a few seconds if you have lost, and try a new tactic again.  The only complain that i have, is, that the most games are decidet with only one base, since it is to risky and expensive to expand in the most cases, since the maps are very small and the enemy can reach your base in just a few seconds. And with the low income that the players has to work, many games will have only Tier 1 units (the cheapest but also the weakest) since you are vulnurable for a very long time when you try to build higher tier units, because they need a very long time to recruit. I think the Multiplayer matches would be even more enjoyable if it would be easier to expand to at least two farms, since Tier 2 and Tier 3 units, that need a better economy to really becoming cost efficient, will play a higher role in more games.
All in all i have to admit, that i really didnt have so much fun in a game in a very long time. I often say to myself to only play a few games only to play for many hours! The game idea is very good done: it is simple to learn, but hard to master, and while you always have to do something, it managed to never become stressful. And while both the single player campain, as well as the Multiplayer, have a few downsides, the good sites are outweighting the bad sides. The community is very friendly, the developers are very active: Lets say it: I would recommend the game for both RTS-Veterans as well as people who didnt enjoy RTS-Games so far, since it is enjoyable for everyone.

Dragon's Dogma didn't make a good first impression on me - it felt and played like a mindless pseudo-sandobx arcade medieval title with a cliché-stacked, bland and absolutely predictable story since minute one. I am usually a very hard judge on storytelling, so that might be just my opinion. The gameplay was enjoyable, nevertheless, and at first it was the only thing that kept me playing. A hundred hours later, my opinion on this game has changed quite a bit.
Despite what the Store Page might say, this product features two completely different games. The first one is Dragon's Dogma, a reasonably good game that is fun to play and comes with nice and catchy gameplay and a story that, while indeed bland, cliché-stacked and absolutely predictable from minute one, gets surprisingly better once you complete it.
The second game is Dark Arisen, a completely different experience that you can begin by talking to a certain NPC prefirably after you've completed the game (And the post-game). Dark Arisen focuses on the exploration of a single dungeon in an island, and it is easily one of the most challenging, spectacular and enticing adventures gaming has given me the chance to experience. The work on the atmosphere of the island is hands down awesome, making it outshine the rest of the game, and it offers an immersive challenge that Dark Souls fans will indeed appreciate.
To sum it up, I thought this game was crap when I got it. And while it's not the game of the century, it got surprisingly awesome. I got it at a Steam Sale and found it worth every penny.
If this game taught me anything, it's that "wolves hunt in packs."﻿

tl;dr - Would recommend, with some serious caveats (see below). Consider buying when discounted, only consider full price (of €29.99 -- price on 28/07/2017) if you _really_ want the game for some reason. I bought the game for about €12.00 and consider that to be a decent price for what this game is.
------
PRO:
- Massive open world.
- Expansive character creation with many options of how you want your main character to be.
- Create your own main ally (called "pawns" in Dragon's Dogma) and customize him/her in every way you like, including personality (which influences it's AI).
- Hire other people's "pawns" and use them to strenghten your own party ; hire out your own pawn and use him to strenghten yourself.
- The combat system is fingerlicking good. The likes of which I've rarely seen. It's a combination of intense hack & slash, with little to no control over your party members (they do their own thing, only redirected by your cry for help) and extreme tactical gameplay, always having to take note of a combination of elements concerning yourself, your enemy and your environment in order to succeed.
- The AI is very good, both this of your pawns as this of the enemies.
- Boss battles are of delisciously epic proportions.
CON:
- Graphicly fine, but the textures are outdated for 2017. (Zoom in close enough and they actually look ugly.) Mods can fix this onto an extent.
- Voice-acting isn't good at all.
- Clunky user-interface which probably worked better on the console version.
- The standard quests are your basic fetch, kill and escort quests. Don't expect anything you haven't done thousands of times before.
- The storyline is... better not spoken of. For me it's easily the worst part of the entire game. In fact, it would have been better if they'd just let the story out of it.
- Thanks to the above two points, the RPG-factor of this game is limited to the character creation part.
IMHO, most fun in this game is had in freely exploring the countryside and just doing what feels right at the time. If it can be combined with a quest for some extra rewards, good, if not, also good.  You can ignore the quests for the most part of the game anyway.
If you like this kind of open world RPG, I would highly recommend it, you will not be disappointed.
If you like RPG's, but aren't all that into massive open worlds, I'd hold off on it until it's really cheap.
