I usually only review games I've finished, since I want to give them a fair chance and, admittedly, I like writing positive reviews more.
There's just too much game here though. 65+ hours in I've completed 3 of the campaign modes, two of which with both endings, and made my way through half of Ambition mode.
I haven't played a core DW game since 4. The problem with the series is that it always does roughly the same thing, so I didn't bother picking up the next 4 games when they came out.
Because of this the contrast is astounding.
DW4 had 42 playable characters from the 3 main factions and assorted extras (like the Nanzhong royalty or antagonists from the start of the various campaigns).
DW8 ups that to 77, and this "Xtreme Legends" version adds another 6. That's almost double the number of characters, across 6 factions (and, still, the extras).
Even just sticking to a single faction this is a long game.
Lu Bu, long-time antagonist and strongest warrior in the land, finally gets a full-fledged campaign and accompanying faction. I started that one first, and it had a LOT to do.
A campaign consists of about a dozen stages (which take 10-40 minutes each), after that you've reached the "Historical Ending". That's right, 8 games in and the series is still trying its best to have some semblance of historical accuracy in there. This means that, generally, things don't end well for your faction of choice.
For people like me, coming from the early PS2-era games, 12 stages might not seem like a lot. Back then the game was divided into Acts, each Act taking up 2-4 stages and each campaign having ~6 Acts.
In DW8 though, there is a big second ending to go for. Around halfway through that dozen stages there tends to be a pivotal battle, something big that the first half of the campaign has been working towards.
If you do everything right and fulfil certain conditions in the battles leading up to that crucial battle you can change history, branch off of the Historical route and head for the "Hypothetical Ending" which usually ends with your faction of choice ruling the lands. That's another 6 stages.
These alternate conditions are initially hidden and up to the player to figure out, but completing the Historical Ending will reveal exactly what you'll need to do to gain access to the second path. Such conditions might involve making sure a specific person, particularly ones that historically don't make it, get rescued.
Along the same lines there are also optional stages, unlocked comparably (and the conditions also get revealed by getting any ending) that are like the Tales interludes between Acts in DW4.
Then there's a set of Extreme Legends levels, added with this expansion, which is another 8 or so fully fledged campaign levels.
That's 30+ stages of hack and slash goodness.
.
Yes, there are 6 fully developed campaigns and another 20 or so levels categorized as "Other" following people like Yuan Shao, Meng Huo and Dong Zhuo. (Don't worry if you don't know who those people are, there's tons of characters, remember?)
~200 stages then, and most of them unlock a version where you can play it from the other side of the conflict once you clear it. It's no wonder then, that only 0.7% of players have the achievement for completing all stages.
The actual gameplay (which I guess deserves covering as well) consists of taking one of the suggested officers (from a roster of 2-4 suggested for the mission in the Campaign Mode. In Free Mode you can pick anybody) and running through a Chinese battlefield completing objectives, defeating enemy officers and carving a path through hundreds upon hundreds of enemy soldiers.
If you're looking for a power fantasy then this is it. There is a wide array of difficulties, the regular Easy-Normal-Hard is pre-faced by a Beginner difficulty which is truly easier than easy. Unless you really, really try to mess up it's almost impossible to lose the stage. Above Hard is Chaos, which will give you a significant challenge, even with characters stronger than level 100 (level caps at 150). Above Chaos is Ultimate, which will make you weep regardless of how much time you put into your favourite character.
Combat relies on the quick attack and strong attack buttons, which you string together into combos. Every single playable character has a different type of weapon with a different move set, but they tend to be easy enough to get into. If you have trouble coming up with 83 significantly different weapons then you'd be correct. There are around ten or so different types of swords, but they actually feel (and look) different. And there's no shortage of outlandish weaponry either. From the fast chakram to maces, to pikes, to bladed shields, to canoes.
Yes, canoes. You will come across some weird, weird weapons in this game.
You get to choose two weapons to take along into battle (and up to 4 skills which boost certain aspects of your character). It's advised to take at least one of the type that 'belongs' to your character of choice, since they automatically have access to two strong EX Attacks, which are basically special moves with that weapon. Other characters can learn to use these as well, but only when the original wielder has been levelled past level 50.
The reason you get two weapons is because all weapons have an elemental affinity (Earth, Heaven, Man) which opposes each other element in rock-paper-scissors style. That means that every enemy officer you meet will be at an advantage, disadvantage or neutral to your weapon. Being at a disadvantage means your attacks won't stun an enemy officer at all and damage is greatly reduced (halved?), and being at an advantage deals (around 50%) more damage and allows for a special Storm Rush manoeuvre when you hit him/her enough.
This means that it's a good idea to carry two weapons of differing elements and switch them out when necessary, which you can do at any time in battle with a press of the button (it even has a special Switch Attack unique to the weapon). This adds a (thin) layer of strategy to what is otherwise a pretty simple gameplay loop.
New weapons are found regularly, every officer you defeat will drop one, so you'll have no shortage of weapons. Each weapon type has 6 grades of weapons, and more stars denote stronger weapons. They also have randomized weapon skills, like dealing Fire damage on heavy attacks or increasing attack speed, adding an extra layer of complexity. This gets even better/worse once you progress far enough in Ambition Mode to unlock a Blacksmith which lets you fuse weapons together, upgrading and merging the weapon skills. With some effort you can make absolutely insane weapons, only adding fuel to the fire that is your power fantasy (although, at higher difficulties, you'll need every help you can get).
Ambition Mode is a completely separate mode where you first set out to build a palace to attract the emperor-in-hiding to your side, completing short randomly generated missions to gather allies, supplies, fame and gold and expand your own base camp. Once you do there is a second phase, new to Extreme Legends, where you set out to conquer China now that you have the backing of the emperor. There is
to do here, and everything carries over to the Campaigns and Free Mode. This easily adds another 30+ hours of stuff to do on top of the already stupid amounts of content.
The only thing missing is a character creator where you get to make your own warrior, a feature I quite liked in DW4 (and Samurai Warriors 1), but there are plenty of characters (roughly a quarter of them female) and you're sure to find plenty you'll like.

I stumbled upon Mass Effect by accident back in 2009. I have not heard of it before then so I expected nothing and was really pleasantly surprised when I started playing. Now I bought it on Steam to have copy here too so that is why the low play time. The gameplay is cover-based third person shooting but the story and the sci-fi setting/design is what makes this game truly great. You explore the galaxy as Commander Shepard who sets out to stop a deadly threat that could destroy all of civilization. On your quest you gather a crew of alien misfits to help you. It has just the right amount of balance between cheesy dialogues/action and sci-fi lore. The gun overheating and skill tree mechanics might be outdated (and replaced in ME2 and ME3) but I always loved them. I also loved the Mako space vehicle rides but I can totally see people finding it too wobbly. The game will occupy you for hours as it is both really fun and replayable. Choices matter and this helps to create your very own story the way you want it to be. Definitely a game worth getting! Actually, the whole trilogy deserves to be played but sadly ME3 is not for sale on Steam, only on Origin. So I advise getting ME2 and if it fits your style then get ME3 too (ME3 is a lot more like ME2 in mechanics).
The CD-key cannot be claimed in Origin unless customer support is involved. Also both DLCs (Bring Down the Sky and Pinnacle Station) are included only in the Origin copy but you can still try to get them

What a great game. Where to start? TL;DR at bottom.
The Good: It's Animal Farm/Redwall - The Game. Clever story, great simple gameplay, great amounts of strategy, all units available from the start, no pay-to-win stuff, cross platform and splitscreen multiplayer. Being the fastest keyboard masher means very little in this game compared to most RTS games; you get to focus on the fun strategy parts and not on the mechanical stuff. The story is clever and poignant. PvP matches are brief but intense, you only need to dedicate about 5-8 minutes to play a solid match. It plays equally well using a controller or keyboard + mouse. Developers that are listening to the player base. This game came out only a few days ago and they've already rolled out some nerfs to overly difficult story missions based on player feedback.
The Bad: RNG. Every single map, whether story missions or PvP is randomly generated, so no two matches or missions will  be the same. Sometimes this works to the extreme in your favor, sometimes it's the extremely bad for you. This makes every single game require different strategies, which can be very fun, but it is possible to feel the the deck keeps getting stacked against you. The counter point to this is that matches are so short, so if you get a difficult map just keep playing and one will fall in your favor. This doesn't mean  it's impossible to win if you get a challenging map, it may just require some quick thinking on your part, but not everyone is going to be a fan of the randomness and you may not be either. Opinions... man. You gotta have 'em.
TL;DR: Very fun game, easy gameplay, lots of strategy, controller friendly, crossplatform and splitscreen multiplayer, brief matches, devs that listen, however random map generation will not be for everyone.
Not only is the game fun, but the game developer is receptive to customer's feedback and made patches and updates very quickly.

Yet another zombie game in an already really crowded genre and yet this still manages to feel a bit fresh. The real focus in this game is survival. You'll need to set up a base, find supplies, recruit survivors all while defending yourself from zombies.
The game has a great open and persistant world. If you see a house or building you can more than likely enter it and search for supplies. When you gather those supplies they won't respawn. So the more you scavenge the less there is and this will make you need to plan things a bit. Will you stay in an area where you have a safe base but you scvenged most of the supplies, or will you uproot and move to a new area which is less safe but has loads of unexplored buildings which may be packed with loot?
You also have to manage your survivors carefully. The great thing is that each survivor has their own strengths and weaknessess and their own personality and since you'll be switching between survivors as they get tired or injured as you'll get attached to some and end up disliking others. Once a survivor dies in the game thats it they're gone, which will really make you think about whether to take risks or not.
There are a few things that let the game down however. Firstly the graphics look outdated. Also i started playing this game with a m+k and just found it too awkward so switched to a controller which was a massive improvement.. I'd strongly recommend using a controller for this game. Even with the controller i found the combat a bit clunky at times.
Also once you've established your base and are living comfortabl enough it starts to get boring. Not helped by the annoying side quests that pop up far too often. Also the near constant stream of reminders you get over the radio about a side quest when your doing something else is irritating to say the least.
Unlike the main quests which can be left for as long as you want not doing a side quest will lead to consequences as they seem to have a time limit in which to be completed. Sometimes these consequences can mean you losing a survivor so didn't like this either.
The worst side quest is the Besieged ones. It basically has you under siege from zombies in a house with other survivors where you'll board up the windows and fight off the zombies which sounds fun but is anything but. As to beat the mission you have to kill all attacking zombies and as zombies can wander into the area you can end up with a constant stream coming at the house which can make this mission drag out for a good 15-20 minutes.
Overall, though this game is still good despite it's flaws. I would recommend giving it a go as for the first 10 or so hours i was hooked on it. It's a 7.5/10 for me.

Rating: 8 out of 10
(I'm still playing breakdown right now, so the whole views are about the original game.)
I would recommend you this game if you like games like DayZ but get tired of getting killed without any reasons.
I've played for like 20 more hours in 3 days and I love this game. However, to be honest, there are lots of things which could be improved about this game.
Pros:
1, The graphic is good.
2, The bgms are appropriate for the atmosphere.
3, Gameplay is fluent and comfortable, though I would recommend you to play this game with a controller.
4, There are main quests and side quests which keep you having objects to achieve (They're fun at the beginning). For instance, you may choose to help neighbor to earn their trust in order to make progress of making them join you or you may choose to search for resources to build more facilities at home or you could kill zombies in order to get your skill level up.(I love the sound effect of blowing up zombie heads and slow motion of finishing them)
5, There are different types of special zombies, which are obstacles for new players at night or during defense quests from neighbors.
Cons:
1, This game is still not gonna be an amazing game which wouldn't make you feel repetitive about its goals and quests. Also, the main quests are too weak to even be considered as main quests. However, it's contradictory that you will find main quests are so short after you finish them because you would expect a lot more from main quests while the game doesn't offer many different quests after you play for a while. Then, what's the purpose of main quests anyway? just to tell you you need to move somewhere with some reasons? Or just try to create a fake sanse of progress with repetitive quests? After beating the game, I could also say the ending isn't like an ending. It's like a shutting down right from your face when you just wonder what's gonna happen next and bang, the game ends...
2, Though there are special zombies, they're not hard after you play for a while and figure out how to battle with them. To be honest, it's fair and it fits the realistic surviving atmosphere. But, it's really boring to fight against them. I would like to say that since this game doesn't bring many conflicts between people and communities (Like pvp in DayZ but with bots), I would like to see more and harder special zombies in this game to make this game more challenging. Not only several types of special zombies but a lot more should be put in. Also, I think it's gonna be great if some special zombies are gonna appear after you continue finishing main quests. Using them to represent an increasing difficulty and challenge of this game would make people who like to shoot feel more interested in making progress in this game. And yes, we need a big♥♥♥♥♥boss zombie to attack our base to make it more like a community and a raid. Imagine the difference between you walk on the street alone with badass guns and you sneak on the street to hunt down some big♥♥♥♥♥zombies with your people. I really would like to see the latter.
3, Side quests could be much better. I would like to see more details about side quests of different people. I believe there are lots to develop about humanities and societies. It's not only big things between different communities but small details about each person. Their feelings, their memories, and their beliefs could all be developed more. A family picture in a house, dead body of couples with hands holding each other, or even a lonely, weak and hungry dog standing near its suicide owner , scenes like these could be put in this game a lot to make gamers feel more desperate when they do their searching in different houses. And then you shall put some inspiring side quests by contrast to make gamers into the game. Zombies and weapons are all about gameplay. People, communities and their stories are creating the atmosphere of this game. When Skyrim is favored by lots of people but more buggy than this game, the importance of side quests should be taken into account.
After all, it's a good game and a good try. Thie game still has its potential and I really hope this game could be amazing in this genre.

Modern RPG's have lose something through all the top notch shaders, CG, and innumerable DLC's. They lost their soul. This game feels like any one of the original infinity engine games I would have been playing in the ninties, but with a modernized interface that provides the level of accessibility you'd expect to find this day in age.
What sets this game apart is simple: the writing. It's rich in analogy, deep with meaning, and too complex to fit into prototypical archetypes of protagonists and antagonists. Whilw most modern RPG's commit themselves to stamping every binary decision their game offers with a simplified 'good-guy' versus 'bad-guy' system that paints the universe as extremely black and white, (to the point of breaking the immersion of players like myself)  Pillars of Eternity strives at it's very core to create many situations that are composed of 'shades of grey.' You'll want to pick an option, but when you really examine the reasoning for both sides of an argument, you'll have an honest moment of moral dilemma. That is something I haven't felt in decades. Most games will slap labels of paragon and defiler on any action you take, complete with pictures and color coding as if you were too stupid to really figure it out. There's a point in which the agency of a system is made so crystal clear that it practically insults the player for not having the wit to determine their own moral code.
Playing Pillars is a rich and rewarding experiance that provided deep player agency, and conveyed a rich plot. Near the end you'll have that revelation, notice the line being drawn between characters and other components of the story, and you won't get that from another EA mass produced garbage RPG.

I stumbled upon Mass Effect by accident back in 2009. I have not heard of it before then so I expected nothing and was really pleasantly surprised when I started playing. Now I bought it on Steam to have copy here too so that is why the low play time. The gameplay is cover-based third person shooting but the story and the sci-fi setting/design is what makes this game truly great. You explore the galaxy as Commander Shepard who sets out to stop a deadly threat that could destroy all of civilization. On your quest you gather a crew of alien misfits to help you. It has just the right amount of balance between cheesy dialogues/action and sci-fi lore. The gun overheating and skill tree mechanics might be outdated (and replaced in ME2 and ME3) but I always loved them. I also loved the Mako space vehicle rides but I can totally see people finding it too wobbly. The game will occupy you for hours as it is both really fun and replayable. Choices matter and this helps to create your very own story the way you want it to be. Definitely a game worth getting! Actually, the whole trilogy deserves to be played but sadly ME3 is not for sale on Steam, only on Origin. So I advise getting ME2 and if it fits your style then get ME3 too (ME3 is a lot more like ME2 in mechanics).
The CD-key cannot be claimed in Origin unless customer support is involved. Also both DLCs (Bring Down the Sky and Pinnacle Station) are included only in the Origin copy but you can still try to get them

Some levels feature vast expanses of open sky - perfect for high speed thrusts and chases. Other levels take place on a firery-brimstone close quarters assembly line that are more home to the close calls and close quarters - flying through narrow corridors and getting up close and person with a rocket launcher. Conversion of town(blue dragon) to mafia (unseen or cult) is incredibly swingy as removing a crucial role.
Lynching a jester (fool) results in losing the fool lynch day, but also the next 2 days. This completely takes the power away from town and focuses it on night actions and kills.

I think the game could still be improved:
There is no stats in game? Easily the best thing about digital mediums for mafia is the ability to track stats.
Achevements? Could easily have achievements based purely on winning as a faction or class to not compromise gameplay.
The amount of neutral classes that spawn add tons of chaos.
It matters a ton about what faction the nightkill is from, and most of the evil factions have little to no way of checking. Again, chaos over information.

In fact, the prince (always BD) and the king (can be anything, but hard to share said info unless town(BD).
Consistency of abilities and their balance changes every patch. The court wizard went from useless to one of the best roles for example.
The game is a great building block but it needs a lot of touch up work. However, because of the developers frequent patching and communication I have reversed my review.

I am a huge fan of RTS games and have been looking for a game that provides a high level of strategy, ease of play and does not require a huge amount of time to play.  Do not let negative reviews influance you as they are comparing this game to other games that Tooth and Tail is not trying to be.  Tooth and Tail nail all of these aspects and here is why:
Strategy: Each unit has its place in play style and countering other units.  You can sell off your old units to buy different units to adapt to your opponents startegy.  I will have to admit I don't use every unit but again that is because of play style.  Before the game starts, you pick only 6 units types from a list of 20 so when you play the game, you have win using only those units so this adds pre-planning to the game.  When you play and look at your opponents base you may think, Oh I see turrents and barbwire, most likely they don't have mines as well.
Map: The best part I feel because the map is a random generated map every game causing you to adapt every game.  "Sweet there is only one entrance into my base and I have high ground vision, I'm going to go early economy."  Some may feel this adds randomness, I feel it creates replayablity.
Easy to Play:  The controls are amazing.  I am a keyboard mouse guy but for this game I use a controller.  Using a controller for RTS I thought would be impossible.  The creative way they solved unit control I take my hat off to.  There is a commader that is used for building, scounting and leading an army.  You right trigger and the entire army will attack the spot you were standing at.  You still have unit micro if you left trigger then only the unit that you have selected will attack.  I could never think of having the skills to micro units like Starcraft demands.  I feel I have a high level of control and enough micro that if I want to attack the minigun Badger in middle of the army I can.  I may lose my entire army to do so but I have that level of control.  Also every minute your commander gain 10 to his max health.  This allows you go deep into a base and live when there are larger armies.  If you commander dies, he responds back at your base but while you wait, your army is leaderless.
Short Games:  8 Minutes is the average length of my games.  This means I can try different strategies and if it doesn't work, let's go again.  I have never felt to Rage quit because the time investment isn't that large. Your farms run out of food in about 4 minutes, so you have to expand.  If your last farm dies, you have 45 sec to build a farm, otherwise you lose.  I have won many games just denying my opponents expansion options to where they starve.  Again that is the beauty of the random map ganeration.  You need to look at yours and your opponents starting location and identify "I can get blocked if I let them control this point of the map. I better defend that spot quickly or if i defend this one spot, they can't expand.
Advanced Play:  Some reviews talk about lack of depth.  Not at all.  I was playing 2v2 and scouted my opponents team.  I could see that they were putting up defences so I started building my best unit at the back of my base which takes a very long time.  Well with it 40 sec from completing, my base got scounted and he saw my tier 3 building.  Once he left, I knew what was going to happen,  They were going to rush me with a bunch of cheap units and I would lose. So I sold my expensive building which gave me tons of money and quickly built turrents on the high ground and mines.  Within 20 sec of being scouted, here comes both armies but I was able to change direction and prepare.  What a surprise when they showed up to a fortress and for a fraction of the cost, all their units died.
Price: Well worth the $20.  I have purchased other copies for friends.
Con:  The sinlge player is ok.  Would not call it a con,  but I only buy multiplayer games anyways.

Honestly, I wish I could give this game a + review, there's a lot I do quite enjoy about it, but there's a huge overlaying factor that really outweighs the rest. I do enjoy the game, and will no doubt continue to play it but it is a bittersweet experience.
+Artstyle
+Music
+Atmosphere
+Unique controls: TaT boils down the RTS genre to a single unit, providing its own hardships and skill requrements, a player will often have to plan in advance what they want to do in order to carry things out.
=Army structure: the game allows player to pick out an army of 6 unit types mixed between 4 brackets to organize their power/cost in tiers, and then a catagory for defensive structures. At the start of a PvP game player choose, blind to what everone else is picking. This can nail a player into a specific playstyle that if too focused, will leave them unable to adapt to a situation if their army is not suited to deal with an issue. Evened out by the fact that your enemy is also limited to their selected decks.
-Randomly Generated Maps: In some genres it would allow for endless gameplay while the Dev team having to do little work beyond setting up how the RNG would work and construct the maps. This is a huge problem for the style of RTS TaT has gone for. Many of the story mission end up being down to "if I can get a good layout" to win the stage. While the needed strat to advance might be in place, if your mill is down hill, or in an open field, or just too close the the enemy, you're out of luck. To have the game decided before it can start is a huge bother to scout a map only to find there no vantage point that will give you the edge you need against a rather one-sided fight. With a recent patch some things have been adjusted but the game is still largly up to RNG, and not skill in many cases.
Pretty alright game, RNG maps can be annoying and cause you to lose but otherwise the game is solid enough. It's not the most complex game but that's alright.

Wait, have I not reviewed this game? It's pretty much the best. If you like twin stick shooters, dark humor, and more or less infinite replay value with runs that surprise me to this day despite having 300+ hours clocked on it at the time I write this, you're probably already playing it, but if not, you should be.

If you liked the original Legend of Zelda for the NES then this is a must-play. It also has a rather interesting backstory to uncover through somewhat cryptic hints. You also may like it if you liked Super Meat Boy, as it has quite a few references to that game.
Honestly, I've never had a single issue with this game. I don't know why anyone would EVER give this game a bad review other than them just not liking it in general, and that's just personal preference. No, this game isn't for everyone, but it is what it advertises to be, and more.
Here's a checklist. If you enjoy these, then you'll probably love this game like I do.
-Nearly infinite replay-ability
-Difficulty that progresses as time goes on
-Very hard to 100% complete, leaving you occupied for a VERY long time (I have 100 hours as of this being posted and I'm not even halfway done with fully completing the game)
-Interesting item combos that will surprise many
-Very similar to the original TLoZ for NES as mentioned above
-Backstory that's entertaining to explore/look into
I could go on, but it'd be ridiculous to list the hundreds of positive things this game has for people to look forward to.
Anyways, with all of that being said, there are only THREE main things that may ward people off. Those things are:
1. Difficulty. While the game may start off easy (depending on how lucky you are sometimes), it DEFINITELY gets bone-crushingly hard after a while.
2. Gore/Grotesque. While I highly doubt anyone would deny a game for gore (especially because this game has pixel graphics), this game certainly does have blood and just straight up nasty stuff in it. No, not the 18+ kind of nasty, but the disgusting kind of nasty. This never really bothered me because of the cartoon + pixel-style graphics, but I could kinda see how someone would be bothered by it.
3. Religion. If you are a very religious Christian, you would probably hate this game's backstory as it has to do with Christianity and can be perceived negatively. Without spoiling much, the most I'll say is yes, you can make deals with the devil, but that option is entirely up to you. In fact, not choosing to do so makes it more likely for angels to grant you rewards. However, if you're really serious when it comes to Christianity and take religious elements in games very seriously, you may not want to play this. It's really hard to explain this without spoiling much, but if you don't mind it being spoiled, I recommend you watch the 'Game Theory' video on this game. It goes in depth about this topic and explains a lot of things.
With all of that being said, I see why people would dislike the game, but I, for one, certainly don't, and there certainly isn't any reason to not recommend it. 10/10 all the way.

I played 62 hours of this game in 2 weeks and I've loved every bit of it.  (I also recognize after writing this that I wrote it in ridiculous order, but I don't feel like fleshing out a review for this game.  It's good, period).
First off, if this game looks trashy to you, then yeah, it kind of is.  The graphics are sub par, it's in subtitles that make you wonder what took so long to port it, and you probably won't figure out how the game works without looking up stuff online.  But Jesus ♥♥♥♥ing Thunder Pants is it fun.
The game is about an hour long on an average playthrough, but you'll be playing through it many many times.  There are multiple endings, pathways, and you can pretty much pull a sword on anybody in conversation.  It reminds of westerado in fact, minus the changing culprit of the main murder.
I should also mention this game typically doesn't take itself seriously.  If you've read other reviews, you probably know that the crime punishment system is an S&M-esque mini-game.  It's not really S&M, it just reminds you of it.  It's mainly deadly traps that would be at home on a saw movie if it had a new coat of blood.  And the other men act like the Gimp from pulp fiction when you try to escape.
I usually find japanese stories lame, or at least japanese characterization.  The women are weak, the motivations are cheesy...but I think they did a good job here.  On one playthrough you think you'll have a character figured out, and then another playthrough shows a completely different side of them that you didn't know about, and yet it never feels out of character.  A leader might seem strong and resilient, but you later realize they are dangerously narrow-minded as well.  It's really well done, and I still find myself saying "Jesus, I didn't know they were like that."
The gameplay is just damn fun.  For such a constricted world of few areas and a short storyline, it feels like GTA.  Sometimes it feels like it gives you more freedom than GTA.  It even reminds me of Skyrim when I start a playthrough going "I'm gonna be good this time," then murdering a bunch of constables because I wanted to level up my sword style.
Sword styles man.  That's what probably makes the game.  There are something like 6 or 7 stances in the game, and each stance has 15 or so styles.  The styles sometimes have overlap with others in their stance, but they also have unique moves.  Some even have counter attacks, and one has a move where you simply walk forward without flinching.  When you hit h, you swing your sword at neck level for huge damage.  You collect styles from killing people, and you can also collect their swords (Better swords on harder modes).
The modes are very interesting.  Soon enough you'll be one hitting people on easy mode once you upgrade your sword enough at the smith (who you can also fight instead of pay.  Great way to upgrade your sword without spending money is not paying, running away, ending your playthrough at the harbor, and repeating).  Hard mode requires better swords and Harakiri mode requires some dodging and charms, and here's where we get into my gripes.
I like charms.  They are passive effects on your sword that you can get from crafting your own swords.  Each sword part can have 3 charm passive effects, and a sword needs 3 of these effects to line up vertically or diagnolly in order to be a full working charm.  If you can get parts with two of the same charm, you can get it to line up in 3 different ways, tripling the charm, but therein lies the problem.  One, only a few of the charms are any good, and that is a waste of space and added frustration to my second gripe.  Getting good charm synergy is pretty much random.  Everytime you disassemble a sword, even if it's the same parts you've used 100 times before, the charms on those parts change.  What people do is get swords, disassemble them into parts, and hope they get a part with double charms.   If they don't, they craft the swords again with the same parts and repeat until they get a part with double charms.  Then they set that part aside and get a new one in it's place.  This is useless RNG (random number generator, drops such as world of warcraft) without any gameplay involved.  This will be a bit of a rant.
Even though I play WoW, Borderlands and Diablo, I think RNG is useless in video games and serves only to add hours without fun in a game.  RNG can be done right, but rarely is.  And if you think there's any other way to get double charms, there isn't.  There's nothing special like killing the hardest character on harakiri mode gives a greater chance for a double big shot charm (one of the only good ones by the way).  They have no system in place.  They made disassembling a priority for getting charms, and it's boring.  It's one of those things where on a good day I'll turn away from the monitor and go "I just spent hours disassembling the same swords for a double big shot charm...Is that worth it?"  There is an alternative, which is repeatedly entering the buy menu from the smith to buy his parts.  Those change everytime you enter it.  While that seems faster, for some reason the smith has way more grip parts than any other parts, so once you get a double charm on your grip you have to try a lot more for a double charm on a blade or guard.  Whatever, it's all for triple charms which greatly help the game (perhaps too much?)
Also one last thing:  Parrying is useless and I find that unfortunate.  Parrying is fun in almost every videogame.  Have you ever parried someone in Dark Souls?  Getthe♥♥♥♥outofhereplease, it's the best.  It seems perfect for a samurai game, but as it stands there is no real system for it... not really with timing or anything.  Certain attacks just get parried easier than others.  There is this push and pull system, but it doesn't seem like pulling works better on pushing attacks than pulling attacks (btw, how many pulling attacks can there really be for a sword?)
The PC Port is great, minus a few things.  One, my lesser alienware computer can hardly run it, which is ridiculous because it looks like a ps2 game.  Two, no mouse.  Da ♥♥♥♥ is that about.  You play it like an arcade machine port.  No Mouse.  Boooo.  EDIT: They have added a mouse function
Still, I'm waiting until relatives leave so I can play it again, cause jesus it's fun.  Highly recommend.

It is actually much more enjoyable than that sentence sounds.  There is always a balance in choosing which missions you can run, and this inability to do everything is the only reason I forgave one of my personal bugbears in games: The Autosave Only system.
Here it actually has a rare useful mechanic of upping the ante on your characters, in that their skills all increase independently and based on their actions, so if you have built up some ubermench they can still be taken down by some bad luck with a feral zombie and then they are gone for good and you continue with some chump that hasn't had any experience.

There were a couple of minor glitches (zombies and npcs getting stuck on objects) but none were game breaking and it was beginning to end a stable experience.

So I wasn't really sure what I was getting myself into with this game when I got it. I had watched a couple of people play the first 20 minutes or so when it first turned up. I am really, completely and utterly pleasantly surprised. I loved every minute of playing it.
I'm a scaredy cat & I normally coward out of things after a short while. Not so with this. It's not really scary at all even for me (though the noises a couple of the special mobs make gives me the creeps).
It's certainly not a difficult game, and while I don't normally use that as a reason for critique it really could stand to be more difficult - though I know some people have said otherwise & I think that comes down to play-style. I lost one survivor but only because I was dumb and in a rush and switched survivors when I thought she was somewhere safe and she mysteriously died in that same spot. That's all. In amidst the pot luck of who will survive when you log back in it was my own lethargy that got her. You become strangely attached to a couple of the members of the group despite them being mostly ambiguous people - you really do feel that it's your responsibility to look after them.
The thing with this game is it is a persistent world. Think animal crossing - if you leave for too long things happen. I played it every day over the holidays logging off each time only once everyone was safe & sound and morale was full. I never returned to any nasty surprises other than a couple of enclaves getting over-run but - that's their own fault ;P If you can dedicate the hours in a short enough time frame it's not a deal-breaker but if you want to put it down and pick it up where you left off a couple of weeks later you might just find it burning around your feet. If you still have feet.
Using an X-box controller at least it was so smooth and satisfying to fight and running over zombies and hearing them pop when you run over them is just, satisfying. They don't really explain much to you but, I didn't find this off-putting but I did have to google what Fame & Influence really did.
For me it really could have stood to be a longer game - to have had the next area open up and be able to move up into a larger home base. But then I was lucky enough to have the time to maintain morale & resources. The OCD in me loves searching buildings & seeing the little X's appear on buildings once you've cleared them.
And finally the story - it's nothing ground breaking or complex but just enough to make me feel a little sick. And for a game that's just a little sick, that's not too bad to me.

The main way the game reduces power usage is to stop rendering the infantry’s details, so you are literally slaughtering faceless peons by the hundreds. The maps are very large and the characters are in no way linked to the world that they live in. When you turn your character, he spins like a top, even while on a horse. The walls are like a half pipe, completely smooth. It is a little jarring how the game gives so little ♥♥♥♥♥ about how the characters interact with the world, but that’s not why we play Dynasty Warriors, we play to be the ultimate warrior. The game’s graphics only go as far as it is needed to show your unlimited power being unleashed upon some faceless cretin trying to either flee or fight, but in the end his only hope is to get out of the high solider density and be by himself. Story: 		1.5/3
There once was a book. It depicted an epic struggle between an orphan who grew into a monster and a man who became a god. Through the many years and endless greedy sequels, we got Dynasty Warriors 8: Xtreme Legends. Characters exist and they struggle in some over vamped high school level drama that is always exploding to the next plot point. With all the high energy I remember none of it. It is the blandest set of campaigns that try their hardest to get in the way of you slaughtering innocent people, and thankfully it even fails at that.
The story takes nothing from the game and is pretty funny how hard it tries. It’s like a Michael Bay movie condensed into a videogame.
Game Play: 	2.5/3
There are two main game modes and some time-attack or free modes on the side. The two main game modes are Story and Empires. The gameplay is straight from dw5 with the addition of a weapon triangle, earth, man, and heaven. Standard one is weak against the other and strong against the third. You can also have any character equip any weapon, and two at a time. Have you ever been play a Dynasty Warrior and thought, “dam it, why is Lu Bu not using a magic harp to kill these ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s”?
The story mode lets you play as a group of heroes in one of the soap opera style stories. At one point I think I fought the son of Lui Bie who was now king of some country and sucked at it so much that I was hired to kill him by his people who were then guarding him. So I was hired to kill the people I was hired by in order to kill their king who was killing the people. Only play for unlocks.
Empire mode lets you run a gauntlet of small battles. On the fifth battle you can fight a large battle to unlock a large number of officers by defeating them in battle. After each battle you can either leave, resetting the gauntlet, or continue and fight harder battles with greater rewards. When you return to camp you can upgrade it so you can get better bonuses during the battles, buy better weapons, or get pets. Finally you can have a majestic eagle kill you enemies. This mode is great for getting your character more powerful when you get stuck in the story mode, or if you just want to kill some people without all the ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t.
Re-Playable: 	.5/1
If you treat replay as starting a new character and using them to kill a small nation, then you can replay this game until the final horn is blown and gods descends from on high. If you consider it completing the game and restarting, good luck doing that before the end days.

A worthy successor to the Tex Murphy series.
The cut scenes and dialogues are all done in high-quality 2K FMV. The acting can be a bit cheesy at times but it's part of the game's charm. Everything is in line with the film noir genre that the games pulls it's roots from.
There's a whole lot of cinematics in this game but the adventure gaming part is also fully present. the game plays from a first person perspective and the controls will feel familiar to any modern gamer. (It's worth mentioning that the controls can't be remapped from the defaults.) I felt at ease with the controls within minutes, although some parts of the UI can be a bit clunky at times. The 3D environment feels a bit dated but it doesn't detract from the gameplay.
The storyline is a classic Tex Murphy adventure and pretty much picks up where Overseer left off. Returning players will feel at home back on Chandler's Avenue, but the story is being told in a way that newcomers won't feel lost from not playing the previous games. The grand theme and tongue-in-cheek humor will reel you in. Most puzzles can be solved with a bit of logic but a small number of them seems a bit nonsensical. There were also a few places where hot spots could be tricky but nothing that would put anyone off.
The game takes about 12 hours to complete, but branching storylines and multiple endings means there's some good replay value in this.
If you're a fan of the previous Tex Murphy titles, then it's a no-brainer. You need this game! Anyone not familiar with the series, but with a liking for good adventure games should also consider this little gem. Let's only hope it doesn't take another 16 years before we see another one.

I thoroughly enjoyed every second of my first playthrough so much that as soon as the credits were done rolling I started a second playthrough right away.
While the 3D enviornments you explore in game are average at best the game lives and dies by it's astonishingly beautiful FMV. If you have any appreciation at all for adventure games you should play this. Even if you've never played another Tex Murphy game you should play this because it's a great example of the form.

Modern RPG's have lose something through all the top notch shaders, CG, and innumerable DLC's. They lost their soul. This game feels like any one of the original infinity engine games I would have been playing in the ninties, but with a modernized interface that provides the level of accessibility you'd expect to find this day in age.
What sets this game apart is simple: the writing. It's rich in analogy, deep with meaning, and too complex to fit into prototypical archetypes of protagonists and antagonists. Whilw most modern RPG's commit themselves to stamping every binary decision their game offers with a simplified 'good-guy' versus 'bad-guy' system that paints the universe as extremely black and white, (to the point of breaking the immersion of players like myself)  Pillars of Eternity strives at it's very core to create many situations that are composed of 'shades of grey.' You'll want to pick an option, but when you really examine the reasoning for both sides of an argument, you'll have an honest moment of moral dilemma. That is something I haven't felt in decades. Most games will slap labels of paragon and defiler on any action you take, complete with pictures and color coding as if you were too stupid to really figure it out. There's a point in which the agency of a system is made so crystal clear that it practically insults the player for not having the wit to determine their own moral code.
Playing Pillars is a rich and rewarding experiance that provided deep player agency, and conveyed a rich plot. Near the end you'll have that revelation, notice the line being drawn between characters and other components of the story, and you won't get that from another EA mass produced garbage RPG.

Sonic CD is an outstanding game, though because it was on the SegaCD, not many people knew about it.
1. **SPOILER ALERT**  Story:
Sonic CD is set on a miniature planet nicknamed "The Little Planet", which is then held captive by Dr. Eggman. Also in this game, we are introduced to two new characthers in the franchise, Metal Sonic and, ugh... Amy Rose... ANYWAY, Sonic must stop Eggman from taking over the Little Planet before it's too late by retrieving the Time Stones, mystical gems that, when found all 7, (sound familiar?) can allow the user to, no, not turn into Super Sonic, but to travel through the flow of time itself!(Amazing, right? yeah. Pretty hard to believe...) After Sonic finds/or fails to find* all 7 Time Stones, he must face off against his metallic doppelganger(?), Metal Sonic. Later, Sonic finds Eggman's/Robotnik's base, the Metallic Madness, which he ends up destroying after the fall of Robotnik. *fakechuckle* After that, he rescues Amy from the collapsing base and runs off leading off into his next adventure.
1.1  **SPOILER ALERT** Endings:
Good Ending: Sonic manages to free the Little Planet after the collapse of the Metallic Madness Zone thanks to the use of the Time Stones, but un-expectinly Eggman/Robotnik still has one of the Time Stones in his possession (somehow?) with Sonic chucking a rock (Chuck Norris Style) at him and destroys his Egg-Mobile, ending off with the Little Planet leaving the Earth(?) with "Sonic Fireworks" and Sonic running off.
Bad Ending: Sonic manages to free the Little Planet after the collaping Metallic Madness Zone, ending off with Sonic leaving the Little Planet, but little did Sonic know that Eggman used the Time Stones to re-build the Metallic Madness Zone and take control of the Little Planet.
2. Graphic: Thanks to the enhancement form Crhristian Whitehead and SEGA, it now looks more like a Sonic 1 remake on the SegaCD and it looks absolutly Amazing! I cannot say that enough without making it seem like i hate the game. The sprites have smooth movements, the texture are great for describing what kind of enviornmet I'm in, and the backgrounds are, meh, Backgrounds.
3. Sound: Since Sonic CD has two seperate soundtracks, SEGA allowed us to switch from the US soundtrack, and the Japanese Soundtrack, and I've gotta say, they are both great to listen to! (especially the JP soundtrack) each zone has its own diverse track, ethier  if you in the smooth-looking present, the shady-metallic future, or the calm and peaceful past.
4. Overall thoughts: This game is really good, from its clean and smooth scrolling, to its well-composed music, this one of the best Sonic games in the franchise.

The best game in the splinter cell franchise, in my opinion. Good story, cool dialogue, nice graphics, and smooth gameplay. A clear 8/10 for me.
Like the previous installment, "Splinter cell: Conviction", you're a lot more mobile than you are in the first three games. You're also free to choose how you want to deal with enemy units. Not only do you have a variety of weapons and ways to dispose of your enemies; you can also use multiple non-lethal methods - like sleep gas, stun gun (like the sticky shocker in Chaos Theory), proximity shocker, and a couple of items to distract your foes. You can also avoid most enemies entirely, which really pays off at the end of the mission.
It may be hard to believe, but the reward system in the game is also pretty well integrated. It's very RPG-like. You get money to buy items and upgrades at the end of each mission (depending on your performance), as well as by picking up dead drops and hacking PCs you find. You'll be able to upgrade Sam's gear in several ways by buying different clothes (boots, gloves, torso, etc), as well as by buying different weapons and weapon upgrades (of which there are many).

Personally, I love games that allow a lot of choices as a player, and this game definitely gives me that. The missions are very non-linear. By that, I mean that you get inserted in an area, and you get extracted in a different area. That's about all there is for linearism. Most of the rest of the mission is your call.
Pick your own playstyle - Ghost, Panther, or Assault - as you go along. In some missions, you might prefer running around blasting everything in sight. Doing so would give you points as Assault. If you'd rather kill silently and keep out of sight, Panther is probably going to be the way you play most often. If you like, you can avoid killing enemies entirely by stunning them with an array of gadgets. That'll give you points as Ghost.
I enjoy it mostly for the freedom and flexibility in the single-player missions. There is a rather interesting multiplayer, also. It's quite a bit different from the normal, and somewhat stale, deathmatch that a lot of shooter multiplayer modes are based around. I'll leave you guys to see for yourself, because the single-player action is really what makes this game great.

This is a lite RTS with with boatloads of flavor, and way more depth than intuition would lead you to believe at first. Importantly, the element most "stripped down" from traditional RTS is actually a key improvement--notably, the ability to command your units is dependent on an in-game avatar that can give three commands --- "attack at my location", "retreat to my location", and "focus fire the target at my location". Rather than dumbing down the strategy, this change actually still maintins the importance of micro-ing units while drammatically lowering the APM needed to play the game at a high level.
Game has online versus (ranked matchmaking and unranked lobbies), offline versus (both against bots and players), and a great, challenge campaigning that absolutely will give players of any level of RTS experience a considerable challenge.
Perhaps most contentious element of this game is the use of random map generation for matches ---single player, ranked versus and unranked versus alike. Personally I quite like this feature, the map generation prioritizes interesting terrain features that naturally create locations of great strategic interest and ensures every match feels fundamentally different from each other.
Absolutely the most fun I've had playing RTS in years.

Stranded Deep…This game has gotten some of the most positive reviews on steam for an early access game that I have ever seen. But online reviewers say that it is just another early access survival game that is unfinished, buggy, and repetitive. These “reviewers” spend two hours on the game and tell everybody their opinion. You cannot truly spend two hours in a game and instantly have a on point review. The critics say that the game is boring, repetitive, and buggy. While the game might still be buggy it says quite explicitly that is is EARLY ACCESS. The games repetitiveness is something that the reviewers have definitely misunderstood. The game is meant to make you think about your survival, in real life surviving in the wilderness means you need a plan. The daily schedule if I may. The first three or four days in Stranded Deep you are scavenging shipwrecks, islands, and sea forts for loot and supplies. You collect coconuts, potatoes, and crabs to eat. On day 10 or 11 you begin to build up your home. You choose an Island and begin building you house and storage areas. The way you survive is you start each day the same. Eat food, drink water. Then you plan out what you are going to do today. Whether it be you go to another island to loot it, or look for shipwrecks out on the sea. The reviewers say that the repetition is a bad thing. The people who are criticizing the game have only written reviews for games with surprises and things that make the game unexpected. They do not have a full understanding of what stranded deep is about. They want FPS and MMO games to review. So when asked to look at this they are unhappy with the lack of action and surprises in the game.
I rate this game a 10/10. And hope for more updates to come.

This has been one week since the release for Throne of Lies,
Once you start the first round, you won't experience ever the same when deductions, the suspense, the conspiracies, daring murders and accusations become more common. Wait common? No, my friend...It's deeper than you can measure with.
You arrive on Castle Adiart back either as member of Blue Dragon, Unseen or you are not afflicted with either side...sword for hire, court jester got tired of being belittled by the king, potion maker? What about the rumors of unnatural murderers across the realm...are you one of them?
You and fourteen other guests have arrived on throne room with the king in his presence until suddenly the castle doors have been sealed away, confused and perhaps afraid what's going on...your survival on the castle begins.
Throne of Lies is medieval fantasy-themed tabletop social deduction game as your goal is to eliminate the opposing faction or playing as neutral you have goal of your own, at day phase you discuss by the round table who is the trusted and traitor as well unsuspected players get affected by day abilities on this phase. During the night phase you decide to make actions such as the investigations, supporting your allies, discussing in secret or murdering the suspect, did you know your fellow healer class is actually now member of Unseen? How did that happen? The 'evil' factions are capable of converting 'good' faction classes, The Blue Dragon. Keep in mind that even few Blue Dragon classes have convert immunity and sometimes, you can earn that immunity when you get resurrected. Do you get roleblocked--I mean occupied too many times as you never get to kill someone? Don't worry! You become immune to occupations after three times in row whether you are killer or not, fewer classes have immunity to occupation as passives at start. During the dead phase, sometimes a Priest will able to talk with the dead as the graveyard is filling with ghosts that belong from the players are dead. You can also bet your gold who dies tonight during day phase and who get executed on trial during night phase. There are a lot of examples what can happen during these days and nights, who need plot twists of the game when this happens unexpecting right at front of your monitor
Throne of Lies offer you gameplay that no match is the old first match you have played before, same players with new names and equipment such as armor and weapons and randomly selected ambience soundtrack give you impression you are still standing by the throne room alive whilst unknown collaborators are plotting with someone's demise, it's in your imagination.
Since one week of the release I have enjoyed the brilliant victories and utter defeats, execellent soundtrack and gameplay play a role to this game, but so do my social deduction and manipulation that can change the tide of the game. The animations of your character hold foundation as you make gestures and open your mouth as you speak as well to react during the execution scenes, each weapon performs different execution styles. You have at night your own class-related bedrooms such as inside the church altar, the dungeon cell, alchemy room, your plate armor display on your room as Knight, magical runes and magical orbs as Psychic and Court Wizard and even throne made of bone and skeleton heads as Reaper and many more!
This is just the beginning. But not for the end.

I played 62 hours of this game in 2 weeks and I've loved every bit of it.  (I also recognize after writing this that I wrote it in ridiculous order, but I don't feel like fleshing out a review for this game.  It's good, period).
First off, if this game looks trashy to you, then yeah, it kind of is.  The graphics are sub par, it's in subtitles that make you wonder what took so long to port it, and you probably won't figure out how the game works without looking up stuff online.  But Jesus ♥♥♥♥ing Thunder Pants is it fun.
The game is about an hour long on an average playthrough, but you'll be playing through it many many times.  There are multiple endings, pathways, and you can pretty much pull a sword on anybody in conversation.  It reminds of westerado in fact, minus the changing culprit of the main murder.
I should also mention this game typically doesn't take itself seriously.  If you've read other reviews, you probably know that the crime punishment system is an S&M-esque mini-game.  It's not really S&M, it just reminds you of it.  It's mainly deadly traps that would be at home on a saw movie if it had a new coat of blood.  And the other men act like the Gimp from pulp fiction when you try to escape.
I usually find japanese stories lame, or at least japanese characterization.  The women are weak, the motivations are cheesy...but I think they did a good job here.  On one playthrough you think you'll have a character figured out, and then another playthrough shows a completely different side of them that you didn't know about, and yet it never feels out of character.  A leader might seem strong and resilient, but you later realize they are dangerously narrow-minded as well.  It's really well done, and I still find myself saying "Jesus, I didn't know they were like that."
The gameplay is just damn fun.  For such a constricted world of few areas and a short storyline, it feels like GTA.  Sometimes it feels like it gives you more freedom than GTA.  It even reminds me of Skyrim when I start a playthrough going "I'm gonna be good this time," then murdering a bunch of constables because I wanted to level up my sword style.
Sword styles man.  That's what probably makes the game.  There are something like 6 or 7 stances in the game, and each stance has 15 or so styles.  The styles sometimes have overlap with others in their stance, but they also have unique moves.  Some even have counter attacks, and one has a move where you simply walk forward without flinching.  When you hit h, you swing your sword at neck level for huge damage.  You collect styles from killing people, and you can also collect their swords (Better swords on harder modes).
The modes are very interesting.  Soon enough you'll be one hitting people on easy mode once you upgrade your sword enough at the smith (who you can also fight instead of pay.  Great way to upgrade your sword without spending money is not paying, running away, ending your playthrough at the harbor, and repeating).  Hard mode requires better swords and Harakiri mode requires some dodging and charms, and here's where we get into my gripes.
I like charms.  They are passive effects on your sword that you can get from crafting your own swords.  Each sword part can have 3 charm passive effects, and a sword needs 3 of these effects to line up vertically or diagnolly in order to be a full working charm.  If you can get parts with two of the same charm, you can get it to line up in 3 different ways, tripling the charm, but therein lies the problem.  One, only a few of the charms are any good, and that is a waste of space and added frustration to my second gripe.  Getting good charm synergy is pretty much random.  Everytime you disassemble a sword, even if it's the same parts you've used 100 times before, the charms on those parts change.  What people do is get swords, disassemble them into parts, and hope they get a part with double charms.   If they don't, they craft the swords again with the same parts and repeat until they get a part with double charms.  Then they set that part aside and get a new one in it's place.  This is useless RNG (random number generator, drops such as world of warcraft) without any gameplay involved.  This will be a bit of a rant.
Even though I play WoW, Borderlands and Diablo, I think RNG is useless in video games and serves only to add hours without fun in a game.  RNG can be done right, but rarely is.  And if you think there's any other way to get double charms, there isn't.  There's nothing special like killing the hardest character on harakiri mode gives a greater chance for a double big shot charm (one of the only good ones by the way).  They have no system in place.  They made disassembling a priority for getting charms, and it's boring.  It's one of those things where on a good day I'll turn away from the monitor and go "I just spent hours disassembling the same swords for a double big shot charm...Is that worth it?"  There is an alternative, which is repeatedly entering the buy menu from the smith to buy his parts.  Those change everytime you enter it.  While that seems faster, for some reason the smith has way more grip parts than any other parts, so once you get a double charm on your grip you have to try a lot more for a double charm on a blade or guard.  Whatever, it's all for triple charms which greatly help the game (perhaps too much?)
Also one last thing:  Parrying is useless and I find that unfortunate.  Parrying is fun in almost every videogame.  Have you ever parried someone in Dark Souls?  Getthe♥♥♥♥outofhereplease, it's the best.  It seems perfect for a samurai game, but as it stands there is no real system for it... not really with timing or anything.  Certain attacks just get parried easier than others.  There is this push and pull system, but it doesn't seem like pulling works better on pushing attacks than pulling attacks (btw, how many pulling attacks can there really be for a sword?)
The PC Port is great, minus a few things.  One, my lesser alienware computer can hardly run it, which is ridiculous because it looks like a ps2 game.  Two, no mouse.  Da ♥♥♥♥ is that about.  You play it like an arcade machine port.  No Mouse.  Boooo.  EDIT: They have added a mouse function
Still, I'm waiting until relatives leave so I can play it again, cause jesus it's fun.  Highly recommend.

Acquire's previous Steam release had gamers defeating vampires, by beating them up with action figures, and then ripping off their clothes. Way of the Samurai 4 isn't
as weird, but veterans and newcomers alike will be surprised, by just how strange the life of a Ronin can be. I've enjoyed this series for quite a long time, and I'm happy to see one of the better titles now available on the service.
As with previous entries, WOTS4 has some basis in historical fact. In the mid 19th century, through treaties and other cooperative efforts, the formerly isolationist Japan worked towards becoming a world power. Due to some questionable decisions by the Shogunate, the country went through something of a semi-colonial period. The British, among other Western powers, held territory in a handful of Japanese ports, where they enjoyed legal immunity.  There was also a rise in xenophobia during this brief yet tumultous period.
It is in these times that you, the wanderer, will find yourself. Will you be the hero that leads Japan to a new age? Will you be their downfall? Maybe you won't be much of anything? Why sacrifice yourself for the greater good, when so many immediate pleasures await? How you answer all these question determines your role as a Samurai. This is the main appeal of the series, the ability to not only make important decisions, but to also interact with a small yet very detailed world.
In this entry there are 10 endings. How you achieve those endings is determined mostly by your dealings with three factions. By participating in events, time will progress, and eventually your fate will be binded with the people you support. Before long, you'll get a feel for how everything works, and future play-throughs will go by very quickly. Way of the Samurai games tend to be short, especially if you know what you're doing. If you want to get the most out of your adventure, you'll want to participate in a lot of extra-curricular activities.
Remember what I said earlier? About "finding yourself"? I meant that in every sense of the word. One of the more enjoyable aspects of the series is creating your ideal Samurai. This can be everything from the clothes you wear, to the weapon(s) you wield, to accessories, hair, face, skin-color, etc. Most of the customization options have to be unlocked, which is a joy to some and a bane to others. Regardless, with enough imagination you can create the look that suits you. How you play games can also have an affect on your days as a Samurai. Dishonorable Samurai tend to make poor decisions, disrespect the dead, and choose violence over diplomacy. This will affect your ranking at the end of every game.
While there are over a hundred weapons, and you'll feel inclined to collect them all, the best one is going to be crafted. For perfectionists, this process is equal parts rewarding and infuriating. Aside from the huge investment of cash, you also have to consider charms. These rarities can be found on every weapon part, and unlocking their potential involves a heap of luck. Still, it's something to consider. For example, if you manage to create a sword with three Life & Death charms, you'll never have to worry about eating during battle to keep your stamina up. Since recovering HP requires stamina, you can see where I'm going with this. A weapon is nothing without a style, and you'll either find or design one that suits you. The style determines not only the moveset, but also special abilities like higher defense. Styles are found off the corpses of your enemies, and must be trained through combat to unlock their full potential. Alternatively, you can find scrolls that perform the same effect.
Whether it's through achievements or simply discovering the mystery behind all of the "???????" in the unlock menu, you may find yourself bound to complete everything in Way of the Samurai 4. This is as far from a trivial task as anyone could imagine. Let's consider the night-crawler portion. During your adventure, you can attempt to gain the interest of the women you pass by. Depending on the time of day, using a line such as "My ship docks at your harbor tonight." can actually work. The following night involves everything from stealth elements to a wrestling match. After all that, you're treated to a love-making segment that's almost as comical as the ones you'd find in Bioware games. This fun little excursion can become a soul-destroying process, if you're crazy enough to take on the "100 night-crawls" achievement.
As the hours pile up, you'll discover that Way of the Samurai 4 takes great joy in making completionists suffer; bedding 100 virtual women is just the tip of the iceberg. While finding the moveset that is perfect for you is entertaining, unlocking the hundreds of moves necessary for a slew of achievements is anything but. Expect to become intimate with the casino, as that is where skill-unlocking scrolls can be purchased. Several clothes and accessories are hidden behind some incredibly obscure unique night-crawls. While everything you need to know can be found on GameFAQs, the process will likely remind you of playing un-translated Japanese games. In short, exercise restraint as much as possible while playing this game. If something ceases to become entertaining, just stop and do something else.
More than anything, Way of the Samurai 4 is what you make of it. This game will draw you in with its allure of being the only Samurai Simulator out there. You will discovers many ways to indulge your innumerable desires. Whether it's the accumulation of wealth, the honor of a high-ranking title, or mere bloodlust, you'll always have something to do. Along the way, you'll stumble into some bizarre situations (such as torturous run-ins with a trio of sadistic sisters), and appreciate the game's many other quirks. This is a unique adventure, one in which you'll want to try everything, and it is extremely addictive. Check it out sometime.

Having only heard of this game series through the mention of name, I found myself intrigued that it had found it's way to the Steam store. Having alured and reeled me in it's arms, it is no wonder why many choose to stay by this franchise. Not having the faintest idea what laid in store for me as I ventured onward to take on the challenge of a Boshin War-era Samurai, I was not dissapointed in what I saw and experienced, not even once.
The combat is swift and merciless, yet it is fully possible to master it with a bit of skill and solid reflexes. The styles of combat ranges from unarmed martial arts, gunslinging revolvery and the use of rifles, the mastery of spear and polearms such as the infamous Japanese Yari or Naginata (Spear and Poleblade respectively), to the legendary Katana - all of which have a combined 180 different fighting styles, ranging from fight techniques seen by Shinobi (Ninjas), Sumo style wrestling punches and grab attacks, and dual wielding whirlwinds of death. It truly is quite overwhelming.
In addition to having this vast array of combat finesse, you also have at your disposal, a rather large assortment of weapons, like before, consisting of the previous mentions of armaments. However, these tools of lethality is not just generic run-of-the-mill swords and sticks with a pointy end - instead, the game offers you, as a Samurai of a Era of strife in Japan, the option to forge your very own customisable, renameable, reforgable, and upgradable deathdealers! Like the hilt of one sword, but like the guard or the blade of another? It's all up to you to choose what weapon you enjoy the most, and as such, one can come up with some pretty hillarious, destructive and impressive creations.
The story is what makes the game shine the most. Like many Japanese games, this one has multiple branching paths which either leads to the player's doom, or his or her fame and success. Having only graced a few of the many paths to choose from, I myself am quite overwhelmed of how much there is to do, and this is not including the countless side-objectives and exploration aspects of the game! It certainly is worth it's weight in gold, and with MANY hours of fun, it is easilly one of the most fun and exciting games I've played.
10/10 - Would slice through ~70 Dragonscales with my custom-made fight style and weapon, again!
