Great game for players who want to pick up the RTS genre or an already established RTS fans who don’t have the time to play games like Starcraft enough to master them. I would mainly recommend it to players interested in playing it online or with friends using the local multiplayer as the main focus of the game is the player vs player experience. If you are hesitant about buying the game or are only interested in the singleplayer experience I would highly suggest checking out the
and getting information about the game there as many of the reviews here are noticeably written without enough experience or understanding of the game.
First of all, I would like to get two things out of the way:
While I can only speak about the alpha community, which I have been part of for over a year now, it is filled with incredible and kind people (including the devs) who care about each other and I hope it will grow bigger now that the game has been released. This is a rather rare find in today’s gaming and something worth mentioning.
Subjective topic, recommend checking out a gameplay video. If you like pixel art you will love this game’s art. The game in general has this dark theme made with pretty colors and the music fits it pretty well.
, the made up language the characters speak is just the cherry on the top in the sound effects department.
The main idea behind the game was to make an easily accessible RTS that has a lot of the difficult mechanics of the genre simplified. This means lower APM requirement, minimal worker and building management, simplified input system that works just as fine with a controller, etc. This results in a much lower skill floor and you reach the part where it’s mainly about outthinking your opponent much quicker. While the skill ceiling is obviously lower as well, there is more than enough room for you to outdo your opponent in.
All of your actions are done through your commander. Be it placing buildings, scouting or controlling your army, all of this is done through your commander that serves as your cursor. In a regular match of T&T, you pick any 6 units from 3 tiers of combat units and a set of defensive structures. You move around the map with your commander to scout and build structures at your base. A build warren will automatically produce its units until its own supply limit is met. You can issue attack move or focus fire orders at your commander’s position to all your units or a single unit type. Player who has no mills left or starves out (has no farms for a minute) loses.
The campaign is split into four parts, one for each faction, represented by their respective commander. Early missions function as a tutorial for you to learn the controls and the basics of how the game works. As mentioned above, the singleplayer missions have procedurally generated maps. This gives the campaign a fair amount of replayability. On the other hand, it creates spikes and drops in difficulty based on how good or bad maps you get and some of the heroic (optional) objectives can be pretty RNG dependent. The other important thing is that many of the missions don’t play like a standard game of T&T with the typical base vs base gameplay and instead you will have missions where you protect certain areas, run around the map with a few units rescuing more on the go, etc.
The game features both local and online multiplayer for up to 4 players. You can either create or join custom matches or play the ranked 1v1 that queues you up against other players. As I said, this also features the procedurally generated maps so you won’t have perfectly balanced maps. The thing you need to realize is that over time the RNG will even out. In 99% of the games, it’s the play that decides the winner, not the map. Also, the shorter game length makes losing due to bad map less terrible. On the other hand, the different maps make every match different and instead of learning map timings and builds you are rewarded for good map read and flexible decision making.
The game is modding friendly. I don’t have personal experience with this but I have already seen some cool stuff. There are also plans on making modding even better in the future. First major thing should be a map editor so people can play their own maps instead of the generated ones. There have been other things mentioned but the map editor is the closest thing to being finished as it has been used for creating the campaign hubs.

I’ve always had a hard time making sequential lists, or deciding what of a certain item is my “absolute favorite.” I have a hard time categorizing them. I tend to not look at things down a linear path and, rather, view it with a broader spectrum. For example, I have a hard time comparing games to “which one I enjoy more,” because in order to do that, I have to define what is enjoyment? Is it how much time you can spend in a game before you grow tired of it? Because, if that were the case, my “most enjoyed” game would have to be DotA 2 with seldom a contender, but it is by far not my “most enjoyed” game. It’s hard to define what’s better within gaming as a whole because there is so much variety within gaming, and so much between every different genre. Defining what game is “better” for me has never before been a thing I have categorized.
Until the release of Dark Souls that is.
The game was such an impactful experience to me that it has cemented itself within my place of “favorite game.” It was unlike any experience a game has left on me previously—the impact was insurmountable. It was something I picked up on a whim, blissfully unaware of what the game contained and ignorant of anything about it. But with everything this game has to offer—the precise, engaging combat; the intricate level design that makes the world feel alive; the history behind the world that you begin to piece together, never quite told to you, but something you’re tasked to figure out yourself—again, contributing to the authentic feeling of this world; and with a brutal learned difficulty that directly reflects the dark, isolated atmosphere—after I had finally put the game down, this game had offered me everything I needed for me to consider it my absolute favorite game.
Easily one of the best games I've ever played!

There are still a few bugs being worked out but the devs have already addressed those issues.
Personally discovered bugs -
Sharks swimming into an island. (Being fixed and even has a sign that jokes about it lol)
Boats spawning on the island and can't be looted unless you climb a tree. (Which can be very dangerous)
Chest items spawning and when opened they fall through the world. (Does't happen often but annoying when it does)
Flashlight no longer putting out light in an area but only into the air. (It will shine but everything on the ground or around you will be shadowed)
When reloading a world it will sometimes spawn a structure you built in a different place and the water cover the island. (Again, not often but annoying. Simple fix is to quit game and reload.)
Cons with Stranded Deep -

Currently there isn't a multi-save feature which would make this a little easier to have different worlds and test different things. (Again, might be added in future update)
Marlins are the most aggressive creature in the game, even more so than a tiger shark or great white. I would really like to see to marlin made more passive and the great whites/tigers/black tips made more aggressive. (Also will most likely be added in future patches)
Now for the amazing parts! -
The world is truly amazing with the details and wildlife. (Can't wait until they add more species since its already amazing)
Can do anything you want from building a small hut to an entire structure that covers the island! (Granted you'll need a ton of sticks)
It truly is an Infinite Procedurally-generated World with tons of islands to explore and use!

My friends and I love Eclipse and were super excited when this came out.  We thought it would give us the chance to play the game as a PBEM over several weeks, rather than having to carve out the time from our busy lives to sit down and play it together in one go.
Sadly, the platform as it stands is too unstable - and too unforgiving - to allow that to happen.
The biggest problem is that, unlike (for example) Civ, where you can set a comfortable deadline to work within and a default number of missed turns which the computer will play for you if life takes over and you can't log-on in time, Eclipse sets a rigidly short time limit and automatically kicks you out if you fail to meet it.  To date, we have yet to finish a game with the same number of players that we started with, as half of us get kicked out for missing the deadline.
I raised this with the Devs, but received no response.
The last straw came when the platform kept dropping me offline for 2 days while I was in the middle of doing my turn - and then kicked me out of the game for not completing that turn!
As it stands, this app is unplayable as a long-term PBEM, and if we actually have the time to sit down and play the game 'live', we'd much rather get together in the same room and play the boardgame.

Disclaimer: I only played this vs. bots. The mechanics of the game is the same as the tabletop version. If you're going to be playing it hotseat or online, I guess it's... alright. Overall I was entertained if frustrated for the lost potential.
As for the game against bots, I was sorely disappointed by the A.I. Perhaps it's a difficult game to make into a good computer-game, but the A.I. played after a strategy that was set in stone. This is absolutely unacceptable for a strategy game, as it essentially forced me to play in a cetain way every game. All the races seemed to play the same way as well, which is actually quite hilarious.
The AI strategy, for every empire would, every game be:
1. get double hulls.
2. attack aliens first turn with the dreadnought they start with, and always win (I never saw them lose to neutrals, not even when they would...)
3. take the middle.
4. put missiles on every ship slot possible. Smart? Not so smart. My intercepters would often win against their dreadnoughts 1-on-1 for this.
5. build monoliths in undefended systems reachable by me.
It means that the replay value is zero for a game otherwise having a great replay value. If you can get rockets, winning is guaranteed. Oh, and did I mention the Hard A.I. is compensated for the lack of engineering hours by starting with a dreadnought? This further ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ the game, forcing you to play defensively until you've managed to scrape together enough research points for the one or two only technologies that will then instantly win you the game?
"Small stuff"
It has a few minor bugs as well and a horrendously poorly made battle design that left me thinking those epic interstellar ships were cardboard boxes, leaving me laughing, and not in a good way. The fighting is slow as well, and there's absolutely no options available to speed it up unless you want it to auto-resolve fights...

So glad I found this game. Up until I found Strike Vector the only games I had for decent dogfighting were FreeSpace2 and the old Ace Combat games (the last one was terrible so I don't play it). The beauty of this thing is you can treat it like a regular fps rather than zip around all the time too. The passive and active abilities on your Vector can be combined with specialities on your weapons to cater to a specific playstyle and if you fly well enough you can play to your strengths while dampening weaknesses (if say for example you had radar jamming + cloak + silent plasma, excellent for sniping but useless in a straight-up fight - know when to relocate and zip through obstacles to stay out of harm's way).
There's a fair amount of content, but really the fights alone will keep you occupied. On the negative side - sometimes the servers can have high latency which can end up with your Vector plastered against a wall that was several hundred metres away just a few moments ago. The extremely fast and precise nature of the flying and shooting also makes it somewhat inaccessbile to gamers that don't have a lot of experience with flying in a 3D environment or fast-paced fps. I find it hard to judge how much this is the case though as I've played space sims for over a decade now. :)

I love this game! The way you can climb everything adds to the fighting and exploration to give this game a unique feel, while sticking to most original rpg elements like the magic and monsters. The pawn system is fun, but makes me wish this game was co-op :(.

Solid gameplay, interesting story that makes you think the more you play it, best lootfest and dungeon crawling I've gotten to see in a long time. Kinda like Skyrim, but better refined in all the right spots. There, tl;dr out of the way.
Combat's pretty varied but a little complicated to a newcomer, not overly hard unless you wander where you aren't ready for yet or find a dragon. Dragons in this game feel like dragons should, in that they will wreck your tiny little protag 4$$ without blinking if you charge them, especially early on. No two-shotting these boys, sorry milk drinkers. LOTS of crazy monsters to run into with unique gameplay mechanics and weaknesses you have to exploit to win with relative ease. Death is obnoxious but not overly punishing, just save often and when you think you should.
Pawns are a great mechanic in my very conceited and obviously best opinion. They learn as they serve you and others, though "WOLVES HUNT IN PACKS" starts to drive you to insanity after the millionth time. Thankfully you can turn that chatter off which I wish I knew about five or six braincells ago. They can help with quests occasionally, and god knows they are good at grabbing loot, so instant plus for a loot fiend like me. You can make your pawn look like a cool thing like a normal person, or make your waifu/husbando like 99% of the players. Me included. Nothing like having an E X T R A T H I C C minio- I mean squire. Busty wenches aside, they can get annoying but overall they're the only companions I like in games. I normally travel alone, but there's something amusing about hearing them say "TIS WEAK TO FIRE" as they cast an ice blast at a wolf.
Worth it if you're a person who likes to encounter Random Monsters who'll Pull a bedsheet over and around your head then proceed to stone you (This may or may not only count for Bitterblack Isle)

Throne of Lies is an epic social deduction game, designed to test your detective skills and pit you against your friends.  I've put over 650 hours into a similar game, "Town of Salem" and I can personally say that Throne of Lies meets and exceeds expectations.
Throne of Lies has an incredible amount of complexity to the roles.  Well balanced, but challenging, the available roles are very unique and have each thier own playstyle.  A scorned (neutral role) gets to use the trollbox to trick the rest of the court into lynching their target.  If that doesn't work, they get to frame them at night to make them look like a member of the opposing faction.
That's just one example of what's available to you as one of the many roles in the game.
Throne of Lies is intense and very entertaining.  I highly reccomend this game to people who enjoy Town of Salem or other similar Social Deduction RPGs.

Played 3 games, died Night 1 in two of them. 10/10 would die again.
In all seriousness, this is a fairly compelling, very deduction focused Mafia/Werewolves style of game, similar to how Town of Salem plays. There's a "Good" faction (The Blue Dragons) and a "Bad" faction (The Unseen) (As well as a Cult faction but you won't run into them when starting) and the goals your trying to accomplish depend on your factions role. The Blue Dragons are trying to out all the Unseen and vice versa for the Unseen members. The twist is the Unseen know who members of their faction are at all times while the Blue Dragons are forced to figure it out through conversation and investigation. There's also a handful of Neutral roles thrown in to spice it up (some are trying to kill everyone else, some are trying to solely survive for example) There's also the King role, which starts Neutral but can be "Converted" onto the Unseen's side (Or the Cult's).
I did say "Converted" and that's another key feature of Throne of Lies, The Unseen start with a Mastermind and an Assassian, and the Mastermind can convert almost any role into an "evil" version of it, but there's always a limit of 3 members in the Unseen at any time. I use Town of Salem as a natural comparison for this style of game since it was the first Werewolves/Mafia game I got heavily interested in, but ToS requires a much smaller level of deductive reasoning required as it's really easy to whip up a mob mentality. In Throne of Lies, the role list of the game is completely hidden, and the only roles that are always there are King, Prince, (and for games with Unseen) Mastermind, and Assassain. Not knowing what could possibly exist means that there's more room for doubt when it comes to potential for claiming, and you have to be almost certain you know the person you're going to send to trial is guilty or not.
Although I haven't "Played" much of Throne of Lies at the time of writing this (That joke at the top wasn't just a joke.) I still see the potential this game has to offer for people who enjoy investigative deception style games like this or ToS, and if you've played ToS before you'd feel right at home with it. And although the community for it is small right now (It DID just launch) it's a very committed one who are willing to help new players along at learning the game. Because if you haven't played something like this before, there is a bit of a learning curve, and I have no idea how the Cult roles will play differently to the Unseen when I get a chance to play games with those enabled. My one concern is just the community size is small and it can take a while for games to start (I had a 10 minute queue time for my third game), so it isn't a sort of "Pick up and play" Like how ToS would be. But that's something that can be fixed with time and more players (The game supports a Minimum of 8 Players and a Max of 16, which is just the right amount for this type of game). I look forward to jumping back in to more sessions of this with my friends and the loyal group of players this game has already accrued, and I think if you enjoy a good session of Mafia/Werewolves this is your style of game.

This is my review for the "Test Of Time" award...
Dark Souls has the best combination of outright fun game mechanics, abundant lore, replayability, and aesthetic style out of any game I have ever played and probably will ever play in my life.
Although Dark Souls has a reputation of being one of the most difficult games to ever be developed, alongside such classics as Ninja Gaiden and Super Meat Boy, the game mechanics are designed such that it is possible avoid virtually any attack in the game. The main contributing mechanic is, of course, the roll, which when executed grants the player invincible animation frames. Therefore, shields and armor are technically unnecessary, and indeed, I myself have in fact done a no shield run wearing only cloth armor. This mechanic among others is what makes Dark Souls a surmountable game, but it also introduces a towering skill ceiling that only the most seasoned and skilled players ever reach. It also has the additional effect of making this game an absolute joy to play time and time again, because the player always feels challenged, and subsequently the player always feels rewarded for improving.
Another factor adding to the replay value of this game is the potential for variety in items, spells, and character builds. With a multitude of impactful and meaningful stats, distinct spell schools, armor and equipment sets, weapons and weapon styles, I imagine one would have to play for at least five hundred to a thousand hours at minimum to experience all of the different builds and flavors available in this game. Personally, I have about 100 hours in this game on PC (and a similar amount on console), and this is across maybe 5-8 playthroughs, and that's just the tip of the iceberg in terms of different builds I could go through the game with. In addition, though I've never had an interest in doing "new game plus" playthroughs, players have the opportunity to play through the game on ramped-up difficulties if they want to continue to play on a single character. I'm not aware of a hard limit on new game plus runs, and players can continue to do NG+++..., etc. runs just as long as they can continue to handle the incremental difficulty.
The music (or lack thereof) and art assets are dark and twisted and perfect for the tone of the game. To me the boss music often sounds hopeless and fills me with dread, like a requiem for a lost cause, yet it has a certain determined energy about it. This is especially applicable to the game's final boss, which is one of my favorite video game soundtracks of all time. (If you have not yet played this game, please do not spoil it by finding a video.) The world between the boss battles are usually absent of any music, which in its own way contributes to the mystery and wonder of the game. As far as art and models go, the monsters are often creepy (the mimic), sometimes weird (the basilisk), and occasionally demented (the bone tower in the Tomb of Giants), but they are all fascinating. There is tons of variety, and the player must learn to approach each monster in a unique way. The bosses are similar in this respect and quite challenging in their own ways. Speaking of bosses, one of the most difficult bosses of all time (in my opinion), Ornstein & Smough, serves as roughly the middle checkpoint of this game.
I contend that this game will stand the test of time as one of the all-time RPG greats. I absolutely recommend this to anyone who has the patience to overcome the game's difficulty hurdle so that he or she can experience one of the most rewarding, complete, and enjoyable video games of our time.

Dynasty Warriors!
A long time ago, an adolescent version of me received a PS2 with Dynasty Warriors 2 as the first game to go along with it. I played the hell out of that game, unlocking every character, beating every campaign, and leveling everyone up to a ridiculous degree. For whatever reason, the Dynasty Warrior series has retained just the right balance of grinding and satisfying gameplay to keep me entertained for years. I've played multiple entries of the series, and even though each game is pretty much the same exact same thing, it always keeps me happy and satisfied.
Based on the Romance of the Three Kingdoms, there is somewhat accurate historical portion of the game, and if you've never heard the story before, it's actually an entertaining period of history. It's not exactly 100% accurate (Dian Wei never wielded an axe that was nearly 2x his size, for example), but almost everything in the game is inspired by a true story in some way.
The port is pretty good, all things considered, but there are a few hiccups. The controller is not bound in a way that makes sense, and you'll need to change things around to get it to play right. Navigating the menu for changing controls is a pain, and you're going to end up taking a ton of screenshots of the menu on accident... Unless you've changed  your steam screenshot key. Other than that, everything has run smoothly for me.
There are multiple gameplay modes, including the story mode, which has multiple characters and paths to play through, a free mode that lets you choose any scenario and side, and some kind of conquest mode that has really weird rules but is satisfying to play.
Make no mistake, this game is a grind. You grind. You grind some more. You grind and grind and grind. There is honestly not much challenge here. The game is pure grind-tastic fun, plain and simple. If you've never played a Dynasty Warriors game, this is a great place to start, and the port is nearly flawless.

Alright, as a Dynasty Warriors fan, this is the best DW game in a while. For people who say  that it's a ripoff because "Complete Edition with blabla DLC's"; well, Koei did screw up with the name, but it means that the original DW 8 game, alongside the Xtreme Legends expansion come in in one game, instead of getting them separately to transfer data, etc. So you get the Story mode of the 3 Kingdoms alongside extra stages and the Lu Bu storyline, alongside Ambition Mode (with a revamped post game) and Challenge Mode (it's not hard but it entertains for an hour or so if you want some achievements).
Overall, the Story is great, for people who kow it and people who are new to it, it does a good job explaining the events (Alas, i recommend the japanese voices, since the English ones don't feature a narrator or base conversations, only events and battle lines, which are still a lot, and better voiced than before, but well depends on one's tastes honestly)
The Shu bias is slowly getting reduced, and every kingdom is amazing in its own right; the missions are great, with the option to pick around 2-3 or even 4 characters per stage for every kingdom, it allows for more characters to shine, and provide more variety in mission objectives. To put an example for longtime fans, at the Battle of Chibi, if one were to play Huang Gai or Han Dang, you get to the Fire Boat, and well, get all the fun; if playing Sun Shangxiang you get to protect Liu Bei and Zhuge Liang while waiting for the wind direction to change for the fire attack to happen, and so on. Which makes it even more interesting on split screen, having 2 people go to different locations to spice things up more.
Alongside the new Hyphotetical objectives to unlock the Hypo route of each faction, it just makes the already good Story Mode, get a lot of replay value, and opens up some interesting scenarios, and gives some characters who don't make the cut in the historical route have some spotlight; though it's not perfect, but no real complaints as it just adds more to the already extensive campaign. (I am looking at you, Shu final hyphotetical stage, for putting in Zhuge Liang and Zhao Yun instead of letting us play as the 3 bros Guan Yu, and Zhang Fei alongside Liu Bei)
The Ambition Mode is an entertaining mode for fighting skirmishes against the cast of the game, recruiting allies, gaining fame and materials to build a massive building to welcome the Emperor and become known throughout the land; a bit silly but it makes for a good inmersive experience when you don't wanna spend time repeating stages on free mode and you rather just fight for the go of it; this mode also allows to build facilities based on your expansion which will benefit the entire game, such as increasing the weapons a blacksmith can make, or fusion weapons to get the best out of the skillset they have, get animals, increase exp, many options are here to keep the player going, alongside the obvious fun that is beating the 3 kingdom founders and Lu Bu to join whoever your character you are using's cause, it is better than the conquest mode in DW7, of that much i am certain, it also allows 2 player coop.
The gameplay well, it's dynasty warriors, sure it's a "button masher" but there is so much depth into it, more to it than what we give credit for, each character being favored by different abilities, such as shadow sprint (cancel strong attack with normal to continue the chain), Dive (lets you escape easier), Whirlwind (more dmg when enemies are sent flying), and Dash (midair jump or cancel an attack into a forward hop); and that's not even counting the different effects of each weapon, which can vary from increasing musou (special attack) power, to increase the raw power of it, to slow enemies, to grant more dmg the longer your chain is, etc. With the double weapon system, alongside the 3 elements (Man-Heaven-Earth) which is a rock-paper-scissors mechanic which grants advantages or disadvantages, resulting in various possibilities out of a well timed switch attack that could become a switch counter when the odds are against you, or a powerful storm rush when you make good use of your advantage; so many mechanics, alongside the musou system which grants 2 ground musous and an air one, each character benefitting differently from the properties of their own moveset; sword fighters usually have good air musous to keep the chain, while other hard hitting characters' air musou sends everyone flying, while having a grab ground musou, and so much more. The gameplay, the most important part of this type of games, is well made, and allows more some good strategic parts, whether to go all out or hit and run depends on how one wants to play, enemies on hard and above are bound to give the player a challenge, specially if underleveled, trust me on this.
And the OST (Soundtrack) is...well, all Warriors games have awesome soundtrack, but this one is just GOD DAMN
Ok, sorry about that,  you get a new Soundtrack, with Battle of Chibi (both historical and hyphotetical), Hefei, Fan Castle, Wuzhang Plains and well, the Lu Bu route soundtrack being hands down one of the best i heard; oh and if you are not satisfied....long time DW fans are in for a surprise for the Hyphotetical routes of the stages which play some well known songs, which i won't spoil for you :D
Alas, but it's not perfect obviously, when it comes to the pc release, we got cut off the online multiplayer and the ps4 graphics, the latter not being that bad, but the other one can be a deal breaker for people who looked to play online with friends, (hoping DW8 empires fixes this) but why am i recommending this version? Well if you get it in a sale like i did, you get PS3 textures but with custom resolution, you also get to select how many enemies you can get on screen, and on PC oh my, it's terrific; and all the waves of enemies falling before you go at 60 fps pretty much all the time, even when events like fire attacks happen, which used to be the main cause of slowdown in consoles, it's fixed in the pc version and runs perfectly, which of course makes it AMAZING to play split screen with a Friend; I still remembered how bad it was in the PS2 and how little it improved in PS3/PS4 but this version was made for local coop, it runs amazing, and this shows how much potential Warrior games have if Koei made a perfect release.
I say this is a good 1st try since Dynasty Warriors 6; and i hope to see more DW games coming to PC and making full use of it's capabilities, the game is amazing, although it does have shortcomings; but Warriors fans having a huge amount of content to look forward into, and newcomers have plenty of mechanics to memorize if you wanna be a True Warrior of the 3 Kingdoms, without spamming Lu Bu's  buffs, which i remind you to not pursue on Hulao Gate, just in case.
Overall Good Experience and sets a good stone for future Warriors games, 8.5 don't let people who are butthurt over lack of online and that claim that hurr hurr DLC; which is not necessary, it adds a couple of stages which well, should cater to longtime Warriors fans as it brings back maps from classic games, (which pro players use to grind on Ultimate since they are hard), and some prototype weapons which would be later chosen to be used in DW8 Empires to change the weapons of some characters, costumes and the like are not necessary, and the game already has huge content by itself.
Mechanics are well instructed in the game, but you can always look up a guide, so no need to be afraid, wheter you are a long time fan or you wanna inmerse yourself in the Era of the 3 Kingdoms, this is one of the best experiences you can get; and if you want online, get the console version, they are just as enjoyable.
Also Lu Lingqi, jesus, Lu Bu's daughter, such a badass, Koei give this woman a spotlight in your next game dammit.

You play as a samurai from far away land, who just happens to get in the middle of a political war and it is completely up to you what you want to pursue during your visit.
You are not forced to take part in any of the story elements if thats your choice, infact, right when you arrive, you can simply turn on your heels and leave the town. Alternatively you can choose to side with one of the various "factions" and help them achieve their goal, if you regret your choice, you are free to simply turn against them instead.
Various other elements are thrown into the mix with missions that either drive the town into chaos or help turn it into a more safe haven for the citizens. If none of that sounds like your thing, you can go around having sexy time with the town folk, gambling, running your own dojo or just causing havoc and eventually getting arrested and tortured.
At the end of each playthrough, be it by dying or finishing a story, your run will be evaluated and you'll gain samurai points based on your actions and how samurai-like your life was, which in turn you will be able to spend on various, mostly visual, unlocks for your next run.
In short, if you do end up liking the game, theres tons and tons more of fun to find, granted it might get a bit repetive but thankfully you can skip through all the dialogue you have already been through.
TL:DR
A very fun game, with a bunch of humor, open story for you to pursue as you wish and tons of replayability.
Do note that there are various crash issues that MIGHT affect you, I've only had some audio disortion myself, which was just fixed in a patch. Also the game runs at 30fps, if you can't deal with that, just close this page.

This is a mediocre port of a great game. If you want the short of it, you should buy this game for anything under 40 dollars if you'd enjoy an East meets West story with a cool sword building system and branching story. Anyways:
Firstly, the bad. In 33 hours of playing, it has crashed three times which is bad but not terrible (save points are fairly common). The window textures glitch out on my powerful pc, but not catastrophically and they are rarely seen. Control prompts are given in controller buttons, not keyboard buttons, even though once or twice it used keyboard prompts instead when I played, so I think somewhere that isnt working correctly. Finally, the game is short but built for replaying with many New Game+ mode stuff so if you don't want to play it multiple times, you won't enjoy that part.
As for the good, it is built with a branching story and many events and characters that your choices can seriously effect. Because the game is short, they allowed many permanent choices such as taking quests that allow you to kill various main characters in the three factions, who in turn often have unique weapons. This goes into the New Game plus mode, which is very neat. All gear and fighting styles are carried over game to game, and even some light story elements change (aiding certain characters in previous playthroughs often has them start elsewhere in the world, so you don't have to redo certain sidequests). The combat is fairly fun, but the reality is this is a loot game with an interesting East meets West theme (with zany elements occasionally thrown in that reminds me of Dead Rising). Almost every weapon can be broken down into three parts, and then those parts put back together any way you wish, the end goal being to make the ultimate sword/spear or at least the coolest looking one. Finally, the story while not always the best written is pretty good and interesting, with each branching path coming to a relatively logical and satisfying conclusion (although certain actions are weirdly unoticed, such as killing a faction's guards but still being allowed to take all their quests). This game has many secrets and there are multiple secret missions I still have not been able to do, and pretty much each new path will net you one to five unique swords you otherwise could not get. I really recommend this game.

Mechwarrior Online, Unreal Tournament with permanent jetpacks, Quake and a bit of Ace Combat squashed together. That sound appealing to you? Then continue.
After having been at this game for an hour or so a day a week, I'm nearly at rank 44 (the current max that I know of) and have 14 hours tracked by Steam... They really need to stop marketing this as a "brutal aerial FPS". "Brutal Aerial Shooter" maybe, but the "brutal" part needs some work...
Before reading the rest of this, do keep in mind that this is one of those "constantly in development" games, so anything can change.
Bear in mind this is a LONG review so you can rack off and read a 1 line review instead if you are the tl;dr sort.
Gameplay video over here.
To begin with the graphics and sound of this game are nice and mediocre respectively; graphically the Unreal Engine has never been underperforming (unless made so by developer, such as, say, Dishonored). You might find yourself reminded of HAWKEN (which is coincidentally another UDK title) given the overall aesthetic of the game. Vectors aren't very streamlined or hyper futuristic - I'd liken them to a RSI craft rather than an Origin Jumpworks in Star Citizen. Textures in the environment are blurry at times, a victim of low resolution, and even in the hangar the Vectors' texture resolution could do some work. There aren't many options to toy with - just bloom and motion blur off the top of my head, but as a whole the game looks nice and runs smoothly, for my mid-range GPU. Textures unload too often though, so stutters happen a lot. Standard UE tweaks can be done though.
Soundwise is a mixed bag. Stuff like the shotgun and plasma cannon sound decent, but need more oomph, the LMG sounds like a pip spitter and the Vectors' afterburners also need more "BAM I'M GOING FAST". Explosions on the other hand are satisfyingly gritty. The absolutely worst aspect of the sound though is the powerups - they mute almost all ambient sound for no reason, and don't give you a... powered up?... feeling.
I don't like the music as a whole, whether it's the trailer's on the game's own. It's a kind of fun-loving peppy country rock thing (I think), which feels at home yet not at the same time. Personally I'd expect this kind of music in a trucker sim or something, but not in a futuristic-ish aerial shooter. I'd go for something more orchestral with some electrical vibes but that's my opinion. Music is a subjective thing.
Gameplay, being the chicken schnitzel and french fries of this title's marketing, is mostly good too. Being both a shooter player and an Ace Combat player as well as a fan of Crimson Skies (High Road to Revenge, that is), but not a Quake/Unreal Tourney player...
The basic piloting, flying your Vector without crashing, if you will, may not be for everybody. It adopts the "follow your reticule" method (i.e. your Vector uses your crosshair as a vector) in the "Vector mode" (jet mode), but this becomes standard shooter aiming in Harrier mode (i.e. hover, or helicopter mode), with the exception of your crosshair moving ahead, somewhat like MWO's arm crosshairs do. Given that you can easily turn on a dime by switching between Vector and Harrier mode, this makes for some very impressive flying antics if you can get the hang of it, plus you can barrel roll and do quick-strafes. Using third person Chase view (which is default, contrary to the marketing subtitle) makes things easier to get the hang of plus you can see things you might crash into more easily. Hitting anything head on in Vector mode is guaranteed to be a suicide, so be certain to try the Solo flight (buried under the Classroom menu button) to get the hang of things first.
Combat wise, the six degrees of freedom afforded by the dual-mode Vectors (it's like flying an Osprey tiltrotor that doesn't suck!) makes for some extremely high paced dart-around combat, especially between two competent pilots who can easily spend minutes just dancing with the angels without shooting each other down. That said, a capable pilot can also quite easily dominate the scoreboard, with or without experience. It's incredibly fun to watch and exhilarating in a way to achieve.
The weapons mostly have some bite to them, but some definitely much more than others. This is the largest flaw of the gameplay right now; weapon balance is nearly comparable to a certain Paul's. Shotguns are certainly devastating up close, but at the same time require some precise aiming even at that range (2 shots will do if you can get within 100m and center the target in your crosshair), but yet I feel they need a damager nerf and a range boost. Plasma is fine, since its a true sniper pro challenge (easier said than done in this game) while the gattling plain outclasses the LMG in general.
Then there's the fact that Unreal/Quake (maybe some TF2) rocket jumpers got attracted. The Rocket Launcher is a commonly encountered weapon, the Homing one more so, and this hits extremely hard and still blasts you with splash even if it doesn't contact directly.
The Swarm Missiles are the most commonly encountered weapon, the developer-declared "newb's weapon" but even long running players will use it, because it's so effortlessly able to kill things. You merely need to hide around a corner and fire them when you detect a Vector incoming on your radar. Aim them properly close range, you outdamage a shotgun. A shotgun coming at you? Move backwards, fire in their direction. Swarm Missiles also leave little dodging room in maps like Iron Fortress. They need a serious nerf, now. They're too rewarding for such an effortless weapon in a "BRUTAL" game, as are the Homing missiles. I feel like I'm playing against MWO's poptarts, and that's not a good feeling.
As a couple of last notes, aiming is -easier- in first person. Flying isn't. And the community is tiny - expect to see the same names over and over.
Modewise there's just Domination (king of the hill(s)) where you have to hold certain areas ala Battlefield Conquest till your score bar reaches the goal. Deathmatch (and Team Deathmatch) plus Bounty Hunter are the remaining few. Bounty Hunter could do some work because it's pretty darn luck based since a random lucky kill will put you in first, plus it encourages those hide-in-corner swarm players. The devs do seem to be working on new stuff in this area though. There's no PvE, only competitive PvP modes, plus it's not machinima friendly nor can you watch replays, spectate, etc. Hopefully those kind of things will come along.
As with most games of this nature, Strike Vector feels a tad unfinished. Not like, say, Warframe, which feels a different kind of unfinished. The server browser can be inaccurate, the servers themselves will boot everyone out and reset themselves at least once in a while, and you might find yourself unable to change your Vector's colors. In my experience though I've had no problems with the client crashing or anything, but there's a lot of annoying short stutters which I believe might be texture loading whenever I do a 90 degree.
So, as Kotaku says, "Strike Vector does one thing - frantic multiplayer action". And indeed it does it well. But no game is ever flawless, and definitely Strike Vector is flawed. Recommended? Yes. If you're a fan of flying, darting around, and heated battles. No, if you get tired of dying easily, really hate Swarm missiles coming around corners, or can't get the hang of flying anything at all. This is hardly a game for everybody. At US$24.99, I'd also pass. It's really hard for me to mark this as recommended at that price, but then again there's going to be no paid DLC, all free.
Don't get me wrong, I like this game. I'm not much of a twitch shooter person and Strike Vector is a twitch shooter. It just requires more thought in it than say playing Duke Megaton online.
Update: Now, SV is $11.49. More worth it.

The majority of people who will come reading these reviews will probably be those who have experience with town of salem and epicmafia but are still on the fence if Throne of lies is worth 10 bucks for the same experience.
Let me start off this review by making the audacious claim that Throne of Lies is a much more complex, engaging, and entertaining game than Town of Salem will ever be. If you have 9 dollars to spare,
and stop wasting your time with town of salem. Here is why.
1.
- Every single role has 3-4 different abilities as opposed to town of salem where each role has 1 ability. Why does this matter? Every single player has the capability to win the game on their own with deception and skill. Town of Salem can be so frustrating where you feel powerless as a spy in a game with no whispers, or as lookout with no results. Even the neutral roles contains so many abilities. These extra abilities add much more thinking to the game. You aren't just a survivor who vests 4 times in this game. The alchemist(survivor equivalent of throne of lies) who also just has to survive till the end of the game, has 2 kill potions, 3 vests, and infinite healing capability. You have to really think who should I heal and keep alive? Should I kill the ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ who is accusing me of being unseen? Should I vest(stone-skin potion) since I'm being accused tonight. The point is you have to actually think when you use your ablitites, it isn't just monotonous, clicking one button every night. With this much power, any player can win with skill, you just have to play smart and you will be rewarded. In town of salem, survivors do literally the same thing every game. put 4 vests and pray town won't execute you and mafia won't kill you, lol. The alchemist is just 1 example of an improved role from town of salem. The entire game can be considered an improvement from town of salem which fixes every problem that game had.
2.
- God bless these devs for implementing shorter timers. In town of Salem, the timers are unbearably long once you learn the game. There is no need for so much time to do 1 generic ability at night or 5 entire minutes to execute a confirmed baddie. When the game drags out and nothing happens, the game feels stale fast, town of salem has had this problem for a while, If you are coming from town of salem, you will really love the shorter timers in throne of lies. The game feels fast-paced.
3.
- The King is just another element added to the game that increases the complexity of the game. He can be good, neutral or evil. You really can't tell right away, but he holds a lot of voting and executing power, as well as the ability to guard himself and other players and can even investigate others. There is 1 king in every single game.
The evil guys, the neutral players, and the good guys don't know the king's faction. Every single players has to deduce the king's faction through his actions/attitude in the game. The king is a very powerful player who can tip the game to either side if he survives till the end. Killing or keeping him alive makes or breaks the game for your faction. What does this mean? Not only do you have to kill everyone in the opposing faction and do your best to complete your role's objective, you have to keep tabs on the king!
4.
- The most frustrating thing for me in town of salem was being asked to post my role's objective in jail to the jailor. That isn't how the game is intended to be played. I'm not expected to post my role's objective to you. You are expected to find my role with clues and anaylsis, not by worthless metagaming lul. Another example is spychecking spies, adding names in will for disguisor, random voting when blackmailed, the list just goes on and on. Town of Salem is riddled with meta gaming which ruins the game immensely.
In Throne of lies, I have not seen any cases of metagaming which ruin the game for me. The game is really well designed and makes it extremely difficult to do so. You will really appreciate that this game is won more so with analysis than ridiculous cheating.
5.
- Another huge point for Town of Salem players. Town of Salem is a FREE game. That means any child on the internet can make an account and plague your games. Especially since Town of Salem is a team-reliant game where half the town roles only have 1 ability and they must communicate to get anything done. This make the game UNBEARABLY frustrating and can honestly convert level-headed players to toxic players in no time at all.
Throne of Lies has a 9 dollar paywall to enter the game. 9 dollars is not much all, but it will block those damned little kids out. The current Throne of Lies community consists of olders players who have played town of salem and epicmafia long ago, or are just trying something new. The players are welcoming and patient. Everyone is learning! Toxicity is limited in this game simply because the game is designed so much better. Better players will win their games single-handedly, they aren't reliant on the team since every player's role has so much power.
6.
- I've only played for a couple weeks and I've already noticed so many constant large game-changing updates and buxfixes. It is very apparent that the devs are passioniate about making the game the best they can. They put the game at just 9 dollars to give you constant updates and constant accessability. I've also noticed there is no stupidly pointless dlc. All the skins and weapons can be bought with in-game currency which is SO much easier to gain than in Town of Salem. In Town of salem, you have to pay an absurd amount for executions, skins, pets, etc. They are milking players for all they got. Especially when their game has remained static it amazes me that they can still do this. The throne of lies developers could have doubled the price of the game, they could have added pointless dlc, they could have turned this entire game into a cash grab, but they didnt.
Why did I make this review? So that Throne of Lies can get the larger player base it deserves.

I don't get it.
I grew up loving the Sonic genesis trilogy, but never got the chance to play Sonic CD. The internet kept telling me about how amazing it was and how it was the best 2D Sonic game ever. I bought the Sonic Gems Collection in 2005 and that was my first chance to play Sonic CD. I didn't see what was so great about it. In fact, I saw a lot of negative stuff. Fast forward to today, and I'm still not sold, although that's not a surprise since this is just a port.
The level design and art style in Sonic CD is just downright atrocious. The color scheme chosen for the later half of the levels is all over the place. The first level, Palmtree Panic, is bright and colorful; something you'd expect a Sonic game's first level to be. Once you're past that though, everything goes crazy. Collision Chaos' bright pink layout or Wacky Workbench's muddled purple shadows don't lend themselves to memorable imagery. I remember Angel Island or Green Hill zone very vividly, as those zones had their own color schemes that while popping out, created a lasting image in your head. How about Ice Cap zone or Lava Reef zone? All of the zones in Sonic 1-3 had character and personality and I can recall them very clearly. Here, I can't remember anything past Palmtree Panic. The worst offenders are the last half of the levels, from Quartz Quadrant onward. These all have a generic industrial feel to them with odd color choices that made my eyes hurt eventually.
And I even haven't gotten to the level design. You thought the colors and art were all over place? You haven't seen anything yet. The level design in Sonic CD is - and I know I've said this a lot but I seriously mean it - ALL OVER THE PLACE. Again Palmtree Panic isn't too bad but you can still see hints of what's to come early on. There are sections in the level that literally look like they've been copied and pasted around. There are tiles that don't connect cleanly with other tiles and then there's just some plain old bad platform placement. Seriously, it's as if someone used a selection tool and highlighted random parts of the levels and shuffled them around in random places. The levels are also filled to the brim with really random gimmicks that don't compliment each other that well, the clearest offender of this being Wacky Workbench, where background objects can hurt you, floor panels can launch you, and other weird stuff. Most of my time playing through the levels I was just struggling to keep Sonic from flying around all over the place and then all of a sudden the level will be over. Overall, the levels are a mess and by the time they're over you will not remember anything about it. There is just no clean flow to the game, and for a momentum based platformer, that is a big flaw.
The cherry on top of all this? This is the first Sonic game to incorparate an actual mechanic about going fast. There are posts sprinkled througout the levels labeled "PAST" and "FUTURE". If you hit one of these signs you'll get an indicator you're ready to go to that time period. To actually pull off the time travel Sonic needs to go fast and maintain a fast speed for a couple of seconds. You can already see the problem with this. Because the level design is so clunky and messy, random obstacles will probably stop you from getting to or maintaing top speed. You remember those stupid little speed traps that were in the original trilogy? You know, like those small little platforms where there was two springs on each side and if you so wanted to you could just drop Sonic in there and he'd bounce back and forth endlessly? In some areas they had to put those kinds of traps next to the posts in order to give players an easy way to time travel. If that isn't proof that something isn't working right with your base level design then I'm not sure what is.
As for the time travelling mechanic itself it's nothing interesting. It's one of the two ways to get the true ending, the other being collecting all of the chaos emer- oh, I'm sorry, "time stones". May I mention that Sonic CD has probably the worst special stages I've seen in the 2D games? Imagine the Sonic 3 special stages but instead of only being able to move at 90 degree angles, you have full 360 rotational control over Sonic. UFOs fly around the stage and you have to destroy them all to get the time stone. Okay, doesn't sound too bad right? Well, first off, Sonic turns like a freaking rock, making hitting the UFOs really frustrating. If you've ever played Sonic R, that's how sluggish Sonic turns. Secondly, the stages themselves are filled with "void" zones, and if you're in these zones even for just a second, you lose a TON of time, and you automatically fail if you run out of time. Overall it's just an annoying diversion and not a fun way to get the time stones, like the Sonic 2 or 3's special stages.
Anyways, so the time mechanic. For starters, it's not really explained that well. What you have to do is go to the past period of the zone you're in and destroy the machines Eggman/Robotnik has placed. Doing so changes the future of the zone into a "good" future, and if you do this for every zone you can get the true ending, instead of having to deal with the silly special stages. The thing is, you have to actually stop and explore levels to find the machines and traditional Sonic level design doesn't lend itself to exploration very well. It's all about going forward and finding new routes at the same time. But see, it's even worse here because the level design in Sonic CD is so messy it's even harder to explore. Aside from that, there is no point in going to the future period until you've destroyed the past machine. I know the bad future zones are supposed to be ruined and nasty looking but the present zones shouldn't look funky too!
To this day Sonic CD is praised almost unanimously and I still don't see why. Just play one of the genesis trilogy games and then play Sonic CD, the difference in quality will be as clear as night and day.

I finally just finished the campaign, and might I say, what a great game! Having never played very many RTS games, this one was really easy to get a hang of and figure out right from the start! And with it being such short battles, it made the countless times I failed on some of the campaign levels more tolerable by knowing I could restart without having to spend a lot of time to get back up again. I also loved the story! Having read all of the Redwall books as a child, this game really brought me back, and I could really see the creatures of Redwall doing things like this as well (and for anyone who thought the story was too dark or creepy or anything, Redwall had animals eating eachother AND it was considered a kid's book!) But after I finally finished the story it gave me that kind of feeling of both joy that I did it, and yet sorrow that it's over, when that main theme played after the credits my heart literaly felt like it jumped from the feelings I got from it. I also thought the last level was just epic in general, and it felt really cool deciding everyone's fate, even though I could pretty much guess at what was going to happen, and when it did, I still tried my hardest to stop it! I almost felt like I was each of those characters! The maps may be unfair sometimes, but it's still the commander who wins or loses the battle and I liked the diversity the changing maps brought! I gotta say, this game is one of my favorite games that I've played all year, if not THE favorite game I've played all year!(and this was the first year I found out about the Steam summer sale!). Well this has gone on long enough, I just have to say GET THIS GAME! You will (hopefully) not regret it!

I love this board game, and this program is a fairly faithful execution of it, from a mechanical standpoint.  Unfortunately, the asynchronous multiplayer is really poor, missing basically all of the features one would expect from online board game play.  It is missing all of the following basic functions that one would expect from a good online board game:
-Basic hosting features (like the ability to name your game, option for random race assignment, or the ability to kick players)
-A game journal
-Out of game method of notification when it is your turn (email or otherwise)
-Any player profile metrics (play speed, games completed, win/loss, etc.)
-No support for live games
Additionally, it seems to disconnect you from any/all of your games if you accidentally disconnect your profile on any of the devices onto which you've previously added it.  All of this adds up to a very slow and low-functioning asynchronus play experience; it seems impossible to finish a turn (much less a game).  Player profile metrics (with play speed and games completed, specifically) would go a long way towards resolving this, as players could set up games for other players that had a similar preferred schedule/pace.
For the devs,
(for the Game of Thrones Board Game) is an excellent example of an implementation that allows for the creation of a solid online board gaming community.

If you are familiar to the last three Way of the Samurai games then there isn't too much to say aside from this being an upgrade from 3.
Unarmed combat is as valid an option now as using spears or any other combat style, as there are now various styles for each form of combat you can switch between without relying exclusively on one sword for certain move sets. Custom weapons make a return, as well as a means to make your own fighting style; both of which can take some time to gather what you need to create it, but if you played the last three then you are familiar with that kind of grind. The game's new ability, Spring harvest, is essentially this special mode where you can go berserk on the controls just slicing everything up, and generally good for large scale fights you want to blaze through or to unleash hell on one really tough opponent.
The story is nothing special, but branches out a good deal based on your choices. It's also a nice touch to add an event chart to look back at outcomes you have explored in past playthroughs and to see how many other paths certain scenes can take.  Once again, like the prior games, all characters you encounter are killable. This includes the main characters of the story, provided you have the skills and equipment to win. While most of the story tries to play itself serious, between the more ridiculous moments you can explore and the even more ridiculous costume options for your character this seriousness (for me at least) can and often goes right out the window and never to be seen again.
Overall, if you liked the prior Samurai games or if you are new and want to play a fashion-attrocity samurai beating his opponents to death with a blunt bamboo stick like its nobody's buisness all while drinking sake then this one is recommended.

***This review was written in 2017***
Short version: 7/10, neat game, was probably really unique for it's time, but feels a little dated 10 years later
Mass Effect is quite an interesting game. I put "this review written in 2017" above because it affects my score. This game came out originally in 2007. I have no doubt that, for the time period, this game was quite revolutionary. It became a very successful franchise with a very successful gameplay formula (branching dialogue, semi-realistic character relationships, a cool story, etc.). This game has some really cool and great things in it, as well as some pretty bad things. Playing this game 10 years after it came out, it's quite easy to see the flaws. So let's focus on those first.
1. The game feels very dated. Graphics aside, the gameplay is not that great. It's a 3rd person cover shooter/RPG hybrid. The cover shooter part does not feel that great. It can feel clunky and awkward at times, and I did not enjoy the gunfights as much as I thought it would. The RPG mechanics are cool, but nothing too out of the ordinary (from my limited experience with this type of game i.e. having a squad that you can command).
2. I have to make this a separate point because I could go on for days about this: the Mako. The Mako is the in-game vehicle that the player uses to drive over long distances on the planets. Put simply: it sucks. Really bad. This vehicle is the single worst vehicle I've ever driven in any game. The controls are awful. The slightest bump in the terrain--the tiniest rock you drive over will cause the whole vehicle to spin wildly out of control and flip over. Holding W on the keyboard (aka the go straight key) causes you to NOT go straight. If you're holding W down and go over a slight bump, guess what? Now you're going sideways. It is INCREDIBLY difficult to control and the player is actually punished for trying to do something as simple as drive straight. The guns on the Mako are powerful and are actually really useful, but the aiming is awkward and inconsistent. The Mako became downright frustrating to use at several points in the game.
3. My last criticism is that the dialogue can be a little cheasy and unrealistic at times. I sometimes said "what? That's not how people speak...at all!"
Now, that aside let's look at the positives of the game:
1. Good characters. The characters feel "real" enough, and despite some cheesy dialouge here and there, overall, I enjoyed the characters and their interactions. They have some interesting backstories and you, as the player, can develop a sort of attachment to them. Each member of the squad is their own person, not just a copy-paste, generic "bald space marine."
2. The story was both unique and cliched. I liked the story despite it being a classic "authority doesn't believe me so I have to do everything on my own" tale. The unique parts were in the execution, which is to say, the lore. The lore is a pretty big part of the story, and it will be interesting to see where it goes in the sequels (which I haven't played yet at the time of this review).
3. Speaking of lore, the atmosphere this game creates is awesome. You really do feel like a space captain/commander. There are big philosophical questions of A.I. and what makes organic life unique, the differences between alien races and a sort of racism towards the different alien races. There are space politics, and there are cool interactions between members of different alien races. Each race has a different and unique backstory. In short, if you like being immersed in space and the possiblities of science fiction, then this game should deliver that for you.
3. The side quests were varied and unique. None of them felt very similar, and they were more than simple fetch quests. To be fair, I did not do too many side quests, but the ones I did do were interesting and varied.
All in all, this is a good game. The story, characters, and lore really made up for the glaring dated feel of the game and absolutely terrible vehicle controls. I give this game a 7/10. Dynasty Warriors 8: XTreme Edition is a Hack and Slash game where you control a single hero and fight your way through a vast horde of enemies to single-handedly win battles. You will regularly kill hundreds if not thousands of enemy soldiers and a dozen or more enemy officers – characters like yourself on the opposing side – every mission. The game is very much about the light experience of running through and killing massive numbers of foes; while the core gameplay is decent enough, and there is some amount of character-to-character variability, on the whole the game itself is fairly repetitive as all of the levels boil down to almost exactly the same thing, just in a different environment with different orders of objectives. There is little meaningful variation in the enemy units, and thus the game is pretty samey from level to level. It is decent enough as a passing experience, but it is not much fun to sit down and spend hours fighting through the game.
Story
The game is based on the Romance of the Three Kingdoms, a culturally-important work of historical fiction about the unification of China in the 2nd and 3rd centuries CE. All of the major characters – all 77 of them – are given unique appearances, and their personalities from the stories tended to be reworked to give them more dramatic impact. As it is an old Chinese story, in many ways it seems odd to modern sensibilities, and many important events occur between battles, summarized in telly text.
On the whole, playing this game for the story is a waste; the English voice acting isn’t great, and while the Japanese voice acting sounds better, in the end it doesn’t matter much as the plot itself is not delivered very well and a lot of characters aren’t very sympathetic – including the characters you play as. Lu Bu, for instance, the star of one of the campaigns, has a personality which would ordinarily be found on a villain – he betrays everyone and believes that might makes right, and at the end of his campaign, he is executed for his crimes and constant betrayals. Indeed, the characters all tend to be rather shallow and uninteresting, and the story itself isn’t terribly interesting because characters keep falling in and out of the story as you follow each path along; only once you’ve beaten all the campaigns are you likely to really understand what is going on, and even then, character motivations often feel strange.
Gameplay
The gameplay itself is all about visceral satisfaction; you play as a single hero who wades his way through hordes of enemies, with some friendly officers and a handful of soldiers at your side who are, by and large, worthless. It is your job to do everything, your job to beat your way through the enemy lines, your job to keep your own officers alive, to complete all the objectives, and to otherwise do everything.
But that’s what you’re here for, right?
The protagonist you play has can switch between two weapons of the player’s choice, though it is always best for their primary weapon to be the weapon that they gain an ex bonus for, which grants them special attacks with it. The character can equip two of the same weapon, or can equip two different weapons to get a bit better versatility. Depending on which weapons enemies are you using, you may get an advantage or disadvantage, and because you have two weapons, you can always work out to at least be on even footing with them.
Each weapon has its own unique attack pattern, and as noted each character additionally has a special set of attacks with their preferred weapon. The character also has three “super” attacks which are built up by killing enemies and collecting dropped items from slain foes, as well as a secondary super meter which causes them to go into a “rage” and make a very powerful area of effect attack which will usually wipe out entire enemy forces by itself, killing hundreds of enemy soldiers and possible multiple enemy officers at the same time.
Each level consists of the player walking around it (or calling in their horse to ride around on it), fighting their way through an enemy army to try and capture various objectives, protect their allies, or just kill the enemy officers or general. These levels tend to mostly feel very similar; while there are differences between the levels, most of the levels are not very different in effect as the environments usually matter little (with a few notable exceptions) and the player is mostly just going from one place to another, fighting their way through the enemy horde.
While the weapons and characters all have their own abilities, ultimately the gameplay isn’t very different, and the enemies tend to feel very samey. Still, there is some satisfaction to be found in occasionally jumping in to murder large numbers of soldiers in a stage or two; it is not the sort of game to be sat down and powered through, but the large number of game modes, levels, alternative levels, collectables, and other things that the game offers means that it is possible to keep playing the game sporadically and still have a feeling of making progress for a very long time.
Presentation
The game is mostly fairly well-presented; the characters look decent enough, and the textures and animations all look fine, though there isn’t anything jaw-dropping in the game. The largest annoyance is that the keyboard controls are shown in the place of controller controls even if the player is using a controller.
Final Summary
Dynasty Warriors 8 XTreme Edition is a game which is best in moderation; it is fun to run through and kill large numbers of enemies, but the gameplay gets monotonous after a few levels and stops being as interesting. Still, as a “sometimes food”, a game that you play on occasion, it works well enough – it just isn’t much fun to run through the whole thing in one sitting. If you’re looking for something other than mindless killing, though, like plot or challenge, you’re better off looking elsewhere.

Lots of people love saying that this game is hard, and that's what makes it fun, but that doesn't really encompass it. It's hard, but what makes that bearable for me is that at least when I die I feel like I screwed up, instead of the game screwing me. There's no "do it again stupid" gameplay, the knowledge you've earned with previous deaths and previous bosses can help you going forward, and that helps you feel like you're progressing even as you die. You're very clearly outmatched by much of what lies before you, but that just makes perserverance feel that much more rewarding.
You are a very small insect it a very large world, and everything about the world's construction and the way you move through it works to make you feel like you've stumbled into more a mythology than a story. There is very little that is explained, but it feels right, because this world isn't about you. Having tons of exposition dumped in your lap would just feel like you were getting a guided tour, instead of organically exploring the ruins of a once great land.
The game is hard, and the setting works with that, but ultimately it doesn't become frustrating or depressing, because there's always a chance to move forward. Every time you die, you learn, and this is a game where mastery is rewarded.
So long as you keep going, you'll win, and so long as you don't give up hope, you won't go hollow.
You do need to have a good sense of humour though, because you are going to die in really stupid ways every once in a while.

Pillars of Eternity was designed from the ground up not only as a love letter to isomeric cRPGs of the past, but also as a continuation of that legacy. From the green character selection circles to the infamous 'You must gather your party' notification, anyone who enjoyed the Infinity Engine games will feel right at home, and still everything isn't just the same as it was. This isn't a remake or rehash: the classic intelligence and dexterity attributes have been tweaked to have more relevance outside of combat, the lion's share of level growth no longer comes from killing monsters but from conversation, reputation is made up several different expected character traits now instead of the single, universal number it was before. But still I felt compelled to collect and read every book I came across, speak to every person I came across (Even the jarring, overly Godlike backer-made NPCs), just like I did when first playing Baldur's Gate.  The world is new, but the feeling is the same, and what's changed has done so in an effort to better support that familiar experience. These improvements, however, can sometimes act as a double-edged sword. While each character that joined the party did so as a fully fleshed out person with their own motivations, those same motivations ask the unanswered question of why they were continuing to follow me on this death defying quest. Knowing many of them had their own important concerns elsewhere made it hard to imagine that they were all as interested in the approaching conclusion as I was. The game's storyline is similarly fully formed which leaves the end with a sense of finality. There's no cliffhanger here to breed anticipation for a continuation of the world. I'm left wanting more and not having any idea of how it will come about. That thought, that all the essential questions about the world have been answered, is troubling, but only if you assume there aren't any new ways to surprise us.

Fans of the Zombie Apocalypse genre should not pass this one up.  It is a good game despite its flaws.
To me, this game feels like what Dead Island should have been.  Things like having actual resource needs for your group and the ability to build and upgrade structures in your home base really help the game stand out from your generic zombie slaying fair.  Also the fact that events can happen while you are not playing, while it can be annoying, makes for a fairly unique game.
I also really like the fact that you can be overwhelmed by zombies if you are by yourself and you aren't careful.  You can't just run out in the street and start mowing down zombies with an unsurpressed assault rifle.  For one, you'll quickly deplete your ammo supply.  And the other reason is because all the noise will draw out all the zombies in the surrounding area and you'll likely be overrun.  It really helps to add some tension when you are a long ways from home on a supply run and you're low on health and don't have a ride nearby.
Unfortunately, the game is not perfect, and there are a few particular areas I feel the game is lacking.  The first of which to me is the camera.  The views for when you are executing zombies can sometimes make it impossible to see whats happening.  Also, the fact that you are encouraged to use foliage to hide from zombies, but the bushes/trees don't dim and go transparent when close to the screen makes for more times when you can't see anything.
Another feature I think this game could sorely use is some sort of weapon modding feature.  Coming off of playing Payday 2 with its amazing amount of weapon mods available, this game has none other than applying one of a few types of suppressor to guns.  It would be awesome if you found a weapon expert survivor and you could then mod your stocks, optics, foregrips and such but, alas, its not possible.
And finally, perhaps the biggest ommission that could have really made this game a gem is its lack of a multiplayer mode.  While you can ask other survivors to accompany you and help out, you can't get them to pick up supplies or give them any orders when they are with you.  They also have a tendancy to follow you right up your butt and then block doorways behind you.  The AI just isn't a good substitute for a few good buddies.
Still, despite lacking in some areas, this game is a fun single-player experience.  To me, it did a decent job of capturing the spirit of zombie apocalypse survival.  I'm hoping the game has a sequel with a bit more polish to put it into GOTY territory.

In my opinion, this game is certainly the best game in the 2D sonic series, I might go as far to say the best game in the franchise. Whilst a lot of people will say this game is overrated and isn't as good as games like Sonic 2 or Sonic 3 & Knuckles, I beg to differ.

Sonic CD is your normal every-day side scroller with our favorite blue hedgehog, whilst a lot of people think this game didn't bring as many new things to the table as it could have, it brought in great new features with the inclusion of Past and Future signs. Once you run into one of these signs, you'll have to keep your momentum and run for a certain period of time. If you lose speed or hit an obstacle you'll lose this ability. But if you keep up your speed, you'll be transported to a Past/Future orientation of the current stage. The past orientations usually show the stage at a much better time, with greenery and a serene atmosphere, a lot nicer in contrast to the future versions of the stage which either look chaotic, rusted or dull and overrun with machinery. Along the game you'll run into collapsed robot transporters, if you go back in the past of the level and return to them you can break them, resulting in a good future for the stage, if you go all the way to the future in the current stage you'll be greeted with a Good Future rendition of the stage, the Good Future's are like the Bad Futures in terms of the technology, but they look a lot more wonderful and are all generally amazing to go through.
An alternate way to get all the good futures (And the good ending) Is to collect all the time stones by finishing the stage with 50 rings and jumping into the giant ring at the end. This will transport you to the special stages of the game. Which compared to the other 2D sonic games, are very unique. They take place in a 3D enviroment in which sonic has to jump and destroy UFO's to complete the stage, it may sound simple but the stages are usually surrounded in water. If sonic lands in the water, 10 seconds are lost instantly making it very hard at times, especially in the last two stages. Whilst I find the controls to be sluggish, these stages are certainly the most unique in the sonic series.
Aside from the tenses in this game, it also presents something new in the sonic series, it posesses 2 sountracks which can be accessed in the steam version. Whilst I believe the US soundtrack has the best tracks, the Japanese soundtrack also has some of the best music, it also contains one of the most iconic themes in the sonic series, the Stardust Speedway Bad Future track.
All in all, I would definitely recommend this game to fans of the sonic series, I'd recommend it to anyone in general. 10/10 from me.
