8.1/10 (I rarely ever give 8 or higher for a game)
Best manager sim ever.  I have played a ton of manager sims (FIFA manager, Football Manager, GoallineBlitz, Blackout Rugby, Powerplay Manager, HSU (Heartland Soccer Union), coupled with dynasty modes in games like Rugby Challenge 1 and 2; EA sports NHL, FIFA, Madden,...; 2k series, PES series, ... and without question this game is superior.
The problem with most online manager sims is that you have to wait for games sometimes hence why a non-online one should be superior.
Football manager and FIFA manager had far too many issues with gameplay (football manager was especially horrendous at this) and horrible options respectively (FIFA manager) to make their games any fun.
Any dynasty mode is never indepth enough to really do a manager sim justice.  You have the league, the juniors, and that is usually about it if even that good...
That leaves this game...as superior as it is better in all regards to the stuff above (well FIFA gameplay is better then it, just the options for FIFA manager were garbage).
It is not perfect mind you...
Graphics: Even 15 years ago these graphics would not be the best, so if you need amazing eye candy this is not it - FIFA manager is better in this regard
Music: a limited selection gets boring after a while (even though the tunes on their own are good), though like any game you can put songs in your game folder, apparently they have a folder they specify to the user to do this but I have yet to see how user friendly it is to find it...
Depth: Germany is ridiculously in depth, every other nation is not.  All other nations have are tier 1 teams (so if you are in the lower tiers and cannot find players in Germany for hire, unless you can find nations with not so good players - (Bermuda, Somalia, St Lucia, ...)  you are going to be stuck.
Tutorial: they really need a good one though that said the hints they give you work, just realizing where the icons are for these hints (right on your main page but like any new game despite them being in your face, you may not realize they are important until later on in your first season as was my case)
Language: While the game is in English there are a few things which you can tell a translator was used to put in English (and did not do a good job).  That said they do update the game so hopefully for those who would have an issue with that eventually those things will be fixed, that said, if you are fluent in English the errors are easy to see and understand what is meant in virutally all cases.
Manual:  Though it is ridiculously detailed, and extensive with tons of info, one glaring deficiency is what they mean by 'grade'.  I know that it judges the skill of the player in the game, but whether 1 means the best or a higher # is a question that the manual does not answer (and after 40 plus hours of playing I am still guessing that 1 is the best, yes I have read the whole manual by the way, plus did a CTRL + F search in relation to it to find stuff).
Stadium: Again the eye candy of FIFA Manager is better, plus FIFA manager has more stadium SEATING options (much more).  That said the revenue generation that Club Manager has (build a restaurant, build a fan shop, better security, bus line to get more fans to the games, better toilets,...) which all influence the amount of fans you get is OUTSTANDING.  Merchandise options to have shirts, bedding, stuffed animals which you can sell to fans all makes this sim MUCH better than its competitors.
The economics of the game are excellent, and overall the game does a much more realistic job at allowing you to run your team with all the options.  An extensive transfer market with a ton of players, financial constraints, plus a ton more options make this game the best by far.
Still not sure about replayability since I am just starting this game (yep 61 hours is starting, but am loving it, my team is tier 3 at the moment, have played 10 seasons thus far), but assuming I get to 100 hours will do an update on this review.
A few hints which you should know if you do get the game:
-invest in at least 400 shirts from the start (you are cut off from buying more shirts as of July 15th), they are your biggest source of merchandise revenue and without this you lose a lot of additional revenue you will want for transfers
-get sponsors (though before you do PLAN).  I find getting better players off the transfer market THEN going for the sponsor that gives you the most revenue per win the best strat for the first few seasons
-set your individual ticket prices and SEASON ticket prices.  This garners you a ton of revenue pre-season which will allow you to get those additional transfer players you want (HINT:  ALWAYS set one section for expansion - usually one of your two cheapest - at a quota of 0 for season tickets so you can expand whenever you want)
-NEGOTIATE those salaries and transfer prices, once it hits orange do not barter anymore on transfer prices.  With season length of contracts realize that players usually get ticked once you go to 3 seasons though some are good with 5.  I would suggest to go for 2 seasons then lower the salary (again once it goes orange, accept).  Realize that if you tick off a player and they break off negotiations they will not talk to you again for the rest of the season (unlike other sims that have a cooling off period of much less time) - the only exception to this is contract negotiations with your own players.
There are other reasons this sim rocks, plus other hints I have though off hand cannot think of them and I have written a ton already so feel free to add me and ask questions if you have more queries about this game, as I noted, it does not have the best eye-candy, and the English can be problematic at times, the depth in other nations could be improved upon, but beyond that it is without question the most in depth manager sim out there and a ton of fun.

The game has a great soundtrack and the art style as well as the presentation managed to grab me. The gameplay itself is fine from what i can tell. You control a single unit that acts like a mouse cursor with restraints. It represents the commander of your army. If it dies, you may not interact with the world for a few seconds. This commander builds your buildings which either produce units or food. Units cost food in mainentance as well as production (which happens automaticall every x seconds).
Food production buildings deplenish fast and for this reason battles are quick and snappy. So far so good. Where the game failed for me was the AI and ramdom map generation. The latter can produce a mission of varying diffliculty with some of them being impossible. Since there is no restart mission button, you may then either quit to the title screen or search something that can kill you. Not a deal breaker, but annoying.
The first problem is far more significant: The AI. The enemy ai commander will move randomly accross the map and build wherever it can. It's units will search the quickest way to your buildings and throw themselves against them. They don't need the commander to move like your troops do, which means the enemy does not play by the same rules. Not only takes this away from the experience when the enemy commander constantly strolls trough your base and dies, but you can also exploit this behavior, making the regular missions quite easy. Allied AI behaves in a similiar way, which can lead to frustrating moments. Though it seems to be more likely to join you when you attack.
I really, really want to like this game. But for me, playing the missions became an increasingly dull experience. Completly on the contray to all the other great things the game has to offer. I can imagine the multiplayer being very interesting with human opponents. But i can't reccomend Tooth and Tail for the single player campagne only.

I'd imagine that all the fuzz surrounding Mass Effect Andromeda has made some people also become interested in the original trilogy. (It's what inspired me to replay it.) Does this first installment still hold up even 10 years after release? Well, that sort of depends on your motvation for playing it.
Arguably the strongsuits of this game are its story, world, atmosphere and characters. Even after my now 3rd playthrough, I still love walking around the Normandy or Citadel and chatting with squadmates and other characters. Most of them are very likable and offer some insight into their lives and morals.
The core gameplay to advance you in this story however is a mixed bag. At its best, gunplay is average. At its worst, it's feels kinda clunky.
Especially in the beginning hours of the game, combat feels incredibly underwhelming, as most guns are very inaccurate and weak. It slowly becomes more tolerable once you start leveling up your weapon traits and unlock stronger guns. It doesn't help that both the enemy and squad AI are pretty terrible.
Also, unless you're an achievement hunter, I do not recommend playing through the game on harder difficulites, as it just multiplies most already present issues. It turns combat into an absolute borefest, since the main thing that changes is that enemies take longer to kill.
So really, my recommendation depends on whether or not you're willing on putting up with this for the story. If you're the type of person that doesn't care much for story or world building, this game is probably not for you. You might be better off just skipping this for one of the later installments.
Otherwise, I'd say it is still totally worth it, especially if you plan on continuing with the other 2 games by importing character profiles. (Choices you make in this game will transfer over to the other 2.)
Be prepared that it's also a pretty lengthy game. Depending on how much time you spend with side quests and character interaction, playtime can range from 15-30+ hours.

TL;DR :
- Can no longer reach the website for the game after repeated attempts.
- Odd silent moments, terrible audio quality
- Still incredibly buggy, this long after release.
-Continue to get black screens when trying to start up.
- Terrible AI, gross HUD
- Relies entirely on a nonsensical, broken temperature system to pad the game
- Being near the sea still makes a lot of people get frame rate drops
- Nothing has really improved since release date, unless you think that a "new" tiny island that's just as buggy as the old one and a basic character customization screen that has no real affect on gameplay counts as an improvement.
I bought this game a long time ago, I think not too long after it's release. I had hoped that I would find a new studio to follow, but from the start it wasn't very good, with terrible AI of all kinds, tons of stuttering when you got to close to or looked at the sea, a tiny map, repetitive enemies, and a "survival system" so basic and annoying that staying alive early on was more than a bit hard.
Sure, I persevered anyway, and through the bugginess I managed to build a small hovel and a fire, which kept me alive long enough to make repeated trips back and forth, but only so far, and only in really one direction, as I could only find one small "village". By that I mean a series of old houses with little to nothing inside and a bunch of skeleton things that wanted to fight you. But the game was so simple and shoddy that at the time it just couldn't hold my attention.
I came back some time later, after hearing that the devs had implemented a new island and character customization, and better optimization. Hoping that meant that meant a fun, fresh start, I hopped back on only to flick through a few basic options for my character and spawn on an island that was honestly not too much different than the original one, save for the dragon. A dragon that never once tried to fight me, even when I charged and tried to scale its tower.
Not much had changed beyond that, bugginess still abounded (especially as you neared or looked at the sea that you start by), AI was still atrocious, the UI was still pretty ugly and odd looking, the survival system was still basic and annoying (If it's that cold, how in the world is there any life growing there?), and I still found myself trying to build and hop from fire to fire only to discover that the map was still really tiny. It became obvious that they were relying almost entirely on ridiculous temperature to pad out there game, which failed miserably.
Still, I pulled out and waited again. Now, December is coming to a close, with 2018 looming in the distance, and things haven't changed. I struggled for a long time to even start the game without getting a black screen, found no help on the website for the game, which appears to have been taken down, and the devs seem to have gone dark, even though some say that the game is just on hold. On hold? I payed for the game back in 2015. If you still need time 2-3 years later, maybe you shouldn't have put it on Steam for this much money.

If you're thinking of skipping out, you'll definitely be missing out on this re-release of﻿ Sonic CD. It has more to offer than the 1996 PC port or Sonic Gems Collection edition ever did.
- Presented in 16:9 widescreen.

- The option to﻿ decide how you want your Sonic physics like (Sonic 2 or the original Sonic CD).
- The option to select which regional soundtrack you want to listen to. Freaking. Finally.
- Each individual music track from the USA and Japanese soundtrack last longer now. The US soundtrack borrows from the Sonic Boom album, which featured the longer versions of Stardust Speedway, for example.

This re-release of Sonic CD is a complete revamped and different entity than the 1996 PC edition, and the Sega CD original for that matter. It has such awesome, game-enhancing features that make this the definitive Sonic CD experience﻿ of all time.

So I hate open world games. Fallout, Elder Scrolls, GTA... just can't ever get into them.
This game, however, I absolutely loved. It's very well crafted and just FEELS good, for many reasons, of which a few are:
It has some of the best monster fighting mechanics I've ever seen, in which you can climb up on top of huge monsters and stab the hell out of them. This lends itself to a feeling of dynamic combat that can make for some great moments, that I'm sure you can find in other reviews. Here's mine: I wanted to cross a rock bridge spanning a deep chasm but a huge extra tough cyclops was standing right in my way. While I sat there, staring at it from a distance, pondering what to do, one of my warrior pawns (a sort of battle companion) ran forth and leapt on the cyclops. Together, they overbalanced and wham! both went over the edge, perishing to their doom below, Gandalf-Balrog style. All that, completely unscripted.
This game's nights and dungeons are REALLY, actually dark. This gives it a great feel, like you're actually in delving deep forbidding dungeons.
While the game has some MMO style "fetch" or "slay" quests, they're rare and never felt onerous. The world feels lived in and real, maybe not quite to the degree of Witcher 3, but then Witcher 3 is the DIAMOND standard when it comes to that.
In short, I'd say that if you like open world games DEFINITELY give this one try. But even if you don't, you may be surprised by how much you enjoy this. I know I did.

This is going to be a long review. And a strange one as well, probably. Way of the Samurai is an extremely straightforward game, and yet there's so much to talk about it. I will try to give it a review as in-depth as possible from the perspective of someone who has *never* played the series, but the TLDR is that for a 20 buck game you should probably pick it up.
Graphically, the game looks okay, despite showing some age. It's not only the fact that it's 4 years old, but that by then those graphics were hardly cutting edge by 2011, the year of Skyrim. There are hardly any gimmicks in that aspect: most of the game occurs in a rather small play area, there is no clothing damage that had appeared in earlier installments and the gore is pretty minimal. Still, they are very functional, and the feeling of cheapness fits super well with the B movie feel of the game, much like in Deadly Premonition, but more on that later. The game is locked to 30 FPS but I really doubt that will ever bother you unless you care more about a counter than a game, in which case I'd urge you to go to Word and type a random 5 digit number and proceed to masturbate furiously for the next bunch of hours. Bottom line, it looks okay. Really okay.
The customization options are also one of the highlights of the game: you can place, move and resize every accessory in your Samurai, allowing you to be as boring or creative as you want to. Want a nude samurai with a medal loincloth? How about Oni nipple tassels? Dude made out of boxes? You got it!
Sound's alright. Music can become a bit repetitive by the 20,000th time you hear a song, but for a 1-track-per-event ost I have no complaints. Sound effects are also functional. The voices is where the game really shines though. Most of the sound bits you can hear when going through ingame text are different and match the voice actor you're talking to. The entire game is in Japanese with English subtitles, and peppered with delicious, delicious Engrish that always gets a chuckle out of me.
Now. Onto the gameplay. First thing you'll notice is that the game is goofy. Extremely so. From the 10-year-old British ambassador to the 3 S&M adept daughters of the Minister, the game proudly turns the camp to 11 and puts you in aggressively cheesy scenes more often than not. Whether you want to cope with that is up to you, but I gotta say that for all the general weirdness the game accomplishes to be fun without going into aggravating territory. Lots of puns, lots of terrible humor and hilarious interpretations of Western culture much like in Deadly Premonition, but easily within parameters, despite everything. Some of the storylines are more grounded, if kinda topical, but again this feels like it's really aiming for B-movie throwbacks while keeping some humor about it. Kinda hit or miss, but I'd be hard pressed to find a moment where I genuinely wanted to just shut down the game, besides, almost everything can be skipped or fast-forwarded. And most of the events are purely accessory. Speaking of which:
The game happens along 5 days, divided into day, evening and night. Time will only advance if one goes to sleep or does the next story mission, which means you can choose what to do and when. At the end of those 5 days (or earlier) , depending on what you've done, you'll get an ending out of the 10 possibles, most of whose are pretty different from each other. At the end of the game you'll carry your items and gear to the next playthrough, and so on. That means the game is crazy replayable, what with the several optional storylines, side activities (like running your own dojo or doing parallel quests), possible outcomes of the primary missions and the customization. But we're still missing the actual meat and potatoes of the replayability factor and the game itself, and those are the weapons and styles.
At the start of the game you can wield swords, spears or do hand-to-hand martial arts. As you unlock further upgrades you'll also be able to equip guns, rifles, claws and akimbo katanas, using the samurai points you'll obtain after each ending (along with new difficulty levels, customization options, etc). On top of that you have the several fighting styles for every weapon type, each based in a stance, of about 11 or so different stances in the whole game. Getting better in a certain style will unlock new moves for that stance, and you'll be able to make your own fighting style using unlocked moves, integrating up to 3 different stances. You can also dismantle every weapon you come across and assemble the parts into new weapons: make them to look how you like, try to stack Charms on them, improve their durability and strength, the like. Missions aside, crafting itself is a quite interesting side activity that invites you to waste your time (and pretty much your time only, as it's pretty much assumed you'll savescum, or at least many hours "fishing" for your wanted part) but not only you're given several ways to make that grinding happen, it's pretty much optional, so you're not confronted by a number wall that you need to vault to continue on your story. And even if you find the game getting too frustrating for your taste, you can always restart the whole thing while keeping your stuff, much like in Majora's Mask.
In brief, this is a pretty hilarious game, with pretty good controls, pretty good fighting, very "horizontal" content (lots of optative parallel stuff) and great customization options. It is not perfect: despite the tutorials at the beginning the game can result pretty frustrating on your first playthrough while you figure stuff out and there's stuff I'd have done differently or at least explained better, but again, in general I think it's a pretty cool game overall.
7.5. Add an extra point if you enjoyed Deadly Premonition's intensely weird, yet clearly love-injected personality.

Firstly, if you have played and enjoyed previous games in the Dynasty Warriors and Orochi series you won't be surprised to find out this game offers more of the same. With several modes to play through, including the popular ambition mode, there is plenty to keep you occupied.
The basic premise of the game is you play a significant character from Chinese history and roam around the landscape on foot and horseback killing thousands of enemy soldiers while levelling up yourself, skills and weapons in the process - sweet. There are loads of characters, moves and special weapons to pickup, plus you can fight from horseback. Generally there are hoards of enemies mixed in with tougher characters for you to wade through - respect.
After turning the Japanese voice option and subtitles on I played through ambition mode for a while to level up some of the familiar characters. After the usual calibration period getting used to how to set the characters and weapons up I went into the Lu Bu story mode, which was pretty cool. After completing several of the story modes I turned my attention back to ambition mode to aquire all the goodies required such as Red Hare and improved weapon skills.
If you have played previous incarnations on Xbox or PS then the first thing you might notice is the improved graphics, especially view distances and slow down issues in busy Musou packed fights, which is greatly improved. Negatives are if you use a game controller the forward and back (red and green) buttons are reversed, although this can be changed. As per usual it can get repetitive but it's always an easy game to come back to or play when friends are around. With a choice of male and female characters and an intuitive control system it's easy for pretty much anyone to play - kickass you guys.
Pure action, you can end up killing thousands of enemies on the first mission, but it is too repetitive and the story too boring.

Those seeking traditional RTS levels of control won’t find it here. However, in its attempt to provide “RTS distilled”, Tooth and Tail has found a recipe of its own that, while having a few hiccups (some bigger than others), comes off as both fun and boasting at least some amount of originality. While I can’t say I’m a fan of the procedurally generated maps and their tendency to be hard to read or of the abrupt difficulty spikes I encountered in a couple of missions, I, ultimately, had a blast playing through Tooth and Tail. Figuring out how to deal with the challenges the missions threw at me harkened back to a time when a younger me was taking his first steps into Tiberian Sun and, although some missions frustrated the heck out of me, I can’t say I regret spending time with Tooth and Tail’s campaign. With multiplayer matches being intense and fairly short in length, Tooth and Tail never overstays its welcome, being a good choice for both longer sessions and for moments when you want to play something but only have 15 minutes at your disposal. Simply put, Tooth and Tail is a great game that’s worthy of attention.

I had been pushing this game aside for years till Mass Effect 2 came along and I wanted to play this game to see what all the fuss was about. I am mainly a FPS gamer, I have steered clear of most RPG games since I knew that they were addictive and took a huge chunk of time to finish. What I didn’t realize back then was the man-hours and creativity that goes into making these games. So Mass Effect was my introduction to the world of RPGs. This was also the first BioWare game I’ve ever played and I’m glad I took the plunge. I played the Mass Effect Trilogy on my PS3 so this review is based on the PS3 version though I'm planning to play this trilogy again on PC now. Before that I wanted to write my first ever review for a game on Steam. I hope you'll like it.
Who’ll love this game:
Do you like feeling all powerful?
Do you like to feel that your every decision will have overreaching and cascading effects through time and on other lives?
Do you like to be a galactic hero who has a reputation for saving millions of lives?
Do you like to fight an alien race that’s so old and powerful that they don’t even consider you worthy of attention like an insect?
If the answer to any of these questions is yes, then you’ve picked the right game.
The Story:
The story is set in a Universe where we have a galactic government and humanity is among the newest species to be inducted into it. Spectres are among the elite who possess great power vested onto them by the government. They can take decisions independently and they even have a license to kill without fear of any repercussions. So as it happens one of these Spectres, Saren has just gone rogue and he is travelling the universe collecting Prothean artefacts which are extremely advanced for their time and these artifacts actually pave the way for the developed, modern technological era. Protheans are an ancient species that have long gone extinct centuries before our story even starts.
The scope of this story is wide reaching and feels daunting at first and makes you realize how high the stakes are. The way the story twists and turns and reaches its shocking ending is brilliant. There’s always something interesting to do and your choices change the course of the story. As the game progresses you have to make harder choices with major consequences. Every decision feels personal and when you mess up it’s heartbreaking. That’s how strongly this story sucks you in.
The Dialogue:
The dialogues in this game are a little rigid and robotic. I think this is the only minor gripe I have in what is otherwise an excellent game. The conversations don’t sound natural. Probably this is the writer’s idea of how a space faring species speaks.
The Characters:
Captain Shepherd is the first human Spectre. You can either choose to play as the Male Shepherd or Fem Shepherd. You can even choose his backstory. He/She has a tragic backstroy but is a bonafide badass with a reputation that precedes him. Over the course of the game you meet your team members: Garrus Vakarian, Kaidan Alenko, Ashley Williams, Tali'Zorah nar Rayya, Liara T'Soni and Urdnot Wrex. They join your team for various reasons and each of them has a compelling reason to join your team. These are well rounded and memorable character. It’s fun to converse with them and get to know more about them between missions and you can also romance (have sex with) some of these team members. Incase you were wondering I did Liara T’Soni and Ashley on my two play-through sessions. I played a Fem Shepherd on both and Liara is a darling.
Villains are aplenty in this game and there’s a lot of variety to the kind of villains that we get to face during the course of this game. Geth, Husks, Asari, Humans, Turians and Colossus Geth etc. Each one of these requires a different strategy to tackle if you want to get past them with minimal damage. After the final reveal we face an enemy that’s just phenomenal in scale.
Weapons Inventory System:
As a FPS gamer I am quite accustomed to “loadouts” but inventory management is something I seldom come across in FPS games and this was a steep learning curve for me as a starter on RPG. This game has a very deep inventory system where you get to choose which one of the weapons or abilities of the team members you’d like to improve. I think this was the most tedious part of the gameplay (besides Mako which I’ll get into later). I’d just say that I would prefer to spend much less time on inventory management and more time in actually playing the game. So sometimes it can be frustrating (they fixed it in Mass Effect 2). However, it should be remembered that this is a very important feature that helps in tackling stronger enemies as the game progresses.
Vehicle Controls:
Oh! Why? Why do I have to drive the Mako through so many terrains? Mako is a multi-terrain vehicle which is mostly helpful during some assignments on uncharted planets. Some of the levels with Mako are definitely worth playing over and over again however, my problem is with Mako itself. If you have played this game already you’d know that the controls for this thing are probably the biggest problem this game has. It seems like Mako has a mind of its own sometimes. Except for the Mako most of the controls are pretty solid in this game.
Missions:
You get to go on a boatload of assignments in this game. Apart from the story based missions you also get the secondary missions which may sometimes feel repetitive. However, playing these missions help in exploring some vital elements which are required to help you level up faster. In that way these are a necessary evil. I’d recommend playing all of these secondary missions.
Soundtrack:
Jack Wall delivers one of the most thoughtful soundtracks for a game. The soundtrack amplifies several scenes in this game and it feels like an integral part of these scenes. It sets the mood and atmsphere with the extensive synth use which feels futuristic even if it should like it belonged in the 80s. This is a great game and a game of this caliber deserved a great soundtrack and that’s just what it is.
Conclusion:
Mass Effect boasts of a great story that’s built around great characters and (for the most part) great gameplay. But by no means is this game easily conquered. You may have to spend atleast 40-50 hours in order to finish this game and that makes me think how hard it must have been for the game designers to create such an expansive world. The voice acting and visuals in this game deserve high praise and they actually account for the strongest visceral impact of this game. I’ve played this game twice in both Paragon and Renegade playstyles, so that’s about over 100 hours of game time and it was totally worth it. Even today there are few games out there that are this immersive. Every time I play this game, I feel like I’m really Captain Shepherd and that’s a testament to how strongly you get attached to this world and the characters. One thing is for certain, once you enter this world you'll never forget it.

Of all the Mass Effect games, this is only one which can be considered a true RPG with all the standard RPG fare intact.
While the other entries in the series do a good job of personifying the Good (ME2), the Bad (ME3) and the Ugly (Andromeda), the original Mass Effect is the most distinct of the series - focusing less on the combat and more on traditional RPG mechanics and exploration of the galaxy.
Graphically the game still looks good, albeit for a game which came out in 2007, although the combat feels dated unless you are of the Biotic God persuasion - although it does have elements which were sad losses from subsequent games in the form of greater squadmate controls and using lots of powers.
Most importantly for a Mass Effect game, the writing of Mass Effect 1 is in another plane of existance compared to the later offerings, although Mass Effect 2 is still well written, and the depth of world building and genuine diversity (OF PERSONALITY) and memorability of the squadmates is excellent.
If you want a sci-fi RPG that's well written, with a universe that you can, and will, get sucked into and fall in love with then Mass Effect is for you. However, this is debatably the high point for the franchise and rather than loving you tenderly and settling down happily ever after, the series will sour later on and leave you with a nasty taste in the mouth if you follow it through to the conclusion.

-dayz has 90+ developers, aproximately 5m of copies sold (and tons of money) a fanbase established since arma 2 mod, completely supported by a veteran company (bohemia) and the best scenario ever possible for an EA game.
-Miscreated has 15+ part time developers, limited budget and basically no visibility.

Splinter Cell Blacklist is a game revolving around a group of special force soldiers part of the fourth echelon team. The player plays as the protagonist known as Sam Fisher who is trying to uncover a case called the 'Blacklist'. As of the game it self, i have to say that this game was very enjoyable to play with the many different play styles available to choose from; including the 'Ghost' (Completely stealth gameplay), the 'Panther' (stealth gameplay with lethal killing) and the 'Assault' (completely full on kick a** mode). I found that playing as a 'Ghost' was the entertaining due to the cautious actions i need to do to complete the levels un-noticed.
The gameplay is pretty straight forwards as a stealthy game where the player is able to hide behind cover and move from places to places with the ability to knockout enemies silently. However, Splinter Cell Blacklist have extended the 'stealth' feature to a furthur extent where shadows become really important to remain off sight thus having the abililty to shoot almost every light source present there.
Something i didnt like was the enemy's AI vision ranges in the game. They literaly cannot see the player in the shadows even if he was 5 meters right infront of him in open space. The logical thinking of the AI also bugs me a little throughout the game  but the game is still pretty difficult at some points due to it which is nice. Also, I didnt like the customization in this game where every single piece of armour available looks almost the same with very limited customization (colours, patterns). Though i do understand that this may be just because of the type of game, but it wuold be nice if this option was available. To extend this point, there isnt much use of purchasing new weapons as well as the default weapons are pretty much all the player needs to complete the game, but I must say that the variaty of gadgets available is very good for different play styles and tastes of the players.
I found the story a little hard to follow through due to the many things which were going on in the campaign but i did manage to understand the general things which was happening throughout the game. This might be because this is the first spliner cell game i've played idk. The whole story in general wasnt every appealing to me as I thought it was a little boring and simple but follow through-able.
Lastly, the optimization of this game is completely wayy off for lower end computers where I was playing at about 5 fps on the lowest settings without modding it further down. My computer is definately good enough though, i could play tomb raider, skyrim, battlefield etc. I do see that this mainly happens in ubisoft games.
To conclude, I would recommend this game to stealth lovers or to people who enjoy generic third person shooters as well as this game would definately fit into their tastes. Enjoy!

For someone who wants to be immersed in the story of an RPG this game just doesn't cut it.  I'm 25+ hours into this game and just not interested.  The whole open world thing is interesting.  Skyrim-esque I suppose, but that's not my jam. While the world itself looks interesting, it mostly just feels lifeless.  The majority of the NPCs appear to only be there for your sake.  While your own character is basically a silent protagonist, the never-ending repeating dialogue of your companions is painful.  I would turn their dialogue off, but they occasionally say important things like "we should check this path here first" or "these dudes are weak to ice attacks"   So I leave the dialogue on.
I hear a lot about how the combat is great, but I found it lacking.  I become extremely bored of combat after discovering that all I have to do is this little charge-stab attack to win 95% of encounters.  By accessing the menu at any time you can INSTANTLY cure your character to full health/stamina during combat, lowering the difficulty to near zero.  Even the whole Shadows of the Collosus "climb on top of the big-bad-guy and then stab him in the eye" gimmick just felt poorly implemented.  Though it was awesome cutting off enemies tails to weaken them, or cutting off one of a bosses 3 heads.
The inventory/crafting system seems decent, but theres just so much junk, and no way to tell what is valueable and what isnt.  There seems to be about 40 different herbs, 80 different potions, and 150 different foods:  which all do slightly different versions of healing you.  All of which clutter your inventory.  Every armor/weapon can be upgraded 3 times, using progressively rarer ingredients WHICH IS AWESOME!  However, there's no easy way to tell if the interesting new sword i found after a dungeon boss is better/worse/same as my current sword, because my current sword is buffed up to level 3.  Game is missing that color coded rarity system that we all know and understand.
The one AMAZING thing this games does is the Pawn system.  It needs to be explored by other games, because that's truely the future of great, interesting RPG worlds.

Meh, just a Baldur's Gate retro-experience, eh? Wrong!  This game has the spirit, but is it's own game. So much about this game is great.  I could go on about how its a great rehash of old school rpgs like baldurs gate, but there is no need. Thousands of others have already done so.
Do I recommend this game? You bet. Especially if you like those style games. This is a solid, well made, high quality game. The story is intriguing, but not mind blowing. Its enough to make you want to play through it. The semi D&D like rules are different enough to seem like a whole new system, but familiar enough so that most can catch on quickly and understand it without reading a 200 page manual.
So does this game fall short anywhere? A bit... mostly with combat. Nothing that makes me not want to play, but enough to make me frustrated a bit more often than it should. (and this is playing on normal mode... i cant imagine playing on harder difficulties due to these issues).
Here they are in no particular order:
- The combat is pause based, like Baldurs gate, only... you will be hitting pause a LOT more often. A LOT LOT LOT LOT more often. Often times you may find yourself wondering "Why didnt they just make combat turn based?" because you are hitting pause every other second to issue commands.
- Your party members are dumb. In combat (not personality/story). If you dont pause to issue commands, they will quite frequently end up not doing ANYTHING at all. Just standing there. Issue an order for your spell caster to cast a spell. Awesome. As soon as they are done casting, they will stand there... and veg out. No matter what is going on.
- Difficulty is way too random. In the same area, you might fight something at your level, and then 15 seconds away stumble across an enemy that is WAY too hard for you to beat, that slaughters your party. And there are often no clues leading up to the sudden increase in difficulty either. This happens in ANY difficulty mode. You will be quicksaving and loading a LOT.
- Characters miss in combat WAY too much. Its boring to miss a lot. Nuff said
- The mechanics with the "dual" life values is a neat concept that ends up being overly complex and messy in actual use. I understand their desire for damage that is only temporary that can heal back without resting, and perm damage that requires a rest, I just think they had to REALLY stretch and reach for a system to make this work. So much that it just sorta gets in the way of having fun in combat. Limiting potions, and healing spells (per rest) is already enough of a challenge for most rpgs. They didnt need to reinvent the wheel here.
- Stealthing is just done very poorly. The whole "Being detected" aspect works fine, and is neat, since its often not immediate... however, the attacking from stealth just seems down right awful. In fact, most of the time its hard to tell if you even GET to attack from stealth (opening attack from stealth), because as soon as you go to attack, the game autopauses and your character is no longer stealthed, even BEFORE the first attack. Are they getting a stealth bonus? Hard to say. Not to mention, if your stealther goes in to backstab and doesnt finish the target off, they will most likely die due to the next point....
- Classes are VERY unequal in balance, challenge level, and ability to just play through the game.  Even on normal, expect to reload your game a LOT if you are playing any class with low HP that lacks the ability to defend well, or dish out so much damage that the enemy doesnt have time to hurt you. I picked rogue starting out, and before you get your full party, the game can be super challenging.
Those points aside, the game is still good as I stated. Its a quality made game, that just has a few opinionated hangups that prevent me from playing more than short bursts of it at a time. Its like a really good tasking fruit, with the occasional thorns that poke your tongue. You are gonna eat it, trying your best to avoid the thorns... but you wont always be successful.

When the world comes alive and the set pieces move in this classically styled game it's a thing of beauty. The rest of the time running around in almost entirely static world is just only kind of neat. However the story more than makes up for this. The nods to table top elements are also a classy touch. The voice acting is very well done but be careful of missing out on outside of direct dialogue conversations because you won't hear them unless your camera is focused on the character that's doing the talking.
Difficulty wise the game straight up tells you to play the game on easy the first time through if that's any indication. Especialy if your party does not include a tank. Character development is a bit confusing initialy as the impact of attributes is sometimes confusingly ambiguous. The game does it's best to provide explanations via tooltip though. Many game concepts are also actually very different from their 3.5 era conventions.
To conclude when the game takes advantage of the animation and textures for which it's hardware requirements call for it's a very pretty thing indeed. Overall if you are a fan of DnD inspired isometric styled games you will have a blast.

Anyway, the gamplay is challenging, even for a guy like me that never played RPG's like Baldurs Gate and Neverwinter Nights, I got my♥♥♥♥♥♥kicked even on the lowest difficulty setting. But once you got used to the control, you wil certainly get the hang of it, since you are mostly of the time clicking with your mouse then using hotkeys if you want to use your abilities.
Although it feels sometimes a bit unfinished for some people, since most of the dialogues are only written text, you feel like your more reading a novel instead of playing a game.
But I recommend this game for RPG/fantasy fans alike!

There have been a lot of Sonic the Hedgehog sequels, but this is probably the only one which closely resembles the art and design of the original game. This re-release isn't perfect due to 1 song being edited to take out the lyrics, but it's easily the best version of the game ever released.
With some additional content and access to both the original Japanese and North American sountracks, this is one Sonic classic that is worth revisiting.

This is probably the best version of Sonic CD that's out there, allowing for both soundtracks, stage select without having to replay the game or having to enter a cryptic cheat code, and even the ability to play as Tails once the game is completed. I also enjoy the small things they have added such as being able to hold more lives than 9, and that just shows Sega really cared when recrafting Sonic CD. I haven't encountered any game-breaking glitches and with my Logitech controller, the game runs no problem, and it's definitely worth checking out if you are a Sonic fan.
The only gripe I would have is the fact that my saves weren't stored on the cloud or even in an obvious folder on my computer (such as the "My Games" folder which has saves for some of my other games) so when I moved to a new PC, I was very disappointed to see my files have disappeared. It's rather unusual too because my high scores are still intact on the leaderboards, so why couldn't the saves be intact as well?
All in all, perfect remake. I don't see anything else Sega can do to "top out" Sonic CD.

Lovely sandbox game with many intense moments (like running out of stamina) and hordes of zombies running your way. The gathering and building aspect of the game comes together well with the third person GTA-style drive and quest gameplay. Overall, it's a very satisfying experience when you drive into a horde of zombies with a great big smear left on your windscreen down to completing an upgrade on your building that gives bonuses and items for you to keep fighting.
There are a few nagging things about this game, namely the short game hours, which I was very surprised about. I was kinda left hanging after the slightly anti-climactic ending fight and discovering my fate. Then I asked myself, "Was that it?" I'm guessing and slightly hoping there is a sequel to download right after. Also the limitation to the building options are very realistic but left me wanting more freedom to design my own end-of-the-world zombie free homebase, although it does give priorities to some important buildings and choices but there are very clear choices and buildings that gave clear advantages to aid in zombie killing than other ones, such as the machine shop being able to repair your vechiles, compared to a garden growing plants.
I do however highly recommend this game to anyone who is a fan of post-apocalyptic or zombie games. However bleak this world seemed, there were plenty of moments where the player will be empathic towards the characters they control. Listening to their well-written dialogues and discovering their special traits added a deeper connection to the survivors and made it that much harder to watch them get devoured by those red-eyed zombies.
Rest in peace, brothers, or see you soon, at the end of my barrel.

This is proberly the best Dynasty Warriors for a long time in my opinion, yeah theres like £150 of DLC but its all vainty with some weapons/animals thrown in, the only DLC you'd proberly want is the japanse voice option which is free anyway. Also this is 2 player couch co-op for pretty much everything, for anyone who maybe deciding to buy for the first time.
There is so much content in this version, the 3 main modes in this is the classic story mode, play out the story of one of the kingdoms, though this time round, you cant just pick a officer from that kingdom then play through the entire story being OP like before, for each story you pick between 3 officers for that mission, if you help plans succed or complete certain tasks other officers will be available on missions further down the line, or may even unlock another story path.
Gameplay wise, this is super smooth for me, not had any graphic lag or delay when loading enemies, the in-game cinematics have been done very nice.
Free mode is what it sounds like, pick any missions and play with any officer, though there are objectives to fulfill if you wish to obtain A rank.
Then Ambition mode, similar to other Xtreme legends, you have your own town and fight battles to help build up your town, upgrading shops, capturing officers, so on and so forth.
There are still the challenge modes like the bridge challenge
So if your un-sure about the game, keep in mind this is one of the best ones to buy, price can be steep at the moment but you get alot of content in return.
Lastly, I would recommended a gamepad, if you have trouble with yours just re-map the buttons, the camera controls didnt work for me til I remapped it. Even though it has gamepad support you still need to push a button on your keyboard to access the title screen menu's which is proberly the only problem I have with it. After that ive been using the gamepad entirely.
TL;DR
Great game, tons of content, 2 player couch co-op, lots of characters. recommeding gamepad.

State of Decay is a brilliant game. It is a good example of a zombie survival game. The fact that you have to search for resources like food, medicine and ammunition makes it a lot more realistic.

You choose where you start, which survivors you allow into your group, and which survivors you leave for dead. And just to make things a little better, you can decide to at any time move to the next level, which basically resets the map, makes it harder, with more zombies and less resources, and you can take 5 survivors with you. This means that the game is more or less endless.
Buy this game if you enjoy survival games and zombie shooters. The only improvement I would like is multiplayer.

"Reach for the stars" were the last words in the Mass Effect credits. Well, the first part of this much hyped space epic almost gets that far. While the main story and some of the characters are compelling, the game constantly stumbles because of a simple but poor design decision: the developers went for quantity of over quality in most aspects of the game and everything ends up feeling more than a little half-cooked as a result. The game is definitely still worth the time to play through but it also leaves you wondering how much better it could have been had they not tried to overreach so much.
+Cool setting, story and a lot of lore if you can be bothered to read it
+Impressive visual design that manages to offset the dated graphics
+Excellent synthwave type soundtrack that meshes well with the space theme
+Decent replay value
+Wrex
-Driving on planets seems to be universally panned among players and for a good reason: controlling the vehicle is often like trying to handle a sentient rubber ball that hates you. And there certainly is a LOT of driving...
-Probably one of the clunkiest cover based shooters ever made
-Lots of horribly slow elevators that you have to use over and over again
-RPG mechanics are very poorly implemented and the whole game reeks of being designed for the Soldier class and everything else is more of an afterthought. You can't even aim properly with half the weapons you ALWAYS carry with you if you have the wrong class!
-Majority of side quests are hollow MMORPG style one time deals that lead nowhere and have no impact on anything beyond your wallet and XP
-A lot of fully voice acted dialogue inevitably leads to writing and acting that vary greatly in quality. There is a comical amount of distinctly awkward pauses and the choices you're offered are infuriatingly inconsistent with what the character will actually say
-To maximize the visual fidelity such as increasing shadow resolution etc. you have to fiddle with .ini settings. This obviously should've been trivial for the developers to do correctly
-Audio volume is sometimes all over the place: squadmates often get very quiet outside of actual dialogue and some cutscenes blare at full volume, ignoring the ingame settings
-Stores and the inventory are slow and clumsy to use. Was it really too much to ask to make better use of a mouse and available screen space? This is further compounded by the sheer amount of items you get and most of them are garbage or otherwise redundant
-Squadmates are very efficient in getting in your way in combat and blocking your path. Oh you're sniping that enemy? Here, let me get in front of you so you can admire my neck
-Enemies and items seem to scale with player level leading to an oddly stagnant status quo where you're not always sure if you're actually making any progress with developing the characters despite all the supposedly nifty gear and added skill points
Can't wait for Shadow of war.

Shadow of Mirror is not Lord of the rings. It's an inspired story that takes from Lord of the rings. It makes the characters from those beloved movies (when they appear) not any more fleshed out or deep. It doesn't add to the original trilogy or the hobbit. It won't make you think more about the movies and you won't be exclaiming "hey there's the shadow of mordor!" In the middle of revisiting the early 2000s greatest trilogy.
That being said no one asked for that to happen. No one asked for an all out fleshed out story and characters that add to the original. No one really saw this game coming. Which was a great stroke of luck for the developer. They were able to take some well known tropes from today's best games and one original idea and make something that built a unique experience.
The long and short of it is that this is assassin's creed type gameplay, with a lot of character. Not in your own player. Not even in your allies, but in the most important part of adventure games and some would argue entire series and films, the antagonist.
Every bad guy can become a villain, and any of the chiefs and captains can become your nemessiss. You combat is a nice mix of Batman and assassin's creed but that's really only the beginning. Taking a familiar playstyle and adding the information and deep antagonists that they have makes this not an all out fantastic experience but one that i will be revisiting many times just so I can beat the snot out of my revanant enemies.
Thus the game has a lot of potential in combat that it instead focused on a unique experience between characters that in most other games would just be another dropped body. While the level up and progression system, the combat, the platforming, and the story itself is above average but just below greatness the core gameplay of making normal grunts into enemies you'll remember is remarkable and elegant. It's something I can't wait to see more of in the future.

TL;DR - Quake meets Descent
If you're into old school FPS games like Quake and Unreal Tournament (or if you're REALLY old like me, Descent), I would suggest picking this up.  It's fast, it's fun, it's (as they advertise) BRUTAL!  Kills are very satisfying and it is a true 360 degree kill zone experience.
-For Newbs-
This is not Call of Duty.  I say this because the FPS genre has been dumbed down dramatically by that series.  Strike Vector is much more skill-oriented than CoD.  That said, if you're looking for a space-like shooter and are willing to not give up after an hour of crashing, then I suggest picking this up. Once you learn the movement system, the game is a marvel.  I can't stress enough the importance of learning the movement.  When I started playing the game, I spent a couple hours literally just crashing everywhere until I finally understood how it worked.  Now I'm just completely unstoppable :D.  If you don't learn the movement, just rename this to Crashing: The Game.
-For High Level Players-
This is, as I originally wrote, Quake meets Descent/Star Fox/X-Wing etc...  There are even some familiar visuals which you can customize your 'Vector' with (ie: star fox and x-wing looking parts).  Most of the weapons are lead based except for the shotgun which appears to be the only hitscan weapon in the game.  Some minor weapon balancing does need to go into the game, however it is pretty balanced as it is.  There isn't anything really OP, you can pretty much dominate with everything.  The inner DMer in me has awoken.
The game has its typical indie hiccups (nothing dramatic or game breaking), but that said, I still recommend picking this up.
(On a side note, I have a Wii Classic Controller plugged into my PC through an adapter.  This was causing some gameplay issues that were immediately fixed upon unplugging the controller from the adapter.  Could have just been my controller inputting commands as the game has controller support.)

For someone who wants to be immersed in the story of an RPG this game just doesn't cut it.  I'm 25+ hours into this game and just not interested.  The whole open world thing is interesting.  Skyrim-esque I suppose, but that's not my jam. While the world itself looks interesting, it mostly just feels lifeless.  The majority of the NPCs appear to only be there for your sake.  While your own character is basically a silent protagonist, the never-ending repeating dialogue of your companions is painful.  I would turn their dialogue off, but they occasionally say important things like "we should check this path here first" or "these dudes are weak to ice attacks"   So I leave the dialogue on.
I hear a lot about how the combat is great, but I found it lacking.  I become extremely bored of combat after discovering that all I have to do is this little charge-stab attack to win 95% of encounters.  By accessing the menu at any time you can INSTANTLY cure your character to full health/stamina during combat, lowering the difficulty to near zero.  Even the whole Shadows of the Collosus "climb on top of the big-bad-guy and then stab him in the eye" gimmick just felt poorly implemented.  Though it was awesome cutting off enemies tails to weaken them, or cutting off one of a bosses 3 heads.
The inventory/crafting system seems decent, but theres just so much junk, and no way to tell what is valueable and what isnt.  There seems to be about 40 different herbs, 80 different potions, and 150 different foods:  which all do slightly different versions of healing you.  All of which clutter your inventory.  Every armor/weapon can be upgraded 3 times, using progressively rarer ingredients WHICH IS AWESOME!  However, there's no easy way to tell if the interesting new sword i found after a dungeon boss is better/worse/same as my current sword, because my current sword is buffed up to level 3.  Game is missing that color coded rarity system that we all know and understand.
The one AMAZING thing this games does is the Pawn system.  It needs to be explored by other games, because that's truely the future of great, interesting RPG worlds.

Probably one of the best combat mechanics I've ever played with! Fighting big monsters is actually exciting for once! The only other game I could think of that made me have this much fun fighting bosses would probably be Monster Hunter. Being able to mount enemies, ride them into the air, and keep stabbing them until they fall down is always fun. Many RPGs can take lessons from this game!
As for the visuals, this game is pretty lackluster. I'm not one who cares a lot about graphics, as long as the visual design is nice to look at. Dragon's Dogma looks like crap that was bleached. For some reason they decided to put a washed out looking filter on the game. Luckily SweetFX exists and I was able to give it a brighter look. The audio on the other hand is not too bad. It's not amazing but it didn't wanna make me play the game muted.
The story... honestly it's not that great and it has a very subtle way to tell it. Unless you're paying close attention you won't really get it. Basically you're a villager in this fishing village and a dragon steals your heart. You wake up and find out you can command this race of humanoid called Pawns, who really seem human except they don't have emotions. You then go on a journey to find out what's going on and take back your heart, although no one is really going to explain things to you in detail.
What the game really shines in is the combat. Again, fighting bosses in this game is a ton of fun. There are 9 classes you can play with and each of them provides a unique experience from each other. You feel strong when playing a warrior type. You feel like a ninja when using the daggers. You feel powerful when using magic. Every hit you deliver and every hit you take actuall feels like it has an impact, which I haven't felt recently from RPG games.
The world itself, sadly, isn't that interesting. There's really only two areas populated by friendly NPCs, a fishing village and a walled up town with a castle. The characters are forgetable and repeat the same lines over and over again. Honestly, only reason I remember them is because of their stupid lines. "They're masterworks all you can't go wrong." Not only that, but unless you know before hand, you'll probably be disappointed with an outcome late in the story. Not going to say anything else because spoilers.
One of the main features in this game is that instead of having multiplayer, you can hire other people's pawns and they can hire yours. The pawn is pretty interesting since it can actually learn how to fight better and help you out the more you play with them, although like any other AI, they can be pretty stupid most of the time. It's an interesting feature though and there's actually a good community for it if you want to delve deeper into the system.
Overall, even though the game is plagued with bad writing, a boring setting, and really weird design choices, the combat makes up for it in my opinion. Grinding just feels really fun and the game provides many dungeons late in the game for you to gather loot in. Definitely worth the price, especially on a sale.

While I never got to play Sonic CD when it was originally released on the Sega CD, I find this particular Sonic game to have always been an underappreciated gem (until now of course).
I find that Sonic CD was overshadowed by Sonic 2 in many ways.  The latter is raved as one of the best Sonic games of all time and has gotten several ports to both other Sega and non-Sega consoles.  Sonic CD had a narrow accessibility for gamers and a pretty shoddy port done for the Gems Collection.  This more or less ensured it would never quite take the limelight like  it deserved.
But it has all come full circle with this multi-platform release that has reinvented a game that, by all means, was and always has been superior to Sonic 2.  It kept the original formula that made the early Sonic games successful, but took up a time travel focus that served to enhance the gameplay in a very compelling way.
Instead of bogging you all down with the technical details, I'll just state the one thing that has stuck with me most prominently.  There are two ways to achieve the good ending, each catering to two different kinds of players: Explorers and speedrunners.  You could even toss aside being classified as either and attempt both approaches, seeing whichever one happens to land you the prize.  It seems like such a small change, but it's the kind of carefully chosen freedom that makes the reward that much more appealing.
Aside from that, you get an actual animated opening and endings, two different soundtracks, an expanded move-set, and a sizable game filled with a variety of interesting locales that  have four distinct looks depending on the time period.  There are also plenty of unlockables, of course.
Find out for yourself why Sonic 2 falls short of this fantastic game.

If you had a PC back in "the good old days," odds are high that you fondly recall the time you spent playing the ultimate computer game of that era: Scorched Earth.

All these years later, ShellShock Live manages to capture the spirit of classics like Scorched Earth while remaining unique enough in its own right to justify its existence.
The graphics are nice, the music and sound effects are high quality, and the game has an unusually high level of polish for an early access title. At the game's current asking price, it's a must-buy for anyone looking to recapture their Scorched Earth glory days.

If you're an RTS fan you should probably pick this game up (I think it's worth the $20, but if it's ever on sale there's no question). The game is very very simple to learn, but seemingly quite difficult to master. I'm only 3 hours in and I already feel like I got my money's worth. This game mixes the perfect amount of simplicity with actual strategy in short bursts that I think pretty much anyone can enjoy.
The game is captivating because it is so simple, yet it's filled with interesting little complexities and synergies that could take dozens of more hours to master. The best part? You hardly have to focus on macro game as your entire base can be built with the click of a button or two... You get to spend more time focusing on strategy and killing your opponent rather than jumping back and forth between all your units and buildings making sure they are all doing exactly what you wanted them to (I'm looking at you Starcraft); it's all very straight forward, making the game much more enjoyable for the average player.
The different "factions" are really just your preference of hero as you get to select the units you want to bring in prior to each game. All units are available for selection regardless of the hero chosen. I think this is a positive feature as it allows people to really synergize the units instead of just picking the most broken faction. This is also a huge benefit to the devs as well because it means they don't have to spend their time trying to balance different factions and can focus on the game content instead.
As far as performance I have not had a single issue other than one minor input issue when trying to play with friends, but we figured out a work-around for the time being and the devs have already recognized the issue and are expected to fix it soon. Very solid for launch day.
I can't wait to see more from this game and I sure as heck hope the devs continue to add to this. I could definitely see this being a game I keep coming back to.

Tooth and Tail, or TnT in short, is simply an RTS for people who don't have the time to play RTSs. With lightning fast matches, it's either think fast or get destroyed. Either that or trap yourself in a corner with a million defenses and wait till your resources run out, but trolling people's always fun too, right?
Moving on, I think Starcraft 2 is the game that resembles this one the closest. Both games have a large emphasis on counter building. The only difference is that in TnT, you have to choose the units that are available. Before the match begins, you are given time to pick 6 of the 20 units and buildings currently in the game. Each unit/building has its own counters, meaning you can get screwed if you don't build correctly - or you can just do what I do and spam defenses in a corner. Yes, I am that guy.
All in all, Tooth and Tail is a great game to play with friends, whether local or online (Probably the only RTS you can play with friends using controllers on the couch).

Alpha tester since late 2016 for the multiplayer branch.
First, before I say anything going into detail, the game is wonderful. It's a fresh RTS that completely seperates itself from other games in the genre. The devs themselves have also been amazing; giving out keys and their plans for the future of the game.
Now to seperate my thoughts:
Now I've said some kind words for the game; it truely deserves the praise it should be getting. However, I've found the single player itself to be... well... mediocre. The story itself it great; no doubt it sets up the universe fine. The characters are both charming and/or intimidating. So, if it has a great story, then why would it be mediocre? Well, I'd say it would be fine if the difficulty didn't spike all over the place.
I'm not the best RTS player; I've always liked turn-based more than anything else. However, I do have moderate experience, and the difficulty is just terrible. You'll start off first being smooth and easy, like any other game in the universe. As soon as you hit the second part, it starts to flicker. You'll be having an annoying time dealing mechanics that are too powerful for you to handle. At points, you'll be depending on RNG just to finish a single mission. I, myself have been stuck for two hours attempting to beat a single mission later on in the game. It's a shame, I'm trying my best to see how the story progresses.
Multiplayer is the main meat of the game in my opinion. While singleplayer puts a hard time on you, you'll be a little more relaxed in multiplayer. You'll be faced against people depending on skill, so there isn't that much pressure on you. Overall, multiplayer is the fun part of the game.
This isn't the final verdict; I'm still progressing through the game and experiencing some content. The game is worth the buy, no doubt about it. I hope they'll take the game beyond and support it as long as possible.
TL;DR
Cute RTS, has most of the standard RTS Mechanics but has it's controls simplified to make it more accessible.

1) Swine, who are sentient, talk, etc, are treated like property and goods, and are straight up farmed an eaten (Gristmills are in fact actually butcheries, the crops above are fed to swine underneath the Gristmill), they are the only ones who eat fruits and vegetables.
2) The Civilized (who are a sort of religious institute led by a flesh eating giant moose) choose people to get eaten, and also eat many of their own converts.
For some unexplained reason this is suddenly not sustainable anymore, and everyone are begining to starve, thus ensuring a civil war between the four factions.
Also there was apparently a Tsarina who was a rat (?) that is implied to have been assassinated by the Civilized for reasons unknown, but she is really just mentioned and used as an excuse for green team to join the war.
Anyway, you play as all four factions: The Longcoats (blue), The Commonpeople (red), the KSR (green) and the Civilized (yellow) in a (very short) campaign of 24 missions total (divided in 6 missions per faction).
The Longcoats are led by Bellafide, who is♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥off about the Civilized choosing his son to get eaten (selfishly so, because he gives no hecks about anyone elses family being eaten, and none of his troops really care about his vendetta either).
The Commonfolk are led by Hopper, a one armed rat, who is mostly mad about starving and the Civilized never choosing their own when selecting sacrifices.
The KSR are the secret police led by The Quartermaster (who is a girl mind you, in case you were confused?), who are only interested in protecting the Tsarina and ensuring peace and order, but join the war because, well, she's dead, and the Civilized betray them because reasons?
The Civilized, led by Archemedes (not technically the leader, but he commands the troops and does things), who are a bunch of psycho creepy cannibals who want to screw everyone over and eat well.
Regardless, none of their followers actually care about the respective leader or their cause, and only fight for meat, going as far as constantly switching sides, etc.
None of the factions are inherently "good", they are all straight up killing each other for the following reason:
"Ew, I don't want to eat fruits and vegetables, only filthy swine and beasts eat those, I'd literally rather die and/or join a faction and commit suicide in pointless skirmishes so I can eat meat and cannibalize my own species instead."
That's the gist of that.
--
Gameplay wise (and overall I guess) I can essentially sum it up in pro's and cons here:
Pros
- Cute art style
- Charming characters (Hopper is gonna be a fave for many for sure)
- Good attention to detail
- Great music
- Easy to learn with simple mechanics
- Good ending
Cons
- Creepy and poorly explained convoluted setting
It piqued my interest, but there is a lot of "what, why?" and "jesus how horrifying, the dev must be sick in the head yo" and not a whole lot of explaining going on, there is even a stupid joke from the dev about it being so vague if you talk to a squirrel in the room with all the troops in the KSR hub.
- Don't really get time to familiarize yourself with the characters and hubs.
4 SEPARATE campaigns of 24 missions would have helped the game, chars and settings a lot.
- Extremely short campaign, at hardly 8 hours if we are being really generous here (and that's me getting stuck on 3 missions for 3 hours total, consider that I'm not a god of RTS or anything either, I'm a drawn out 1+ hour siege warfare man, not a starcraft mcageofempires2 aggressive rush mobile defense pro).
- Unit management works poorly in large scale/spread engagement - turrets are GOD in this game.
- "Soft" time limit that punishes defensive play/drawn out battles severely, you turtle, you die. Simple as that.
- Poor unit balance with some units being clearly superior, and others being memes and jokes.
- Game heavily favors T1 healer + mook spam over higher tier investment - even Uncle Butter will eat dirt to T1 spam.
- Awkward mission balance/difficulty, ranging from borderline impossible, to cakewalk at random.
- Atrocious luck based map RNG, you'll see exactly what I'm getting at as you go through the campaign.
- Poorly tested campaign missions with often bogus Heroic objectives, with good classics such as "Protect 10 farmers" and said farmers immediately being killed off the second you spawn, just to name the first best example.
- Poor map variety, the majority of maps feel the same, the saving grace in the campaign is that each map has some sort of gimmick/objective that makes it a little different from the previous mission I guess?
- The animation for the gristmill can go f itself, jesus christ, I don't ever want to look at this thing ever again.
While I agree that "endless" and "replayable" are indeed words that exist within the english language, they are defenitely not applicable to this game. Just because a game has procedually generated maps it doesn't mean that each map is a magical fresh experience that will keep you interested forever, let alone for a week.
The game shouldn't had banked so hard on the whole furry cred, multiplayer thing and marketing the concept of a gristmill spawning next to a hill instead of 2 trees and a river, or a player potentially (but probably not) opting to choose distillery brothers as T1 mooks over the lizards as a big selling point, and should instead have focused more on fleshing out the campaign and setting, and ensuring a larger unit and map variety.
Then again, it's 20 bucks, it is what it is I guess.
It wont really hurt to buy it anyway, suppose it's good for an afternoon or two, but you wont miss out if you don't either.
Could always just watch a no commentary walkthrough on youtube or whatever.
It's just a real shame about the lost potential.
And also, no sass or anything here guys, but I'm glad that a good deal of you are enjoying the game as it is still, I sincerely hope the multiplayer stays active for you lads and that people don't like... forget the game within 3 months, 'cause that's sort of been happening a lot with games that don't really leave a lasting impression these days.

Shadow of Mirror is not Lord of the rings. It's an inspired story that takes from Lord of the rings. It makes the characters from those beloved movies (when they appear) not any more fleshed out or deep. It doesn't add to the original trilogy or the hobbit. It won't make you think more about the movies and you won't be exclaiming "hey there's the shadow of mordor!" In the middle of revisiting the early 2000s greatest trilogy.
That being said no one asked for that to happen. No one asked for an all out fleshed out story and characters that add to the original. No one really saw this game coming. Which was a great stroke of luck for the developer. They were able to take some well known tropes from today's best games and one original idea and make something that built a unique experience.
The long and short of it is that this is assassin's creed type gameplay, with a lot of character. Not in your own player. Not even in your allies, but in the most important part of adventure games and some would argue entire series and films, the antagonist.
Every bad guy can become a villain, and any of the chiefs and captains can become your nemessiss. You combat is a nice mix of Batman and assassin's creed but that's really only the beginning. Taking a familiar playstyle and adding the information and deep antagonists that they have makes this not an all out fantastic experience but one that i will be revisiting many times just so I can beat the snot out of my revanant enemies.
Thus the game has a lot of potential in combat that it instead focused on a unique experience between characters that in most other games would just be another dropped body. While the level up and progression system, the combat, the platforming, and the story itself is above average but just below greatness the core gameplay of making normal grunts into enemies you'll remember is remarkable and elegant. It's something I can't wait to see more of in the future.

At first I thought this game wasn't up my alley, but I have to say, anyone who enjoys games like DayZ, Unturned, Rust or anything of that nature, owes it to themselves to try this game out. And the developers are actively working on it, which makes me think they are actually proud of their product and want to continue improving upon it.
Experiences with other players in this game varies, and you'll find this game as a whole is really more of a social experiment of a sort. I can say that the mental aspect of this game really is the entire driving point. It's powerful in it's effect upon your psyche. The shock when someone has the drop on you, the edgy feeling you get when confronting someone, asking if they'd like to team up with you. The excitement of discovering a gun with a few bullets in it. Because those bullets somehow ease the anxiety by a small margin, which makes what is otherwise incredibly stressful situations less overwhelming due to the shear prospect of having more than the two options of running or hiding in the bushes while a couple of bandits are poking around looking for trouble. At least you can try to surprise them by taking at least one with you before you go down. And yes, believe me when I say that the fights can be so intense that you really feel cornered, like you don't have a shot, which summons up the wild thought that you'll fight tooth and nail to make their day as ♥♥♥♥ed up as they're trying to make yours.
And when you die, it sucks, but you also feel excited because the journey has begun again. New friends, new challenges, new loot.
The game is in early access but growing steadily, and the developers don't seem to plan to slow down and drag it out for our money.
I couldn't suggest this game more, even if I tried. Get it, now. Seriously.
