When I first purchased this, I had very immense interest in this, as my play hour count indicates.
I've had a little time to think since then, however, and now... Honestly, I can't much recommend this.
Now, mind you, when the game is fun, it's *very* fun, at least in my opinion. The choice systems are also very empowering. I also like the realistic political and power play sub-plots.
However, the main reason I don't recommend this is the event prioritization. Note: Spoiler-bearing Examples will be entailed.
At first, I *like* how the events flow; they do so smoothly, seamlessly carrying the story and intrigue. This carries on for the earliest part of the game.
...Then, it gets to where you're supposed to go to the different planets- and that's when the deal-breaking (for me) downsides kick in.
For one, the sense of direction is rather poor. Perhaps this is only an issue for a moron like me, but getting lost is very easy in this game. I can't tell you how many times I lost my way in a ruin or even an office building in this game, and eventually had to just stick to taking every right turn to wind up where I'd started. The mini-map can help in understanding the landscape, which actually makes it fantastic for the derelict planet exploration missions, but it offers no help in finding the actual objectives.
This isn't just limited to complex indoor structures, either. I recall at least several times trying to play the game through, I just zipped from one end of a long vehicle-entailing track to another, and wound up going back to the starting point several times. the Scenery is seldom well-distinguished enough to facilitate differentiation of direction. If you're an intelligent sort like most people, this shouldn't be a problem. However, for a moron like myself, this means having no choice but to just keep holding the drive button, never stopping, and hoping that I don't get flipped. When there are foes ahead who want to blow me and my buggy to hell and back, I must stop well ahead of the threat to get out and shoot them; otherwise I risk losing direction if I try to fight them via tank, or getting killed if I press on to avoid losing track.
Additionally, the flow of events on individual planets is absurdly disorganized. Things seem to happen in a strange sequence that makes the visits seem more like fever dreams than missions. Perhaps Bioware assumed that we were going to follow a specific sequence ourselves, and programmed the events likewise?
Anyway, scenes themselves also seem to introduce characters and factors more quickly than I for one can take them in, and seldom (although thankfully not never) provides a means to clarify who someone or what something is. This often entails characters and objects that are very important to story and, in fact, to gameplay.
Even when I manage to make it through the assorted missions, I often find myself coming out- and this is even after repeated playthroughs- wondering what just happened.
This might only be an issue for my own inferior mind. Even so, I don't think I can recommend this game.

Hello developers,
Firstly, I just want to explain my reasoning for a thumbs down. I do not outright hate this game; I love it to be honest. It's still in early development and needs a bunch of work, but it's good for what it's priced at. The thumbs down is mainly due to the next paragraph...
I have played the heck outta this game before the recent major update. My boyfriend got the game after the update and we played through together. I wanted to experience the new content with him and I was super hyped. However, there were a lot of issues that put me off and made me set down the game. First of all, the dialog is extremely hard to read within the latest content, and it would be nice to have it fixed. It feels like there was absolutely no spell check or any attention payed to grammar. I can understand a few mistakes here and there, especially with a smaller team. But if I have to stare at a box of dialog and try to make out what is meant, somethings needs to change... Part of why this bothers me so much is that I'm a third-year student in college and I'm rather particular when it comes to dialog. Secondly, there are some issues with the hitboxes for ranged attacks; you have to pretty much get a direct hit. It would be nice to see larger hitboxes. Finally, the two 'parts' of the game feel rather disjointed. Yes, there is a connection where Ashley saves you and brings you to the forest, but beyond that and the fact you need to rescue the hearts, I felt no true connection to the snow world. That being said, the two worlds are completely opposite and I just may be crazy in picking that apart.
While I did nitpick about a few things, I would like to say that I'm honestly excited for where you guys take this game. I genuinely enjoyed the feel of the first section and was in love with the look of the new forest area. The soundtrack also is adorable and relaxing. There are things that really offput me from the game, but I'm sure that I'll get into it again.
One more thing to mention; I give you guys kudos for working on the game through your troubles and hardships. I may not personally know what you guys are going through, but I have had some pretty horrible things happen in my life as well.
Overall, I hope the rest of development goes well for all of you and I wish you the best!

As a kid this was one of my alltime favorite 2-D sonic games. Does it hold up today? The answer is no, not really. There's a dime a dozen old sonic games (read: 4) and this one has a neat little mechanic to set it apart from the others, namely the time travel element. It's a neat idea but by modern day gaming conventions a pain to utilize. That doesn't mean the levels aren't still spectacular right? Wrong. The levels are actually quite annoying, with paths that can be skipped because they just make you go out of the way for some reason.
But while I'm here talking about the steam version let me make it clear that this port is top notch. Unlike the Sonic Adventure DX port this one is optomized, given new menu's, the ability to use japanese or english music, a hostful of extras, and even the ability to play as Tails, something which was not in the original game.
So in conclusion there are really only two parts of this game that did not age for me: The boss battle between Metal Sonic (quite fun actually), and the Sonic Boom song at the opening of the English version.

I enjoyed this game.  Sure, there were a few gripes I had here and there but overall I definitely think I stole it for $10.00.
I enjoyed the gameplay mechanics a lot.  I thought that the keyboard/mouse handled the game well for the most part, but it the game does show certain areas that were truly designed for a controller.  The stealth component was largely intact although nowhere near as stealthy as the first splinter cell.  There were some segments of the game where you were forced to do things that I really didn't think Sam Fisher would ever do in those situations.  The gun play was tight and the game had a fairly good weapon selection.  I've always been a good fan of the game series putting emphases on pistol gameplay and this game follows through with that again.  One thing I found kind of annoying about the gun play were killing the AIs wearing helmets.  Even if you hit them in the face or chin, one shot always counts to remove the helmet and then another to get the headshot.  Kinda silly especially when you hit an AI in the chin and hear a helmet 'dink' noise.
There was only one really buggy part of the game and that was at the end. For whatever reason I can't see the ending cinematic once I beat the game, and only the audio comes through.  I played the last mission twice and it did this both times.  This was a crumby way to the end game, but not the end of the world I suppose.
I can't review the multiplayer because it really does not exist in the fact that nobody is playing it.  Despite it being on the best seller list for the summer sale, I could not connect to a single game after multiple attempts.
Overall I think it was a pretty decent game, especially for the price.  Buy it if you're looking for a good single player experience, with a typical but none the less solid story.  If you're looking for a stealth multiplayer or something of the sort, look elsewhere.  Also, the game runs  pretty well on PC and the bugs, tearing, clipping, etc were minimal, at least for me.

But, when sneaking up on enemies they will hear you unless you do it fast. Until you start seeing heavys that is. They have heavy armour and the only way to kill them quietly is to sneak up on the but they will always hear you so you can't stealth kill them. Another annoying thing is that enemies start to wear helmets so you can't one shot them and are forced to sneak up on them. This is usually fine until in almost every level you will be in the middle of enemies all close to one another. The gameplay as I stated can be very annoying but the stroy is pretty solid and should be played through. Lastley the voice of Sam Fisher is different from a deeper darker voice to a higher (yet still manley) voice. It was annoying at first but you get used to it.

This is, as I just said, a Real Time Strategy game. However, Pocketwatch opted to have the player take a more active approach to commanding an entire legion of ♥♥♥♥massive forest animals. Instead of clicking on units to select them and tell them to go butcher

The gameplay can be broken down as follows: you and your opponent(s) will start on a randomly-generated map. You each have a Gristmill to your name. Said mill has 8 farms encircling it. These farms are worked by Swine (or Fat Boris, as they have also been referred to in some circles). The Swine will churn out Food, which is your building resource. Food is used in three ways: to expand to a new Gristmill, to place down Warrens/Defenses, and to recruit new units.
Now, after about five minutes, your farms will go barren, and will not produce any more Food, at which point, you'll have to start a new farm to keep production going and your army fed (if you don't, you'll starve, resulting in a loss). This, of course, is a problem, because as previously mentioned, your army units have two costs: one to build their "bunkers" so to speak, and one to
♥♥♥♥ing use them. The more bunkers you build, the more units of that type you can bring in, but that also means the more Food you'll spend on recruitment. It's a brilliant way to keep the game flowing.
Oh, and your opponents will be very well aware of these rules, and they
hunt you down with a vengeance that would strike Ghost Rider with awe. Yes, even the A.I. in offline battles. I have no shame in admitting that the Medium difficulty A.I. gave me a run for my money.
I may have just compared this game to a "stupid Anton Chekhov novel about a black-humor Russian Revolution spiked with cannibalism," but I gotta be honest here, I [l]love[/l] the story and the lore behind it.

Bellafide was, naturally,

to see who becomes a snack. As one does.

The only thing I have difficulty surviving is...the boredom.
Walk around for two hours, find one .223 round, but no gun.
Walk around for another hour, find a 1911 handgun, no .45 rounds.
Walk around for another hour, find a second flashlight even though you spawn with one.
Walk around for another hour, find anothe player, get killed with an axe.
Start over.
Walk around for an hour, find a rifle, but no ammo.
Walk around for another hour, find bat finally.
Walk around for an hour, see a mutant. Attach it with a bat, lose 70% of your health and find nothing on its corpose. Great reward for the risk.
Walk around for an hour, get attacked by a guy with a gun.
Start over.
Check out an entire airfield, find 1 can of peaches.
Check an entire city block, find 15 water bottles, 15 rations, 7 t-shirts, 3 tan combat boots, 1 rope, 7 cans of oil, 15 stow packs, and two .223 rounds but no gun.
The game is beautiful. The night is truly dark and immersive. The rain/storms add the right effect. The detail to the buildings and clutter make the world feel great. Nothing beats the first time you experience a night cycle and are slowly moving through homes.
Here's the problem: surviving is easy. Finding food and water is a piece of cake, so there's no tension or "game" involved in that. I ran around for 2 hours eating and drinking as I went and simply replacing my food with stuff I was finding. I have NEVER had an issue finding food or water.
Weapons, especially guns and ammo, though? Impossible to find. More importantly, when you do, the game sucks the life out of you by saying, "Hey! Thanks for playing for 2 hours, here's a pistol with 1 round of ammo!" Great. Thanks game.
This game is in serious need of some action. We need more guns and ammo spawns. Hell, I'd take more melee weapon spawns at this point. Right now, you have a glorified walking simulator with no story or characters.
It probably wouldn't hurt to increase the number of mutants. Have them patrol through towns or fields. Put them inside of buildings and rooms so searching/looting isn't so care-free.
Right now, this game is worth skipping for one that has more game in it. Sadly, all it would take is a dramatic increase in weapon spawns.

Now I know this game is quite old, but I have finally been able to sit and dive into the deep space of Mass effect. From the vast amount of planets to explore, to the commanding of my squad to take on the ventures unknown, I had one heck of a time.
In the beginning I jumped in being prepared to get through the game as quickly as possible. Now it is not the best way to play this game, even though I had that mindset, I found myself veering off course to the different side quests the universe had to offer. Right from the start, you are given a variety of choices in dialogue in which molded your character with the personality you wanted to give. Now being the person I am I will always be the that knight in shining armour, but the choices were still very hard to choose from, sacrificing others for the good of mankind, or maybe saving a whole species but risking another catastrophe of war, it was a very hard decision.
Putting aside the dialogue for a moment, there was still a lot of decision making when it came to the combat. Different weapons, with different upgrades and stats, then choosing if to keep the best weapon for yourself (of course you do) or giving it to your squad members. I have to admit I did spend a lot of time deciding which upgrades were best on which guns to make certain situations easier for me, some bullets did better against synthetics while others organics, and at the time of the fight you could just decide by thinking
Im not saying this a life or death decision but it really. REALLY. helped in some such situations but yeah I like combat to go smoothly when Im involved.
Overall this game is a must play. I would advise getting it for the cheap price it is now than the full retail price it once was.

"As Commander Shepard, you lead an elite squad on a heroic, action-packed adventure throughout the galaxy."
My very first experience with Mass Effect was when I saw the cover of the third game on a shelf when browsing around a shop. I have heard good things on the internet about the franchise and since I couldn't find any copies of the games, I brought this one. When I got home I started up my PS3 and played the game. Obviously I felt a bit lost at first and knew that some things were missing because I hadn't played the previous games, but the experience sure was fun. I then purchased the other two games and a bit of DLC as time went by from the PlayStation Store and played the entire franchise from start to finish. It quickly became one of my favorite gaming franchises. Recetly I bought Mass Effect 1 for PC since it was on sale. I managed to get the two DLCs for free and installed a mod that enchanced the game's overall quality and textures. The perfomance was vastly improved when compared to the console. Instead of the game being locked on 30FPS, I now get around 80 to 130 frames-per-second.
So, is this game so good that it was worth a re-purchase? Yes, it is. It's been months since I touched the series and being back sure feels good. Unlike last time, I kind of rushed in order to get to the third game, but this time around I'm going slow. I've already spent forty hours in this and I'm still not finished. I'm taking my time to explore every corner and quest that the game provides.
Pros:
- You can create your own Shepard and modify his or hers facial features, background and even select a Class. Vanguard is my favorite, but it all depends on taste after all.
- The story is great. One of the best out there. No wonder this game was a hit back on 2007.
- You control your character at 100%; you make your own choices and the story is tailored by how you play. Most of your choices lead to consequences that will impact future games.
- You will either love or hate your companions. They are great characters and will surely provide you aid in combat. Each one of them has a different role, so be sure to think before heading out.
- It has one of the best voice-acting out there. Jennifer Hale is the best.
- Being a 2007 most computers and laptops nowadays can handle this game with ease and it still looks amazing ten years later. BioWare sure knew what they were doing with their engine back then.
- The Mako can be fun and there's some variety put into the side-quests in terms of looks and feel.
- This game only came to be thanks to KOTOR, so obviously you will find some nice Star Wars references here and there. Besides those, there are also some other Easter Eggs and even references to older games and subjects.
- The RPG and Shooter elements were combined rather nicely. You can select all sorts of gear for your character and companions.
- Great soundtrack.
- And many others...
Cons:
- For some people the game might feel outdated... for whatever reason. Most people prefer ME2 and ME3. I personally find all of them good at their own pace.
- It's a bit hard to create a good-looking Shepard... but not as hard as some other BioWare games that's for sure.
- If careless, you will be blocked from certain choices that will eventually ruin your experience.
- The AI isn't amazing. Some enemies will sometimes stare at the walls and your companions will sometimes shoot at you rather than the enemies themselves.
- Some people can find the Mako a bore due to its clunky physics and the familiar feeling of most side-quests. There is also a lack of variety in music choice when it comes to these quests.
- Some backtracking during missions.
- Sometimes the DLC can can be removed by itself. Be sure to save a copy of their installers and a copy of your save files somewhere. However, your computer might consider these save files as malware.
- Little variety put into the DLCs. Pinnacle Station feels like it was done by a completely different team.
- Even though you have several dialogue choices, some of them can lead to the exact same outcome.
- And others.
WARNING: The Steam version DOES NOT include any of the DLC. You can easily find it for free just by browsing it on Google with no issues.

Outdoes the original in every aspect, especially the physics. After playing the Megadrive CD version last week, I figured I'd have to rehash my recommendation. Sonic CD features gameplay very similiar to Sonic 2, with slight changes to the spindash (reversible to S2 standards in the new port), and a time traveling mechanic. At certain points of the level, there are signposts that start a time traveling sequence you trigger by simply going fast. This will either make you go into the Future, or the Past. Each Level has 4 different versions of itself. A Present version, a Bad Future version (representing the bad guy winning), a Good Future version (representing Sonic stopping him), and a Past version, where you have to travel to in order to save the future. While this is a straightforward Sonic platformer in the quaint essence, it has a good variety of exploration as levels are laid out to be two-directional, which is necessary in this game as you have to sometimes go back in a level after you traveled to the Past in order to prevent Robotnik taking the area over, and as you might think, there are multiple endings reflecting your actions or lack of it. It's was a fantastic game back then, and still is nowadays, and the added widescreen support, new engine that fixes physics woes, the option to play as Tails as well as being able to choose the soundtrack wrap this well up as something you should definitely not miss having played if you are a platformer enthusiast, as being back as Sonic enthusiast since Generations, I can say it's definitely the franchise's best.

Honestly, a great game for anyone who enjoys the Dynasty Warriors series.
I had originally played Dynasty Warriors 2-6 (including Extreme Legends and Empires), and had acquired this in hopes of reliving my childhood. One thing that this game has that differs from the older titles is the ability to swap between two weapons (both can be chosen from a LARGE assortment of different weapons). This allows many different combos to be made. This also allows you to switch out a particular character's weapons out of that character (ie: Zhao Yun using Pang Tong's weapon instead of his own + another weapon), which, personally, I am not a huge fan of, for I enjoyed using a new character and seeing what his strengths and weaknesses are.
Addionally, a new feature called "Storm Rush" was introduced. When using a weapon which has a type advantage over an enemy officer, you will see a blue crystal ontop of the officer. After using the weapon with the type advantage and breaking all 3 sections of the crystal, your character will enter a mode where he unleases a bunch of powerful attacks on enemies infront of (or around) him/her. While this may seem good, having a weapon with a type DISADVANTAGE on an enemy officer will result in your attacks not causing flinch to them. This makes it so switching between weapons with different types almost neccesary.
Additionally, switching weapons allows you to break some officer's attacks while they are charging them, and breaks guard. This is different than the older titles where an enemy's officers guard was a pain to get through. Personally, I still prefer the old system, as it encouraged repositioning.
The soundtrack of this game is AMAZING (just like the soundtrack of the older titles). The additional characters and Jin add a lot to this game.
Overall, a game I definitely recommend. Now if only I had more time to play it...

Pillars of Eternity is the first cRPG I've played and I played it on the Beginner setting. Everyone else already talked about how great it is, so I'm just going to list mostly the things that annoyed me in the hopes that they might make this better in the future.
First thing's first. The amount of loading screens in this game is ridiculous. The maps themselves are quite small and not complicated, and there's no real reason for there to be a 10 second loading screen with every map change. On top of that, they did not do anything to reduce the amount of loading screens you'd have to experience. For example, I got a quest to go and get an invite to a meeting. It goes like this:
- Quest giver gives quest
- Go downstairs (loading screen)
- Leave house (loading screen)
- Move to edge of map
- Change to another district of city (loading screen)
- Walk to invitation giver's building
- Enter building (loading screen)
- Get invitation - like 2 lines of dialogue
- Leave building (loading screen)
- Move to other district (loading screen)
- Enter house (loading screen)
- Go up stairs (loading screen)
- Tell quest giver I got the invite
- Go downstairs (loading screen)
- Leave house (loading screen)
- Enter place of meeting (loading screen)
Like.. they could just not have had the quest giver be on an upstairs floor, and could have skipped the part where I have to go back and say I got the invite - that would take out like five loading screens. I spend half of this game tabbed out. On top of that, running across maps that you've already explored is slow and boring, even with fast mode enabled.
Speaking of slow, annoying things, the way the game deals with "being in combat" and looting is very annoying. There's a few second pause between killing the last creature and being able to loot - the game perceives you as being in combat for a little while after the creatures are dead. So after every fight I have to wait for a few seconds before I can loot. In isolation, this is not the end of the world, but over an entire playthrough it became pretty frustrating.
Other things that I disliked where the system of attributes and skills, where there is pretty much twice the amount of keyworded skills/attributes/traits/talents than would actually be necessary to make a fun game. It adds a ton of reading and complexity without really adding anything to gameplay. The tooltips for the attributes are not enough to be able to determine if one stat is better than another - like, I dunno if this belt with +1 fortitude is better than one with +1 constitution or +1 endurance or +1 deflection. It's all defense-ey abilities, why do we need so many variations of it? It's very rare that I picked up an item that was a clear upgrade to something I already had, and this was the case even though I got unique-titled fancy-sounding new items all the time. Maybe some people find this lack of clarity fun, but for me it was just unsatisfying that I never really had a moment where I was like, "holy♥♥♥♥♥♥ what a beast of a weapon!". Instead I got to spend ages poring over tooltips trying to work out if +% damage was better than might or +DR.
The stronghold was a nice idea but it never really became relevant for me and was just more annoying than anything. Especially due to loading screens, if I want to go there and rest that's at least three loading screens, and the bonuses I get for resting are way worse than anything I could get in an inn for 200cp. When you take into account the cost of building upgrades to improve the resting bonuses, you would expect that travelling home to your stronghold would be worth it. As it is, you have no real reason to go to your stronghold, other than to pick up herbs and bits and pieces your adventurers got on missions, but there's not really much point, as by the time you start gaining anything, the game is almost complete anyway. The game was also way shorter than I was expecting.
The UI for using the abilities of your party was just terrible as well. You can set hotkeys, but can only use them if you have the character that will cast the spell selected, so you barely save any time over not using a hotkey.
The game is still good, but the above mentioned stuff makes it a 6/10. Things I particularly liked were:
- Even on beginner difficulty, the game is still slightly challenging in the beginning, although it became extremely easy towards the end.
- The story is intriguing and the named party members were interesting characters that weren't just flat generic fantasy warriors.
- The opening phase of the game was cool.
As it is, I'm near the end of the game, and I'm struggling to motivate myself to finish it, due to the stuff I mentioned above and more, so I can't really recommend it to others.

Do not, under any circumstances, pay full price for this game. Unless of course you happen to be a millionaire on a videogame kick, in which case splurge away, my friend.
Because of the above I cannot give PoE a thumbs-up, as I only give thumbs-up to games that deserve their full price. Here is why PoE does not.
- Loading screens. Loading Screens of Eternity, I think. Travel is a chore, whether exploiring or backtracking. Let's say you wake up at an inn and want to visit a character who lives on the second floor of a mansion in the nearby district. Loading screen 1: Exit the inn. Loading screen 2: transition to the district. Loading screen 3: walk into the house. Loading screen 4: get up to the second floor of the house. After a while, the screens interrupt the flow enough to want to just give up. This isn't 1999.
- The game is mostly combat, or at least it feels heavily skewed towards combat. Sneak for a few steps, fight trash mobs, loot. Sneak a few steps, disarm a trap, fight trash mobs, loot. Don't get me wrong, I like combat, but after a while it gets dreadfully same-y. And even with the joke of the AI introduced in 2.0 you can't really program or automate your characters' repetitive actions. It feels tactical and cool at first, but after the 100th repetition, it's just... BAAAWWWRING.
- It looks, plays and feels like something built on the ancient Infinity engine (see: Baldur's Gate, Icewind Dale). Obsidian basically took Unity (which is pretty good as far as engines go) and saddled it with all idiosynchracies of an early-2000 isometric RPG. Forget rotating the camera to get a better view of the scrum on the screen when bigger battles erupt. Forget even turning on silhouette display for your characters when they are obscured by something, like a corner wall. It makes even the limited camera of Divnity: Original Sin look advanced by comparison.
- Graphics are likewise quite basic. It is nearly impossible to create a good-looking character; not that it matters (given zoom levels). Whereas environments look very pretty, characters models are straight out of early 2000s, again. It made me miss D:OS's bodybuilder dudes and permanently-in-do-me-high-heels chicks. (Yes, I know, second comparison to D:OS in as many paragraphs. Sorry).
- Pauseable real-time combat is a drag. Real time just doesn't work in isometric RPGs that aren't straight-up actioners like Diablo.  Opponents nearly always charge you at turbo-speed and you are left guessing just where to plop that AoE spell so it doesn't whiff because by the time your caster finished mumbling, the enemies are three blocks away. On the other hand, close combat quickly becomes a chaotic scrum, where characters and spell effects obscure each other, and bad pathfinding forces unintentional comedy on both sides.
- Finally, and this really sticks in my craw: Obsidian decided to reinvent the wheel with regards to the ruleset for the game. It seems that they tried to improve upon AD&D... somehow... and ended up with a hodge-podge mess instead. There are complex RPGs systems that do a beautiful job at creating an intricate stat system (take, for example, Das Schwarze Auge). And there are systems that are simplified right down to bare basics, and those are fine too. PoE tried to do... all things at once I guess? Take Might for example: for some reason, it increases your physical damage, your spell damage, your healing and your ranged damage (including guns). There is literally no reason not to max it out, regardless of what kind of character you are. Simple, right? Except this results in some kind of muscle-man spellcaster that can also swing a greatsword and lift someone off the ground by their throat (my scholarly cipher did just that in one of the dialogue-driven scenes and I just went "EH?"). At the same time you have a bunch of derived statistics, defenses that influence your offensive capabilities, health that represents your global survivability and endurance that represents your per-battle survivability (which literally means you can die at full health). It is all unnecessarily convoluted and was done before, by smarter people, and better.
It doesn't help either that the man in charge of balancing game mechanics, Josh Sawyer (AKA JSaw or Balance Man) is a shameless nerf herder with a chip on his shoulder against spellcaster classes. (In his own words, CRPG spell casters are too flexible and powerful). This doesn't strike me as a level-headed and neutral individual who should be in charge of a single-player game mechanics; and according to Obsidian Forums' hangers-on, "the Balance Man hath not yet truly begun balancing". Already over the course of several patches the game has experienced wild and massive nerf-buff cycles normally seen in MMOs, and apparently there are more coming. And since Obsidian promises minimal to no mod support, modding out these "balance changes" will be that much more difficult. For now, if you play the game, do yourself a favor and download IEMod.
Overall, PoE tells a good story. It isn't a bad game by any stretch of imagination. But when it tries to price itself on a par with much higher-budget games, it certainly reaches WAY beyond its station.

Not as fun as I hoped it would be.
I love the old Infinity Engine games; "Baldur's Gate II" and "Planescape: Torment" are two of my favorite games of all time. That's why I expected to also love "Pillars of Eternity". Unfortunately, instead of enjoyig the experience, it felt more like a chore. Normally in a great and addictive game, you rarely reach a point where you want to stop playing once you've first started; you want to keep going to explore and discover the new content. While Pillars of Eternity started out promising, it failed to consistently hook me. I still played quite a lot of hours in a short timespan because I wanted to really give it a chance, but as I kept playing, it started to feel more and more like it was something I was just forcing myself to get through. In the rest of the review, I will describe what I liked about it and what I didn't like.
The first impression of the game is very good. It has a nice aesthetic and interface, good music, good voice acting, and decent production values all-around. The character creation system is interesting at first, presenting options that all seem balanced in terms of game-play; in other words, you could create a random character with random options and it will still be relatively as powerful as a character that has been min/maxed. This makes it seem like the focus of the game will be more on role-playing, or that at least the characters built for role-playing won't be at a severe disadvantage during game-play; I appreciate the effort that was made to balance the game mechanics in this way. Most of the dialogue has options that are available only when certain character requirements are met, and selecting different options frequently leads to different outcomes; other games have such a feature, but not usually to quite such an extent. Much of the interface and game-play is similar to the old Infinity Engine games, and that familiarity is pleasant for someone who loves those old games.
The biggest problem with the game is that the main story and plot are not interesting. It doesn't help that none of the story flow makes much sense. You arrive to the region as a random level 1 character looking for a new place to settle down... and then that's totally forgotten for the rest of the game, even when you somehow manage to get your own keep within a couple game-world days??? Your motivation is not terribly clear or believable after that. Even the main quests in the journal didn't offer a good context for your future actions. The hollowborn thing and its impact on the behavior of the world was also an incredibly dumb plot point. There's a lot I could say about how much I hate the lore, the universe, and the story, but I want to move on to the actual game-play. It seems like it should be good and fun, but it's actually really boring and tedius. Bear in mind that I started on the Hard difficulty level, and didn't play anything lower than that. The places that have mobs have a lot of mobs, and they are littered all over the maps. You can't take 5 steps without running into a trap or a mob. That's not too bad and is even a positive when talking about a game like Diablo, but in a game that requires you to play turn-based on the harder difficulties, it gets old really fast. Sure, you can use the stealth mechanic to avoid most of the combat if you already know the maps inside and out, but on your first play-through, you absolutely have to fight and fight a lot. I enjoy turn-based combat when the fights are interesting / unique / thoughtful / rewarding / good, but the vast majority of the fights here are against trash mobs that will wipe the floor with you if you don't meticulously go through the same combat setups, use the same 3-4 skills, in the same order, etc. When you are brand new to the game, each fight can take like 5 - 10 minutes, and there can be like 15 of them in one small 3-floor dungeon. Later in the game, once you know what you're doing, the fights don't take as long, but they're still incredibly boring to slog through. In a game like BG2, most of the fights are basic auto-attack affairs that just add a tiny bit of resistence and flavor to an area, and it makes sense that death does not indeed lie around every corner; the epic fights that require a lot of planning and prolific use of the pause button are rare and thematic, and it feels really good when you win those fights. But in Pillars of Eternity, even a room full of lowly spiders can be a challenge that requires a lot of repetitive and tedius micromanaging to get through. And once you get through the first room of spiders, oh look, the next room has just as many spiders and is essentially the same fight (one wonders how an ogre can survive in such a place). The combat mechanics that go into a fight, like accuracy, damage reduction, deflection, flanking, and such, seem reasonable enough, it's just the fights themselves that are lackluster. Beyond fighting, there are small little adventure checks that require you to have a certain, say, mechanics or athletics skill level, or they require that you have certain items. Well, since you only need one character to have a high skill level usually, and there is no weight mechanic and basically no inventory restriction, those adventure checks are mostly pointless. They might be interesting if they were less trivial, but as they are now, they might as well not even be in the game. That really goes for all of the non-combat skills.  Instead of making the game feel more rich, they just make it seem kind of bloated instead. Believe me, when I first started playing, I was hoping against hopes that these skills could be meaningfully used to avoid combat, provide solutions to quests, and offer differing styles of game-play, but sadly, they're merely easily obtainable check boxes for extremely minor outcomes. The same is largely true of the reputation system and the dialogue checks. The amount of actual role-playing feels very light with too much emphasis on boring fights with trash mobs. Is that really supposed to be entertaining?
Everything about this game feels contrived and over-designed. It's like they built a game around the mechanics they wanted rather than fitting the mechanics to the game and player experience they wanted. Maybe this review is harsh, but I honestly can't say that I enjoyed this game, and I would not recommend it.

Very fun little RTS with an interesting setting. The campaign from what I've seen thus far reminds me a bit of a very specific graphic novel series called "FABLES", specifically "The Farm" but with a more industrial era setting. It's fairly gritty given each faction is fighting over who literally gets to eat who and the side conversations you can have by talking to people hanging around in each factions hideout between missions gives some dark context.
Each mission has a sub objective to make things a little more interesting and add some longevity to the campaign which (going by the achivements) seems to have about 28 missions spanning four factions. Ultimately, a nicely planned out context for teaching you the mechanics and doing some worldbuilding along the way. Matches are relatively short and move quickly and are more about positioning and decision making than getting fussy with build queues. The maps themselves are randomly generated (including the campaign) which is worth noting. It's not trying to be an esport or anything crazy like that and I honestly think its better for it. If you're looking for some RTS fun you can jump into, play around a bit in and not have to dedicate your life to it to get some enjoyment out of it, this seems like a pretty cool option so far.
Also worth noting it controls just fine with a controller since there isn't a huge micro focus and the contextual input gets the job done just as well.

If you're looking for a good SP and/or Co-Op game, buy this now!

"As Commander Shepard, you lead an elite squad on a heroic, action-packed adventure throughout the galaxy."
My very first experience with Mass Effect was when I saw the cover of the third game on a shelf when browsing around a shop. I have heard good things on the internet about the franchise and since I couldn't find any copies of the games, I brought this one. When I got home I started up my PS3 and played the game. Obviously I felt a bit lost at first and knew that some things were missing because I hadn't played the previous games, but the experience sure was fun. I then purchased the other two games and a bit of DLC as time went by from the PlayStation Store and played the entire franchise from start to finish. It quickly became one of my favorite gaming franchises. Recetly I bought Mass Effect 1 for PC since it was on sale. I managed to get the two DLCs for free and installed a mod that enchanced the game's overall quality and textures. The perfomance was vastly improved when compared to the console. Instead of the game being locked on 30FPS, I now get around 80 to 130 frames-per-second.
So, is this game so good that it was worth a re-purchase? Yes, it is. It's been months since I touched the series and being back sure feels good. Unlike last time, I kind of rushed in order to get to the third game, but this time around I'm going slow. I've already spent forty hours in this and I'm still not finished. I'm taking my time to explore every corner and quest that the game provides.
Pros:
- You can create your own Shepard and modify his or hers facial features, background and even select a Class. Vanguard is my favorite, but it all depends on taste after all.
- The story is great. One of the best out there. No wonder this game was a hit back on 2007.
- You control your character at 100%; you make your own choices and the story is tailored by how you play. Most of your choices lead to consequences that will impact future games.
- You will either love or hate your companions. They are great characters and will surely provide you aid in combat. Each one of them has a different role, so be sure to think before heading out.
- It has one of the best voice-acting out there. Jennifer Hale is the best.
- Being a 2007 most computers and laptops nowadays can handle this game with ease and it still looks amazing ten years later. BioWare sure knew what they were doing with their engine back then.
- The Mako can be fun and there's some variety put into the side-quests in terms of looks and feel.
- This game only came to be thanks to KOTOR, so obviously you will find some nice Star Wars references here and there. Besides those, there are also some other Easter Eggs and even references to older games and subjects.
- The RPG and Shooter elements were combined rather nicely. You can select all sorts of gear for your character and companions.
- Great soundtrack.
- And many others...
Cons:
- For some people the game might feel outdated... for whatever reason. Most people prefer ME2 and ME3. I personally find all of them good at their own pace.
- It's a bit hard to create a good-looking Shepard... but not as hard as some other BioWare games that's for sure.
- If careless, you will be blocked from certain choices that will eventually ruin your experience.
- The AI isn't amazing. Some enemies will sometimes stare at the walls and your companions will sometimes shoot at you rather than the enemies themselves.
- Some people can find the Mako a bore due to its clunky physics and the familiar feeling of most side-quests. There is also a lack of variety in music choice when it comes to these quests.
- Some backtracking during missions.
- Sometimes the DLC can can be removed by itself. Be sure to save a copy of their installers and a copy of your save files somewhere. However, your computer might consider these save files as malware.
- Little variety put into the DLCs. Pinnacle Station feels like it was done by a completely different team.
- Even though you have several dialogue choices, some of them can lead to the exact same outcome.
- And others.
WARNING: The Steam version DOES NOT include any of the DLC. You can easily find it for free just by browsing it on Google with no issues.

Mass effect is developed by bioware and published by EA in 2007. Bioware is known for the great lore, deep narrative and belivable charecters. Can this game hold the reutation that bioware has or will it be a let down. Let's see down here
Mass effect by no means a perfect game. It has it's own fair share of flaws.
The combat. It's not what we except from a third person shooter. Ofcourse it's a bioware game. you need to pause. Need to plan. Give orders to your teammates. But this feels little clunky. This breaks the flow, the immeresion. gunplay is also not satisfying. Not all the guns have a punch to it. Only assult rifle and pistol are fun to use.
Side mission. Like all other Bioware games this also provides side missions. But all the side missions feels the same. you'll be dropped in mako on surface of the other planets. you need to drive around got to the place. Kill certain number of enimies. then press a key to activate/deactivate or rescue a target. All the worlds feel same. Visually the look different. But all the planets have same gravity, .even moon to has same gravity as other planets.This feels kind a wierd.
The M35 MAKO. This thing by far is the weakest pont of the game. Exploration is one of the main features of the game and mako is the all tarrian APC used for exporation. But the physics of the vehicle make me scratch my head, and it feels like it was not a well thought out ideaa. No uncharted world is made keeping the vehicle in mind. The mako comes as a afterthought which is became mandatory because of slow movment speed of charecters. The mako also provides Fire power for the combat. But you cannot shoot downwords or upwards. it's annoying during the combat.
By reading all this you may feel like I hate this game to the core. But as a surprice even for myself, I absolutly adore this game. Why you ask. Reason is Story, Charecters and their interactions, and the universe the bioware has created. Here the story is not about becoming the hero. No you are already a established hero. You are not the choosen one. You earned it. And now you need to save the whole galaxy with the help of your team mates. And your team mates they are also as colourfull and interisting as the main charecter. Your interactions it depends on what you choose to do. The finale will not entirely be different. Just a slight variation. The graphics still holds to this day. It looks beautyfull. The uncharted worlds have their own vibe. As told before  each one is visually different. even the skyboxes are amazingly detailed.
The lore is extreamly deep. Once you get in to it, it is not possible to satisfy your hunger to know more about this Universe. This game has flaws But it raises above all those and presents a whole galaxy of fun and belivable charecters and story. It's a must buy. Don't miss out on this galaxy touting experince that everone should enjoy.

Strategic Warfare in Europe (SWiE) is a Grand Strategy video game with comparisons to playing a more complicated game of chess.  Assume control of a nation from the Second World War with the aim to lead it to victory.  Select from seven historical start-dates.  Build army, airforce and naval units to obliterate your enemies.  Unlock research to give your units a technological edge.  Use diplomacy to recruit allies to your cause or stop the enemy recruiting for their side.   Re-enact battles from the most destructive era in human history.  Will you succeed where others have failed!?
+ Seven historical scenarios.
+ Play as Axis, Allies or Commitern.
+ Custom games allow multiple nations to be played.
+ Slow, methodical gameplay.
+ Simplified, robust mechaics.
+ Enjoyable military soundtrack.
+ Can simultaneously play more than one nation.
- Clunky interface.
- Glitched and/or broken achievments.  Production ones have to boosted in 1 (one) game!!!
- Terrible feedback.  AI turn is too fast to register.  No log to tell you what happened.
- Basic air and naval combat play second fiddle to the land war.
- Overly limited diplomacy, research and production for this genre.
- USA is unrealistically nerfed.
- Smaller nations are not scaled to be played individually.
- A few CTDs on Win10.
- Some bugs exist mostly with naval combat/production.
- Too few strategic/political events.
- Seems hardcoded to play out fairly historically.
* Basic but adequate tutorials.  Needs more info for casual players.
* Medium learning curve at the start for new players to the genre because of the dated GUI.
* Most military strategy options are available, even if they are not comprehensive.
* Limited to the European/North African theatre.  Another game covers the Pacific theatre.
* Mostly good AI behaviour.  Large nations use assets well.
* There are nukes but no V1/2s.
* Limited strategic warfare (submarine/bombers).
At the end of the day SWiE is your basic WWII grand strategy video game.  It feels more like advanced RISK than Hearts of Iron-lite.  There is little actually wrong with the game but its limited in every aspect compared with modern versions.  While I enjoyed my time with SWiE it never really felt like it got beyond second gear given my extensive experience with Hearts of Iron, the daddy of this genre.
The biggest surprise for me was the gameplay.  It flows quite well so you do not get bogged down in to much detail.  The turn-based gameplay also helps keep playing a scenario down between hours or days, instead of weeks.  Given its scenario selection, range of military units and capable A.I., SWiE is actually not far off being a recommendation - if only just.  The soundtrack too is a good point adding to the WWII ambience, reminding me of those WW2 films from the seventies and eighties.
However the game has a fair few negatives.  Scope and scale are just to limited, maybe to the point of the game being an operational wargame not grand strategy.  Graphically it shows it age at a glance.  Turn-based mechanics make combat a little hit-and-miss, with the advantage going to who has the initiative.  Amphibious operations are not as initutive as they could be. Air combat is also lacklustre compared to newer games.  While naval combat is too basic to be of much interest.  Scenarios seem stacked to play out fairly historically with hardcoded events to ensure declarations of war occur roughly on schedule.  There arent enough leaders nor are their numbers increased as play goes forwards.   But it is the lack of detailed strategic options that impact on experience; diplomacy and research are just to basic and only occasionally impact how the war plays out.
Problems with achievements persist despite given alot of attention by the developers, remaining broken/glitched even today.  Production counters for instance do not seem to update unless they pass a threshold to register.  Its biggest downfall is the lack of feedback given to players.  On faster PCs it can be easy to miss which units where destroyed for instance.  The turn-based timescale may throw gamers with experience of real-time WW2 grand strategy for there is less time to achieve aims and correct mistakes.
Ultimately this genre has moved on and SWiE shows its age.  While its not a bad game I can really only see hardcore fans being interested in this and only if they are a completionist.  You'd be better off starting with a modern incarnation from this genre.  Only bother with SWiE if you are a fan of older games or have an ancient PC or you want a war-focused grand strategy game limited to the European theatre.  I would suggest getting SWiE as part of a bundle, at extreme discount in a sale or wait to see if its offered for free.  Thats how I got my copy.  If you skip it, you wont be missing a life-altering experience.

Often called the "lost" Sonic game, which was true for a while. Time was, this was actually a reasonably hard game to come by. Unless you were the rich kid in the neighborhood, you were stuck with the plan ol' Genesis, none of this Sega CD stuff. The rumor of a Sonic Game with animated cartoon sequences and CD-quality music and TIME TRAVEL and METAL SONIC and all kinds of other crazy♥♥♥♥♥♥in it became the stuff of legend among us poor cartiridge-bound schlubs.
Even well into my adulthood, this one one of the ones that got away, swallowed deep in the halcyon dreamtime that was the early 90s, before there were Rules™ governing the attainability to the masses of what should've been flagship titles, particularly for for ill-concieved system attachments that some ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ executive thought up because they were told this Full Motion Video thing was gonna revolutionize gaming forever (kinda like how touchscreen is supposed to be the next big thing now).
So the game stayed weirdly hard to get throughout the early 'aughts. Emulation was possible but not simple until way later, and good luck tracking down an .iso, the Sega CD system BIOS, and an emulator that would actually smoosh all that crap together. eBay was also an option but that took a fair bit of money to chase down what amounted to an ephemeral youth-dream, for me anyway. Not to mention the ♥♥♥♥ing headache of purchasing and setting up the godforsaken electrical-engineering night terror that was the Sega CD. Ever seen what it takes to get that goddamned thing up and running? It's not fun. You have to, like, bolt it onto the side or maybe underneath of your Genesis, give it its own power supply, configure the hell out of it so it would boot from the CD instead of the cartridge slot but still let you play the cartridge slot, wire up the sound output to supercede the crappy Genesis sound and it just kept getting worse the more you dug into its labrynthine, pre-Google-translate manual. More than one parent probably pitched the whole thing out the front door on Christmas day when it became clear upon trying to set it up for their screaming spawn what an unholy time vampire that shitheap was going to be.
So yeah. This poor game never got played much. The slow, choking death of its parent console didn't help, and given that Sega seemed weirdly reluctant to even admit its existence (let alone re-release it for modern ANYTHING), it remained somewhere in fantasy nostalgia orbit for a lot of people far longer than most classic games starring major, world-recognized characters really should.
It was the lost, legendary Sonic Game.
Now you can buy it on Steam for the price of an expensive coffee.

Sonic CD is absolutely one of the greatest and most replayable games of the 16 bit era, and stands tall as a wonderful platformer even by today's standards. Of course, the original version didn't run half as well as this new one does, so this is Sonic CD... as you TRULY IMAGINED IT (sorry).
But in all seriousness, there's a lot to love about this game. It has multiple endings (lovingly animated in a vintage 90's style, complete with fuzziness, cels, ink, and paint); it has a deceivingly large amount of levels to trek; there are secret bonuses to unlock; the level designs have a very "sandbox" feel to them unlike anything (16 bit) Sonic had ever explored; and to top it all off, there are two soundtracks accompanying the game, each of them being incredible achievements in music in their own ways, one being upbeat and energenic and the other taking a more atmospheric (if a bit serious) approach. You can even play as a certain two-tailed friend when you finish the game at least once...
This is what Sonic was always meant to be, and is easily the best Sonic game not called "Sonic the Hedgehog 2". The fact that it got the star treatment for its appearance on modern platforms makes it that much better. Highly recommended, especially for its price; it's a steal even when it's not on sale!

Hello Survivalists all over the world!
This is my review to Savage Lands.
The developers said you get:
"Open-World Fantasy. Traverse a uniquely ominous fantasy world scattered with the remains of a lost culture. Brutal Combat. Defend yourself against an intimidating array of hostile creatures from towering giants to rabid wolves. Manage your equipment and plan your attacks wisely, or the next fight may be your last. Crafting. Create a vast arsenal of unique items, powerful armor, devastating weapons, and much more. Intuitive Build System. Construct shelters, useful items, and entire villages to improve your chances of survival in the Savage Lands. Multiplayer. Join a server to battle other Savages for resources and supremacy, or forge alliances to build a thriving village and tame the land. Carry your hard-won inventory between servers to play easily with friends. Resource gathering. Harvest natural resources, hunt the island’s fauna, and loot the remains of fallen foes to build, craft, and prosper in the unforgiving wilderness.
Character Customization. Stand out from the crowd with versatile character creation and unique armor. Band Together. Form alliances with fellow savages and end Kur’s reign over the land."
...errmm...
Whooot???!!!
Dear fellows here the truth:
a) The World of Savage Lands ends on an Island. Compare to other "open world" games, it took me roughly 20 Minutes to run from one end to the other on this island. If you feel the increased desire to run around the island, it will cost you around 2 hours of your life.
b) Brutal combat without blood, cutting limbs or heads. Far away from brutality. This game is for kids, age +6 or +7
c) Well, somewhere are hostile creatures. Roughly counted I saw max. three or four different species, devs produced twentytwo. Well, I didnt found them so far. Sorry my fault. These creatures are listlessly animated and lousy opponents. They hide well. Why?

d) Multiplayer. Well. When you find 3 players online on a good day than you have multiplayer with 3 players. This is certainly not a mistake of the developers, but indirectly already, because if they had transferred more passion and time into this game, then this game would play more people.
The game certainly includes the usual features of a survival game, but unfortunately everything feels unfinished and without passion.
A lack of sound, a lack of creatures in behavior, count and design, a lack of environment design, a lack of animations. Well, these circumstances allow a good overall performance.
If you are wealthy game collector, go for it. All others should be carefully watch vids on gameschannels, rather to spend hard earned cash in this game.
Take care guys,

This game is a pretty great rpg. The character customization is better than most games out there. If you want to make your character a buff old man with a greatsword then by all means go for it. The combat is pretty good. In my opinon it is second only to vindictus when it comes to how versitile the fighting is. You also have the ability to climb larger foes to aim for their weak spots or to hold onto them if they take flight.
Their is a pretty sizeable list of equipment as well. You could make your character look like anything from a dragon-slaying badass to a court jester. I'd give this game a 8.5 out of ten. I would have bumped it up to a 9 but the PC port didn't have two of my favorite armor sets (White hawk and swordsman) due to licensing issues.

i grew up playing games like baldur's gate, icewind dale, neverwinter nights, etc and loved all of them. pillars of eternity really did a fantastic job playing to the nostalgia of consumers like us. poe was marketed as a modernized equivalent of those titles but in the end it really fell short. i really wish steam would change their rating system to stars/points instead of a simple thumbs up/down. i would give this 2 or 3 out of 5. but because of the way it was hyped and marketed, i'll have to give it a thumbs down. you can read all the glowing reviews before me, so i'll just focus on why i just couldn't bring myself to finish the game despite being nearly at the end. i really recommend that you play divinity original sin instead.
character progression is very bland in poe. i remember agonizing over which skills to take in baldur/nwn because there are so many fantastic ones to choose from. in poe, a vast majority of skills are pretty useless and most builds will be forced into very similar paths. some levels you will be stuck with only 1-2 garbage skills to choose from. some classes and weapons are so overwhelmingly more powerful than others that you feel gimped not to use them. enemies hit so hard that you end up dumping stats like constitution. dual-wielding or two-handers are very tough to pull off without micromanagement. even if try to use different classes and builds, in the end most of your party will be in the mid/back rows shooting guns with the same exact talents. while your nearly zero dps tanks try desperately to hold the line.
magic is really what really makes rpgs well... magical. there's nothing more satisfying than nuking your enemies with massive aoe spells. in poe, spell damage is pathetic. your casters, regardless of class, will be doing crowd-control and shooting guns for damage. all this together really made combat a dreadful chore. every battle began with the same formation, same tactic, same opening crowd-control spells, etc.
on top of all that i found the story uninspiring and the recruitable npcs were painfully dull. also, their stats are terrible. in fact, you might as well just hire 5 random characters that you can build from scratch.
Will be grate in the future!

Truly the spiritual sequel to the Infinity Engine games that Obsidian promised in their Kickstarter. Anyone familiar with those old titles will be at home with the games interface straight away. Pillars of Eternity (PoE) is set in an original world where reincarnation is a major force and the gods have a great deal of influence on the lives of the people. The player enters this world, and after certain events in the early part of the game, is dragged into a massive conspiracy that threatens the entire frontier of Dyrwood. The plot is well written and very intriguing, though for spoiler reasons I won't go into it to much than I already have. There are usually multiple ways to resolve the quests and situations you come across which is always good in these kind of games, so you can feel free to be a hero or a ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ as you choose. Quite a few situations feature choices that are morally ambigious too, another aspect I appreciated.
The roleplaying system is also an original from Obsidian and you may want to play a few test runs with different character builds to get a feel for it before you settle on something. Overall I feel the system works quite well once you get used to it and I can see myself replaying the game as a different class once Im finished, using my knowledge of the systems to make a much smarter build.
The graphics are quite good, the game is done in a fixed isometric view like Baldurs Gate et al with 3D characters wandering around on pre-rendered backgrounds. The backgrouns are quite well done and feature a lot of detail. The monster and character models are also quite detailed, though for tactical reasons you will rarely be focused too closely. The music is also solid, being both epic and melancholy at the same time, reminding me a little of The Lord of the Rings theme in the overall atmosphere it creates.

Cat Meat is a fun little platformer that is below your average gamer's radar. It has a simple premise and isn't hard to play at all. For what it is, its not a bad game at all but is definitely not an award winner.
Gameplay: The gameplay is relatively simple. Your goal on each stage is to get to the exit at the opposite side of the screen opposed to where you started. All the while you have to avoid death via cliffs, water, spikes, blobby lava guys, falling meatballs, etc. To achieve this all you really do is run and jump while waiting for the correct time to do both. There are also gems you can collect that give you score but they don't do anything and might as well not be in the game. You start out with nine lives but their doesn't seem to be a way to earn more which is made worse by the fact that you can't save and that every game over means you need to restart the entire game. Other than that though the game is pretty fun.
Overall Score for Gameplay: 7/10
Graphics: The graphics are simple and cute looking. There are some nice backgrounds and the characters and foreground are pretty detailed. The effects in the game such as the meteor animations look pretty nice too.
Overall Score for Graphics: 8/10
Soundtrack: There's only two tracks in the entire game, the title theme, and the one that plays during the actual game. There alright sounding but get annoying to listen to pretty fast.
Overall Score for Soundtrack: 5/10
Sound: The sound is pretty minimal and that's okay in a game like this. There's a jumping sound effect, cannon sound effect, death sound effects, etc. It gets the the job done and makes the game feel like a classic SNES or Sega game.
Overall Score for Sound: 8/10

The Binding of Dory tells the biblical story of Dory, the short term memory loss fish that was abandoned by her parents at a very early age. Her mother and papi tried to sacrifice Dory to their mighty God that lived on land. Her parents beat the crap out of Dory, attempting to make her into sushi in order to please God, but they only caused Dory to have short term memory loss. Dory escaped her parents and forgot everything about her past. In this game you have to survive the harsh, procedurally generated  open ocean, alongside the effects of your mental state(memory loss).
Dory was raised in a fish aquarium and she has never faced the dangers of the the ocean life. She will have to battle the unknown seas with her procedurally brain damaged cells. Each brain cell has a procedural chance to be damaged, making this game unique in its own way with each new run.

Dragon's Dogma is by far the most unique Action Adventure JRPG i've experienced. Capcom did a great job at establishing a fictional European setting. You'll find yourself immersed into the world with the setting and the npc's of the game. The game is a party based game, kinda like Kingdom Hearts. You have pawns that fight alongside you. One that you create and 2 more that you can hire. The cool thing is that the 2 that you hire are actually other player pawns! Which means your pawn will also be available for hire in another player's game. They will learn more of the world, gain exp, and may recieve a gift from the person who hired your pawn! Overall Dragon's Dogma is great and deep experience with lots of memorable moments. I loved it!
Pros (+)
+ Very interesting lore
+ Creating your own character! Has a decent character creation menu with lots of options to make your character look however you like. Your character will also be in cutscenes
+ Combat! Very satisfying, fluid, and pretty
+ Combat is dynamic and deep!
+ Lots of vocations (classes) and customization of your character and your created pawn. You have all of the vocations to your disposal and can be switched at the inn at gran soren or certain npcs. Your pawn also recieves the same treatment, just not the tier 2 vocations
+ Very great sound design. Swords, daggers, and magic explosions are crisp and sound great
+ BOSS BATTLES ARE INSANELY EPIC. You're gonna find a lot of mythological creatures. You can climb and scale them too! That's how big boss battles should be done.
+ Soundtrack is beautiful with a lot of epic tunes
+ Voice acting is superb!
+ A beautiful world
+ Purchasing and collecting gear to make your character look bad♥♥♥♥♥
+ Bond/Romance system.
+ Lots of playtime and replay value
+ End game world is tough
Neutral (=) Some may enjoy this
= Travel is always on foot! Fast travel is very limited via ferrystones/portcrystals. It's about the adventure :)
= The Bond/Romance system is simple but not very fleshed out. Prepare to choose a hubby/waifu mid-game or you're gonna get some weird♥♥♥♥♥♥end game lol
= Your travel companions (pawns) will talk a lot! You can change the pawn chatter setting to "off" in the menu if you don't want them to talk
= Spikes in difficulty! Prepare yourself with curatives and level wise
= The same bandits/mobs you killed in an area will respawn after a time. (-) Those damn wolves and harpies will annoy the♥♥♥♥♥♥out of you on your travels.... (+) A positive to the respawns though is that you'll be earning exp after killing them and you won't remain stagnant level wise.
Cons (-)
- You're gonna see a lot of the same places because of your travel on foot. Travel can become tedious and feel like a chore.
- Some quest descriptions can be unclear
- Not very many romance options
- NPC escort quest
- No dialogue choices. Your character is mute and has no personality.
- No timed save files! Why?! What if I want to go back to a certain point if I messed up? (=) Well, chances are you can use the return to last checkpoint and you'll be fine but you realized that you just lost a lot of progess and have to start over. So make sure to rest at an inn or save frequently.
- No other save files, which means no multiple character slots for other family or friends to play.

An absolutely phenomenal game! I wish I had not been so poor when the Kickstarter had launched, else I would have funded this for sure. Obsidian and their team took great care to emulate the classic games like Baldur's Gate, Icewind Dale and Neverwinter Nights. Their attention to detail, story, atmosphere and art style all meshed together nicely to weave a fantastic tale! I have to say that this is probably the best money I have spent in a long time. With so many ways to play this game, many different character options, and fun challenges, it is infinitely replayable.
I do appreciate the fact that they included an achievement for soloing the game on the hardest difficulty as well :P I remember playing Baldur's Gate so much that I challenged myself to beat the game with a single character. It was fun to run through this game in that same way and get a little badge of honour for it ;)
If you like in-depth RPG's, rich back story, reading and challenging tactical combat, this is definitely the game to buy. I look forward to the next thing that Obsidian puts out. I also hope that this shows off how well a publicly funded game, dedicated to fans, can be amazingly successful and so much fun to play!
On the down side: I was hoping that the characters the backers were able to create would have been a bit more involved in the story and not just some background text that could be glazed over. I would have loved to have seen some kind of mechanic involving souls or something. If you played it, you know what I am talking about.
The game was initially a bit buggy, and in some places still is. I waited a while before playing through so that fixes could be released, as well as balances. I got stuck in a house because the icon to exit the door disappeared. No amount of pressing Tab or running around the room helped and I had to restart my game, being that I was playing on Trial of Iron.
I do greatly recommend this game for those of you that are fans of any of the old Isometric RPGs.

First of all, few disclaimers:
- I backed the PoE on KS, with more money than most of other KS pledges combined, I was really looking forward to it
- The most important one: Most of the stuff I'll criticise is my problem with this kind of approach to RPGs. They are OK, that's why if backed the game, but I enjoy different kind of mechanics in RPG more. I have my preferences and I'll review it from my PoV. But that's the problem, I know that they are done exactly as they should be, it's just not the most enjoyable approach for me any more.
- I don't like DnD(-ish) rules much, I've never did. When I was playing DnD with friends a lot, we became so agitated towards the rules that we started to create our own system
- I'm not a hardcore player, I don't min-max, I don't go into too much of a depth in combat mechanics in DnD games
* While I was waiting for my friend to check my Engrish I've thought about it a lot and I have to change to review to lower score. BTW, she ignored me so sorry for my Engrish*
The actual "review":
The game is visually stunning and gorgeous, the soundtrack is heart warming and beautiful, the writing is skillful and enjoyable to read (especially the little bits when you are looking into a soul of random people, their history). The voice overs brings the game to a whole new level, I couldn't get enough of them.
Same goes for your companions, they were both well written and had great voice overs. I really enjoyed their personality and if not I didn't have them in my party. At the end I loved all of those who were travelling with me on this journey. One small problem was that the terms of their entry to your group were cheesy most of the time. And the big problem was a bug, missing voice overs. This really broke my immersion every time it happened (which was a lot, unfortunately).
The number of quests could have been bigger and most of them didn't really do anything for me. But the ones that did had really big impact on me and after dialogues with particular characters it really made me think. I had to stop playing and just thing about stuff for a while. But if I'm completely honest, I've excepted much much much more. When there is Chris Avellone and Joshua Sawyer, there has to be  perfection in quests. And there wasn't at all:( The more I think about it the sadder I am. Great and interesting quests are integral part of epic RPG and there is only an extremely small amount of them here. The story as a whole was interesting but nothing exceptional. I really like the world and lore they created.
The mechanics are... well, better version of DnD rules, which is still not enough for me. I've played a wizard and I had to switch after 10-15 hours because I was bored. Per rest abilities are a bad game design in my opinion, so I've switched to Cypher and it was great fun. This is were Obsidian shines. They take well known approach and mechanics and they just add something small which changes the game a lot (like QTEs in JRPG style combat in SP:SoT).
The cypher is really interesting new character class, as is the Chanter. All classes have their specific abilities and then there are some common abilities and perks that everyone can get. This should give you freedom to make whatever character you'd like, but only within set boundaries.
The character progression for me is too slow, 12 levels in 70+ hours is not enough for me. And if I have to wait so long for a level up, I would like to see my characters getting more powerful than they did. The item progression is a little bit better, I've changed equip quit a bit during my play through. The addition of item enchantment helped the game. My only problem is that the unique historic items you'll find have same enchants as you can give them. I would like to see some unique enchants on them, that you can't acquire any other way. The crafting system was very streamlined, easy to get into which I really like. I don't enjoy crafting most of the time, I don't want to waste time by searching for recipes and I don't have to in PoE.
The combat is like any other DnD based combat, with few tweaks. If you liked combat in BG or IWD you'll like it here as well. If you didn't I don't think that their little evolution will help much. The combat is real time tactical, and you can pause it whenever you want to. You have up to 6 characters in your party so you have a wide variety of skills, spells, buffs and debuffs at your disposal. On higher difficulties you have to combine all of them for you to survive and enjoy the fights. The biggest problem of a combat (other then the DnDish rules:P) is the AI. More often than not, after you kill one enemy, some of your companions will just stand there and do nothing until you give them another actions.
You can be a lord of a keep which has a 15 floor dungeon underneath. You can build new rooms in it, hire guards, send companions on random adventures, imprison some special characters, build a place for shopkeepers and such. It sounds really interesting but it gets tedious after a while. The building takes too much of a time. The sleeping bonuses don't stuck as you build more of them so you get better bonuses in every inn. The shopkeepers don't have much to offer and if you want to visit all of them you will be looking at a quite a lot of loading screens because all of them have their own buildings. Because of this, the keep is basically a waste of time.
The loading at general is one of the biggest problems of the game. If you are running between areas and buildings in them, you will spend more time looking at the loading screen then actually play the game.
In conclusion:
The game as a whole is nearly what Obsidian promised it would be. It's nearly what we backers wanted. Everything is as it was in the IE times, with some nice tweaks here and there, but with weak quests for the most part. The world, graphics, music, writing, everything is beautiful. The mechanics are heaven for old school players.
The biggest problems are quests and, as always, bugs. I watched the game going through all the patches up until now (1.06) and they fixed a lot of things.
But the break out of immersion bug still remain - missing voice overs. Bad AI is also still there. The bad optimization i.e. too long and too much of loading screens breaks immersion and lowers the enjoyment of the game quite a lot.
I hope they fix these two things (maybe add some more UX tweaks like the ability go from one map to next without the need of going to the edge of the map if you visited it previously and if there is no encounter waiting for you) and I'll gladly play through it again when all of the expansions are out.
7.5/10 (I'm very sad in the end)
