One of my favourite games due to the fact that it is NOT perfect at all.
Visuals:
"Let's start with Visuals, Arisen."
At the time of the first release on consoles, the game looked reasonable. On PC, there is no change except for the draw distance and lighting/shadows. The rest looks exactly as it did. I was hoping this would be the "Snazzy Remastered Edition 2002" but nope. The game still looks fabulously disgusting so i'm happy with it.
Gameplay:
"Next up is gameplay, Ser."
It's a heavy(ish) hack and slash with verticality/grabs/scaling monsters Shadow of the Colossus style and cool hats. It feels lIke a basic single player MMO in a way. You're able to see other player's pawns which usually roam the streets and nearby roads and you may interact with them to hire them and...well that's pretty much the only online interaction it has apart from a "Magical Boss" which everyone contributes to.
The combat in this game is great but it lacks a lock-on mechanic which isn't really needed but it can help in certain situations. Apart from that, mashing buttons and stuff is pretty much all there is to it.
Sound/Music:
"Do you enjoy the sweet sounds ARISEN?"
The music in this game is nice. It definitely fits in with the atmosphere and setting however.. I do believe that there is music from the base game which is missing from the Dark Arisen version. A blend of both soundtracks would have been nice but i'm not complaining because it all sounds great. ALSO, the sound of 10+ enemies dying at once can blow your eyes out simply because of the sharp blast of soundwaves through your cranium. You'll understand if it happens.
Story:
"Shall I read you a story, Arisen?"
The story is alright. It's what you'd expect for a game like this. It has cheesy cutscenes with exaggerated facial expressions which definitely add to the tension of a scene, making the story so much more believable. I just think the story is a bit too simple, it could have more depth or a darker atmosphere to the story. It does get sad at times and rather dark but it is fairly predictable.
Conclusion:
Try it out, you've got nothing to lose but your clothes...eventually. #StoleTheKing'sWaifu
Also, you'll be hearing the titles "Arisen" and "Ser" literally every second of the game.
Thank you, Ser.

I played this until my eyeballs fell out, and now with hollow sockets I sit down to write my review.

What we have here is an honest to goodness Role-Playing Game. Not a linear, turn based mess just a step above a game of checkers in terms of action, nor is it a fussy disaster of dialogue trees with binary "good or bad" moral choices and NPC partners judging your every decision.
Dragon's Dogma's gameplay is pretty solid. Character building and leveling are slightly handicapped by the character growth system. Characters are class-based, and classes can be changed almost at any time (by visiting one of two characters), but statistics grow based on what class the character is in when they go up a level.
Often this can leave the player with a sense that they're eventually going to end up with abilities too low to finish the game, though this never really ends up being the case. Equipment is a much greater component then leveling, and even the hardest end-of-game enemies can be defeated by a sub-optimal character.
The story seems pretty standard for the first half of the game or so; a great dragon steals the player character's heart, and he or she must take up arms, grow in strength, and eventually challenge and slay the dragon. It does a good job of luring the player into a false sense of familiarity before twisting around during the final third of the game. If I offer any more details than that, it will absolutely ruin the best parts of the story, but it really is more complex than it looks on the surface.
Dragon's Dogma has a few special, almost unique features that deserve mention. The first is the grab button, which allows the player to bodily pick up and carry or throw around humanoid-sized and smaller creatures. When used on larger, giant monster type enemies, the grab button allows the characters to freestyle climb around to reach hard to get weakpoints. It is occasionally used for puzzle solving, such as adding weight to trigger switches faster by picking up a team mate, or weighing down flying enemies by dog-piling all over it.
The second feature deserving special mention is the online multiplayer, which is super-unique in that it includes the other players in a very indirect way. Early in the game, you'll be instructed to create a partner character to assist your main character, choosing their class, appearance, what general strategies they favor, and their personality. The player is also allowed to bring one or two other partner characters along, which are the main sidekick characters of other players. There's a system for rating and reviewing the partner characters before sending them back home, and a partner charactercan exist in several games at once (they don't have to disappear from your team to hang out with someone else,).
It's an interesting approach to multiplayer without any multiplayer gameplay, even if it does occasionally feel like a little bit of a chore.
The PC release of Dragon's Dogma is missing one notable special feature of the original release; two sets of special costumes based on the armor of the Griffith and Guts characters from the Berserk comic are sadly not available. However, for the list price, the PC release of Dragon's Dogma contains all existing DLC and expansion content along with the original game. The performance of the PC port is overall very good; I have only experienced a tiny handful of bugs or crashes in over 300 hours of gameplay.
Dragon's Dogma really is a game worth playing. Take up arms and fight, or flee and abandon all illusions of control.
The choice, as ever, is yours, Arisen.

My first impressions of this game are great but I will update my review as I put more time into it.
Ruin of the Reckless has a very simple gameplay loop of trying to ascend a tower by finding the key and then the elevator on each floor until you die or succeed and then repeating. While doing this you attempt to acquire weapons and equipment to help you fend of attackers so you can gather currency and experience. Money allows you to purchase items at shops as well as cards that act as modifiers to your run equipable in the lobby. Experience allows you to gather more orbs that add passive upgrades or extra attacks to your character during the run. The combat is melee focused but also has a spell system with limited charges to add range or crowd control options. The dodge roll and secondary attacks are also affected by random pickups throughout each run.

The art style and animations on the characters is very nice but the backgrounds seem very minimal and plain aside from the hub area. The game could also use an option to return to the lobby after death so you can adjust which cards you have equipped rather than needing to select ‘return to lobby’ from the menu.
All in all really enjoyable rogue-lite so far with a decent challenge!
Edit 1
After 3 hours I'm really disappointed in the weapon and equipment selection. Combat is becoming very repetitive and builds rarely seem all that different from each other. The weapons in general are extremely similar and sparse. As far as the skill cards, which act as permanent modifiers to each run, I’ve only unlocked around 4 and none of them are particularly interesting. If these complaints continue further through the game I’d have a much harder time recommending it.
Edit 2
4 hours in and I have now made it past the first boss. I’ve encountered 7 different melee weapons, 6 different spells, and 3 different sub attacks. The main problem I continue to have is that nothing feels unique and all of the runs start to blend together. Since it only took me four hours to reach this point I can’t recommend Ruin of the Reckless. Everything feels too similar and the combat has almost no nuance. I really want to like this game but it’s not looking like I’ll be able to continue playing for much longer.

Full Discloser I backed this game on kickstarter.
Ruin of the Reckless is great, it's like a melee focused Nuclear Throne with the difficulty curve of Spelunky. The reason I like the game is the card system where you basically can make your own load out. When you accomplish some feat in the game you can receive a card that you can equip in the main lobby, which can alter the game in some way. From making the floors easier to giving you different starting items, it’s pretty diverse and keeps the game interesting.
The controls are smooth, my only minor gripe is the default keyboard layout is a little clunky. But that is easily fixed with a few quick rebinds.

I really wanted to like the game, but the melee combat just does not seem to fit in with the genre.
Think of Ruin of the Reckless like Nuclear Throne with melee feel. Traverse the tower levels, kill the monsters, get the key to go to the next floor and then escape via elevator. All that until you are free! As you progress through the tower, gain levels and collect “power orbs” – the orbs that amplify your abilities / enhance your character. Think of those as of mostly passive skills: vampirism, pet follower, “more money drops. You can also gather new spells that are more like active abilities (but you can have one at a time).
•	Good item / spell variety. You can also unlock different cards that affect the gameplay: be it a new starting item / spell loadout, more enemies on levels (for harder difficulty) or more money drops to make the game easier.
•	Characters / Monster are very well-detailed for a pixel art. You can see that a lot of effort went into this.
•	The music/sound effects are decent.
•	Interesting approach to difficulty: no traditional difficulty settings per se, but a special “cards” that you can equip in the game lobby. Those cards affect the gameplay modifiers, making the game easier or more difficult: your character can have more hp, more monsters can spawn on the level, levels become easier, etc.
•	The tower that you are climbing feels like a part of its own world: the characters you meet have their own personality and it adds to immersion.
•	Challenging difficulty
•	The melee mechanics just do not seem to work. Technically, everything is there, but the process becomes pretty straightforward and repetitive: go to the monster and kill him. If he rushes – stay a bit back, wait until he attacks, find an opening and perform your own strikes. The weapons do not feel different: they have different hit patterns, but mostly the attacking process feels the same over and over again. Spells save the situation a bit, but this is not enough (charges are limited and you are holding 1 spell at a time, right?).
•	Backgrounds / Tiles are rather bland. They do the trick and they fit into the style color-wise, but overall they are not detailed well-enough compared to other characters.
•	The Game is made in Game Maker, which might not be the best choice to show so many details / monsters on the levels. My setup is I5-4670 @ 3.4GHz / 8 GB Ram / GTX 760 – the game’s fps would drop significantly when a lot of monsters appear.
I really wanted to like the game: you can see how much effort went into making it. However, the core idea of melee combat just did not seem to work well. It is done with a lot of attention, but that does not make it interesting or exciting. If we compare it to the Nuclear Throne: there, you have different weapon shooting patterns, but so do enemies. You need to get creative when dodging the attacks and shooting on the run, trying to avoid the enemy touches / bullets like a plague. On the contrary, the process here feels repetitive and not captivating: there’s some dodging involved, but most of the time (when you are not using spells) the end of the combat is the same. You need to approach the monsters and hit them in melee. You don’t care much about the environment / hiding like you did in Nuclear Throne. The challenge of masterfully evading and keeping the distance is gone here, and while it seems like a minor thing, it changes everything. Because eventually the ending of every melee combat is the same: you need to approach the enemy and hit him.
From what I've played so far, definitely worth the purchase and though it may be hard to complete, you get a great sense of achievement when you go up the levels in the tower.

Been having a lot of fun with this throughout its development.
Combat is fast and fun. It's really satisfying to weave through enemies, methodically taking them out in order of current threats. This does get harder to do on the higher floors though, as the enemies will quickly overwhelm you. You'll need a plan of action for that.
This is a pretty hard game. But it gets easier as you figure out the best ways to take out everything. Or you can just dash up to them and hit them. That works too. If you're bored of melee, there are various spellbooks which can offer you ranged, AoE or other attacks. They don't have any cooldowns, but they can only be used a limited amount of times before you need to find a new spellbook.
There's a unique way of "leveling up" that I like as well.
Rather than getting a guaranteed upgrade of some sort when you have enough exp, you simply get another slot to hold an orb. Orbs float around the tower, each offering a random power up, such as vampirsm, alchemy, pet affinities, or agility. The orbs are fragile however, and will explode violently if hit by a single attack from you or an enemy. While your foes won't target the orbs intentionally, they may unintentionally blow one up while targetting you.
Don't get too confident when you have a lot of items you feel are powerful, though. Just look at the game's name...

I'm a huge fan of Chaos Theory and consider it to be one of the best stealth games in history for its design. When Conviction came out I played it only to be blown away at how everything that was great about Chaos Theory had been thrown away. While Double Agent (game prior to Conviction) was much more streamlined, it still contained many things from Chaos Theory that made it work. Conviction was such a mess that I didn't even make it halfway through the game before I dropped it and went back to CT. I had very low expectations for Blacklist, but for once I was glad I was wrong.
First off, lets make it clear that Blacklist is NOT Chaos Theory. If you wanted Chaos Theory then you should play Chaos Theory; nevertheless Blacklist brings a game that encourages a kind of stealth that suits the more fast moving hard hitting gameplay, tons of gadgets, and good old coop and spies vs merc modes. As a game I got 16 hours out of just the single-player content in BL.
While things like the mark and execute system from Conviction return, it acts as more of an option than a must use tactic like it was in conviction. In addition to this, non-lethal options are much more common place and maps are open to more tactical options (though still nowhere near CT's giant interconnected maps, nevertheless its still a far cry from Convictions linear design).
There are alot of things I wish Blacklist did but in the end I found myself charmed (to say the least) by the game's competence in what it did do. As long as you acknowledge that BL will not be CT you'll have a great time and hope that the next game, Ubisoft will bring back the detailed light and sound meter, along with Michael Ironside as Sam's Voice Actor.

Middle-earth: Shadow of Mordor is an action/adventure game in the style of the ‘Batman Arkham Series’ but in the Middle-earth world.
You play as a ranger who is possessed by an Elf (how this happens is the story, so no further spoilers in this review). This means you have the powers of a ranger and an Elf.
The story is very well told and is a sort of prequel to the Lord of The Rings. In the game, you must complete different quest to follow the story. As I have told the fight system is in the style of the Batman series and is very well done and gives a lot of satisfaction. You play with sword/dagger/bow so you can imagine that the game is very bloody with impressive finishing moves. The more you play and complete quests and tasks the more points and experience you gain to level up your character.
The game also has what is called the ‘nemesis system’. This is something unique to this type of game. It means that by the way you play captains and war chiefs (they are bosses in the game) are randomly generated and climb up in the ranks of Sauron’s army. It’s your task to kill them or to turn them over to your side.
The graphics, music and sound effects are very impressive. I can confirm that the game supports ultrawide resolutions and the 21:9 aspect ratio. I tested with 2560*1080.
In game, everything is 21:9 but the movies are letterboxed.
I have bought the premium edition with all the DLC. Having played the DLC I would not recommend buying these separately.
I highly recommend this game, it’s a lot of fun and very satisfying to play.

Single Player:
As I've played more and more, I've gotten quite used to how the game plays and have managed to easily beat all of the infiltration levels on Perfectionist difficulty and mastered Ghost in 3 of the 4 levels (one of the levels is from the DLC content). I say this because at first I felt the controls were not so fluid feeling, but by playing a bit more I got used to the controls. It's actually been a great experience so far. If you're a Splinter Cell die hard fan like me, then you should definitely get this game if you were like me and just didn't because they hadn't got Ironside to make Sam Fisher the character I've come to love, or if you just don't have it yet for whatever reason. It actually feels and acts sort of like Conviction, but also resembles a lot of earlier Splinter Cell games to the extent of making the game reward the truly stealthy tactics more-so than going into a run-n-gun playstyle (you get higher scores if you're a ninja). It's a really nice blend of all of the Splinter Cell games so far into one jam packed set of awesome stealthiness.
Spies Vs. Mercs
The multiplayer is also surprisingly still somewhat alive as I've gotten into several matches even though I just got the game 3 days ago. Granted, I haven't gotten very far into the multiplayer Spies vs. Mercs, so I am not sure of the level of cheaters/hackers/aimbotters etc on it, but I can say that it is fun even if you get killed a lot because you don't know what's going on at first and you suck at being a merc like me. It also feels great to be a spy and get a kill. And in this game, unlike the earlier spies vs. mercs, your chances of getting kills as a spy are MUCH higher. You can actually melee kill from the front of the merc in this one. And you do have a weapon of somesort, as well as gadgets. The interesting starting classes for the spy and mercs come equipped with decent ranges of playstyles. So, with a decent team, you can win games on either side of the playing field. Overall I definitely feel this should be fun for most everyone as long as they enjoy the game enough to feel like it's awesome even when they die :P Although, I am a little wary of the hacking/cheating level into higher spies vs mercs rankings because I've read some things about that, but hopefully it's not like some people like to say. A guy can be hopeful right? Either way, the single player is a blast, and with a friend the multiplayer of any game is always better. :)

I suppose the best way I could describe how I feel about this game is probably by giving the pros and cons...
Pros
For me personally I enjoyed to hop around in mordor killing orcs and learing about the orc hierchy with the nemesis system.
The combat is fun especially with the shield bearers and berserkers and lets not forget the ranged units to give you a heck of a time when you think you're being awesome :)
If you're going to kill a captain or warchief, you have to be at least somewhat sneaky about it or you end up with half the camp on you.
The nemesis system is fairly interesting.
The orc chatter is quite entertaining sometimes and it's cool how their grumbles and boasts ususally keep up with the current events.
Some of the captains and warchiefs are a pain to kill.
The different skins are fun to try out, and mess around in.
There are many more pros beyond what I have here in this list that you can probably find in other reviews but basically this game will keep you entertained at least until you beat it and probably a while afterwards.
Cons
I think it's kind of silly that often the captains you've killed come back multiple times swearing revenge when you did something obviously leathal to them.
The stealth is really easy most of the time and the orcs on watch must be blind, it's pretty bad, think something like  vanilla World of Warcraft (I say vanilla because I don't know how it is now) style of stealth, except you stay stealthed when you backstab and are just crouched a little instead of transparent.
The combat is way too easy in the majority of situations, the varient types of orcs do make it a little harder, but once you get it down it can get a little boring.
The story line was really, really hard to follow, put quite simply you'll get the jest of the story of Celebrimbor and Talion but not in a way that makes complete and total sense, or rather in a way that skips a lot of what, I at least, think is important material for a good story and to make one flow properly.
For all I know there could be more cons as well, but those were just my main gripes with the gameplay.
All in all this game was definatly worth the 10 bucks I paid for it, though be forewarned, you need to download 42,1 GB which took me 10 hrs at about a constant 1.6-1.5 mbps. Also, I advise you to mess around a bit while you complete the main missions, don't just run through them and then feel like you're done, the nemesis system and branding orcs, sending them out and about, gives you a ton of opportunites to entertain yourself, while leaving a few main missions out there and taking a break every now and then will keep you interested. If you catch this game on sale for sure get it, and even if you don't you're getting probably more than your moneys worth for only 20 bucks on this purchase.

I was hoping by the time this released that the game would have some way of easing in how to improve at the game, and that it would be pretty awesome. Instead I'm greeted with a "Just hop into a server, and good luck." Which really doesn't work out when you have one experienced player from before release, or just a flight combat veteran dominating primarily the rest of everyone else due to inexperience.
There wasn't a moment that it felt like being outside of Jet mode served purpose to battling as much as it does to make really sharp turns around obstacles to try and shake off anyone on your tail. I hate to see this game does not refresh the server listings properly with incorrect player counts, maps, and modes as I found myself many times joining a server that said it was in TDM mode with 11/12 players as a regular DM with just myself in it.
Under the menu I wasn't too surprised that there isn't many graphical options being this came from a small team. That didn't become an issue for me as I had solid performance all the way through on a GTX 760. At least you can rebind all your keys from what it seemed, but that won't help much when you're trying to get into this game.
It's just that I could of played War Thunder or Star Conflict for free and end up having a better time.
I wouldn't pick this up unless you're a hardcore fan of flight combat because the learning curve is really high.

Einmal getestet und BANG!!!
Hatte Miscreated als eines von mehreren Games aus einem HB-Bundle erworben. Da ich zigtausende Games im Backlog habe, checke ich manchmal 10-20 an einem Tag ab und ich muss zugeben das meiste davon wandert innerhalb von einer Minute in den Müllordner.
Im übrigen bin ich so gar kein Freund von MP, spiele fast nur Singleplayerspiele offline.
Nun das hat sich mit MIscreated gewaltig geändert, ein einziger Schritt in diese geniale und wunderschöne Welt und es war um mich geschehen. Was für eine Prachtgrafik und das alles sehr flüssig. Der wahre Star des Spiels ist nicht das PvP-Gemetzel, dem ich sowieso nicht viel abgewinnen kann und auch nicht die Mutanten die meist eh zu dumm sind um ernsthaft Widerstand zu leisten, nein es ist die geniale Grafikengine von Crytek die dem Spiel zu wunderbaren Landschaften und im Zusammenspiel mit der realistischen Beleuchtung zu einer enorm stimmigen Athmosphäre verhilft.
Wer mal im aufsteigenden Bodennebel durch den Sumpf gewandert, bei Sonnenaufgang im Gebirge geklettert oder auch nur in der Dämmerung durch den dichten Wald geschlichen ist, der weiss wovon ich hier rede, es ist einfach überwältigend.
Und an jeder Ecke gibt es in der recht großen Karte was zu sehen, ob man per Tauchgang oder Kraxeleien Höhlen plündern will, ein abgestürztes Flugzeugwrack samt Leichen entdecken oder durch ungenutzte Atombunker kriechen will, überall ist was zu finden und sei es nur ein versteckter weil nur per zu aktivierendem Aufzug erreichbarer Level in einem Hotel in der Hauptstadt. Man kann ganze Wochen mit der Erkundung verbringen und findet irgendwie immer noch was neues, zumal immer mal wieder neue Gebiete freigeschaltet werden. Selbst Motorboote sind vorhanden mit denen man die Flüsse und das Meer befahren kann.
Klar kommt dann auch noch der Storypart dazu, wobei Story bedeutet das man überleben muss, egal wie. Das ist eigentlich nicht so schwer, denn Nahrung und Wasser gibts ja reichlich in den Häusern. Nur blöd das Banditen und Monster da oft auf einen warten.  Da hilft es natürlich bewaffnet zu sein, am besten noch ein Auto zusammenzubasteln, denn damit kriegt man jeden Mutanten klein.
Lustigerweise kann man bei MIscreated sehr gut sehen zu welcher Sparte Spieler die Leute so gehören, da gibts die reinen PvP-ler, die nur glücklich sind wenn sie so viele Mitspieler wie möglich killen können. Aber auch regelrechte Logistiker die ihen Basenbau vorher am Reißbrett planen und die Teile dafür zusammensuchen gibt es. Auch als Wandersimulator ist das Spiel geeignet und so kommen auch verkappte Naturforscher zu ihrem Recht wenn sie Rehe, Wölfe oder Eichhörnchen jagen.
Ich hänge nun schon seit mehr als 100 Stunden an dem SPiel, ein Wert den ich nicht so oft in so kurzer Zeit erreiche und es macht immer noch Spaß! Wenn ich mich durch Hayward schlage und bei jedem Schritt schauen muss das mich weder Mutanten noch PvP-ler erwischen, dann ist das schon ein geiles Feeling. Werde jetzt mal langsam mit dem Basenbau beginnen, das einzige was ich noch nicht gemacht habe. Mal sehen wie ich damit klarkomme.

So, I've been playing PC games for years now, its 2017 and I'm bored, looking around for something fun to play. Looking at my library I remember I bought ME 1 and 2 about a year ago when they were on sale for 4.99 each. I've always been reticent about playing legacy games as they tend to be getting high reviews from people with nostalgia tinted glasses on and not nearly as good compared to more modern titles.
Mass Effect, howeve, holds up with the best of them. In fact, I'd say there are few modern RPGs that are anywhere near the experience.
There are only two things that give away this game's age: The graphics and the irritating infrequency of autosave locations (seriously, you're going to want to save FREQUENTLY). In terms of gameplay and worldbuilding however, I'd argue that many modern titles have yet to catch up.
The best way to describe it is that the developers seem to have thought of everything. Somehow they make squad based combat feel fluid and intuitive. The maps are easy to navigate, you will never find yourself lost. The weapons only can overheat, there is no irritating ammo system. There ARE weapon upgrades but they are class specific and can easily be transferred to a different weapon when you find a better one. The story progression is both exciting and intriguing, and kept me glued to my screen for hours on end just to push through and find out what happens. \
TL;DR, everything just... works. Really well. Its a fun, fast paced sci-fi RPG with some of the best squad based combat that you will ever encounter and a story that keeps you on the edge of your seat.
So what are you waiting for, buy the game already.

I bought the game, having known about it a while, and waited until I saw some polishing and patching before plunging as I tend to get into these kinds of cRPGs and play the heck out of them.
Note: This is as close to the old Baldur's Gate series, Icewind Dale series and Torment that you're going to get today. So this game should strike a cord with all the people that are nostalgic for these older games. Having gone through the game, the game is quite similar to these, with a long unraveling story line that is pretty good. All of these games are rather linear, as in, the story doesn't change as you play or alter the outcome (the way the old Fallout series did). But it plays very similar, the story depth and length is similar.
Overall, a good game. I have about 80+ hours now. I've played through twice at this point. The game is replayable. While the story doesn't change, how you play it can. I enjoyed going through with one party, and then re-doing it with a completely different party. And will do it again with a third party soon, just to experience that too.
There are expansions coming for this game, so it will grow and give you even more do experience soon.

Every character can be shaped into whatever you want. Wizards can wear plate and be tanks. Fighters can be naked and beat up stuff. There is not ultra-class that takes the cake (Cleric, for example, in the older D&D games). You can play solo, or in a party. Lots of fun difficulties to do this with too making it a challenge.
I definitely feel like this game was worth the admission price (I bought it for $30 or so here on Steam). I don't say that often for a lot of games.

Reasons to love this game:
1) The writing is very well done - the choice of words and eloquent images painted make reading what amounts to at least a novel's worth of text enjoyable.
2) The artwork. I have a decent rig with an HD monitor, and I have to say that I was blown away by some of the scenes in the game. I have seen it running at lower resolutions, and it still looks excellent.
3) Character building. Not just the writing, but the sheer abundance of choices that you have in customizing your character.
4) The novelty of the new classes. The cipher and chanter were great classes to play and required a different playing style than I was used to. I also loved reading the names of the chants.
5) The music. It was flowery, subtle, intense, and brooding where necessary. The composer chosen for this game is quite an artist.
6) Nostalgia. I, like many gamers from the 80s and 90s, I suspect, have many great memories about sitting in front of their computers for hours and hours playing these types of games. Every choice was agonized over and the characters felt like people you knew by the end. This game evokes that same feeling, with a 21st century nod to the significant improvements in graphics and sound.
However, I have to ding this game for the following:
1) The Kickstarter "perks" in-game. The backstories and characters were excellently written and fun to read, but I felt like I was reading a plaque stapled to the character's forehead instead of getting insight into the character. If those characters were woven into the game (there were murderers, pirates, saviors, and all other sorts), this game would have probably been my favorite released in recent memory. The characters did not react to the PC at all, and there was nothing you could really "do" with your insight into their lives, minds, and hearts.
2) The end-game of the plot. While the first 3/4 of the game had a very intruiging plot - souls that exist across time and are reborn, the slow reveal of the PC's involvement with the main villain - the last 1/4 of the game felt like I was having a philosophy debate shoved at me in quite a ham-fisted manner. While you can ultimately choose how you feel about the subject matter of the game, as is a staple of this type of game, the writer's stance on the subject was quite blatant and made the game feel a little less "free".
3) Some of the voice acting - in some scenes where you could tell the character was supposed to be outraged or feeling other strong emotions, the voice acting came across as a bit flat. While, overall, the voice acting was great, the few instances of flat performances pulled me out of the game temporarily.
Overall, this game is a must-play for those of you that loved Baldur's Gate or Planescape: Torment, or just enjoy a game where you can pick your own path and play the type of character that you love to play with as few instances of being shoe-horned into a specific path as possible.

I rarely take the time to write reviews for games and in fact I believe this is one of the first or THE first review I've bothered to write about on Steam. The only reason I'm taking the time to do this is to warn potential buyers. I bought this game a year ago. I bought the 4 pack so that me and my friends could all play together. The game looked cool and seemed like a cool concept and though I've always had some hesitation about buying into Early Access games, I saw the potential for this game. When my friends and I played this game at the time it was barely functioning. While I could play, I found the gameplay to be absolutely bare bones with little to do. Two of my friends on the other hand could not even run it properly without it crashing every half hour. Their hardware is not bad enough that this game should do that. I believe that the issues they experienced were due to poor optimization. The poor gameplay combined with the poor performance left a bad taste in all our mouths but we figured that the game was in very early access and while I can't fathom why any developer would want to release their game in such an unfinished state to the public, we hoped that this game would improve. We tried playing it again some months later and sadly it was the same story. No improvements had been implemented as far as any of us could tell and my friends who had gotten new machines were still plagued with stability issues.
Fast forward to now. I decide to check the updates on this game, figuring that it had been some time and I see a post from the developer that explained that they were working on another project as of July and attributed that project for the reason why development on this game had stalled. We're near October and no word for the developer on the steam front has shown up. Honestly this game shouldn't have been allowed to be put up on the store. It allowed the dev team to make money which most likely went toward other projects. They preyed on the good will, hope, and ignorance of their customers and will continue to do so in all likely hood. This game should be taken down from the store and the developers should be called out on their poor business practices.
I know that in their post they said they had contractual obligations they needed to meet for other projects and implied that this game was more of a "passion project" but that doesn't change the fact that they accepted money from other people not for a product they had but a product they promised and with the little to no progress they've made in delivering that product I cannot recommend that anyone give these guys any more money.
TL;DR:
Don't buy this game! It's just a trap for the developer to take your money and use it for other projects. This is pretty much abandon-ware that they are hoping to make some quick cash off of and will only update it when the fanbase gets riled up enough to scream bloody murder. Save yoru cash.

Ruin of the Reckless is a fantastic game built on a unique premise. It ends up as a simultaneously maddening and satisfying challenge. The game favors those who are reckless, willing to try different styles of gameplay, and move fast. It’s got a unique art style, great characterization, a retro feel, and enough to keep you interested and likely coming back to the tower many times.
To read the full review, check out Gamer's Almanac:

Ruin of the Reckless is a rogue-lite game developed by Faux-Operative Games. RotR succeeds in offering fast paced action with great levels of build variety.
Graphics
_______
While lacking in variety in some cases, RotR drives home that 16-bit feel with a fairly vibrant color palette, smooth animation, and some fun character / enemy designs. While progressing up through the tower, the environments do get a bit redundant, but it's never enough to take away from the game overall.
Music & Sound
_______
Kicking off with an extremely catchy theme performed by SLIME GIRLS, the games music continues to be catchy and fairly unobtrusive through the game. Sounds are also well placed throughout and provide a satisfying thump when attacking enemies or utilizing spells lending well to the overall feel of the game.
Gameplay & Game Feel
_______
The controls handle well especially when utilizing an Xbox One or Xbox 360 controller. Character movement is responsive and in the event of most deaths I couldn't find myself blaming the game or the controls, just myself for making the wrong decision or moving at the incorrect time. The dashing mechanics are very similar to what you'd find in something like Hyper Light Drifter, and combat feels very similar to a melee version of Enter the Gungeon. The game handles well, and the variety in enemies provides enough of switched up experience, especially when fighting certain enemies in different combinations as you ascend the tower.
With a multitude of weapons and orb combinations to choose from, each run feels in its own way "unique" so to speak. Some weapons do feel a bit more powerful than others, and I believe this is more of an issue with some enemies being very difficult to tackle with certain weapon types over others. Overall I'd say the variety in weapons, magic, orbs, and trinket combinations yields a fairly unique experience each time you die and respawn in the tower.
Overall
_______
While I'm not normally a huge fan of rogue-likes in this style, I found myself enjoying my romp through RotR while not feeling exhausted each time I would die and have to restart. The gameplay doesn't particularly stand out amongst the pack of similar titles, and the environments can lack variety, but it's satisfying and fun to replay. If you're a fan of games such as Enter the Gungeon, or Binding of Isaac, I'd strongly recommend picking this up!

Simply incredible. This is twitch gaming reborn. Ludicrously polished from concept to execution. Take an incredible art style (like Hawken done right) and pair it with blisteringly fast and fun gameplay and you've got one hell of a combination. The vectors look and feel amazing and what the weapons lack in originality they make up for in balance and punch. As you may have already been let on by other reviews this game is VERY hard to pick up and play but your patience will be more than rewarded. While I've played enough twitch shooters to navigate the maps and avoid incoming fire easily enough I initially simply could not figure out the homing and dismissed it as near-useless. Game takes a while to get good at and yields a very satisfying experience once you get there.
Tribes Ascend is a decent comparison, but doesn't really do the game justice. Even though they both emphasize combat in all dimensions, the SPEED and variety of ways you can move in SV is what really sets it apart from any other shooter. It appears lag-free (playing from NA), runs perfectly, and provides competitive visuals that do well to compliment the mechanics. Gameplay can be VERY fast and twitchy, with varying skill floors across the levels. Suicide (crashing) is penalized in most game modes, and the combination of level design and mobility make it very difficult to play as a camper. At the same time, there is opportunity for sniping sprees, depending on the map, provided you consistently change location to avoid being spotted out. In general though, you can expect a need to be constantly moving, and those able to navigate tight spaces at high speeds while taking shots at other fast movers results in a very high skill cap for the game.

Ohhhhhh, Miscreated.... What things it's done for me. The thing about Miscreated is, yea you can do it alone, but if you have friends that have it, it's WAYYYYY better. My friend convinced me to buy Miscreated at the beginning of summer, and oh my what things we have done. Even though I only played with one friend, it was still a blast none the less. Miscreated has pretty much carried me through the summer and strengthened many bonds. What started out as people I ran into and asking for a can of soup have become some of my best friends. Through the many many nights my friends and I have stayed up till 4-6 am in the morning, it has all been worth it.
I usually go by a rule with games, for every dollar I spend, I at least want 1 hour of playtime. And while my ~80 hours doesn't look like much compared to other games I have like CS:GO and Rust with ~600 hours each (BTW great games, if you haven't bought them already, look into them) the hours I spent on here were some of my funest. Miscreated is very weird in the way that you don't need to be stacked to have fun. Whether it was running around towns ♥♥♥♥ing up freshies with our hundreds of ammo, or just running around 'usting' (our term for kicking) geared kids. The strange thing is, me and my friends can almost recall every fun moment we had with the game, all dating back to the beginning of summer 2016.
As a conclusion to this review, I just wanted to say how much this game has done for me, if I haven't shown you already. Just a recap, it carried me through summer, we stayed up many nights playing it, we met awesome people on the way, and we had so many good times with it. And the last thing I said, which is very important to me, was strengthening bonds with my friends.  The reason this is so important you ask? Because I had moved 3-4 years prior to today, and me and my old friends hadn't talked for the majority of that time. All until I first made contact with one of them while they were having a party. We met on Skype and I didn't really think much of it, I just thought it was a one time thing and then we were going to stop talking. But it most definitley wasn't. They added me on Skype and we chatted every now and again, but it was very awkward at first. We moved to Discord and even though I was pretty close with most of them, some of them I barley knew. That was until Miscreated came into my life, and those friends I barley knew have become some of my closest friends. Anyways, long story aside, this game is amazing, and it is definitley worth it's $20 price tag.
-Thanks "Ratio" for the inspiration to write my long review again.

Baldur's Gate.
Baldur's Gate II: Shadows of Amn.
Baldur's Gate II: Throne of Bahl.
These, particularly the last two, forever exist in my experience as high pinnacles of storytelling and gaming. When I first played them in my early teens I had no idea what D&D was. I did not know the 2ed Rules. I cheated extensively just to continue the story and interact with my companions. The Baldur's Gate series set the bar for any and every future RPG, and for the most part, set it too high.
At times my nostalgia and heart have been tickled by others... By Mass Effect, by Neverwinter Nights and its expansions, and Dragon Age II (yes... the second one). However, nothing has ever given me half a whiff of what BGII did; to the point that I bought BGII again on GoG just to be able to play it on a modern OS.
Until Pillars of Eternity.
The engine? Basically the same. The character details rarely mattered; the portraits and interactions always did. PoE isn't like Skyrim or Mass Effect: You won't be spending 2-3 hours designing your protagonist. Instead, you'll choose a look and then actually step into their shoes through choices and dialogues.
The settings and backgrounds range from "Yeah, this really is a dirt road through nowhere" to "Bawls, that is a beautiful set-piece!" More than once I stopped or backtracked to look at a particular sculpture again, or re-loaded just to get another glimpse before a fight. There are some stunning places and things to be at and look at in this game.
The characters are strong. By that, I mean they are consistent, different from each other, and overall endearing. I have not tried them all (I, apparently, didn't find all of them through my first complete playthrough!), but the ones I eventually settled on were living, breathing beings with their own pasts, desires, and beliefs. Not every one is an enigma wrapped in a riddle wrapped in a bow -- but not every single one needs to be.
The major fights in this game, as I played on Normal, were on the easy side with the exception of the dragons.
The story was long. Much longer than I thought -- both to my delight and occasional frustration. There are weaker parts and stronger parts, but the pressure of the main plot only felt light once or twice. The mystery is well played, and I didn't see the ending coming at all; though (reminiscent of other RPGs) the final few acts felt somewhat underwhelming. When I replay it (and it's definitely a "when") I'll have a much narrower idea of what I want to do, and I believe I'd even enjoy one more playthrough after that.
The game's mechanics are easy to get a jist of, but too ambiguous to really min-max on your first go through. A second playthrough is warranted based on what options you missed by 1 stat or 1 skill alone.
Who will like this game? Anybody and everybody who enjoyed the Baldur's Gate series. Anybody who likes RPGs with squad-based micro-management and has the patience to play a game like this through (60 hours was my minimum, though I think you could squeak by your first time with 40-50 hours).
It may only be 85% of what Baldur's Gate II: SoA + ToB is to me, but to be likened to my personal pillar of gaming is high praise from me since so many others claimed BG2's heritage and didn't just underdeliver, but fell painfully short. PoE is a good game, and will be a good game whenever I play it again and again.
It's the type of game I may not play for months, or years, but when I do it will fulfill a very specific need: The need to immerse myself in a different world and with fully formed characters to go on an adventure.
Heartily recommended.

I have played Baldurs Gate, Icewind Dale, Fallout, Torment, as well as Neverwinter Nights 1&2. I have played just about every obsidian game that has come out as well, with my favorites by and far being NWN2 Storm of Zheir, and Fallout: New Vegas.
However when I play this game, it is (to my surprise) boring. The problem is a vast majority of the game is combat, tedious number rolling save-scumming low damage limited spells combat. There are no instant-kill abilities or vibrant graphic spells to break up the monotony such as Torment, it is largely just putting a tank or two at a bottleneck and picking apart packs of monsters. It almost feels that most enemies exist of the sake of existing. There are other things I dislike about the combat (especially the engagement system) but I will save my figurative breath.
As with any Obsidian game the dialogue is well-written, although I find that a majority of  dialogue choices loop to the same outcome. Most quests end up with you fighting the person regardless if you want to or not, a vast majority of people are more than willing to just charge in and die to a group of random strangers for no discernible reason instead of going to jail or opting to run away. It seems most "persuasive" options involve threatening people until they tell you what you probably already know.
That being said I don't really enjoy this game, it holds a lot of potential that just isn't realized and ends up executing ideas poorly. Obsidian has an undeniable talent for writing, but they are just not up to balancing a game. The leveling system is a mess of must-have or don't-touch abilities, and even with a 6 person party it just feels completely underwhelming.

I still remember the days when I would play DW 3 back on my uncle's PS2 more than ten years ago. Comparing the two, it was mad repetitive and didn't teach you much about the actual history. Now it does. As someone who constantly re-reads the Romance of the Three Kingdoms classics, I really appreciate how much they abide by the history now compared to before. Of course, the actual history is a lot sadder and for people who have no idea what's going on, they might wonder why their side in Story mode still "loses" when they won the battle. And another nice thing they did to make things not as repetitve was giving you the option between 3-4 characters each stage of Story mode.
Combat wise, I like the Switch system, you effectively get to use two weapons per battle. That definitely mixes things up compared to previous DWs. Ambition mode is like Xtreme mode in past DWs. Only difference was that in the past Xtreme modes, your playthrough was done once you died. I remember how brutal that was, even as Lu Bu. But here, if you lose a campaign, you don't get penalized for it.
And if you want a challenge, then don't play beginner/easy/normal difficulty. The real game begins beyond.
As for cons, this game is a massive time dump. Moreover, I highly recommend you get a controller like I did, makes life a lot easier and it'll be a good investment since you'll use it for other games as well. Framerate was a little shaky for me and I think graphics could have been done better (though honestly, who's looking at the trees when you got a thousand soldiers to hack through?). Also since I actually like to read through the storyline on the loading screen, the lines go by too slow...But yeah, nothing major to worry about.
Overall: 8.5/10

We'd reached the end of a particularly stressful journey.  Harpies hounded us along the way with goblins joining in later, and there was no end to the traps that met us along the path.  As one could imagine, it was quite a relief seeing our destination so close, lit up in the night as if it were a beacon of hope.  But as we passed the ruins of what seemed have formerly been part of the town toward which we were traveling, I spotted a figure standing next to torch.  They seemed to be standing by the road, almost as if they were waiting for something or hurt, but there was only one of them in sight.  Thus, I dropped my guard and walked ahead of the group, hoping to interact with them.  When I was close enough, however, before I was even able to realize exactly what was going on, the figure lunged at me, irritated and surprisingly powerful, nearly ending my journey just before it would meet its proper conclusion.  Fending them off, they faced the light, and as they did it was clear that this was a member of the undead.
This was probably the first encounter in Dragon's Dogma that really stuck out to me.  While it may not seem like much, that encounter lends itself well to the game's emphasis on proper lighting.  Should you follow the game's suggestion, night will be suitably dark, and beings off in the distance will be obscured by the darkness.  While this may seem trivial, it was a lot of what made the game work as well as it did for me, and I honestly would not recommend playing any other way.  Largely because nothing about the encounter above was scripted or premeditated.  The zombie
there by default, but that experience was particularly unique due to how information was presented and acknowledged.
That is just one of various examples of why Dragon's Dogma stands out as a solid Open-World Action RPG in a world sorely lacking in them.  Solid ones specifically, that is.
The gameplay in DD revolves mostly around team building and synergy.  While there is no multiplayer in Dragon's Dogma, the game is built around the Pawn System.  Pawns are NPCs that are created by other characters and sent to aid other players.  You can have up to 3 pawns, and these pawns can be any of the available classes in the game, of which there are several.  While it's not required, the key to success in Dragon's Dogma is making a team that works well and balances off of each other.
For instance, a team of four Sorcerers may have immense damage potential and crowd control, but against a group of sturdy enemies or something particularly fast, they may quickly find themselves with a horrible case of death.  Meanwhile a group consisting of a healer, a tank, and some DPS will fare far better.  On average.  One thing to remember about this game, and to keep in mind, is that this is an Action RPG.  Don't feel the need to be tied to definites, try things out.  I've personally had a lot of fun just playing with my personal pawn and no other members- it's challenging but it certainly makes for a different experience.
Speaking of classes, while some of the classes are off-shoots of others, the classes themselves tend to be particularly diverse.  If you're a Strider, you'll be zooming across the battlefield, damaging as many enemies as you can as quickly as you can, and dealing damage to larger enemies from atop them.  As a mage, you'll heal your cohorts, attack with powerful elemental magic, and aspect your team's weapons to exploit enemy weaknesses (which, compared to other games, makes for one hell of a boon).  As a Fighter you'll be grabbing the enemy's attention, soaking damage, and occasionally springing your teammates off of your shield to attack airborne enemies.
For the most part, these classes feel unique and don't end up feeling like each other until you unlock the hybrid classes.  Changing classes is no big deal either and is encouraged, as you can change simply by going to an inn and class progress is saved upon changing.  So if you want to try out any and all of the classes, feel free.  This is an easier option than making a new character, as the game doesn't really support multiple characters natively.
As a port, Dark Arisen is surprisingly competent for something came at such a short notice.  Running at 1080p+ out of the box and supporting 60 FPS natively when the original release didn't.  Overall, on this GTX 970, the game runs as smooth as butter, which, having played the original release, can be pretty breathtaking.  Probably the biggest advantage that the PC release has, though, is that you can finally return things to the way they were meant to be and replace the DA theme with Into Free by Bz.
Seriously.  Do it.  It makes the make 100% better.

The second in the Tex Murphy games, Martian Memorandum sees you once again as PI Tex Murphy, down on your luck despite your success with your previous case, Mean Streets.  You need a job, and you need it soon.  Lo and behold, Marshall Alexander, CEO of the TerraForm Corporation, hires you to find his daughter, who was abducted -- and something "else" . . .
Gone is the dialogue puzzle of the previous game, which disappointed me a bit.  There are times when you need to do more than just talk to people in these screens, such as give them items in order to move the story along, and I didn't realize this until I read a guide.  Granted, it's entirely possible that such was clearly mentioned in the manual that would have come with this game if you bought it hard-copy (in 1991).
Also removed from this game is the driving mechanic from Mean Streets, which was difficult at best and caused you to miss out on a lot of the previous game's flavor.  Another mechanic taken out is the side-scrolling shooting gallery.  I am pleased that neither of these mechanics made it into Martian Memorandum.  That said, the game then becomes rather linear, but it's still a pretty neat story even today.
People who are genuinely interested in seeing what constituted gaming in the early dawn of the industry should have this in their library.  That's the only reason I do.  I grew up in the 90s, and there's nothing wrong with taking a trip down Memory Lane.

I got this game at a huge discount from its usual price, so it hardly cost me anything at all. But the time I spent playing it - 7 hours - is time I wish I could get back now.
To call the game mediocre is being generous. Thinking back on my standards around the time this game came out, I would have found it lackluster and tedious even back then. The dialogues are a meandering choose-your-own-adventure that sometimes matter and sometimes don't, and sometimes are dead-ends unless you interrupt with an inventory item. This wouldn't be too bad, were it not for the extremely low-fi voices. I give it points for being one of the first "talkie" games, but those points are taken away for the dialogue being very grating. There is also a lot of reading, which I am fine with in games, but the font style, size, and color used made it difficult to read, whether in a window or full-screen.
The graphics were a weird hybrid of detailed and abstract, so while you'd sometimes have a grainy photo of a real-life object, other times there would be two beige pixels nestle unobtrusively in a scene, that you were supposed to realize were important and click on (because it was a piece of paper or something.) And since this is before the days of highlighting, there was never an indication of what was and wasn't an important pixel, so you could click all over an object and get a generic response, not knowing that the slightly lighter pixels were the ones that would give you the clue you actually needed. This wasn't a problem unique to this game, but it was rampant within it.
And of course there were the psychic puzzles where the only way you knew what to do was die and time travel. (See if that supports your weight. It didn't? You're dead? Well, good thing you can relive that moment.) Again, this wasn't the only game to do things like this (Sierra was notorious for it), but when the rest of the game is lackluster, things like this just add to the aggravation.
After finishing the game and seeing the arguably anticlimactic ending, I was amazed that this went on to have a half dozen more sequels. (Though I've started into the next installment, and it's light-years ahead of this one in every way and will probably get a thumbs up from me.) My advice is to skip this one and go to the next in the series.

A masterpiece of a series; Mass Effect is a three part space opera with rich lore and great action. While definitely showing its age the original Mass Effect is still a great game that opens the door for writers to take the story in any direction, it is the best possible introduction to an incredibly large universe and I recommend playing it before starting Mass Effect 2.

Codex entries, Mars Rovering and squad-based shootouts: the Mass Effect experience.
Relatively massive aRPGs are always a highly subjective experience. There's so many ways to play them that it can be argued that no two people are playing the exact same game. So it's only fair that I just detail how I played Mass Effect, so you can choose, no circle menu needed, how relevant this review is to you.
Vanguard class, on Veteran difficulty, completed all the missions (even the garbage collection ones) and explored every planet before taking on the story missions, read all the codex entries, concentrated on using all powers and abilities, and constantly switched out companions.
This means that absolutely everything in the following review is so highly subjective that you can append everything with "playing the way I played it." So that's exactly what we're going to do, every time something subjective comes up I'm going to mark it with an asterisk (*).
Playing the way I played is dangerous. A Renegade choice, even, chewing through all the optional stuff first. It was obviously not intended to be played in that way and I don't recommend it *.
If anything, you really want to pace yourself. As it is, playing my way, you get a flat 60% of the game's worst content upfront, the 60% of garbage filler planet exploration * and exposition, followed by 25% of decent filler content (Hackett's errands, Citadel quests, and a half dozen missions that end in hilariously anticlimactic text prompts), and finally the 15% of excellent story content.
So do one story mission, then a third of the planet exploration, and so on. All this takes you through two main forms of gameplay and some fairly hefty conversations.
The core firefight gameplay is pretty consistenly good *. You have a lot of tools at your disposal and get incredibly overpowered by the end with double-stacked mods and the best gear that credits can buy *. With Barrier-spamming and a shotgun in hand you're encouraged to run into firefights instead of just toeing it behind cover, which leads to satisfyingly aggressive fights, and your other abilities range from debuffs, to disablers, to squad-wide revival *.
All this is supported by some great sound design - meaty gun blasts and hard-hitting shield displacement - and gives you some unique eye-candy to look at while doing it, outside of a few notably awkward armour designs and some very drab interiors in the planet exploration stages *.
When the music is great, it's great. When it's not, you're listening to the same three lazy space ambient tracks while mountain-climbing your way through the game's endless supply of Steam Greenlight-tier empty barren maps with the Mako *, the game's Mars-Rover-Tank thing.
Now the Mako itself controls fine. Even great, I'd say. Pulling off some manoeuvres like jumping over a trio of rockets and returning with one back that just reduces a squad to shreds, before landing with a satisfying clunk, never got old *.
But the maps are absolutely awful, outside of the story maps. The Mako works best when you're forced to continually get in and out of it, not just driving to the same two dungeons filled with different assets, struggling with the physics engine to get over mountains and getting bored to sleep treading through endless plains.
So that's the bulk of the gameplay *.
There's some "under the hood" RPG systems ala Deus Ex, which mostly amount to "equip the thing that makes your points go higher", but switching armour and weapons does lend some visual variety to the game and there are some endgame ammo types and power-speccing that allow for different playstyles - even within classes *.
Now this is a game that is designed for gamepads first and foremost. Use a gamepad if you can. The menus are designed for crab people. The auto-aim and stat-based aiming is so ridiculous it's not like that's a concern. It's completely playable with a keyboard and mouse if you can think like a crab-person for said menus, it's just awkward and the RPG aiming means you can be staring right at an enemy and still miss.
A word of warning: Steam's version of Mass Effect is fairly buggy. If anything you're probably better off buying the Origin version, since you get the DLC and a fair few bug fixes, but if you have an inherent aversion to Origin you can still enjoy audio/BGM constantly cutting out and characters having a tenuous connection to the material plane.
No asterisk there, note that.
The widely lauded story is fairly good, if very Bioware tropey, but the majority of the dialogue and flavour text is based around exposition around various worldbuilding elements. Even at the most dramatic moments, Mass Effect has no problem dropping its in-universe jargon to enforce how consistent it's world is.
This isn't a bad thing, but people who like reading codex entries and discovering how a new world works are probably going to get more out of the story out of people looking for a standard RPG or action plot *.
Characters have their own driving motivations and backstories, and even the most alien races are driven by fear, anger or plain boredom, and unless you're completely averse to conversations, at no point does it feel like a slog getting through them.
Shame that they're underwritten *. As a rule of thumb, you'll get about three conversations out of a squad member, and one conversation out of a regular NPC. Most of them trigger just after a few travel screens, but a few trigger after story missions - this means that for half the game, half your squad will just repeat itself, and vice-versa for the other half*.
For some inane reason, most of the inter-squad conversations are reserved for the elevator transitions, elevators that you will absolutely want to skip at every possible moment *.
Ignore that asterisk, everyone should skip the elevators. They're awful. Use the rapid transit system when you can.
Mass Effect is a good game that's held back by filler content that doesn't use the core gameplay as much as it should. That and really bad, bland maps for most of that filler *.
Is it worth playing? Absolutely. Mass Effect is a one-of-a-kind space opera RPG. Nothing else quite like it out there.
And you don't need an asterisk on that.

If you're reading reviews to decide whether or not you should get this game, I'm going to tell you off the bat that if you want to immerse yourself in a gorgeous scifi universe while enjoying some action and light RPG elements, click that "Add to Cart" button now. The Mass Effect Trilogy from 1-3 delivers engaging and visceral cinematic player involvement all the way through. The first game in the series of course will seem a little lacking in a few areas (read on for details on that) but it doesn't fall short in narrative, one that feels like a movie theatre experience catered directly to you.
When the dust settles and we're faced with deciding our favorite part of a series, we tend to go with the first impression that made an impact on us. All bias aside, I take a step back and look at the trilogy objectively (because many of you might be wondering how this stacks up against ME2 + 3), and I feel each of the games has a distinct aura about them. The first game in the series does an incredible job setting the stage, effectively instilling that "something big is going on and I feel I'm on the cusp of something historical" feeling, while at the same time giving the player enough room as to not feel like their entire playthrough has to be a race against time.
Mass Effect 1 has the most RPG elements out of any of the three games, as they become more and more action-oriented focusing on narrative, interaction with crew members and combat more than anything else. Even still, the elements are so subtle that only feels like an RPG at certain times, most notably the usage of text passages to describe an ending of a sidequest, or the more in-depth skill system. You really need a bit of patience if you want to enjoy this game world, as there are a few things in this game where you can see they had to cut due to some development constraint or another. Most of the levels feel a little bare, as the environments look like textured block-ins with a few static meshes to decorate. This is just fine in most cases, however the more you get into the game world, you'll eventually be wishing they had time to add more just to convey a more complete display of the game world's lore.
There's a wealth of weapons and armor, and the variety in the first game compared to the 2nd and 3rd is exponentially higher. There has to be hundreds of weapons, armor, omni-tools, biotic amps and mods that can be added to weapons and armor to give you stat buffs. You won't find anything like this in the rest of the trilogy where the other two games simplify the player loadout so much that you'll feel suffocated when comparing it to what ME1 offers. Aside from the narrative, there are tons of sidequests of course. Many of these can be found by talking to NPC's, overhearing conversations even listening to the news guy in the elevator intercom on the Citadel. When you start to stack up these quests, you can hop into the Normandy and travel to different star systems within the galaxy, searching for solutions to these quests. You can read detailed information about planets that you click, and some of them can be scanned for materials or other quest-related items. Some of the planets are open for exploration with the Mako, which is hysterical and fun to drive (you'll form a love-hate relationship with the performance). Sometimes you can land on a planet just to check it out, discover anomalies, find items from wreckages and even observe wild life (which is scarce in the game). For me, traveling to other planets and just checking them out is the most attractive feature, but even that feels a little bare, and could use some more things to discover.
I could go on writing for hours, as I've designated this as my #1 all time favorite game, but suffice it to say that if you haven't been aboard the Mass Effect train, you need to jump in and see what it's all about. It truly lives up to the hype you've been hearing since the release, there's always been so much talk of it in the industry, and there's a good reason why. This universe makes you feel so small yet instills enough ambition in you that you'll want to travel the galaxy and see it all, and you can, aboard the SSV Normandy SR-1...

In terms of an interesting campaign, this Total War probably takes the cake. The blood and gore DLC makes battles especially entertaining. I've spent 145 hours playing and won two campaigns (Visigoths and Geats, both H/H), and spent other hours trying different factions.
On the pro side:
- Vastly different campaigns depending on what you're interested in; nomads bent on killing and destorying, barbarian kingdoms starting small and creating empires, and vast empires fighting to retain their incessantly raided borders.
- Blood and gore DLC, plus battle mods from the workshop, make battles realistic.
- Friendly fire exists.
- Tactics appear to be more essential in this title vs. others.
- Interesting dilemmas.
- Family tree, intrigue, dominion, and control are great features for controlling inner politics.
- Traits for generals and governors add another interesting element to the game.
On the con side:
- Glitches... there was a glitch in my Geat campaign where a whole portion of my family tree (including my heir) were listed as other nobles, so I couldn't use normal family intrigue with them--had to declare a new heir in fear that giving the crown to a potential non-family member could wreck my campaign. Very minor stuff outside of this.
- Siege battles tend to get repetitive. I got bored of the DLC with the Roman Expedition pretty quickly, because every siege battle started looking exactly the same--same garrison, same terrain, everything. Probably a coincidence, because I've never encountered this before.

Crusader Crash is an old school platformer/hack and slash game inspired by the nes.  The game has a very nice retro look and a good retro soundtrack and if you enjoy retro platformers this game is a definite must buy.
The controls in this game are simple and very responsive.  You have 3 buttons, attack, jump, and reflect.  Attack and jump are exactly what you would expect, when you hit the reflect button your knight sounds out a wave in front of him.  This wave does not damage enemies at all but will destroy any projectile on impact.  Use of this mechanic is mandatory to fight certain enemies and get over tricky jumps which would otherwise be impossible due to streaming projectiles.  It is implemented well and adds an extra layer of gameplay to the game.
The game is split into 8 worlds.  You are given 3 lives and unlimited continues, you can also stop at anytime and contine from the last level you left off at.  Extra lives are awarded at 15000 and 35000 points(I never got any higher than that), and a typical playthrough of most levels will grant you at least 15000 points meaning you will usually have 4 lives to complete a level.  Each level is divided into 2 sections than a boss battle, if you die you start from the last checkpoint, if you lose all your lives you start back from the beginning of the stage.
The level design is great, has all the typical locales one would expect, and the game has a nice smooth difficulty curve.  The first few levels are nice and easy as are the bosses but the difficulty ratchets up a few levels into the game.  This is a challenging game, expect to die while you learn the levels, but it is not a frustratingly difficuly game.  You could probably get through the early levels without continuing and in the later levels you may have to continue a few times but you won't be smashing any controllers cursing at the screen.  Most of the challenges in the game are fair and when you die it is your fault, there are a very small handful of times where you get killed by something you had no way of knowing was there but these are so infrequent they are not worth worrying about.
Overall crusader crash is an incredibly fun retro throwback that gets just about everything right.  Solid retro graphics and music, fun and varied level design, tight controls, and a decent challenge, the game sells for $4 and for that price this game is a steal .

Of course, the actual history is a lot sadder and for people who have no idea what's going on, they might wonder why their side in Story mode still "loses" when they won the battle. And another nice thing they did to make things not as repetitve was giving you the option between 3-4 characters each stage of Story mode.
Combat wise, I like the Switch system, you effectively get to use two weapons per battle. That definitely mixes things up compared to previous DWs. Ambition mode is like Xtreme mode in past DWs. Only difference was that in the past Xtreme modes, your playthrough was done once you died. I remember how brutal that was, even as Lu Bu. As for cons, this game is a massive time dump. Framerate was a little shaky for me and I think graphics could have been done better (though honestly, who's looking at the trees when you got a thousand soldiers to hack through?). Also since I actually like to read through the storyline on the loading screen, the lines go by too slow...But yeah, nothing major to worry about.

ATA–203, originally designated ATR–130, was laid down by the Gulfport Boiler and Welding Works, Port Arthur, Texas, 10 September 1944; launched 26 October 1944; and commissioned 1 January 1945, Lt. J. E. Fuld, Jr., USNR, in command.
Following shakedown, ATA–203 departed Texas for Coco Solo, thence with 2 YTBs in tow, she headed for Pearl Harbor, arriving 9 March. Exchanging the YTBs for pontoon barges, the auxiliary tug steamed westward, 16 March, and on 22 May cast off her charges in Nakagusuku Wan, Okinawa. She performed towing jobs in the Okinawa area, then on 11 June, headed south to Leyte. From there towing assignments took her to the New Hebrides, New Guinea, and finally back to Okinawa where she reported for duty to ComMinPac, 30 August.
On 8 September, she got underway for the Japanese home islands, reporting to ComMinDiv 7, off Kyushu, 11 September. Until 29 December she conducted hydrographic surveys off Sasebo, Omura, and Nagasaki, acted as a mine destruction vessel and assisted storm damaged ships. Then detached from all duties in Mine Force, Pacific, she took up towing services for the occupation forces.
On 14 March 1946, ATA–203 headed home, reporting to ComServLant 22 June. Assigned to the 16th (Reserve) Fleet, she decommissioned 20 October 1946 arid was berthed at Orange, Texas. Named Navigator, 16 July 1948, she was transferred to the Maritime Administration in August 1960 and was laid up at Mobile, Alabama, as a unit of the National Defense Reserve Fleet. She remains there into 1970.

Similar to the Zuma series or Luxor, you shoot colored balls at a slowly moving ball-snake (my termonology) that is trying to get to a hole in the ground.  If the ball-snake reaches the hole, you lose the level.  After a few levels you get some power ups that randomly appear after making matches.  Every 4 or 5 levels you get a key that lets you unlock more power ups.  You can choose which power ups you want to unlock.  It's always nice to have control over what special powers you have so you can play in your style.  The levels get tougher as the game progresses:  2 ball-snakes at once, zig-zag paths that make it difficult to shoot balls where you want them, tunnels where you can't get at part of the ball-snake while it goes through, etc.
Power ups include:
Slow - always useful!
Backwards - the ball-snake creeps backwards for a few seconds
Shooter (I forget what it's called) - you shoot a fire dart, first only one but later you can upgrade to 3.
Blast - creates a big blast that takes out all balls in the area of the blast, small at first but can be upgraded
Orb of Decay - This is a good one, though it sounds like it would slowly decay them it actually does it instantly.  A trail of black smoke destroys orbs in a certain area when you use this one.
And more that I have not unlocked yet.
The main gameplay area is shown as a map that you progress across (I can't remember if there was some kind of story).
There is also a Challenge area where you try to play levels as long as you can.  Those unlock as you go along in the main map gameplay.  I'm not sure if there are leaderboards or if you are just playing for your own record.
There are Achievements.
There are Trading Cards.
There are 3 Difficulty settings including "Nightmare" for those who want a challenge!
Graphics aren't the greatest (looks like a phone game) and the music is probably that free stuff but I just want to play, I don't care how things look and sound.  There is one music track I like that is fun and quirky.  I assume it randomly picks a track.
It's a great game for short bursts of play.
((For the record, I bought this on Steam with my own money.)
