If you like zombie survival games, you want this one. State of Decay is one of those rare gems that started out on the Xbox Arcade and was developed under that whole 2GB limit. I honestly would love to have seen what Undead Labs would have been able to do with this if they were not working under such restraints.
The base game itself can play out in a number of ways. You have several bases to choose from, various weapons, vehicles that have their own set of stats (fast and flimsy or slow and durable). The main game has a storyline that can take a while to complete, an advancement system that lets you choose a set of skills to specialize for each person as you level them up (easy to miss if you're new, second tab in the character screen), and a colorful set of characters.
The Breakdown DLC is the survival mode you want to play. This does have some drawbacks though; luckily it's not that expensive. Breakdown removes the story mode and puts you in the Trumbull map. After a while you'll find an RV, repair it, and move on to the next map. The next map is the same map but with harder zombies, more spawns, and a higher chance of being torn to pieces.
Where my grievances come in with this DLC is the character parts were done a bit lazy. Most don't have their regular voices from the original game. Pastor Will has Ed's voice in mine and was once telling me how he got laid behind a park bench or something. So while minor, it's noticeable.
(Edit: Adding in some new info now that I've had a chance to play Lifeline and the updates to fix things are likely finished) There are still some lingering glitches even after several updates, one of the most notable being that some zombies can at times run through the house and get stuck in the floor, Big'un zombies can sometimes glitch through doors and lead to mission failures or the death of a playable character if you're really unlucky.
The Lifeline DLC is it's own map and introduces several new characters, weapons, and vehicles. While it's a fun little game with its own unique story to the SoD world, it offers less freedom than the original. In Lifeline you will have access to many new techs to help fight off the zombie hoards while you evacuate survivors. But as time goes on, you'll lose some of these advantages. Luckily you can get them back later, but the tradeoff is you'll have to sacrifice your outposts to certain areas to maintain them. You also work on a bit of a timer throughout the game. Hoards will periodically atack your base and you'll need to be back there to help fight them off or bad things will happen.
All in all, Lifeline is a pretty decent story on its own, but I think the original game still stands as the better of the two.
Overall, I can't recommend this one enough for fans of zombie survival and building games. With any luck Undead Labs will have a chance to expand on this one in the future and make something truly unique.

Recommended at the price I got it at, but hard to recommend in general because the contorls are such a pain.
They can be rebound, but there's the issue of too many things to do.
Don't Starve Together for instance has: wasd (move), space (interact), f (attack), 12345 (switch between tools)
Feel The Snow has: wasd (move), shift (run, painful to keep held down with your pinky because it lasts quite a while), e (intenract), f (attack), space (dash), q (block), 12345 (switch between tools). Just from that, you're sort of fine, except shift to run is pretty hard on the pinky. However then later in the game you need two or three more buttons for special abilities, one or two buttons for potions, and you just start to run out of space for your left hand.
As for your right hand, DST allows you to move with the mouse, you can't do that in Feel The Snow but you still need to use your mouse for crafting and other things. You could bind special abilities and potions and simialr to your right hands keys (jkl etc), but then you'd be switching your hand between mouse and keyboard, because the mouse isn't really optional.
And this problem has the potential to get worse with updates. If they add more features (for instance different weapons which you're encouraged to switch between mid combat, they already have that actually but...) rather than streamlining things, the button overload could get even worse. It's already confirmed that they're adding a fourth ability for each tree.
Four abilites works in league of legends because you can move with your mouse! So your mouse moves and your hand qwerftd etc.
So the whole thing just leads to an uncomfortable experiance, and I'm not sure if i'll finish the game (in that windy dark cave with the iron right now).

At first I fell in love with this game. It is very similar in nature to other top-down pixel style RPG's however it adds in an MMO mechanic that otherwise doesn't exist in some other games. While I enjoyed the game at first, over time I have come to feel that the developers are not objective to what it is that they do, the timing in which they do it, and the people whom they do it too.
My first example will be daily logins. For months you would be able to login and get daily login rewards on your character over a 7 day streak. At the end of day 6 / 7 you would get an in-game currency called 'Platinum' that can then be spent for unique transformations, morphs, mounts etc. however Platinum can also be bought with $$$. What occurred was that individuals took advantage of that system, creating several characters so that they were pulling in 100's of plat a month. This of course saturated the Platinum market, however instead of simply punishing the players whom took advantage of this loop-hole, the developers turn off daily logins all together - and then re-activate however you are only allowed to get the dailies once per IP. Reasonable solution in my eyes, however this does not punish those whom have already taken advantage. Instead they opted to raise the prices on all platinum purchases, with some items costing 250+ platinum; with the response of "It's a bonus item, its not needed; price does not matter" Essentially negating the possibility that anyone who plays for free (250 platinum, you get 7 platinum a week from logins...) would be able to get any of these items.
It's not pay to win, but if you want some of the cool stuff they are releasing you sure as hell have to pay. Otherwise the only people who will get any of the new items released by developers are those who spend tons of $$$, take advantage of the system, or are privvy to information from the developers so that they can prepare for when things are released.
Another example would be the most recent halloween event, in which PAST halloween (11/02/17)  a new halloween boss was released for a period of 8 hours (During the night while people are sleeping), which then dropped Platinum shop items! But nobody would have been online to farm this boss on release unless they KNEW it would be dropping on a Friday night for a period of 8 hours. So again those who were privvy to information or 'buddy buddy' with developers were able to better prepare and take advantage of a situation. Yet again placing items into the hands of the SAME PEOPLE, so that 3-4 people within the game have nearly anything worthwhile making the market unstable, unreliable, and overall the game just not enjoyable. The logical timing for this event would have been the night of Halloween (10/31/17), instead they delay it several days and drop it randomly in the night time; no day-to-day player would have known this. However there are 3-4 people who farmed it the entire 8 hours and I am sure got a plethora of platinum shop items.
Final example will be the 3 hours of time that I (and a group of 6+) wasted on a recent raid release, only for the developers to DELETE the loot table so that items would not drop as we fought the boss. All because we were playing the game AS IT WAS DESIGNED, and were punished for utilizing what was available to us as players. Instead of correcting it and then speaking to that person they just made it so nobody got any loot. So 7 individuals had 3 hours of raid time completely negated, because the Developers thought it would be fun to exercise their 'power' and make it so nobody got loot. Overall, I must say I am disappointed in the way the developers present themselves, and the way that they isolate players due to their preferential treatment.
If you are looking to play solo and play from time to time, this game will entertain you for a week or two. However if you are looking for something a little more serious that will provide you a good community experience in which the gameplay is set fairly for all, with none getting advantages or preferental treatment, then this would not be for you. It is unfortunate I have spent several weeks enjoying this game only to have it destroyed because those running this game are obviously giving information or leaking forthcoming material to normal players, giving them unfair advantages. I am disappointed, I really enjoyed this game.

Ah, how do i start with Isaac.
Isaac is essentially, the best Rouge-Like you could ever buy, full stop. I have played at this point, 135 hours and have only unlocked half of the items and stuff, which is why i so goddamn love this game - there is just so much stuff in it. You could have thousands of hours, with all unlocks, and still find a new synergy that tickles yur fancy, it is highly likely with the amazingly large, strange array of items you can find. From shooting blood beams of death out your mouth, to shooting bombs, to having infinite airstrikes, you can find all sorts of items which synergysie in ways you would not believe. Ever wanted to have an on-demand airstrike that shoots out knives when it lands? Now you can! Ever wanted to become a demon and shoot beams of mega death at your enimies? Now you can!
The core gameplay of Isaac is pretty simple, walk from room to room, killing enemies and getting to the boss, then killing the boss and advancing. You shoot in for directions with basic tears to start with, but the more you progress through floors the weirder items you will pick up, changing your tear type into all sorts of different things. When you first start playing Isaac the sheer wonder of "Hey, what does this do?" literally anytime you find an item is magical, then picking it up, it not seemingly doing anything, then it blowing up in your face is even better; and once you get to know what items do the feeling of "Oh, should i take this?" is also magical. As with most Edmund games it is littered with other Edmund game references like Steven (Time ♥♥♥♥), The Triachnid (Spewer i believe), Dr. Fetus (Super Meat Bouy) are just a few off the top of my head, and there are probably more. Like i said, there are about a bazillion different items, each with their own way to synergize with one another. While yes, it can be rage enducing at times *cough cough* The Lost *cough cough* it is really all part of the fun, i thnk at times it can be a little unfair with it being based a little on luck with the items you get, but i dont think that is too bad. Isaac is, an all-round amazing game.

Man, what a ride! Obsidian really delivered on their promise. The game will certainly have an added appeal for any nostalgic Infinity Engine fan, but it's nevertheless a solid standalone effort delivering outstanding gameplay. After putting in about 70 hours into a single playthrough, here are my five cents:
The pros (in no particular order):
1) Infinity engine. It helps PoE imbue the adventure with a sense of wonder and immersion that has been missing from the recent AAA titles. I've put in more than 100 hours into Dragon Age: Inquisition, and while the visuals were great, I couldn't shake off the feeling of the world being too inanimate and generic. Same goes for Skyrim, which, while joyfully interactive, suffered from predictable copy-and-paste patterns in many of its environments. Paradoxically, while Infinity Engine is supposed to basically present the environment as an isometric drawing, it really makes the world come alive and feel inhabited not only by the PCs, but by everyone else, including the foes you encounter. The artwork here is top-notch, with every area, including, for example, such mundane things as inns, having a unique feel and presentation that really urges you to explore every bit of it.
2) Exploration. PoE plays like a true RPG should, with traps, surprises, hidden passways and more to be found in every cave and dungeon. And they feel very organic and logical. The game is brimming with content, and a small dungeon level can easily take up 40+ minutes of game time even without any wipes. And yet it never feels repetitive, as you always have a sense of purpose. There is a 15-level dungeon, and all of the levels are interesting in their own way. This speaks volumes about the approach of Obsidian, and it's really showing. Having a pen-and-paper RPG cut-ins (texts that describe you jumping over a ridge etc.) was also a greatly appreciated touch.
3) Combat. Hands down, this is the best combat system of any RPG I played, and I started with Might&Magic 6 back in the day. It elegantly improves on the classic D&D formulas that were so awesomely implemented by BioWare in Baldur's Gate, and makes combat dynamic and enjoyable. It also feels very balanced, with different character classes adding different flairs to the whole gig. I guess the greatest compliment to the combat system is that you are forced to use different tactics throughout the game, not just stick to the same "optimal" formula for every encounter (I'm looking at you, Dragon Age). As in any true RPG, the combat in PoE strarts with carefully selecting gear for your party. The system that Obsidian came up with (balance between attack speed, damage, interrupt chance, recovery speed, damage reduction and accuracy/deflection) is so obvious and fair that I'm inclined to call it genius. I have played pen-and-paper D&D starting with 2nd edition, and this honestly beats any of the systems that they had, which is saying something.
4) Gear. I just love the fact that while there is an abundace of loot in the game, you are not spoiled for choice when it comes to equipping your guys. There are no overpowered "no-brainer" choices in PoE, and it all comes down to balancing everything. Item buffs don't stack, which is a great little tweak that does wonders for you item and party management. Enchanting is also realized very well, but I have to say that IMHO Dragon Age did crafting better.
5) Story. Of course, with the game coming from Obsidian, it shouldn't come as a suprise, but the story in PoE is great. It doesn't necessarily reach BG2's or Fallout2's heights, but it's compelling and balanced. The team set out to introduce you to a new campaign setting (i.e. world), and they achieve just that, with you steadily gathering information and making sense of the whole history of the region the game unfolds in. That, to me, proved to be a very important aspect, because the main plot ties into the whole context of the world history brilliantly, and they basically enrich one another. There are enough fantasy tropes in play for the story to be accessible for any type of player, and while nuances are there for an inquisitive player to unearth and enjoy, you can do just fine without them.
6) Companions. PoE can't quite match the nuanced stories and personalities that BioWare offered for DA:I's companions, but interaction with them is still perfectly enjoyable. I loved some of the routes Obsidian decided to go with companions' quests, with most of them having thought-provoking, satisfying conclusions.
The cons (in no particular order):
1) A.I. Such a compelling combat system would be much better served by a stronger A.I. Opponents are not the brightest bulbs, and your party members will often run around frantically, lose track of their orders and generally require micromanagement, especially in tighter underground encounters. This has been a feature of virtually every Infinity Engine game, and it's kind of sad to still experience it in 2015. But this is a minor frustration, with key encounters wisely giving you the space you need to operate.
2) Voice acting. While it's admirable for such a low-budget project to have so much voice acting, it leaves much to be desired. While the dialogues themselves are quite ok (although they do suffer from being a bit too "generic fantasy" at times), the delivery is sometimes cheesy and uninspired. The game also insists on adding flavor text describing emotions and behaviour of the person you are talking too, and while it worked really well for me in general, adding voice acting on top of that text makes both hard to follow and enjoy.
3) Size of the world. I feel kind of guilty mentioning this, but PoE could really use more areas to be explored. The game is filled with content as it is, but I can't help but think back to the sense of wonder that the first Baldur's Gate brought with its myriad optional areas. The average size of an area in PoE is also not that large. I guess you could squeeze out about 100 hours of gameplay by doing absolutely everything, but that's it. I'm not a big "replay value" kind of guy, and I just wish that the game delivered more content, since the content that is in the game is absolutely outstanding. The world map is also a bit deceiving in this regard, with large area left without any of the zones to discover and explore.
Overall, I highly recommend this game to any RPG fan. It's a solid 9/10 in my book. I'm very excited for the upcoming expansion, because this is the type of world that really draws you in and clearly has more stories to tell.
P.S. I mostly play on consoles now, but I had no trouble hooking up my laptop to the TV and just kicking back with a remote keyboard/mouse, ps4-style. I had no problem whatsoever with reading text in the game. And, contrary to some opinions, I didn't think that there was too much reading involved.

As much as I would like to reinforce much of the existing reviews about how well the game is, let me just say that the game overall was amazing, beautifully looking, wonderful soundtracks and well written dialog and naration.
That said, there were 4 things I think they could have really improved on:
(incoming bug report)
1. Slightly buggy pathing. Sometimes the character will run back and forth over an area to try to find a path to attack an enemy in melee and it can be lead to your character dieing for running by another enemy and provoking an attack of opporutunity and or just not find how to get there and stop moving all together.
2. Sometimes area spells become buggy and cause the caster to run straight to the center point of where you want to cast with the cast icon above them, and then not cast it. This is a bug I think they could fix. Several times my priest and or wizard would run to the center of where i was targeting a spell instead of casting it and i would have to resend the action again before they would immediately do it now they were in range.
3. The difficulty of this game is significantly easier than any of its predecessors. Even on the most insane difficulty, I found most fights to be fairly easy. There were probably only 3 significant fights that truely were worthy of that difficulty in the game.
4. The character highlighted icon (green circle) in game when you select a character was barely noticable compared to the non-selected character icons. This was a poor decision and I think they could have made this stand out more.
Overall I would give the game 9/10 if the 4 issues I would say could be addressed. Until then 8/10.

I Would like to start of by saying, Well done on this game Ubisoft.
It runs fantastic on pc, any kind of pc really. The PC port is stunningly good.

The other downside to the versus mode is that as mercenary you play in first person. Now this in itself isn't a negative thing, but the FOV is very narrow and can't be adjusted.
This said, the versus made is really fun.
I'd say, purchase this game if you're a splinter cell fan or a general fan of stealth games. If this is not the case, you might still want to give it a try when it goes on sale.

One of the most chalenging Stealth games I've played!
Play as a ghost where absolute silence and non-lethal aproach is your strengh. Stealth is your thing but you don't have time to wait or your just a but more agressive? Then Panther playstyle is your thing where flashbang to quickly kill enemies before they see you (or vanish) and silent weapons like pistols, Smgs and snipers could all have silencers. But hey, you wanna be a total agresive ninja with guns? Then your in for Combat where you come in lock and loaded and loud where grenades and explosive traps with the very loud shotguns (or any other weapon without silencer) are the total ninja brute!
I've played the majority of my time playing as a ghost (but you can mix match your loadout to compensate for any situations) but sometime time isn't on my side and lethal aproaches are need to avoid direct confrontations.
The scoring system let's you master all three playstyles on all maps with offcourse the level of difficulty as a bonus point from Easy, normal ,professional to perfectionist. For those who likes the biggest of chalenge, Perfectionist trully is a hardcore chalenge to overcome!
I haven't played any coop game as of yet. I plan to finish the game on solo before it. But there is alot more chalenge to overcome when in coop. Commandos and Heavy enemy types can take hostage your companion if he ever got caught and both can help each other out to reachs higher places or to dual-breach zones.
The Spy Vs. Mercs multiplayer is very difficult to master since there is a lot of very good players who can either kill you as swiftly and quietly as a true ninja or spot your hiding spot as the Mercenary. Teamwork is non the less the most important thing.
** 8/10 **
+ Very fun and chalenging stealth mechanics for 3 different playstyle in single player and Coop.
+ Vs. Multiplayer is very fun with communications and even better with 1 to 3 other friends
- Vs. Multiplayer is imposible in a 4 vs 4 game when your P.U.G team are all over the map and there's no temawork
- 4 vs 4 games aren't Dark and full of shadows like in 2 vs 2 games making stealth more difficult to play as a spy.

I absolutely love the game. Think Dark Souls (ish) combat - with less rolling, and more abilities to use - mixed with a follower/party system. There is high-replayability, mainly because of starting new and doing different builds, as well as the fact that even after 6 or so times, the quests haven't gotten boring. Each encounter can go wildly different than the last. At first, some encounters may seem to be long, especially with the larger creatures, but that gets better with time. Yes, your character and followers (called pawns in-game) are getting better stats, but it is mainly because you will learn the detail that has gone into all of the enemies - their strengths/resistances and their weaknesses. Also, the more your followers play and experience combat, the more about the enemies and quests they learn. When implemented, this ranges from using a spell in accordance to a monster's weaknesses, to chiming in to help you on how to finish a quest. Definitely a great game for those of us that like rpgs, dungeon crawlers, and min-maxing.

Attila is often rated among Total War fans as the most difficult of the series. If you're not used to the game-style that is unique to TW series, this is likely not the place to start unless you're looking for a challenge. It also suffers from a general lack of optimization that can make it run rather slowly in places. The only other major negative is that some of the DLC races really aren't that impressive, and are oddly held behind DLC just because.
With that said, there are a ton of things to enjoy about this! The start positions can vary between fleeing populations desparately attempting a safe place to find home, a dwindling but massive empire, a fledgling empire about to take on the world, a world-crushing horde, or merely a group of tribesmen attempting to survive through the apocalypse happening around them. What do you feel like starting as?
Beyond that, balancing your cities is actually a thought process beyond just mindlessly building the best of everything. Most high-income buildings have some serious detriment to your economy in some way, and you need to balance that out with other setups. In the end, this generally results in different provinces having quite different makeups based on the resources available there.
The combat as well is quite good, with cavalry (especially cavalry archers) being the most powerful types of unit in the game. This is generally accurate for the time period, but even then most cavalry have to be somewhat micromanaged to not just get caught up on spearmen.
Overall, Attila is a challenge, but because of this it feels extra rewarding when you manage to carve out your little corner of the mediterranean despite the chaos raging around you.

At the time I'm writing this, I've finished "Part I" of the game. So I'm far from finished, but I think I've got a good sense of the game overall at this point.
I've played the classics this is based upon -- the Baldur's Gate series, Icewind Dale, Planescape: Torment -- and immediately upon starting the game, it's clear that this is a lovingly-crafted work by the masters, who've learned much in their years of experience. If you've enjoyed any of those games, you'll most likely love this. If you've never played those games, I also recommend this, but be sure to make use of the ingame "help" system, because this game is light on tutorials, and there are a lot of gameplay conventions to learn.
The writing is excellent, and the dialogue is quite good. The story seems a mature one -- it's not simply the power fantasy that most CRPGs are, and there are hints that this story is actually exploring some deeper questions about ethics and meaning. You encounter people who commit atrocities, but even they have reasons for what they've done -- no one is Evil with a capital E, just because. This is not to say that everything's grey and there's no right and wrong, but you do have to pause every now and then and think about what your opponents are saying.
They use voice-acting for the highlights, but much of the dialogue is in text only. This is good, in my opinion, because it means that they don't skimp on the writing in order to fit it into the constraints of what can be voiced. Most of the voice-acting is very good to excellent; there were a few bits that sounded flat, but those were mostly minor NPCs. The major characters all are well done.
This doesn't use a D&D rules set. It's mostly familiar in style, and you can get a feel for how it works fairly quickly. But the differences tend to trip me up. It's hard to decide which skills and spells to select without advice. It was actually a relief when my party wizard could use the "fireball" spell, and it turned out to work just like dear old fireballs of D&D. The class balance seems pretty good, but it's not perfectly balanced; in particular, I notice that rangers, who are overpowered in most D&D-derived CRPGs, seem to be underpowered here. The paladins in the game, though recognizable thematically, do not have the guaranteed good guy status they usually do; this is good, as that always undermined the potential for roleplaying through ethical problems.
The "health" system is different from what I've seen in any other game, and it's a bit confusing at first, though I think it actually makes a lot of sense. You've got two different, but related stats: endurance, and health. Damage in combat mostly effects endurance, and when your endurance hits zero, you're knocked out. Your health bar goes down more slowly, but it's related to endurance; I'm not sure how the math works, but there seems to be some proportionate damage to health when your endurance is damaged. At the end of a fight, your endurance quickly recovers, but you still have some damage to your health. The important thing to notice is that almost all game references to healing refer to endurance, not to health; there are few ways to heal damage to health aside from resting. In practice, this means that you can quickly recover from a fight, but you're also gradually worn down over the course of several fights; this makes sense to me, intuitively. If an NPC's health gets down into the red, they're likely to die in a fight.
Combat is quite challenging. Even trivial encounters require some thinking. Overall, this is positive, but it can be wearying. As in classic Black Isle / Obsidian games, you can explore maps completely, and it's generally rewarding to do so, but it gets tedious to fight every random monster populating an open field. It's worth noting that stealth is generally a viable option, and you can avoid a lot of fights if you're careful about it.
In particular, in Part I, there was one major fight -- the climax to a sidequest, but one you're unlikely to skip -- that was much, much more difficult than anything prior to that in the game.
I spent hours on that fight, with my party of four characters at 4th level. From what I read on forums, my party was typical of what you'd expect to have at that point, and many people claimed to have succeeded with such a party. I finally decided to postpone it until I had a party of six, at 5th level, and it was still difficult.

Look upon my hours spent on this game, ye mighty, and despair.
I'm not saying you too will be spending over 280 hours killing hordes of Chinese peons upon buying the latest version of
, but there is something innately satisfying to the series. If all you have is a PC and you haven't played any games from the franchise since Warriors Orochi, then you owe it to yourself to shell out for this version. Especially if there's a steam sale or some such.
Dynasty Warriors 8 is uncomplicated yet deep, with a huge cast of characters just waiting to be experimented upon, each character with their own unique gimmick/playstyle. This really needs to be stressed: Omega Force, the developer of the series, has done a bang-up job establishing exclusive weapon mechanics for each of its 82 characters that will keep you engrossed in finding out how to best maximize your slaying prowess. They're introduced 3 at a time at the beginning of each stage in Story Mode and even their higher functions are unlocked through leveling, so you're never intimidated by having everything thrown to you at once.
At least, not in Story Mode. Outside of Story Mode are scores of extraneous game mechanics which ultimately add nothing to the game, forcing new enthusiasts to run to any of the (honestly quite excellent) player submitted FAQS for help. The weapon system in particular needs to go, where a character's fighting style will be based on the weapon rather than the character. So if Lu Bu is equipped with Guan Yu's crescent spear, he'll start fighting like Guan Yu. Meaning you can have Lu Bu jump around like a little girl by equipping him with, say, Daqiao's magical sticks. My point is that giving every character the choice of every weapon allows cheesing and actually takes away from the uniqueness of the characters. The focus of the game shouldn't be on inanimate objects anyways.
Then there are game modes which will confuse potential players with poorly thought out goals, such as Ambition Mode. The levels are grindy, repetitive and mostly there for the gems and materials needed for upgrading your weapons or artificially leveling your characters. All the money you'll gain playing Story Mode will be spent on the faculties you've built in Ambition Mode, but you have to play Ambition Mode to get the materials that upgrade these faculties into something useful.
Tied to that is my huge disappointment stemming from my experiences playing ye olde Dynasty Warriors 3 on the PS2 in that for a game mode based upon the stated goal of reunifying China, there is little to no strategy involved at all! Ambition Mode introduces Bodyguards, friendly generals whom you can order around the map and change the course of a battle with their special abilities. In practice however, their influence on the battlefield remains minimal. So Ambition Mode becomes randomly generated stages where you unify China under a single Emperor by killing every Chinese general personally and thus bringing them forth to your cause. Bodyguards are a great idea on paper but suffers from no one on the development team having any faith behind it, leading to another extraneous and useless game mechanic.
Free Mode is Story Mode but with added goals. Optional goals. And you can play with the Bodyguards unlike in Story Mode. But it's the same goddamn thing. Offers literally nothing that couldn't be added to Story Mode. Like I said: lots of useless clutter in this game.
I (most probably) won't be buying a Wii U but it'll be interesting to see just how Hyrule Warriors compares to the Dynasty Warriors franchise. I remain optimistic in promoting DW8XL, though: as useless as the new options are, Hyrule Warriors doesn't seem to offer any new options themselves. And for all the mistakes that Omega Force have made, they have managed to create 82 characters each with their own engaging fighting style. And that is an achievement in itself.

The game is frustratingly vague with just about everything, the menu's feel clunky, the game often incorporates the day and night cycle into quests but there's no actual way to tell the exact time anywhere. Worst of all, the game throws a massive difficulty spike at you completly out of nowhere after probably the dullest first 2/3 hours of a game I've ever played, and the only way to overcome this particular spike is to level up and buy new gear. To buy new and level up at a reasonable pace, you have to complete quests. To do this, you have to walk for about half an hour (real time) to do a series of quests that dish out such meager rewards that you'll wonder why you even bother, when you'd need 10x as much money and experience to even make any progress in the quest that's another 30 minutes walk away.
Also, when doing a quest when I was asked to evict someone from their house, after stumbling about looking for the 3 people I had to talk to and having one of them bug out on me, The patriarch of the family I was trying to evict suddenly demanded 30,000 coins. This was the only way to progress his quest. The average quest I was doing would pay out 500 coins.
I'll struggle on for a bit more, as I really want to like this game, but currently all it's positives are locked behind a big wall of stupid decisions and poor design choices.

Total War: Attila
"You built an empire beyond imagining. The pinnacle of human achievement and the envy of the world. Did you think it would last? The eternal city. That glorious monument to power, culture and learning. But the Old Wolf lies wounded; surrounding by jackals; circled by vultures. Worried to death by a thousand, tiny vicious mouths— brought low by your own arrogance. These are the death throes of Rome. The light of civilisation dims and gutters. And if such precious time was left to hide your women, for your children to cry, even at the moment of your final defeat you would still take no comfort in oblivion. For I am coming for you. I RIDE WITH A MILLION WARRIORS! I BRING THE END OF DAYS!!. I AM!! THE SCOURGE!! OF GOD!!!. And I will watch your world... Burn. “
These are the words that Attila greets you with into the world of Attila Total War. His world, so it would seem.
Total War: Attila is the installment in Total War, a franchise of turn based strategy games. Total War's unique selling point is combining turn-based campaign management in the continental scope, with real time battles with a potencial of many thousands of troops battling it out in a map, with you in total control of one side. After a mostly failed launch of Rome II installment, plagued by performance issues and bugs, the developer, Creative Assembly was focused on fixing Rome II and developing Attila. Not only they managed to redeem Rome II from its technical issues, but they also managed to churn out an excellent upgrade to it, which is what we should regard Attila Total War as. It is a great improvement in both the game mechanics and climate.
The Setting
“The walls shall shake at the noise of the horsemen, and of the wheels, and of the chariots”
- Ezekiel, XXVI, 10
The year when the campaign starts is 395 AD and the grim and cruel promise by our friend Attila could not have hit a better time. Years of mismanagement and the subsequent splitup of the Roman Empire, has brought its western half down to its knees. The Eastern Roman Empire fares only somewhat better. Internal struggles tear the Rome apart. As if it wasn't enough, the climate changes. It gets colder and not only the fertility of the Roman lands will fail, causing famines and further disorder, but the barbarians that once lived beyond Rome will be compelled to move out of their homes, right into the falling empire. And on top of the food chain of the desperates and hordes, admits the smoke, blood and cold, the Huns, will come. With them, death, war, pestilence and hunger. Above them, Attila. Flaggorum Dei.
Regardless of which faction you pick to play as, the Total War, up until now being all about ascending into great and soon sole power in the world, offer you much different prospects, both in theme, and in situation. The game slogan puns Rome II's “How far will you go for Rome?”, going “How far will you go to survive?” And indeed, the first choices you will make will not determine your ascendancy: Just your survival as a realm.
Otherwise, the game does not differ much from the usual Total War deal. Settlements with buildings, armies that you lead to your own and enemy territory, all on turn-based, good-looking map. The two primary aspects of the faction you play as on the campaign map, are its settlements which make you money as you develop them and its armies, which are raised from your cities. The said armies can move out on the map to defend your possessions and to expand them. That's a very basic description.
The Campaign
“Nothing happens to anybody which he is not fitted by nature to bear”
-Marcus Aurelius
Much like Napoleon Total War was more or less a fixed Empire Total War, this can be best described as an upgrade to Rome II system. The food mechanic actually matters now, with the introduction of provincial fertility system: Some provinces will yield more food than others. Fertility decreases overtime, giving you that sense of the nature itself turning against you and conveying in a perfect way what drove the Great Migration that was a nail in the coffin of Roman Empire. For if you are non-Roman, your land stops supporting you and you are faced with prospect of a famine (or when the Huns start molesting you), you have an option to become a migrating horde: The star and prime mechanic of the game.
When you start a migration, all your settlements are razed and abandoned (provinces can actually be ownerless now), but your armies are given the additional aspect: The transition to nomadic lifestyle is manifested in the armies being given population and ability to make buildings, essentially becoming mobile cities. However, unlike static settlements, those cities would be lost for good if their army was unmade. They have unique building chains and will be on the move until they can find a place you deem worthy of conquering, upon which you lose your city aspect of your armies. Or stay mobile forever. It's up to you.
The user interface can be a bit of a pain to learn to control, espeically if you're not familiar with Total War. Perhaps such is the fate of interfaces conveying the amount of information that Attila one does, but it's still compounded by a relatively high difficulty level. Every choice will have to be weighted carefully, unless you fancy reloading saves as often as some do in XCOM games (read: often.) Nonetheless the game does not condemn you to that gloomy apocalyptic feel of the call to migrate being a matter of life or death. Depending on what you choose to play as you could start out as a migrant horde, or be Sassanid Empire, living it up in the ever-hot and fertile Middle East. Or you could lead Huns and eventually, the Scourge of God himself. Or, if you are up for an ultimate empire building, no, empire survival challenge, you can place yourself at the helm of Western Roman Empire. Can you turn the tide of history and make the Rome great again? Or will Attila watch your world burn? It has its issues, though: major league micromanagement being one of them. It's also nigh-impossible to win while maintaining Christian temples, which are all very, very expensive in upkeep. Seriously, I understand that excessive Church spending is what brought down the Byzantium and that Catholics like me love their church bling, but this stuff is extreme. Get a mod that buffs Christianity if you're going for Western Rome.
Speaking of religion, its relevance is further fleshed out and manifests itself in tensions of heathen populaces and diverse bonuses provided by religious buildings. A realm that accumulated enough populace of a certain faith, can make that faith its official religion, which will influence the aesthetics of its army and what its troops talk about, further boosting the immersion in the culture you lead.
Politics were a painful aspect of Rome 2 that were too irrelevant unless something really started to break the order. Attila fixed them. Now, the low and high power balances bring along both benefits and disadvantages,with absolute political dominance coming with high debuffs, making it justifiable in only few select situations. Even armies have integrity value: losing battles and not resting in friendly territory will cause them to revolt against you.
Each general and family member is now of certain loyalty, which is a variable that handles rising of civil wars from now on. Total political balance is influenced by A: How much influence (sort of political mana) your family as a whole has compared to other generals/characters and B: By level of control, which is a static value influenced by the political events. Your ruler can also have children. Male children will eventually become generals or governors, depending on your pick, whilst female children can be sold... eeh, married, to powerful non-family member characters to shift the political balance in favor of your family, or sent to marry abroad, to gain you a foreign ally.

Originally played this on the PS3 when it came out in a set for the trilogy, and it's even better on PC.
Pros:
- Compelling and well written story; the story sets up the game's villains very well with a worthy payoff. There's a real sense of urgency and discovery.
- Interesting characters; if you don't at least like Garrus, you're lying to yourself.
- Amazing video game world with a wonderful attention to detail; probably one of the best universes created in an RPG. Not every location is amazing but as a whole they serve the story quite well and were always fun to learn about.
- Decisions!; pretty self explanatory, if you've heard of Mass Effect you've most likely heard of the dialogue and decisions. While it isn't terribly nuanced and it often restricts you or creates a plot point that doesn't make much sense, the dialogue tree adds a nice little bit of artificial control  to the game and it's always entertaining to see whatever choice you made pan out.
Cons:
- Clunky gameplay; the shooting and cover mechanics are woefully outdated. You can often get stuck on cover and the assault rifle reticle is too big.
- Forgettable sidequests; the first game always suffered from a massive number of fetch quests and generally uninteresting distractions that didn't add to the main game.
- Inventory management; this can also be attributed to the fact that the game is relatively old, but managing the items you pick up is a pain. This is slightly better on PC because of the mouse, but it still isn't fun.
The cons that I've listed were fixed for the most part in Mass Effect 2 & 3.
Verdict:
While the UI and gameplay definitely show the game's age, I think Mass Effect is still worth playing if you're a fan of RPGs. The highlight is definitely the world, lore and story that the first game in the series sets up so well.
Still one of my favorite game series ever.

A fun and relaxing little game that combines resource gathering and crafting mechanics with a simple RPG-esque story. Still in Early Access as of writing this. My friend and I purchased this together because we were looking for something we could play in co-op.
Things I like so far:
-Visual aesthetics and music are cute, simple, and calming.
-Crafting recipes found as drops (primarily from enemies), so your ability to craft scales with your progress through the game.
-Making shelters is simple, modular, and straightforward.
-Co-op works well. Haven't had any connectivity issues.
Things that I dislike (and hopefully they will polish up in future releases).
-Combat is a little clunky. You can only attack in one of the four major directions, and lining up special attacks can be a pain.
-Level up tree could be cleaned up a little. It took me and my friend a while to learn that you can level up base attributes (damage and defense) instead of just leveling special attacks.
-Story could use a bit of polish. You are bounced around from questgiver to questgiver, each of whom has little characterization.
I look forward to seeing what new content is released and improved upon as time goes on. I feel like I got a lot of content for an early access game (compared to other early access experiences I've had in the past).

I'll be honest, having only played those in the last year or so, I was somewhat underwhelmed.  I get why they were great over a decade ago.  The plot and characters and general themes stand the test of time.  The gameplay makes me wish I had a time machine to 10 minutes from now.  Yet...
Actual Review:  I loved Pillars of Eternity.  The combat is very fluid, using individual character cooldowns instead of turns.  This makes things much more dynamic with a lot less waiting (though the waiting aspect is absolutely still there, just less prominent and annoying).  The world is dark and unique (it may have used D&D as a jump off point, but it JUMPED OFF).  The characters generally make sense within their world.  The visuals are beautiful - straddling modern aesthetic and past games.
The dialogue / actual role-playing is a big step up from many games, which I enjoyed.  You get a reputation based on your dialogue and action, and it's not just good or bad.  I ended up being rational, honest, and diplomatic (aka what I try to be but cannot seem to manage in real life).
The large-party RPG is fun, and this one is simply fantastic.  If you're new to the genre, I think this is a great starting point.  If you liked older ones, I do honestly think this is a great leap forward.  The classes and races are pretty interesting, the story is definitely compelling, and the character customization is deeper than I really had time for (in a good way - I like when I can learn new things on multiple playthroughs if I want).  Like I said, the combat is fluid and fun.  I will say that I think balance is slightly off, especially toward the end.  The first act has a pretty steep learning curve, while in the third act it was rarely difficult.  I played on normal, so this was fine.  There are harder difficulty levels, though.
Give it a shot.

So, Exile's End. I knew it looked a ton like Inescapable, and, well, it's the same guy. There are some big-name Japanese veterans in on the game as well, including Keiji Yamagishi (Ninja Gaiden composer) and some folks that worked on Secret of Mana, among other titles.
Interestingly, the game doesn't bill itself as a Metroidvania, but by some measures, it is. It lacks the sort of level-up progression of the Castlevania side, but it definitely includes its fair share of unlocked abilities to enable progression, a map system to get around (something Inescapable lacked!), and a few hidden rooms for optional upgrades as well. But it does feel a bit closer to its stated inspiration, Commodore 64/Amiga games of a somewhat non-linear nature. There's probably a little Flashback/Out of This World as well, although the controls are much more responsive.
Early on, the game is pretty tough, but this gradually starts to smooth out, especially once you get the shock absorbers so you can fall from any height without taking damage. There are also some instant death spikes to worry about... but the game is quite lenient, giving a checkpoint each screen with the auto-save, and four save slots, which record progress at each screen transition.
Graphically, I love the look of the game. It really does look like a period piece in a lot of ways, with some spiffy-looking but somewhat repetitive tiling that would have indicated a lack of memory back in the day. The executable itself was a whopping 31 MB, of which you have to figure a fair amount was the soundtrack.
Gunplay is fun, once you get one. You've got a bit of a pause between shots that you have to account for, and the weapon is governed by an energy meter. Enemies will cough up crystals to restore that, though. You'll also find other guns, but they tend to consume a lot of juice. There are also a few limited-ammunition items like a machine gun, grenades, and a grenade launcher. You'll also find first-aid kits scattered about, but these do not replenish, so be careful you don't use 'em all up. You can only carry one of those at a time, too, so feel free to use one if you're almost dead and come across one in an area you'll never revisit. Enemies will also drop restoratives, although not quite as often as you'd like.
There are a few boss battles, with the best option there being the grenade launcher, if you have it, then finishing things off with your SMG. Or throwing grenades, that works too.
I wish that the game did a little better job building up suspense in spots, because it doesn't always feel like it maximizes parts of its story. I would have loved to have known a bit more about the protagonist outside of the intro sequence. I also wish the game would lead you just a little bit more. It can be quite cryptic about where to go next. One particular spot is quite egregious, and if I hadn't decided to check a Let's Play, I would likely have been stuck for a while... although I'd probably have uncovered some other secrets in the process.
Anyway, for the whopping $5 I dropped on the game, I definitely got my money's worth. I probably should have bought it a while back, despite the "Mixed" reviews on Steam. This, like Inescapable, was a game that somehow was greater than the sum of its parts.

Despite the fact that the second sentence in the game's official description on Steam declares it to be emphatically "NOT a Metroidvania," I can assure you, gentle reader, that it is. Or at least, it pushes enough of those buttons to qualify as such in my book. I view that as a plus, counting Symphony of the NIght and Super Metroid among my all-time favourite games, period, let alone in this genre.
I can see where the developers may be coming from, though. It incorporates elements of other games/genres, notably Flashback, Out Of This World, and the C64/Amiga aesthetic, blending it into at most, a gritty subgenre of Metroidvania. I'm not sure why they wanted to distance themselves from that label, but it's not helpful to generate confusion amongst potential buyers.
On to the game itself. It's short. That's not necessarily bad, but it's something that needs stating. What it lacks in length, it makes up for in flavour and feel. The mood is just right, aided by the backgrounds and soundtrack. The game also features cut scenes that are very much in the style of the NES NInja Gaiden series. There's mostly still images and basic dialog, that serve to tell a story with a lot more implied background than what is covered in game; lends the impression that the setting is more fleshed out than it probably is (a plus, I'd say).
It also has, what I'd call "genre expectations" that lie squarely between that of Flashback and Metroid - you start out completely unarmed and un-powered, in a hostile environment where even a fall from sufficient height can damage or kill you very easily. Health ups are few and far between (at first), and your first foes will be killed literally by throwing found rocks at them. Along the way, it transitions somewhat, so that by end-game, it feels like the early part of most Metroid games. You've got your double-jump, a couple guns, all but one with limited ammo. There are no crazy shinesparking abilities, wall jumps, or anything like that.
As to the shortness - it's metroidvanian in that you need to do a little backtracking, but you don't need to do a lot of it. More if you want to find all the secrets, but there aren't a ton of those to be had, but finding them without using a map may take some time. All are visible though, so it may involve a bit of "pixel hunting" to discover them all.
I'd give this game a recommendation based on the fact that I liked all of its main inspirations, and it resulted in a "just right" experience that meets in the middle of all of them, but it's something I"d certainly want to wait for a sale. It's good, but it's no Axiom Verge.

Before I really get into this, don't let my hours fool you. I have well over 200+ hours because I played back on Xbox.
I found this little gem at my nearest Gamestop almost by accident and I loved it, there are cons as well as pros.
Pros: Decent PC port though the textures could look better sometimes. (it's not perfect and lower end PCs might run slower.)
Incredibly fun monster fights: fighting bigger monsters is a blast, it's very tactical deciding whether to let your pawns tank and fire from the back, or reign them in and try to work as a team. there's also the grapple system that lets you grab onto bosses and stab their various weak points.
Pawn System: the pawn system is usefull beyond measure and it's fun making parties of characters from vastly different players/places. (ie. Gerralt from The Witcher, or Guts from berserk, among many other cosplays.)
The DLC: the Dark Arisen DLC is what all DLC should try to be, new somewhat varying areas. (though they mostly "feel" the same) TONS of new enemies, equipment,  and bosses. a few new NPCs and a somewhat engaging plot, more so than the main story. (though you'll probably be playing for the gameplay anyway)
Cons: Boring Quests: the Main story is pretty slow in the beginning and mid point, but goes into overdrive near the end where most of the fun is had. the menial quests are just that, meanial. though there are some memorable ones.
boring eneimes: most of the enemies in the game are pretty common fantasy enemies, even some bosses (they are still badass to fight though) and all of the enemies spawns are exactly the same no matter when/what time you cross an area. a pack of goblins will always spawn in that one bush you passed 50 times.
Lacking Fast Travel: the Fast travel in this game is pretty sub-par, and wasn't even added until after the DLC patch on console. there's no horse riding in this game, and the map is Elder Scrolls-sized. make sure to keep those fairy stones on you at all times.
missing content: I won't complain about this one too much since it's been pretty well covered by 90% of the other reviews, but they removed some content including the Berserk equipment (Gut's/Griffith's armors and weapons.) and the Japanese voice overs. I personally don't mind this too much, but to some it's a big deal.
Pawn's callouts: turn off pawn voices in the options before you even start playing. they will repeat themselves over and over, calling out the same enemies sometimes 3-4 times in the same fight. Or they'll tell you what the monster in question is weak to many times.
All in all I'd give this game a 7.5/10 which is perhaps a little too good. and I'd take all my praise with a grain of salt. I love this game, and I could probably be considered biased. I hope this review is inciteful, and helps you to decide where your money goes. ^^

You've probably heard of this game/series and the seemingly endless stream of positive feedback it has gotten, and while it certainly is deserving of its praises, those same opinions would probably give the impression that it has minimal to no flaws so I thought I'd list some of them down for you.
1) Too many elevators - you'll spend a needless amount of time watching your squad standing in elevators. Yes, they are literally just standing there doing nothing until the elevator reaches its destination.
2) Horrible vehicle controls - there's a lot of exploration involved which would've been great had the vehicle controls been simple, but instead you'll ragdoll your vehicle all over the place because of how unnatural the controls feel.
3) Poor companion control - if you've ever played Dragon Age, another IP by BioWare, you understand what good control over your squad/party is, but in this game, the only character you can control fluidly and easily is Shepard.
4) Underwhelming final boss fight - I won't go into detail with this one to avoid spoilers, but it was extremely one-dimensional, lacking any sort of variety compared to previous encounters which involve adapting to the situation. Beating a final boss is supposed to feel exhilarating, but this fight left me feeling a bit flat.
Now don't get me wrong, I thoroughly enjoyed the game and definitely think it is worthy of all its praises. I simply believe it's worth mentioning that it is far from perfect and understandably so since it was developed when its genre was still in its infancy. If you're looking to get it, I do recommend it. Just bear in mind it has annoying quirks you wouldn't ever expect to find in more recent games.

I got this during sale, and I just finished the game recently.
One of the best action hack and slash games I've ever played, Imagine Assassin's Creed, Batman Arkham, set in the world of The Lord of the Rings(MIddle-Earth), with their own original gameplay system (Nemesis System)
Being a fan of Lord of the Rings(although the story is non-canon), I was familiar with the lore of the game at the very start. I would admit the game story isn't that great ~ the game is kinda short, and the open-world maps kinda small. The combat system, while fluid and fun, has flaws ~ enemies tend to attack you one at a time, there are a few occasions where two would attack at the same time, but never three. that's where suspension of disbelief comes in. The game is fun despite those issues above, and it makes a great action hack and slash game. That's what matters, not everything has to have logic in it. (the logic as to why would the orcs attack one at a time)
What made it really fun was the Nemesis system, your enemies are not just mindless nameless thugs to kill, they have names. ranks, personalities, ambitions, strengths, weaknesses, etc. get killed by an Orc, and that orc gets promoted, Kill an Orc, and it may come back in revenge for you later, with scars and a damaged body. Get killed multiple times by the same orc over and over again, he gets more powerful all while making you more thirsty for some personal vengeance, and the feeling of finally killing said orc = satisfaction.
You can  possess a high ranking captain and make him an ally to let him do your bidding (e.g. assassinating other orc captains), possess a bodyguard of a high ranking warchief and order him to backstab that chief, so he can take his place as warchief, and let him to your bidding, this is just one of the many things to do with the orc faction in the game
Worth my money and time

Today, I’m here to tell you about Strike Vector, from the French indie developer, Ragequit Corporation.They have gone from a 4 man team to a 9 man team that has made a “fast brutal aerial FPS” in 15 months. It’s an extremely fun game. It’s fast-paced and plays like an arena shooter. The game is by no means a graphical masterpiece, but it looks and sounds great.
Like I said before, this game is extremely fun. And a bit addicting, that is if you’re into flight games. I even got to play with some of the developers, and they’re extremely fun to talk to. Whether you’re into obliterating the opposition with rockets and mines, shredding the competition with Gatling guns or shotguns, or taking aim and coming out on top with the plasma gun, you’ll have fun and get your heart pumping with any play-style.
When you think aerial combat, you might think Ace Combat or the more recent, War Thunder, but Strike Vector is more fast paced and intensely aggressive than those. It harkens back to the old days of classic arena shooters, such as Quake. As such, the learning curve is a tad high, but with time anyone can master the game.
The map design is intuitive and it can play a huge role in each match. The maps range from very compact and great for closed quarters dogfights, to vast open areas with very few places to hide. Despite the variety in size and hiding spots, each map is designed to allow for quick getaways or horrifying accidents for enemies, as well as yourself. So be careful where you turn, you never know what’s around the corner. My suggestion, quickly learn the maps and you’ll do well in most situations.
How have I not touched on customization yet, it is one of the best parts of the game. You can customize not only your arsenal, but the look of your Vector. You can pick two (left/right) weapons from 8 choices, one specialization out of 7, and one special action out of 8. And don’t forget to choose a color scheme and logo.
The controls are what you’d expect in a shooter, with minor differences. Controllability on the other hand, is fantastic and manuevering is super responsive. The ability to switch to harrier mode on the fly makes it very easy to turn on a dime and derail the competition. You can even use harrier mode to hide in a corner and wait for your unsuspecting prey or seize the opportunity to take aim with your plasma gun.
Though when it comes to graphics, they’re good, but it’s nothing too special. It’s got some blurry textures up-close, but at least it looks great from a far and while blazing around the map, which is what you’re doing most of the time anyways. It also lacks graphical options, but at least I love the post-apocalyptic ambiance. Aside from the graphics, the sound effects, such as the guitar riffs played throughout the game or the sweet release of a homing missile, are awesome. Each weapon has it’s own unique look, sound and feel.
If you’re like me, you can play this game constantly just trying to hone your skills. No leaderboard has been implemented as of yet, but I could see one being added very soon. Players are given quite an array of customization to mess around with, so I can’t imagine you getting bored very quickly. Plus they’re going to release free content in the future, for anyone that somehow becomes bored.
This game is reminiscent of Quake and brings back the classic style of arena shooters, with an aerial twist. At a $25 price tag, I would definitely recommend this game to anyone interested in some fast FPS action, or if you’re just a plain old adrenaline junkie. After all, it is a “fast brutal aerial FPS”, and don’t forget it.

Since I've whinged on about how the game is handled- Let's talk about the game itself.
It's plagued by lazy primative copy/paste/recolor content from gear/crafting to maps that are X amount of the same tile with color variances. Anything that isn't a "unique" piece of gear (The items of said numbering in the low dozen at best) is a tick up in stats and a color shift to match the color of the materials used to make it.
Mechanics that are either broken outright or obfuscated so heavily they might as well be invisible- Defense in this game is broken, and as small of a difference as 5 points can mean that at certain areas or VS certain mobs you go from eating 3 shots to being invincible- Until a random one shot happens because ???
Skills and classes are also outright broken.   Classes and their associated subclasses have different stat scaling percentage values and or damage increases/decreases.. These are however literally invisible unmarked values that you can only find out by being lucky and asking a developer or a player who has spoken to a developer directly- So you start off nice and blind even if you made an educated choice.
Notably physical damage classes largely have worthless skills with poor stat scaling and as you hit middling levels- Your auto swings will easily outpace them even when level capped (A process accomplished by mindlessly spamming them until a times used value fills and it blips to the next rank, maxxing out at 3.)
And a goodly half of them don't have enough unique skills (And share enough skills) that there's little difference between some subclasses.  With maybe two tops being major departures from their base class at best out of a list of around 9 classes.
And there is simply not much to do and hardly any content besides mindless grind over what amounts to a single digits worth of zones and no, I'm not feeling generous enough to count submaps in said zones.
That good will was long ago spent by the team behind the game.
It could have been a fun little comfy sandbox RPG- But an utter lack of direction, drive and general incompetence makes it not so.

A pretty cool mix of Flashback with heavy leanings towards Metroid best describe the feel of this game. The music score is quite simply phenomenal. Composed by Keiji Yamagishi himself, of "Ninja Gaiden" fame. The Royal Bath melody in particular I never grow tired of hearing. Enough can't be said about having really good background music to set the mood and accompany you while traversing around the depths of the planet.
Most would agree that controls are very important in a game like this. Thankfully you'll come to find the controls are very solid, tight, and responsive. Far to many indie games drop the ball when it comes to controls, but Exile's End certainly got it oh so right.
The plot itself is rather typical sci-fi fair with some interesting undertones. A lone survivor of a spaceship wreck, finds himself stranded on an alien planet. You'll find yourself surrounded by a hostile environment, trying to figure your escape, while unraveling this foreign worlds mysteries without giving away to much.
Level design is very well done indeed. I really have to commend the developers when it comes to this particular area. So many little touches all come together to pull off a well crafted game. For example, generally when you're forced to back track (in order to use a key item you just discovered in a previous area) you're usually given a handy short cut nearby to use. Back tracking is kept to a minimum as much as possible. Unlike some of the lesser enjoyable games of this style; Exile's End doesn't make the mistake of purposely using backtracking as a tool to pad the game in order to make it seem longer. It also features a helpful mapping guide very much like Super Metroid's, which fills in new areas as you explore them.
The puzzles you encounter are fairly easy to solve. If not a little vague at times. Which encourages some old fashion problem solving skills. The solutions always make sense. It is nice that the game doesn't give you to many hints, or constantly try to hold your hand at every step of the way. In this way it stays true to it's retro roots.
Graphically it's very much up to par with some of the top SNES games of the golden era. The animated cut scenes look fantastic. Each of the area's has it's own unique look and theme which differentiates itself from the last in distinct ways. Keeping the game fresh each time you move into a new zone. Bosses, enemy monsters and other characters fit the unearthly forms that you would expect.
Difficulty is only moderate in normal story mode. The game allows for saves and also autosaves at the start of every screen you enter. This make it's pretty forgiving. Trying to find all of the items and secrets can be the most difficult part. I never found myself stuck for very long or felt any part of the game was unfair and overly frustrating. People looking for more a real challenge have Survival Mode avaliable.
Had this game been released on a 16 or 32-bit console of the day, I think the magazines of the time would have probably rated it atleast an overall 8.5 out of 10. It doesn't really do anything new, but what it does do well is bringing together elements from many classic games. Blending them into a different perspective with top quality gameplay.
Very high quality indie game that deserves a chance. If you've been searching for a game that can stand up to some of the best that 90's classic console gaming had to offer look no further than Exile's End!

Ever wanted to revisit wolf3d on a machine that which has performance that would have been unthinkable back when that game was released? Did you maybe lack the appreciation of the evolution of gaming during the past decade? Is your view of the early 90s gaming era coated with a heavy rose tint?
Well here comes Intrude! Take a trip down memory lane, back when computers couldn't handle all the unnecessary "features" modern games pester players with!
Gone are all the great features that you've grown to like over the years!
Minimap? Nope! Remember - you're playing Wolfenstein. Enjoy the glorious feeling of getting lost over and over in the game's labyrinth-like levels!
Texture variation? What do you you're playing, a modern game, in a modern machine? We've got limited RAM to work with here! This game has to be run in the worst rig possible - so we've decided to omitt such feature that would have a trivial effect to the game's performance. Enjoy the same recolored enemy models over and over again, along with walls in spectacular colors like: light grey, lighter grey, dark grey and brown - over and over again!
Level design to rival that of the original Wolfenstein 3D! Good luck trying to find your way in this mess of levels! No easily-discernible landmarks and no map, coupled with maze-like levels will make sure you'll lose your sense of direction completely! Helpful if you thought you'd be done with it quickly, great for artificially padding out the game's length!
It has secrets! They are also ridiculously easy to find! From blatantly obvious cracks in the walls to blatantly obvious invisible walls with pckups to guide you to them! If you can never find any secrets in any other game, you'll easily find most if - not all - of them in this one! Gone are the days when you actually had to put some effort - instead, rely to ammo and serendipity to find hidden areas!
Extremely limited weapon selection! Simple and easy! Four cliche weapon categories - pistol, shotgun, automatic (chaingun) and explosive (rocket launcher) - making it absolutely easy to choose between weapons, without pesky things like weapon "variety" to confuse you!
Simplistic AI! Ever gotten outsmarted by computer-controlled enemies? No more! Enjoy totally predictable movement patterns, rush tactics and explosives-wielding enemies shooting using them way too close for their own good!

Over ten hours into the game and so far I can say that the game has wonderful pacing, a vast tree of stories that branch out and well placed character developments. While the overall theme is nothing special, it is a well excuted. Zombies are a threat, you're generally not rewarded for destroying them and thus making too many mistakes in combat can result in the perma-death of one of your characters.
You are able to meet new characters and befriend them by assisting them when they require it and eventually they will join your headquarters and become playable, each having their own skill sets, such as being good with guns, or quick with a melee weapon.  The combat system is simple and functions easily in a pinch, melee attacks, kick, push and dodge, which is incredibly fun and fluid when you're beating on a group of three or more like it were the Matrix.
The game has the typical open world dynamic events system where you are waypointed to missions, but there is no shortage of them. Most of the buildings in the game are open and searchable for loot, weapons and ammo are generally quite easy to find and you will constantly need to haul goods back to the headquarters to stop chaos breaking loose. All in all, I recommend this game for all of the aforementioned reasons and the small price it is fetching for.

It was only recently, as I stumbled late into work with a distinct lack of sleep that caused me to curse my own existence, that a single thought kept re-occurring in my head; This is all The Binding of Isaac: Rebirth’s fault. It had proven so addictive, and so compelling, that I’d completely lost sight of what time it was - realising too late the error of my ways. Never mind the fact I should have been a responsible adult and paid attention to my schedule, the truth shone through – this game was too damn good to be considered healthy.
TBOI: Rebirth is a rogue-like title where you play a child fleeing from his psychotic, murderous mother. During his escape he is forced to battle his many demons via firing his own tears at them, all the while picking up things which make him stronger but which mutate his body into grotesque forms. If that sounds pretty weird to you – well, you’d be right. Yet despite it being a bizarre tone for a game to take, it still works, with everything that occupies this strange world adding to its atmosphere in both bleak and darkly comedic ways.
When it comes to actual gameplay, it’s very much in the same vein as most twin-stick shooters; make you way through room after room, avoiding traps and killing enemies, until you reach the boss. Kill that, descend to the next floor, rise and repeat. You’ll be grabbing keys and bombs to help you along the way, but it’s one of the many unique items that can be found on each floor that you really want to get your hands on. Some are boring but practical, such as merely providing health, while some are much more exciting… Blood lasers? Fear shots? The ability to produce an army of attack flies? They’re all here, and they’re all pretty crazy.
With rooms, enemies and items being randomly generated each time you play, it creates a situation where when I say each run is different, I sincerely mean it. The bulk of the enjoyment that comes from this comes from the fact that items can work with each other to create synergies that take things into really absurd territories. For instance; there’s an item that lets your tears bounce off walls, and another that lets them split into multiple shots once fired. Pick up both, and suddenly there’s a thousand different shots rapidly bouncing off the walls in every direction. That’s just the start of it as well; even after all my time with the game, I’m still finding combinations that make me laugh, or simply leave me in awe at the fact they’re so powerful I’m wiping out rooms in the blink of an eye. Your luck can easily swing the other way, however; not all item drop or combinations work in your favour, and if you’re unfortunate you can find yourself in a desperate fight to survive with what little damage you can dish out. Manage to pull a victory of what seems like a crushing defeat, however, and it just makes that victory that much sweeter. There’s never a dull moment.
One of the main key points that make TBOI:R so genius, however, is in the way that more items and features will unlock as you keep playing and defeat its many challenges. Wind your way down to any of the (multiple) final bosses and succeed in vanquishing it, for instance, and the unlock you receive as a result has the potential to pop up in any of your future runs. This means there’s more scope for diverse runs, more room for crazy item synergies, and more of a chance for you to end up with a big grin on your face. It’s a great mechanic, and one that makes you keep coming back in the hope and desire of unlocking even more stuff to play around with. With so many bosses to beat, and so many characters to beat them with... Well, trust me when I say it’s going to take a nigh-on herculean effort to unlock everything the game has to offer.
That’s because this game is a pretty serious challenge. Everything’s out to kill you, and managing to keep your cool as a plethora of enemies and obstacles appear in the tiny room you’ve just wandered into is a key skill you have to learn pretty quickly if you want to stand a chance of getting anywhere fast. Sometimes this difficulty gets cranked up to even more brutal levels where you need to be really on the ball to even cope, and sometimes (and in one of my few criticisms I have) it just gets plain unfair. There are some scenarios where damage simply feels inevitable, and some enemies and bosses (You will hate the word “Bloat”, trust me) are notably harder to the point you feel the developers where just being mean-spirited. This runs even truer if you purchase the DLC, which provides challenges so incredibly frustrating you'll wonder where the fun is meant to be at times. Most damage is fair, don’t get me wrong, but you will likely feel your rage levels rising at points.

The other issue that runs in sync with this is that things feel a little overtly reliant on luck at times. Luck always plays a role in rogue-likes, of course, but in most rogue-likes good play and a healthy dose of effort can pull you through in anything but the direst of situations. Here, if you keep getting items that basically serve little to no practical purpose (of which there are a few), you’re going to have to be some supreme guru of skill and patience to triumph. When the same situation reoccurs over multiple runs… Well, the fun levels drop a little.
