Stranded Deep is one of the unique survival games on Steam.
You play as the role of a castaway stuck in the void of Pacific ocean.
: Since every island has limited resources, you'll find yourself constantly wandering around the vast open ocean to find another island with yet another scarce resources.
There are three ways in which you can travel from island to island: Swimming, paddling, and using a motor boat.
Not to mention, sharks will occasionally draw an interest unto the player.
You can do a lot of things on an island: Build simple structures, find/cook food, and sleep.
In the vast deep sea, you can: loot shipwrecks, and hunt fish/shark for food.
The crafting in this game is very unique compared to other games; You craft materials in front of you instead of the traditional craft-it-in-your-inventory/backpack.
You need to watch out for three things: Your Health, Hunger, and Thirst.
Everything that you do is a necessity for survival.
: The graphics of this game is breathtaking. The water's effects are some of the best I've seen. Seeing water quality in other games is rarely done. In fact, they do not act like water at all. This game is an exception to that; moreover, this is an Indie game.
The islands are filled with flora elements which makes up the beautiful island scenery.
The water world is also perfect.
You'll see tons of detailed biomes and aquatic fauna.
The only disturbing thing to see in the game is when the player is poisoned and your flashlight/torch is opened. This gives me goosebumps whenever I see this.
In conclusion, The graphics is superior in proportion to the file size of the game.
: Throwing things around and cutting trees are the most realistic scenarios I can think of.
There are many flaws in the Physics of the game: •Raft sinking in the presence of light objects, •You can climb a tree while chopping it down, •You can chop a tree while freely walking afar from it, •Swimming is faster than paddling, •You can use a tree as a raft, • and many more...
: Most of the fish travels in schools.
The three types of sharks has their own attitude towards the player.
Great AI script.
There are still a lot of bugs and glitches present in the game since it is still on Alpha stage.
I would gladly share how to reproduce those bugs and glitches, Just message me.
Stranded Deep is an extremely promising Early Access Game!

The last great Total War Game. (as of 2017).

This game is a slight improvement on Rome 2, but is overall a shortcoming in the Total War franchise. Its battle repeatedly pressure you into the same scenarios while you fight the same clunky AI on the same of about 3-4 battlefields (Mainly due to the repetitive nature of towns) and inevitably either win, or are cheated out of a victory by morale penalties that force your men into breaking.
There is no significant improvement in the franchise and the game feels as if it only has less features. Added buildings don't appear in the cities the way they did in earlier Total War titles either. This is a lazy repolish of a much better game with added resource management based on arbitrary numbers that were not properly balanced (referring to food and public order) Naval combat is still as simple as spamming artillery ships. Hadrian's Wall has no impact on gameplay. You still cannot control the direction your army routes. Towns and forts inexplicably decide not to add gates so as to speed up the gameplay. Diplomacy is as lacking as ever. About 5 random events will be cycled through to give the (false) impression of depth to politics in the game.
If you want Rome Total War Barbarian Invasion with updated graphics and no soul, this is your game.

It's Dynasty Warriors. It's got all kinds of modes that are all Dynasty Warriors. It's got more playable characters than I've ever heard of in a game, all with unique move sets and nearly all with unique weapons.
If you've never played Dynasty Warriors, here's how it works: You are a massive badass, and you run around the battlefields of Three Kingdoms era China obliterating everything. Depending on your character and weapon you have different abilities, move reach, and combos, but basically you run around decimating entire armies of enemies. This is all reasonably easy unless you've cranked up the difficulty, but really it isn't about skill; it's about efficiency and killcount. KIllcount is astronomically high, often passing 2000 in one level.
Basically don't get this game if you want something technical or cereberal. Get this game if your life feels difficult and you want to do something easy but satisfying.
[As an aside, this claims to be the complete edition, but there is a lot of DLC available that isn't included. Those of us who played this on console expected that DLC to be included with the Complete Addition, but it isn't. That said, if you can get the DLC on sale some of it adds levels and weapons/movesets, which can extend replay value]

This game is an absolute HOOT!
I don't play a load of games, but I bought this one for 20 bucks. It is currently 9.99, which is a steal!
YUP! You will kill orcs, actually Uruks, which are a little different. That may be out of canon, but given the many and varied ways you can kill them, it really doesn't matter. The thing is, you advance in the story by completing specific missions. But you don't have to complete them sequentially. You can build up your character by playing side missions, accumulating runes (which power your sword, bow and dagger) and increasing your ability (through gaining XP and Mirian).
I'm not all the way through the story; I've had too much fun going on combat missions at lunch or before work, so I'm not in any hurry to finish the game. Each Uruk captain has different strengths and weaknesses, but by the time you are half-way through the game, you can pretty much destroy any captain one-on-one. The problem is that these Uruk captains are accompanied by other Uruk captains and hosts of regular Uruks! Things can get exciting real quick!
Part of the fun is finding new and ever more cool ways of wasting Uruks. Like eating Lays potato chips, you just aren't satisfied with just one! Getting Uruks to kill other Uruks is fun; but biting the heads off Uruk captains with Graugs is a blast! Blowing them up, burning them, exploding their heads (Scanners-style), and having Caragors bite them to death are just a few ways to get your orc killing game on. Its kind of like the "choke and chuck" in Jedi Academy; it never seems to get old for me. But I'm a simple soul...
I can't speak to the canon, although I first read the LOTR in the 70s. This feels very close to the time between the Hobbit and the Fellowship of the Ring. And they found a way to bring Celebrimbor, from another part of the canon, into the story. I really feel like I am in part of the story I haven't heard before.
Buy this game; you won't be sorry!

The game is just a huge testament of how to show the world what can go wrong with a multimillion dollar budget.
- The plot is extremely banal and far from immersive
- The classes - while detailed - suffer from being half finished - there are no tradeoffs there, character building is fully binary (you do it the right way or don't), no multiclassing or anything. If you played one class, no reason to play it again ever.
- The 'difficulty' of the game comes from stat boosted enemies in superior numbers. The higher the difficulty the more enemies there are and they have better stats. The AI is so horribly dumb that your regular DotA player is a genius compared to it. No aggro management, no positioning, no setting up traps. The AI just charges you - and if they are boosted enough they will kill you otherwise you will win. Makes combat extremely stale.
- The quests are really a hit or miss - some are good, some are extremely bad and most of them lack any cohesion to the main quest ('go there hero, kill stuff because reasons' kind of).
- The companions. Some are extremely captivating and interesting. Which is basically a bad thing as there aren't enough interactions with them.  I mean you will spend with them hours, who wouldn't want to listen to the same 3 comments over and over again and finish the 'companion special quest' in about 4 minutes?
All in all it's a solid 6/10. It's an okay game, I wouldn't give more than 15 EUR for it though.

It's currently impossible to ignore new players, and boy do they get annoying. Others are readily available to help, but those people are usually the level 55s, and they are farming the bosses in game for loot to sell, and are not your friends.  I had one demand that I give him the items which dropped for me and my partner because he hit the boss a couple of times, but we had killed that boss several times before, so his help was unneeded.  Regardless, he had been helpful with advice, so I traded him the items, despite me really having a use for one.  I asked if he wanted to trade for it, and the cost of getting my drop back was exorbitant, how silly of me.  One item even goes for 5 million gold, which is outlandish and insane.  The level 55s run the show and make the game miserable for others, all for the sake of gold, which at the top tier is meaningless.  So what we have is a game that is so blatantly unbalanaced that the top people play it for petty gain which prevents others from playing the game for personal enjoyment, and that is how this game is designed.
Server lag is atrocious, sometimes with 3 second freezes, resulting in you not knowing how you died, since mobs can spawn on your square and attack instantaneously.
Quests require a certain level to do, even if you slaughtered 50 of those same monsters prior to leveling, you cannot accept said quest until you are the proper level.
There is no roleplaying in this game.  There are no heroes or villains, just cutthroats and exploiters.  The lack of customization shocks me as to how this game can even advertise any level of roleplaying.  There are no choices to make.  It simply does not exist.
Character classes are completely broken and imbalanced.  Some are worthless, and others are beyond meta.
TL;DR this game is for the people who have already been playing it, not you.  28 hours in and I realize it is nothing like advertised, and being an early release Alpha does NOT explain the lack of advertised content, which I see no way to add without overhauling the game.  You will be preyed upon by other players.  You will die to unavoidable server issues.  You will not be roleplaying.  You will be killing thousands of the same mobs in order to level, and you will never roleplay in any action that you take.  I will never recommend this game, nor will I play it again.

Exile's End has fantastic environmental graphics for a 2D platformer, making me think of the old Flashback game. Unlike Flashback, however, the environment looks very empty and bland. It is a shame that such beautiful graphics are paired with such lackluster level design. The soundtrack is nothing special, and even becomes very repetitive and droning after a while. The story is very simple as well - the protagonist is part of a rescue mission right when something goes horribly wrong. With no way out, the only thing left to do is to go further in and find out what is going on. Storywise, there is no real drive to continue playing the game. It is not very exciting and it all seems rather predictable.
The controls of the game are great, which is the most important aspect of a 2D platformer. However, the mechanics and level design are outright mediocre. Due to getting falling damage at the beginning of the game, you are pushed to explore your environments carefully before advancing. However, moving the screen around to do this is terribly slow and takes away from the platforming. The environmental dangers such as floor and ceiling spikes feel terribly cheap as you just can't be bothered to wait for your screen to move up or down.
Enemy design is mostly lackluster. Each area usually has one or two enemy types that do little else but walk back and forth at the same pace. They feel out of place and offer no challenge what so ever, making them feel like filler content. The only exception is the first "tough" dog-like enemy you encounter, which sprints and jumps at you and requires a trick to escape from. The rest are just badly designed. Touching an enemy bumps you back a bit, but you get no invulnerability frames. Thus, if you are stuck in a corner or walking forward, you keep getting more and more damage.
The level design makes most screens feel like filler content (with monsters feeling like pointless bullet sponges), and often enemies spawn right in front of you when you transition from one screen to the next.
Exile's End allows you to save in any screen, but it's rather stingy when it comes to healing items. The only way to heal are from the limited number of health packs, and the rare pill drop from enemies. As a result, if you are low on health you'll find yourself grinding for such a pill drop. Fortunately, the game - outside of bosses - is not challenging at all. The majority of the damage you will get is from not being careful enough with the environment as you try to traverse filler content areas as fast as possible, desperately waiting for something exciting to happen.
The game would be great if enemies were more interactive and varied and the level design would do the graphical design justice. It's a real shame that the level design is so bad, because it is the one flaw making me not recommend this game. As it is, the game is bland and boring because of it.

A great game that I don't think is getting nearly enough attention!  I'm including the first video of my Let's Play here for visuals, as I think the start of the game does a great job of setting the tone.
While the developer states 'NOT a Metroidvania', I have to humbly disagree.  However, it is also very reminiscent of games like Flashback in its style, presentation, and puzzle-solving.  Where it deviates greatly from Flashback are in the controls, which are tight and responsive.
Exile's End follows the journey of old soldier Jameson upon his team crash-landing on a foreign planet, one actively preventing him from escaping.   Story elements are told through communication with your ship's AI, through computer entries found in the environment, and through beautifully drawn cutscenes.  All to the sounds of a great retro-sounding, yet atmospheric, soundtrack.
You start off the game entirely defenseless, to the point where even falling more than a few feet will cause significant damage or certain doom.  Much like Flashback, a simple rock becomes an important tool for the beginning of the game.  As you progress your suit is upgraded to handle more and more dangerous environments along with an ultimately impressive array of weapons, tools, and items.
Much like Metroid, as you acquire new suit upgrades, new areas will become open to you.  While you can follow a somewhat linear path through the game, there's a ton of hidden items and secrets to be found if you take the time to explore.  In fact, during my playthrough I only found 56% of the items (according to the endgame screen) and I thought I had been fairly thorough!
Exile's End does a solid job of presenting the player with puzzles and challenges that require you to think a little more.  The design feels, again, very similar to Flashback in that the solution to puzzles is not always immediately obvious but generally requires manipulation of the environment through whatever tools you have available.  This could be as simple as throwing something to hit a switch, or triggering a sequence of events to open a door.  While some of the solutions can be a bit obtuse, it's clever for the most part and one of the game's strong points.
It should be noted that Exile's End isn't a particularly long game, especially if you're not hunting for all of the secrets and items.  My final playtime on Steam for my first playthrough was 5.3 hours, with an in-game time clocked at 4:10.  I died / loaded saves a number of times, so that's where the discrepancy comes in.
All told, I like it quite a bit.  It's not a perfect game, but it had me hooked.  The majority of my playtime game within a single session; I always wanted to see what was beyond that next door, solve that next puzzle, see the next piece of the story.

I got into Total War from the Warhammer franchise so when I started playing this game, I was shocked how much complexity the game offers compared to Warhammer. I now know what they meant by "streamlining". Therefore this review is for people who have played Total War: Warhammer and not any previous installment.
TWA has what TWW doesn't have.
= Weather Conditions: Rain, fog, dryness determines the battle a lot. The fog of war as well as flamability can be affected by these.
= Varying Tax Rates: You can set the national tax rate to different values in addition to exempting regions from taxes.
= Flammability: You can set stuff on fire and it can affect the enemies morale. Some people (like Atilla) want to watch the world burn.
= Court Intrigue: You can have heirs, wives, court system.
= Varying arrow ammunition. Heavy, Normal, Fire, Whistling Arrows all have their special uses. You can switch during the battle. Fire boulders and normal boulders for artillery.
= Sea Battles and Naval Invasions: Something that TWW cannot have unfortunately.
= Better Siege Battles: You can actually surround a city as well as having actual towns in fights.
= Disease (Not like the Skaven disease)
So far, I'm having a blast with the game but I did prefer playing AoC due to the setting.

No, this isn't a first-person EVE Online, this is a completely different game. Strike Vector is amazing, expecially considering it's made by a team of nine people, and that it is currently in Beta.
Unlike your average FPS, like Call Of Duty or Battlefield, you start the game with all gameplay elements unlocked, giving you complete freedom to do what you want straight away. This also creates an almost level playing field for all players, as the only advantage you start with is your skill level. Using this customization system, you can create a massive amount of effective classes. There are six weapons to choose from, with different advantages and disadvantages, and each can take two of four to seven perks, such as accuracy or damage. You get one overall perk for your Vector, which can give you extra speed in Jet or Harrier mode, or extra defense. You get a special ability, such as Mines, or Turbo-Boost, which can only be used every thirty seconds. This system allows for a massive amount of 'classes' to choose from. You can use a balanced combat fighter, with a Gatling Gun and Swarm Launcher (each with Damage and Fire Rate perks), Mines, and Saurian. You could also create a specialist sniper class, with Plasma Guns (with Accuracy and Fire Rate), Cloak, and Copernicus. The system is amazing.
At the end of each game, you get XP, which levels you up, and unlocks new cosmetic items, such as ship camos, cockpits, engines, decals, thumbnails for your playercard (you start off with a pretty rainbow), and game artwork.
There are four game modes: Team Deathmatch, Deathmatch, Domination, and Bounty Hunter. TDM and DM are very similar to your average shooter TDMs and DMs. You get points for getting kills. Domination works similarly to the game mode of the same name within Call Of Duty. Bounty Hunter, however, is very unique. Each time you get a kill, you get money (officially called Bounty). The player with the most Bounty at the end of the game wins, obviously. Each time you are killed by an enemy player, they get most of your bounty. If you crash, your money is dropped as floating '$'s, which can be picked up by you, or another player.
During any game mode, Drones will enter the map, which fly around and can be destroyed for one of three Bonus Crates. These Crates are also deployed randomly by fixed Dispensers on the map. To obtain the Crate, you must simply fly through it. The blue Crates (Strike Shield) make you almost invulnerable for about thirty seconds. Which can be quite effective. Enter Harrier mode while using it, and hound enemy players as they try to kill you, taking one or two points of damage at a time, for easy kills. Be careful though, as you still crash just as easily. Red Crates (Strike Damage) boost your damage. Yellow Crates massively increase the speed of your Vector, while also increasing your Fire Rate and reload speed.
Of course, there are bugs in the game. Small ones (sometimes you'll be crash, but the scoreboard will say that you were killed by another player), and some very big, and annoying ones. Firstly (this isn't necessarily a bug), many are finding that the game won't start. Launching will open the Steam preperation window, the close almost straight away. This can be fixed quite easily by going to C:\Program Files\Steam\SteamApps\common\StrikeVector\Binaries\Redist and opening the application there. This will install the application, which is required to play the game. When I did this, my computer restarted to do updates, and I had to do it again. After doing this, the game opens fine.
There is, however, one very annoying bug. In the first hour and a half (roughly) of playing the game, was constantly disconnected from online games, but the game worked fine in a practice session. I played through it, as I greatly enjoyed the small amounts of time I was able to play. Eventually, the I was able to play full games without being disconnected, since after that first hour and a half of mayhem, I have only been disconnected two or three times during a total of probably five hours gameplay. I bought Mass Effect recently for my run through of the entire series, and I have to say, I am impressed. I expected a really bad game that I would play "for the story." I was wrong. This was an absolutely great experience. There are a few things that were frustrating, such as the repetative land rover missions, and the way the Citidel was laid out. The Citidel is your center hub of trade and activity, for people that don't know much about the Mass Effect universe. The story was fantastic, the characters so belivable, however the combat was a bit rough due to the sheer age of the game. It doesn't take long to get used to the outdated combat and graphics, and once that is aside, everything is so much fun. One of the best RPGs of it's kind.

So... this game. What is there to say, really?
ME is a space opera third person shooter roleplaying game. It's the first of the original Mass Effect series trilogy and is
to play through, if you want to play the trilogy, as the choices you make here really do MATTER (a lot).

, even without these precautions. I was a dummy on my first playthrough and went with infiltrator, didn't look up controls well enough and overall my first experience sucked. When creating a character, choose a power based class (Adept for example) and not weapon based ones (Soldier or infiltrator for example). Do not worry, if you don't like the class that much, you can change it in the beggining of next game (ME2). That being said, this is just advice based on my experience, if you wanna pop some heads with infiltrator build, you are free to do so.
Yeah, you are better off to just ignore the DLC.
Many people get stuck in Mako sections of the game. Don't worry, most of us have been there.
Avoid spoilers like the plague.

All jokes aside, this is just the beggining of what Mass Effect has in store.

I finished this in 4 hours, 27 minutes, but that is a bit deceptive. There was a major bug at release and I lost the first 6 hours or so of play and had to start over. I knew what to do then and repeated that 6 hours worth in like 2 hours. That 4:27 apparently doesn't count loading a saved game either (which I didn't have to do very often). Steam shows 12.7 hours total. I'm guessing it would take a new player about 6-8 hours.
The graphics, sound and music are all fine. Nothing sepectacular, but adequate and even fairly good for the most part.
The game has a few flaws, but I found it quite fun and worth the asking price.
My biggest problems with the game were:
1) The beginning area (forest) is not really very fun. You start with nothing and you take fall damage. It is very easy to die by stepping off the wrong ledge. They did add a way to look down (hold "down" for a few secs) so this part should be a little better now.
2) Most of the bosses are too easy. At least two of them have a "safe spot" where you can stand with almost no danger and kill them with your infinite ammo default handgun.
As to whether it's a a Metroidvania or not, I would say "yes". At first it feels a little more like "Out of This World", but as you progress and start finding power-ups and new weapons, it defintely starts feeling more like a Metroidvania.
When you die, you restart on the screen you are on, from an auto-save so your hp, ammo, etc. are all restored to when you first entered the screen. There are no checkpoints and you can save anywhere. When you re-enter a screen, all the enemies have respawned, making it easy to farm hp or ammo.
I wish there was a hard mode.
Edit: I also should point out that at the end of the game I got a message saying I had found only 46.7% of the items, so there was a lot more exploring and discovery that could have been  done.

I don't play a load of games, but I bought this one for 20 bucks. It is currently 9.99, which is a steal!
YUP! You will kill orcs, actually Uruks, which are a little different. That may be out of canon, but given the many and varied ways you can kill them, it really doesn't matter. The thing is, you advance in the story by completing specific missions. But you don't have to complete them sequentially. You can build up your character by playing side missions, accumulating runes (which power your sword, bow and dagger) and increasing your ability (through gaining XP and Mirian).
I'm not all the way through the story; I've had too much fun going on combat missions at lunch or before work, so I'm not in any hurry to finish the game. Each Uruk captain has different strengths and weaknesses, but by the time you are half-way through the game, you can pretty much destroy any captain one-on-one. The problem is that these Uruk captains are accompanied by other Uruk captains and hosts of regular Uruks! Things can get exciting real quick!
Part of the fun is finding new and ever more cool ways of wasting Uruks. Like eating Lays potato chips, you just aren't satisfied with just one! Getting Uruks to kill other Uruks is fun; but biting the heads off Uruk captains with Graugs is a blast! Blowing them up, burning them, exploding their heads (Scanners-style), and having Caragors bite them to death are just a few ways to get your orc killing game on. Its kind of like the "choke and chuck" in Jedi Academy; it never seems to get old for me. But I'm a simple soul...
I can't speak to the canon, although I first read the LOTR in the 70s. This feels very close to the time between the Hobbit and the Fellowship of the Ring. And they found a way to bring Celebrimbor, from another part of the canon, into the story. I really feel like I am in part of the story I haven't heard before.
Buy this game; you won't be sorry!

Alright, so I've played several Total War games. Played Medieval and Medieval 2 when they came out and honestly was never very good at the games. But I enjoyed myself no less. I've poked around at a couple other Total War titles, Rome 2 felt weird and I saw a lot of peopple didn't like it. Total War Shogun 2, I haven't touched much, so can't say much there either. But Attila is what hooked me. That said, let's get on with it.
Total War Attila has several layers to it. But nothing horribly overhwelming, at least in terms of actually learning the game. Figuring out the way dominion, power and such balance out is a bit of trial and error, but once understood it's an aspect of the game easily controlled. But when taken advantage of and using politics as a means of gain over just battle and territory gain can come at a massive advantage later in the game. Especially when the star of the game shows up, Attila the Hun and his Mongol horde. But we'll talk about the horde in a moment. Other gameplay elements remain very similar to the other Total War titles I've played. A modest but fleshed out variety of units with a great unit-counter tree with a somewhat clunky UI that can feel like it's throwing a lot of information at you. It's another trial an error thing, but hardly confusing, just requires practice to the uninitiated.
Graphics look fantastic for it's time and still look good. However the game can have it's slow downs and sharp drops in fps. I'm no coder 'nor do I understand computing language. So whether it's just poor optimization or the game simply requiring a bit more processing power than it says is a mystery to me. I'll drop my PC's specs at the end of review for comparison. But for the most part, things run fairly smooth and I think it should be expected for things to chug a little bit when there are over 4000+ units on the field engaged in battle. If you've ever played major 4x games like Civilization 5 & 6 or Sins of a Solar Empire, I'm sure you'll understand the late game struggle when your fps slowly but surely drops due to the sheer amount of things going on at any given time by that point.
I do feel some of the game was chopped up for additional content, but I honestly feel like the base game still has a modest wealth of content. Nothing mindblowing, but it hasn't left me wanting, considering a single grand campaign can potentially take twenty hours at the bare minimum, but of course, I'm hardly an expert at this game. But I suppose the developer/publisher needs that little extra revenue stream if that ensures we get more great Total War games in the future, if of course, that is the intent.
Now, the horde. And one other thing. First we'll talk about the issue with the horde. They've overpowered a bit. At first it's not so much, be given about sixty or so turns in the game, they turn into not only a force to be reckoned with, but depending on several variables, they become just short of unstoppable. Though this isn't entirely the development teams fault, as they DO give the option for quite a bit of diplomacy and even forewarn that only your struggling barbarian empire or divided Roman empire cannot hold back the horde alone. But even then, the Huns have the uncanny ability to just roll over almost everything in sight. So it's one of those cases where they are in fact overpowered, but can be overcome with strategic planning and not overextending your empire.
I'm not doing very good with this review. So let us talk about that other thing. Difficulty. The AI is really only so smart and from what I can tell, will usually use the same tactics no matter the difficulty. I'm not sure, but I highly suspect the change to difficulty only modifies the amount of money other empires get, giving them an edge against your empire, which, mid to late game, becomes almost traumatic and tremendously difficult. Especially the Hunnic empire, which will have cash bleeding out of every orifice.
Now I haven't even touched multiplayer yet due to both a lack of confidence in myself and my general distaste of playing multiplayer games in general. So my opinion there is a blank, sorry.
Now a quick note involving the dlc packs. One of which is garbage and should be made free for the game. A dlc that adds blood and dismemberment, along with some other animations that would steep this game into the Mature rating. This content wasn't added to keep a Teen rating which is ridiculous and outright theft. Now that may be a bit of a leap and really isn't terribly damaging to reputation, but a very stupid move by the publisher to reach other demographics while alienating others due to highly questionable business tactics.
Not much else to say I guess. Game looks good, plays good and overall has a nice fit to it. Though it still sells for something like $45(USD) I think it's almost worth it's price. If you see it on sale and have enjoyed the Total War series before, get this game without hesitation. I know at this moment, on sale, it's about $12(USD) which is quite a discount. Though to be honest, I feel the base price should be lower due to the overpriced DLC which comes with the game, but doesn't do anything truly interesting. But yea, I'd recommend this game. Just buyer beware and pay attention to what the DLC has to offer and check out other reviews. It really is a fun game, but it's certainly not for everyone.

I am an oldschool RPG fan, and I have to say that I played every big RPG back in the days and some I have finished multiple times like Planescape Torment, all Fallout games, all Black Isle games like Baldurs Gate, Icewind Dale etc. so I think that I am a person who can give a really sober and neutral review for someone who needs the kick before buying the game.
The first thing that caught my attention after starting the game were the visuals. The graphics are just amazing. I was really amazed when I saw it, especially after I re-played Icewind Dale the so called HD edition. That graphic compared to Pillars is like from B.C. Pillars look gorgeous. I really really appreciated the zoom in/zoom out featuire which these types of 2D isometric RPG's were always lacking.
The music is also very good, and some songs are epic. Remind me the good old times from Baldurs Gate. Fits very very well to this fantasy world. My only problem here was, that after a while it felt repetetive. I am not sure of the songs are just similiar or there arent many of them ( didnt heard the ost ) but I had the feeling when I entered a map that the same music is playing .... again, or atleast a very similiar one.
The story overall, is basicly what makes these games so good. The story is always huge and complicated in these games. Yes, you read a lot in this game. I am a person who not only read in games ( RPG's ) , but I also read a lot of books and not only fantasy. I must say that the story in Pillars for me was mediocre, or below avarage at its best compared to other games aswell, like Final Fantasy, Baldurs Gate, Planescape Torment ( one of the best ). Pillars just doesnt catch up here. People who never played a good story based game, or never read a very good book... they might like Pillar's story but dont expect something mind blowing or something that gives you chills everytime you think about it. It's just not there for me.
Speaking asbout the story, I think that the NPC's I had in my group or Castle ( waiting for me to pick them up ) werent interesting. Eder ? Aloth ? I really wanted to like them I really tried.... I just couldnt care less about their story. It's not Minsc and Boo from BG, it's not Morte or the Nameless One, It's not Morrigan from Dragon Age. Thats why I created 4 characters on my own and just ignored almost all the NPC sidequests. I didnt enjoyed them. But you dont have to care about this if you didnt played any of these games, it is my little little note which I wanted to share.
The biggest feature of this game is always the combat, which is amazing in Pillars. It is very dynamic, fast, colorful, bautiful... and also chaotic at the beginning. You can slow it down anytime, or even pause to assign commands. Basicly it works like this. You press spacebar to pause the game, assisng command with every party member. For example, the Paladin activates this spell, atatck with Warrior this enemy, Cast a Fireball with the Mage, Cast a AoE defensive buff with your priest etc.... once you done, you unpause the game and every command you did during the pause will trigger and happen at the same time. Then, you press pause and again.... you assign command ans so on. Easy enemies can be beaten easily without the pause button, but tougher bosses or encounters literally are unplayable without the pause. But thats ok, combat is designed around this in these games.
The lack of D&D features, names, spells is also a letdown for me. This is not the Baldurs Gate 3 I wanted. I want my Magic Missile not some other looking ( similiar ) spell which is called Minoletta Missiles, it is very confusing at the beginning. You know what was really good in all the previous games ? Once you played any of them and then you jumped on the other one, you didnt had to study all the spells because in the world of D&D every spell did always the same. You had a Magic Missile, Mirror Image, Fireball wtc. in every Black Isle fantasy game. Here I had to read, study, find out what works and what not on my own... I didnt liked it too much, but again IGNORE all this if you never played the previous games. This is my personal note. I understand that implementing the D&D rules is a matter of a lot of money and license but.... oh well.
Took me 60 hours exactly to beat the game. At 51 hours, I was at the final boss, but sadly I couldnt beat him because I was level 7-8 with my party. Had to return here at max level which is 12 btw, and it was suddenly super easy. The point is, that the game didnt told me to do all these sidequests to actually even have chance to beat the final boss. I always thought sidequests are optional, not recommended. A mistake. so dont do the same. You cannot beat the boss I think under level 10, but max is recommended.
Overall the game is really really good. A lot of gametime, possible replayability with multiple and different endings. Looks very pretty, plays very smooth. I had a great time. A comeback of a classic RPG. A reminder in the modern days, what we loved so much in the late 90's. Definitely recommended.

It's a first person shooter, yes. But don't be fooled by it's retro looks. It's not a wolf3d clone at all. If you die, you have to restart from the beginning of a level. No midlevel saving. Pistol starts are a common thing due to that, because if you die you lose all your weapons too. You are in a constant need for ammo as well. Furthermore, the game includes moving lasertraps and other shenanigans that make your survival a hell. Weapons fire extremely slow too, projectiles are freaking fast and almost impossible to avoid. Over the last years there has been quite an influx of FPS games attempting to imitate the success of the classic games of the 90's era and failing miserably to keep their promises. However this game it's a big exception; it's not another over hyped, buggy early access tittle but a perfectly playable -albeit- simplistic shooter. As it’s been stated multiple times before it takes inspiration from classics games like DOOM and Wolfenstein 3D so if you’re not a fan of 2.5D First Person Shooters I don’t see why would you purchase this in the first place. However if you are into this type of games you might be as pleasantly surprised as I was.
While simplistic in nature it remains challenging and it doesn’t take too long to get into. It’s not very long and it will take one to two hours to finish depending how much of an explorer or scavenger you are so it doesn’t overstay its welcome. The levels while somewhat mazy they are actually well designed and vary from corridors to more open areas; and no, the levels are not randomly generated this time around. The game is self-aware of its limitations and while it lacks a map feature (Which might understandably frustrate some) I didn’t get lost that much and I was able to memorize the levels quite well after a while.
Something to keep in mind is that this game lacks a conventional save feature (Instead there is a checkpoint save system that will instantly save when you finish a level) meaning that if you die or quit halfway through on a level you’re forced to start the level from scratch. While this is not a necessarily a bad thing (And it makes the game more challenging) the checkpoint system can be annoying especially if you miss a secret or an item meaning that the only way to recover them is to re-start the game
making it frustrating if you’re achievement hunting or you’re going for a 100% run for there is no way to check the stats for a level until you’ve finished said level. Something else worth pointing out is that the control customization while present is quite limited; by default the game uses WASD which on itself isn’t a problem but at the time it only allows to change the buttons for the weapons and nothing else which is a bit of a left down (Especially if you use another type of controls). While the defaults suit me perfectly I wasn’t fond of the mouse wheel cycle order and many times while playing I wished I could change it. Hopefully they’ll improve this in the future.
The weapon variety while not big or creative gets the job done and each weapon handles differently making them appropriate for different scenarios but are also well balanced and remain useful from start to finish. I never ran out of ammo and I found myself using all weapons often. That combined with how the weapons allow for fast or slow paced gameplay made them quite a joy to use. My only gripe is the lack of gibs for using the rocket launcher but at the very least it remains quite satisfying to use despite that. While there are only 4 weapons (5 total with the knife) I prefer a small but perfectly usable arsenal over a big arsenal where I only end up using a few weapons anyway.
There is some decent replay value thanks to the achievements, 2 game modes you unlock after beating the game for the first time (Both which really change the gameplay drastically) and the included level editor which is really easy to use (However with the lack of a steam workshop feature sharing any level you create is a little tricky but not impossible). I really appreciate what they were going for and that the final result is a non-pretentious game that is fun to play and get into that you can get for a reasonable price.

The best way I can sum up Intrude is the gameplay of Wolfenstein with the attitude of Doom... and its great!
I loved pretty much every second of this gem of a game, and the soundtrack definitely added to that. No joke, this is probably my favourite OST this year so far. The gameplay is simple and well defined, being a good example of less is more, and has the rare sense that when I die, it feels like it was my fault and not the fault of the game. The only part of this game I wasn't a fan of is the final boss, however while I was enraged by my 10th death, all the while it still felt like I was the one messing up and it wasn't flawed game design.
I saw many complaints regarding the lack of a map, and while it could have helped, I really didn't feel like I needed one. I got seriously lost and had no idea what to do twice, and even then it was often just me missing a door. Admittedly a map would have helped me find that, but the exploration just added to the game in my opinion. Weapons feel great too, shotty especially, and the enemies give nice feedback. You wouldn't expect such satisying gunplay from this sort of game, but Intrude pulls it off, and then some.
I can not recommend this game enough. For £2.99 it's an absolute steal, and is well worth your money. Buy it right now.

I'm not quite finished playing this game as of writing, but there are some things you should know going in:
This game does not refill health between levels, and has no checkpoints to speak of. You die, you restart the entire level. It's a shame because the game feels great to control and I love its style, but if you start a hard level with little health you're going to need to master it before you get any leeway back. Personally I got stuck on level 2-5 for a good while. Also, the game never pauses. There's a pause feature, but it doesn't stop enemy movement or attacks.
-SPOILERS-
Alright, I'm at the final boss and I must say, it's total garbage.
One, the design of the boss itself is basically a sphere with a bullet sphincter on it. It really feels like this was someone's first game but, come on dude. I know you can do better than that.
Two, the way this boss works is it moves to a position, and chooses from a set of three attacks. Thing is, there's no way to know where the boss will stop moving to attack you, so it could very well (and probably will, at least once) move maybe two pixels and rattle off two attacks in quick succession. Like say, the rocket launcher (in which you shouldn't use cover) immediately followed bu the machine gun (you need cover to survive this attack at all.)
Three, the rocket launcher attack it has can destroy the pillars in the room which you NEED to evade the machine gun attack, as it never misses you. This is the only time the game ever punishes you for using cover, and how it does this is incredibly punishing. If you lose the last pillar, you'd better hope the Death♥♥♥♥♥♥doesn't use its machine gun, which will all but ensure you need to start over. If they at least played a cutscene of the roof collapsing when that last pillar goes, that'd actually make things a lot better. At least then there's no false hope of "maybe I can still do it" before being annihilated.
Four, the RNG that selects attacks is just that. Random. It can drag out the machine gun five times in a row because there's nothing regulating it, forcing you to just kind of sit around for a while. Honestly the whole fight is the epitome of tripping at the finish line.
-END SPOILER-
It speaks to the strengths of the level design and game engine that I'm still willing to recommend it. Even at four dollars though, you should wait for a sale.

I
wanted to love this game. As soon as I saw the splash art on Chrono.gg I bought it instantly, but alas, it's not what I hoped for. Some of the disappointment is my own fault, but there is also failures on the developers fault.
So to preface my review:
1. If the devs ever read this, don't take this at all as an attack against yourselves. We're clearly both fans of the classic FPS genre and if anything I say seems to be meanspirited it's out of passion I'm sure you also have.
2. I like the game.
This is one of those situations where the binary Steam recommend system sucks. My recommendation lies somewhere in the middle for a multitude of reasons and to different people.
Intrude wears it's influences on it's sleeve and one quick glance at a screenshot shows it's going for a Wolf3d/DOOM style shooter. In some ways it accomplishes this but in others not so much.
First what the game does right:
And that's kinda where the positive end. Not a lot to most people and in reality it's not. For fans of classic FPS games however this should be enough to carry you over.
The pitfalls of the game can be summed up to a lack of understanding and/or implentation of what made classic FPS's good.
The game looks like a classic FPS, it feels like a classic FPS, but so many aspects are missing.
Immediately after 2 seconds of the game red flags were raised. Testing the buttons, I press tab, which showed my ammo stocks. There are only 4 weapons in the game. Wolfenstein 3D only had 4 weapons, but Wolfenstein 3D came out in 1992. This in itself isn't something inherently bad; it just made me cautious because if the game failed in other departments this could be bigger than expected. And it does.
The first chapter, simply put, is dull from a level design perspective. I think even my mother knows about DOOM's Episode 1 - Level 1. It's iconic. It's the pinnacle of level design in a first person shooter and for me to compare any game to this is unfair, but that level highlights many of the issues most of the levels in this game have.
Firstly, everything looks the same. This is one reason why I much prefer DOOM to Wolf3D. The maze type levels were not as strong as DOOM's gauntlets that felt hand crafted rather than computer generated (even though they're not). In EP1,LV1, you know exactly where everything is without the help of a map. In Intrude, you don't know where anything is because everything looks the same. To top it off, there's no map, which in later levels is massively annoying.
Secondly, the secret is not hard to find, something that also carries over into other levels. If it's not in plain sight, shoot a barrel and you've found it. The limited interaction with the levels makes them feel so stale in terms of exploration and secrets.
On the topic of exploration, it's not really needed. In classic FPS's, not exploring was a sure fire way to ensure you don't progress. After playing Blood this week where finding ammo and weapons is vital, Intrude seems so elementary. I only ever died once and that was because I walked into an insta death laser. Weapon switching is hardly needed because ammo is so plentiful. In Wolfenstein or DOOM, conserving ammo plays such a pivotal role in how well you do. Ammo surplus is a problem modern FPS's have so to have this game also have that problem is a major downfall.
Enemy variety is extremely weak. You have pistol guy, melee guy and machine gun guy. They're the most common enemies from what I've played, the only other being a droid, which is actually well designed for one reason; projectile.
Another reason I prefer DOOM to Wolf3D is because how hitscan heavy Wolf is. Speed and mobility are crucial in DOOM because enemies fire projectiles you can dodge. Speed is not a factor in Intrude, lacking a sprint key.
Intrude is a heavily flawed game. I can see through the flaws* and enjoy it for what it is and I hope the developers build on this in the future if they plan of trying this again. I only recommend this if you are a big fan of the shooters of the past, and even then you have to lower your standards a bit for what is essentially a watered down modern Wolfenstein 3D.
*or at least I could if the game wouldn't crash everytime I'm about to complete level 2-3...

Intruder is a game that technologically fits right between Wolf3D and DOOM.
From Wolfenstein it takes movement and level design, although not as maze-like as in W3D; from DOOM it takes enemies composition, and variety of weapons - each having its purpose and ammo type.
I bought game for 1.99$, and after one hour I can say it is worth it. Rather simple, yes, but still fun.
Mix of melee and range enemies making you switch weapons; levels not too big to make you lost but big enough to make you memorize some sections for navigation purpose, satisfying shooting, minimalistic enemy sprites that look good even on big screen (1080p), smooth movement and framerate. No technical difficulties. I recommend it for all retro fans.
tl:dr - small game, but FUN.

Let me preface this by saying that I played Mass Effect 2 first on the XBox Before I played Mass Effect 1 on the PC. (Exit OG ME fans and PC loyalists)
Let me also say that I believe ME1 to be the better game (Exit ME2 fans).
Where to begin? To start, this game is much harder than ME2. Not only is it more difficult (this coming from someone who has beaten both on Veteran difficulty as an Adept), but ME1 is harder in a better way than ME2 is hard. Let me explain: In ME1, there are situations where you can get overwhelmed by enemy numbers, but the difficulty of the encounters usually arise from having to balance tech, biotics, and guns in the right way to beat your enemies. As an adept, I found that abilities like Barrier were indispensible for any engagement because it gives me increased survivability that I can't get from armor (Adepts are restricted to Light Armor). There was a distinct feeling of tactical combat where you had to plan around your enemy's abilities (which they use more liberaly in ME1) and where your abilities seemed useful. In ME2, the difficulty arises almost exclusively from large numbers, constant gunfire, and a Shepard whose shields seem to evaporate almost instantly. Fighting any one enemy in ME2 is the same as fighting any other enemy: remove shields, barriers, and/or armor, hit them with one of the biotic abilities that ragdolls them, spray, and repeat.
Another thing that jumps out from my memory is cover in both games. ME2 is a cover-based third-person shooter; to have any hope of surviving an engagement for longer than ten seconds, you MUST find cover. If you aren't close enough to target them with abilities, tough luck. ME1 has cover and incorporates it, but several times I remember the game punishing me for staying in cover for too long. I have lost track of how many times I was sniped or blown up with a rocket for taking cover at inopportune times while dangerous enemies were about. To top it off, if I faced a situation in ME2 analagous to an ME1 situation where I was punished for going into cover, ME2 would reward me by making me impervious to all damage while I wait for my health and shields to regenerate. Cover is not the catch-all solution in ME1 that it is in ME2.
ME1 isn't without faults, dear reader. Preach this to the choir: ME1 is slightly uglier, the Mako sections go from "adorable" to "abysmal" real quick (and they are a sizable part of the game), large exporatory bits like the Citadel are frustrating to navigate, the inventory interface is not the best, the "quest" interface is equally frustrating, the gameplay is somewhat unforgiving during the late-game, and the voice acting and writing in ME2 has an edge over ME1 because ME2 has the confidence of a second iteration and it doesn't ham in nearly as much exposition about the universe. I'm sure I'm missing some things, but for all its faults, the things ripped out of the game in ME2 make my playthroughs of ME2 melancholic and boring. No **truly** heat-based weapons, no inventory on the scale of ME1, no modifying weapons on the fly, a MUCH less complex leveling system than in ME1, and the implimentation of regenerating health à la "most mainstream shooters."
At the last, I will leave you, reader, with this anecdote: When I loaded my ME1 save in ME2 to see what Bioware had in store for people who bought the first game, it was cool to see the choices in the last game reflected in some little blurbs in the early game, but I could not get past the "thermal clip" that they pushed on you right out of the gate. In ME1, the fully-voiced Codex explained why reloading was unecesary due to the advent of Mass Effect technology. It was an interesting mechanic that that allowed for some interesting plays to occur, removing some technical difficulty ("I ran out of ammo and now I have to face this boss. How have I failed to arrive at this situation?") and adding some new opportunities for meaningful difficulty ("That Asari overheated my weapon, which gave her enough time to put me in stasis, expose me, and kill me dead. How can I overcome?"). In ME2, they scrap that unique mechanic with the generic, tried and true "bullets-in-a-magazine" mechanic for ammo that you see in almost every other shooter. Not only is this disappointing considering what ME1 was like, but ME2 even teases you with those little blurbs that appear while loading a section of the game. One of them says something along the lines of "Guns use thermal clips. When it overheats, eject the thermal clip and load in a new one!" So harshly do I scream at my monitor saying "THE GUN ISN'T OVERHEATING, THIS IS EA DEMANDING THAT BIOWARE MAKE THE GAME "MORE ACCESSIBLE" TO THE GENERAL MARKET!"
For those of you into people, ME1 is like a kind of ugly stutterer who has these deep and interesting elements to them that make them a joy to be around. ME2 is like a charismatic, physically attractive person who has a bit of an empty head. They're cool to look at, but beyond first impressions, interactions with them get old REALLY fast, especially in light of your interactions with the ugly stutterer.
Playing this game after playing Mass Effect 2 makes the sequel look like it was made for children.
tl;dr: After beating both ME1 and ME2, I must say that ME1 is the better game, so buy it.

Dragon's Dogma is a unique, brilliant yet flawed underrated gem.
I bought the game on it's PC release and didn't really get into it. I was fresh out of Dark Souls 1 and 2, and 3 was about to release. The game had it's charm, but looked kinda dated and lacked complexity in both story and gameplay compared to the Souls series I was infused in. I played a couple hours and forgot about it.
After a year of DS3, Rocket League and getting back into Skyrim among other things, I looked for new games to play. I was craving something new to lose myself into like I did with the Souls series. I noticed Dragon's Dogma being mentioned by a small fraction of Souls enthusiasts, which puzzled me as I personally didn't get the vibe from it. For lack of better options though, I decided to give it another try.
Dragon's Dogma isn't Dark Souls, or Skyrim, or Shadow of the Collossus, or Final Fantasy or any other RPG. Dragon's Dogma is unique in that it attempts to combine complex existing features in a coherent, living world and adds innovations on top. Such an ambitious attempt comes with flaws, but also with unexpected brilliance.
Dragon's Dogma is open world, in that you have a vast world to explore. While most of the game's content resides in the main storyline, the game does allow you to freely roam the world at any point, and has many side quests.
The main storyline may appear pretty weak and generic at first. I know it did for me. Not until the very end of my first playthrough did I realize the true scale of it. I really recommend playing this game with an open mind, as it is much deeper than it originally seems. And yes, if you get into it, you -will- want to do a second playthrough. ;)
DD is an Action-RPG. Combat is real time and occurs as you run into enemies. You have a wide variety of classic classes to chose from, and can switch vocations indefinitely. Each vocation's skill trees unlock as you level them, and reach unsuspected levels of complexity, resulting in an extremely varied gaming experience depending on which class you play.
Combat is one of the strongest points of the game. It manages to be both fast paced and tactical. And epic! Yes a lot of it will be mowing down goblins and thieves, but run into one of the bigger monsters and that's where the real fun begins. The way to bring down these will be up to you, but they all have their weaknesses and depending on your class you'll have a different role in that. Hack at it's feet to weaken it's defense, or cling to it's leg to unbalance it, while your archer companion snipes at it's one eye and the mage rains bolts upon it. Or climb all the way to it's head to remove it's giant helmet and stun it while the warrior concentrate all of his strength in his massive two-handed sword to deliver the killing blow. Add the epic orchestral choir driven soundtrack in the background, and there you have it: the game absolutely succeeds in giving you this grand feeling of fighting giant monsters as a team while giving you total freedom and keeping it fast-paced, and this is quite an achievement in my opinion.
Speaking of team, let's talk of pawns. Dragon's Dogma is a single player game. With a twist. On character creation, you'll be able to create a secondary non playable character: your "pawn". Ingame, you'll gain access to special stones, which allows you to recruit 2 other pawns on top of your main one. These other pawns were created by other players and you can hire them for free if they are your own level or below, or use a special currency for higher level ones. Your own pawn will be available for rent to other players as well.
This may seem trivial at first, but there's more to it. As you progress through the game, explore the map, complete quests and fight enemies, your pawn will gradually learn about all these things. He will learn to not run head first into this particular foe, but to target specific parts. He will also learn when he travels with other players, and may surprise you by showing you the path to a hidden cave you didn't notice, or giving you hints on a quest you didn't complete yet. All of these he will know because he experienced it while being rented by someone else. He will also learn from your actions and behavior, and gain certain orientations from it. You'll have the possibility to shape and reorient these by talking to him in certain locations. This gives whole new aspects to the game, as how your pawn shapes will directly alter his fighting performances, and the rental system expand the illusion of the world's existence beyond your own experience. Your pawn will also collect a particular currency while being rented which becomes really useful in later parts of the game, which gives more incentive to perfect him. Should be noted that there's still a quite active community of very friendly pawn trading players if you would so wish to give into that kind of online interactions. By no means a necessity though.
So there you have it. A classic looking single player open world action RPG with hints of multiplayer, a story with a twist, super epic battles and a LOT of content.
Beat the main game ? If you're like me you'll feel compelled to go ng+. The game strongly encourages you to do so anyway. Feeling overpowered ? Why not head to Bitterblack Isle, the DLC area of the game ? The Dark Souls vibe is strong with that one, and it'll kick your♥♥♥♥♥even if your second playthrough of the main game felt like a breeze. And yes, there's a hard mode if you want extra challenge. Want more Dragon action ? The Ur-Dragon becomes available on ng+. You'll be able to take the offline version on your own afer a while, but the online one takes days of players from the entire world fighting it to take down, and you can claim your part of the loot when it finally does. There's lots to do, but if you end up falling in love with the game like I and others did, you'll be left wishing the game was more successful and got more DLCs, and join the club of people praying it finally gets the sequel it deserves.
The game has it's flaws, naturally. You forgive them after a while when you measure how ambitious it was. The pawn system can be frustrating at times, as well as the questing one. The game also introduces an "affinity" system, with which you naturally build gradual relationship bonds with any NPC you interact with in the world, which is both interesting and flawed as well. The main story goes through confusing and/or incoherent and sometimes plain uninteresting moments, but redeems itself in the end. The main gaming events themselves will sometimes get boring with a lot of back and forth, only to surprise you again with a sudden unexpected epic confrontation ... It's a game that by it's overambitious nature would have necessitated much more polishing and optimization, but still managed to achieve a surprisingly great amount of it's goals.
All in all, yes: flawed in many ways ... yet unique, brilliant and epic. I really, really recommend you give it a real try if you're a RPG enthusiast.
Oh and the soundtrack is a-ma-zing.
Cheers~

After about 100h gameplay on my friend's pc, I finally decided to buy myself a own copy of this. Blacklist is one of the best infiltration games currently in the market (another one is Hitman). As a hardcore speedrun player, I fully understand how much effort Ubi have put on this game. Here are the points.
1) Outstanding characters' motion capture --- Blacklist's characters motions are very natural and smooth.
2) Enjoyable single player experience --- good plot, good stage settings and truly exciting infiltration experience.
3) lore-friendly gameplay --- my 640m laptop can run this game smoothly.
4) Good gaming mechanics adjustments --- In Conviction, the gameplay style is rather combative. Now Blacklist is encouraging players to have a infiltration-focus style for the highest point, which makes it a real infiltration game.
Yet this game is not perfect. These are the things I don't like in this game
1) Character control is imprecise and uncomfortable --- I always got wrong inputs and wrong actions because of this.
2) Enemies' AI is strange --- sometime they will start searching you not knowing why
3) Mult-player is disappointing because of the presence of cheaters, plus you can't kick them or quit a game. Most of the time, you will be either playing with noob teammates or dealing with god-like opponents.
4) Armored enemies in single player is so overpowered.
Overall, I highly suggest anyone to buy this game. It is outstanding by many means. Ubi has earned a bad reputation on ALWAYS releasing lore-unfriendly, buggy and unfinished games. But this one is not. It worths 3 years of waiting. I am very satisfied. And you will be.

So there I was, on a steep cliff. A cyclops stood in my way. I engaged it and me, along with my 3 pawns (basically npc party members) fought valiantly...until....the Cyclops knocked my primary pawn, Keela into the horizon...well...more like off the cliff. So she died. Then me and the rest of the party finally beat the cyclops by knocking him off the cliff...he probably fell on Keela's corpse... So then I cleared a bandit fort and decided to walk back to the capital. On the way to the capital I got ambushed by dozens of bandits and undead, but that wasn't a problem...and then it began...A group of invisible lizard-people attacked us. We fought them for 5 whole minutes and couldnt win, so I decided to retreat....then  I ran into a bunch of ghosts...who ended up possessing my mage/healer - Alisander. He died, and since he isn't a primary pawn like Keela, I can never get him back. He will forever be remembered for his ice boners that pierced the heavens themselves, along with the cyclops. So then it was just me and my warrior pawn - Hera. We could see the capital in the horizon. We ran as fast as we could, and on the way we got ambushed by more undead, a necromancer, more bandits and even goblins. Not to mention the invisible lizard-people and ghosts that were still chasing us. Oh and we also ran into a giant chimera...not one step without getting ambushed by some mob or even boss. And the entire time after Alisander's death, I was at 10-20% hp, since I was out of healing herbs and my healer was dead. So after a 20 minute run, with countless mobs chasing me, I finally got to the capital.
10/10 would get attacked by invisible lizards again.
